title: Which of the following is NOT key characteristic of greedy
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: Which of the following is NOT a key characteristic of a greedy algorithm ?

options.label: A
options.html: Makes locally optimal choices at each step

options.label: D
options.html: Suitable for solving problems with optimal substructure

solution: A greedy algorithm is defined by its strategy of making the locally optimal choice at each step with the hope that these local choices will lead to a globally optimal solution. A defining characteristic of this approach is that once a decision is made, it is never reconsidered or revised. This means greedy algorithms do not employ backtracking to undo previous choices, which distinguishes them from other techniques like dynamic programming or exhaustive search. Therefore, the statement that a greedy algorithm 'might require backtracking to revise choices' is incorrect and represents the exception among the options. While it is true that greedy algorithms do not always guarantee a globally optimal solution (Option B) and are suitable for problems with optimal substructure (Option D), the fundamental rule is to commit to a choice immediately without looking back. Option A correctly describes their core mechanism of selecting the best immediate option.

title: Which of the following are limitations of Greedy algorithms? Choose

Which of the following are limitations of Greedy algorithms?

A. They always fail for NP hard problem.

C. They are faster than dynamic programming in most cases.

D. They make local choices without looking ahead.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. A, C Only

  2. B, C Only

  3. A, B, C, D

  4. B, D Only
solution:
The correct answer is:

B and D

Explanation:

  • A. Incorrect
    Greedy algorithms do not always fail for NP-hard problems. In fact, they are often used to find approximate solutions for such problems.

  • B. Correct
    Greedy algorithms may not always produce the optimal solution unless the problem has the greedy-choice property (e.g., Dijkstra's Algorithm works, but not all problems do).

  • C. Incorrect
    While greedy algorithms are often faster than dynamic programming, this is not a limitation. It’s actually an advantage.

  • D. Correct
    Greedy algorithms make decisions based only on the current step (local optimum) without considering future consequences, which can lead to suboptimal results.

title: The correct sequence of constructing Huffman tree is Repeat until
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
The correct sequence of constructing Huffman tree is
A. Repeat until root formed
B. Create leaf nodes
C. Build priority queue
D. Combine lowest frequency nodes
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Correct sequence: Create leaf nodes, Build priority queue, Combine lowest-frequency nodes, Repeat until root formed.

  1. Create leaf nodes: Make a leaf node for each symbol with its frequency.

  2. Build the priority queue: Insert all leaf nodes into a min-priority queue (min-heap) keyed by frequency.

  3. Combine the two lowest-frequency nodes: Remove the two nodes with smallest frequencies, create a new internal node whose frequency is their sum, and insert the new node back into the priority queue.

  4. Repeat until a single root remains: Continue removing and combining the two smallest nodes until only one node (the root of the Huffman tree) remains.

Why this order matters: You must first have leaf nodes to populate the priority queue. The queue provides the two lowest-frequency nodes at each step; combining them creates larger nodes that are reinserted, and repeating this process produces the final Huffman tree.

bodyHtml: Given an array F = {10, 5, 100, 60, 25, 11}. Assume the array content F[i] indicates the length of the ith file and we want to merge all these files into one single file. Find the total number of record moves in the optimal solution.
solution:
Key idea: always merge the two smallest files first (a greedy Huffman-style algorithm) to minimize the total number of record moves.

Start with the file sizes:

F = {10, 5, 100, 60, 25, 11}.

Sort (or use a min-heap) and repeatedly merge the two smallest files:

  1. Initial (sorted): [5, 10, 11, 25, 60, 100].

  2. Merge 5 and 10 → 15; cost = 15. New list: [11, 15, 25, 60, 100].

  3. Merge 11 and 15 → 26; cost = 26. New list: [25, 26, 60, 100].

  4. Merge 25 and 26 → 51; cost = 51. New list: [51, 60, 100].

  5. Merge 51 and 60 → 111; cost = 111. New list: [100, 111].

  6. Merge 100 and 111 → 211; cost = 211. New list: [211].

Total number of record moves is the sum of all merge costs:

15 + 26 + 51 + 111 + 211 = 414.

Answer: 414 record moves.

Why this is optimal: merging the two smallest files at each step minimizes the incremental cost and yields the optimal total (this is the same greedy principle behind Huffman merging).

19

These five jobs occupy slots 1 through 5 and give a total profit of 12 + 25 + 30 + 19 + 15 = 101, which is the stated maximum.

Now bring in J5 (profit 10), whose deadline is the variable A. J5 can be scheduled — and would add its profit, pushing the total above 101 — only if there is a free slot at or before slot A. Slots 1 through 5 are already full, so the earliest free slot is slot 6. Hence J5 stays unscheduled (total remains 101) exactly while A ≤ 5; as soon as A ≥ 6, J5 takes slot 6 and the total rises to 111.

Cross-check

At A = 5 the optimal profit is 101; at A = 6 it becomes 111. So the largest deadline for J5 that keeps the maximum profit at exactly 101 is 5.

title: The time complexity of Fibonacci series with using dynamic programming
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: The time complexity of Fibonacci series with using dynamic programming and without using dynamic programming are respectively is?
solution:
Correct time complexities: Using dynamic programming: O(n). Without dynamic programming (naive recursion): O(2^n) (exponential).

Why dynamic programming is O(n):

  • With memoization or an iterative approach, each Fibonacci number up to n is computed once and reused when needed, so the total work is proportional to n.

Why naive recursion is O(2^n):

  • The naive recursive relation T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) results in a recursion tree whose number of nodes grows exponentially with n (approximately proportional to φ^n, which is O(2^n)).

Additional notes:

  • An iterative DP implementation can achieve O(n) time with O(1) extra space by keeping only the last two values.

  • Memoized recursion achieves O(n) time but uses O(n) space for the memo table and recursion stack.

  • Note that any appearance of O(2n) in the original text is likely a typo for O(2^n); O(2n) denotes linear time and would be written simply O(n).

title: Which of the following problems can be solved by Dynamic
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: Which of the following problems can be solved by Dynamic Programming (DP) ?
solution: Dynamic Programming (DP) is an algorithmic technique used to solve optimization problems by breaking them down into simpler subproblems and storing the results of these subproblems to avoid redundant computations. The key characteristics required for a problem to be solvable by DP are overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Optimal Binary Search Tree (OBST) involves finding the most efficient BST for a given set of keys and frequencies, which exhibits both overlapping subproblems (calculating costs for subtrees) and optimal substructure. Similarly, the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem finds the longest sequence common to two strings by comparing prefixes, where solutions to larger problems depend on smaller subproblems. The Knapsack Problem determines the maximum value of items that fit into a limited capacity, relying on decisions made at each step based on previous optimal solutions. Since all three problems possess the necessary properties of overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, they are classic examples solvable using Dynamic Programming. Therefore, the correct answer is 'All of the above'.

title: What is the time complexity of the classical Dynamic Programming
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: What is the time complexity of the classical Dynamic Programming approach using nested loops for the LIS problem?
solution:
Concept

The Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) problem asks for the length of the longest subsequence whose elements are in strictly increasing order. The classical dynamic-programming formulation defines dp[i] as the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i. The governing recurrence is: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over every earlier index j < i for which arr[j] < arr[i], and dp[i] = 1 when no such j exists.

Application to this problem

Evaluating that recurrence with two nested loops proceeds as follows:

  1. Outer loop: iterate i from 0 to n-1, initialising each dp[i] = 1.

  2. Inner loop: for each i, scan every earlier index j from 0 to i-1 and, whenever arr[j] < arr[i], update dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1).

  3. Answer: the LIS length is the maximum value over all dp[i].

The inner loop performs up to i comparisons for each i, so the total work is 1 + 2 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2 comparisons. This sum is of the order n2, because the two nested loops each run proportional to n.

Cross-check

A faster n log n method exists (patience-sorting with binary search), but that is a different algorithm, not the nested-loop DP being asked about. A single pass would be n, which cannot examine all earlier elements; a triple nesting would be n3, which the recurrence never requires. The nested-loop DP sits exactly between these.

title: Given the optimal substructure of the Longest Common subsequence(LCS) problem
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: Given the optimal substructure of the Longest Common subsequence(LCS) problem gives the recursive formula. Find the corresponding values of A and B is?
solution:
Recurrence: For i = 0 or j = 0, LCS[i, j] = 0. If i, j > 0 and X_i = Y_j then LCS[i, j] = LCS[i-1, j-1] + 1. If i, j > 0 and X_i ≠ Y_j then LCS[i, j] = max(LCS[i, j-1], LCS[i-1, j]).

Therefore the two values A and B in the formula correspond to the left and top neighbours of the (i, j) cell:

  • A = LCS[i, j-1] (the value from the cell to the left)

  • B = LCS[i-1, j] (the value from the cell above)

Intuition: when characters match you extend the diagonal value by 1; when they do not match you consider skipping one character from either sequence, which corresponds to taking the maximum of the left and top cells.

bodyHtml: Consider product of three matrices M1, M2 and M3 having w rows and x columns, x rows and y columns, and y rows and z columns. Under what condition will it take less time to compute the product as (M1M2)M3 than to compute M1(M2M3) ?
solution:
Let M1 be w×x, M2 be x×y, and M3 be y×z.

Computing (M1M2)M3 requires wxy multiplications for M1×M2, resulting in a w×y matrix. Multiplying this by M3 takes wyz multiplications. Total cost: wxy + wyz.

Computing M1(M2M3) requires xyz multiplications for M2×M3, resulting in an x×z matrix. Multiplying M1 by this takes wxz multiplications. Total cost: xyz + wxz.

For (M1M2)M3 to be faster, we need wxy + wyz < xyz + wxz. Dividing by wxyz gives 1/x + 1/z < 1/w + 1/y.

A1 is 5x6

A2 is 6x7

A3 is 7x8

A4 is 8x10

Find the minimum number of multiplications required to compute A1 A2 A3 A4 is _______?
solution:
To find the minimum number of multiplications for matrix chain multiplication, we use dynamic programming. The matrices have dimensions: A1 (5×6), A2 (6×7), A3 (7×8), A4 (8×10).

We compute the cost for all possible parenthesizations. The optimal way is (((A1A2)A3)A4).

Step 1: Compute cost of (A1A2): 5×6×7 = 210 multiplications.

Step 2: Compute cost of ((A1A2)A3): (5×7) × 8 = 280 multiplications.

Step 3: Compute cost of (((A1A2)A3)A4): (5×8) × 10 = 400 multiplications.

Total cost: 210 + 280 + 400 = 890 multiplications.

Thus, the minimum number of multiplications required is 890.

title: The complexity of matrix multiplication of two matrices and whose
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: The complexity of matrix multiplication of two matrices A and B whose orders are m×n and n×p respectively is
solution:
Concept

The cost of standard (naive) matrix multiplication is governed by one rule: the work equals the number of entries in the product matrix multiplied by the work needed to fill each entry. Each output entry is a dot product over the shared (inner) dimension, so it costs a number of scalar multiply-add operations equal to that inner dimension.

Application

  1. A has order m×n and B has order n×p; multiplication is defined because A's column count (n) matches B's row count (n).

  2. The product C = A·B has order m×p, so it contains m·p entries that must be computed.

  3. Each entry C[i][j] is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, taken over the shared dimension n: it needs n multiplications and n−1 additions, i.e. O(n) work.

  4. Total work = (number of entries) × (work per entry) = (m·p) × O(n) = O(m·n·p).

Cross-check

The triple-nested loop (over the m rows, the p columns, and the n shared terms) runs the inner statement m·n·p times, which confirms O(m·n·p). The product dimensions m and p and the shared dimension n each appear exactly once, with no squared factor — so no inner dimension is raised to a power.

title: What is the correct recurrence relation for all pair shortest

bodyHtml: What is the correct recurrence relation for all pair shortest path using floyd-warshall algorithm is?

options.label: A
options.html: AK(i, j) = min{ AK-1(i, K) + AK-1(K, j), AK-1(i, j)}

options.label: B
options.html: AK(i, j) = min{ AK+1(i, K) + AK+1(K, j), Ak+1(i, j)}

solution:
Interpretation: A_k(i, j) denotes the length of the shortest path from i to j whose intermediate vertices (if any) are all in the set {1,...,k}.

Recurrence: A_k(i, j) = min(A_{k-1}(i, j), A_{k-1}(i, k) + A_{k-1}(k, j)).

  • Base case: A_0(i, j) is the direct edge weight from i to j (use 0 for i = j and infinity if there is no direct edge).

  • Meaning of the two terms: The first term A_{k-1}(i,j) is the shortest path that does not use vertex k; the second term A_{k-1}(i,k) + A_{k-1}(k,j) is the length of a path that goes from i to j via k (with intermediates from {1,...,k-1}).

  • Iteration: Run k from 1 to n to progressively allow more intermediate vertices; after k = n, A_n(i,j) is the shortest path between i and j using any vertices.

solution:
The Floyd-Warshall algorithm computes all-pairs shortest paths using a dynamic programming approach. It strictly executes three nested loops running from 1 to n, regardless of the graph's structure, edge weights, or density. Therefore, its best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexities are all identical at Θ(n3).

Thus, the correct option is D.

title: The time complexity of computing transitive closure of binary relation
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: The time complexity of computing transitive closure of a binary relation on a set of n elements is known to be
solution: The transitive closure of a binary relation on n elements represents all pairs (a, b) such that there is a path from a to b in the relation graph. The most standard algorithm to compute this is the Floyd-Warshall algorithm, which iteratively updates reachability between all pairs of vertices using an intermediate vertex. This involves three nested loops, each running from 1 to n, resulting in a time complexity of O(n³). While faster algorithms exist for sparse graphs or using matrix multiplication (O(n^2.376)), the general worst-case complexity for dense graphs remains O(n³). Option A (O(n)) and Option B (O(n log n)) are too optimistic as they cannot account for checking all pairs. Option C (O(n^1.5)) is also incorrect as it falls below the cubic bound required for all-pairs reachability in the general case. Thus, O(n³) is the standard accepted complexity.

title: Suppose that the minimum spanning tree of the following edge-weighted
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Suppose that the minimum spanning tree of the following edge-weighted graph contains the edges with weights x, y, and z:

What is the maximum value of x + y + z?
solution:
Answer: 25

Key idea: Use the cut property (an edge can belong to some MST if it is a minimum-weight edge across some cut separating its endpoints). For each edge, pick a cut that isolates one endpoint's component and compare the other crossing edges to get an upper bound on the weight.

  • For the edge between F and G (weight x): consider the cut that isolates vertex F. The edges crossing that cut are A–F = 11 and F–G = x. To have the F–G edge included in some MST we need x to be at most the other crossing edge, so x ≤ 11.

  • For the edge between D and E (weight y): consider the cut that separates the pair {C,D} from the rest of the graph. The edges crossing that cut are C–H = 12, D–H = 9, D–I = 6, and D–E = y. The smallest competing crossing edge has weight 6, so to ensure D–E can be chosen in some MST we must have y ≤ 6.

  • For the edge between B and C (weight z): consider the cut that isolates vertex B. The edges crossing that cut are A–B = 13, B–G = 14, B–H = 8, and B–C = z. The smallest competing crossing edge has weight 8, so we must have z ≤ 8.

Therefore the maximum possible values that still allow those edges to appear in an MST are x = 11, y = 6, z = 8. The maximum sum is 11 + 6 + 8 = 25.

Achievability note: these bounds can be met simultaneously (ties in selection can be broken to include the specified edges). For example, with x = 11, y = 6, z = 8, Kruskal's algorithm can be ordered (or ties broken) so that the edges of weights 11, 6, and 8 are included in the resulting MST.

solution:
Concept — A spanning tree of a connected graph on n vertices is a cycle-free subgraph that keeps every vertex connected, and it always uses exactly n − 1 edges. Among all such trees, the minimum spanning tree is the one whose edge weights add up to the smallest total. Kruskal's algorithm builds it greedily: sort all edges by non-decreasing weight and accept an edge only when its two endpoints currently lie in different components; an edge whose endpoints are already joined would close a cycle and is rejected.

Application — The figure has 8 vertices (A to H) and 11 weighted edges, so any spanning tree of it must contain exactly 8 − 1 = 7 edges. Listing the edges in non-decreasing order of weight:

Edge

Weight

B–D

1

G–H

A–F

2

B–C

2

F–G

2

A–B

3

C–H

3

E–G

3

D–E

4

C–E

5

E–H

6

Applying Kruskal's rule to that sorted list:

  1. B–D (1): B and D lie in different components, so this edge is accepted.

  2. G–H (1): G and H lie in different components, so this edge is accepted.

  3. A–F (2): A and F lie in different components, so this edge is accepted.

  4. B–C (2): C joins the component {B, D}, so this edge is accepted.

  5. F–G (2): the component {A, F} merges with {G, H}, so this edge is accepted.

  6. A–B (3): the component {A, F, G, H} merges with {B, C, D}, so this edge is accepted. Six edges are now in place, with a running total of 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 11.

  7. C–H (3): C and H already lie in the same component, so this edge would close a cycle and is rejected.

  8. E–G (3): E is still isolated, so this edge is accepted. It is the seventh edge, and the total becomes 11 + 3 = 14.

  9. D–E (4), C–E (5) and E–H (6): all eight vertices are already connected by seven edges, so none of these is needed.

Cross-check — Prim's algorithm started from A selects A–F (2), F–G (2), G–H (1), A–B (3), B–D (1), B–C (2) and E–G (3) — the same seven edges, with the same total 2 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 14. A lower bound agrees: the seven smallest edge weights anywhere in the figure are 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3 and 3, which already add to 14, so no seven-edge subgraph of this graph can cost less than 14.

Result — The minimum cost of a spanning tree of the given graph is 14.

title: Consider the following graph: Which of the following is/are represent
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Consider the following graph:

Which of the following represents the sequence of edges added, in order, to build a minimum spanning tree using Prim's algorithm?
solution:
Concept

Prim's algorithm grows one connected tree from an arbitrary start vertex. At each step it adds the minimum-weight edge that crosses the cut between the in-tree vertices and the outside vertices, so the chosen edge always has exactly one endpoint already in the tree.

A sequence is a valid Prim order only if every listed edge actually exists in the graph, attaches a brand-new vertex (one endpoint inside the tree, one outside), and is the cheapest such crossing edge available at that moment.

Edges of this graph

a-b = 4, a-d = 3, a-c = 8, b-e = 9, b-d = 7, c-d = 5, d-f = 4, d-g = 3, d-h = 9, e-f = 5, e-h = 4. Note there is no edge between d and e.

Application (trace starting at vertex e)

  1. (e-h), weight 4: cheapest edge leaving {e} beats e-f (5) and b-e (9). Tree = {e, h}.

  2. (e-f), weight 5: cheapest crossing edge now; h offers no cheaper new edge. Tree = {e, f, h}.

  3. (d-f), weight 4: f-d (4) is the cheapest crossing edge. Tree = {d, e, f, h}.

  4. (d-a), weight 3: d-a (3) ties d-g (3); take a first. Tree = {a, d, e, f, h}.

  5. (d-g), weight 3: the remaining weight-3 crossing edge attaches g. Tree = {a, d, e, f, g, h}.

  6. (a-b), weight 4: cheapest crossing edge (vs d-c 5, d-b 7). Tree = {a, b, d, e, f, g, h}.

  7. (d-c), weight 5: attaches the last vertex c (cheaper than a-c 8). Tree = all 8 vertices.

The seven chosen edges span all 8 vertices and total 4 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 28, the minimum spanning tree weight.

Cross-check (why the other sequences fail)

  • Any sequence that lists edge d-e is invalid: there is no d-e edge in the graph, so it can never be a Prim step. Vertex e connects only via b-e (9), e-f (5), or e-h (4).

  • Any sequence that picks an edge whose both endpoints are still outside the current tree (for example taking e-f or e-h before either endpoint has joined) breaks Prim's single-connected-component growth.

  • Any sequence that takes a costlier crossing edge while a cheaper crossing edge is available (for example attaching c with d-c before bringing in b with the cheaper a-b) violates the greedy minimum-cut rule.

title: Let (V,E) be directed graph, where is the set of

bodyHtml:
Let G (V,E) be a directed graph, where V={11,12,13,14,15,16} is the set of vertices and E is the set of directed edges, as defined by the following adjacency matrix A.

A[i][j]={1, 11≤ i ≤ j ≤ 16

A[i][j]={ 0, Otherwise A [i][j]=1 indicates a directed edge from node i to node j.

A directed spanning tree G, rooted at r∈V, is defined as a sub graph T of G such that the undirected version of T is a tree, and T contains a directed path from r to every other vertex in V. The number of such directed spanning trees rooted at vertex 11 is _______________
solution:
Answer: 120

Reasoning:

The adjacency matrix has A[i][j] = 1 for 11 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ 16, so there is a directed edge from a vertex p to a vertex q exactly when p ≤ q. (Self-loops p = q appear in the matrix but are not used as tree edges.) We count directed spanning trees (arborescences) rooted at vertex 11.

  • Vertex 12: its parent must be one of the earlier vertices {11} → 1 choice.

  • Vertex 13: its parent can be any of {11, 12} → 2 choices.

  • Vertex 14: its parent can be any of {11, 12, 13} → 3 choices.

  • Vertex 15: its parent can be any of {11, 12, 13, 14} → 4 choices.

  • Vertex 16: its parent can be any of {11, 12, 13, 14, 15} → 5 choices.

Each non-root vertex chooses its parent independently from the allowed earlier vertices, so the total number of directed spanning trees rooted at 11 is the product 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 = 120. Equivalently, for n = 6 vertices the count is (n−1)! = 5! = 120.

Note: The original solution used the term "MST" and gave an unclear sequence of examples. This improved solution gives a direct combinatorial count based on the adjacency rule.

title: Complete undirected graph is given on the vertex set to
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: A complete undirected graph G is given on the vertex set 0 to (n – 1) for a fixed value of ‘n’. Draw the minimum spanning tree (MST) of a graph G, for the following cases and find the cost of MST: i) weight of the edge (u, v) is |u – v| ii) weight of the edge (u, v) is |u + v|
solution:
Case i — weight w(u,v) = |u - v|: The smallest possible positive weight is 1, which occurs for every pair of consecutive vertices (k, k+1). Choose the edges (0,1), (1,2), …, (n-2, n-1) to form a path connecting all vertices. Each chosen edge has weight 1, so the MST cost is 1 · (n-1) = n-1.

  • Example (n = 4): edges 0–1, 1–2, 2–3 each weight 1, MST cost = 3.

Case ii — weight w(u,v) = |u + v| = u + v (labels are nonnegative): For each vertex i > 0 the smallest edge incident to i is (0,i) with weight i. Taking all edges (0,1), (0,2), …, (0,n-1) yields a spanning tree (a star centered at 0) whose total cost is sum_{i=1}^{n-1} i = n(n-1)/2. No spanning tree can have smaller total cost because every vertex i>0 must be connected by some edge of weight at least i, and (0,i) achieves that minimum for each i.

  • Example (n = 4): edges (0,1)=1, (0,2)=2, (0,3)=3, MST cost = 1+2+3 = 6.

Final answer: For the weight |u-v| the MST cost is n-1. For the weight u+v the MST cost is n(n-1)/2.

solution:
Concept: When several equal-weight edges compete during Kruskal's algorithm, the minimum total weight is still unique, but the SET of edges chosen among a tie can vary. Counting distinct minimum spanning trees means counting, at each weight tier, how many ways the tied edges can be chosen without creating a cycle.

  1. The unique smallest edge is (a, d) with weight 5. It is forced into every MST, merging a and d into one component.

  2. Both weight-6 edges, (a, b) and (b, e), connect distinct components without forming a cycle, so both are forced as well. The component is now {a, b, d, e}.

  3. Vertices c and f are still outside this component. Edge (d, e) also has weight 7, but both its endpoints already sit inside {a, b, d, e}, so it would only close a cycle and is skipped. The weight-7 edges that can actually extend the tree are (b, c), (c, e), (c, f), and (e, f).

  4. Two of these four edges are needed to bring in both c and f. Checking every pairing (table below) shows exactly one pairing closes a cycle; the rest are valid.

Pair of weight-7 edges

Connects c and f without a cycle?

(b,c) + (c,e)

No — recreates cycle b–c–e–b through the existing (b,e) edge

(b,c) + (c,f)

Yes

(b,c) + (e,f)

Yes

(c,e) + (c,f)

Yes

(c,e) + (e,f)

Yes

(c,f) + (e,f)

Yes

The remaining edge (b, d) has weight 9 — higher than every weight-7 edge — so it never appears in a minimum spanning tree.

Cross-check: every valid pairing gives the same total weight, 5 + 6 + 6 + 7 + 7 = 31, confirming each is genuinely minimum-cost; substituting (b, d) for any weight-7 edge would total at least 33, which is heavier and is correctly excluded. Counting the cycle-free pairings above — five of the six possible pairs — gives the number of distinct minimum spanning trees for this graph.

title: Which of the following statement is false about Prim’s algorithm?
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: Which of the following statement is false about Prim’s algorithm?

options.label: A
options.html: Initially the root's key is initialized to 0 and all other nodes to infinity

options.label: B
options.html: It may use binomial max heap to represent the priority queue

options.label: C
options.html: The complexity is O(E log V) using binary heap

options.label: D
options.html: The time complexity is O(E + V log V) using Fibonacci Heap

solution:
Concept: Prim's algorithm grows a Minimum Spanning Tree from a start vertex by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that crosses from the tree to a vertex outside it (the cut property). To pick that cheapest crossing edge fast, every vertex keeps a key = the smallest edge weight connecting it to the current tree, and these keys are stored in a min-priority queue so that extract-min always returns the next vertex to attach.

Initialization: every vertex starts with key = infinity, then the start (root) vertex's key is set to 0 so it is the first one extracted. So the root's key is 0 while all other vertices begin at infinity and are lowered as cheaper edges are discovered.

Application — checking each statement against this method:

  • "binomial max heap for the priority queue" — Prim's needs the MINIMUM-weight vertex each step, which a min-priority queue (min-heap) provides. A max-heap returns the largest key, so it cannot drive Prim's; this claim does not hold.

  • "root key initialized to 0" — consistent with the initialization above: the start vertex's key is set to 0 (others are infinity), so this holds.

  • "O(E log V) using a binary heap" — with a binary heap each of the O(E) decrease-key and O(V) extract-min operations costs O(log V), giving O(E log V); this holds.

  • "O(E + V log V) using a Fibonacci heap" — a Fibonacci heap does decrease-key in O(1) amortized and extract-min in O(log V) amortized, giving O(E + V log V); this holds.

Cross-check: three statements match standard Prim's behaviour, so the single statement that is false about Prim's algorithm is the one claiming a binomial max heap can represent the priority queue.

title: Which of the following algorithms is not used for finding
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: Which of the following algorithms is not used for finding a Minimum Spanning Tree?
solution:
Concept

A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of a connected, weighted, undirected graph is a subset of edges that connects all vertices with the minimum possible total edge weight and contains no cycle. MST algorithms grow or prune a single tree/forest using a cut or cycle rule. This is a fundamentally different problem from the shortest-path problem, which finds the minimum-weight path between vertices and may use negative-weight edges.

Application

Classify each offered algorithm by the problem it solves:

  • Kruskal's Algorithm: builds the MST by adding the globally cheapest edge that does not form a cycle (greedy on sorted edges) - an MST algorithm.

  • Prim's Algorithm: grows the MST from a start vertex, repeatedly adding the cheapest edge leaving the current tree - an MST algorithm.

  • Boruvka's Algorithm: repeatedly adds, for every component, its cheapest outgoing edge, merging components in parallel rounds - an MST algorithm.

  • Reverse-Delete Algorithm: starts from the full edge set and deletes the most expensive edges whose removal keeps the graph connected - an MST algorithm.

  • Bellman-Ford Algorithm: computes single-source shortest paths and can handle negative edge weights - a SHORTEST-PATH algorithm, not an MST algorithm.

Four of the five listed methods construct a minimum spanning tree; the remaining one solves the shortest-path problem. Hence the algorithm not used for finding an MST is Bellman-Ford.

Cross-check

MST algorithms output a set of edges forming a tree spanning all vertices; their correctness rests on the cut property (the cheapest edge crossing any cut is safe) or the cycle property (a strictly heaviest edge on any cycle is unsafe). Bellman-Ford instead outputs a shortest-path distance/predecessor table from one source and is the standard choice when negative weights are present - confirming it belongs to the shortest-path family, not the MST family.

title: In the context of minimum spanning trees, the "cut property"
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: In minimum spanning trees, the cut property is used to justify Prim's algorithm. What does the cut property state?

options.label: A
options.html: A maximum-weight edge in the graph must be part of every MST.

options.label: B
options.html: A minimum-weight edge in the graph is the only edge Prim's algorithm can choose.

options.label: C
options.html: A minimum-weight edge crossing the current cut is safe to add to an MST.

options.label: D
options.html: A maximum-weight edge crossing a cut is safe to add to an MST.

solution:
CONCEPT

A cut partitions the vertices of a connected, weighted, undirected graph into two non-empty sets. A crossing edge has one endpoint on each side of that partition.

The cut property says that a lightest edge crossing a cut is safe for the minimum spanning tree: it can be included in some MST. When all edge weights are distinct, that crossing edge is forced into the MST.

APPLICATION

  1. In Prim's algorithm, the vertices already in the growing tree form one side of a cut, and the remaining vertices form the other side.

  2. The candidate edges are the edges crossing that current cut.

  3. Choosing a minimum-weight crossing edge is safe, so adding it preserves the possibility of completing a minimum spanning tree.

  4. Therefore, the cut-property statement that fits Prim's algorithm is: a minimum-weight edge crossing the current cut is safe to add to an MST.

CONTRAST

  • A maximum-weight edge rule can add unnecessary cost and is not justified by the MST cut property.

  • A globally minimum-edge rule misses the cut restriction used in Prim's step-by-step growth.

  • A maximum-weight crossing-edge rule keeps the cut setting but reverses the light-edge condition.

RESULT

The answer is: a minimum-weight edge crossing the current cut is safe to add to an MST.

title: Assume Dijkstra Algo is used to find shortest path, find
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Assume Dijkstra's algorithm is run on the graph below, starting from source vertex G, to find the shortest path from G to every other vertex.

Find the number of edges in the graph that are NOT used in the resulting shortest-path tree.
solution:
Dijkstra's algorithm finds, from one chosen source vertex, the shortest distance to every other vertex: starting from the source, it repeatedly picks the nearest unvisited vertex and relaxes — attempts to improve — its neighbours' tentative distances. An edge becomes part of the shortest-path tree only if it ends up as a vertex's FINAL shortest-distance predecessor at the moment that vertex is finalized; an edge that is tried during relaxation but is later superseded by a shorter route (and so never becomes any vertex's final predecessor) remains unused, along with every edge that plays no role in relaxation at all.

Applying this to the given graph with source G:

  1. Initial distances from G: G = 0, A = 2 (via G–A), T = 3 (via G–T), M = 5 (via G–M), E = ∞.

  2. Pick the nearest unvisited node A (distance 2). Update neighbors: E via A = 2 + 7 = 9, M via A = 2 + 6 = 8 (no improvement to M).

  3. Pick the next nearest unvisited node T (distance 3). Update neighbors: E via T = 3 + 4 = 7 (improves E), M via T = 3 + 4 = 7 (no improvement to M since M = 5).

  4. Pick M (distance 5). Its neighbors do not improve any distances (E via M = 10 > 7). Finally pick E (distance 7).

The edges chosen when each node received its final shortest distance form the shortest-path tree:

  • Used edges in the shortest-path tree: G–A, G–T, G–M, T–E

  • All edges in the graph: G–A, A–E, E–T, T–G, G–M, A–M, E–M, T–M

  • Unused edges = (all edges) − (used edges) = A–E, A–M, E–M, T–M

Cross-check: a shortest-path tree spanning all 5 vertices (G, A, T, M, E) must contain exactly 5 − 1 = 4 edges, since any spanning tree on n vertices has n − 1 edges — this matches the 4 tree edges found above, confirming the tree is complete and correctly formed.

Count: the graph has 8 edges in total; the shortest-path tree uses 4 of them, so 8 − 4 = 4 edges are not used. The correct answer is 4.

title: If there is cycle in graph that is reachable from
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: If there is a cycle in a graph that is reachable from source then Dijkastra’s shortest-path algorithm may relax an edge more than once in the graph ?
solution:
Answer: False

Explanation: In the standard Dijkstra algorithm implementation that uses decrease-key, each vertex is finalized (settled) when it is extracted from the priority queue. A finalized vertex is processed exactly once, and its outgoing edges are relaxed at that time. Therefore each edge is relaxed at most once, so a reachable cycle does not cause repeated relaxations of the same edge.

  • Key idea: a vertex is given its final shortest-path distance when popped from the priority queue and is not reprocessed.

  • Outgoing edges are relaxed only when their source vertex is settled, so each edge is considered at most once in that step.

  • Cycles reachable from the source do not change this property.

  • Note: Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights; with negative weights the algorithm is not valid.

Implementation note: Some implementations that avoid decrease-key insert duplicate entries for a vertex into the priority queue and may examine a vertex multiple times before ignoring stale entries. That is an implementation detail; the standard correctness argument relies on settling each vertex once, which prevents repeated effective relaxations due to cycles.

title: Which data structure is used to maintain the distance of
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: Which data structure is used to maintain the distance of each node in a Dijkstra’s algorithm?
solution:
Answer: Priority queue (min-priority queue).

Explanation: Dijkstra’s algorithm repeatedly selects the vertex with the smallest tentative distance and updates neighbors. A min-priority queue efficiently supports selecting the minimum-distance vertex each time.

  • Key operations: extract-min (remove the node with smallest tentative distance).

  • Key operations: decrease-key (update a node’s tentative distance when a shorter path is found).

  • Key operations: insert (add nodes into the priority queue as needed).

Implementation note: A binary min-heap is a common implementation (giving about O((V+E) log V) time). Using a Fibonacci heap improves decrease-key and yields O(E + V log V) in the theoretical bound.

title: Match the following time complexities of Dijkstra’s algorithm with the
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Match the following time complexities of Dijkstra’s algorithm with the corresponding priority queue implementations.

List-A List-B

P: Binary heap X: O(v2 )

Q: Array Y: O(E log2 V)

R: Fibonacci Heap Z: O(V log2 V +E)
solution:
Final mapping:

  • Binary heap → O(E log V). Reason: extract-min and decrease-key cost O(log V), and across the algorithm these give O(E log V) overall (extract-min done up to V times, decrease-key up to E times).

  • Array (unsorted) → O(V^2). Reason: selecting the minimum vertex from an unsorted array takes O(V) and is repeated V times, giving O(V^2).

  • Fibonacci heap → O(V log V + E). Reason: decrease-key is amortized O(1) so most edge relaxations are cheap; extract-min costs O(log V) done V times, yielding O(V log V + E).

Key intuition: if decrease-key is O(log V) (binary heap) the cost is dominated by E log V; if decrease-key is O(1) amortized (Fibonacci heap) the cost reduces to V log V + E; an unsorted array forces linear scans leading to V^2.

title: In the Dijkstra algorithm the shortest path always passes through
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: In the Dijkstra algorithm the shortest path always passes through the least number of vertices?
solution:
Answer: false — Dijkstra finds the path with minimum total edge weight, not the path that passes through the fewest vertices.

Why: Dijkstra's objective is to minimize the sum of edge weights along a path. The count of intermediate vertices is not considered, so a path with more vertices can have a smaller total weight than a shorter path in terms of vertex count.

  • Counterexample: vertices A, B, C with edges A–B weight 5, B–C weight 5, and A–C weight 15.

  • From A to C, the path A→B→C has total weight 10 and uses three vertices, while the direct path A→C has total weight 15 and uses two vertices. Dijkstra picks A→B→C because its total weight is smaller, even though it visits more vertices.

Note: Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights. If negative-weight edges are present, use an algorithm designed for that case (for example, Bellman-Ford).

title: Let be the directed, weighted graph shown below. What is
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Let G be the directed, weighted graph shown below.

What is the cost of the shortest paths from ‘a’ to all other remaining vertices in the above graph?
solution:
Solution (apply Dijkstra's algorithm from source a):

  1. Initialize distances: a = 0; set direct neighbors from a: b = 50, c = 45, d = 10; set e = ∞, f = ∞.

  2. Pick the unvisited vertex with smallest distance: d (10). Relax edges from d: d -> e with cost 15 gives e = 10 + 15 = 25. Other relaxations do not improve a (a is already 0).

  3. Next pick e (25). Relax edges from e: e -> b with cost 20 gives candidate b = 25 + 20 = 45, which improves b from 50 to 45. e -> c (cost 35) would give 60, so c remains 45. f is not reached from e.

  4. Next vertices to consider are b and c (both 45). Processing b does not improve c (b -> c = 10 would give 55). After processing, no further improvements are possible.

Final shortest-path costs from a:

  • a: 0

  • b: 45 (one shortest path is a -> d -> e -> b with cost 10 + 15 + 20 = 45)

  • c: 45 (directly a -> c with cost 45)

  • d: 10 (directly a -> d)

  • e: 25 (via a -> d -> e: 10 + 15 = 25)

  • f: ∞ (no path from a to f; the only edge involving f is from f to e)

Therefore the correct answer is: a = 0, b = 45, c = 45, d = 10, e = 25, f = ∞.

solution: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source node to all other nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. To implement this efficiently, the algorithm repeatedly selects the unvisited node with the smallest tentative distance. A Priority Queue or Min-Heap is ideal for this task because it allows efficient retrieval of the minimum element and supports fast updates when shorter paths are found. This reduces the time complexity to O((V + E) log V), where V is vertices and E is edges. Using a simple Queue or Stack would not guarantee processing nodes in order of distance, leading to incorrect results or inefficiency. Similarly, a Binary Search Tree could work but is generally less optimized for this specific use case than a heap. Therefore, the Priority Queue/Min-Heap is the standard choice for an efficient implementation.

title: Which of the following is/are false?
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: Which of the following is/are false?

options.label: A
options.html: For every weighted graph with starting vertex at S, Bellman Ford algorithm always gives shortest path to any given vertex V.

options.label: B
options.html: If a graph contains a negative weight cycle then Dijkstra’s algorithm may not terminate

options.label: C
options.html: For a directed graph, the absence of back edges across a complete DFS forest means there is no cycle.

options.label: D
options.html: A complete graph of 4 vertices can have maximum 16 minimum cost spanning trees.

solution:
Concept

A statement of the form "this algorithm/theorem always guarantees X" is false the moment it drops the precondition that the guarantee depends on. So evaluate each claim against the exact requirement of the underlying result: Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra each need a specific condition on negative weights, DFS back edges characterise directed cycles, and Cayley's formula counts spanning trees of a complete graph.

Applying it to each statement

  1. Bellman-Ford "always" for "every" weighted graph: this overstates the guarantee. Bellman-Ford returns correct shortest paths only when no negative-weight cycle is reachable from the source; with a reachable negative cycle the shortest paths are undefined and it reports the cycle instead.

  2. Dijkstra and a negative-weight cycle: the standard algorithm extracts and finalises each vertex from the priority queue exactly once, so its main loop is bounded to exactly |V| iterations on any finite graph, whatever the edge weights are. A negative cycle cannot make this loop run forever — it can only leave an already-finalised vertex holding a distance that a later relaxation along the cycle would have lowered further, so the reported distances come out wrong while the algorithm itself still halts. The claim that it 'may not terminate' overstates what a negative cycle actually breaks: correctness fails here, not termination.

  3. DFS back edges in a directed graph: a back edge points to an ancestor on the recursion stack and exists exactly when a directed cycle exists, so no back edges across the DFS forest means the graph is acyclic.

  4. Spanning trees of K4: Cayley's formula gives n(n-2) spanning trees, i.e. 42 = 16; with all edge weights equal, every one of these 16 trees is a minimum-cost spanning tree.

Cross-check

The over-general guarantees are the false ones; the structural facts (DFS back-edge characterisation, Cayley count) hold exactly as stated.

title: Which of the following statements are incorrect: Adding number on
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Which of the following statements are incorrect:

S1: Adding a number on every edge of a graph may change the shortest path.

S2: A graph where all edge weights are distinct can have more than one shortest path between two vertices.
solution:
Answer: None of the statements is incorrect; both statements are correct.

  • Explanation for the first statement: Adding the same constant to every edge can change which path is shortest. This is because each path’s total increases by (constant × number of edges in that path), so paths with different edge counts can swap order after the addition.

    Example: Path X uses two edges of weights 1 and 1 (total 2). Path Y uses a single edge of weight 3 (total 3). Initially Path X is shorter (2 < 3). If we add 2 to every edge, Path X becomes 6 and Path Y becomes 5, so the shortest path changes.

  • Explanation for the second statement: Distinct individual edge weights do not guarantee a unique shortest path. Different combinations of distinct weights can sum to the same total, producing multiple shortest paths.

    Example: Edges with weights 1, 4, and 5 are all distinct. One path could use edges of weights 1 and 4 (total 5), while another path could use the single edge of weight 5 (total 5). Both paths tie as shortest.

Conclusion: Since both statements are true, none of them is incorrect.

title: The bellman-ford algorithm takes _time to detect the presence of
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: The bellman-ford algorithm takes _time to detect the presence of a negative weight cycle in a graph.
solution:
Answer: O(VE)

Reason:

  • Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge in the graph for V-1 iterations to compute shortest paths. Each iteration scans all E edges, so these passes cost O((V-1)·E) = O(VE).

  • To detect a negative weight cycle, the algorithm performs one additional pass over all edges. If any distance can still be reduced in that extra pass, a negative cycle exists. That extra pass costs O(E), so it does not change the overall O(VE) bound.

Therefore, the time to detect the presence of a negative weight cycle using Bellman–Ford is O(VE).

title: Graph is such that every vertex is connected to every
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: A complete graph G has a direct edge between every pair of distinct vertices. If Bellman–Ford is used to find a shortest path, what is its asymptotic running time in terms of V, the number of vertices?
solution:
Concept: For any weighted graph (including ones with negative edge weights), Bellman–Ford's running time is the product of two governing quantities: the number of relaxation rounds, V − 1, and the work per round, which relaxes every edge once, i.e. Θ(E). This gives the general bound O(V × E), valid regardless of how many edges the graph has.

Application:

  1. Per-round work: every edge is relaxed once per round, costing Θ(E).

  2. Number of rounds: V − 1, so multiplying the two gives a total of O(V × E).

  3. Edge count for this graph: G is complete, so every distinct pair of vertices has an edge. The exact count is V(V−1)/2 — for V = 4 that is 4×3/2 = 6, not 42 = 16, so the exact count and 'V2' are not the same number.

  4. Asymptotic order of that count: Big-Θ notation describes growth rate, not an exact value at one V. As V grows, V(V−1)/2 grows in proportion to V2 (the −1 and the 1/2 factor don't change the growth rate), so we write E = Θ(V2) — meaning 'grows like V2', not 'equals V2 exactly'. That is why 6 (the true edge count at V = 4) and 16 (literally V2 at V = 4) can both be consistent with E = Θ(V2).

  5. Substituting E = Θ(V2) into the general bound O(V × E) gives O(V × V2) = O(V3), the running time for Bellman–Ford's shortest-path search on this complete graph.

Cross-check: Doubling V roughly quadruples the exact edge count V(V−1)/2, consistent with quadratic growth, which confirms E = Θ(V2) is the right order to substitute. A final extra round to detect negative-weight cycles costs one more Θ(E) pass and does not change this asymptotic bound. Note also that if all edge weights were guaranteed non-negative, a priority-queue-based algorithm could run faster in practice — but Bellman–Ford is needed precisely because it correctly handles negative edge weights, which a plain priority-queue approach cannot.

title: Consider the following statements: The Bellman-Ford algorithm applies to instances
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Consider the following statements:

S1: The Bellman-Ford algorithm applies to instances of the single-source shortest path problem which do not have a negative-weight directed cycle, but it does not detect the existence of a negative-weight directed cycle if there is one.

S2: A weighted directed graph G = (V, E, w) and let X be a shortest s-t path for s, t ∈ V. If we double the weight of every edge in the graph, setting w of (e) = 2w(e) for each e ∈ E, then X will still be a shortest s-t path in (V, E, w ).

Which of the following option is correct?
solution:
Answer: Only S2 is correct.

  • Why the first statement is false: Bellman-Ford does detect negative-weight directed cycles. After performing |V|-1 relaxation rounds to compute shortest paths in a graph without negative cycles, the algorithm performs one additional relaxation pass; if any distance can still be decreased in that extra pass, the algorithm reports the existence of a negative-weight directed cycle.

  • Why the second statement is true: Multiplying every edge weight by the positive constant 2 scales the length of every s–t path by 2, so the relative ordering of path lengths is preserved. Therefore any shortest s–t path before scaling remains a shortest s–t path after scaling. (This reasoning holds for any positive scaling factor.)

Summary: The first statement is incorrect because Bellman-Ford detects negative cycles; the second statement is correct because positive scaling preserves shortest-path ordering. Hence only the second statement is correct.

title: Consider graph G(V, such that every vertex of is connected
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml: Consider a graph G(V, E) such that every vertex of g is connected to every other vertex through direct link. What is the time complexity to compute the shortest path using bellman ford algorithm?
solution:
Key idea: the Bellman–Ford algorithm performs up to V−1 relaxation passes over every edge, so its time complexity is O(V * E).

Number of edges in a complete simple undirected graph:

  • E = V(V−1)/2 = Θ(V^2)

Substitute into the Bellman–Ford complexity:

  • O(V * E) = O(V * V^2) = O(V^3)

Conclusion: For a complete graph where every vertex is directly connected to every other, the shortest-path computation using Bellman–Ford takes O(V^3) time.

title: Given Graph, Assume that if it takes time to travel
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Given Graph, Assume that if it takes time T to travel from vertex a to b, then it takes the same time to travel from b to a. We wish to select a walk from vertex 1 to some other vertex, back to vertex 1 and so on till each vertex (except vertex 1 - the source) is visited exactly once.

Let the initial instant be T= 0. Let the times of visit of vertices 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 from T = 0 be T2, T3, T4 , T5, T6 and T7. We wish to minimise the sum of T2, T3, T4, T5, T6 and T7. Find out the minimum possible sum of the given times [ Note: Each edge cost is nothing but travel time] ______
solution:
Corrected reasoning and final calculation:

Key idea: Each visit to a vertex starts at vertex 1, and between consecutive visits we return to vertex 1. For the k-th vertex visited (in the chosen order) its arrival time equals the sum of all previous round trips plus the one-way travel to this vertex. This makes earlier chosen edges contribute more to the total sum, so assign smaller edge times to earlier visits.

Derivation of coefficients for six vertices:

  • If the chosen visit order has edge times w1,w2,w3,w4,w5,w6, the arrival times sum to:

  • w1 + (2w1 + w2) + (2w1 + 2w2 + w3) + ... + (2w1 + 2w2 + 2w3 + 2w4 + 2w5 + w6).

Thus the coefficients multiplying w1..w6 are 11, 9, 7, 5, 3, 1 respectively. To minimize the total, sort edge times in ascending order and assign them to these coefficients in that order (smallest time gets coefficient 11, next smallest gets 9, and so on).

Edge times from vertex 1 to each vertex (from the diagram):

  • Vertex 2: 2

  • Vertex 3: 5

  • Vertex 4: 3

  • Vertex 5: 7

  • Vertex 6: 8

  • Vertex 7: 6

Sorted edge times (ascending): 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8.

Assigning coefficients and computing the sum:

  • 11 × 2 = 22

  • 9 × 3 = 27

  • 7 × 5 = 35

  • 5 × 6 = 30

  • 3 × 7 = 21

  • 1 × 8 = 8

Total minimum sum = 22 + 27 + 35 + 30 + 21 + 8 = 143.

One optimal visiting order (by vertex number) is: 2, 4, 3, 7, 5, 6, giving the minimal sum 143.

title: Match the following table showing algorithm and its application. Scenarios
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Match the following table showing algorithm and its application.

Scenarios

Algorithms

(P) A person wants to visit from one place to another place in shortest period

(i) Floyd's algorithm

(Q) A person wants to visit M places in shortest period

(ii) Multi-stage graph algorithm

(R) All N persons wants to visit all M places in shortest period

(iii) Dijkstra's algorithm
solution:
Concept

Shortest-path algorithms are distinguished by the query model and graph structure. Floyd–Warshall precomputes all-pairs distances, Dijkstra handles non-negative weighted single-source queries and can be repeated for several sources, and the multi-stage graph method uses the layered structure of a directed acyclic graph.

A matching question must therefore be read using the particular operational interpretation adopted by its source examination.

Application

  1. For P, the official ISRO interpretation uses Floyd’s algorithm: an all-pairs distance table can answer a requested place-to-place query.

  2. For Q, the visit through M places is interpreted as movement through successive stages, so it is paired with the multi-stage graph algorithm.

  3. For R, Dijkstra’s algorithm is interpreted as being run from each relevant person’s starting vertex to obtain routes to the M destinations, assuming non-negative edge weights.

Cross-check

  • The revised final ISRO Computer Science answer key for the 2025 A-series Question 37 selects the mapping P–(i), Q–(ii), R–(iii).

  • The wording is not algorithmically exclusive: Dijkstra can also answer a single source-to-destination query, while Floyd–Warshall is the direct all-pairs method. The accepted mapping here follows the official PYQ key rather than claiming those alternatives are impossible.

Therefore, the officially accepted matching is P–(i), Q–(ii), R–(iii).

title: Arrange the following algorithms from the most efficient to least

Arrange the following algorithms from the most efficient to least efficient using their standard worst-case time complexities:

title: Which of the following algorithms use Greedy strategy? Dijkstra’s algorithm
subject: Algorithms
bodyHtml:
Which of the following algorithms use Greedy strategy?
A. Dijkstra’s algorithm
B. Kruskal’s algorithm
C. Huffman coding
D. Bellman-Ford algorithm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Answer: Dijkstra’s algorithm, Kruskal’s algorithm, and Huffman coding.

Explanation:

  • Dijkstra’s algorithm: Greedy. At each step it selects the vertex with the smallest tentative distance and finalizes that choice, never needing to revise it.

  • Kruskal’s algorithm: Greedy. It repeatedly picks the smallest-weight edge that does not create a cycle, making locally optimal edge choices to build a minimum spanning forest.

  • Huffman coding: Greedy. It repeatedly merges the two least-frequent symbols to build an optimal prefix code, making a locally optimal merge at each step.

  • Bellman-Ford algorithm: Not greedy. It uses repeated relaxation of edges and can update previously made choices based on information found later, which is characteristic of dynamic programming/iterative relaxation rather than a greedy one-pass choice.

Therefore the correct set of algorithms that use a greedy strategy is Dijkstra’s algorithm, Kruskal’s algorithm, and Huffman coding.

{
    float a = 123.456;
    printf("%.2f, %7.3f, %12e", a, a, a);
}
solution:
Concept — how a printf conversion is built

A conversion specification here has the form %[flags][width][.precision]conversion; optional flags may also appear right after the % sign, and none of the three conversions in this call uses one. The width is a minimum total field width: with no flag, if the converted text is shorter, spaces are added on the left, and if it is already that long or longer nothing is added — printf never truncates a number to make it fit. The .precision is the count of digits printed after the decimal point for both f and e; it defaults to 6, and the value is rounded to that many digits, never cut. An e conversion also normalises the number as d.dddddde±dd, that is, one non-zero digit before the point.

Application — the three conversions in this call, with a = 123.456

  1. %.2f: no width is given and the precision is 2, so 123.456 is rounded to two decimal digits — the third digit 6 rounds the 5 up — giving 123.46.

  2. %7.3f: the precision 3 gives 123.456, and that text is already 7 characters long (three digits, the point, three more digits), so the minimum width of 7 is exactly met and no spaces are added.

  3. %12e: no precision is written, so the default 6 applies — mantissa 1.234560 and exponent 2, that is 1.234560 × 102, written 1.234560e+02. Count its characters: one digit, the point, six digits, the letter e, the sign and two exponent digits — 12 in all. The minimum width of 12 is exactly met, so here too no spaces are added.

Cross-check — what each width actually did

Conversion

Width asked for

Text produced

Its length

Spaces added

%.2f

none

123.46

6

0

%7.3f

7

123.456

7

0

%12e

12

1.234560e+02

12

0

So the widths 7 and 12 only reserve room; here the text already fills them, which is why no padding appears. Had the call used %15e, the same 12-character text would have been printed with three leading spaces, and %9.3f would print two leading spaces before 123.456. Without a flag, a width can only add spaces on the left — it never adds digits and never cuts; a - flag would left-justify the text instead, and 0 would pad it with zeros.

One more detail: a is declared float, and a float argument is promoted to double before printf reads it. 123.456 is not exactly representable in binary, so the stored value is about 123.456001, but at 2, 3 and 6 decimal digits it still rounds to the digits shown.

Result: the three fields print as 123.46, 123.456, 1.234560e+02.

A valid C identifier must start with a letter (A-Z or a-z) or an underscore, and every character after the first must be a letter, digit, or underscore; a digit can never be the first character, and a reserved keyword cannot be used as an identifier.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q53
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml: Which of the following is not a valid C data type?
solution:
Concept

In C, a type name must either be defined by the language or introduced by the program through a declaration such as typedef. The standard arithmetic type family includes integer types and floating types.

Application

Among the given values, int, float, and char are standard C type specifiers. real is not a predefined C type name; a program may use it as a type name only after explicitly defining an alias such as typedef float real;. Therefore, the value that is not a built-in C data type is real.

Contrast

  • int denotes a signed integer type for whole-number values.

  • float denotes a floating type for finite-precision real-number approximations.

  • real is an ordinary identifier unless the program declares it as a typedef name.

  • char denotes the character-sized integer type; sizeof(char) is 1 byte.

Cross-check

A declaration such as int x;, float y;, or char c; uses a standard type specifier. By contrast, real z; requires a prior declaration such as typedef float real;, confirming that real is not predefined by C.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q43
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml: In the conventional data model of a 16-bit C compiler, the size of long int is:
solution:
Concept

In C, integer-type widths are implementation-defined, but long int must represent at least the range −2,147,483,647 to 2,147,483,647.

Traditional 16-bit C data models use a 16-bit int and a 32-bit long int.

Application

  1. Use the conventional 16-bit C data model named in the stem: long int occupies 4 bytes in that model.

  2. Convert bytes to bits using 8 bits per byte: 4 × 8 = 32 bits.

Contrast

  • 8 bits is one 8-bit byte, which is narrower than even the conventional 16-bit int in this model.

  • 16 bits is two 8-bit bytes and is the conventional width of int, not long int, in this model.

  • 24 bits is three 8-bit bytes and is not the conventional long int width used by this data model.

Cross-check

A signed 16-bit object reaches only 32,767, whereas long int must represent values through at least 2,147,483,647. A 32-bit signed representation meets that minimum range, confirming 32 bits.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q47
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml: In C, for an 8-bit two’s-complement signed char, the range of the char data type is:
solution:
Concept

An n-bit signed integer in two’s-complement form has the range −2n−1 through 2n−1−1. An 8-bit signed char therefore has 256 bit patterns: one bit carries the sign contribution, and the remaining bits determine the magnitude pattern.

Application

  1. Set n = 8 because the question specifies an 8-bit signed char.

  2. The minimum value is −28−1 = −27 = −128.

  3. The maximum value is 28−1−1 = 27−1 = 127.

Cross-check and contrast

  • −128 to 127 contains 256 signed values and is the interval obtained from the 8-bit signed formula.

  • 0 to 255 also contains 256 values, but it is the usual range of an 8-bit unsigned char.

  • 0 to 32767 contains 32,768 non-negative values and corresponds to a 15-bit unsigned magnitude range, not an 8-bit range.

  • None of these would apply only if every listed interval failed the stated 8-bit signed assumption.

Therefore, the required range is −128 to 127.

title: <iostream> using namespace std; int void fun() int int cout
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml:
What is the output of the following C++ program?

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
int x = 10;
void fun() {
    int x = 2;
    {
        int x = 1;
        cout << ::x << endl;
    }
}
int main() {
    fun();
    return 0;
}
solution:
Concept

The unary scope resolution operator :: (with nothing on its left) always names an identifier from the global namespace. It bypasses every local or block-scope declaration that may be shadowing the same name, so it is unaffected by any inner variable of the same name.

Application

  1. A global variable x is defined at file scope with value 10.

  2. Inside fun() a local x = 2 shadows the global, and an inner block declares yet another x = 1 that shadows both. These two only affect an unqualified x.

  3. The print statement is cout << ::x << endl;. Because the name is qualified with ::, lookup goes straight to the global x, ignoring the block-scoped 1 and the function-scoped 2.

  4. Hence the value sent to cout is the global value, 10.

Cross-check

The code is syntactically valid C++, so it compiles and runs cleanly. If the same line were written as an unqualified cout << x it would instead print the nearest enclosing local, 1; the :: prefix is exactly what forces the global value, 10.

title: Which among the following operator has the right to left

bodyHtml: Which among the following operator has the right to left associativity?
solution:
In programming, associativity determines the order in which operators of the same precedence are evaluated. Operators can be left-associative (evaluated from left to right) or right-associative (evaluated from right to left).

Arithmetic, logical, and relational operators are generally left-associative. However, the increment (++) and decrement (--) operators are unary and are right-associative. This means that in an expression with multiple increment/decrement operators, they are evaluated from right to left.

For example, in the expression ++x++ (if valid), the rightmost operator is evaluated first due to right associativity.

Thus, among the given options, only the increment/decrement operators have right-to-left associativity.

title: Find the output of the following #include<stdio.h> int main() int
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml:
Find the output of the following

#include<stdio.h>
int main()
{
int x = 5, y = 9;
x = (x = x + y) - (y = x - y);
printf("%d %d", x, y);
return 0;
}
solution:
The core of this problem lies in the expression: x = (x = x + y) - (y = x - y);. This is an example of an expression that technically results in undefined behavior in standard C because it modifies the same variable multiple times without a sequence point. However, most modern compilers (and competitive exam environments) evaluate it using a specific mathematical sequence.

  1. Initial Values: x = 5, y = 9.

  2. Evaluating the Parentheses:

    • First sub-expression (x = x + y): x becomes 5 + 9 = 14. The value of this sub-expression is 14.

    • Second sub-expression (y = x - y): Now, x is 14. So, y becomes 14 - 9 = 5. The value of this sub-expression is 5.

  3. Final Assignment for x:

    • x = (14) - (5) = 9.

  4. Final Result: x = 9, y = 5.

title: What is the output of the following program #include<stdio.h> int
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml:
What is the output/behavior of the following C program?

#include<stdio.h>
int main()
{
   int i = 5;
   printf("%d %d %d", i++, i, ++i);
   return 0;
}
solution:
Concept: In C, a sequence point marks a place where all side effects of prior evaluations are guaranteed complete before evaluation continues. Between two sequence points, modifying the same scalar object more than once, or modifying it while also reading its value for something other than computing the new stored value, is undefined behavior. The C standard also leaves the order in which a function call’s arguments are evaluated unspecified — a compiler may evaluate them left-to-right, right-to-left, or in any other order, and may schedule the associated side effects at different points.

  1. The call is printf("%d %d %d", i++, i, ++i); with i initialized to 5.

  2. All three arguments — i++, i, and ++i — are evaluated as part of setting up the same function call; the only sequence point here occurs right before the actual call, after every argument has been evaluated.

  3. i++ modifies i (post-increment), ++i also modifies i (pre-increment), and the middle argument reads i directly — that is two modifications and one plain read of the same object across the three argument evaluations, with no sequence point separating them from each other.

  4. Because no sequence point separates these evaluations, the compiler is free to choose any order among the three arguments and to apply the two increments at any point relative to the plain read — the standard places no obligation on what value the plain i sees or in which order the increments occur.

Cross-check: Different compilers, and even the same compiler under different optimization settings, are free to print different values for this exact program without violating the standard, because the standard simply does not define an outcome here. Assuming one specific evaluation order — say, strict left-to-right with each side effect applied immediately — only reproduces ONE of the many results a conforming compiler could legally produce; it does not establish what "the" output is.

Therefore, the only defensible classification for this program is undefined behavior — not any specific triplet of printed numbers.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q180
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml:
What will the following C code print?

int value, x, y;

value = (x = 10, y = 5, x + y);

printf("Value = %d", value);
solution:
Concept. Used as an operator, the comma in C is a sequencing operator: in an expression a, b the left operand is evaluated first and its value is discarded, and the value and type of the whole expression are those of the rightmost operand. Each comma is a sequence point, so every side effect of one operand is complete before the next operand begins.

Application.

  1. The parentheses in (x = 10, y = 5, x + y) enclose one comma expression with three operands, so the operands are evaluated strictly left to right.

  2. The first operand x = 10 is evaluated: it stores 10 in x. The value it produces is discarded at the comma.

  3. The second operand y = 5 is evaluated: it stores 5 in y. Its value is discarded at the next comma.

  4. The third and rightmost operand x + y is evaluated with the stored values: 10 + 5 = 15. Because it is the rightmost operand, 15 is the value of the whole parenthesised expression.

  5. That value is assigned to value, so value holds 15 and printf("Value = %d", value) writes Value = 15.

Cross-check. The snippet is well-formed C: the commas in the declaration int value, x, y; are declarator separators, the commas inside the parentheses form a comma expression, and the %d conversion specifier is paired with an int argument, so nothing here is a constraint violation. Treating only the first assignment as the expression’s value would give 10, and treating only the second as its value would give 5; both readings ignore that a comma expression takes the value of its last operand, which is why the sum 15 is what reaches value.

title: The correct way to round off floating number to an
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml: The correct way to round off a floating number x to an integer value is
solution:
Correct expression: y = (int) (x + 0.5)

Why this works (for non-negative values):

  • Adding 0.5 shifts numbers with fractional part 0.5 or greater up to the next integer threshold.

  • Casting to integer then truncates the fractional part, producing the expected rounded integer.

  • Example: x = 2.3 → x + 0.5 = 2.8 → (int)(2.8) = 2; x = 2.6 → x + 0.5 = 3.1 → (int)(3.1) = 3.

Important caveats and alternatives:

  • For negative numbers this method may fail because many languages truncate toward zero when casting. For example, x = -2.6: x + 0.5 = -2.1 and casting toward zero gives -2, while mathematically rounding should give -3.

  • Behavior is language-dependent: in Python, int(x+0.5) resembles this approach but still truncates toward zero for negatives. Prefer using the language-provided round function (for example round(x) in many languages) which handles sign correctly.

  • If you need mathematical rounding (round half up) that works for negatives, use floor(x + 0.5) for real-to-integer conversion when floor is defined to be the mathematical floor, or use a dedicated rounding routine.

Summary: The expression y = (int) (x + 0.5) correctly rounds non-negative floating values in the usual cast-truncate languages. For robust behavior across positive and negative values, prefer built-in round functions or a floor-based approach.

Therefore, printf("%d", x); prints 10.

title: What is the output of the following pseudocode print(x
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml:
What is the output of the following C-style pseudocode?

x = 5
y = x++
z = ++x
print(x + y + z)
solution:
Concept: The increment operator has two forms. In post-increment (v++), the expression yields the variable's old value and the variable is increased by 1 afterward. In pre-increment (++v), the variable is increased by 1 first and the expression yields the new value. In both forms the variable's stored value permanently increases by 1; only the value handed to the surrounding expression differs.

Application: Trace each statement and keep track of the stored value of x after every line.

  1. x = 5: store 5 in x. Now x = 5.

  2. y = x++: post-increment, so y receives the old value y = 5, and afterward x becomes x = 6.

  3. z = ++x: pre-increment, so x first becomes x = 7, and that new value is assigned, giving z = 7.

  4. print(x + y + z) uses the current stored values: x = 7, y = 5, z = 7.

Result: x + y + z = 7 + 5 + 7 = 19.

Cross-check: Each increment raises x by 1, so after two increments x rises from 5 to 7 — it does not stay 5. The only value that is captured before an increment is y (the post-increment), which is why y alone keeps the original 5 while both x and z end at 7.

title: Which of the following is wrong about the data types?
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml: Which of the following statements about data types is wrong?

options.label: A
options.html: The number is always positive when the qualifier 'unsigned' is used.

options.label: B
options.html: The number can be positive or negative when the qualifier 'signed' is used.

options.label: C
options.html: The range of values for signed data types is more than that of unsigned data types.

options.label: D
options.html: The leftmost bit in an unsigned data type is used to represent the value.

solution:
Concept

A data type's storage is a fixed number of bits, and that width fixes the total count of distinct values it can hold (2^n for n bits). 'signed' versus 'unsigned' does not change how many values exist — it only changes which values those bit-patterns are mapped to. A signed type dedicates one bit to recording the sign, so its patterns are split between negative and non-negative numbers; an unsigned type uses every bit for magnitude, so all its patterns are non-negative.

Applying it to each statement

Read every statement and decide whether it is true; the question asks for the one that is wrong.

  • Unsigned removes the sign, so it cannot store a negative number (it stores non-negative values) — a true description of unsigned behaviour.

  • Signed reserves a sign bit, so it can store both negative and non-negative numbers — a true description of signed behaviour.

  • Signed has a greater range than unsigned — this is the claim to test below.

  • In unsigned, no bit is reserved for a sign, so every bit (including the leftmost) carries magnitude — a true description.

Cross-check the range claim with an 8-bit example

  1. Unsigned 8-bit uses all 8 bits for magnitude: it covers 0 to 255, so its maximum value is 255.

  2. Signed 8-bit (two's complement) spends one bit on the sign: it covers -128 to 127, so its maximum value is 127.

  3. Both hold 2^8 = 256 distinct values, but the unsigned maximum (255) is larger than the signed maximum (127).

Result

Because the unsigned type reaches a higher maximum value for the same width, the statement claiming that signed types have a larger range than unsigned types does not hold. The other three statements correctly describe how signed and unsigned types behave.

title: The symbol shown in the figure represents flowchart.

title: In flowchart, the diamond-shaped symbol (used to represent conditional statements)
subject: C Programming
bodyHtml: In a flowchart, the diamond-shaped symbol (used to represent conditional statements) has:

options.label: A
options.html: two incoming lines and two outgoing lines

options.label: B
options.html: one incoming line and one outgoing line

options.label: C
options.html: one incoming line and two outgoing lines

options.label: D
options.html: two incoming lines and one outgoing line

solution:
Concept

A flowchart symbol's number of connectors is fixed by its logical role. A decision (conditional) symbol — drawn as a diamond — tests a single condition and must split the flow into separate paths, one for each possible outcome of that test (e.g. true/false).

Application

A condition has exactly two mutually exclusive outcomes, so the diamond receives the flow from one place and sends it to two:

  • one incoming line: control reaches the diamond from a single preceding step.

  • two outgoing lines: after the condition is evaluated, flow leaves along one of two branches, typically labelled 'Yes'/'No' (or 'True'/'False').

Contrast

Checking the other counts against the decision role:

  • 'two incoming lines' would describe a merge/connector joining paths, not a test that originates a branch.

  • 'one incoming line and one outgoing line' is a straight-through process/action box (rectangle): it transforms data but makes no choice.

  • 'two incoming lines and one outgoing line' merges paths into one — the opposite of branching, so it cannot encode a condition.

Only one entry feeding two exits matches a conditional test: one incoming line and two outgoing lines.
