title: Consider the following specifications of disk: An average seek time
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Consider the following specifications of a disk:

An average seek time of 5ms
A 6000 RPM rotational speed
A 10 MB/s average transfer rate
1 ms of overheads (controller)

How long does it take to read a 512B sector?
solution:
Given:

  • Average seek time = 5 ms

  • Rotational speed = 6000 RPM → rotation period = 60 / 6000 = 0.01 s = 10 ms

  • Average rotational delay = half a rotation = 10 ms / 2 = 5 ms

  • Transfer rate = 10 MB/s → transfer time for 512 B = 512 / (10,000,000) s = 0.0000512 s = 0.0512 ms (≈ 0.05 ms)

  • Controller overhead = 1 ms

Total time = average seek + average rotational delay + transfer time + controller overhead

Total time = 5 ms + 5 ms + 0.0512 ms + 1 ms = 11.0512 ms ≈ 11.05 ms

Therefore, reading a 512 B sector takes approximately 11.05 ms.

title: Total time to access disk block is given by the
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Total time to access a disk block is given by the –
solution:
The total time to access a disk block consists of three components:

  1. Seek Time

    • Time taken to move the read/write head to the desired track

  2. Rotational Delay (Latency)

    • Time waiting for the required sector to rotate under the head

  3. Transfer Time

    • Time taken to actually read/write the data

Therefore:

Total Access Time=Seek Time + Rotational Delay + Transfer Time

title: Consider the disk which has average seek time of ns
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Consider the disk which has average seek time of 32 ns and rotational rate of 360 rpm (round per minute). Each track of the disk has 512 sectors, each of size 512 bytes.

What is the time taken to read four continuous sectors? And What is the data transfer rate?
solution:
Correct answer: Option B (0.0843 s and 1536 KBps)

Important unit note:
KBps means kilobytes per second. Kbps means kilobits per second. Since each sector size is given in bytes, the computed transfer rate is in KBps. If converted to bits, 1536 KBps = 1536 × 8 = 12288 Kbps.

Given:
Average seek time = 32 ns ≈ 0 s
Rotational speed = 360 rpm = 6 rotations/second
Sectors per track = 512
Sector size = 512 bytes

Track size:
512 sectors × 512 bytes = 262144 bytes = 256 KB

Average rotational latency:
One rotation takes 1/6 s.
Average rotational latency = (1/2) × (1/6) = 1/12 = 0.0833 s

Transfer time for 4 continuous sectors:
Data to read = 4 × 512 bytes = 2048 bytes = 2 KB
Transfer rate = 6 × 256 KB/s = 1536 KBps
Transfer time = 2/1536 s ≈ 0.00130 s

Total time:
Seek time + average rotational latency + transfer time
≈ 0 + 0.0833 + 0.00130
≈ 0.0846 s, represented by the closest option 0.0843 s.

Therefore, the intended answer is 0.0843 s and 1536 KBps.

title: Which of the following is the major part of time
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Which of the following is the major part of time taken when accessing data on the disk ?
solution:
Concept: The total time to access data on a disk is made up of several distinct delays that happen before the transfer itself: seek time (the read/write head physically moving to the correct track), rotational latency (waiting for the target sector to rotate under the head), and settle time (a brief pause for head vibration to damp out once it reaches the track). Because seek time involves mechanically repositioning the actuator arm — a comparatively slow, physical motion covering anywhere from one to hundreds of cylinders — it is typically the largest of these components, often several times longer than rotational latency and orders of magnitude longer than settle time.

Application: For this question, the head must first travel to the target track before any reading or writing can start, and that mechanical travel consistently takes longer (commonly several milliseconds) than the roughly half-a-revolution wait for rotational latency or the sub-millisecond settle time. This is exactly why disk-access-time analysis (and standard OS/COA references) identifies this head-positioning delay as the dominant, major part of total disk access time.

Cross-check — why the other listed timings are not the major part:

  • Settle time is only the microsecond-scale pause for head vibration to damp once positioning is done — a small fraction of the total, not the major part.

  • Rotational latency is bounded purely by the disk's spin speed (on average, half a revolution) — a real delay, but one that doesn't involve any mechanical repositioning, so it is generally smaller.

  • Waiting time (queueing time) is the delay a request spends waiting in a scheduling queue before the disk even starts servicing it — that is a contention/scheduling concept external to the disk's own physical access-time components, so it cannot itself be counted as part of the disk's access time.

title: Consider the following statements: Comparing the time taken for single
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Consider the following statements:
S₁: Comparing the time T₁ taken for a single instruction on a pipelined CPU with time T₂ taken on a non-pipelined but identical CPU we can say that T₁ ≤ T₂.
S₂: The performance of pipelined processor suffers if the pipeline stages have different delays.
Which of the following option is correct?

options.label: D
options.html: None of S₁ or S₂ is correct

solution:
S₁ is false (not necessarily true).

  • Pipelining improves throughput, not necessarily the latency of a single instruction. The latency of one instruction in a pipelined CPU equals the sum of stage delays plus any pipeline-register overhead. A non-pipelined (monolithic) implementation does the whole work in one cycle whose delay might equal the same sum without the register overhead. Thus a pipelined instruction can have equal or larger latency, not necessarily smaller. So the claim T1≤T2T_1 \le T_2T1​≤T2​ is not guaranteed.

S₂ is true.

  • If pipeline stages have different delays, the clock period must accommodate the slowest stage; faster stages idle waiting for the clock. This increases the cycle time and reduces pipeline throughput (performance), so performance suffers.

Final answer: S₁ — False, S₂ — True.

title: Consider the program which was made to run on two
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Consider the program which was made to run on two different machines the machine 2 results 30% speeder however the CPI is increased by 25%. If the clock frequency of the machine 1 is 2 MHZ what is the clock frequency of machine 2?
solution:
• Machine 2 is 30% faster than Machine 1 (i.e., performance2 = 1.3 × performance1).

  • CPI on Machine 2 is 25% higher than Machine 1: CPI2 = 1.25 × CPI1.

  • Clock frequency of Machine 1: f1 = 2 MHz.

  • Find clock frequency f2 of Machine 2.

Definitions and relations

  • Execution time T = IC × CPI / f (IC = instruction count; same for both machines).

  • Performance ∝ 1 / T.

  • Given performance2 = 1.3 × performance1 ⇒ T2 = T1 / 1.3.

Compute ratio T2/T1 using the execution-time formula: T2/T1 = (IC·CPI2 / f2) / (IC·CPI1 / f1) = (CPI2 / CPI1) · (f1 / f2)

Set equal to 1/1.3: (CPI2 / CPI1) · (f1 / f2) = 1 / 1.3

Rearrange to solve for f2: f2 / f1 = 1.3 × (CPI2 / CPI1)

Substitute CPI2 / CPI1 = 1.25: f2 / f1 = 1.3 × 1.25 = 1.625

Therefore: f2 = 1.625 × f1 = 1.625 × 2 MHz = 3.25 MHz

Quick numeric check

Assume IC = 1 and CPI1 = 1 for simplicity:

  • T1 = 1 / 2 = 0.5 (time units)

  • CPI2 = 1.25 → T2 = 1.25 / 3.25 ≈ 0.384615

  • T1 / T2 ≈ 0.5 / 0.384615 = 1.3 ⇒ performance2 is 30% higher ✔

Answer: f2 = 3.25 MHz.

title: What is the main advantage of instruction pipelining
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: What is the main advantage of instruction pipelining?
solution:
Instruction pipelining splits instruction execution into stages (fetch, decode, execute, memory access, write-back) and overlaps these stages across successive instructions, so a new instruction enters the pipeline before the previous one has fully finished. Because several instructions are in flight simultaneously, the average time to complete each instruction, and hence overall throughput, improves, even though a single instruction's total latency through all stages is unchanged.

Applying this here: the direct effect of that stage-overlap is a lower average completion time per instruction, which is exactly what makes 'Reduced instruction execution time' the main advantage being asked about.

Checking each other option against this by value:

  • Increased memory access speed, a cache/RAM property, not something pipelining's stage-overlap changes.

  • Improved data transfer rate, a bus/interconnect bandwidth property, again unrelated to overlapping instruction stages.

  • All of these, fails because the two properties above are unaffected by pipelining, so grouping them with execution time overstates pipelining's effect.

title: The process when processor fetch or decode another instruction during
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: The process when processor fetch or decode another instruction during the execution of current instruction is called
solution: Pipelining overlaps stages of instruction processing. While one instruction is executing, another instruction can be fetched or decoded.

title: The right sequence of suboperations that are performed in arithmetic
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
The right sequence of suboperations that are performed in arithmetic pipeline is –
A. Align the mantissas
B. Add or subtract the mantissas
C. Normalize the result
D. Compare the exponents
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Correct sequence: Compare the exponents → Align the mantissas → Add or subtract the mantissas → Normalize the result.

  1. Step 1 — Compare the exponents: Determine which operand has the larger exponent so you know which mantissa (if any) must be shifted.

  2. Step 2 — Align the mantissas: Shift the mantissa of the operand with the smaller exponent to match the larger exponent (align the binary points).

  3. Step 3 — Add or subtract the mantissas: Perform the arithmetic on the aligned mantissas.

  4. Step 4 — Normalize the result: If the result's mantissa is out of range, shift it and adjust the exponent accordingly; then apply rounding if required.

Why other orders fail:

  • Trying to add or subtract before aligning produces incorrect results because the binary points do not match.

  • Normalizing before the arithmetic makes no sense because normalization depends on the arithmetic result.

  • Alignment requires knowing which exponent is larger, so exponent comparison must come first.

title: Consider stage pipeline system. Assume that there is no cycle
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Consider a 5-stage pipeline system. Assume that there is no cycle-time overhead of pipelining. An application is executing on this pipeline system. What is the speedup achieved with respect to non-pipelined execution if 42% of the instructions incur 2 pipeline stall cycles? ______ (up to 2 decimal places)
solution:
Concept: In an ideal pipeline one instruction completes every clock cycle, so the pipelined machine needs 1 cycle per instruction and every stall cycle adds directly on top of it: CPIpipelined = 1 + (average stall cycles per instruction). A non-pipelined machine has no overlap at all — it must finish all k stage-cycles of one instruction before starting the next — so CPInon-pipelined = k.

When pipelining adds no cycle-time overhead, both machines run at the same clock period, so the cycle counts alone decide the ratio: Speedup = k / (1 + average stall cycles per instruction).

Application: substituting the data given in this question.

  1. Pipeline depth k = 5, so the non-pipelined machine spends 5 cycles per instruction.

  2. Average stall cycles per instruction = (fraction of instructions that stall) × (penalty per stall) = 0.42 × 2 = 0.84.

  3. CPIpipelined = 1 + 0.84 = 1.84 cycles per instruction.

  4. Speedup = 5 / 1.84 = 2.7173913…

Cross-check: multiplying back, 1.84 × 2.71739 ≈ 5.00, which recovers the non-pipelined cycle count, so the ratio is consistent. The value also lies inside the expected bounds — with no stalls at all the speedup would be the full depth 5, and 0.84 stall cycles per instruction pull it down to roughly 2.72.

Answer: Speedup = 5 / 1.84 = 2.7173913… . Expressed to two decimal places this is 2.71 if the remaining digits are truncated and 2.72 if they are rounded, so both 2.71 and 2.72 are accepted.

New CPI = (1 + 0.2 * 3)

title: Five-stage pipeline has stage delays of and nanoseconds. The registers
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: A five-stage pipeline has stage delays of 50, 60, 80, 75, 80 and 70 nanoseconds. The registers that are used between the pipeline stages have a delay of 10 nanoseconds each.The total time to execute 500 independent instructions on this pipeline, assuming there are no pipeline stalls, is _______ nanoseconds.
solution:
Answer: 45360 ns

  • Given: number of pipeline stages k = 5, number of instructions n = 500.

  • Stage delays provided: 50, 60, 80, 75, 80, 70 ns. The cycle time is set by the slowest stage plus the register delay.

  • Compute cycle time tp = max(stage delays) + register delay = 80 ns + 10 ns = 90 ns.

  • Total time = (number of stages + number of instructions - 1) × tp = (k + n - 1) × tp = (5 + 500 - 1) × 90 = 504 × 90.

  • Compute: 504 × 90 = 45360 ns. (Or equivalently pipeline fill = 5 × 90 = 450 ns, plus remaining 499 × 90 = 44910 ns; total = 450 + 44910 = 45360 ns.)

title: The instruction pipeline of processor has the following stages: IF
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: The instruction pipeline of a processor has the following stages: IF (instruction fetch), ID (instruction decode), OF (operand fetch), PO (perform operation), and WB (write back). The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for every instruction. Consider a sequence of 50 instructions. In the PO stage 20 instructions take 3 clock cycles each, 18 instructions take 2 clock cycles, and the remaining 12 instructions take 1 clock cycle each. Assume that there are no data hazards and no control hazards. The number of clock cycles required for completion of execution of the sequence of instructions is ?
solution:
Key idea: The pipeline has 5 stages (IF, ID, OF, PO, WB). If every stage took 1 cycle, the total cycles for 50 instructions would be number of instructions + number of stages - 1 = 50 + 5 - 1 = 54.

Variable PO stage: each instruction i spends k_i cycles in the PO stage. Each instruction that needs more than 1 cycle in PO causes (k_i - 1) extra stall cycles.

  • Total PO cycles = 20×3 + 18×2 + 12×1 = 60 + 36 + 12 = 108.

  • Total extra stall cycles = (sum of PO cycles) - (number of instructions) = 108 - 50 = 58.

  • Total cycles = base pipeline cycles (54) + total stalls (58) = 112 cycles.

Answer: 112 cycles.

title: Consider the two processors and MIPS Million instruction per second)
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Consider the two processors P1 and P2. MIPS ( Million instruction per second) of P1 is 100 and P2 is 200. Which of the following options are correct?
solution:
Short answer: Using only MIPS you cannot determine which processor is better.

  • Key formula for performance: Execution time = (Instruction count × CPI) / Clock rate

  • Relation to MIPS: MIPS = (Instruction count / Execution time) / 10^6, which can also be expressed as Clock rate / (CPI × 10^6) for a given instruction mix. MIPS depends on CPI and the instruction mix, so it can be misleading across different architectures or compilers.

  • Illustrative example: Suppose P1 reports 100 MIPS and P2 reports 200 MIPS. If a program requires 50 million instructions on P1, its execution time on P1 = 50,000,000 / (100,000,000 instructions/sec) = 0.5 s. If the same task requires 200 million instructions on P2, its execution time on P2 = 200,000,000 / (200,000,000 instructions/sec) = 1.0 s. Here P1 is faster despite lower MIPS, showing why MIPS alone is inadequate.

  • Recommendation: Compare processors using execution time for representative workloads or standardized benchmarks (for example SPEC). When needed, use Instruction count, CPI, and clock rate together to compute and compare real performance.

title: Non-pipeline processor has clock rate MHz and an average CPI
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: A non-pipeline processor has a clock rate 4 MHz and an average CPI of 5. An upgrade to the processor introduces 5 stage pipeline. However, due to internal delay the clock rate of the new processor has to be reduced to 3 MHz. What is the speed-up of pipeline over non-pipeline?
solution:
Step-by-step calculation:

  1. Non-pipeline processor:

    Cycle time = 1 / clock rate = 1 / 4 MHz = 0.25 μs. Execution time per instruction = average CPI × cycle time = 5 × 0.25 μs = 1.25 μs.

  2. Pipelined processor (5-stage):

    New cycle time = 1 / 3 MHz = 0.333... μs. With an ideal pipeline throughput of one instruction per cycle, execution time per instruction ≈ 1 × 0.333... μs = 0.333... μs.

  3. Speed-up calculation:

    Speed-up = execution time (non-pipeline) / execution time (pipeline) = 1.25 μs / 0.333... μs = 3.75.

    If the pipeline cycle time is approximated as 0.33 μs, the quoted approximate value becomes about 3.78; the exact ratio using repeating decimal 0.333... is 3.75.

Final answer: The speed-up of the pipelined processor over the non-pipelined one is 3.75 (which lies within the provided range 3.7–3.78).

title: Consider an instruction pipeline with four stages and each with
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Consider an instruction pipeline with four stages (S1, S2, S3 and S4), each with a combinational circuit only. The pipeline registers are required between each stage and at the end of the last stage. Delays for the stages and for the pipeline registers are as given in the following figure:

What is the approximate speed up of the pipeline in steady state under ideal conditions when compared to the corresponding non-pipeline implementation?
solution:
Concept

In a pipeline whose stages take unequal amounts of time, the pipeline's clock cycle time is fixed by the slowest stage plus the delay of the pipeline register (latch) that follows it -- every stage must wait for the longest stage to finish and for the register to latch its output before the next cycle can start. Once the pipeline is full (steady state), one instruction completes every clock cycle, so the achievable speedup over a non-pipelined implementation is the ratio of the total non-pipelined execution time to this single pipeline clock cycle time.

Application

  1. Non-pipelined execution time per instruction is the sum of all four stage delays: 5 + 6 + 11 + 8 = 30 ns.

  2. The slowest stage is S3, with a delay of 11 ns.

  3. The pipeline clock cycle equals the slowest stage delay plus the pipeline-register delay: 11 + 1 = 12 ns.

  4. Steady-state speedup equals the non-pipelined time divided by the pipeline clock cycle: 30 / 12 = 2.5.

Cross-check

If all four combinational stages had the same delay d, the speedup with a 1 ns register overhead would be 4d / (d + 1), approaching the stage-count ceiling of 4 only when the register overhead is negligible relative to d. Here the unequal stage delays make the 11 ns stage the bottleneck, and substituting the actual 12 ns clock interval gives 30 / 12 = 2.5.

title: Consider three different processors executing the same instruction set. has

solution:
To find the number of instructions executed by each processor, use the formula:

Instructions = (Clock Rate × Time) / CPI

Given: Time = 10 seconds

For P1:

Clock Rate = 3 GHz = 3 × 10⁹ Hz

CPI = 1.5

Instructions = (3 × 10⁹ × 10) / 1.5 = 30 × 10⁹ / 1.5 = 20 × 10⁹

For P2:

Clock Rate = 2.5 GHz = 2.5 × 10⁹ Hz

CPI = 1.0

Instructions = (2.5 × 10⁹ × 10) / 1.0 = 25 × 10⁹

For P3:

Clock Rate = 4 GHz = 4 × 10⁹ Hz

CPI = 2.2

Instructions = (4 × 10⁹ × 10) / 2.2 = 40 × 10⁹ / 2.2 ≈ 18.18 × 10⁹

Thus, the number of instructions executed are: 20 × 10⁹, 25 × 10⁹, and 18.18 × 10⁹.

CPI = 1.5

CPI = 1.0

P3 के लिए:

क्लॉक दर = 4 GHz = 4 × 10⁹ Hz

CPI = 2.2

title: Which of the following statements with respect to K-segment pipelining
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Which of the following statements with respect to K-segment pipelining are true?

(A)  Maximum speedup that a pipeline can provide is 𝑘 theoretically

(B)  It is impossible to achieve maximum speed up 𝑘 in 𝑘-segment pipeline

(C)  All segments in pipeline take same time in computation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Final answer: The correct true statements are the one that says the theoretical maximum speedup of a k-segment pipeline is k and the one that says it is impossible (in practical terms) to achieve that maximum. The claim that all segments take the same time is not generally true.

Explanation:

  • Theoretical upper bound on speedup: For a k-segment pipeline, the ideal (theoretical) maximum speedup is k. This assumes perfectly balanced stages, no pipeline register overhead, no hazards, and a steady stream of independent tasks.

  • Practical achievability: In practice, achieving the ideal k-fold speedup is effectively impossible because of register and latch overhead, imbalanced stage latencies, pipeline hazards (data, control, structural), and the cycles needed to fill and drain the pipeline. So the statement that reaching the theoretical maximum is impossible is intended in a practical sense and is correct as a real-world observation.

  • Equal-stage-time claim: It is not generally true that all segments take the same time. Equal stage durations are an ideal design goal to maximize utilization, but real pipelines often have unequal stage latencies; the slowest stage determines the pipeline clock period and thus limits speedup.

  • Conclusion: The theoretical maximum is k (true), the practical impossibility of reaching that maximum is a valid real-world statement (true in practice), and the claim that all segments take equal time is false in general. Therefore the correct selection includes the first two statements only.

title: Consider an instruction pipeline as shown below: program having instructions
subject: CO & Architecture

Consider an instruction pipeline as shown below:


A program having 80 instructions is executed in the pipelined processor. Instruction I6 is the unconditional jump instruction and branch address is known after EX stage. The time needed to complete the execution of the program if the branch target address is 78th instruction is ________________ns
solution:
Key idea: the pipeline has four stages (IF, ID, EX, MO) and buffer delays between stages. The clock period must accommodate the longest stage plus its following buffer delay.

  • Compute clock period: the EX stage is 6 ns and the buffer after EX is 3 ns, so clock period = 6 + 3 = 9 ns.

Which instructions actually execute: the program executes instructions 1 through 6, then instruction 6 is an unconditional jump to instruction 78, so the executed instructions are 1–6 and 78–80, a total of 9 instructions.

Cycle count and branch penalty:

  • Base pipeline cycles without hazards = number of executed instructions + (pipeline depth − 1) = 9 + 3 = 12.

  • Because the branch (instruction 6) is resolved in the EX stage, two following instructions (the ones fetched in the two cycles between the branch IF and branch EX) are speculatively fetched and must be flushed, adding a penalty of 2 cycles.

  • Total cycles = base cycles + branch flush penalty = 12 + 2 = 14 cycles.

Total time = total cycles × clock period = 14 × 9 ns = 126 ns.

title: Assume an instruction mix of conditional branches, unconditional branches, all
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Assume an instruction mix of 20% conditional branches, 5% unconditional branches, 75% all others. 65% of the conditional branches are taken. We have a 5-stage pipeline where branch target locations are computed in the 2nd stage and branch conditions in the 4th stage. Assume no other sources of pipeline stalls.

We want to decide whether to implement "predict taken" or "predict not taken" for branch prediction for this machine. For "predict not taken", even unconditional branches are assumed not taken. Which of the following is correct?

options.label: A
options.html: "predict taken" is better for this machine.

options.label: B
options.html: "predict not taken" is better for this machine.

options.label: C
options.html: For "predict taken" branch predictions, CPI is the 1.54

options.label: D
options.html: For "predict not taken" branch predictions, CPI is the 1.54

solution:
We compare the two static strategies by computing the average branch penalty per instruction and the resulting CPI (base CPI = 1).

Predict taken:

  • Taken conditional branches (20% * 65%): resolved at stage 2 → 1-cycle penalty when predicted taken: 0.2 * 0.65 * 1 = 0.13

  • Not-taken conditional branches (20% * 35%): mispredicted until the condition is resolved at stage 4 → 3-cycle penalty: 0.2 * 0.35 * 3 = 0.21

  • Unconditional branches (5%): treated as taken → 1-cycle penalty: 0.05 * 1 = 0.05

Total branch penalty = 0.13 + 0.21 + 0.05 = 0.39, so CPI = 1 + 0.39 = 1.39.

Predict not taken:

  • Taken conditional branches (20% * 65%): mispredicted until stage 4 → 3-cycle penalty: 0.2 * 0.65 * 3 = 0.39

  • Not-taken conditional branches (20% * 35%): correctly predicted → 0-cycle penalty: 0.2 * 0.35 * 0 = 0

  • Unconditional branches (5%): mispredicted (predicted not taken) → 3-cycle penalty: 0.05 * 3 = 0.15

Total branch penalty = 0.39 + 0 + 0.15 = 0.54, so CPI = 1 + 0.54 = 1.54.

Conclusion: predicting taken is better because it gives a lower CPI (1.39) than predicting not taken (1.54).

Final answer: 154 ms

  • Clock period: The pipeline clock must accommodate the slowest stage. The stage delays are IF=5 ms, ID=3 ms, EX=5 ms, MEM=7 ms, WB=6 ms, so the clock period T = 7 ms.

  • Number of executed instructions: The program executes instructions I1 through I6 (6 instructions) and then jumps to I19 through I28 (10 instructions), so total executed instructions = 6 + 10 = 16.

  • Branch penalty: The branch at I6 resolves (target becomes available) in the EX stage. Two instructions that were fetched after the branch (the ones currently in IF and ID) must be flushed, producing a 2-cycle penalty.

  • Total cycles = base cycles + penalty = 20 + 2 = 22 cycles. Total time = 22 × 7 ms = 154 ms.

Assumption: "No branch prediction" is interpreted as fetching the next sequential instruction each cycle until the branch is resolved, and if the branch is taken the wrongly fetched instructions are flushed when the branch resolves in EX.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q90
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: In a 5-stage pipeline, branch is resolved in EX stage. If branch frequency = 15% and misprediction penalty = 2 cycles, what is pipeline CPI?
solution:
Concept: In a pipelined processor achieving an ideal one-cycle-per-instruction throughput, the baseline CPI is 1. Any instruction that forces the pipeline to stall raises the effective CPI above this baseline. A branch instruction whose outcome is not known until a later pipeline stage forces the pipeline to stall for a fixed number of cycles on every occurrence; this fixed per-branch stall cost is the branch (misprediction) penalty. Since the item supplies only a single branch frequency and a single fixed penalty value, with no separate misprediction-rate figure, the standard convention for this class of numerical is to apply that penalty uniformly to every branch instruction encountered. Averaged over all instructions, the overall CPI is: CPI = Ideal CPI + (Branch Frequency x Branch Penalty).

Application:

  1. Identify the given quantities: ideal CPI = 1 (one instruction completes per cycle in a hazard-free pipeline); branch frequency = 15% = 0.15 (fraction of instructions that are branches); branch penalty = 2 cycles (stall cycles incurred per branch, since the outcome is known only in the EX stage).

  2. Compute the average stall contributed by branch instructions: Stall per instruction = Branch Frequency x Branch Penalty = 0.15 x 2 = 0.30 cycles.

  3. Add this stall contribution to the ideal CPI: CPI = 1 + 0.30 = 1.30.

Cross-check with a per-100-instruction count: out of 100 instructions, 15 are branches; each branch adds 2 stall cycles, giving 15 x 2 = 30 extra cycles; total cycles = 100 (base) + 30 (stalls) = 130 cycles; CPI = total cycles / total instructions = 130 / 100 = 1.3, which matches the formula result.

Hence, the pipeline CPI is 1.3.

title: Which of the following is/are cause hazard in pipelined CPU
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Which of the following is/are cause hazard in pipelined CPU ?

options.label: A
options.html: 2 consecutive instruction and both need to read memory at same time.

options.label: C
options.html: 2 consecutive instructions and one instruction uses the result of previous instruction.

solution:
Explanation: The following situations each cause a hazard in a pipelined CPU:

  • Structural hazard — Two consecutive instructions both trying to read memory at the same time compete for the same hardware resource (for example, a single memory port), causing a stall or conflict. Mitigations include adding memory ports or caches, or stalling.

  • Control hazard — An instruction that contains a jump or branch creates uncertainty about the next instruction address until the branch is resolved. Common solutions include branch prediction, delayed branches, and pipeline flushing or stalling.

  • Data hazard — When one instruction uses the result produced by the immediately preceding instruction, a read-after-write dependency arises. Mitigations include forwarding/bypassing, instruction scheduling, or inserting stalls.

Conclusion: The three described situations (simultaneous memory reads, a jump/branch instruction, and an instruction using a previous result) are all causes of pipeline hazards. Therefore, the statement that none of these is a hazard is incorrect.

title: Consider the following set of instructions executed for program to
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Consider the following set of instructions executed for a program to be accomplished.

How many anti data dependencies and true data dependencies are present in the above instructions?
solution:
Concept

A pipeline's true (data) dependency — RAW, Read-After-Write — exists whenever an instruction reads a register whose value was produced by the nearest earlier instruction that wrote it; every such governed read counts as one dependency. An anti-dependency — WAR, Write-After-Read — exists whenever a later instruction writes a register that an earlier instruction had already read, because letting that write happen too soon would return the earlier instruction the wrong value. Both types are counted per read-write pair across the full instruction sequence, not merely between instructions that sit next to each other.

Application

First list every register this six-instruction sequence reads from and writes to:

Instruction

Reads

Writes

I1: STORE M[100], R1

R1

—

I2: MOV R2, M[700]

—

R2

I3: DIV R1, R2, R1

R2, R1

R1

I4: ADD R2, R1, R2

R1, R2

R2

I5: STORE M[500], R2

R2

—

I6: STORE M[200], R1

R1

—

Anti-dependencies (WAR) — an earlier instruction reads a register that a later instruction then writes:

  1. R1: I1 reads R1, and I3 later writes R1 — one anti-dependency.

  2. R2: I3 reads R2, and I4 later writes R2 — one anti-dependency.

  3. No other earlier-read-then-later-write pair exists for R1 or R2 across the sequence, so the anti-dependency count is 2.

True dependencies (RAW) — an instruction reads a register whose most recent value came from an earlier write:

  1. R1 is written only once, by I3. Every later read of R1 traces back to that same write, since nothing else writes R1 afterward: I4 reads R1 after I3, and I6 reads R1 after I3 — 2 true dependencies from R1.

  2. R2 is written twice — first by I2, then later by I4. I3 reads R2 before I4's write, so I3's value comes from I2. I4 also reads R2 as a source operand before its own write takes effect, so that read also comes from I2. After I4 writes R2, I5 reads R2, so I5's value comes from I4 — 3 true dependencies from R2 (two tracing to I2, one to I4).

  3. Total true dependencies = 2 (from R1) + 3 (from R2) = 5.

Cross-check

Confirm by tracing each register's own access timeline in program order:

Register

Access sequence (in program order)

R1

I1 reads → I3 reads and writes → I4 reads → I6 reads

R2

I2 writes → I3 reads → I4 reads and writes → I5 reads

Reading this timeline left to right and drawing an edge from every write to every read that follows it before the next write reproduces the same 5 true dependencies found above; drawing an edge from every read to the next write that follows it reproduces the same 2 anti-dependencies. A narrower check that only compares directly consecutive instructions (I1-I2, I2-I3, I3-I4, I4-I5, I5-I6) misses non-adjacent pairs — such as I1's read of R1 reaching all the way to I3's write, or I2's write of R2 still governing I4's read — and undercounts both totals.

So this instruction sequence contains 2 anti-dependencies (WAR) and 5 true dependencies (RAW).

title: The following assembly code is to be executed in 3-stage
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
The following assembly code is to be executed in a 3-stage pipelined processor with hazard detection and resolution in each stage. The stage are IF, OF (one or more as required) and execution (including write-back operation). What are the number of possible RAW, WAW and WAR hazards in the execution of the code.
Instruction Meaning
I₁: Inc R₀ R₀ ← (R₀) + 1
I₂: Mul ACC, R₀ ACC ← (ACC) × (R₀)
I₃: Store R₁, ACC R₁ ← (ACC)
I₄: Add ACC, R₀ ACC ← (ACC) + (R₀)
I₅: Store M, ACC M ← (ACC)
solution:
Final answer: RAW = 5, WAW = 1, WAR = 2

Definitions:

  • RAW (read after write): a later instruction reads a location that an earlier instruction writes.

  • WAW (write after write): two instructions write the same location; the order of writes matters.

  • WAR (write after read): an earlier instruction reads a location that a later instruction writes.

Identify hazards by location touched (R0, ACC, R1, M) and by instruction order.

RAW hazards (5 pairs):

  • I1 → I2 (I1 writes R0; I2 reads R0)

  • I1 → I4 (I1 writes R0; I4 reads R0)

  • I2 → I3 (I2 writes ACC; I3 reads ACC)

  • I2 → I4 (I2 writes ACC; I4 reads ACC)

  • I2 → I5 (I2 writes ACC; I5 reads ACC)

WAW hazards (1 pair):

  • I2 → I4 (both write ACC)

WAR hazards (2 pairs):

  • I3 → I4 (I3 reads ACC; I4 later writes ACC)

  • I2 → I4 (I2 reads ACC as source and I4 later writes ACC)

Notes: The same instruction pair can appear in more than one hazard category when one instruction both reads and writes the same location (for example, the pair I2 → I4 is both a RAW and a WAW/WAR interaction depending on which access is considered). The final tallies under the pipeline timing given are RAW = 5, WAW = 1, WAR = 2.

I6: Branch if R4 != 0

Let A be the number of true (RAW) dependencies, B the number of anti (WAR) dependencies, and C the number of output (WAW) dependencies. Find A + B + C.
solution:
CONCEPT

A dependency is identified from the read and write order of the same register. RAW means a later instruction reads a value written earlier; WAR means a later instruction writes a register read earlier; WAW means two instructions write the same register.

The scope here is register dependencies within one loop iteration. Memory-location dependencies and loop-carried dependencies are therefore outside the count.

APPLICATION

First record the register read/write sets:

Instruction

Registers read

Registers written

I1

R2

R1

I2

R1

R1

I3

R2, R1

None

I4

R2

R2

I5

R4

R4

I6

R4

None

  1. RAW dependencies: I1 → I2 through R1; I2 → I3 through R1; and I5 → I6 through R4. Hence A = 3.

  2. WAR dependencies: I1 reads R2 before I4 writes R2, and I3 reads R2 before I4 writes R2. Hence B = 2.

  3. WAW dependency: I1 and I2 both write R1. Hence C = 1.

  4. Therefore, A + B + C = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

  • R2 contributes two WAR relationships.

  • R4 contributes one RAW relationship. In particular, I5 → I6 is not WAR because I6 reads R4 and does not write it.

solution:
Dependencies present in the program: write-after-write (WAW), read-after-write (RAW), and write-after-read (WAR).

title: Which of the following are NOT true in pipelined processor
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Which of the following statements are NOT true in a pipelined processor?

I. Bypassing can handle all RAW hazards.

II. Register renaming can eliminate all register-carried WAR hazards.

III. Control hazard penalties can be eliminated by dynamic branch prediction.
solution:
CONCEPT

Pipeline-hazard remedies address different constraints. Forwarding resolves a RAW dependency only when the producer value is available in time; register renaming removes name dependences such as WAR; branch prediction speculates on control flow but must recover from a wrong prediction.

APPLICATION

  1. Statement I: A load-use pair can need a stall because the loaded value becomes available after the immediately following consumer needs its execute-stage input. Therefore, bypassing does not handle every RAW hazard.

  2. Statement II: Assigning a new physical destination to a later write prevents it from overwriting the architectural name before an earlier read. Thus register renaming can eliminate register-carried WAR hazards.

  3. Statement III: Dynamic prediction reduces average control stalls, but a misprediction still flushes younger speculative instructions and redirects fetch. Therefore, it cannot eliminate every control-hazard penalty.

CROSS-CHECK / CONTRAST

  • I and II only combines one unsupported universal claim with one valid renaming claim.

  • II and III only combines the valid renaming claim with an unsupported prediction claim.

  • All of these would require the renaming claim to be false, although renaming removes the relevant name dependence.

Result: Statements I and III are NOT true, so the answer is I and III only.

title: The expression for machine which is having m-bit instructions that
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: A machine uses m-bit instructions and supports zero-address, one-address, and two-address formats. Its memory contains 2p words. Assume every m-bit pattern encodes one of these instructions. If r, s, and t denote the numbers of zero-address, one-address, and two-address instructions, respectively, which expression relates m, p, r, s, and t?
solution:
Concept

A fixed m-bit instruction word has 2m possible bit patterns. A p-bit address field has 2p possible values.

Independent address fields multiply the number of complete instruction patterns, while an instruction format with no address field contributes one pattern per opcode.

Application

  1. Because the memory has 2p words, one memory address requires p bits.

  2. Each of the r zero-address instructions has no address field, so this class contributes r patterns.

  3. Each of the s one-address instructions can use any of 2p addresses, so this class contributes s · 2p patterns.

  4. Each of the t two-address instructions has two independent p-bit addresses, so this class contributes t · 2p · 2p = t · 22p patterns.

  5. These disjoint classes fill the m-bit instruction space, giving 2m = r + s · 2p + t · 22p.

Cross-check

When p = 0, each address field has one possible value and the expression reduces to 2m = r + s + t. This matches the one-word-memory case, where address fields add no extra choices.

Result: 2m = r + s · 2p + t · 22p.

title: Processor has integer registers and floating point registers It uses
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: A processor has 16 integer registers (R0, R1, …, R15) and 64 floating point registers (F0, F1, …, F63). It uses a 2-byte instruction format. There are four categories of instructions: Type-1, Type-2, Type-3 and Type-4.Type-1 category consists of two instructions, each with 2 integer register operands and one floating point register operand(2Rs+1F). Type-2 category consists of eight instructions, each with 2 integer register operands (2Rs). Type-3 category consists of 14 instructions, each with one integer register operand and one floating point register operand (1R+1F). Type-4 category consists of N instructions, each with a floating point register operand (1F). The maximum value of N is ________.
solution:
Instruction size = 2−byte.

So, the total number of instruction encodings = 2^16

There are 16 possible integer registers, so no. of bits required for an integer operand = 4

There are 64 possible floating-point registers, so no. of bits required for a floating-point operand = 6

Type-1 instructions:

There are 2 type-1 instructions and each takes 2 integer operands and one floating point operand

No. of encodings consumed by type-1 = 2 × 2^4 × 2^4 × 2^6 =2^15.

Type-2 instructions:

There are 8 type-2 instructions and each takes 2 integer operands.

No. of encodings consumed by Type-2 instructions = 8 × 2^4 x 2^4 = 2^11.

Type-3 instructions:

There are 14 type-3 instructions and each takes one integer operand and one floating point operand.

No. of encodings consumed by Type-3 instructions = 14 × 2^4 x 2^6 = 14336.

So, no. of encodings left for Type-4 = 2^16 − (2^15 + 2^11 + 14336) = 16384.

Since type-4 instructions take one floating point register, no. of different instructions of Type-4 = 16384 / 64 = 256.

title: The number of machine instruction(s) required by accumulator CPU to
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: The number of machine instruction(s) required by accumulator CPU to execute X = (A + B)C is/are_______ format and addressing mode
solution:
Answer: 4 instructions.

Explanation:

  1. Load A into the accumulator: ACC ← M[A]. This brings A from memory into the accumulator (1 instruction).

  2. Add B to the accumulator: ACC ← ACC + M[B]. This performs the addition using the accumulator (1 instruction).

  3. Multiply the accumulator by C: ACC ← ACC * M[C]. This performs the multiplication using the accumulator (1 instruction).

  4. Store the result into X: M[X] ← ACC. Write the final result from the accumulator back to memory (1 instruction).

Total instructions = 4 (load, add, multiply, store).

Addressing mode: each instruction uses direct memory references (for example M[A], M[B], M[C], M[X]) with operations performed via the accumulator.

title: Processor has distinct instructions and general purpose registers. 32-bit instruction
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: A processor has 200 distinct instructions and 50 general purpose registers. A 32-bit instruction word has an opcode, two register operands and an immediate operand. The number of bits available for the immediate operand field is__________
solution:
Solution:

  • Determine opcode bits: To encode 200 distinct instructions requires ceil(log2(200)) = 8 bits.

  • Determine register operand bits: There are 50 registers, so each register operand needs ceil(log2(50)) = 6 bits.

  • Compute immediate field bits: Instruction word is 32 bits. Subtract opcode (8 bits) and two register operands (6 bits each): 32 - (8 + 6 + 6) = 12 bits.

  • Answer: 12 bits are available for the immediate operand.

title: Consider system with 16-bit instructions and 6-bit addresses. If there
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Consider a system with 16-bit instructions and 6-bit addresses. If there are 14 2-address instructions and 100 1-address instructions, what is the maximum number of 0-address instructions that can be formulated?
solution:
Concept

In an expanding-opcode design, an instruction format with fewer address fields frees bits that can extend the opcode.

If an address field has a bits, each unused opcode prefix at one level expands into 2a longer prefixes at the next level.

Application

  1. A 2-address instruction uses 2 × 6 = 12 address bits, leaving 16 − 12 = 4 opcode bits. Therefore, there are 24 = 16 possible 2-address opcode prefixes.

  2. Fourteen of these prefixes are assigned, so 16 − 14 = 2 prefixes remain available for expansion.

  3. For a 1-address instruction, each remaining prefix gains 6 opcode bits. This produces 2 × 26 = 128 possible 1-address opcode patterns.

  4. After assigning 100 of those patterns, 128 − 100 = 28 expanded prefixes remain for 0-address instructions.

  5. A 0-address instruction uses all 16 bits as opcode bits, so each of the 28 remaining prefixes gains the final 6 bits: 28 × 26 = 28 × 64 = 1792.

Cross-check

The complete 16-bit code space has 216 patterns. The assigned instructions consume 14 × 212 + 100 × 26 patterns, leaving 216 − 14 × 212 − 100 × 26 = 1792 patterns.

Therefore, the maximum number of 0-address instructions is 1792.

Solution: 896 is the correct answer
Instruction size = 24 bit
Address bit = 6 bit
No. of 3 address instruction = 50
No. of 2 address instruction = N

Total no. of instructions = 3-address instruction + 2-address instruction

2^24 = 50 2^18 + N 2^12
2^24 = 2^12 (50 2^6 + N)
2^12 = 50 64 + N
N = 4096 - 3200
N = 896

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q96
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: What is the main reason for separating the opcode field and addressing mode field in instruction formats?
solution:
An instruction format is described as orthogonal when its constituent fields, the operation code and the addressing-mode specifier, can each take any of their permitted values independently of one another. That property is achieved by keeping the addressing-mode information in a field of its own rather than folding it into the opcode field, so that changing the addressing mode used with an operation never requires changing, or reserving a new value for, the opcode itself.

  1. Take a single operation, say ADD, and list the addressing modes it might need to access its operand: immediate, register, direct, and indirect.

  2. If the opcode field alone had to encode both the operation and the addressing mode, four separate opcode values, one per mode, would be needed just for ADD, and the same multiplication would repeat for every other operation in the set.

  3. Placing the addressing-mode choice in its own field instead lets one ADD opcode combine with any addressing-mode value the field can hold, since the two fields are decoded and interpreted independently, though a particular architecture may still choose to disallow a specific combination for practical reasons.

  4. This same independence, applied across the whole opcode field rather than only to ADD, is what makes the instruction set orthogonal: operation and addressing mode can be varied and combined largely independently, rather than every valid combination needing its own reserved opcode.

Checking this against the alternative explanations confirms the fit: the overall instruction length is set by the total bit budget and by techniques such as opcode expansion, not by whether the addressing-mode bits sit in their own field; control-unit complexity instead depends primarily on the implementation, such as whether the decode logic is hardwired or microprogrammed, with field organization only a secondary factor, so orthogonality rather than reduced complexity is the primary reason for the separate field; and variable-length opcodes commonly arise from opcode-expansion techniques that trade opcode bits against operand bits within a fixed-width format, unrelated to separating out the addressing-mode field. Only the independence argument, orthogonality, is what a separate addressing-mode field directly produces.

title: The immediate addressing mode can be used for Loading internal
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
The immediate addressing mode can be used for

1. Loading internal registers with initial values

2. Perform arithmetic or logical operation on data contained in instructions

Which of the following is true?

options.label: D
options.html: Immediate mode refers to data in cache

solution:
What immediate addressing means: The operand value is encoded directly in the instruction as a constant (an immediate), so the CPU uses that value without fetching it from memory or cache.

Common uses:

  • Load a register with an initial constant value, for example: LOAD R1, #100.

  • Use an immediate operand in arithmetic or logical instructions, for example: ADD R2, R2, #5.

Limitations: Immediate fields are limited by the instruction format, so very large constants may require loading from memory in multiple steps.

Summary: Both statements are correct. Immediate addressing is used both to load registers with initial values and to perform arithmetic or logical operations using constants encoded in instructions.

title: Consider 24-bit hypothetical processor. The memory is byte-addressable. Assume there
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Consider a 24-bit hypothetical processor. The memory is byte-addressable. Assume there is a program having 300 instructions. Let the program is required to be stored in the memory with a starting address of 300(in decimal), then the value of PC at the last instruction of the program is ______.
solution:
Key facts: The processor is 24-bit so each instruction occupies 24 bits = 3 bytes. Memory is byte-addressable.

  • Number of instructions = 300.

  • Size per instruction = 24 bits = 3 bytes.

  • Total program size = 300 × 3 = 900 bytes.

  • Starting address = 300 (decimal).

Program Counter semantics: The PC holds the address of the next instruction. After the last instruction has been placed/executed, the PC will point to the address immediately after the program.

Therefore PC after the last instruction = starting address + total program size = 300 + 900 = 1200

title: In which of the following modes will the operand value
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: In which of the following modes will the operand value be stored in the relevant register?
solution:
Answer: Register Mode

Reason: In register mode the instruction specifies a particular processor register that holds the operand value. The operand is located directly in that register rather than in memory or within the instruction encoding.

  • Immediate mode: The operand is encoded as a constant inside the instruction itself. It is not provided by a register unless a separate instruction moves it there.

  • Direct addressing: The instruction contains a memory address where the operand resides; the CPU accesses memory to read or write the operand.

  • Register indirect addressing: A register holds the memory address of the operand. The register points to memory where the operand is stored — the register contains an address, not the operand value itself.

  • Decrement (autodecrement) addressing: The register is adjusted (decremented) to form a pointer for memory access; the operand is accessed in memory using that pointer rather than being simply stored in the register.

Summary: Of the modes listed, only register mode places the operand value directly in a processor register; the other modes involve the operand being a constant in the instruction or being located in memory (with registers used as addresses or adjusted pointers).

title: Data-memory references for indirect addressing
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Consider a three-address machine. Each instruction occupies one memory word. Count only data-memory references made while executing the operands; do not count instruction fetches.

Use these addressing conventions:

  • Ri: register-direct operand; the value is already in register Ri, so it needs no data-memory reference.

  • (Ri): register-indirect operand; Ri holds the effective address, so reading or writing the memory operand needs one data-memory reference.

  • (A): direct memory operand at address A; accessing it needs one data-memory reference.

  • @(A): memory-indirect operand; first read M[A] to obtain the effective address, then access the operand at that address, so a read needs two data-memory references.

For an instruction OPCODE A, B, C, execution means A ← B OPCODE C. Determine the total number of data-memory references needed to execute both instructions:

MUL (R1), (R2), @(5000H)
DIV R3, R2, (800H)
solution:
Concept

An addressing mode determines where an operand is found and therefore how many data-memory accesses it costs. Register-direct operands cost 0; direct and register-indirect memory operands cost 1 per read or write; a memory-indirect read costs 2 because the processor first obtains the effective address from memory and then reads the operand.

For a three-address instruction A ← B OPCODE C, count every memory read of B and C and every memory write to A. Instruction fetches are excluded here.

Application

  1. For MUL (R1), (R2), @(5000H), read the source (R2) once: 1 reference.

  2. Read the source @(5000H): one reference reads the pointer stored at address 5000H and a second reference reads the operand at that pointer: 2 references.

  3. Write the product to destination (R1): 1 reference. Thus MUL uses 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 references.

  4. For DIV R3, R2, (800H), R2 is read directly from a register and R3 is written directly to a register, so neither costs a data-memory reference. Reading direct operand (800H) costs 1 reference. Thus DIV uses 1 reference.

Cross-check

Listing the actual memory operations gives three reads and one write for MUL, plus one read for DIV. Therefore, the total is 4 + 1 = 5 data-memory references.

Result: 5

title: Consider the following statements: in the immediate addressing mode the

Therefore both statements are true.

title: Digital computer has memory unit with bits per word. The
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: A digital computer has a memory unit with 32 bits per word. The instruction set consists of 110 different operations. All instructions have an operation code part (opcode) and two address fields: one for a memory address and one for a register address. This particular system includes eight general-purpose and eight user-addressable registers. Registers may be loaded directly from memory, and memory may be updated directly from the registers. Direct memory-to-memory data movement operations are not supported. Each instruction stored in one word of memory. How many bits are needed for the memory address?
solution:
Answer: 21 bits.

Reasoning:

  • Opcode bits: need enough distinct codewords for 110 operations, so bits = ceil(log2(110)) = 7 bits.

  • Register field bits: there are eight general-purpose and eight user-addressable registers, totaling 16 registers, so bits = ceil(log2(16)) = 4 bits.

  • Memory address bits: each instruction is 32 bits and contains an opcode (7 bits) and one register address field (4 bits), so memory-address bits = 32 - 7 - 4 = 21 bits.

Conclusion: The memory address field requires 21 bits, which allows 2^21 addressable memory words.

title: Two word instruction is stored in the memory is designated

bodyHtml: Two word instruction is stored in the memory is designated by the symbol p. and address field of instruction is stored at p+1 designated by Q.The operand used during the execution of instruction is stored at an address symbolized as S, if direct addressing is used find correct relation
solution:
Answer: S = Q

Explanation: In direct addressing the address field of the instruction contains the effective address of the operand.

  • The instruction is at location p, and the address field (the value that gives the operand address) is stored at p+1 and denoted by Q.

  • Because the address field itself holds the operand address in direct addressing, the operand address S equals Q.

  • For contrast: in indirect addressing the address field holds a pointer to the operand address, which would give S = M[Q].

Short example: if the address field value (Q) is 200, then the operand is stored at address 200, so S = Q = 200.

title: Computer uses memory unit of words of bits each. binary
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: A computer uses a memory unit of 512𝐾 words of 32 bits each. A binary instruction code is stored in one word of the memory. The instruction has four parts: an addressing mode field to specify one of the two-addressing mode (direct and indirect), an operation code, a register code part to specify one of the 256 registers and an address part. How many bits are there in addressing mode part, opcode part, register code part and the address part?
solution:
Key facts: memory = 512K words, word size = 32 bits, instruction stored in one word, addressing modes = 2, registers = 256.

  • Address part: number of words = 512K = 512 × 1024 = 2^9 × 2^10 = 2^19, so address needs 19 bits.

  • Register code part: to specify 256 registers requires log2(256) = 8 bits.

  • Addressing mode part: two addressing modes (direct and indirect) require log2(2) = 1 bit.

  • Opcode part: remaining bits = 32 − (addressing mode + register code + address) = 32 − (1 + 8 + 19) = 4 bits.

Final bit allocation: addressing mode = 1 bit, opcode = 4 bits, register code = 8 bits, address = 19 bits.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - December 2010 - source row 34
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: The register or main-memory location that contains the effective address of an operand is known as:
solution:
Concept

In computer architecture, an effective address is the address of the memory location containing the operand to be accessed.

In indirect addressing, an instruction names a register or memory location whose stored value is that effective address. That address-holding register or memory location is a pointer.

Application

The stem describes a register or main-memory location that contains the operand’s effective address. This definition corresponds to a pointer.

Contrast

  • Pointer: stores an address that is used to access the referenced operand indirectly.

  • Special location: a generic phrase, not the standard computer-architecture term for an address-holding location.

  • Index register: contributes an index to an address calculation, commonly represented as EA = A + (R); it need not contain the complete effective address by itself.

  • None of these: does not apply because pointer is an offered standard term.

Therefore, the required term is pointer.

title: Which of the following addressing mode is/are suitable for program
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Which of the following addressing mode is/are suitable for program relocation at run time?
solution:
PC-relative addressing: This mode calculates the effective address by adding a displacement value to the Program Counter (PC). This makes instructions refer to memory locations relative to their current position in the program. Since the offset is relative, the program can be loaded at any memory location without needing modifications.

Base register addressing: Here, the address is computed by adding a displacement value to the contents of a specific base register. This base register often points to the starting address of a program segment. Similar to PC-relative addressing, instructions refer to memory locations relative to a base point, allowing relocation without code changes.

Absolute addressing: The address of the operand is directly embedded in the instruction. If the program is relocated, these addresses would need to be updated.
Indirect addressing: The address of the operand is stored in another memory location. While the instruction itself might not need modification, runtime resolution of the indirect address adds complexity during relocation.

title: Consider the following micro operation The given micro operation depicts…..
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Consider the following micro operation

The given micro operation depicts….. ?
solution:
Answer: Indirect cycle — this sequence resolves an indirect address to the actual (direct) address.

Key steps:

  • MAR ← IR[address]: Copy the address field from the instruction register into the memory address register to set up the memory read.

  • MBR ← memory: Read from memory at the address in MAR into the memory buffer register; this fetches the actual operand address (the indirect target).

  • IR[address] ← MBR[address]: Update the instruction's address field with the fetched address so the instruction now contains the direct/effective address.

Why this is the indirect cycle: The micro-operations explicitly fetch an address from memory and store it into the instruction's address field. That action resolves indirection (turning an indirect address into a direct address), which defines the indirect cycle. This is different from a normal instruction fetch (which only loads the instruction), the execute phase (which performs the operation), and interrupt handling (which deals with control transfer and state saving).

title: The reason of sequencing the micro- instruction in the control
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: The reason of sequencing the micro- instruction in the control memory is

options.label: C
options.html: Sequential control memory access for specific operation task

solution:
Key idea: sequencing microinstructions lets the control memory deliver the micro-operations for a specific machine instruction one after another.

  • Simplifies the control unit: fetching microinstructions in sequence reduces the complexity of control flow logic needed to execute an operation.

  • Enables implicit next-address generation: a next-address generator can increment or step through addresses to fetch the following microinstruction without requiring explicit address calculations for every step.

  • Facilitates implementing a specific operation as a sequence of micro-operations, making microprogram control flow straightforward and easier to design.

  • Note common misconceptions: sequencing does not by itself make control words smaller or reduce control memory size; those depend on microinstruction encoding and count.

Therefore, the primary reason for sequencing microinstructions in control memory is to allow sequential control memory access for a specific operation task, simplifying the control unit and enabling implicit next-address generation.

title: Choose the correct statement from the following regarding RISC and
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml: Choose the correct statement from the following regarding RISC and CISC architectures.

options.label: D
options.html: RISC architecture support variable size instruction format.

solution:
Answer: CISC supports variable-size instruction formats.

Why this is correct:

CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) architectures commonly use variable-length instruction encodings. This allows the instruction set to include many complex operations and multiple addressing modes, so instructions can occupy different numbers of bytes depending on their operands and addressing.

  • Benefit: Variable-length instructions can make code more compact and express complex actions in single instructions.

  • Trade-off: Decoding variable-length instructions is more complex and can complicate pipelining and instruction fetch.

Contrast with RISC:

  • RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) designs favor a small, simple instruction set with fixed-size instruction formats (commonly a consistent width such as 32 bits).

  • This fixed-size format simplifies decoding and supports efficient pipelining and parallel execution, at the cost of needing more instructions to express some complex operations.

Summary:

  1. CISC: variable-length instruction formats, larger/complex instruction set, more addressing modes.

  2. RISC: fixed-size instruction formats, smaller/simpler instruction set, pipeline-friendly design.

title: Match List with List II: List List II CISC Processors
subject: CO & Architecture
bodyHtml:
Match List - I with List - II:

List - I

List - II

A. CISC Processors

I. Operating system controls overall assignment of tasks

B. RISC Processors

II. Uses explicit parallelism

C. EPIC Processors

III. These possess so many processing features, making the job of machine language programmers easier

D. Multicore Processors

IV. Have a small instruction set
solution:
Understanding Processor Type Matching

This question requires matching different types of computer processors with their defining characteristics. Let's break down each processor type and its corresponding feature:

CISC Processors Explained

CISC stands for Complex Instruction Set Computer. Processors of this type are designed with a large number of instructions, including complex ones that can perform multiple low-level operations in a single command. This complexity aims to make the job of machine language programmers easier by reducing the number of instructions needed for a task.

Therefore, CISC processors match with characteristic III: "These possess so many processing features, making the job of machine language programmers easier".

RISC Processors Explained

RISC stands for Reduced Instruction Set Computer. In contrast to CISC, RISC processors feature a smaller, highly optimized set of instructions. These instructions are typically simpler and execute faster, often within a single clock cycle. The focus is on simplicity and speed.

Therefore, RISC processors match with characteristic IV: "Have a small instruction set".

EPIC Processors Explained

EPIC stands for Explicitly Parallel Instruction Computing. This architecture aims to improve performance by exposing parallelism explicitly. The compiler plays a crucial role in identifying and grouping independent instructions into bundles that can be executed in parallel. This differs from architectures where parallelism might be hidden or managed implicitly.

Therefore, EPIC processors match with characteristic II: "Use explicit parallelism".

Multicore Processors Explained

Multicore processors are processors that contain two or more independent central processing units (cores) on a single chip. In such systems, managing which task runs on which core is essential for efficient operation. This task assignment is primarily handled by the operating system, which schedules threads and processes across the available cores.

Therefore, Multicore processors match with characteristic I: "Operating system controls overall assignment of tasks".

Correct Processor Matching Summary

Based on the explanations, the correct matching between List - I (Processor Type) and List - II (Characteristics) is as follows:

List - I (Type of Processor)

List - II (Characteristics)

A. CISC Processors

III. These possess so many processing features, making the job of machine language programmers easier

B. RISC Processors

IV. Have a small instruction set

C. EPIC Processors

II. Use explicit parallelism

D. Multicore Processors

I. Operating system controls overall assignment of tasks

Thus, the correct option is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

solution:
Concept

A language-processing system converts a program written in a source language into a target form that a computer can execute.

For a compiled language, a compiler performs this translation before the program runs; later stages may assemble, link, and load the generated code.

Application

A C program begins as human-readable source code. The compiler translates that source into lower-level target code, which is then processed into an executable machine-language program.

Contrast

  • An editor is used to enter and modify the source-code text.

  • An operating system manages hardware resources and provides the environment in which programs run.

  • A compiler is the language processor that translates C source code into target code before execution.

Therefore, C programs are converted with the help of a compiler.

title: Which of the following is the CORRECT sequence of the
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following is the CORRECT sequence of the phases of a compiler?

options.label: A
options.html: Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, intermediate code generation, code generation, code optimization

options.label: B
options.html: Lexical analysis, intermediate code generation, syntax analysis, code generation, code optimization

options.label: C
options.html: Lexical analysis, intermediate code generation, syntax analysis, code optimization, code generation

options.label: D
options.html: Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, intermediate code generation, code optimization, code generation

solution:
Concept: A compiler transforms source code into target code through a fixed pipeline in which each phase consumes the previous phase's output: lexical analysis (characters -> tokens), syntax analysis (tokens -> parse tree), semantic analysis (type/scope checking), intermediate code generation (parse tree -> intermediate representation), code optimization (improves that intermediate representation), and code generation (intermediate representation -> target code).

Application: Trace the five phases named in this item through that dependency chain:

  1. Lexical analysis must run first, since it is the only one of these phases that reads raw source characters.

  2. Syntax analysis runs next, because it needs the token stream that lexical analysis produces.

  3. Intermediate code generation runs after syntax analysis, since it needs a validated parse tree as its input.

  4. Code optimization runs after intermediate code generation, because it improves the intermediate representation that phase produces.

  5. Code generation runs last, emitting target code from the optimized intermediate form.

So the order among these five phases is: lexical analysis, syntax analysis, intermediate code generation, code optimization, code generation.

Cross-check: Reading the dependencies backward confirms it: code generation needs the optimized intermediate code, which needs the unoptimized intermediate code from intermediate code generation, which needs the parse tree from syntax analysis, which needs the tokens from lexical analysis -- a clean chain with no phase used before its input exists. (Semantic analysis, which normally sits between syntax analysis and intermediate code generation, is not among the phases listed in these options.)

title: Which of the following phase of the compiler, gathers type
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following phase of the compiler, gathers type information and saves it in either the syntax tree or the symbol table, for subsequent use during intermediate code generation?
solution:
Concept: In the classical compiler pipeline, the front end has three distinct phases: lexical analysis (produces tokens), syntax analysis (uses those tokens to build a parse tree/AST reflecting only grammatical structure), and semantic analysis (checks static semantics -- most importantly type compatibility -- and attaches the derived type information onto the syntax tree's nodes or into the symbol table). Only after this annotation is the tree "type-complete" and ready for the back end (intermediate code generation, optimization, code generation) to consume.

Application: The question asks for the phase that "gathers type information and saves it in either the syntax tree or the symbol table, for subsequent use during intermediate code generation." That is precisely the semantic analyzer's job: it type-checks expressions and declarations, then records the results (types) on tree nodes or in symbol-table entries so intermediate code generation can use them.

Cross-check: Contrasting with the alternatives confirms this: syntax analysis only builds the parse tree's structure and has no notion of types; lexical analysis only produces a token stream (identifiers, keywords, operators) with no structural or type information at all; and "Code Analyzer" is not one of the standard compiler phases. So among the given options, only the semantic analyzer performs the type-gathering role described.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q37
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Under the usual introductory classification, which errors can a C compiler point out while parsing source code?
solution:
Concept

A compiler checks source code against the formal rules of a programming language. During parsing, it compares the token sequence with the language grammar; a grammar violation is classified as a syntax error.

Application

For example, if a closing brace is missing, the token sequence cannot form the grammatical structure required for the program. The parser therefore produces a diagnostic before normal translation can complete.

Contrast

  • Semantic errors concern meaning-related constraints, such as incompatible types or undeclared identifiers; diagnostic coverage depends on the language rules and compiler analysis.

  • Logical errors arise when a grammatically valid program expresses the wrong algorithm and usually appear through incorrect output or behaviour.

  • None of these would deny that grammar violations are diagnosed during parsing.

Cross-check

GCC provides the -fsyntax-only mode specifically to check source code for syntax errors without continuing to later compilation stages.

Result

Therefore, in the stated introductory parsing context, the compiler points out syntax errors.

title: The compiler for high level language that runs on one
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: The compiler for high level language that runs on one machine and produces code for another machine is called
solution: A compiler that runs on one machine and produces code for another different machine is known as a cross compiler. This differs from native compilers which generate code for the same architecture they run on.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 34
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: When a compiler runs on one machine and produces code for a different machine, this is called:
solution:
Concept

A compiler is classified by the relationship between the machine it runs on (the host) and the machine its generated code is meant to run on (the target). When host and target are the same platform, the compiler is called a native compiler. When host and target differ — for example, compiling on an x86 desktop to produce code for an ARM microcontroller — the compiler is called a cross compiler, and the process is cross compilation.

Application

  1. The stem describes exactly this host/target split: "runs on one machine" (the host) and "produces code for a different machine" (the target).

  2. This host-vs-target distinction is precisely the definition of a cross compiler, so the compiling activity described is cross compilation.

  3. "One pass" and "two pass" instead classify a compiler by how many times it scans/traverses the source program during translation — a completely different axis (single-machine internal architecture) that says nothing about whether the host and target machines differ.

  4. Since cross compilation directly and uniquely matches the stem's description, "None of the above" does not apply.

Cross-check

Real-world toolchains confirm this: GCC and LLVM/Clang both document a "host" (machine running the compiler) and a "target" (machine the generated code runs on); when a single toolchain build sets these to different architectures, its documentation calls it a cross compiler. This matches option 0 and rules out the pass-count based distractors, which describe an unrelated property of the compiler.

title: Compiler for high level language that runs on one machine
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: A compiler for a high level language that runs on one machine and produces code for a different machine is called :
solution:
Correct answer: Cross compiler

Explanation:

  • A cross compiler runs on a host machine with one architecture and operating system but generates executable code for a different target machine or architecture. This is useful when the target environment cannot run a compiler (for example, compiling code for an embedded ARM device on a desktop x86 machine).

  • Optimizing compiler: Applies transformations (such as loop unrolling, constant folding) to produce faster or smaller code for the same target; not specifically about compiling for a different machine.

  • One-pass compiler: Processes the source code in a single pass (reads input once) to perform translation; this describes the compilation strategy, not whether the output targets a different machine.

  • Multipass compiler: Performs multiple passes over the source or intermediate representations to handle complex analyses and optimizations; again, this concerns compilation stages rather than host/target differences.

title: The action of parsing the source program into proper syntactic
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: The action of parsing the source program into proper syntactic classes is known as
solution:
Correct answer: Syntax analysis

Explanation: Parsing the source program into proper syntactic classes means taking the stream of tokens and organizing them according to the grammar to produce a parse tree or abstract syntax tree. This process is called syntax analysis (parsing).

  • Lexical analysis: converts the raw character stream into tokens (identifiers, keywords, literals, operators). It does not build syntactic structures.

  • Syntax analysis: takes tokens and builds the parse tree or abstract syntax tree according to the language grammar. This is the parsing step.

  • Semantic analysis: checks meaning, type correctness, and scope on the AST produced by syntax analysis.

  • Intermediate code generation: produces an intermediate representation from the AST for optimization or final code generation; this occurs after parsing and semantic checks.

Therefore, the correct term for 'parsing the source program into proper syntactic classes' is syntax analysis.
