title: Which analyser will erase the white space and other components
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which analyser will erase the white space and other components from the identified source program?
solution:
Correct answer: Lexical analyser (scanner).

What the lexical analyser does:

  • Removes whitespace and comments that are not significant for parsing.

  • Scans the source code and groups characters into tokens (identifiers, keywords, literals, operators, separators).

  • Produces a stream of tokens and passes them to the syntactic analyser (parser).

  • Detects lexical errors (for example, invalid tokens or unterminated literals) and may record identifier occurrences for later phases.

What it does not do:

  • It does not perform syntax checking — that is the job of the syntactic analyser (parser).

  • It does not perform semantic checks like type checking — that is the job of the semantic analyser.

title: Which of the following grammar can be used to design
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following grammar can be used to design Lexical Analysis of Compiler?
solution:
Lexical analysis describes tokens using regular languages, so regular grammar is exactly sufficient and is the natural formalism for specifying a lexer.

However, any language that can be generated by a regular grammar can also be generated by more powerful grammars such as context-free or recursively enumerable grammars. This means those grammars can, in principle, also be used to describe the same token languages, even though they are more expressive than needed.

  • Regular grammar: directly models regular expressions and finite automata used in lexical analyzers, and is the minimal and standard choice for token specification.

  • Context-free grammar: strictly more powerful than regular grammars and capable of generating all regular languages, so it can describe the same token patterns but is typically used for syntax analysis rather than for implementing lexical analyzers.

  • Recursively enumerable grammar: the most general class in the Chomsky hierarchy and also capable of generating all regular languages, so it can in principle specify lexical tokens, but is far more complex than necessary and not used in practical lexer design.

In summary, all three listed grammars can theoretically be used to design the lexical analysis phase because they can generate regular languages, but regular grammar is the appropriate and sufficient choice for real lexical analyzers, while context-free and recursively enumerable grammars are unnecessarily powerful for this purpose.

title: Which of the following is an input to lexical analysis?
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following is an input to lexical analysis?
solution:
Correct answer: Sequence of characters

Explanation:

  • What lexical analysis takes as input: The raw source code represented as a sequence of characters. The lexical analyzer reads these characters and groups them into meaningful tokens.

  • What lexical analysis produces: A sequence of tokens (identifiers, keywords, literals, operators, punctuation, etc.), which are then passed to the syntax analyzer (parser).

  • Why other choices are incorrect: A parse tree is generated by the parser during syntax analysis, not by the lexical analyzer; therefore it is not an input to lexical analysis. "None of these" is incorrect because there is a valid input listed: the sequence of characters.

title: Consider the following statements: Lexical analysis check the grammar rules
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Question :
Consider the following statements:
S1: Lexical analysis check the grammar rules and construct a parser tree.
S2: Lexical analysis break the source code into tokens and generates a token stream.
Which of the following is correct?
solution:
S1: Incorrect. Lexical analysis does not check grammar rules or construct a parser tree. It is responsible for breaking the source code into tokens (lexemes) and generating a token stream. Checking grammar rules and constructing a parse tree are tasks handled by the syntax analysis phase (parser).

S2: Correct. This statement accurately describes the role of lexical analysis. It scans the source code, identifies tokens, and generates a stream of tokens for further processing by the parser.

title: Which of the following option having lexical error?
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following option having lexical error?
solution:
Correct answer: int 3y12 — variable names cannot start with a digit, so this is a lexical error.

  • int float; The lexer produces valid keyword tokens ('int' and 'float'). The issue is that a keyword is being used where an identifier is expected, which the parser will flag as a syntactic error. This is not a lexical error.

  • int x = 2; This is lexically and syntactically correct: tokens include the keyword 'int', identifier 'x', the assignment symbol, numeric literal '2', and a semicolon. It is a valid declaration with initialization.

  • int 3y12 This is a lexical error because identifiers cannot begin with a digit. The lexer cannot form a valid identifier token from '3y12' (it would start a numeric token at '3' and then encounter letters), so lexical analysis fails.

  • int y = y/0; This is lexically and syntactically valid: tokens and structure are correct. Division by zero is a runtime or semantic error (undefined behavior in many languages), not a lexical error. Also beware of using y before it is initialized.

title: Which of the following can be used to design Lexical
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following can be used to design Lexical Analysis?
solution:
Answer: DFA can be used for designing a lexical analyzer.

Why this is correct: Lexical patterns are regular languages, and regular expressions that describe tokens can be converted into deterministic finite automata for efficient scanning.

  • Write regular expressions for each token type.

  • Convert each regular expression to an NFA (nondeterministic finite automaton).

  • Apply subset construction to obtain an equivalent DFA, then minimize it if desired.

  • Use the resulting DFA(s) to implement the lexer for fast, deterministic token recognition.

Why the other choices are not suitable: Pushdown automata are for context-free languages and parsing nested structures; a parse tree is the parser's output showing syntactic structure, not a machine for token recognition.

title: Regular expression is used in Lexical analysis to model The
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Regular expressions are used in lexical analysis to model the following. Consider the two statements:

S1: The structure of tokens, with fixed-length identifiers included.

S2: The structure of lexemes, with variable-length identifiers included.

Which of the above statement(s) is/are False?
solution:
Concept: In lexical analysis a token is an abstract category (a token name, optionally with an attribute) whose valid spellings are described by a pattern written as a regular expression. A lexeme is the concrete sequence of characters in the source program that matches such a pattern. A pattern like letter(letter|digit)* deliberately matches strings of many different lengths, so neither tokens nor the identifiers they cover are restricted to one fixed length.

Applying this to the statements:

  • S1 says the structure of tokens has fixed-length identifiers. Tokens are pattern-based categories, and the identifier pattern letter(letter|digit)* matches names of any length, so identifiers are not fixed-length. S1 is therefore false.

  • S2 says the structure of lexemes has variable-length identifiers. Lexemes are the actual matched character strings, and identifier lexemes such as a, sum or counter1 clearly vary in length, so S2 is true.

Cross-check: In the code int value = 3; the lexeme 'value' (five characters) and a lexeme 'x' (one character) are both matched by the same identifier token pattern. One pattern accepting strings of different lengths confirms identifiers are variable-length lexemes, not fixed-length tokens.

Result: Exactly one statement is false, namely S1, while S2 is true.

title: Which of the following cannot be functionality of scanner?
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following cannot be functionality of a scanner?
solution:
Answer: Type checking is not a functionality of the scanner.

Explanation: The scanner (lexical analyzer) only reads characters and groups them into tokens. Type checking requires syntactic and semantic context (such as declarations, scopes and symbol-table information) that become available after parsing and during semantic analysis.

  • Removing white spaces: scanners typically skip or use whitespace only to separate tokens.

  • Token generation: the scanner produces tokens (token type and lexeme) for the parser.

  • Ignoring comments: comments are usually recognized and discarded by the scanner so they do not affect later phases.

Conclusion: Type checking is performed during the semantic analysis phase, not by the scanner.

title: In lexical analysis, pattern is generally described using
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: In lexical analysis, a pattern is generally described using __________.
solution:
In lexical analysis, a pattern is generally described using Regular Expressions (Regex).

How it Works

A lexical analyzer reads the source code character-by-character and groups them into meaningful units called lexemes (like keywords, identifiers, operators, or literals).

  • A Lexeme is the actual text string (e.g., 125, totalCount, if).

  • A Token is the abstract category assigned to that string (e.g., NUMBER, IDENTIFIER, KEYWORD).

  • A Pattern is the descriptive rule that dictates what characters can form a given token.

These patterns are defined mathematically and practically using Regular Expressions. For example:

  • An identifier pattern might be written as: [a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]* (starts with a letter or underscore, followed by any number of alphanumeric characters).

  • A digit/number pattern might be written as: [0-9]+.

During the generation of a compiler, these regular expressions are converted behind the scenes into Finite Automata (specifically Deterministic Finite Automata, or DFAs) to physically execute the matching process on the input text.

title: What is the primary function of LEX in the context
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: What is the primary function of LEX in the context of lexical analysis in compiler design?

options.label: C
options.html: To generate scanners based on regular expressions

solution: LEX is a lexical analyzer generator tool used in compiler construction that takes regular expressions as input to generate efficient scanners (lexical analyzers). Its primary function is to convert source code into a stream of tokens by matching patterns defined via regular expressions. This makes Option C the correct answer because LEX automates scanner generation, handling token recognition and whitespace skipping without manual coding. Option A is incorrect because code optimization occurs in later compiler phases, not lexical analysis. Option B describes YACC or Bison, which handle context-free grammars for parsing, not lexical analysis. Option D is also incorrect as abstract syntax trees are constructed during semantic analysis or parsing, not by LEX. Thus, LEX specifically focuses on tokenization using regular expressions.

title: Which of the following is valid real-world application where Finite
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following is a valid real-world application where a Finite State Machine (FSM) model is appropriately used?

options.label: A
options.html: Managing dynamic memory allocation in operating systems

options.label: D
options.html: Modeling the behavior of lexical analyzers in language processing

solution:
Finite State Machines (FSMs) are computational models ideal for systems that transition between a finite number of states based on inputs. In compiler design, lexical analyzers use FSMs to scan source code character by character and recognize tokens like keywords, identifiers, or operators. Each token type corresponds to a specific state sequence, making FSMs the standard tool for this task.

Option A is incorrect because memory allocation involves complex data structures and dynamic resource management, not simple state transitions.

Option B is wrong since matrix multiplication relies on arithmetic operations and linear algebra algorithms rather than state logic.

Option C involves recursion, which uses a stack data structure for function calls, it is not primarily modeled as an FSM.

Option D is the only valid application where FSMs are appropriately used.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2010 - source row 35
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which compiler component groups a stream of input characters into tokens?
solution:
Concept

Lexical analysis is the first phase of a compiler. It reads the source program as a stream of characters and groups them into tokens such as identifiers, keywords, literals, and operators.

The component that performs lexical analysis is called a scanner or lexical analyzer. Its token stream is then passed to the parser.

Application

The stem asks for the compiler component that groups input characters into tokens. That operation is lexical analysis, so the relevant component is the scanner.

Contrast

  • A parser consumes tokens and organizes them according to the grammar, typically producing a parse tree or syntax tree.

  • A code optimizer transforms an intermediate representation to improve properties such as execution time or code size while preserving program behavior.

  • A code generator translates an intermediate representation into target assembly or machine code.

  • A scanner reads the source character stream and emits lexical units such as identifiers, keywords, literals, and operators.

Result

Therefore, the required compiler component is the scanner.

title: Which of the following features cannot be captured by CFG.
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following features cannot be captured by a CFG.

options.label: C
options.html: Whether a variable is declared before its use

solution:
Key idea: Context-free grammars (CFGs) generate languages by rewriting single nonterminals and can express recursive and nested syntactic structures, but they cannot enforce context-sensitive relationships that require matching or comparing identifiers across distant parts of a program.

  • Syntax of a recursive procedures: Can be captured by a CFG. A production can include the same nonterminal to model recursion, allowing arbitrarily deep recursive structures.

  • Syntax of if-then-else statements: Can be captured by a CFG. Nesting of conditionals is context-free; grammar ambiguities such as the dangling-else are resolved by grammar design or parser rules.

  • Whether a variable is declared before its use: Cannot be captured by a CFG. This is a context-sensitive semantic requirement that needs tracking of declarations and scopes (for example via a symbol table) and comparing identifier identities across different parts of the program.

  • Matching nested parentheses: Can be captured by a CFG. Balanced nesting is the classic example of a context-free language (e.g., S -> '(' S ')' S | ε).

Therefore, the feature that cannot be captured by a CFG is whether a variable is declared before its use.

title: Which grammar will have the left recursive production reference within
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which grammar will have the left recursive production reference within the given string?
solution: Left Recursive Grammar will have the left recursive production reference within the given string. If within the given context-free grammar G, there is a production expression that is in the form of Z->Za; where Z is a non-terminal symbol that has a left recursive production reference and a is a set of terminals, then the grammar is said to be Left Recursive Grammar. Right Recursive Grammar will have the right recursive production reference within the given string. If within the given context-free grammar G, there is a production expression that is in the form of Y->Ya, where Y is a non-terminal symbol that has a right recursive production reference and a is a set of terminals, then the grammar is said to be Right Recursive Grammar.

title: Consider the grammar. SxSxS For string “xxxxxx”, How many total
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the grammar.
S -> SxSxS | ϵ
For a string “xxxxxx”, How many total number of parse tree/s are possible.
solution:
Key insight: each application of the rule S -> S x S x S adds two terminal symbols 'x'.

Step 1: Determine how many times the rule must be applied.

  • Let k be the number of times S -> S x S x S is used. Each use contributes 2 x's, so 2k = 6, giving k = 3.

Step 2: Count the number of distinct parse trees for k = 3.

  • Each internal node of the parse tree has exactly three ordered children (a full ordered ternary tree). The number of such trees with k internal nodes is given by the Fuss–Catalan (generalized Catalan) formula:

  • Number = 1/((3-1)k + 1) * binomial(3k, k) = 1/(2k + 1) * C(3k, k).

  • For k = 3: binomial(9, 3) = 84, and 2k + 1 = 7, so the number = 84 / 7 = 12.

Conclusion: There are 12 distinct parse trees that generate the string "xxxxxx".

title: Find the Ambiguous CFG.
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Find the Ambiguous CFG.
solution:
Answer: The ambiguous grammar is S → 1S | S0 | 2.

Explanation and explicit ambiguity example:

  • Two different leftmost derivations for the string 120 show ambiguity:

  1. Derivation 1 (use production that adds a leading 1 first): S ⇒ 1S ⇒ 1 S0 ⇒ 1 2 0

  2. Derivation 2 (use production that adds a trailing 0 first): S ⇒ S0 ⇒ 1S0 ⇒ 1 2 0

These two derivations produce the same terminal string but have different parse-tree shapes, so the grammar S → 1S | S0 | 2 is ambiguous.

Why the other grammars are unambiguous:

  • Grammar S → 1S | 0S | 2: This generates strings by repeatedly prepending a 1 or 0 until the base 2 is produced (strings of the form (1|0)*2). For any final string, the sequence of prepended symbols is exactly the prefix before 2, so the derivation is unique.

  • Grammar S → 1S0 | 2: This generates strings of the form 1^n 2 0^n. The number of recursive steps n is fixed by the counts of 1s and 0s in the string, so there is exactly one derivation for each string.

Conclusion: S → 1S | S0 | 2 is ambiguous (example: 120). The other two listed grammars are unambiguous.

title: Consider the following context free grammar SS SS*| Which of
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the following context free grammar

S → SS + | SS*| a

Which of the following statement/s is/are correct with respect to the grammar?

S1: The grammar has leftmost derivation for the string aa + a*

S2: The grammar has rightmost derivation for the string aa + a *

S3: Since the grammar has left most derivation as well as right most derivation so it is ambiguous grammar.

options.label: B
options.html: All S1, S2 and S3 are true.

solution:
The leftmost derivation for string aa + a* is:

S = lm ⇒SS* ⇒SS + S* ⇒aS + S* ⇒ aa + S* ⇒ aa + a*

So the statement S1 is true.

The right most derivation for string aa + a* is:

S = r m ⇒ SS* ⇒Sa* ⇒ SS + a* ⇒Sa + a* ⇒ aa + a*

So the statement S2 is true.

Statement S3 is not true i.e., since the grammar has left most derivation as well as right most derivation but it is not capable of generating different parse trees for any

string generated by the grammar and hence it is not ambiguous grammar.

Please note a grammar is ambiguous if it has two different parse tree for any string by using either LMD only or by using either RMD only.

title: Which of the following is true AS aXb aAbS aAb
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Which of the following is true :
G1: S → AS | ε
A → axb | ε
G2: S → aAbS | ε
A → aAb | ε

(a, b and x are all terminal symbols; S and A are the only non-terminals.)

options.label: C
options.html: G1 is LR(1) while G2 is not LR(1)

options.label: D
options.html: There exists a string in the language of G1 for which G1 has an infinite number of parse trees.

solution:
Concept

A grammar is ambiguous when some string in its language has two or more distinct parse trees (equivalently, two or more distinct leftmost derivations) — even one such string is enough, and infinitely many parse trees for one string still counts as ambiguous.

Two grammars are equivalent only if they generate exactly the same language; a single string produced by one but not the other already disproves equivalence.

Every LR(1) grammar admits a unique deterministic parse for each string, so an ambiguous grammar can never be LR(1).

Application

  1. Trace ε through G1: S → ε directly gives one parse tree. S → AS with A → ε then S → ε gives a second, distinct tree. Repeating S → AS any number of times, using A → ε at each step before the final S → ε, gives a further distinct tree for every repetition count — all yielding the same string ε. So G1 already has infinitely many parse trees for ε alone, which makes it ambiguous and confirms that the statement about an infinite number of parse trees for some string of G1 holds.

  2. Compare the languages: in G1, A → axb | ε lets A produce the terminal string "axb" (a, x and b are all terminals), so "axb" belongs to L(G1). G2's productions (S → aAbS | ε, A → aAb | ε) only ever combine the terminals a and b, so no string containing x can ever appear in L(G2). The two languages therefore differ, so the two grammars are not equivalent.

  3. Check G2 for ambiguity: each application of S → aAbS (or A → aAb) nests one matching a…b pair around whatever comes next, and the only way to stop is A → ε or the final S → ε — there is no way to insert an extra ε-step without changing the resulting string, so every string of G2 has exactly one derivation. G2 is therefore not ambiguous, so the claim that both grammars are ambiguous does not hold — only G1 is. For example, take the string "ab": the only way to produce it is S → aAbS with A → ε (contributing nothing between a and b) and the trailing S → ε (contributing nothing after b) — any other choice for A or the trailing S adds more terminal symbols and yields a longer string, so "ab" has exactly one derivation, not two.

  4. Since G1 is ambiguous, and an ambiguous grammar can never be LR(1), G1 cannot be LR(1) — so the claim that G1 is LR(1) while G2 is not fails immediately, regardless of G2's own LR(1) status.

Cross-check

Re-deriving axb in G1 (S → AS → (axb)S, then the trailing S is terminated with S → ε) confirms it belongs to L(G1); and it too has infinitely many parse trees, not just ε — extra A → ε steps can be inserted before or after the A → axb occurrence any number of times without changing the resulting string, exactly like the ε case. This is consistent with G1 being ambiguous purely because of its unrestricted ε-recursion in S → AS, and with G2's strictly nested a…b matching giving every string a unique derivation.

Result: "Both are not equivalent" and "There exists a string in the language of G1 for which G1 has an infinite number of parse trees" are TRUE; "Both are ambiguous" and "G1 is LR(1) while G2 is not LR(1)" are FALSE.

title: Consider the context free grammar SS SS*| Consider the statements:
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the context free grammar G

S → SS + | SS*| b

Consider the statements:

S1: G has leftmost derivation for the string bb + b*

S2: G has rightmost derivation for the string bb + b*

S3: G is ambiguous in nature.

Which of the above statement is/are TRUE?
solution:
Conclusion: Only S1 and S2 are true; S3 is false.

Leftmost derivation for the string bb+b*:

S => SS* => SS+ S* => bS + S* => bb + S* => bb + b*

So statement S1 is true.

Rightmost derivation for the string bb+b*:

S => SS* => Sb* => SS + b* => Sb + b* => bb + b*

So statement S2 is true.

Why the grammar is not ambiguous:

  • Each derivation corresponds to a full binary tree where leaves are the terminal b and internal nodes are binary operators (+ or *).

  • Postfix notation (the form produced by this grammar) encodes that binary tree uniquely, so a given postfix string determines a single parse tree.

  • Therefore there is no string with two different parse trees; the grammar is unambiguous.

So statement S3 is false.

Also The statement S3 is FALSE because the grammar does not generate more than one parse tree for the same valid string.

For ambiguity, a grammar must allow:

  • more than one leftmost derivation, or

  • more than one rightmost derivation, or

  • more than one parse tree

For the string bb+b*, only one valid grouping is possible:

(bb+)b∗

Since no alternative parse structure exists for the same string, the grammar is not ambiguous.

title: Consider the grammar SaS For string “bababab”, the number of
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the grammar G
S→ SaS | b For a string “bababab”, the number of parse tree that can be generated are ______
solution:
Answer: 5 parse trees.

Explanation:

1) Count the number of b terminals in the string "bababab". There are 4 b's.

2) Key insight: Each application of the production S → S a S corresponds to an internal node of a full binary tree, and each terminal b corresponds to a leaf. A parse tree for a string with n leaves (b's) is a full binary tree with n leaves.

3) The number of distinct full binary trees with n leaves is the Catalan number C_{n-1}. For n = 4 leaves, we need C3.

  • Compute C3 using the formula Ck = (1/(k+1)) * binomial(2k, k).

  • C3 = (1/4) * binomial(6, 3) = (1/4) * 20 = 5.

Therefore, there are 5 distinct parse trees for the string "bababab". (The original image shows these five parse trees.)

title: Consider the following statements about the context free grammar {S→SS,
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the following statements about the context-free grammar:

G = { S → SS, S → 01, S → 10, S → ε }

S₁: G is ambiguous.
S₂: G produces all strings with an equal number of 0s and 1s.

Select the correct option:

options.label: C
options.html: S₁ is correct, but S₂ is false.

options.label: D
options.html: S₁ is false, but S₂ is true.

solution:
S₁ is true. The grammar is ambiguous because S → SS allows different groupings of the same concatenation. For example, 011010 can be grouped as (01)(1010) or as (0110)(10), giving different parse trees.

S₂ is false. The grammar generates concatenations of the blocks 01 and 10, along with ε. Therefore every generated non-empty block contributes one 0 and one 1, but not every string with equal numbers of 0s and 1s is generated. For example, 0011 has two 0s and two 1s, but it cannot be formed as a concatenation of 01 and 10 blocks.

Thus S₁ is correct and S₂ is false, so option C is correct.

title: Given the following expression grammar: id Which of the following
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Given the following expression grammar:

E → E * F | F + E | F

F → F − F | id

Which of the following is true?
solution:
Correct answer: - has higher precedence than *.

  • Grammar level matters: Operators generated inside the lower nonterminal F bind more tightly than operators generated at E level.

  • Subtraction: The rule F → F − F defines − within F, so a subtraction expression can behave as a single F when used inside an E production.

  • Multiplication and addition: Both * and + are introduced in productions for E, so they do not bind more tightly than the operator inside F.

Therefore, the true statement among the options is that − has higher precedence than *.

title: Which of the following features cannot be captured by CFG?
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following features cannot be captured by CFG?
solution:
Summary: The features that cannot be captured by a context-free grammar are matching of function arguments and declaration of a variable; these require semantic/context-sensitive checks.

  • Syntax of nested if-else: Can be specified by a CFG. Nested constructs are syntactic and grammars can generate arbitrarily deep nesting; parsing techniques and grammar rules can also address the dangling-else ambiguity.

  • Matching of parentheses: A classic context-free language (balanced parentheses) that a CFG can describe. For example, productions like S -> ( S ) S | ε generate all correctly matched parentheses strings.

  • Matching of function arguments: Cannot be enforced by a CFG alone. Verifying that the number and types of actual arguments match a function's parameter list needs semantic information (symbol tables and type information) and is performed during semantic analysis or via syntax-directed translation.

  • Declaration of a variable: Cannot be enforced by a CFG alone. Ensuring a variable is declared before use and handling scopes requires context-sensitive checks using a symbol table in the semantic analysis phase (for example, with SDT).

title: Which is equivalent CFG without useless symbols for the given
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Which is equivalent CFG without useless symbols for the given grammar:

S → PQ | p , P → p
solution:
A symbol is useful if it is both generating and reachable.

  1. Generating Symbols: S and P derive terminals (S → p, P → p). Q has no production rule, so it is non-generating.

  2. Elimination: Since Q is useless, the production S → PQ is eliminated.

This leaves S → p and P → p. Now, P cannot be reached from the start symbol S, making P unreachable. Removing P leaves only S→ p.

Correct Answer: S → p (Option B).

Correct options: A, C and D

Short explanation (together):

  • [A] True – ε-productions can always be removed from a CFG (except possibly allowing S → ε if ε is in the language).

  • [B] False – Any CFG, even with ε-productions, can be converted to CNF using standard steps (ε-removal, unit production removal, etc.).

  • [C] True – For a given string, every leftmost derivation corresponds to a rightmost derivation; hence the number of LMDs and RMDs is always equal.

  • [D] True – Left recursion can always be eliminated from a CFG using known algorithms.

✅ Final Answer: A, C and D

title: What is the space complexity of the CYK algorithm for
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: What is the space complexity of the CYK algorithm for the P table, where n is the number of words in the sentence and m is the number of non-terminal symbols in the grammar?
solution:
Concept: the space a dynamic-programming parser needs is (number of table cells) times (space one cell occupies). For a chart-parsing table the cells are indexed by the contiguous substrings, called spans, of the input, and each cell stores the set of grammar symbols that can derive that span - so the two factors are how many spans exist and how large a symbol set can be.

Application - CYK on a sentence of n words with a Chomsky-Normal-Form grammar of m non-terminals:

  1. The table P has one cell per span. A sentence of n words has n(n+1)/2 spans, which is O(n2) cells.

  2. Cell P[i, j] holds the set of non-terminals that derive the span starting at word i with length j. A set drawn from m non-terminals occupies O(m) space - m bits as a bit-vector, or at most m symbols as a list.

  3. Multiplying the two factors gives O(n2) times O(m) = O(n2m) for the whole P table.

Cross-check - what each of the four expressions actually counts:

Expression

What it counts

O(n3)

(start, split, end) index triples - the loop count behind CYK’s running time, not anything that is stored

O(nm2)

ordered non-terminal pairs (B, C) at each of n word positions - one span length, not all spans

O(n2m)

every span paired with every non-terminal - exactly the contents of the P table

O(n2m2)

every span paired with every ordered non-terminal pair - pairs are examined transiently while a cell is filled, they are not stored in it

Hence the P table occupies O(n2m) space. The often-quoted O(n3·|G|) figure is CYK’s time complexity, driven by the extra split-point loop, and must not be confused with its storage.

title: Which of the following derivation does top-down parser use while
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following derivation does a top-down parser use while parsing a input string? The input is assumed to be scanned in left to right order.
solution:
The correct option is C (Leftmost derivation).

A top-down parser constructs the parse tree from the root (start symbol) down to the leaves (input tokens). When scanning the input string from left to right, it always expands the leftmost non-terminal symbol first at each step. This process corresponds exactly to finding a Leftmost Derivation (LMD) for the input string.

title: Why must left recursion be eliminated in top-down parsers?
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Why must left recursion be eliminated in top-down parsers?

options.label: B
options.html: It leads to ambiguity in the grammar

options.label: C
options.html: It slows down the execution of compiled programs

options.label: D
options.html: It cannot be represented using regular expressions

solution:
Top-down parsers, such as Recursive Descent and LL parsers, expand grammar rules recursively from the start symbol. If a grammar contains left recursion, a non-terminal immediately calls itself before consuming any input.

Example:

Expr → Expr + Term | Term

Here, Expr tries to expand into Expr + Term repeatedly, causing infinite recursion. Therefore, left recursion must be eliminated or converted into right recursion for successful top-down parsing.

title: Which of the following statements are true about parsing in
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Which of the following statements are true about parsing in Compiler design?

i. A parser converts tokens generated by the lexical analyser into a parse tree.

ii. A top-down parser can handle left-recursive grammars without any modifications.

iii. A shift-reduce parser can make decisions based on the current input symbol and the top of the stack.

iv. LL(1) parsing is a type of bottom-up parsing technique.

Choose the correct answer from the option given below.
solution:
Statement i is true because parsers convert lexical tokens into parse trees. Statement ii is false as top-down parsers cannot handle left recursion without modification, causing infinite loops.

Statement iii accurately describes shift-reduce parsing mechanics using the stack and input symbols. Finally, statement iv is incorrect because LL(1) is a top-down technique.

Therefore, statements i and iii are true, making option 1 the correct choice.

solution:
Given grammar: S → ( S ) | a and B → B , S | B, with S as the start symbol.

  • In the production S → ( S ), the symbol immediately following S is ')', so ')' is in FOLLOW(S).

  • Because S is the start symbol, the end marker '$' is also in FOLLOW(S).

  • In the production B → B , S, the non-terminal S appears at the end, so FOLLOW(B) is included in FOLLOW(S). From B → B , S, the symbol immediately after B is ',', so ',' is in FOLLOW(B) and therefore ',' is also in FOLLOW(S).

Thus FOLLOW(S) = { ')', ',', '$' } and the number of terminals in FOLLOW(S) is 3.

title: What will be the “First” and “Follow” of and for
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
What will be the “First” and “Follow” of E and F for the following grammar?

E -> TE'
E' -> +TE' / ε
T -> FT'
T' -> *FT' / ε
F -> id / (E)
solution:
Concept: First(X) is the set of terminals that can begin some string derivable from X (plus ε if X can derive the empty string). Follow(X) is the set of terminals that can immediately follow X in some derivation from the start symbol, and the end-marker $ always belongs to Follow(start symbol). Both are propagated through every production where the non-terminal appears, using the nullable-tail rule: if whatever comes right after X in a production can itself vanish (derive ε), then whatever follows that vanishing piece also flows into Follow(X).

Applying this to the grammar: E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → id | ( E ).

  1. F → id | (E), so First(F) = {id, (}.

  2. T → F T′, and F can never derive ε, so First(T) = First(F) = {id, (}.

  3. E → T E′, and T can never derive ε, so First(E) = First(T) = {id, (}.

  4. E is the start symbol, so the end-marker $ belongs to Follow(E).

  5. The only production placing a symbol right after E is F → ( E ), which puts ) immediately after E, so Follow(E) = {$, )}.

  6. T appears only in E → T E′. Since First(E′) = {+, ε}, the terminal + is added directly to Follow(T); because ε ∈ First(E′), Follow(E) is also inherited, giving Follow(T) = {+, $, )}.

  7. F appears in T → F T′ and T′ → * F T′. Since First(T′) = {*, ε}, the terminal * is added directly to Follow(F); because ε ∈ First(T′), Follow(T) is also inherited, giving Follow(F) = {*, +, $, )}.

Cross-check: Trace the string id + id * id. After the first id, the next token is +, matching the + in Follow(T) and Follow(F); after the final id the input ends, matching the $ present in every Follow set; and any parenthesised sub-expression such as (id) always closes with ), matching the ) member of Follow(E) and Follow(F). Every predicted Follow member shows up at a real boundary in the string, confirming the sets.

Result: First(E) = {id, (}, Follow(E) = {$, )}, First(F) = {id, (}, Follow(F) = {*, +, $, )}.

title: Which of the following grammar is are not LL
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following grammar is / are not LL (1)?
solution:
To determine if a grammar is LL(1), we check for: 1) no left recursion, 2) no ambiguity, 3) no common prefixes (i.e., First sets of productions must not overlap).

• S → SS | ∈: This grammar has epsilon production and left recursion. It is ambiguous because multiple parse trees can be generated. Ambiguous grammars cannot be LL(1).

• S → bSc | bc: Both productions start with 'b', so they have a common prefix. The First sets of both productions are {b}, leading to a conflict in the parsing table. Hence, not LL(1).

• S → Sb | c: This grammar has left recursion because S appears as the first symbol in a production. LL(1) grammars must be free of left recursion. Therefore, it is not LL(1).

• S → bS | c: First(bS) = {b}, First(c) = {c}. The intersection of First sets is empty. There is no conflict in the parsing table. This grammar is LL(1).

title: Consider the following grammar SaSb cQq Qm It can be
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the following grammar

S → SaSb | cQq Q → Qm | ε

It can be ______

options.label: A
options.html: Parsed by LL(0) but not by LL(1) parser

options.label: B
options.html: Parsed by LL(1) but not by LL(0) parser

options.label: D
options.html: Cannot be parsed by LL(0) or LL(1) parse

solution:
Answer: The grammar cannot be parsed by LL(0) or LL(1) parsers.

Reason: Both nonterminals are left-recursive.

  • S → SaSb is left-recursive because the right-hand side begins with S.

  • Q → Qm is left-recursive because the right-hand side begins with Q.

Impact on LL parsing:

  • Top-down LL parsers expand nonterminals by their productions. With left recursion, expansion leads to infinite recursive calls (nonterminating), so LL(0) and LL(1) cannot parse the grammar as given.

  • To make the grammar suitable for LL parsing, left recursion must be eliminated (rewrite productions to be right-recursive or use equivalent non-left-recursive forms).

Example (for Q only):

  • Original: Q → Qm | ε

  • After removing left recursion: Q → Q' and Q' → m Q' | ε (produces the same language: zero or more m's), which is suitable for LL parsing.

Conclusion: The grammar as written is left-recursive and thus cannot be parsed by LL(0) or LL(1) without transformation.

title: Consider the following grammar The grammar is [Hint: is not
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the following grammar G

The grammar G is [Hint: 's' is not a terminal]
solution:
Grammar (with 's' in the image interpreted as the nonterminal S):

S → i E t S A | a

A → e S | ε

E → b

Key point:

  • This is the standard dangling-else grammar (an if-then-else style grammar). It is a context-free grammar but it is ambiguous.

Show ambiguity with the example token sequence: i b t i b t a e a (read as: if b then if b then a else a).

Two distinct leftmost derivations that yield the same token sequence:

  1. Derivation where the else associates with the inner if (inner else):

    1. S ⇒ i E t S A

    2. ⇒ i b t S A

    3. ⇒ i b t i E t S A A (expand the S on the right)

    4. ⇒ i b t i b t S A A

    5. ⇒ i b t i b t a A A (inner S ⇒ a)

    6. ⇒ i b t i b t a e S A (inner A ⇒ e S)

    7. ⇒ i b t i b t a e a A (that S ⇒ a)

    8. ⇒ i b t i b t a e a (remaining A ⇒ ε)

  2. Derivation where the else associates with the outer if (outer else):

    1. S ⇒ i E t S A

    2. ⇒ i b t S A

    3. ⇒ i b t i E t S A A (expand the S on the right)

    4. ⇒ i b t i b t S A A

    5. ⇒ i b t i b t a A A (inner S ⇒ a)

    6. ⇒ i b t i b t a A (make the inner A ⇒ ε)

    7. ⇒ i b t i b t a e S (outer A ⇒ e S)

    8. ⇒ i b t i b t a e a (that S ⇒ a)

Because the same token sequence has two distinct parse trees, the grammar is ambiguous. It is a context-free grammar but not unambiguous and therefore not LL(1). Thus the correct choice is the description "none of the above."

To determine if the grammar S → m | mn | mno is LL(k), we find the minimum lookahead k to distinguish productions.

  • FIRST3(m) = {m}

  • FIRST3(mn) = {mn}

  • FIRST3(mno) = {mno}

Since all three lookahead sets of length 3 are completely disjoint, a parser needs exactly 3 symbols of lookahead to make a unique decision. Thus, it is LL(3).

Correct Answer: The grammar is LL(3) (Option B).

title: Which type of grammar is required for predictive (non-backtracking) top-down
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which type of grammar is required for predictive (non-backtracking) top-down parsing?
solution:
In compiler design, a predictive top-down parser constructs the parse tree from the root node (the start symbol) down to the leaf nodes (the terminals/tokens) without ever rolling back or changing its mind.

To construct a deterministic parsing table for such a parser, the context-free grammar must satisfy the LL(1) properties:

  1. L: Left-to-right scanning of the input string.

  2. L: Leftmost derivation is used to construct the parse tree.

  3. (1): One token of lookahead is sufficient to make a non-backtracking decision.

For a grammar to be LL(1), it must not contain any Left-Recursion or Left-Factoring issues. When the parser looks at a non-terminal variable and the current lookahead token from the input, there must be exactly one valid production entry in the parsing table. If a grammar meets these mathematical conditions, the parser can predict the correct derivation path instantly, rendering backtracking completely unnecessary.

title: LL grammar for the language is
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
LL grammar for the language
L = { an bm cn+m | m ≥ 0, n ≥ 0 } is

options.label: E
options.html:
Both of the following are correct LL grammars for L:
S → aSc | S1 ; S1 → bS1c | λ
AND
S → aSc | S1 | λ ; S1 → bS1c | λ

solution:
Concept: A top-down (LL) parser must pick a production for a nonterminal using only the next input symbol, so a grammar can be an LL(1) grammar only if, at every nonterminal, no two alternatives can be triggered by the same lookahead symbol — and in particular, at most one alternative of a nonterminal may derive the empty string λ, since two alternatives that both reach λ create exactly such a clash.

For a concatenation language like { an bm cn+m }, the standard construction pairs the outer a/c layer with its own recursive nonterminal and hands off to a second nonterminal that generates the inner b/c layer down to λ, keeping the empty-string case reachable through exactly one path.

Application:

  1. Define S to generate the outer layer: S → aSc | S1. Peeling the aSc alternative n times gives an S1 cn.

  2. Define S1 to generate the inner layer: S1 → bS1c | λ. Peeling this m times gives bm cm.

  3. Substitute S1 = bm cm into an S1 cn: the result is an bm cm cn = an bm cn+m, matching L for every n, m ≥ 0 (including n = 0, or m = 0, or both).

  4. Check the lookahead sets at S: SELECT(S → aSc) = {a}; SELECT(S → S1) = {b} ∪ FOLLOW(S) = {b, c, $} (FOLLOW(S) includes c from the recursive aSc wrapping, plus end of input). These two sets are disjoint, so the choice at S is deterministic.

  5. Check the lookahead sets at S1: SELECT(S1 → bS1c) = {b}; SELECT(S1 → λ) = FOLLOW(S1) = {c, $}. These are disjoint too, so S1 is deterministic and the whole grammar S → aSc | S1, S1 → bS1c | λ is a valid LL(1) grammar.

Cross-check: Run the same two tests on each of the four base grammars offered — does the grammar generate exactly L, and does S have two ways to reach λ on the same lookahead?

Grammar

Generates exactly L?

Empty-string paths at S

S → aSc | S1 ; S1 → bS1c | λ

Yes

Reaches λ only via S → S1 → λ (one path); no lookahead clash, so this grammar is LL(1).

S → aSc | S1 | λ ; S1 → bS1c

No

S1 never derives λ, so a string such as "bc" (one b, no a) cannot be produced.

S → aSc | S1 | λ ; S1 → bS1c | λ

Yes

Reaches λ via S → S1 → λ AND directly via S → λ — two paths on the same lookahead set {c, $}, a lookahead clash, so this grammar is not LL(1) even though it generates L.

S → aSc | λ ; S1 → bS1c | λ

No

No production of S ever hands off to S1, so no string containing a b can be produced from S at all.

Result: So exactly one of the four listed grammars is both a correct generator of L and a valid LL(1) grammar — the one with S → aSc | S1, S1 → bS1c | λ. The grammar that additionally gives S a direct λ generates the same language but fails the LL(1) lookahead check, so the option asserting that both of those grammars are valid LL grammars does not hold up.

(Some circulated answer keys for this item have listed the second grammar as acceptable alongside the first; that pairing does not survive the LL(1) lookahead check worked out above, since it introduces two derivations of λ at S on the same lookahead set.)

title: Consider the grammar with the following productions id id/ id
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the grammar G with the following productions
S → S & id / S # id/ id
The handles in right sentential form of the reduction for the string “id & id # id”, are:
solution:
Grammar: S → S & id | S # id | id. Target string: id & id # id.

Rightmost derivation (forward):

  1. S ⇒ S # id

  2. S # id ⇒ S & id # id

  3. S & id # id ⇒ id & id # id

A handle is the substring that matches the RHS of a production and whose reduction corresponds to one step in the reverse of the rightmost derivation. Perform the reverse reductions (rightmost derivation reversed) to find the handles:

  1. Start with: id & id # id. Reduce the leftmost terminal "id" (which matches RHS 'id') to S, giving S & id # id. Handle: id

  2. Now reduce the substring S & id (which matches RHS 'S & id') to S, giving S # id. Handle: S & id

  3. Finally reduce the substring S # id (which matches RHS 'S # id') to S, giving S. Handle: S # id

Therefore the sequence of handles (in the order they are reduced during the reverse of the rightmost derivation) is: id, S & id, S # id.

title: Which of the following is an action of bottom up

bodyHtml: Which of the following is an action of bottom up parser
solution:
Correct actions: for a bottom-up parser.

  • Shift: move the next input symbol onto the parser's stack (read and push the symbol).

  • Reduce: replace the sequence of symbols on the top of the stack that matches the right-hand side of a production with the production's left-hand side (apply a production in reverse).

  • Accept: indicate successful parsing when the input is fully consumed and the stack has been reduced to the start symbol.

Note: Substitution is not a standard parser action in bottom-up parsing; it is not used as a formal action name.

title: Which of the following statements is TRUE for the grammar
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Which of the following statements is TRUE for the grammar given below?

S -> (L) | a
L -> L,S | S

options.label: A
options.html: The grammar can be parsed by LR(0) parser only

options.label: B
options.html: The grammar can't be parsed by LR(0) but it can be parsed by SLR(1)

options.label: C
options.html: The grammar can be parsed by LL(1) and LR(0) parsers

options.label: D
options.html: The grammar can be parsed by LL(1) parser only

solution:
Concept

Parser-class hierarchy: For the LR family, LR(0) ⊆ SLR(1) ⊆ LALR(1) ⊆ LR(1). A grammar is LR(0) when its LR(0) item-set (canonical collection) has no shift–reduce or reduce–reduce conflict in any state — i.e. no state holds a completed item [A → α·] together with a shift item, and no state holds two completed items. Separately, a grammar with left recursion (e.g. L → L , S) can never be LL(1).

Application to this grammar

  1. LL(1) check: The production L → L , S is immediately left-recursive, so the grammar is not LL(1). Any statement asserting LL(1) is therefore false.

  2. Build the LR(0) item sets. Augment the grammar with S′ → S and walk CLOSURE/GOTO state by state (dot · marks how far each item has been matched):

  1. I0 = {S′ → ·S, S → ·(L), S → ·a} — no completed item; pure shift/goto state.

  2. On '(' from I0: I2 = {S → (·L), L → ·L,S, L → ·S, S → ·(L), S → ·a} — no completed item; pure shift/goto state.

  3. On S from I2: I5 = {L → S·} — the only item in this state, so it is reduce-only; no shift item shares the state, hence no shift–reduce conflict.

  4. On L from I2: I4 = {S → (L·), L → L·,S} — both items have the dot immediately before a terminal (either ')' or ','), so this is a pure shift state with no completed item.

  5. On ')' from I4: I6 = {S → (L)·} — single completed item, reduce-only.

  6. On ',' from I4: I7 = {L → L,·S, S → ·(L), S → ·a} — no completed item; pure shift/goto state.

  7. On S from I7: I8 = {L → L,S·} — single completed item, reduce-only.

  8. On 'a' (from I0, I2, or I7): I3 = {S → a·} — single completed item, reduce-only.

  9. On S from I0: I1 = {S′ → S·} — the accept state.

Across all nine states, every state is either a pure shift/goto state (no completed item) or holds exactly one completed item (reduce-only) — no state ever mixes a completed item with a shift, and no state holds two completed items. So there is no LR(0) conflict anywhere: the grammar is LR(0).

Cross-check

Because LR(0) ⊆ SLR(1) ⊆ LR(1), an LR(0) grammar is automatically SLR(1) and LR(1) too — FOLLOW(L) = { ) , , } and FOLLOW(S) = { $ , ) , , } are never even needed to resolve a conflict, since none exists. Among the four statements, the only one consistent with “LR(0) = yes, LL(1) = no” is “The grammar can be parsed by LR(0) parser”. The word “only” is loose — every LR(0) grammar is trivially also SLR/LALR/LR(1) — but it is the intended reading, since it is the lone option that does not contradict the automaton just built.

title: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up parsing
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up parsing?

options.label: A
options.html: Top-down parsing starts from the start symbol/root, while bottom-up parsing starts from the input symbols/leaves.

options.label: B
options.html: Top-down verifies rules against previous tokens, bottom-up constructs the parse tree

options.label: C
options.html: Top-down is more efficient for smaller grammars, bottom-up for larger ones

solution:
Top-down and bottom-up parsing differ mainly in the direction in which the parse tree is constructed.

In top-down parsing, the parser starts from the start symbol/root of the grammar and expands productions until it matches the input string. It builds the parse tree from root to leaves.

In bottom-up parsing, the parser starts from the input symbols/leaves and repeatedly reduces substrings to non-terminals until it reaches the start symbol. It builds the parse tree from leaves to root.

Hence, the correct answer is: Top-down parsing starts from the start symbol/root, while bottom-up parsing starts from the input symbols/leaves.

title: What type of grammar can be used for both top-down
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: What type of grammar can be used for both top-down and bottom-up parsing ?
solution: A Context-Free Grammar (CFG) is the broad class of grammars that encompasses both top-down and bottom-up parsing techniques. While specific subsets like LL(1) are designed exclusively for top-down parsing and LR(0) is strictly for bottom-up parsing, the general CFG definition does not restrict itself to one direction. Top-down parsers (like recursive descent) build the parse tree from the root down, whereas bottom-up parsers (like shift-reduce) construct it from leaves up. Since any grammar that can be parsed by either method must fundamentally adhere to the rules of a Context-Free Grammar, CFG is the correct classification. Therefore, Option C is the right answer because it represents the superset capable of supporting both parsing strategies depending on the specific algorithm chosen.

title: XA yB xA yA Which of the following is correct:
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
S → xA | yB | 𝜀

A → xA | 𝜀

B → yA | 𝜀

Which of the following is correct:

options.label: A
options.html: G can be parsed by LR(1) but not SLR(1)

options.label: C
options.html: G can be parsed by LL(1) parser

options.label: D
options.html: Grammar G is an SLR(1) but not LR(0) grammar.

solution:
Final classification: the grammar is LL(1) and SLR(1), but not LR(0).

  • First sets: First(S) = {x, y, ε}; First(A) = {x, ε}; First(B) = {y, ε}.

  • Follow sets: Follow(S) = {$}; Follow(A) = {$}; Follow(B) = {$}. (A and B occur only at the ends of right-hand sides, so their Follow equals Follow(S).)

  • LL(1) check: For each nonterminal the First sets of different alternatives are disjoint (for S: {x}, {y}, {ε}; for A: {x}, {ε}; for B: {y}, {ε}). Where ε appears, the corresponding Follow sets do not intersect the First sets of other alternatives. Therefore the LL(1) parsing table has no conflicts, so the grammar is LL(1).

  • LR(0) check: The LR(0) automaton produces a shift/reduce conflict. Concretely, a state can permit a reduction by A → ε at the same time that a shift on terminal x is possible for the production S → xA. Because LR(0) has no lookahead, it cannot decide between shifting and reducing, so the grammar is not LR(0).

  • SLR(1) check: Using Follow sets to qualify reductions resolves the LR(0) conflicts. The reduction by A → ε is placed only under lookahead tokens in Follow(A) = {$}, not under x; similarly for B → ε. Thus the previous shift/reduce conflicts do not occur in SLR(1), and the grammar is SLR(1).

  • Conclusion: The grammar can be parsed by an LL(1) parser and is SLR(1), but it fails to be LR(0).

title: Which of the following correctly describes feature of Simple LR
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following correctly describes a feature of Simple LR (SLR) parsing?

options.label: A
options.html: Parsing tables are not used in the SLR technique.

options.label: B
options.html: SLR parsing constructs a leftmost derivation of the input string.

options.label: C
options.html: FOLLOW sets are used in constructing SLR parsing tables.

options.label: D
options.html: SLR parsers rely on backtracking to analyse input strings.

solution:
SLR(1) parsing is a bottom-up (shift-reduce) LR technique: it builds an LR(0) automaton from the grammar's items and then places its reduce actions using FOLLOW sets computed from the grammar -- a reduce-by-A entry is added only under the terminals in FOLLOW(A) for a completed item A → α•. (If a shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflict still remains after this, the grammar is not SLR(1).) This FOLLOW-set step is exactly what separates SLR from a plain LR(0) parser and from the stronger canonical-LR(1)/LALR(1) parsers, which instead compute per-state, context-sensitive lookaheads.

Building the SLR parsing table therefore means: for every LR(0) state containing a completed item A → α•, a reduce-by-that-production action is added in every ACTION-table column headed by a terminal in FOLLOW(A). This is precisely the feature that correctly describes SLR parsing among the options given.

Each of the other statements fails for a specific reason:

  • Claiming parsing tables are not used contradicts the core SLR mechanism -- SLR is entirely table-driven, using ACTION and GOTO tables built from the LR(0) automaton.

  • Claiming a leftmost derivation is constructed describes top-down (LL) parsing, not SLR -- every bottom-up/LR-family parser, SLR included, instead produces a rightmost derivation of the input in reverse.

  • Claiming SLR relies on backtracking is false -- its table-driven shift/reduce decisions are fully deterministic, so no backtracking over the input is ever needed.

So the FOLLOW-set-based reduce-action rule is the feature that correctly describes SLR parsing.

bodyHtml:
Consider the grammar G with the following productions:
S → SaP | P
P → PbQ | Q
Q → QcR | R
R → d
Let CLR(1) parser is used to construct the sets of CLR(1) canonical items for G, then number of look-ahead for an item Q → •QcR in initial state are _______
solution:
Grammar: S → SaP | P ; P → PbQ | Q ; Q → QcR | R ; R → d

Goal: find the lookahead set size for the item Q → •QcR in the initial CLR(1) state.

  • Start from the initial item S' → •S, $ and take closure. This produces S → •SaP, $ and S → •P, $.

  • From S → •SaP, $ we add S → •SaP, a and S → •P, a (because FIRST(aP$) = {a}).

  • From S → •P, $ and S → •P, a we add P → •PbQ and P → •Q with lookaheads $ and a respectively. These P items generate P → •PbQ and P → •Q also with lookahead b due to the item P → •PbQ (FIRST(bQ…) = {b}).

  • Therefore P → •Q appears with lookaheads { $, a, b }. Taking closure of each P → •Q, LA gives Q → •QcR and Q → •R with lookaheads $, a, b.

  • Because Q is left-recursive, for any item Q → •QcR, X the dot before Q causes closure using β = cR, so we add Q → •QcR and Q → •R with lookahead FIRST(cR X) which is {c}. Thus c is also introduced into the lookahead set.

Conclusion: the lookahead set for Q → •QcR in the initial CLR(1) state is {a, b, c, $}, which has 4 terminals.

title: Which derivation is also known as canonical derivations?
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which derivation is also known as canonical derivations?
solution:
In the Theory of Computation and Compiler Design, formal languages use context-free grammars to derive strings. A derivation is a sequence of production steps that replaces non-terminals with terminal/non-terminal strings.

  • Rightmost Derivation (RMD): At each step of the derivation sequence, the rightmost non-terminal in the current sentential form is strictly chosen and replaced first.

  • Canonical Derivation: By formal computer science definition, a Rightmost Derivation is uniquely termed a Canonical Derivation. This specific relationship forms the structural foundation for bottom-up parsing techniques (like LR parsers), which implicitly trace a rightmost derivation in reverse order.

title: The following grammar is: Aa bAc dc bda
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
The following grammar is:

S → Aa | bAc | dc | bda
A → a
solution:
CONCEPT: A state in the canonical LR(0) automaton carries a shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflict only when TWO DIFFERENT items in that SAME state compete for the same lookahead symbol. SLR(1) restricts each reduce action to the lookaheads in FOLLOW of the reduced nonterminal — one GLOBAL, context-blind set covering every place that nonterminal ever appears in the grammar. LALR(1) instead computes, per state, the precise lookaheads a valid derivation can actually deliver there, which is never broader than FOLLOW (FOLLOW is the union across every context, not just the ones reaching this one state) — so wherever SLR(1)'s coarser FOLLOW-based check already avoids a clash in a state, LALR(1)'s narrower, state-specific lookaheads cannot manufacture a new clash there. So if a state in this grammar's LR(0) automaton never holds more than one completed item, and never holds a completed item alongside a shift action on the same symbol, there is only ONE production's item present to begin with — no amount of lookahead splitting can introduce a second, competing item into that state, so both SLR(1) and LALR(1) succeed there.

APPLICATION:

  1. FOLLOW(A): A occurs in S → Aa (followed by 'a') and S → bAc (followed by 'c'), so FOLLOW(A) = {a, c}.

  2. Build the canonical LR(0) item sets. The start state contains S′→•S, S→•Aa, S→•bAc, S→•dc, S→•bda, A→•a.

  3. On symbol 'a' from the start state, the automaton moves to the state {A→a•} — a single completed item with no other item sharing that state.

  4. After prefix 'b', the state {S→b•Ac, S→b•da, A→•a} also transitions on 'a' to that SAME state {A→a•} (identical item set), so the two paths converge on one state instead of colliding inside it.

  5. Every other position that completes a handle — {S→Aa•}, {S→dc•}, {S→bAc•}, {S→bda•} — is likewise reached as a state containing exactly that one completed item, with no shift action or second reduce competing for any symbol in that same state.

  6. So no state in the LR(0) automaton ever holds two competing actions on the same input symbol — the construction has zero shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflicts even before any lookahead restriction is applied.

CROSS-CHECK: Every reduce-bearing state found above — {A→a•}, {S→Aa•}, {S→dc•}, {S→bAc•}, {S→bda•} — carries exactly one item, so there is never a second, competing item for LALR(1)'s finer per-state lookaheads to clash with. The FOLLOW(A) = {a, c} overlap only matters when it forces two DIFFERENT items into the same state, which never happens here. So the grammar succeeds under SLR(1) (the coarser check), and therefore also under LALR(1), whose lookaheads are never broader than SLR(1)'s.

Result: the grammar is parsable by both SLR(1) and LALR(1).

title: Consider the following program: int main() int switch case printf("One\n");
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the following C program:
int main() {

    int x = 5;

    switch (x + 1.5) {  

        case 1:

            printf("One\n");

            break;

        case 2:

            int y = x;  

            break;

        case 1:  

            printf("Duplicate\n");

            break;

        default:

            extern int z;  

            z = 10;

    }

    return 0;

}

Assume a standard two-pass compiler for C where type checking, scoping, and uniqueness constraints are handled post-parsing. The primary error in this program that prevents successful compilation is detected during which phase?
solution:
Correct phase: Semantic Analysis

Reason: Lexical analysis and syntax analysis would accept the program tokens and grammar. The errors that prevent successful compilation are detected by type checking, scope/unicity checks, and constant evaluation — all performed during semantic analysis.

  • Non-integer controlling expression: The expression x + 1.5 has a floating-point type. In C the switch controlling expression must have an integral type; using a floating type is a semantic (type-checking) error detected after parsing.

  • Duplicate case label: The same case constant appears more than once (case 1 is repeated). Duplicate case labels within the same switch are a uniqueness/scoping error caught during semantic analysis.

Conclusion: Both the non-integral switch expression and the duplicate case labels are semantic errors detected in the semantic-analysis phase, so compilation fails at that phase.

S → c {print(“(“)} S1 (print(“)+(”) S2 {print(“)”)}
S → d {print(“(“)} S1 (print(“)-(”) S2 {print(“)”)}
S → num {“print(“num.val”)”}
Select the odd one out:
solution:
Answer: The odd one out is the sequence "c 6 b / 36 + 9 9" because it is not a valid expression under the given grammar.

Token mapping: a = '*', b = '/', c = '+', d = '-', num = numeric literal

How to check validity (prefix binary operators):

  • Use an arity-count method: start with need = 1. For each token from left to right: if token is an operator (a, b, c, d) do need = need - 1 + 2 (net +1). If token is a number do need = need - 1. A valid expression finishes with need = 0.

Check each given sequence:

  • "c b 10 2 b 10 2": valid. Need progression: 1 -> 2 (c) -> 3 (b) -> 2 (10) -> 1 (2) -> 2 (b) -> 1 (10) -> 0 (2).

  • "c 6 b / 36 + 9 9": invalid. It contains literal operator symbols '/' and '+' mixed into the token stream rather than the grammar terminals (a, b, c, d), and the token sequence cannot satisfy the prefix arity requirement, so it cannot be parsed by the grammar.

  • "d a 4 10 a 4 10": valid. Need progression: 1 -> 2 (d) -> 3 (a) -> 2 (4) -> 1 (10) -> 2 (a) -> 1 (4) -> 0 (10).

  • "c b c 6 3 9 9": valid. Need progression: 1 -> 2 (c) -> 3 (b) -> 4 (c) -> 3 (6) -> 2 (3) -> 1 (9) -> 0 (9).

Conclusion: The sequence "c 6 b / 36 + 9 9" is the odd one out because it does not conform to the grammar terminals and fails the prefix arity check; the other three sequences are valid parses.

title: Consider the SDT: xSy {S.val S.val ySx {S.val S.val {S.val
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the SDT:
S → xSy {S.val = S.val + 2}
| ySx {S.val = S.val + 2}
| ϵ {S.val = 0}
The SDT:

options.label: A
options.html: Counts the total number of x’s and y’s

options.label: B
options.html: Counts even number of x’s and y’s

options.label: C
options.html: Counts the number of pairs of x’s and y’s

options.label: D
options.html: Counts odd number of x’s and y’s

solution:
Given SDT:

S → x S y {S.val = S.val + 2} | y S x {S.val = S.val + 2} | ε {S.val = 0}

Key idea:

  • Base case: ε sets S.val = 0.

  • Each use of a recursive production adds one x and one y and increments S.val by 2.

  • Therefore S.val equals 2 times the number of recursive expansions, which is exactly the total number of x and y symbols in the derived string.

Example: Consider the string x x y x y y (six terminals). The derivation requires three recursive expansions, so S.val = 0 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, which equals the total number of x's and y's.

Conclusion: The SDT computes the total number of x and y symbols in the generated string.

title: Which of the following is/are true for symbol table
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following is/are true for symbol table ?

options.label: A
options.html: Lexical analyzer only stores value in the symbol table.

options.label: B
options.html: Syntax analyzer only stores information in the symbol table.

options.label: C
options.html: Semantic analyzer stores and fetch information present in the symbol table.

options.label: D
options.html: Intermediate code generator only fetches information from symbol table.

solution:
Revised solution: Only the statement about the semantic analyzer is correct; the other statements are inaccurate as worded.

  • "Lexical analyzer only stores value in the symbol table."

    Evaluation: False. The lexical analyzer does not only store value; it recognizes tokens and often enters identifiers and literals into the symbol table with their lexeme and token type, and may record literal values. Additional attributes are added by later phases.

  • "Syntax analyzer only stores information in the symbol table."

    Evaluation: False. The syntax analyzer primarily builds and checks the syntactic structure; it may consult and add scope- or reference-related information to the symbol table, but it does more than just store information.

  • "Semantic analyzer stores and fetch information present in the symbol table."

    Evaluation: True. The semantic analyzer both retrieves information from the symbol table (for type and declaration checks) and stores semantic attributes (such as resolved types, bindings and other attribute information).

  • "Intermediate code generator only fetches information from symbol table."

    Evaluation: False. The intermediate code generator does fetch information (addresses, types, sizes) from the symbol table, but it may also create entries for temporaries or record intermediate results and their attributes.

Summary: The correct statement is the one describing the semantic analyzer's use of the symbol table. The other statements are incorrect because they assert an exclusive or incomplete role using the word "only" or are otherwise imprecise.

The front-end phase is significant as it performs lexical, syntax, and semantic analysis to translate source code into an intermediate representation.

P→ QR {Q.a = R.a}

R→ id {R.a = id}

Which of the given option is correct:
solution:
Key observations: examine each production and how attribute "a" is used.

  • For S → P Q with semantic rule S.a = P.a + Q.a: the attribute a of S is synthesized because it is computed from attributes of the children P and Q.

  • For P → Q R with semantic rule Q.a = R.a: the attribute a of Q is being set using R (a right sibling), so this is an inherited attribute for Q that depends on a right sibling.

  • Because a appears as both a synthesized attribute (in S) and an inherited attribute (in Q), it is neither only synthesized nor only inherited.

  • An L-attributed definition requires that inherited attributes of a symbol may depend only on the parent’s inherited attributes and attributes of symbols to its left, not on symbols to its right. Here Q.a depends on the right sibling R, so the SDT is not L-attributed.

title: Consider the SDT. {P.val= Q.val R.val} Q.R {P.val Q.val R.val
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the SDT.

S2: P → Q.R {P.val = Q.val * R.val and Q.val = R.val}

Which of the given option is correct w.r.t the above SDT?

options.label: A
options.html: S1 is L attributed but S2 is not L-attributed.

options.label: B
options.html: S1 is S attributed and S2 is L-attributed.

options.label: C
options.html: Both S1 and S2 are S attributed.

solution:
Conclusion: S1 is L-attributed but S2 is not L-attributed.

Reasoning:

  • S1: For the production P → Q R with semantic rule P.val = Q.val + R.val, only a synthesized attribute (P.val) is computed from attributes of its children Q and R. This fits the definition of an S-attributed grammar (only synthesized attributes), and such a grammar also satisfies the L-attributed requirements (L-attributed allows synthesized attributes). Therefore S1 is both S-attributed and L-attributed.

  • S2: For the production P → Q R with rules P.val = Q.val * R.val and Q.val = R.val, the rule Q.val = R.val makes Q depend on R, which is to the right of Q. This creates a dependency of a right-hand symbol on a symbol to its right, violating the L-attributed restriction that an inherited attribute of a symbol on the right-hand side may depend only on symbols to its left and on the left-hand side. It also prevents S2 from being S-attributed, since synthesized-only definitions should not require sibling-to-sibling dependencies. Therefore S2 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed.

Consider the SDD

Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.html: Q.val is synthesized attribute and A.val is inherited attribute.

options.label: B

solution:
Synthesized attribute: A synthesized attribute at node N is defined only in terms of attribute values at the children of N and at N itself.

Inherited attribute: An inherited attribute at node N is defined only in terms of attribute values at N's parent, N itself, and N's siblings.

  • For the production P → Q R with the semantic rule Q.val = R.val: Q.val is an inherited attribute. This assignment defines Q.val using its sibling R (the rule is given at the parent), so Q.val depends on a sibling value and is therefore inherited.

  • For the production A → B C with the semantic rule A.val = B.val × C.val: A.val is a synthesized attribute. It is computed from the attribute values of its children B and C, so A.val is synthesized.

Conclusion: Q.val is an inherited attribute and A.val is a synthesized attribute.

title: Select the correct option: &Optimization
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Select the correct option(s):

options.label: A
options.html: Every L-attributed attribute is also a synthesized attribute.

options.label: B
options.html: Every inherited attribute satisfies the L-attributed restriction.

options.label: C
options.html: A basic block is a sequence of instructions where control enters the sequence at the beginning and exits at the end.

options.label: D
options.html: Live variable analysis can be used for dead code elimination.

solution:
Concept: Each statement here names a formal definition from a different area of compiler theory. An L-attributed definition allows, for every attribute, either a synthesized attribute (computed bottom-up from the children's attributes) or an inherited attribute restricted to depend only on the parent and on symbols to its left in the same production — the class permits both kinds and places a specific dependency restriction only on inherited attributes. Separately, a basic block is a maximal sequence of consecutive instructions with a single entry point (the first instruction) and a single exit point (the last instruction), and live variable analysis is a backward data-flow analysis that finds, at each program point, which variables may still be read later — an assignment outside that live set can be dropped as dead code.

  1. "Every L-attributed attribute is also a synthesized attribute" is false: the L-attributed class explicitly includes restricted inherited attributes alongside synthesized ones, so membership in the class does not force an attribute to be synthesized.

  2. "Every inherited attribute satisfies the L-attributed restriction" is false: an inherited attribute is L-attributed only when its dependencies are limited to the parent and left siblings; an inherited attribute that reads a right sibling's attribute (a common pattern in general attribute grammars) violates this restriction and is not L-attributed.

  3. "A basic block is a sequence of instructions where control enters at the beginning and exits at the end" is true: this is precisely the textbook definition — single entry at the first instruction, single exit at the last, with no internal branch targets or branch-causing instructions in between.

  4. "Live variable analysis can be used for dead code elimination" is true: once live variable analysis determines a variable is not live immediately after an assignment (and the assignment's right-hand side has no other externally observable effect), the optimizer can treat that assignment as dead code and remove it — this is exactly how live-variable data flow feeds dead-code elimination.

Cross-check: The two false statements both mishandle the direction of a subset relationship in L-attributed grammar theory (synthesized-in-L-attributed and inherited-in-L-attributed are not "every member automatically qualifies" claims), while the two true statements are independent, standard definitions from code optimization that hold without exception. Hence the correct options are the basic-block definition and the live-variable-analysis/dead-code-elimination statement.

title: Choose the correct expression for the given below DAG. &Optimization
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Choose the correct expression for the given below DAG.
solution:
Final expression: a + a*(b-c) + (b-c)*d

Explanation:

  • Compute the subexpression (b - c) once; the DAG reuses this value rather than recomputing it.

  • Form a*(b - c) by multiplying a with the reused (b - c).

  • Form (b - c)*d by multiplying d with the reused (b - c).

  • Add the three terms to get the final expression: a + a*(b - c) + (b - c)*d.

Why the other expressions are incorrect:

  • (a*(b-c))+ (a*(b-c))+(b-c)*d duplicates the product a*(b-c), which contradicts the DAG that uses a and the reused (b-c) without duplicating that multiplication.

  • (a+a)*(b-c)+(b-c)*d adds a to a before multiplying by (b-c), implying two a terms combined; the DAG instead yields a as a separate term plus a*(b-c), not (a+a).

  • 'None of these' is incorrect because the correct expression appears among the provided choices.

title: Directed Acyclic graph can be used &Optimization
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Directed Acyclic graph can be used
solution:
Answer: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) are used to represent expressions within a basic block, enabling optimization.

Key ideas:

  • Eliminate common subexpressions — identical expressions are represented by a single DAG node, so repeated computations are detected and computed once.

  • Generate optimized three-address code — traverse the DAG and emit code only for distinct computations, reusing results from shared nodes to reduce temporaries and instructions.

Example:

  1. Original code: x = a + b; y = a + b;

  2. Optimized using a DAG: t1 = a + b; x = t1; y = t1

title: What are the benefits of using intermediate code instead of
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: What are the benefits of using intermediate code instead of directly generating machine code ?

options.label: A
options.html: Allows for different code generation backends for various platforms

options.label: B
options.html: Simplifies the parsing and semantic analysis phases

options.label: C
options.html: Reduces the memory footprint of the compiler

solution:
The correct answer is 1) Allows for different code generation backends for various platforms.

Using Intermediate Representation (IR) is a fundamental strategy in modern compiler design (like LLVM or GCC) because it acts as a universal bridge between the source language and the target hardware.

Key Benefits of Intermediate Code

  • Portability: As mentioned, you can target new hardware (ARM, x86, RISC-V) just by swapping the back-end.

  • Machine-Independent Optimization: Most code optimizations (like removing "dead code" or simplifying math) are the same regardless of the CPU. IR allows the compiler to optimize once before reaching the hardware-specific stage.

  • Easier Debugging: IR is typically more human-readable than raw binary, making it easier for compiler developers to verify that the logic remains intact during the translation process.

title: Consider the intermediate code given below: If the above code

If the above code is converted into static single assignment, the minimum number of variables required is?
solution:
Key insight: In static single assignment (SSA) form every variable that is assigned must get a distinct name/version. Variables that only appear on the right-hand side and are never assigned can keep their original names (or be considered single versions).

Step-by-step SSA renaming for the given code:

  • a = c + d -> a1 = c + d

  • b = f * g -> b1 = f * g

  • h = b * a -> h1 = b1 * a1

  • i = j + h -> i1 = j + h1

Now list the distinct variable names in SSA:

  • Right-hand-side (never assigned): c, d, f, g, j

  • Left-hand-side (new SSA names): a1, b1, h1, i1

Total distinct SSA variable names = 5 (inputs) + 4 (assigned versions) = 9.

Conclusion: The existing solution's renaming steps were messy and its final count (stating 9 but written inconsistently) needs clarification. The corrected SSA naming above shows 9 distinct variables are required in SSA form.
