title: Consider the following SDT for generating three-address code: id gen(
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the following SDT for generating three-address code:

S → id = E { gen(id.name, '=', E.place) }

E → E1 + T { E.place = newtemp(); gen(E.place, '=', E1.place, '/', T.place) }

E → T { E.place = T.place }

T → T1 / F { T.place = newtemp(); gen(T.place, '=', T1.place, '+', F.place) }

T → F { T.place = F.place }

F → (E) { F.place = E.place }

F → id { F.place = id.name }

F → num { F.place = num.value }

For the input statement: x = a + b / c + d / e

Which of the following is the correct sequence of three-address code instructions generated by the SDT?
solution:
Key insight: the SDT's semantic actions swap the operators: the production for addition generates a division, and the production for division generates an addition.

Apply the SDT step by step to x = a + b / c + d / e:

  1. For b / c: use T -> T1 / F which does T.place = newtemp(); gen(T.place, '=', T1.place, '+', F.place).

    Generates: t1 = b + c

  2. Combine a + (b/c): use E -> E1 + T which does E.place = newtemp(); gen(E.place, '=', E1.place, '/', T.place).

    Generates: t2 = a / t1

  3. For d / e: again T -> T1 / F gives an addition.

    Generates: t3 = d + e

  4. Combine the two E parts: final E -> E1 + T uses the addition-production action (which generates a division).

    Generates: t4 = t2 / t3

  5. Assignment: S -> id = E produces

    Generates: x = t4

Final sequence of three-address instructions produced by the SDT:

  • t1 = b + c

  • t2 = a / t1

  • t3 = d + e

  • t4 = t2 / t3

  • x = t4

Therefore the correct generated sequence (following the given SDT exactly) is the five instructions listed above.

title: Consider the following program: int gate(int rank) int for printf("Gate
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Consider the following program:

int gate(int rank)

{

int i;

for (i = 1; i < 10; i++)

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

return 1;

}

Which of the following code optimization can be applied on the above C-code?
solution:
Answer: Loop unrolling is the appropriate optimization.

Why: The loop runs a fixed number of times (from i = 1 to i < 10, so 9 iterations) and each iteration performs the same printf call using the unchanged parameter rank. Unrolling reduces the loop-control overhead (increment, comparison, branch) by replicating the loop body multiple times.

Example (manual full unroll):

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

Example (partial unroll):

for (i = 1; i < 10; i += 3) {

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

printf("Gate rank = %d", rank);

/* handle remaining iterations if needed */

  • Why code motion is not appropriate here: Code motion (hoisting) is only safe for loop-invariant code that has no side effects. The printf call has an observable side effect (it prints each iteration), so hoisting it outside the loop would change program behavior.

  • Why strength reduction is not appropriate here: Strength reduction targets expensive arithmetic operations (e.g., replacing multiplication with addition when updating an index). This loop uses a simple increment and has no such expensive operations to reduce.

  • Compiler note: Modern compilers can automatically perform loop unrolling (full or partial) when the trip count is known or when guided by optimization flags.

title: Find the correct code optimization technique that can be applied
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Find the correct code optimization technique that can be applied to the following given code.
X＝1
Z = 3
y = x*3 +a
b = z + a
c = y*c+ b
solution:
Explanation: all four listed optimizations can be applied if performed in the right order. Below are the stepwise transformations and why each optimization applies.

  • Constant folding — evaluate expressions involving known constants.

    Original (normalized):

    x = 1

    z = 3

    y = x * 3 + a

    b = z + a

    c = y * c + b

    After constant folding (x = 1 makes x*3 = 3; z is 3):

    y = 3 + a

    b = 3 + a

    c = y * c + b

  • Common subexpression elimination — detect that y and b compute the same expression.

    Since both y and b are 3 + a, compute it once and reuse the result (introduce a single definition or make one variable copy the other).

    Example transform:

    y = 3 + a

    b = y // reuse the computed value

  • Copy propagation — substitute the copy where it is used.

    Replace uses of b with y in later code to eliminate the extra variable:

    c = y * c + y

  • Dead code elimination — remove assignments that are no longer needed.

    After propagation the assignments to x and z are unused and can be removed. The temporary b is also eliminated.

    Final optimized code (after these passes):

    y = 3 + a

    c = y * c + y

Notes:

  • The optimizations interact: constant folding exposes the common subexpression; eliminating the common subexpression creates a copy that can be propagated; propagation enables dead-code elimination.

  • Further algebraic simplification (e.g., factoring c = y*c + y into c = y * (c + 1)) is possible but is a different transformation (algebraic simplification/strength reduction).

title: In the context of compiler design, "reduction in strength" refers
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: In the context of compiler design, "reduction in strength" refers to

options.label: A
options.html: code optimization obtained by the use of cheaper machine instructions

options.label: B
options.html: reduction in accuracy of the output reduction in accuracy of the output

options.label: C
options.html: reduction in the range of values of input variables

solution:
Reduction in Strength is a classic code optimization technique applied during the optimization phase of a compiler.

  1. The Goal: To replace an operation that is computationally expensive (takes more CPU cycles or complex circuitry) with an equivalent operation that is computationally cheaper (faster and simpler).

  2. Classic Example: Replacing an expression involving multiplication (×) with an equivalent expression using repeated addition (+) or bit shifts (<<) within loops. For example, replacing i×2 with i+i or i<<1. Division and exponentiation can similarly be replaced by cheaper operations when possible.

Result: This leads to more efficient machine code, which means the program runs faster.

title: What is the goal of constant propagation optimization
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: What is the goal of constant propagation optimization ?

options.label: A
options.html: Remove redundant expressions by replacing constants with their values

options.label: B
options.html: Eliminate unnecessary function calls for known outcomes

options.label: C
options.html: Reduce memory usage by allocating variables only when needed

options.label: D
options.html: Improve branch prediction accuracy by analyzing control flow

solution: Constant propagation is a compiler optimization technique designed to improve code efficiency by tracking the values of variables throughout execution. When a variable is assigned a constant value, such as x = 5, the compiler replaces all subsequent uses of that variable with the literal value 5. This process eliminates redundant expressions because operations involving known constants can often be simplified or computed at compile time rather than runtime. For instance, if an expression is 5 + 3, constant propagation replaces it with the pre-calculated result of 8. Option B is incorrect because eliminating function calls relates more to inlining or dead code elimination, not specifically constant propagation. Option C describes memory optimization techniques like register allocation or stack management, while Option D refers to control flow analysis for branch prediction. Therefore, the primary goal is replacing constants with their values to remove redundant computations.

title: In the bodies of the two loops are merged together
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: In _______, the bodies of the two loops are merged together to form a single loop provided that they do not make any references to each other.
solution:
Answer: Loop jamming

Explanation: Loop jamming, also known as loop fusion, merges the bodies of two separate loops into a single loop when the loops do not have dependencies on each other. This transformation combines iterations so the combined loop performs the work of both original loops.

  • When it is allowed: The two loops must iterate over the same bounds (or compatible bounds) and there must be no loop-carried dependencies or cross-references between the loop bodies that would change program semantics.

  • Benefits: Improved cache locality, reduced loop overhead, and sometimes better opportunities for further optimization (e.g., vectorization).

  • Caution: Do not apply loop jamming if the order of updates between the two loops matters or if merging would introduce dependencies that change results.

  • Example before merging: for i in 1..N: A[i] = f(i) for i in 1..N: B[i] = g(i)

  • Example after loop jamming (merged): for i in 1..N: A[i] = f(i); B[i] = g(i)

  • Why other choices are incorrect: Loop unrolling replicates the body of a single loop to reduce control overhead; strength reduction replaces expensive operations with cheaper ones; loop concatenation usually means placing loops sequentially and is not the standard term for merging bodies.

title: Consider the following code: if(a<50) goto return If variable then
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml:
Question.

Consider the following code:
1. a = 10
2. b = a / 1 L1:
3. c = c * b
4. d = b*3
5. if(a<50) goto L1
6. return c
If variable a ⇒ 1, b ⇒ 2, c ⇒ 3, d ⇒ 4 , then write the number of the variable which is live throughout the program.
solution:
Answer: 3 (variable c)

Variable mapping: a → 1, b → 2, c → 3, d → 4.

Reasoning:

  • The return statement uses c, so c is live at the point of return.

  • The statement c = c * b reads the previous value of c, so c must be live just before that assignment (the assignment does not kill the need for the old value).

  • Because the code loops back (if a < 50 goto L1), the need for c propagates backward through the loop to earlier program points, making c live across the loop and at program entry.

  • Other variables are not live at every program point: a and b are used locally and d is never used after its definition, so only c remains live throughout.

Therefore, variable number 3 (c) is live throughout the program.

title: Which of the following is NOT common data flow analysis
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following is NOT a common data flow analysis technique used in compilers ?
solution: Data flow analysis techniques are used in compilers to gather information about how data moves and changes throughout a program. Constant propagation, reaching definitions, and liveness analysis are all classic examples of data flow analyses. Constant propagation tracks constant values through the code, reaching definitions determine which assignments reach a particular point, and liveness analysis identifies variables that hold values needed in the future. Type inference, however, is not a data flow analysis technique. It is part of type checking and compilation processes that determine the types of expressions without explicit annotations, often used in languages like Haskell or TypeScript. While type inference involves analyzing code structure and relationships, it does not fit the definition of data flow analysis, which focuses on variable values and their usage across control flow paths. Therefore, type inference is the correct answer as it is not a standard data flow analysis technique.

title: In activation record control link point to
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: In activation record control link point to
solution:
Correct answer: the activation record of the caller.

Explanation: The control link (dynamic link) in an activation record points to the activation record of the caller. It records where to return control when the current procedure finishes and maintains the dynamic call chain.

  • Purpose: restore control to the caller and support stack unwinding on return.

  • Distinction: the access (or static) link points to a lexical parent’s activation record for accessing non-local variables; the control link tracks the dynamic caller.

  • Return values are handled separately (for example via registers or a result location), not by the control link.

title: What are the main components of runtime environment
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: What are the main components of a runtime environment ?
solution: The main components of a runtime environment include memory management, function call stack, and heap. These are essential for program execution.

title: Which of the following is not the part of activation
subject: Compiler Design
bodyHtml: Which of the following is not the part of activation record?
solution:
Concept: An activation record (stack frame) is the block of storage a compiler allocates for a single procedure call. The classical runtime-environment model fixes its standard fields as actual parameters, returned value, control link, access link, saved machine status, local data, and temporaries — nothing beyond that list is a distinct field.

Application: checking each option against that standard field list —

  • Actual parameters — named directly in the standard list, so this is a field of the activation record.

  • Returned value — named directly in the standard list, so this is a field of the activation record.

  • Saved machine status — named directly in the standard list; it holds the caller's register values, program counter, and return address needed to resume execution, so this is a field of the activation record.

  • Formal parameters — not named in that list. A formal parameter is only the name a function's own code uses for an incoming value; the compiler binds that name to the storage already reserved for the actual parameter (or treats it as ordinary local data), so no separate field is ever reserved for it.

Cross-check: three of the four options map onto fields explicitly named in the standard activation-record layout; the fourth, formal parameters, maps onto no field of its own — it is only an alias for storage that already exists elsewhere in the record, never a fresh allocation.

Therefore, the item that is not part of the activation record is formal parameters.

title: Assume that each character code consists of bits. The number
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Assume that each character code consists of 8 bits and the asynchronous serial line uses binary signaling, one start bit, two stop bits, and no parity bit. The number of complete characters that can be transmitted per second at 2400 baud is:
solution:
Concept: In asynchronous serial transmission, each data character occupies a complete frame. The frame length equals the data bits plus start, stop, and parity bits. Baud counts signal elements per second; with binary signalling, each signal element carries one bit, so 2400 baud provides 2400 bit-times per second.

Application:

  1. Find the frame size: 8 data bits + 1 start bit + 2 stop bits + 0 parity bits = 11 bit-times per character.

  2. Convert the line rate: binary signalling makes 2400 baud equal to 2400 bit-times per second.

  3. Divide the available bit-times by the frame size: 2400 / 11 = 218.18 characters per second.

  4. Count only complete frames: floor(218.18) = 218 complete characters per second.

Cross-check: 218 frames require 218 × 11 = 2398 bit-times, which fits within 2400. By contrast, 219 frames require 219 × 11 = 2409 bit-times, which exceeds the available capacity. Therefore the maximum number of complete characters is 218.

title: The acronym of NCP used in ARPANET is:
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The acronym of NCP used in ARPANET is:
solution: The correct option is A (Network Control Protocol). In ARPANET, NCP stands for Network Control Protocol. It was the first standard network protocol implemented to allow computers (hosts) to communicate over ARPANET, which was later replaced by the modern, more robust TCP/IP suite on January 1, 1983.

title: ARPANET was developed in

solution: ARPANET, an early packet-switching network and precursor to the Internet, was developed in 1969.

title: Benefits of network do not include
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Benefits of a network do not include
solution:
Concept

A computer network connects multiple devices so they can communicate and share resources. Its classic advantages fall into three buckets: sharing information/data, sharing hardware (peripherals like printers and storage), and centralised management of users and resources. These are the benefits a network is built to deliver.

Application

The question asks which listed item is NOT a benefit. Checking each against the cost/benefit reality of running a network:

  • Improved information sharing — a core purpose: connected machines exchange files and data freely, so this IS a benefit.

  • Better monitoring of worker performance — central servers and logs let an administrator track usage and activity, so this IS a benefit.

  • Sharing of peripherals — one printer, scanner or storage device can serve many users over the network, so this IS a benefit.

  • Low maintenance cost — a network adds cabling/hardware, security, backups and ongoing administration; it raises maintenance effort and cost rather than lowering it. This is NOT a benefit.

Cross-check

Three of the four items are textbook reasons organisations install networks, while increased setup and upkeep cost is a well-known drawback of networking. So the item that does NOT belong among the benefits is “Low maintenance cost.”

title: What is the full form of ARPANET, which was an

bodyHtml: What is the full form of ARPANET, which was an experimental computer network that was the forerunner of the Internet?
solution: ARPANET stands for Advanced Research Projects Agency Network. It was the experimental network that became a forerunner of the Internet.

title: Is set of formal operating rules, procedure or conventions that
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: A .......... is a set of formal operating rules, procedure or conventions that govern a given process.
solution:
A protocol is a set of formal operating rules, procedures, or conventions that govern a given process. In networking, protocols define how data is transmitted and received between devices. They ensure compatibility and standard communication across different systems.

This definition aligns with the concept of a protocol, which establishes the rules for interaction. Other terms like routing or switching refer to specific actions or layers within a network architecture, rather than the governing rules themselves.

title: Which of the following options is an example of full-duplex
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following options is an example of a full-duplex transmission device?
solution: The correct option is C (Telephone). A full-duplex transmission device allows data to be transmitted simultaneously in both directions over a single channel. A telephone network is a classic example because both communicating parties can speak and listen at the same time without any interruption.

title: Which of the following option is example of half-duplex communication
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following devices is an example of half-duplex communication?
solution:
Concept

A communication mode is classified by whether information can travel in one or both directions and, if it travels both ways, whether the two directions can be active simultaneously. In half-duplex communication, both ends can transmit and receive, but only one end transmits at a time.

Application

Walkie-talkies use a shared push-to-talk channel. One user presses the transmit button and speaks while the other user listens; the users then exchange roles to reply. Thus communication is bidirectional but not simultaneous.

Contrast and cross-check

  • Radio broadcasting has a one-way station-to-receiver path, so it illustrates simplex communication.

  • A conventional telephone call permits simultaneous two-way speech, so it illustrates full-duplex communication.

  • Broadcast television has a one-way station-to-viewer path, so it illustrates simplex communication.

  • Walkie-talkies permit both users to transmit, but turn-taking prevents simultaneous transmission; this matches the half-duplex rule.

Therefore, walkie-talkies are the half-duplex device among the given choices.

title: Remote batch-processing operation in which data is solely input to
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: A remote batch-processing operation in which data is solely input to a central computer would require
solution:
Concept

Transmission mode classifies a communication link by the permitted direction and timing of data flow. It is independent of the physical medium or signalling service used by the link.

Transmission mode

Direction and timing

Simplex

One endpoint always sends; the other endpoint always receives.

Half-duplex

Either endpoint may send, but the endpoints do not send simultaneously.

Full-duplex

Both endpoints may send simultaneously.

Application

  1. Identify the data path: the remote terminal supplies a batch of records to the central computer.

  2. Read the qualifier “solely input”: during the described operation, data travels from the remote terminal to the central computer, and no reverse transfer is required.

  3. Match the direction to the definition: fixed one-way flow corresponds to simplex transmission.

Cross-check and contrast

  • A telegraph line names a communication service or physical line; the phrase alone does not specify a direction-of-flow mode.

  • “Mixed band channel” is not one of the standard simplex, half-duplex, or full-duplex direction-of-flow modes.

  • “All of the above” would require every listed choice to establish the required one-way mode, which the medium and band descriptions do not do.

Result

Therefore, the remote input-only operation requires simplex lines.

title: What is the primary purpose of tunneling in internetworking?
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the primary purpose of tunneling in internetworking?

options.label: A
options.html: To encrypt data between two different networks

options.label: B
options.html: To connect two similar networks through a dissimilar intermediate network

options.label: C
options.html: To increase the bandwidth of a WAN connection

options.label: D
options.html: To prevent unauthorized access to the Ethernet frames

solution:
Concept

A network tunnel creates a logical point-to-point link by encapsulating an original packet inside a packet of another protocol. The outer protocol carries the packet across an intermediate network, and the tunnel endpoint removes the outer header.

Application

Here, the two endpoint networks use the same inner networking protocol, while the intermediate network uses a different protocol or infrastructure. Encapsulation lets that intermediate network transport the original packets without needing to interpret their inner protocol, so the tunnel connects the two similar networks across the dissimilar network.

Contrast

  • Encrypting data protects confidentiality; it is an optional security property of some tunnels, not the defining purpose of tunneling.

  • Increasing WAN bandwidth changes link capacity; encapsulation instead adds a header and usually adds a small overhead.

  • Preventing unauthorized access is an access-control or link-security function; tunneling by itself does not authorize users or devices.

  • Connecting similar networks through a dissimilar intermediate network describes the logical link created by encapsulation and decapsulation.

Cross-check

RFC 2473 defines a tunnel as a virtual link between endpoints: one endpoint encapsulates the original packet and the other decapsulates it. That mechanism directly matches connecting compatible endpoint networks across a different transit network.

Therefore, the primary purpose is to connect two similar networks through a dissimilar intermediate network.

solution:
Bus topology uses one shared backbone cable. As the number of devices and cable length increase, signal degradation, collisions, and troubleshooting problems increase. A break in the backbone can also affect the whole network.

Star and ring topologies also have limitations, but they can be expanded using switches, repeaters, or managed/dual-ring designs. Among the given options, the topology generally least suitable for larger networks is Bus topology.

Therefore, option B is correct.

Apply the formula with n = 8:

title: Let us assume that there are four network segments in

bodyHtml: Let us assume that there are four (4) network segments in Bus topologies: A1–A2, B1–B2–B3, C1–C2 and D1–D2–D3. If A1, B1, C1 and D1 are interconnected in mesh, then how many mesh connections are required?
solution:
To determine the number of mesh connections required, we use the formula for a full mesh topology: n(n-1)/2, where n is the number of nodes.

Here, the nodes to be interconnected are A1, B1, C1, and D1, so n = 4.

solution: Mesh topology provides the highest redundancy because every node is connected via dedicated point-to-point links. If a single cable fails, only the communication between those two specific nodes is affected; data can easily be rerouted through alternative paths. Therefore, the correct option is A.

title: Which network topology is typically used in local area networks
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which network topology is typically used in local area networks ?
solution: Star topology is the most common topology used in modern Local Area Networks (LANs), such as Ethernet networks. It connects all devices to a central hub or switch. This layout offers high reliability, easy troubleshooting, and scalability. Therefore, Option B is correct.

title: Linear LAN architecture in which transmissions from various stations on
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: A linear LAN architecture in which transmissions from various stations on the network are reproduced over the length of the medium and are accepted by all other stations on that network is known as
solution:
Concept

A network topology describes how stations and communication links are arranged. In a shared-medium topology, every station attaches to the same communication path, so a signal injected by one station travels through that common path and can be observed by the other attached stations.

A linear shared-medium LAN uses one backbone cable with stations connected along its length. This differs from layouts built from dedicated point-to-point links or from a central switching device.

Application

  1. The stem specifies a linear LAN, so the physical communication path is a single line rather than a collection of independent links.

  2. It says transmissions are reproduced over the length of the medium, which identifies one shared backbone carrying the signal past the attached stations.

  3. It also says the other stations accept those transmissions, which is the broadcast behavior of a bus topology. Therefore, the described architecture is Bus Topology.

Contrast

  • Mesh Topology uses several point-to-point links and can provide multiple routes between stations.

  • Star Topology gives each station a separate link to a central hub or switch.

  • Cell Topology divides wireless coverage into geographic cells served by base stations.

Cross-check

Replacing the shared backbone with a central hub would make the layout star-shaped, while adding dedicated interconnections would make it mesh-like. Keeping one common linear backbone preserves the bus structure.

Result

The linear shared-medium LAN described in the question is Bus Topology.

title: LAN physical topology with end points on the network converging
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: A LAN physical topology with end points on the network converging at a common central switch (known as hub) using point-to-point links is known as
solution: The correct option is B: Star topology. In a star topology, all devices are connected to a central controller (hub/switch) via dedicated point-to-point links. If a device wants to send data, it goes through the central hub, preventing direct traffic between endpoints.

title: What is the name of the topology which has bidirectional
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the name of the network topology in which every pair of nodes has a bidirectional link?
solution:
Concept

Network topology describes how nodes and communication links are arranged. In a full mesh, every distinct pair of nodes has a dedicated point-to-point link; a bidirectional link permits communication in either direction.

For n nodes, the number of physical links in a full mesh is n(n − 1)/2 because each link joins one distinct pair. This pairwise-connectivity rule distinguishes a full mesh from hub-based or hierarchical layouts.

Application

The stem states that every pair of nodes has a bidirectional link. That is the defining connectivity rule of a full mesh, so the required topology is Mesh topology.

Contrast and cross-check

  • Star topology connects peripheral nodes through a central hub or switch rather than directly connecting every pair.

  • Tree topology arranges nodes in parent-child branches across hierarchical levels.

  • “None of these” would apply only if none of the named topology categories described the stated link arrangement.

  • With four nodes, a full mesh has 4(4 − 1)/2 = 6 links, one for each node pair, which cross-checks the definition.

Result

The topology is Mesh topology.

title: In which type of network is each device connected directly
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In which type of network is each device connected directly to a central network switch?
solution: The correct answer is C (Star). In a star network topology, all peripheral nodes (computers/devices) are connected directly to a central networking device, such as a switch or a hub. All data transmission passes through this central controller.

title: In which of the following network topologies, failure of one
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In which of the following network topologies can the failure of one individual node break the entire communication path of the network?
solution:
Answer: C (Ring)

  • In a standard ring topology, nodes form a closed loop. Data is passed from one node to the next.

  • Because each node is part of the forwarding path, failure of one individual node can break the loop and disturb the whole network communication.

  • In a bus topology, the important distinction is that the backbone cable can affect the whole network. Failure of one attached node is different and usually does not stop the remaining nodes.

So the topology asked in the question is Ring, not Bus.

bodyHtml: Which of the following network topology has more complex structure?
solution: A Hybrid topology integrates two or more different standard topologies (such as Star, Bus, or Ring) into a single network. Managing, troubleshooting, and configuring the diverse architectures, hardware interfaces, and distinct complex routing rules makes its structure the most complex. Therefore, Option D is correct.

title: Example of fibre distributed data interconnect (FDDI) is
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following best describes the network arrangement used by Fibre Distributed Data Interface (FDDI)?
solution:
Concept

A token-passing network grants transmission permission through a control token that circulates among stations. Ring arrangements provide a closed path for this circulation; a dual counter-rotating ring adds resilience when one path is disrupted.

Application

FDDI carries data over optical fibre at 100 Mbps and uses token passing on two counter-rotating rings. The primary ring normally carries traffic, while the secondary ring provides an alternate path during a fault.

Contrast

  • Token Bus uses a shared physical bus with a logical token-passing order.

  • Star topology connects all outer stations through one central hub or switch.

  • Mesh topology uses many direct point-to-point links between stations.

  • Token ring circulates transmission permission around a closed ring, matching FDDI's token-passing dual-ring design.

Result

Therefore, among the given choices, FDDI is best described as Token ring.

title: What is the drawback of using BUS topology?
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the drawback of using a BUS topology?

options.label: A
options.html: Only a pair of nodes can be connected

options.label: B
options.html: Performance degrades as additional computers are added or on heavy traffic

solution:
Concept

A bus topology connects every node to a single shared backbone cable, which acts as one common broadcast medium. Because the medium is shared, only one device can transmit successfully at a time; access to the cable is governed by a media-access / collision-handling scheme, and the cable's total bandwidth is split among all active senders.

Applying it here

  • Every computer taps into the same backbone, so all of them compete for the one channel.

  • Adding more computers, or sending more traffic, increases contention for that single shared cable.

  • More simultaneous attempts to transmit mean more collisions, which force retransmissions and add delay.

  • The fixed cable bandwidth is now divided among more active nodes, so each node's effective throughput and response time get worse.

So the defining weakness is that throughput and responsiveness fall as the number of computers grows or as traffic rises — the network does not scale well under load.

Why the other choices fail

  • "Only a pair of nodes can be connected" — false; a bus's whole purpose is to let many nodes share one cable, not just two.

  • "There are no drawbacks" — false; the contention, collisions, and single-cable point of failure are exactly its well-known weaknesses.

  • "Very slow data rates" — a bus is not inherently slow; under light load it performs fine. The problem is degradation as load and node count rise, not a low baseline rate.

title: For devices in network, number of duplex-mode links are required
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: For n devices in a network, how many full-duplex point-to-point links are required in a full mesh topology?
solution:
Concept

In a full mesh topology, every unordered pair of distinct devices has one direct point-to-point link. A full-duplex link carries traffic in both directions, so the same device pair needs one physical link, not two directional links.

Application

  1. Each of the n devices is incident to n − 1 links, giving n(n − 1) link-ends in total.

  2. Every physical link has two ends and is therefore counted once from each endpoint.

  3. Dividing the link-end count by 2 gives n(n − 1)/2 physical full-duplex links.

Cross-check

For n = 4, the unordered pairs are {1,2}, {1,3}, {1,4}, {2,3}, {2,4}, and {3,4}: six links. The formula gives 4 × 3 / 2 = 6.

Result

Therefore, a full mesh of n devices requires n(n − 1)/2 full-duplex point-to-point links.

title: Which of the following is true for Circuit Switching handling
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Using “path” to mean an end-to-end reserved circuit or channel (not necessarily a separate cable), which statement best describes how circuit switching handles multiple simultaneous connections?

options.label: A
options.html: A single path is used and shared for all data

options.label: B
options.html: It encodes all data into a single channel

options.label: C
options.html: Separate physical paths are allocated for each channel

options.label: D
options.html: All connections are multiplexed into a single channel

solution:
Concept

Circuit switching is connection-oriented: before data transfer begins, the network establishes an end-to-end circuit and reserves transmission resources for that connection until the circuit is released.

A circuit is a dedicated channel through the network. A physical link may carry several circuits in fixed time or frequency slots, but each connection retains its reserved share instead of contending for capacity packet by packet.

Application

For several simultaneous connections, the reservation rule is applied independently to each connection. If N connections are active, the network maintains N separately reserved circuits or channels through the switching fabric.

Cross-check and contrast

  • A single shared path for all data describes pooled use of one transmission resource without a dedicated circuit for each connection.

  • Encoding all data into one channel is a signal-combining operation, not the connection-reservation rule used by a switching network.

  • Multiplexing all connections into one channel describes stream sharing; circuit switching may use fixed multiplexing on a link, but the resulting circuits still have separately reserved resource shares.

  • Question not attempted is a response-state label rather than a statement about circuit switching.

Therefore, among the offered statements, the best description is that separate physical paths are allocated for each channel. Here “paths” means separately reserved circuits or channels; it does not require a different cable for every connection.

title: Which switching technique establishes dedicated communication path between source and
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which switching technique establishes a dedicated communication path between source and destination for the duration of a conversation ?
solution: Circuit switching creates a dedicated physical path for the entire conversation duration.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q70
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: When an e-mail is sent over a network, the message is broken into smaller pieces called:
solution:
Concept

Packet-switched communication divides application data into manageable transmission units before sending it.

Each unit carries a payload and control information so intermediary devices can forward it and the receiver can reassemble the data.

Application

An e-mail message is application data. During transmission over a packet-switched network, the message is divided into packets.

Contrast

  • Bytes are groups of eight bits used to represent digital data; they are not the delivery units named by the question.

  • Digits are symbols used to write numbers; in binary notation, those symbols are 0 and 1.

  • A process is a running instance of a program managed by an operating system.

  • Packets are formatted units that carry payload and delivery-control information across a network.

Result

Therefore, the message pieces are called packets.

title: Which of the following is the most common method of
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following is a commonly used home internet access method?
solution: Fiber optic cable is a commonly used home internet access technology that transmits data using light through optical fibers. It provides high bandwidth, low latency, and reliable connectivity, making it the preferred broadband solution for homes today.

title: Which of the following is NOT type of wireless network
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following is NOT a type of wireless network ?
solution: The correct answer is Option D (Ethernet). Ethernet is a wired networking technology that uses physical cables, typically twisted-pair copper or fiber optic strands, to connect devices within a local area network. Unlike wireless standards that transmit data through radio waves or light signals, Ethernet requires a direct physical connection between the network interface card and the switch or router. In contrast, Wi-Fi (Option A) utilizes radio frequencies to enable wireless internet access over a range. Bluetooth (Option B) is a short-range wireless protocol designed for connecting peripherals like headphones and keyboards without cables. NFC (Option C) allows for close-range wireless communication between devices, often used in contactless payments. Since Ethernet relies on physical cabling rather than wireless transmission methods, it is the only option listed that does not qualify as a type of wireless network.

Correct answer: Radio waves (microwave-frequency RF)

  • Wi-Fi uses radio-frequency electromagnetic waves, commonly in bands such as 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.

title: The token management i.e. preventing two parties from attempting the
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The token management i.e. preventing two parties from attempting the same critical operation at the same time, is the responsibility of
solution:
Session Layer (Answer: A) is responsible for token management to prevent simultaneous access to critical resources by multiple entities.

Other layers (e.g., Data Link, Network) handle different responsibilities such as error control, flow control, and routing. Hence, the correct layer for this task is the Session layer.

title: The physical layer is responsible for (Physical Layer)
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The physical layer is responsible for –
solution:
The physical layer is responsible for the transmission of raw bits over a physical medium. It defines the electrical, mechanical, and procedural specifications for activating, maintaining, and deactivating the physical link between devices. This includes the transmission of data as electrical signals, light pulses, or radio waves.
Key responsibilities of the physical layer include:
Bit transmission: Sending and receiving individual bits over a communication channel.
Signal encoding: Converting data into signals suitable for the transmission medium.
Physical topology: Defining the layout of devices and connections.
The physical layer does not handle error detection, flow control, or addressing—these are managed by higher layers. It only ensures that bits are transmitted correctly over the physical medium.

title: Which layer is associated with log in and log out
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which layer is associated with log in and log out from the network?
solution: The Session Layer (Layer 5) establishes, manages, maintains, and terminates connections (sessions) between local and remote applications. This directly includes authentication and authorization steps like logging in and logging out.

title: In SDN architecture, what is the primary role of the
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In SDN architecture, what is the primary role of the control plane?

options.label: A
options.html: To forward packets based on routing tables

options.label: B
options.html: To manage flow rules and make decisions about where traffic should go

solution:
Concept — The work a network does splits into planes. The control plane is the decision layer: it builds a view of the network, computes paths and writes the forwarding entries that devices will use. The data (forwarding) plane is the execution layer: it moves each arriving packet out of a port by looking those entries up. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) pushes this split further by lifting the control plane out of the individual devices into a logically centralised controller.

Application — In an SDN network the controller keeps a global view of the topology, decides which path traffic should take, and installs the resulting flow rules into every switch’s flow table over a southbound interface such as OpenFlow. The primary role of the control plane is therefore to manage flow rules and decide where traffic should go, while each switch is left with the fast lookup-and-forward job.

Cross-check — Each activity below belongs to a different part of the system:

Activity

Where it belongs

Forwarding a packet against installed table entries

Data (forwarding) plane inside the switch

Managing flow rules and choosing traffic paths

Control plane, centralised in the SDN controller

Physically connecting devices

Cabling, connectors and physical-layer hardware

Encrypting data before transmission

Security protocols such as IPsec or TLS

Result — The control plane manages flow rules and makes the decisions about where traffic should go.

title: In the OSI model, which layer is responsible for end-to-end
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In the OSI model, which layer is responsible for end-to-end error recovery and flow control ?
solution: The correct answer is the Transport layer. In the OSI model, the Transport layer (Layer 4) is specifically designed to manage end-to-end communication between source and destination hosts. Its primary responsibilities include ensuring reliable data delivery through error recovery mechanisms, such as retransmitting lost packets, and managing flow control to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver. While the Data link layer handles error detection and flow control, it operates only between adjacent nodes on the same network segment (hop-to-hop), not end-to-end across the entire path. The Network layer focuses on routing and logical addressing, while the Session layer manages dialog control between applications. Therefore, because it guarantees complete data integrity and regulates transmission rates across the entire network path, the Transport layer is the definitive answer for end-to-end error recovery and flow control.

title: Which of the following is not related to data link
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following is not related to data link layer?
solution:
Concept: The OSI model assigns framing, error control, and medium access control (including MAC addressing) to the Data Link Layer (Layer 2) — all single-hop responsibilities between two directly-connected nodes. Congestion control, by contrast, regulates the overall volume of traffic flowing across a network that spans multiple links and routers, so it is a Network Layer function (reinforced at the Transport Layer), not a Data Link Layer one.

Application: Checking each listed function against the data link layer's scope:

  • Framing: encapsulates packets received from the network layer into discrete frames by adding header/trailer boundaries, which are then transmitted as a bit stream — a Data Link Layer function.

  • Error control: detects and corrects bit errors introduced during transmission over a single link — a Data Link Layer function.

  • MAC addressing: uses physical hardware addresses to deliver frames to the correct node sharing that link — a Data Link Layer function.

  • Congestion control: manages traffic load across the entire network path, involving multiple routers and links — NOT a Data Link Layer function.

Note the distinction the question is testing: flow control (pacing transmission to match a receiver's capacity on a single link, e.g. via sliding-window protocols) IS performed at the Data Link Layer, but congestion control (preventing network-wide overload across many links and routers) is not — the two are often confused, but only flow control belongs to Layer 2.

Cross-check: Framing, error control, and MAC addressing are covered in every standard treatment of the Data Link Layer, while congestion-avoidance mechanisms (leaky bucket, token bucket, RED, TCP congestion control) belong to the Network/Transport Layer chapters. Of the four functions listed, congestion control is the one not related to the data link layer.

title: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for logical
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for logical addressing and routing ?
solution: The Network Layer (Layer 3) handles logical addressing and routing.

title: In TCP/IP stack, which layer is equivalent to transport layer
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In TCP/IP stack, which layer is equivalent to transport layer of OSI model?
solution:
Concept

A protocol stack layer is identified by the SERVICE it provides, not only by its name. The OSI Transport layer (Layer 4) provides end-to-end delivery between two hosts: segmentation, end-to-end flow control, and error control, using port-based connections.

Mapping to the TCP/IP model

In the classic four-layer TCP/IP (DoD/ARPANET) reference model, the layer that performs exactly this end-to-end host-to-host job is the Host-to-Host layer (also written as the Transport layer in modern descriptions). It is where TCP and UDP live, providing port-addressed, end-to-end communication between processes on two hosts.

Why the other layers do not match

  • The Internet layer carries IP packets and does logical addressing and routing — that is the OSI Network layer (Layer 3), not Transport.

  • The Application layer of TCP/IP rolls together the OSI Application, Presentation and Session layers (Layers 5-7) — well above Transport.

Conclusion

The end-to-end, TCP/UDP-bearing layer is the Host-to-Host layer, so it is the TCP/IP equivalent of the OSI Transport layer. Note: "Host-to-Host" and "Transport" are two names for the SAME layer; since the option set offers "Host-to-Host Layer" and not a literal "Transport layer" choice, "None of these" is not required — Host-to-Host is the matching layer.

title: In the OSI model, which layer is responsible for error
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In the OSI model, which layer is primarily responsible for error detection and correction of frames between adjacent network nodes?
solution:
The intended context is frame-level communication between adjacent network nodes. In the OSI model, this responsibility belongs to the Data Link Layer (Layer 2).

The Data Link Layer packages bits into frames and uses mechanisms such as FCS/CRC to detect transmission errors. In some protocols, it may also support correction or retransmission at the link level.

The Transport Layer may handle end-to-end reliability/error recovery, but it is not the layer responsible for frame-level error detection and correction.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option C: Data Link Layer.

subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In the OSI model, which layer is responsible for routing and forwarding data packets?
solution: In the OSI model, the Network Layer (Layer 3) is responsible for routing and forwarding data packets. It determines the best path for data transmission across networks and handles logical addressing (e.g., IP addresses). The Data Link Layer (Layer 2) manages node-to-node communication and error detection but does not handle routing across networks. The Transport Layer (Layer 4) ensures reliable end-to-end data transfer and flow control but does not perform routing. The Physical Layer (Layer 1) transmits raw bit streams over a physical medium and does not interpret data or manage routing. Since the Network Layer is not listed among the options, the correct choice is 'None of the above'.

title: When data is transmitted from device to device header from
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: When data is transmitted from device A to device B, header from A layer 5 is read by B’s ______ layer.
solution: In the OSI model, Layer 5 is the Session layer. When data travels between devices, headers added by a specific layer on the sender are processed by the corresponding peer layer on the receiver. Therefore, Device A's Layer 5 header is read by Device B's Session layer.

title: Why was the TCP/IP model designed with fewer layers than
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Why was the TCP/IP model designed with fewer layers than OSI?
solution:
The OSI Approach (Theoretical): The Open Systems Interconnection model was built as an academic exercise. The designers mapped out every conceivable service a network could offer and isolated them into 7 strict boundaries. Because the model was built before the software existed, some layers turned out to be nearly empty or highly redundant in actual practice.

The TCP/IP Approach (Pragmatic): The TCP/IP suite was engineered by programmers who were actively building working network nodes. They grouped tasks based on how software functions are naturally implemented in an operating system's protocol stack.

title: Which of the following is not associated with the session
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following is not associated with the session layer ?
solution:
Answer: Semantics of the information transmitted is not associated with the session layer.

Explanation: The session layer is responsible for managing dialogues and sessions between applications, including control and coordination tasks. The semantics (meaning, representation, translation, encryption, compression) of the data is the responsibility of the presentation layer.

  • Dialog control: Manages start, maintenance, and termination of communication sessions.

  • Token management: Controls which party may transmit to avoid conflicts in multi-party or half-duplex sessions.

  • Synchronization: Inserts checkpoints or recovery points to enable recovery from failures during a session.

  • Semantics of the information transmitted: Handled by the presentation layer (data representation, translation, encryption, compression), so it is not a session-layer function.

title: Which of the following layers is an addition to OSI
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which option lists all the layers that exist as separate layers in the OSI model but not in the TCP/IP model?
solution:
Concept: A layered network model assigns a distinct responsibility to each layer and specifies how neighboring layers interact. Comparing two models requires checking which responsibilities exist as separate layers and which are consolidated into a broader layer.

Application

The OSI upper stack separates application services, data representation, and session control into the Application, Presentation, and Session layers. The TCP/IP model groups these application-facing responsibilities under its Application layer instead of defining separate Presentation and Session layers.

Contrast

  • Application layer: provides network services to user applications and appears as a named layer in both model families.

  • Presentation layer: handles representation tasks such as translation, compression, and encryption in OSI.

  • Session layer: handles dialog establishment, synchronization, and termination in OSI.

Cross-check and result

OSI has seven layers, whereas the traditional TCP/IP model has four. Consolidating the two OSI-specific upper-layer functions explains the smaller TCP/IP count. Therefore, the complete choice is Session and Presentation layer.

title: Network has data transmission bandwidth of bits per second. It
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: A network has a data transmission bandwidth of 38.6 x 106 bits per second. It uses Pure ALOHA. The round trip time is 2 µs. The packet length is 1484 bits. The vulnerable time for such a network is ____________ ms. (Correct upto 3 decimal places).
solution:
Key formula: Vulnerable time for Pure ALOHA = 2 × transmission time.

Transmission time = packet length / bandwidth.

  • Compute transmission time: 1484 bits / (38.6 × 10^6 bits/s) = 1484 / 38,600,000 s ≈ 0.0000384456 s = 0.0384456 ms.

  • Vulnerable time = 2 × 0.0384456 ms = 0.0768912 ms ≈ 0.077 ms (rounded to 3 decimal places).

Note: The given round trip time (2 µs) is not required for this calculation because the vulnerable period in Pure ALOHA depends on the packet transmission time only.

title: In slotted ALOHA with G-stations attempting to transmit in one
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In a slotted ALOHA with G-stations attempting to transmit in one slot, the throughput is equal to –
solution:
In slotted ALOHA, a station may start a transmission only at the beginning of a fixed-length time slot, so every attempt in a given slot is synchronized with every other attempt. If stations together offer G transmission attempts per slot on average, the number of attempts landing in any one slot follows a Poisson distribution with mean G: P(exactly k attempts in a slot) = (Gᵏ × e⁻ᴳ) / k!. Throughput is the probability that a slot carries exactly one attempt (k = 1), since zero attempts wastes the slot and two or more attempts collide and destroy each other.

Applying the Poisson formula for a successful (collision-free) slot:

  1. Write the general Poisson probability of exactly k attempts in a slot: P(k) = (Gᵏ × e⁻ᴳ) / k!.

  2. A slot is successful only when exactly one attempt lands in it, so set k = 1: P(1) = (G¹ × e⁻ᴳ) / 1!.

  3. Simplify the factorial and the exponent: P(1) = G × e⁻ᴳ.

  4. Throughput S is this success probability, so S = G × e⁻ᴳ.

As an independent check, differentiate S with respect to G and set the result to zero: this locates the maximum at G = 1, giving S = 1 × e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368. That matches the well-known textbook result that slotted ALOHA peaks at about 36.8% throughput — exactly double pure ALOHA's peak of about 18.4% — which confirms the formula.

So the throughput of slotted ALOHA is S = G × e⁻ᴳ.

title: There are stations in slotted LAN. Each station attempts to
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: There are n stations in a slotted LAN. Each station attempts to transmit with a probability p in each time slot. What is the probability that only one station transmits in a given time slot?
solution:
This problem is based on probability in a Slotted ALOHA-like system.

There are n stations

Each station transmits with probability p

We want the probability that exactly one station transmits

Step-by-step logic:

Choose 1 station out of n → n ways

That chosen station transmits → probability = p

Remaining (n − 1) stations do NOT transmit → probability = (1 − p)^{n−1}

Multiply all:

P=n⋅p⋅(1−p)n−1

title: Maximum throughput of slotted ALOHA network is:
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Maximum throughput of slotted ALOHA network is:
solution: The maximum throughput (S) of Slotted ALOHA is achieved when the load G = 1, given by S = G . e-G. For G = 1, S = 1/e = 0.368 or 36.8%. This is exactly double the efficiency of Pure ALOHA (18.4%).

title: At what value of load the maximum throughput of PURE

bodyHtml: At what value of load G the maximum throughput S of PURE ALOHA occurs ?

The Throughput Formula: \(S = G \cdot e^{-2G}\)

  • Maximum Throughput Load: \(G = 0.5\)

  • Max Throughput Percentage: \(\approx 18.4\%\)

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 6
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The throughput of pure ALOHA is given by:
solution:
Concept: Throughput S of a random-access protocol equals the offered load G multiplied by the probability that a transmitted frame survives without a collision — i.e. S = G × P(no collision). In pure ALOHA a station transmits the instant it is ready, with no time-slotting, so any two transmissions that overlap even partially collide.

  1. A frame with transmission time Tt sent at time t0 collides with any other frame whose transmission begins in the interval (t0 − Tt, t0 + Tt); this vulnerable period therefore has length 2Tt — twice the frame time (in slotted ALOHA, slot alignment shrinks the vulnerable period to just Tt).

  2. Frame arrivals are modelled as a Poisson process with average rate G frames per frame-time, so the number of arrivals k in an interval spanning τ frame-times has probability P(k) = (Gτ)ᵏ e−Gτ / k!.

  3. A frame survives only if zero other frames arrive during its own vulnerable period, τ = 2. Substituting k = 0, τ = 2 gives the success probability P(0) = e−2G.

  4. Multiplying the offered load by this success probability gives the throughput: S = G · e−2G.

Cross-check: Differentiating S = G·e−2G with respect to G gives dS/dG = e−2G(1 − 2G); setting this to zero gives G = 0.5, and substituting back gives Smax = 0.5 × e−1 ≈ 0.184 — the well-known 18.4% peak efficiency of pure ALOHA, confirming the derived formula. (The analogous derivation for slotted ALOHA drops the factor of 2 in the vulnerable-period length, giving S = G·e−G with a higher peak of 36.8% at G = 1 — consistent with slotting halving the vulnerable period.)

title: Assume that and are only active stations on an ethernet.
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Assume that A and b are only active stations on an ethernet. Both have a steady queue of frames to send. To get the control on the channel they use a binary exponential algorithm. Both are attempting to transmit the frame. The probability that both are successfully allowed to send the frame on the 4th round and in earlier attempts both A and B collides is ________. (Upto 2 decimal places)
solution:
Key idea: compute the probability of collision in each round, then multiply the probabilities that collisions happen in the first three rounds and that no collision happens in the fourth round.

  • 1st round (window size = 1): both must transmit immediately, so collision probability = 1.

  • 2nd round (window size = 2): each picks a slot uniformly from 2 slots; collision occurs if they pick the same slot, so collision probability = 1/2.

  • 3rd round (window size = 4): collision probability = 1/4 (they pick the same slot among 4).

  • 4th round (window size = 8): probability of no collision is 1 minus the probability they pick the same slot, so no-collision probability = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.

Multiply the probabilities: P = 1 × 1/2 × 1/4 × 7/8 = 7/64 ≈ 0.109375

Final answer (rounded to 2 decimal places): 0.11

title: Let and be two stations attempting to transmit on an
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Let P and Q be two stations attempting to transmit on an Ethernet. Each has a steady queue of frames to send. After each frame is sent (from both sides), they collide for the first time and contend for the channel, using the binary exponential backoff algorithm. What is the probability that the contention ends after 3 successful transmissions?
solution:
What is happening in the question?

Two stations P and Q are trying to transmit.

  • They collide initially, so they start binary exponential backoff.

  • After each collision, they pick a random number from a range:

Range = {0,1,2,...,2^k − 1}

  • If both pick the same number → collision again

  • If they pick different numbers → success

Backoff Rounds:

Round 1 (k=0) :

Choices = {0}

  • Both must pick 0 → collision is guaranteed

Round 2 (k=1) :

Choices = {0,1}

  • Total pairs = 4

  • Collision cases = (0,0), (1,1) → 2 cases

P(collision)= 2/4 = 1/2

Round 3 (k=2) :

Choices = {0,1,2,3}

  • Total pairs = 16

  • Collision cases = (0,0), (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) → 4 cases

P(collision)= 4/16 = 1/4

What does " contention ends after 3 successful transmissions " mean ?

This means:

  • Collisions happened in earlier rounds

  • Finally, in the next round (k = 3), they succeed

So we only need:

Probability of NO collision in round 4 (k = 3)

Round 4 (k=3) :

Choices = {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}

  • Total pairs = 8×8=64

  • Collision cases = when both pick same number = 8 cases

P(collision) = 8 / 64 = 1 / 8

​P(no collision) = 1−(1 / 8) = 7 / 8

So, Final answer is 7/8.

title: What is the minimum frame size (in Mbits) required in
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the minimum frame size (in Mbits) required in a CSMA/CD network with bandwidth of 1 Gbps and one-way propagation delay of 40 ms?
solution:
Key idea: the minimum frame must be long enough that the sender is still transmitting when a collision signal can travel to the sender (i.e., at least one round-trip propagation time of the link).

  • Compute the round-trip time: 2 × one-way propagation delay = 2 × 40 ms = 80 ms.

  • Convert bandwidth to bits per second: 1 Gbps = 1 × 10^9 bits/s.

  • Minimum frame size (in bits) = round-trip time × bandwidth = 80 ms × 1 × 10^9 bits/s = 0.08 s × 1 × 10^9 bits/s = 80 × 10^6 bits.

  • Convert to Mbits: 80 × 10^6 bits = 80 Mbits.

Answer: 80 Mbits (which lies within the provided acceptable range of 78–82 Mbits).

title: Consider CSMA/CD with frame size 20KB, and transmission rate 10Kbps,the
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Consider a CSMA/CD with a frame size 20KB, and a transmission rate 10Kbps,the maximum length of cable (km)required , if signal speed is 15 km/sec?
solution:
Key formula: For CSMA/CD the round-trip propagation delay must be no greater than the frame transmission time.

  • Write the inequality: 2 × distance / propagation_speed ≤ frame_size_bits / data_rate

  • Convert frame size to bits: 20 KB = 20 × 8 × 10^3 = 160,000 bits (using decimal kilo for clarity).

  • Case 1 (likely intended interpretation in many networking contexts): data rate = 10 Mbps (10 × 10^6 bps) and propagation speed = 15 km/s.

  • Compute transmission time: 160,000 bits / 10,000,000 bps = 0.016 s.

  • Solve for distance: distance ≤ (transmission_time × propagation_speed) / 2 = (0.016 s × 15 km/s) / 2 = 0.12 km = 120 m.

  • Case 2 (if the question actually meant 10 Kbps): transmission_time = 160,000 / 10,000 = 16 s, so distance ≤ (16 s × 15 km/s) / 2 = 120 km.

  • Common mistake (seen in the provided image): omitting the factor 2 (using one-way delay instead of round-trip) gives distance = transmission_time × propagation_speed. For the 10 Mbps interpretation that incorrect step yields 0.24 km (240 m).

Final note: The image-only solution is ambiguous about units and the data rate (it appears to use 10 Mbps rather than 10 Kbps) and it omits the round-trip factor required for CSMA/CD. The correct maximum cable length depends on which data rate the problem actually intends; using the common 10 Mbps interpretation gives 120 m (0.12 km).

title: To support CSMA CD transmission time is double the propagation
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
To support CSMA / CD transmission time is double the propagation time.What is the length of cable in meters used in fast ethernet?
Note: bandwidth = 100 x 106 bps frame size= 64 bytes velocity = 2 x 10 8 meter /sec
solution:
Key formula: transmission time = 2 × propagation time

  1. Compute frame size in bits: 64 bytes × 8 = 512 bits.

  2. Transmission time (Tt) = frame bits / bandwidth = 512 / (100 × 10^6) = 5.12 × 10^-6 s.

  3. Propagation time (Tp) = Tt / 2 = 5.12 × 10^-6 s / 2 = 2.56 × 10^-6 s.

  4. Length = velocity × propagation time = (2 × 10^8 m/s) × (2.56 × 10^-6 s) = 512 m.

Answer: 512 meters

title: Determine the efficiency of CSMA/CD if the maximum cable length
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Determine the efficiency of CSMA/CD if the maximum cable length for transmitting data at a rate of 80 Kbps is 16 KM. The signal speed in the cable is 8 * 105 m/s and the frame size is 1264 bits.
solution:
Given: distance = 16 km = 16,000 m; signal speed = 8 × 10^5 m/s; data rate = 80 kbps = 80,000 bits/s; frame size = 1,264 bits.

  • Propagation delay (Tp) = distance / speed = 16000 / (8 × 10^5) = 0.02 s (20 ms).

  • Transmission time (Tt) = frame size / data rate = 1264 / 80000 ≈ 0.0158 s (15.8 ms).

  • Ratio a = Tp / Tt = 0.02 / 0.0158 ≈ 1.2658.

  • Use the CSMA/CD efficiency approximation: Efficiency ≈ 1 / (1 + 5.65 × a).

  • Compute efficiency: 1 / (1 + 5.65 × 1.2658) ≈ 0.1227 = 12.27%.

Answer: 12.27%.

title: Suppose two nodes, and are attached to opposite ends of
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Suppose two nodes, A and B are attached to opposite ends of the cable with propagation delay of 12.5 μs. Both nodes attempt to transmit at time t = 0. Frames collide and after first collision, A draws k = 0 and B draws k = 1 in the exponential back off protocol. Ignore the jam signal. Then at what time (in seconds) is A’s packet completely delivered at B in μs, if Bandwidth of the link is 10 Mbps and packet size is 1000 bits
solution:
Key data: packet size = 1000 bits; bandwidth = 10 Mbps; one-way propagation delay = 12.5 μs; k for A = 0, k for B = 1.

  1. Compute transmission time for the packet: transmission time = packet size / bandwidth = 1000 bits / (10 × 10^6 bps) = 100 μs.

  2. Collision detection and backoff: both nodes start at t = 0 and detect the collision when the other node's signal reaches them, at 12.5 μs. After that, A uses k = 0 and B uses k = 1.

  3. When can A retransmit? Both nodes stop transmitting as soon as they detect the collision (at 12.5 μs). The last transmitted signal fragments still propagate for another one-way delay (12.5 μs), so the medium becomes idle at 12.5 + 12.5 = 25 μs. With k = 0, A can start retransmission immediately when the medium becomes idle, i.e., at 25 μs.

  4. Check B's retransmission: the slot time here equals the round-trip propagation (2 × 12.5 μs = 25 μs). B waits one slot after collision detection and will attempt at 12.5 + 25 = 37.5 μs, so A's retransmission (starting at 25 μs) proceeds without further collision.

  5. Compute completion time at B: A finishes sending at 25 + 100 = 125 μs. The last bit then needs one-way propagation (12.5 μs) to reach B, so the packet is completely delivered at B at 125 + 12.5 = 137.5 μs.

Final answer: 137.5 μs.

Note: the original solution used the same reasoning but was provided as an image. This text version clarifies why 25 μs is added (medium remains busy until in-flight signals clear) and shows each timing step explicitly.

title: With each successive collision in CSMA/CD Protocol
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: With each successive collision in CSMA/CD Protocol
solution:
Answer: Collision probability decreases exponentially.

Reason: CSMA/CD uses a binary exponential backoff. After the x-th collision, each station chooses a random backoff K uniformly from 0 to 2^x - 1 (in practice this range is often capped after a maximum number of attempts).

  • For two stations both at the same backoff stage x, there are 2^x possible choices for each station, so total ordered pairs of choices = 2^x × 2^x = 2^(2x).

  • A collision occurs when both stations pick the same K. There are 2^x such matching pairs.

  • Therefore probability of collision = (number of matching pairs) / (total pairs) = 2^x / 2^(2x) = 1 / 2^x.

  • Example: x = 1 → probability = 1/2; x = 2 → probability = 1/4; x = 3 → probability = 1/8. The probability falls by a factor of two for each additional backoff stage, i.e., it decreases exponentially.

  • Note: In real implementations there is a maximum backoff stage (a cap), so the exponential decrease holds until that cap is reached.

title: Suppose that Ethernet stations, all trying to send at the
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Suppose that ‘N’ Ethernet stations, all trying to send at the same time, require N / 2 slot times to sort out who transmits next. Assuming the average packet. Size is 5 slot times, express the available bandwidth as a function of N.
solution:
Time per transmission cycle: Each station needs N/2 slot times to resolve collisions + 5 slot times (average packet size).

Total time per transmission cycle = (N/2) + 5

Available bandwidth: Bandwidth is inversely proportional to the total time.

Available bandwidth = Packet Size / Total Time = 5 / ((N/2) + 5) = 10 / (10 + N)

title: Consider CSMA/CD network running at 1Gbps over 1Km without repeaters.
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Consider a CSMA/CD network running at 1Gbps over 1Km without repeaters. Given signal speed is the minimum frame size is: (Assume Speed : 2 * 10^8)
solution:
Given Data:

- Bandwidth (B) = 1 Gbps = 1,000,000,000 bits/sec

- Distance (d) = 1 km = 1000 meters

- Signal Speed (v) = 2 * 10^8 m/s (Standard assumption)

Formulas:

1. Propagation Delay (Tp) = Distance / Signal Speed

2. Round Trip Time (RTT) = 2 * Tp

3. Minimum Frame Size (L) = RTT * Bandwidth

Step-by-Step Calculation:

Step 1: Calculate the Propagation Delay (Tp)

Tp = 1000 m / (2 * 10^8 m/s)

Tp = 0.000005 seconds

Step 2: Calculate the Round Trip Time (RTT)

RTT = 2 * 0.000005 seconds

RTT = 0.00001 seconds

Step 3: Calculate the Minimum Frame Size (L)

L = 0.00001 seconds * 1,000,000,000 bits/sec

L = 10,000 bits

Convert to bytes:

L = 10,000 / 8 = 1250 Bytes

Final Answer:

The minimum frame size required for this network is 10,000 bits (or 1250 bytes).

title: Which of the following Multiple Access Protocols is not suitable
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following Multiple Access Protocols is not suitable for wired networks?
solution:
In Multiple Access Protocol, different protocols are used depending on whether the network is wired or wireless.

CSMA/CD (Collision Detection) → used in wired Ethernet networks

CSMA/CA (Collision Avoidance) → used in wireless networks (Wi-Fi)

Wired networks can detect collisions directly, but wireless networks cannot easily detect them, so they use avoidance instead.

title: Consider CSMA/CD network that transmits data at the rate of
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Consider a CSMA/CD network that transmits data at the rate of 100 Mbps over a 1 Kilometre cable with no repeater. If the minimum frame size required for this network is 1250 bytes, what is the signal speed (km/sec) in the cable.
solution:
Solution:

  • Convert the minimum frame size to bits: 1250 bytes × 8 = 10000 bits.

  • Compute the transmission time at 100 Mbps: 10000 bits / 100,000,000 bps = 0.0001 s = 100 μs.

  • For CSMA/CD the transmission time must be at least the round-trip propagation time, so one-way propagation time ≤ 100 μs / 2 = 50 μs.

  • Signal speed = distance / one-way_time = 1 km / 50×10⁻⁶ s = 20,000 km/s.

Answer: 20000 km/s.

title: Which of the following is true? Hidden terminal can be
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
Which of the following is true?

S1: Hidden terminal can be handled using RTS/CTS

S2: RTS/CTS exchanges help to reduce collisions but it uses the more channel resources and not efficient use of channel resources .
solution:
Answer: Both statements are correct.

Explanation:

  • Statement S1 (hidden terminal): RTS/CTS can mitigate the hidden terminal problem. The sender issues an RTS and the receiver replies with a CTS; nodes that hear the CTS know to defer, which prevents collisions caused by transmitters that cannot hear each other.

  • Statement S2 (overhead and efficiency): RTS/CTS reduces collisions but introduces additional control frames (RTS and CTS) and timing overhead, which consumes channel resources. This extra overhead can make RTS/CTS inefficient for small data frames or in low-contention environments.

Practical note: Use RTS/CTS when the risk of costly collisions is high (large frames or many hidden terminals). Skip RTS/CTS when frames are small or contention is low to avoid unnecessary overhead.

title: Network Allocation Vector (NAV) is associated with which of the
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Network Allocation Vector (NAV) is associated with which of the following MAC technologies?
solution:
Concept

In an IEEE 802.11 medium-access system, carrier sensing has physical and virtual components. Physical sensing observes radio energy, while virtual sensing uses timing information carried in frames.

The Network Allocation Vector (NAV) is the virtual-sensing countdown. A station updates it from the Duration/ID field and treats the medium as reserved while the countdown remains positive.

Application

  1. Suppose a station overhears an IEEE 802.11 frame whose Duration/ID field reserves the medium for 500 microseconds.

  2. The station loads that interval into its NAV and defers a new transmission while the timer counts down.

  3. This virtual carrier-sensing procedure is part of the IEEE 802.11 MAC used by Wi-Fi, alongside CSMA/CA.

Cross-check and contrast

  • CSMA/CD belongs to the classic shared-Ethernet collision-detection procedure rather than this wireless reservation timer.

  • Bluetooth uses its own short-range radio access procedures and is not the IEEE 802.11 MAC family.

  • Ethernet names the IEEE 802.3 family; classic shared Ethernet senses and detects collisions instead of maintaining this IEEE 802.11 reservation state.

  • Question not attempted describes a response state, not a MAC technology.

Therefore, the MAC technology associated with NAV is Wi-Fi.

title: At transmission rate of Mbps and propagation speed of m/μsec,

Distance covered during this delay:

Distance = Propagation Speed × Bit Delay
= 200 m/μsec × 0.2 μsec = 40 meters

title: If the packet size is bits, the rate of channel
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: If the packet size is 5000 bits, the rate of channel is 4 kbps and distance between the hosts is 20 km. Speed of propagation over the transmission media is 200 m/s. Calculate the link utilization for stop and wait flow control mechanism.
solution:
Given: packet size = 5000 bits; channel rate = 4 kbps (4000 bps); distance = 20 km (20000 m); propagation speed = 200 m/s.

Transmission time (Tt): Tt = 5000 bits / 4000 bps = 1.25 s.

Propagation time (Tp): Tp = 20000 m / 200 m/s = 100 s.

Stop-and-wait utilization formula: U = Tt / (Tt + 2·Tp) = 1 / (1 + 2a), where a = Tp / Tt.

  • Compute a: a = Tp / Tt = 100 / 1.25 = 80.

  • Compute utilization: U = 1 / (1 + 2·80) = 1 / 161 ≈ 0.00621.

title: Calculate the link utilization (throughput) for the stop-and-wait flow control
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Calculate the link utilization (efficiency) for the stop-and-wait flow control mechanism if the frame size is 4800 bits, bit rate is 9600 bps, and the distance between the devices is 2000 km. Given propagation speed is 200000 km/s.
solution:
Concept: In stop-and-wait flow control, the sender transmits one frame and then waits idle for its acknowledgement before sending the next. Link utilization (also called efficiency) is the fraction of time the link actually carries data, given by Tt / (Tt + 2Tp), where Tt is the transmission time and Tp is the one-way propagation time. The factor 2Tp accounts for the round trip the frame and its acknowledgement travel. This is a pure dimensionless ratio between 0 and 1 — it is not the throughput in bits per second.

Application: Substitute the given values step by step.

  1. Transmission time Tt = frame size / bit rate = 4800 / 9600 = 0.5 s.

  2. Propagation time Tp = distance / propagation speed = 2000 / 200000 = 0.01 s.

  3. Efficiency = Tt / (Tt + 2Tp) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 2 × 0.01) = 0.5 / 0.52 = 0.9615.

Cross-check: Because the transmission time (0.5 s) is much larger than the round-trip propagation overhead (2 × 0.01 = 0.02 s), the sender stays busy almost the whole time, so the efficiency must be close to 1 — and 0.9615 ≈ 0.96 confirms this. (For reference, the actual data throughput would be 0.96 × 9600 ≈ 9231 bps; the utilization asked here is the ratio 0.96, not this bps value.)

Result: The link utilization is approximately 0.96.

title: In an Ethernet LAN, if cumulative acknowledgments are used and
