bodyHtml: In an Ethernet LAN, if cumulative acknowledgments are used and an acknowledgment for packet 2027 is received, which of the following statements is/are true?

options.label: A
options.html: All packets up to 2027 have been successfully received

options.label: B
options.html: Packet 2027 has been received, but packet 2026 might still be in transit

options.label: D
options.html: Packets 2026 and 2027 were dropped by the network

solution:
Answer: All packets up to 2027 have been successfully received.

Explanation:

  • In cumulative acknowledgment schemes, the acknowledgment for a packet number indicates that the receiver has obtained a contiguous sequence of packets up to that number. Therefore, an acknowledgment for packet 2027 confirms receipt of packet 2027 and all preceding packets.

  • Because the ACK confirms a contiguous sequence through 2027, packet 2026 cannot still be in transit when ack2027 is received.

  • The acknowledgment alone does not imply that packet 2027 was duplicated; duplication would require observing duplicate sequence numbers or duplicate deliveries at the receiver.

  • An ACK for 2027 also rules out that packets 2026 and 2027 were dropped, since the receiver would not send that cumulative ACK unless those packets had been received.

title: The selective repeat protocol is similar to Go back except
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The selective repeat protocol is similar to Go back N except in the following way

options.label: A
options.html: Frame Formats are similar in both the protocols

options.label: B
options.html: The sender has a window defining maximum number of outstanding frames in both the protocols

options.label: C
options.html: Both uses piggybacked acknowledgements where possible and does not acknowledge every frame explicitly.

options.label: D
options.html: Both uses piggyback approach that acknowledges the most recently received frame

solution:
Correct selections: the statements concerning piggybacked acknowledgements and the practice of acknowledging the most recently received frame represent the exception (difference) between selective repeat and Go-Back-N.

Key differences (why those statements are the exceptions):

  • Acknowledgement behavior: Go-Back-N uses cumulative acknowledgements that effectively acknowledge the highest in-order frame received (it does not send an individual acknowledgement for every received frame). Selective Repeat, by contrast, acknowledges each frame individually so the sender knows exactly which frames were received and which need retransmission.

  • Retransmission and buffering: Go-Back-N discards out-of-order frames at the receiver and the sender retransmits from the missing frame onward. Selective Repeat allows the receiver to buffer out-of-order frames and only retransmits the specific missing frames.

  • Piggybacking: both protocols can use piggybacked acknowledgements when the receiver has data to send back. However, piggybacking does not change the fundamental difference in acknowledgement granularity described above.

Why the other statements are not the exceptions:

  • Frame format similarity: both protocols use similar frame structures because both are sliding-window protocols; this is a similarity, not the distinguishing feature.

  • Sender window: both protocols use a sender window to limit outstanding frames. That is a shared characteristic of sliding-window schemes, not the exception asked for.

Summary: The main exception (difference) is in acknowledgement and retransmission behavior: Go-Back-N uses cumulative acknowledgements and retransmits multiple frames after a loss, while Selective Repeat uses individual acknowledgements and retransmits only the missing frames.

title: How many check bits are required for bit data word
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: How many check bits are required for a 16-bit data word to detect 2-bit errors and correct single-bit errors using a Hamming code (SEC-DED)?
solution:
A Hamming code built only for single-error correction (SEC) needs the smallest check-bit count r satisfying 2r ≥ m + r + 1 for an m-bit data word. To also detect double-bit errors (SEC-DED), one further overall parity bit is added on top of that SEC code, so the total check-bit count p must instead satisfy 2(p−1) ≥ m + p.

  1. For a 16-bit data word, m = 16. Testing p = 5 in the SEC-DED inequality: 2(p−1) = 24 = 16, and m + p = 16 + 5 = 21; since 16 is less than 21, 5 check bits do not satisfy the inequality.

  2. Testing p = 6: 2(p−1) = 25 = 32, and m + p = 16 + 6 = 22; since 32 is at least 22, the inequality is satisfied.

  3. Since p = 5 fails and p = 6 is the smallest value that satisfies the inequality, 6 is the minimum number of check bits required.

Independent check: build the SEC-DED code from a plain SEC Hamming code. For m = 16, the smallest r satisfying 2r ≥ m + r + 1 is r = 5, since 25 = 32 ≥ 16 + 5 + 1 = 22, while 24 = 16 does not cover 16 + 4 + 1 = 21. Adding the one extra overall parity bit needed for double-error detection gives 5 + 1 = 6 total check bits, matching the result above.

So a 16-bit data word needs 6 check bits for a SEC-DED Hamming code, which matches the official ISRO 2013 Computer Science answer key.

title: Which sublayer of DLL is responsible for error detection?
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which sublayer of DLL is responsible for error detection?
solution:
Concept. Handling errors on a link is two separate jobs, and the IEEE 802 model places them in two different sublayers of the data link layer. Detection answers one question — are the bits that arrived the bits that were sent? — and is answered by a redundancy check carried inside every frame. Error control, or recovery, is what happens afterwards: acknowledging frames, keeping them in sequence and retransmitting whatever did not survive.

Applying the split to the data link sublayers:

  1. The sending station’s Media Access Control sublayer runs a cyclic redundancy check over the frame’s fields and writes the result into the frame check sequence, the trailer that closes every IEEE 802.3 frame.

  2. The receiving Media Access Control sublayer recomputes that same CRC over the bits it actually received and compares the result with the frame check sequence it was handed. A mismatch means the frame is damaged, and the frame is discarded. This recompute-and-compare step is precisely what “error detection” names.

  3. Logical Link Control, IEEE 802.2, sits above it and defines no check field of its own. Its acknowledged and connection-mode services number frames, acknowledge them and retransmit the missing ones — that is error control and recovery, which can only run after some other mechanism has already detected the damage.

Cross-check against the standards and the other candidates:

  • IEEE Std 802 lists among the Media Access Control sublayer’s functions “protection against errors, generally by means of generating and checking frame check sequences”, and IEEE 802.3 assigns frame check sequence generation and validation to that sublayer while stating that it provides no error recovery.

  • The physical layer moves an unstructured stream of bits and defines no frame fields at all, so there is nothing there to compute a check over.

  • The application layer operates on user-level messages several layers above the link between two directly connected stations.

A word on the exam shorthand. IEEE 802 is often summarised in one line as “LLC — flow control and error control; MAC — media access”, and that line is what makes Logical Link Control look attractive here. It is a statement about error control — the acknowledgement-and-retransmission machinery. The step that actually detects a corrupted frame is the frame check sequence, and that field is generated and verified by the Media Access Control sublayer.

Answer: MAC.

title: The main function of Data link layer is
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The main function of Data link layer is
solution:
Concept: In the OSI reference model, each layer is assigned its own distinct set of responsibilities so that node-to-node link handling stays separate from end-to-end network and application concerns. The Data Link layer's mandate covers framing (dividing the bit stream into frames), physical (MAC) addressing between adjacent nodes, medium access control, flow control on the link, and — the responsibility most emphasized in standard curricula — error control: detecting bit errors introduced by the physical medium and recovering from them, using detection methods such as CRC/parity together with correction mechanisms such as Hamming/Reed–Solomon codes or ARQ-based retransmission.

Application: Among the given options, only “Error detection and Correction” matches this mandate: the Data Link layer both detects errors (CRC/parity) and recovers from them, either via a forward error-correcting code (e.g., Hamming) or by having the sender retransmit the frame after a NAK/timeout (ARQ) — so “correction” here does not require the receiver to always fix bits itself; requesting a clean retransmission is itself a standard, textbook form of error correction at this layer. This is why the reported concern (“only detection, not correction”) does not hold: correction is achieved through retransmission-based ARQ (the common case) and, on some links (e.g., wireless/satellite), through FEC codes as well — both are documented Data Link layer mechanisms, not just detection.

Cross-check — why the other options do not fit:

  • Routing selects a path for data across multiple interconnected networks using logical (IP) addressing; this is a Network layer function, operating beyond a single physical link.

  • Encryption is generally provided at higher layers (e.g., TLS, IPsec) or as an optional feature of specific link technologies; it is not this layer's principal, defining responsibility.

  • “None” is ruled out because this layer does have well-documented responsibilities of its own — framing, physical addressing, flow control, and media access, in addition to error control.

Result: The main function among the options offered is “Error detection and Correction.”

solution:
Concept

In minimum-distance (nearest-neighbour) decoding, a received word is corrected to the valid codeword that lies at the smallest Hamming distance from it. The Hamming distance between two equal-length bit strings is the number of positions in which they differ. A correction is committed only when exactly one valid codeword is strictly closest; if two or more valid codewords share that smallest distance, no unique nearest codeword exists and the error cannot be resolved unambiguously.

Application

Compute the Hamming distance from the received word 01000 to each valid codeword by counting the differing bit positions:

Codeword

Bits

Differing positions vs 01000

Hamming distance

A

00000

position 2

1

B

01110

positions 3 and 4

2

C

11000

position 1

1

The smallest Hamming distance is 1, and it is achieved by two different valid codewords, 00000 and 11000. Because the minimum distance is shared rather than held by a single codeword, there is no unique nearest codeword to decode to.

Cross-check

For the decoder to commit a correction, the winner must beat every other codeword strictly. Here the closest distance (1) ties between two codewords while the third (01110) sits farther away at distance 2. A tie at the minimum violates the strict-uniqueness requirement, so the system reports that it is unable to correct the error.

title: What will be the minimum Hamming distance for the following

bodyHtml: What will be the minimum Hamming distance for the following coding scheme?
solution:
Concept: The minimum Hamming distance (dmin) of a coding scheme is the smallest number of bit positions in which any two distinct valid codewords differ. The Hamming distance between two equal-length codewords is the count of positions where their bits disagree.

Application: The four valid codewords are 00111, 01001, 10101 and 11100. Compare every one of the six possible pairs and count the differing positions:

  1. 00111 vs 01001: differ at positions 2, 3, 4 → distance = 3

  2. 00111 vs 10101: differ at positions 1, 4 → distance = 2

  3. 00111 vs 11100: differ at positions 1, 2, 4, 5 → distance = 4

  4. 01001 vs 10101: differ at positions 1, 2, 3 → distance = 3

  5. 01001 vs 11100: differ at positions 1, 3, 5 → distance = 3

  6. 10101 vs 11100: differ at positions 2, 5 → distance = 2

Cross-check: The smallest of the six distances {3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2} is 2, achieved by the pairs 00111–10101 and 10101–11100. No pair differs in only one position, so the distance cannot be 1.

Result: the minimum Hamming distance of this coding scheme is 2.

title: Let is the message to be transmitted using Hamming code
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Let M = 1000 be the message to be transmitted using the Hamming code with odd parity. Which of the following is the valid 7-bit codeword corresponding to the message M?
solution:
Goal: encode the 4-bit message M = 1000 (read as M1 M2 M3 M4 = 1, 0, 0, 0) into a 7-bit Hamming(7,4) codeword using odd parity.

Standard layout, counting positions from the left (1 to 7): P1 P2 M1 P3 M2 M3 M4. Parity bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4; data bits at positions 3, 5, 6, 7.

Place the message bits: position 3 (M1) = 1, position 5 (M2) = 0, position 6 (M3) = 0, position 7 (M4) = 0.

Odd parity means each parity bit, together with the bits it covers, must contain an odd number of 1s.

  1. P1 covers positions 1, 3, 5, 7. The data bits there (3, 5, 7) are 1, 0, 0 = one 1 (already odd), so P1 = 0.

  2. P2 covers positions 2, 3, 6, 7. The data bits there (3, 6, 7) are 1, 0, 0 = one 1 (already odd), so P2 = 0.

  3. P3 covers positions 4, 5, 6, 7. The data bits there (5, 6, 7) are 0, 0, 0 = zero 1s (even), so P3 = 1 to make it odd.

Assemble positions 1 to 7: P1 P2 M1 P3 M2 M3 M4 = 0 0 1 1 0 0 0. The valid 7-bit codeword is 0011000.

title: Hamming code is used to correct 1-bit error. If the

bodyHtml: Hamming code is used to correct 1-bit error. If the number of parity bits are 6 then the maximum number of message bits can be_____.
solution:
Key formula: 2^p ≥ p + m + 1

This formula arises because p parity bits produce 2^p distinct syndromes, which must cover every possible single-bit error position among the total bits (m message bits + p parity bits) plus the no-error case, hence the +1.

  1. Let p = 6.

  2. Apply the formula: 2^6 ≥ 6 + m + 1

  3. 64 ≥ m + 7

  4. m ≤ 57

Therefore, the maximum number of message bits is 57.

solution: The primary reason block parity (Longitudinal Redundancy Check) was invented was to catch burst errors (where multiple consecutive bits are corrupted during transmission). title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 2
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In order that a code is ‘\(t\)’ error correcting, the minimum Hamming distance should be :
solution:
Concept: For a code to correct up to t bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance between any two valid codewords must satisfy d_min ≥ 2t + 1. This follows from the nearest-codeword decoding rule: every valid codeword defines a sphere of radius t (all words reachable by at most t bit-flips from it), and decoding is guaranteed to recover the correct codeword only when no two such spheres overlap.

Application: Applying this rule to the item:

  1. Let C1 and C2 be any two valid codewords, decoded by nearest-codeword matching.

  2. First check that a distance of only 2t is NOT enough: if d(C1, C2) = 2t exactly, construct a received word W that agrees with C1 in t of the differing positions and with C2 in the other t differing positions. Then d(C1, W) = t = d(C2, W), so a single t-bit error pattern produces a W equidistant from both codewords — decoding is ambiguous, so 2t cannot guarantee correction.

  3. Now check that d(C1, C2) ≥ 2t + 1 IS enough: if C1 is transmitted with at most t errors producing W, then d(C1, W) ≤ t.

  4. By the triangle inequality, d(C1, C2) ≤ d(C1, W) + d(W, C2), which rearranges to d(W, C2) ≥ d(C1, C2) − d(C1, W) ≥ (2t + 1) − t = t + 1.

  5. Since d(W, C2) ≥ t + 1 > t ≥ d(C1, W), the received word W is always strictly closer to C1 than to C2, so nearest-codeword decoding always recovers C1 correctly. So 2t + 1 is both necessary (step 2) and sufficient (steps 3–4), i.e. the minimum Hamming distance of the whole code must satisfy d_min ≥ 2t + 1.

Cross-check: The well-known (7, 4) Hamming code has d_min = 3 and is documented to correct exactly 1-bit errors (t = 1). Substituting into the derived relation: 2t + 1 = 2(1) + 1 = 3, which matches d_min = 3 exactly — confirming the relation independently.

Result: The minimum Hamming distance required for a code to be t-error-correcting is 2t + 1.

title: Consider information bit polynomial is Let the g(x) then find
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Consider information bit polynomial is x4 + x2 + x. Let the g(x) = 1011 then find the codeword corresponding to these information bits if g(x) is used as the generator ?
solution:
Final codeword: 10110000

  • Convert the information polynomial x^4 + x^2 + x to bits (coefficients from x^4 down to x^0): 1 0 1 1 0 → 10110.

  • Generator g(x) = 1011 has degree 3, so append three zeros (multiply message by x^3): 10110 → 10110000.

  • Perform binary polynomial division of 10110000 by 1011. The divisor cancels the leading bits and the remainder after division is 000.

  • Attach the remainder (000) to the original message bits to form the codeword. Since the remainder is 000, the final codeword is 10110000.

title: The message is to be transmitted using the CRC polynomial
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The message 1001 is to be transmitted using the CRC polynomial x³ + x + 1 to protect it from errors. The message that should be transmitted is –
solution:
Concept: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) detects transmission errors using binary (mod-2) polynomial division. For a generator polynomial of degree r, the sender appends r zero bits to the message, divides the result by the generator's binary bit pattern using XOR (mod-2, no-borrow) division, and replaces the appended zeros with the resulting remainder — the Frame Check Sequence (FCS) — to form the transmitted frame. The receiver divides the received frame by the same generator; a zero remainder confirms that no error altered the frame in transit.

Application: For this message, the generator polynomial x3+x+1 corresponds to the binary bit pattern 1011 (coefficients of x3, x2, x1, x0), so its degree is r = 3.

  1. Append r = 3 zero bits to the message 1001, forming the augmented dividend 1001000.

  2. Divide 1001000 by 1011 using mod-2 (XOR) division: the leading 4 bits 1001 XOR 1011 = 0010; bring down the next bit (0) to get 0100.

  3. The leading bit of 0100 is 0, so no XOR is applied; bring down the next bit (0) to get 1000.

  4. 1000 XOR 1011 = 0011; bring down the last bit (0) to get 0110.

  5. The leading bit of 0110 is 0, so the division stops; the final 3 bits give the remainder = 110.

  6. Replace the 3 appended zero bits of the augmented dividend with this remainder: 1001 followed by 110 gives the transmitted message 1001110.

Cross-check: A correctly formed frame divides evenly (remainder 000) by the generator. Dividing 1001110 by 1011 using the same mod-2 process leaves remainder 000, confirming 1001110 is the valid transmitted message.

title: Which of the following functions of the Data Link layer
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
Which of the following functions of the Data Link layer are correct?
1.Framing: Framing is a function of the data link layer. It provides a way for a sender to transmit a set of bits that are meaningful to the receiver. This can be accomplished by attaching special bit patterns to the beginning and end of the frame.

2.Physical addressing: After creating frames, Data link layer adds physical addresses (MAC address) of sender and/or receiver in the header of each frame.

3.Error control: Data link layer provides the mechanism of error control in which it detects and retransmits damaged or lost frames.

4.Flow Control: The data rate must be constant on both sides or else the data may get corrupted thus, flow control coordinates that amount of data that can be sent before receiving an acknowledgement.

5.Access control: When a single communication channel is shared by multiple devices, MAC sub-layer of the data link layer helps to determine which device has control over the channel at a given time.
solution:
All five statements are correct. Brief explanations of each function follow:

  • Framing: The Data Link layer organizes raw bits into frames and marks frame boundaries so the receiver can identify meaningful units.

  • Physical addressing: The Data Link layer adds MAC (physical) addresses to frame headers to identify the sender and/or receiver on the local network.

  • Error control: The layer detects corrupted frames and can request retransmission to provide reliable delivery over a noisy link.

  • Flow control: Flow control regulates the rate of frame transmission so the sender does not overwhelm the receiver.

  • Access control: When multiple devices share a medium, the MAC sublayer decides which device may use the channel at a given time (e.g., CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA).

title: What is true about MAC frame? There is restriction on

a. There is a restriction on the minimum size of the data

c. FS field not included in CRC calculations

d. FS field uses only one set of A & C flags.
solution:
Answer summary:

  • There is a restriction on the minimum size of the data: Correct. Token Ring defines a minimum frame length to ensure reliable token passing and proper error detection.

  • Access Control (AC) field is available in data frames as well as in token frames: Correct. The AC field is used in both token and data frames to control access and priority on the ring.

  • Frame Status (FS) field not included in CRC calculations: Incorrect. The Frame Status field is part of the frame status information and is not properly characterized as being excluded from frame integrity mechanisms.

  • FS field uses only one set of A & C flags: Incorrect. The Frame Status field conveys Address-recognized and Copy flags and can represent multiple flag combinations rather than a single fixed set.

Conclusion: The correct selection is the option that selects the two true statements: the minimum-size restriction and the presence of the Access Control field in both token and data frames.

title: Stations Alpha and Zeta are the transmitting on an Ethernet.

bodyHtml: Stations Alpha and Zeta are the transmitting on an Ethernet. Both Alpha and Zeta attempt to transmit a frame but they collide and Zeta wins the first backoff race. With what probability, Zeta wins the first backoff race?
solution:
A) 0.25

At every attempt to transmit a frame, both Alpha and Zeta chooses value of ‘K’ randomly. Based on the value of ‘K’ we will decide by looking at the backoff time who will win the race. We know that the station having smaller backoff time will win and it will send the frames earlier.

Attempt 1: Value of K is 0 <= K <= 2x-1 (x is the attempt number). Since Zeta won the race that means Zeta must have chosen the smaller number. Now K can be 0 or 1. So Zeta chose 0 and Alpha chose 1.

Total possibilities are (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1).

Probability = Favorable Outcome / Total outcome.

Favorable Outcome = (1,0)

P = 1 / 4 = 0.25

title: Consider the following statements High speed Ethernet works on optic

bodyHtml:
Consider the following statements :

A. High speed Ethernet works on optic fiber.

B. A point to point protocol over Ethernet is a network protocol for encapsulating PPP frames inside Ethernet frames.

C. High speed Ethernet does not work on optic fiber.

D. A point to point protocol over Ethernet is a network protocol for encapsulating Ethernet frames inside PPP frames.

solution:
Answer: The statements "High speed Ethernet works on optic fiber." and "A point to point protocol over Ethernet is a network protocol for encapsulating PPP frames inside Ethernet frames." are true; the other two statements are false.

  • "High speed Ethernet works on optic fiber." — True. Many high-speed Ethernet standards (for example 100BASE-FX, 1000BASE-X and other Gigabit variants) use fiber-optic media for long-distance or high-bandwidth links.

  • "A point to point protocol over Ethernet is a network protocol for encapsulating PPP frames inside Ethernet frames." — True. PPPoE (Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet) carries PPP frames within Ethernet frames to provide PPP services over an Ethernet link.

  • "High speed Ethernet does not work on optic fiber." — False. This directly contradicts the true statement that high-speed Ethernet can and does use fiber-optic media.

  • "A point to point protocol over Ethernet is a network protocol for encapsulating Ethernet frames inside PPP frames." — False. The encapsulation direction is reversed: PPPoE encapsulates PPP frames inside Ethernet frames, not Ethernet frames inside PPP frames.

Conclusion: The correct selection is the one stating that the first two statements are true and the last two are false.

title: The efficiency of ethernet increases
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The efficiency of ethernet increases
solution:
Formula: efficiency = 1/(1 + 6.44·a)

Definition: a = Tp / Tt

Where Tp is the propagation delay and Tt is the transmission time (frame transmission duration).

Key insight:

  • Because efficiency = 1/(1 + 6.44·a), reducing the ratio a increases efficiency.

  • To reduce a = Tp/Tt you can either decrease Tp (propagation delay) or increase Tt (transmission time).

Practical implication: decrease propagation delay (for example by shortening cable length or improving propagation speed) or increase frame transmission time (for example by using larger frames) to increase Ethernet efficiency.

Conclusion: Efficiency increases when propagation time decreases and transmission time increases.

title: IPv4 payload size from header fields
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The first 10 bytes of an IPv4 datagram header are: 45 00 00 5B 00 03 00 00 59 06. What is the IPv4 payload (data) size in bytes?
solution:
Concept

In IPv4, the Total Length field gives the size of the entire datagram, including the header and payload.

The IHL field gives the header length in 32-bit words, so header bytes equal IHL multiplied by 4. Therefore, payload size equals Total Length minus header length.

Application

  1. Split the given header prefix into bytes: 45 00 00 5B 00 03 00 00 59 06.

  2. From the first byte 0x45, the low hexadecimal digit is 5, so IHL = 5.

  3. Header length = 5 × 4 = 20 bytes.

  4. The Total Length field is 0x005B, which is 5 × 16 + 11 = 91 bytes.

  5. Payload size = 91 − 20 = 71 bytes.

Cross-check

Adding the 20-byte header and 71-byte payload gives 91 bytes, matching the Total Length field. Hence the IPv4 payload (data) size is 71 bytes.

title: Which of the following field is not there in IP

bodyHtml: Which of the following fields was introduced in the IPv6 base header and has no direct counterpart in the IPv4 header?
solution:
Concept

Protocol versions may either rename an existing header function or introduce a new field. A direct counterpart performs the same operational role even when the field name changes.

Comparing IPv4 with IPv6 therefore requires checking both the header diagrams and each field’s function.

Application

The IPv6 Flow Label is a 20-bit field used to identify packets that belong to the same flow for special handling. IPv4 has no field with that role, so FLOW LABEL meets both parts of the question.

Contrast

  • VERSION appears at the beginning of both IPv4 and IPv6 headers and identifies the header format.

  • CHECKSUM refers to the IPv4 Header Checksum; IPv6 removes that base-header field rather than adding it.

  • HOP LIMIT is the IPv6 form of IPv4’s Time to Live field, so the two names serve the same per-router lifetime function.

Cross-check and result

The standard IPv4 header diagram has Version, Header Checksum, and Time to Live, while the IPv6 base header has Version, Flow Label, and Hop Limit. The functional comparison leaves FLOW LABEL as the introduced field without an IPv4 counterpart.

title: What is the maximum length of an IPv4 address
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the maximum length of an IPv4 address ?
solution: An IPv4 address is a numerical label assigned to each device connected to a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication. The '4' in IPv4 stands for version 4, which uses a 32-bit address format. This means the maximum length of an IPv4 address is exactly 32 bits, typically represented in dotted-decimal notation as four decimal numbers separated by periods (e.g., 192.168.0.1). Each of the four octets represents 8 bits, totaling 32 bits (4 × 8 = 32). Option A (16 bits) is incorrect because it only represents half the required address space. Option D (128 bits) refers to IPv6 addresses, which were developed to address the exhaustion of IPv4 addresses. Therefore, the correct answer is 32 bits.

title: What is the hexadecimal representation of single IPv6 address block
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the size of an IPv6 address (in bits)?
solution:
Concept

An IP address is a fixed-length binary identifier. IPv6 was introduced to greatly expand the limited address space of IPv4, so it defines a longer fixed-length address whose size is standardised by RFC 4291.

Applying it here

RFC 4291 fixes the length of every IPv6 address at 128 bits. This length is organised as eight 16-bit groups called hextets, so 8 × 16 = 128 bits. When fully written out, each 16-bit group becomes four hexadecimal digits, giving 8 × 4 = 32 hexadecimal digits (32 × 4 = 128 bits, a consistent cross-check). The written form can be shortened by omitting leading zeros and using :: compression, but the underlying address is always 128 bits.

Why the other values do not fit

  • 32 bits is the length of an IPv4 address, the predecessor protocol.

  • 64 bits is the width of the interface identifier that fills the host portion of a standard /64 IPv6 subnet.

  • 256 bits is not used as an IP address length.

Therefore, an IPv6 address is 128 bits long.

title: What does the term ‘IP Address’ stand for
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What does the term ‘IP Address’ stand for ?
solution: An IP Address stands for Internet Protocol Address. It is a unique numerical label assigned to each device connected to a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication.

title: Length of IPv4 address is bits.
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Length of IPv4 address is _________ bits.
solution:
The correct option is B (32).

An Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) address is a 32-bit numeric address used to uniquely identify a device on a network.

  • It is written in dotted-decimal notation, consisting of 4 octets (groups of 8 bits) separated by periods (e.g., 192.168.1.1).

  • Calculation: 4 octets x 8 bits/octet = 32 bits.

  • The total number of possible unique IPv4 addresses is 232, which is approximately 4.3 billion.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q117
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Why are IP addresses required even though MAC addresses are globally unique?

options.label: D
options.html: MAC addresses cannot be used for routing across networks

solution:
Concept: In the OSI/TCP-IP layering model, a MAC address is a Layer 2 (Data Link) address burned into a network interface by its manufacturer -- it is globally unique but flat, meaning it carries no information about which network the device sits on. An IP address is a Layer 3 (Network) address with a hierarchical network-plus-host structure, and routers use only that network portion to decide the next hop when forwarding a packet between different networks.

Application: Because a MAC address has no network component, a router receiving a frame cannot tell from the MAC address alone which network, among many separate networks, the destination belongs to. Global uniqueness only guarantees that no two interfaces share the same MAC value; it does not organize interfaces into networks. The IP address's network portion is what lets a router look up a route and forward the packet toward the correct destination network, so IP addressing is required in addition to the MAC address even though the MAC address is already globally unique.

Checking each option against this concept:

  • Routers strip MAC addresses permanently -- at each hop, a router replaces the frame's Layer 2 header with new source and destination MAC addresses for the next physical link; it re-addresses the frame at every hop rather than permanently removing MAC addressing from the network.

  • IP addresses are faster -- address lookups for MAC-based forwarding (switching/ARP tables) and IP-based forwarding (routing tables) both run as hardware-assisted operations at comparable speeds; raw lookup speed is not the property that makes network-layer addressing necessary.

  • MAC addresses expire periodically -- a manufacturer-assigned MAC address is burned into the interface and stays fixed for its lifetime, with no built-in expiry or renewal cycle (software-based MAC randomization for privacy is a separate, optional mechanism).

  • MAC addresses cannot be used for routing across networks -- this matches the concept above: a flat, non-hierarchical Layer 2 address carries no network-membership information, so it cannot serve as the basis for forwarding across separate networks, which is exactly why the hierarchical IP address is needed alongside it.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q61
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the full form of IP?
solution:
Concept

An initialism is expanded by mapping each letter to the full word whose initial it represents in the standard term.

In computer networking, standardized names distinguish protocols, which define communication rules, from service providers, programs, and hardware interfaces.

Application

Here, I corresponds to Internet and P corresponds to Protocol. Therefore, IP expands to Internet Protocol.

Contrast

  • Internet Provider is a generic phrase for an organization that supplies internet connectivity.

  • Internal Program is a generic phrase for software used inside an organization or system.

  • Interface Port is a generic phrase for a connection point through which a component exchanges data.

Cross-check

Internet standards use Internet Protocol as the title of the protocol specified for IP packet addressing and delivery.

Therefore, the full form of IP is Internet Protocol.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q62
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following is not a standardized Internet Protocol (IP) version?
solution:
Concept

Internet Protocol versions are identified by standardized specifications and by the version field carried in an IP packet.

A historical or experimental protocol label is not automatically a standardized Internet Protocol version; the specification status must be checked.

Application

The IANA IP Version Numbers registry marks decimal values 2–3 as unassigned, value 4 as Internet Protocol with RFC 791, and value 6 as Internet Protocol version 6 with RFC 8200.

Cross-check and contrast

  • IPv3: its numeric version value, 3, is unassigned in the IANA registry.

  • IPv4: a standardized Internet Protocol version with 32-bit addresses.

  • IPv6: a standardized Internet Protocol version with 128-bit addresses.

  • None of these: would require every listed named version to be standardized, which the specification check does not support.

Result

Therefore, IPv3 is the version name that is not valid in the standardized IP-version sense used by the question.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q19
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In standard dotted-decimal notation, an IPv4 address is divided into how many blocks?
solution:
Concept

An IPv4 address contains 32 bits.

Standard dotted-decimal notation groups those bits into 8-bit octets, and each octet is written as a decimal value from 0 to 255.

Application

  1. Divide the 32 address bits by 8 bits per octet: 32 ÷ 8 = 4.

  2. For example, 192.168.1.10 has the four decimal blocks 192, 168, 1, and 10.

Cross-check

Four octets account for 4 × 8 = 32 bits, so the IPv4 address is divided into four blocks.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q21
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the length of an IPv4 address?
solution:
Concept

Protocol specifications define address widths in bits, and 8 bits make 1 byte.

IPv4 uses a fixed 32-bit address, regardless of how the address is displayed in dotted-decimal notation.

Application

  1. Start with the IPv4 address width: 32 bits.

  2. Convert bits to bytes: 32 ÷ 8 = 4 bytes.

Contrast

  • 8 bytes represents 64 bits, which is twice the IPv4 address width.

  • 16 bytes represents 128 bits, the address width used by IPv6 rather than IPv4.

  • 6 bytes represents 48 bits, a width commonly used for MAC addresses rather than IPv4 addresses.

Result

Therefore, an IPv4 address is 4 bytes long.

title: MPPSC State Forest Service Main Exam 2023 Q11
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Each device on the Internet is given a unique network address known as its ____.
solution:
In computer networking, every device connected to a network must be uniquely identifiable so that data sent across the network reaches the correct destination. This identification is provided by a network address assigned at the Network Layer of the OSI/TCP-IP model, which routers use to locate and route data across interconnected networks.

The Internet is a global network of interconnected networks that runs on the TCP/IP protocol suite. On the Internet, the network-layer address used to route data toward a device is called its Internet Protocol (IP) Address. An IP address (a 32-bit number in IPv4, or a 128-bit number in IPv6) is bound to a device's network interface, and routers use it, hop by hop, to forward packets toward that device. (In practice, a device may sit behind Network Address Translation, NAT, sharing one public IP address with other devices on the same private network, with port numbers distinguishing the individual devices behind that shared address; even so, the IP address remains the network-layer identifier used for Internet-wide routing, which is exactly what this term refers to.)

  • Media Access Control Address: a 48-bit hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card, operating at the Data Link Layer.

  • Specific Address: does not appear in networking standards (IETF, IEEE, IANA) as a named address type; it has no defined bit-length, notation, or assigning authority.

  • Port Address: a 16-bit number that operates at the Transport Layer to distinguish individual processes or applications on a device.

Hence, the network-layer address used to route data to each device on the Internet is its Internet Protocol (IP) Address.

bodyHtml: Consider an IP link with a maximum transfer unit of 700 bytes and each datagram size to send is 2400-bytes. Assume that the datagram which has been recently sent has an identification number as 422. What is the total number of fragments that has to be sent to transfer the full datagram and what is the offset value of the 2nd fragment from all the fragmented datagrams. solution:
Key data: MTU = 700 bytes; IPv4 header = 20 bytes; total packet length = 2400 bytes (includes header) → data payload = 2400 − 20 = 2380 bytes.

  • Maximum data per fragment = 700 − 20 = 680 bytes (must be a multiple of 8; 680/8 = 85 OK).

  • Number of full 680-byte fragments = floor(2380 / 680) = 3.

  • Remaining data = 2380 − (3 × 680) = 340 bytes → final fragment carries 340 bytes.

Fragment details (data + header) and offsets (number of data bytes before the fragment):

  1. Fragment 1: 680 bytes data + 20 bytes header = 700 bytes total; offset = 0 bytes.

  2. Fragment 2: 680 bytes data + 20 bytes header = 700 bytes total; offset = 680 bytes.

  3. Fragment 3: 680 bytes data + 20 bytes header = 700 bytes total; offset = 1360 bytes.

  4. Fragment 4: 340 bytes data + 20 bytes header = 360 bytes total; offset = 2040 bytes.

Answer: Total number of fragments = 4; offset of the second fragment = 680 bytes.

title: Router with MTU of bytes has received an IP packet

bodyHtml: A Router with MTU of 1024 bytes has received an IP packet of size 4240 bytes with an IP header of 20 bytes. The value of MF and offset of the 3rd fragment is
solution:
Given: MTU = 1024 bytes; IP packet size = 4240 bytes; IP header = 20 bytes.

  • Compute total data payload: 4240 - 20 = 4220 bytes.

  • Maximum data per fragment = MTU - header = 1024 - 20 = 1004 bytes. Fragment data must be a multiple of 8 bytes, so use 1000 bytes per fragment.

  • Number of full 1000-byte fragments = floor(4220 / 1000) = 4; remainder for last fragment = 4220 - 4000 = 220 bytes.

  • Offsets are in 8-byte units. Fragment offsets (in units of 8 bytes):

    • Fragment 1: offset = 0

    • Fragment 2: offset = 1000 / 8 = 125

    • Fragment 3: offset = 2000 / 8 = 250

    • Fragment 4: offset = 3000 / 8 = 375

    • Fragment 5 (last): offset = 4000 / 8 = 500

  • MF (More Fragments) = 1 for all fragments except the last one. The third fragment is not the last, so MF = 1.

Therefore, for the third fragment: MF = 1, OFFSET = 250.

title: Consider the following fields in IP header and choose correct
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Consider the following fields in IP header and choose correct combination:
solution:
Correct matching: P – 4, Q – 3, R – 1, S – 2

  • P — MF (More Fragments): The MF flag is 1 when more fragments follow and 0 for the last fragment. Therefore MF corresponds to 'Zero for the last fragment.'

  • Q — DF (Don't Fragment): When DF=1 the packet must not be fragmented. Thus DF corresponds to 'If it is 1, then fragmentation is not allowed.'

  • R — Fragment Offset: The fragment offset is 0 in the first fragment and nonzero in later fragments. Therefore it corresponds to 'Zero for the first fragment.'

  • S — Strict Source Routing option: Options that must be copied into all fragments (those with the copy bit set), such as source routing, are present in every fragment. Therefore this corresponds to 'It must be available in all fragments.'

Hence the correct answer is the mapping shown above: P – 4, Q – 3, R – 1, S – 2.

title: Suppose all the bits in the IP4 packet including the

title: IP header checksum must be recomputed in each router before
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
IP header checksum must be recomputed in each router before being forwarded to next router, the reasons may be

a. TTL field b. Fragment offset field

c. 16 – bit datagram length field d. 16-bit datagram identification field

Find the correct reasons.
solution:
The IP header checksum covers only the IP header. Routers must recompute this checksum whenever they modify any header fields.

  • TTL (Time To Live): The TTL is decremented by each router, which changes the header and therefore requires recomputing the checksum.

  • Fragment Offset: If a router fragments a datagram, it assigns fragment offsets for the resulting fragments. That modification to the header necessitates updating the checksum.

  • 16-bit Total Length (Datagram Length): When fragmentation occurs, the total length of each fragment differs from the original datagram; routers that create fragments update this field, so the checksum must be recalculated.

  • 16-bit Identification: This field is set by the sender to help reassemble fragments and is not modified by routers. It does not by itself require checksum recomputation.

Conclusion: The header checksum must be recomputed for changes to TTL, Fragment Offset, and the 16-bit total datagram length. The 16-bit identification field is not changed by routers and is not a reason to recompute the checksum.

title: An IP router with maximum transmission unit (MTU) of bytes

bodyHtml: An IP router with a maximum transmission unit (MTU) of 2000 bytes has received an IP packet of size 5000 bytes with an IP header of length 20 bytes. The values of the relevant fields in the header of the second IP fragment generated by the router for this packet are:
solution:
Solution summary:

  1. Compute total data payload: 5000 (total packet) - 20 (IP header) = 4980 bytes.

  2. Maximum payload per fragment before alignment: MTU - IP header = 2000 - 20 = 1980 bytes.

    Payload must be a multiple of 8 bytes, so choose the largest multiple of 8 ≤ 1980: 1976 bytes.

  3. Number of fragments: ceil(4980 / 1976) = 3 fragments.

  4. Sizes, offsets, and MF flags for each fragment:

    • First fragment: payload = 1976, datagram size = 1976 + 20 = 1996, MF = 1, fragment offset = 0.

    • Second fragment: payload = 1976, datagram size = 1996, MF = 1 (more fragments follow), fragment offset = 1976 / 8 = 247.

    • Third (final) fragment: remaining payload = 4980 - 2×1976 = 1028, datagram size = 1028 + 20 = 1048, MF = 0, fragment offset = (2×1976) / 8 = 494.

  5. Therefore, the correct values for the second fragment are: MF = 1, datagram size = 1996, fragment offset = 247.

title: In IPv4, packet fragmentation and reassembly is handled by IPv4
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: In IPv4, packet fragmentation and reassembly is handled by –

options.label: A
options.html: using the More Fragments and Fragment Offset Fields

solution:
Concept

Every physical link imposes a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) — the largest payload a single frame on that link may carry. When an IPv4 datagram is bigger than the MTU of the next link, the datagram is split into fragments, and only the destination host puts them back together. IPv4 keeps all of the bookkeeping for that split-and-rejoin inside its own header, in the Identification field, the Flags field (which contains the More Fragments bit) and the Fragment Offset field.

The general rule: fragmentation is a Network layer operation driven by IPv4 header fields, and reassembly happens end to end at the destination, never hop by hop.

Applying it to this question

The stem asks which mechanism actually performs fragmentation and reassembly. The three IPv4 header fields that carry fragmentation state work together like this:

IPv4 header field

What it carries

Job during split and rejoin

Identification (16 bits)

The same value copied into every fragment of one datagram

Groups arriving fragments that belong to the same original datagram

Flags — More Fragments (MF)

Set to 1 on every fragment except the last one

Tells the receiver whether further pieces are still on the way

Fragment Offset (13 bits)

This fragment's position in the original payload, counted in units of 8 bytes

Places each fragment at the correct byte position in the rebuilt datagram

So the mechanism the stem is asking about is "using the More Fragments and Fragment Offset Fields": the MF bit signals that the datagram is still incomplete, and the Fragment Offset says exactly where each received piece belongs. Together they are what lets the destination rebuild the original datagram.

Cross-check against the other mechanisms

  • Header Checksum — a 16-bit check computed over the IPv4 header bytes alone and recomputed at every hop. It detects a header damaged in transit, but it carries no information about how a datagram was divided.

  • Encapsulating packets in larger data frames — a Data Link layer packaging step. A link will not accept a frame larger than its own MTU, so making frames bigger is simply not available as a way to move an oversized datagram.

  • MAC Header — a Data Link layer header holding hardware addresses for one hop only. Each router strips it and writes a fresh one for the next link, so it never reaches the destination and cannot carry reassembly state.

This confirms the reading: reassembly state has to survive the whole path, and only the IPv4 header — through the More Fragments flag and the Fragment Offset — carries it end to end.

In the IPv4 header, fragmentation is supported using specific fields. One of them is the Fragment Offset field.

The size of this field is 13 bits

This allows proper reassembly of fragmented packets at the destination

So, the Fragment Offset field in IPv4 is always 13 bits long.

title: Consider very large network of routers. Sender and receiver are
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
Consider a very large network of 6000 routers. Sender and receiver are connected with this network. Sender sends data to receiver and after some time sender receives ICMP time exceeded message for the same transmitted datagram. The maximum number of routers that can be travelled by datagrams when ICMP message reaches back to sender is __________

&Protocols
solution:
Key facts: the TTL (Time To Live) field in an IP header is 8 bits, so its maximum value is 255.

  • Forward datagram: If the sender sets the TTL to 255, the datagram can be forwarded across up to 255 routers. At the 255th router the TTL becomes zero and that router drops the packet and generates an ICMP Time Exceeded message.

  • ICMP reply: The ICMP Time Exceeded message sent by that router can itself use a TTL up to 255. To count the total routers traversed by both the original datagram and the returning ICMP without double-counting, note that the router that generated the ICMP is included in the forward path already.

Calculation: 255 (forward) + 255 (return) - 1 (shared router counted once) = 509.

Answer: 509 (assuming both the original datagram and the ICMP response use the maximum TTL of 255).

title: Which protocol is used to automatically assign IP addresses to
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which protocol is used to automatically assign IP addresses to devices on a network ?
solution: The correct answer is DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol). DHCP is specifically designed to automatically assign IP addresses and other network configuration parameters, such as subnet masks and default gateways, to devices on a network. When a device connects, it broadcasts a request for an IP address, and the DHCP server responds with available configuration details. This automation eliminates the need for manual IP assignment, reducing errors and administrative overhead.\nDNS (Domain Name System) resolves domain names to IP addresses but does not assign them. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps known IP addresses to physical MAC addresses within a local network, rather than assigning new IPs. RARP (Reverse ARP) is an older protocol that allows a device to discover its own IP address from its MAC address, but it is largely obsolete and not used for automatic assignment in modern networks. Therefore, DHCP is the standard protocol for this purpose.

title: Name the protocol used to find MAC address from IP
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which protocol is used to find a MAC address from an IP address?
solution:
Concept

Address resolution links a network-layer protocol address to the link-layer hardware address needed to deliver a frame on a local network.

The direction of the mapping matters: a protocol-address-to-hardware-address lookup is different from a hardware-address-to-protocol-address lookup.

Application

  1. A sender knows the destination IPv4 address but needs a destination MAC address for the local Ethernet frame.

  2. ARP broadcasts a request for the device that owns that IPv4 address.

  3. The matching device replies with its MAC address, which the sender uses in the frame.

Cross-check and contrast

  • RARP begins with a known MAC address and obtains an IP address.

  • ICMP carries IP control and error messages, including ping-related messages.

  • SMTP transfers email at the application layer.

Therefore, the required protocol is ARP (Address Resolution Protocol).

title: What is the role of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the role of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) in computer networks?

options.label: A
options.html: To translate domain names into IP addresses

options.label: B
options.html: To discover the hardware address (MAC address) corresponding to an IP address

options.label: C
options.html: To identify the route with the shortest path in a network

solution: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps known IP addresses to unknown MAC addresses on a local network. When a device needs to communicate with another, it broadcasts an ARP request asking for the MAC address associated with a specific IP. The device owning that IP responds with its MAC address, enabling proper frame delivery at the data link layer.

title: What is the purpose of the Internet Control Message Protocol
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the purpose of the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) in the TCP/IP protocol suite ?

options.label: A
options.html: To provide secure communication over the internet

options.label: C
options.html: To facilitate the exchange of routing information

options.label: D
options.html: To report errors and control messages related to network operations

solution: ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is used for error reporting and diagnostic functions in IP networks. It helps identify network issues by sending control messages like destination unreachable or time exceeded, enabling tools such as ping and traceroute to function properly.

title: What protocol is used to find the hardware address of
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What protocol is used to find the hardware address of a local device?
solution:
Concept

Every device on a local network has two addresses: a logical IP address and a physical hardware (MAC) address. Address resolution is the process of discovering the unknown hardware address that corresponds to a device whose IP address is already known, so that a frame can actually be delivered on the local link.

Applying it here

To send data on a LAN, a host knows the destination IP address but must learn the matching hardware address. The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) does exactly this: the sender broadcasts an ARP request asking which device owns a given IP address, and the device that owns that IP replies with its hardware (MAC) address, which the sender then caches. This IP-to-hardware mapping on the local network is precisely what the question asks for.

Contrast with the other choices

  • RARP works in the opposite direction: a diskless host that already knows its own hardware address uses it to obtain its IP address, so it maps hardware to logical, not logical to hardware.

  • IP is a network-layer addressing and routing protocol; it carries packets using logical addresses and performs no hardware-address lookup.

  • ICMP is a diagnostic and error-reporting protocol (used by tools like ping); it reports delivery problems and does not resolve addresses.

title: What is the primary function of the ARP in an
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the primary function of the ARP in an IPv4 local network?

options.label: B
options.html: To resolve domain names into IP addresses

options.label: C
options.html: To determine the MAC address corresponding to an IP address

solution:
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is used in an IPv4 local network to find the MAC (hardware/physical) address that corresponds to a known IPv4 address. Hosts identify each other logically by IP address, but to actually deliver a frame on the same LAN segment they need the destination's Layer-2 MAC address — ARP bridges this gap.

When a host wants to send data to an IP address on the same network and does not have the matching MAC address cached, it broadcasts an ARP request ("Who has IP X? Tell me your MAC."). The host owning that IP replies with a unicast ARP reply carrying its MAC address, which the sender stores in its ARP cache for future use.

Therefore, the primary function of ARP is to determine the MAC address corresponding to a given IP address — i.e., to map an IP (network-layer) address to a MAC (link-layer) address. This makes option (3) correct.

Why the others are wrong: assigning IP addresses dynamically is done by DHCP; resolving domain names to IP addresses is done by DNS; encrypting communication is the job of protocols such as IPsec/TLS; and forwarding packets between different networks is performed by routers (the IP routing/forwarding function).

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q115
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: How does tunneling enable IPv6 communication over IPv4 networks?
solution:
Tunneling is a transition technique in which packets belonging to one network-layer protocol are wrapped, unchanged, inside the packets of a different network-layer protocol so that they can be carried across a network built for the second protocol.

For IPv6 traffic crossing IPv4-only infrastructure, a dual-stack router or host at the tunnel entry takes the complete IPv6 packet (its own header and payload) and places it as the payload of a new IPv4 packet:

  1. The source generates an ordinary IPv6 packet with a full IPv6 header and payload.

  2. At the tunnel entry point, that entire IPv6 packet is encapsulated as the data portion of a new IPv4 packet, and the IPv4 header's Protocol field is set to 41 to mark the payload as an IPv6 datagram.

  3. The resulting IPv4 packet is forwarded hop by hop through the IPv4-only network using ordinary IPv4 routing, since every intermediate router only ever sees a normal IPv4 packet.

  4. At the tunnel exit point, the IPv4 header is removed, recovering the original, unmodified IPv6 packet, which is then delivered onward on the IPv6 side.

Cross-check: this is distinct from header translation, which rewrites an IPv6 header into an IPv4 header (or vice versa) instead of wrapping the packet, and from dual stack, where a device runs both protocol stacks natively without needing to wrap one protocol inside the other. Per RFC 4213 (Basic Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 Hosts and Routers), encapsulating IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets is exactly how tunneling achieves IPv6-over-IPv4 connectivity.

Therefore, the process is caching.

title: Router outside the organization received packet Consider following steps taken
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
A router outside the organization received a packet 224.240.7.91. Consider following steps taken by router.

1.The router looks in its routing table to find out how to route the packet to the destination.

2.The router looks at the first byte of the address to find the class.

3.The default mask for the class is ANDED (logical AND operation) and address is found.

Which of the following shows correct required step for finding the route?
solution:
To route the packet, the router follows these steps:

Step 1: The router looks at the packet's destination address (224.240.7.91) and checks its routing table to determine where to forward it.

Step 2: The router examines the first byte of the address to identify the class of the address. In this case, 224.240.7.91 falls under Class D (multicast).

Step 3: The router applies the default mask for the class using a logical AND operation with the address to determine the network portion of the address.

Thus, the correct sequence is 2 - 3 - 1.

title: IP currently uses 32-bit addresses, if we could redesign IP
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
IP currently uses 32-bit addresses, if we could redesign IP to use the 6-byte MAC address instead of the 32 bit addresses, how many statements are true about the system.

(i) Allows IP addresses to be dynamically allocated when the hardware moves to the different network

(ii) Mapping is necessary to enable indirection from IP address to the MAC address

(iii) As we use static IP addresses, routing will be much less efficient

(iv) No effect on the system
solution:
(i) False: MAC addresses are hardware-specific and static. They do not change when the device moves to a different network. IP addresses, however, can be dynamically allocated (e.g., via DHCP), allowing network flexibility.

(ii) False: If the MAC address is used directly as the address, there would be no need for mapping between an IP address and a MAC address. The whole concept of ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) would be redundant.

(iii) True: Static MAC addresses are not optimized for hierarchical routing as IP addresses are. This lack of structure in MAC addresses would make routing tables larger and routing less efficient, as every address is unique but not structured hierarchically like IP addresses.

(iv) False: Using MAC addresses instead of IP addresses would have significant effects on routing, address allocation, and network management, leading to various inefficiencies and complications.

Only one statement (iii) is true

title: Which technique is used to allow multiple devices to share

title: What is the subnet mask for Class network with default
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What is the subnet mask for a Class C network with default subnetting ?
solution: In IPv4 addressing, networks are divided into classes (A, B, C, D, E) based on the first octet. A Class C network uses the first three bits of the address to identify it, leaving 24 bits for host addressing. With default subnetting, no additional bits are borrowed from the host portion to create subnets.\nTherefore, the first three octets (24 bits) are reserved for the network ID, and the last octet is used for host IDs. This results in a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0, where each '255' represents 8 bits of network address (11111111 in binary) and '0' represents the host portion.\nOption A (255.0.0.0) is the default mask for Class A networks, and Option B (255.255.0.0) is for Class B networks. Option D (255.255.255.255) represents a single host address (/32), not a standard network mask.

title: Which of the following class of IP addressing is used
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following class of IP addressing is used for multicasting?
solution: The correct option is B (Class D). IPv4 addressing is divided into five classes (A to E). Class D IP addresses (ranging from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255) are explicitly reserved for multicasting protocols, which allow a single source packet to be efficiently delivered to a specific group of destination hosts simultaneously.

title: The length of IPv6 addresses is bits.

bodyHtml: The length of IPv6 addresses is _________ bits.
solution: The correct option is C (128). Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) addresses have a length of 128 bits, organized into eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. This expanded address space was designed to replace the limited 32-bit architecture of IPv4, providing 2128 unique addresses.

title: The default subnet mask for Class IP addresses is:
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The default subnet mask for Class B IP addresses is:
solution: The correct option is C (255.255.0.0). In classful routing, a Class B IPv4 address uses the first 16 bits for the network ID and the remaining 16 bits for host IDs. Therefore, its default subnet mask sets the first two octets to all 1s and the last two octets to all 0s, resulting in 255.255.0.0 (or /16 prefix).

solution: The correct option is C (Multicast). An IPv4 address prefixed with the binary bits 1110 belongs to Class D. According to the internet addressing architecture, Class D addresses are specifically reserved and configured for multicast transmission, enabling data distribution to a designated group of devices.

subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The first octet higher order bits for class D IP addresses is:
solution: The correct option is B (1110). In classful IPv4 addressing, Class D addresses are reserved for multicast traffic. They are architecturally identified by setting the four highest-order bits (most significant bits) of the first octet strictly to 1110, establishing a decimal range from 224 to 239.

Classes A, B, and C are used for unicast routing, Class D is reserved for multicast, and Class E is kept for research/experimental purposes. Therefore, Option B is correct.

bodyHtml: For class C IP address, first octet highest state bit is _________
solution: In classful addressing, Class C IP addresses are identified by their most significant bits (highest state bits) in the first octet, which are fixed as 110. This bit pattern establishes the Class C decimal range from 192 to 223. Therefore, Option B is correct.

title: Which of the following is loopback IP address?
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Which of the following is a loopback IP address?
solution:
The correct option is A (127.0.0.1).

A loopback IP address is a special IP address used by a host to send network traffic to itself. It is primarily used for troubleshooting, testing network software locally, and verifying that the local network stack (TCP/IP stack) is functioning correctly without sending packets out onto the physical network.

  • Reserved Range: The entire Class A block from 127.0.0.0 to 127.255.255.255 (or 127.0.0.0/8 in CIDR notation) is reserved for loopback functions.

  • Standard Localhost: Among this block, 127.0.0.1 is the most commonly used loopback address and is usually mapped to the hostname localhost.

title: What part of is the Network ID, assuming default subnet
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: What part of 192.168.10.51 is the Network ID, assuming a default subnet mask?
solution:
Concept

An IPv4 address is split into a Network ID (which network the host belongs to) and a Host ID (which host within that network). With a default classful subnet mask, the class of the address — decided by the first octet — fixes how many leading octets form the Network ID:

  • Class A (first octet 1–126): mask 255.0.0.0 → Network ID = first 1 octet.

  • Class B (first octet 128–191): mask 255.255.0.0 → Network ID = first 2 octets.

  • Class C (first octet 192–223): mask 255.255.255.0 → Network ID = first 3 octets, host = last octet.

Application

  1. Read the first octet of 192.168.10.51 → it is 192, which lies in 192–223, so this is a Class C address.

  2. The default mask for Class C is 255.255.255.0, so the masked (network) portion is the first three octets and the last octet is the host.

  3. Apply the mask: keep the first three octets, zero the host octet → Network ID = 192.168.10 (full network address 192.168.10.0), and the host part is 51.

Cross-check

Reverse it: every address from 192.168.10.1 to 192.168.10.254 shares the same first three octets, so they must share one Network ID — 192.168.10 — confirming the host byte (51 here) is what varies. Hence the Network ID of 192.168.10.51 under the default mask is 192.168.10.

title: UGC NET Paper 1 June 2010 Set W — Question 48
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: At the network layer, a device connected to the Internet is identified for Internet Protocol communication by which type of address?
solution:
Concept

Internet Protocol communication uses logical network-layer addressing. An address at this layer identifies a network interface so packets can be routed across interconnected networks.

Application identifiers and physical-location identifiers serve different purposes and do not replace the network-layer identifier used in an IP packet.

Application

For a device exchanging packets over the Internet, the relevant identifier in the Internet Protocol header is its IP address. Routers use the destination IP address when forwarding the packet toward the receiving network.

Contrast

  • An e-mail address identifies a mailbox for electronic messaging, not a network interface in an IP packet.

  • A street address identifies a physical postal or geographic location, not an Internet Protocol endpoint.

  • An IP address is the logical network-layer identifier carried in IP communication.

  • “None of these options” would apply only if no listed address type served this network-layer role; the list includes IP address.

Result

Therefore, the required identifier is an IP address.

title: In IPv4 addressing, block of address can be define as
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
(A) In IPv4 addressing, a block of address can be define as x.y.z.t/n in which x.y.z.t define one of the address and /n define the mask
(B) The first address in the block can be found by setting the rightmost 32-n bits to 0s
(C) Address of class C is used for multicast communication
(D) There are five classes in IPv4 address
(E) Supernetting combine several networks into one large network
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Explanation: Evaluate each statement.

  • In IPv4 addressing, a block can be defined as x.y.z.t/n where x.y.z.t is an address and /n is the prefix length (network mask). This is correct (CIDR notation).

  • The first address in the block is found by setting the rightmost 32−n bits to 0. That yields the network address (for example, 192.168.1.10/24 → network 192.168.1.0). This is correct.

  • The claim that Class C addresses are used for multicast is incorrect. Multicast addresses are in Class D (224.0.0.0–239.255.255.255).

  • There are five IPv4 address classes historically (A, B, C, D, and E); this statement is correct. Note that Class D is used for multicast and Class E is reserved.

  • Supernetting combines several networks into a larger network (used with CIDR to aggregate routes). This statement is correct.

Conclusion: The true statements are the ones describing CIDR notation, the rule to compute the first address by zeroing host bits, the existence of five IPv4 classes, and that supernetting aggregates networks. The correct answer is the choice that lists those four true statements.

title: Consider the address and subnet mask Find the subnet id?
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: Consider the address 141.14.196.46 and subnet mask 255.255.192.0. Find the subnet id?
solution:
Key idea: Apply the subnet mask to the IP (bitwise AND) to get the subnet ID.

  • Convert the mask 255.255.192.0 to binary for the third octet: 192 = 11000000. This mask is /18.

  • Convert the IP's third octet to binary: 196 = 11000100.

  • Perform bitwise AND on the third octet: 11000100 AND 11000000 = 11000000 (which is 192).

  • Set all host bits to zero (the lower 6 bits of the third octet and the entire fourth octet). The subnet ID becomes 141.14.192.0.

Final answer: 141.14.192.0

title: An organization has class-C network of It is submitted with
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: An organization has a class-C network of 195.32.7.0. It is submitted with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.240. What is the broadcast address of the last but one sub network?
solution:
Key steps: determine subnet size and find the second-to-last block.

  1. Identify the mask: 255.255.255.240 is /28.

  2. Compute block size: 256 (addresses in last octet) ÷ 16 (because /28 leaves 4 host bits → 2^4 = 16) = 16, so subnets increase in steps of 16 in the last octet.

  3. List the final /28 blocks in the /24: 208–223, 224–239, 240–255.

  4. The second-to-last block is 224–239, so its broadcast address (the last address in that block) is 195.32.7.239.

Final answer: 195.32.7.239

title: The Direct Broadcast Address of the subnet is the subnet
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: The Direct Broadcast Address of the subnet is 201.15.16.31. W the subnet mask of the network is ___________
solution:
To determine the subnet mask from the direct broadcast address:

  • Convert the last octet (31) to binary: 00011111.

  • Count the consecutive 1s starting from the least-significant bit (the right side): there are 5 ones. These are the host bits.

  • Calculate the prefix length: 32 − 5 = 27, so the mask is /27.

  • Write the subnet mask: /27 = 255.255.255.224.

title: If the directed broadcast address of subnet is Which of
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: If the directed broadcast address of a subnet is 213.122.163.31. Which of the following will be the subnet mask?
solution:
Answer: 255.255.255.224 ( /27 )

Reasoning:

  • The directed broadcast address given is 213.122.163.31, so focus on the last octet value 31.

  • 31 in binary is 00011111. A directed broadcast has all host bits set to 1, so the pattern 00011111 shows that the host portion occupies 5 bits in the last octet.

  • If there are 5 host bits, the subnet mask has 8−5 = 3 network/subnet bits in the last octet, so the prefix is /27.

  • The subnet mask in dotted decimal is 11111111.11111111.11111111.11100000 = 255.255.255.224.

Notes:

  • Any mask that produces subnet increments of 32 in the last octet yields broadcast addresses ending in .31, .63, .95, etc. That corresponds to /27 (255.255.255.224).

  • Values like 255.255.255.198 are invalid as subnet masks because mask bits must be contiguous ones followed by zeros.

title: One organisation has one of the IP addresses is and
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: One organisation has one of the IP addresses is 184.26.21.97 and subnet mask is 255.255.255.192. Which is the correct option for another valid IP address and the total number of the host of the organisation?
solution:
Subnet mask: 255.255.255.192 = /26 (binary: 11111111.11111111.11111111.11000000)

  • Host bits = 6 → usable hosts = 2^6 - 2 = 62.

  • Subnet size = 64 addresses (2^6).

  • Given IP: 184.26.21.97. Determine the subnet block containing 97 by finding the multiple of 64 that contains it: 64–127.

  • Network address = 184.26.21.64.

  • Broadcast address = 184.26.21.127.

  • Usable host range = 184.26.21.65 to 184.26.21.126.

Therefore another valid IP address in the same organisation subnet is 184.26.21.121, and the total number of usable hosts for the subnet is 62.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • 184.26.21.65, 32: 184.26.21.65 is a usable host but the host count 32 is incorrect (should be 62).

  • 184.26.21.127, 64: 184.26.21.127 is the broadcast address (not usable) and the listed host count 64 is incorrect for usable hosts.

  • 184.26.21.131, 62: 184.26.21.131 is in the next subnet (184.26.21.128–184.26.21.191), so it is not in the same organisation subnet as 184.26.21.97; the host count 62 itself is correct for a /26.

Final answer: 184.26.21.121, 62

title: Two computers and are configured as follows: has IP address
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml:
Two computers C1​ and C2​ are configured as follows:
C1​ has IP address 197.168.76.24 and network mask 255.255.192.0.
C2​ has IP address 197.168.114.28 and network mask 255.255.224.0.
Which one of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.html: C1​ and C2​ both assume they are on the same network.

options.label: B
options.html: C2​ assumes C1​ is on the same network, but C1​ assumes C2​ is on a different network.

options.label: C
options.html: C1​ assumes C2​ is on some network, but C2​ assumes C1​ is on a different network.

options.label: D
options.html: C1​ and C2 both assume they are on different networks.

solution:
Method: compute each host's network ID by applying its subnet mask, then apply each host's mask to the other host's IP to see what each assumes.

  • First computer (IP 197.168.76.24, mask 255.255.192.0 (/18)): network ID = 197.168.64.0 (third octet 76 is in the 64–127 block).

  • Second computer (IP 197.168.114.28, mask 255.255.224.0 (/19)): network ID = 197.168.96.0 (third octet 114 is in the 96–127 block).

Now apply each host's mask to the other host's IP to determine what each host assumes:

  • Applying the first computer's mask (/18) to the second computer's IP 197.168.114.28 gives network ID 197.168.64.0, which matches the first computer's own network. Therefore the first computer assumes the second is on the same network.

  • Applying the second computer's mask (/19) to the first computer's IP 197.168.76.24 gives network ID 197.168.64.0, which is different from the second computer's own network 197.168.96.0. Therefore the second computer assumes the first is on a different network.

Conclusion: The first computer believes they are on the same network, while the second believes they are on different networks. Thus the correct statement is that the first computer assumes the second is on some network, but the second assumes the first is on a different network.

title: How many hosts can be configured using subnet mask
subject: Computer Networks
bodyHtml: How many hosts can be configured using a subnet mask 255.255.255.248?
solution:
Concept

In IPv4 a subnet mask splits an address into a network portion (the 1-bits) and a host portion (the 0-bits). The number of distinct addresses in a subnet is 2 raised to the number of host bits; of these, two are reserved — the all-zeros address is the network ID and the all-ones address is the broadcast — so the count of usable (configurable) hosts is 2h − 2, where h is the number of host bits.

Application

  1. Write the last octet of the mask in binary: 248 = 11111000. The first three octets are 255 (all 1-bits), so every host bit lies in the last octet.

  2. Count the 0-bits (host bits): 11111000 has three trailing zeros, so h = 3.

  3. Total addresses in the subnet = 23 = 8.

  4. Subtract the two reserved addresses (network + broadcast): usable hosts = 8 − 2 = 6.

Cross-check

This mask is a /29 (32 − 3 = 29 network bits). A /29 is the standard small block that yields 6 usable host addresses — a common allocation for point-to-multipoint links and tiny LAN segments — which confirms the result.
