title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 22
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which of the following join operations does ORACLE support?

options.label: C
options.html: inner join, outer join and semi join only

options.label: D
options.html: inner join, outer join, semi join and anti join

solution:
Concept: A relational join is classified by which rows survive the match. An inner join keeps only matched rows. An outer join (LEFT/RIGHT/FULL) additionally keeps unmatched rows from one or both sides. A semi join and an anti join are existence-based joins that never pull in columns from the second table: a semi join returns each first-table row once when a match exists elsewhere (the EXISTS/IN pattern), and an anti join returns each first-table row when NO match exists elsewhere (the NOT EXISTS/NOT IN pattern).

Application: Oracle's SQL engine implements all four categories. Inner joins and one-sided (LEFT/RIGHT) outer joins have been available since Oracle's earliest SQL releases through Oracle's own equijoin and "(+)" outer-join syntax; a FULL outer join needed a UNION-based workaround until ANSI-standard JOIN keywords -- including native FULL OUTER JOIN -- arrived in Oracle 9i. Semi joins and anti joins are not written with a dedicated JOIN keyword; instead Oracle's optimizer can recognise an eligible EXISTS/IN subquery as a semi join and an eligible NOT EXISTS/NOT IN subquery as an anti join, executing them as such -- visible in an execution plan as operations like HASH JOIN SEMI and HASH JOIN ANTI. This optimizer-level support for semi and anti joins has been present since Oracle 8, well before this question was set, alongside Oracle's long-standing inner/outer join support.

Cross-check (contrast every listed option by its own value):

  • inner join and outer join only -- accurate about those two categories, but omits semi and anti joins, which Oracle also implements at the optimizer level.

  • outer join and semi join only -- accurate about those two, but omits inner join (Oracle's most basic join type) and anti join.

  • inner join, outer join and semi join only -- covers three of the four categories Oracle implements, leaving out anti join.

  • inner join, outer join, semi join and anti join -- names all four categories that Oracle's SQL engine and optimizer implement, with none omitted and nothing added beyond what Oracle supports.

Result: Oracle supports inner joins, outer joins, semi joins, and anti joins, so the option naming all four -- inner join, outer join, semi join and anti join -- is correct (per Oracle SQL Language Reference on joins and subquery-driven semi/anti-join execution plans).

title: Given table Students with columns StudentID, Name, Age, Score, which
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Given a table Students with columns StudentID, Name, Age, Score, which of the following SQL queries will return the highest score for each age group?

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT Age, MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age;

options.label: B
options.html: SELECT Age, Score FROM Students GROUP BY Age;

options.label: D
options.html: SELECT Age, Score FROM Students WHERE Score = (SELECT MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age);

solution:
The query SELECT Age, MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age; correctly returns the highest score for each age group.

Why this works: GROUP BY groups rows by age, and MAX(Score) computes the highest score inside each group. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT must appear in the GROUP BY.

  • The query "SELECT Age, Score FROM Students GROUP BY Age;" is invalid under standard SQL because Score is neither aggregated nor grouped. Some databases may return an arbitrary Score per group when nonstandard grouping is allowed, but that result is not reliable.

  • The query "SELECT Age, MAX(Score) FROM Students;" is missing GROUP BY Age. Without GROUP BY, MAX(Score) would be computed over the whole table (or produce an error), not per age, so it does not return the maximum per age.

  • The query that uses a subquery: "SELECT Age, Score FROM Students WHERE Score = (SELECT MAX(Score) FROM Students GROUP BY Age);" is incorrect because the inner subquery returns multiple values (one max per age) and is not correlated to the outer row. Comparing to a multirow subquery with '=' is invalid.

If you prefer a subquery approach, use a correlated subquery that finds the maximum for the same age, for example:

SELECT Age, Score FROM Students s WHERE Score = (SELECT MAX(s2.Score) FROM Students s2 WHERE s2.Age = s.Age);

This returns the student(s) in each age group whose Score equals the maximum for that age (ties will return multiple students).

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT a1, COUNT(*) FROM Knowledge GROUP BY a1;

solution: If aggregate functions are used in the select clause along with the attribute list we must use group by clause for grouping the attribute values.

title: In SQL, which clause is used to filter groups created
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: In SQL, which clause is used to filter groups created by GROUP BY ?
solution: In SQL, the HAVING clause is used to filter groups created by GROUP BY. The WHERE clause filters individual rows before grouping occurs, whereas HAVING operates on the aggregated groups.

title: What is the primary purpose of the GROUP BY clause
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: What is the primary purpose of the GROUP BY clause in SQL?

options.label: A
options.html: To sort rows in ascending or descending order

options.label: B
options.html: To group rows with identical values in specified columns for aggregate processing

options.label: C
options.html: To permanently remove duplicate rows from a table

solution:
The GROUP BY clause groups rows that share the same values in one or more specified columns into summary groups, so that aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX can be applied to each group separately rather than to the entire result set.

For example, the query below returns one row per department together with the number of employees in that department:

SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees GROUP BY department;

Here the rows are collapsed into one group per distinct department value, and COUNT(*) is computed per group. This is the defining purpose of GROUP BY, which is why option B is correct.

The other choices describe different SQL features: ORDER BY sorts the result set, the DISTINCT keyword removes duplicate rows from output, the WHERE clause filters individual rows before grouping, and JOIN combines rows from multiple tables — none of these is what GROUP BY does.

title: Which of the following is true about the HAVING clause?
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which of the following is true about the HAVING clause?

options.label: A
options.html: Similar to the WHERE clause but is used for columns rather than groups

options.label: B
options.html: Similar to WHERE clause but is used for rows rather than columns

options.label: C
options.html: Similar to WHERE clause but is used for groups rather than rows

solution: The HAVING clause is used to filter groups after the GROUP BY clause has been applied. It operates on aggregate functions (like SUM, COUNT, AVG) and is applied to the result set of grouped rows. Unlike the WHERE clause, which filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters the groups themselves. This means HAVING is used when you need to apply conditions on aggregated data.

title: Which SQL query will correctly raise the salary by for
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which SQL query will correctly raise the salary by 10% for employees in the 'HR' department who currently earn less than 50,000?

options.label: A
options.html: MODIFY employees SET salary = salary + 10% WHERE department = 'HR' AND salary < 50000;

options.label: B
options.html: UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE department = 'HR' AND salary < 50000;

options.label: C
options.html: UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 10% WHERE department = 'HR';

options.label: D
options.html: UPDATE employees SET salary = salary + 5000 IF department = 'HR' AND salary < 50000;

solution:
To modify existing records in a relational database, standard SQL uses the UPDATE statement alongside a SET clause to specify the modifications, and a WHERE clause to filter the targeted rows.

To increase a value by 10%, you mathematically multiply the current value by 1.10 (which represents 100% + 10%). The conditions specified in the problem statement require checking two things:

  1. The department must be 'HR' (department = 'HR').

  2. The current salary must be strictly less than 50,000 (salary < 50000).

Combining these requirements yields the standard SQL syntax:

UPDATE employees  
SET salary = salary * 1.10  
WHERE department = 'HR' AND salary < 50000;

title: Which of the following queries will correctly return the names
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which of the following queries will correctly return the names of students who have received the highest grade in any course?

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades WHERE Grade = (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades);

options.label: B
options.html: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades WHERE Grade IN (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades GROUP BY CourseID);

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades sg WHERE Grade = (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades WHERE CourseID = sg.CourseID);

options.label: D
options.html: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades GROUP BY CourseID;

solution:
Answer summary: Two queries correctly return students who received the highest grade in each course. Both approaches handle ties (multiple students with the same top grade).

  • Using a grouped subquery: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades WHERE Grade IN (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades GROUP BY CourseID); — The inner query returns the highest grade for each course, and the outer query returns students whose Grade equals any of those per-course maxima. Ties are included; add DISTINCT StudentName if you want unique names.

  • Using a correlated subquery: SELECT StudentName FROM StudentGrades sg WHERE Grade = (SELECT MAX(Grade) FROM StudentGrades WHERE CourseID = sg.CourseID); — For each row, the subquery computes the maximum grade for that row's course, and the outer query returns students that match that maximum. This also returns ties. On large datasets, consider indexes on CourseID and Grade for performance.

Why the other approaches are incorrect:

  • A query that uses MAX(Grade) without grouping returns only the single highest grade across all courses, not per course.

  • Grouping solely by CourseID while selecting StudentName without an aggregate yields an invalid or ambiguous result and does not guarantee the returned name has the highest grade.

title: Consider the relation and query: Project (P.no. Pname, price, city)
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider the relation and query:

Project (P.no. Pname, price, city)

SELECT Pname FROM Project WHERE NOT (price > = ANY (SELECT price for FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI')

Which of the following output produced by above query?

options.label: A
options.html: Name of project whose price is greater than the price of every project in DELHI city.

options.label: B
options.html: Name of projects whose price is less than the price of every project in DELHI city.

options.label: C
options.html: Name of project whose price is less than equal to the price of project in DELHI city.

options.label: D
options.html: Name of projects whose price is greater than equal to the price of every project is DELHI city.

solution:
Key idea: The condition NOT (price >= ANY (SELECT price FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI')) is equivalent to price < ALL (SELECT price FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI').

  • The inner query returns the set of prices of projects located in DELHI.

  • price >= ANY (inner set) is true when the project's price is greater than or equal to at least one DELHI price.

  • Negating that condition means there is no DELHI price that the project's price is greater than or equal to, i.e., the project's price is strictly less than every DELHI price.

  • Therefore the query returns names of projects whose price is less than every project price in DELHI.

A clearer equivalent SQL form is:

SELECT Pname FROM Project WHERE price < ALL (SELECT price FROM Project WHERE city = 'DELHI')

Important note: If the subquery returns no rows (there are no projects in DELHI), the ALL comparison is vacuously true, so the condition holds for every project and the query would return all project names.

title: Given table Sales with columns SalesID, ProductID, SaleDate, and SaleAmount,
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Given a table Sales with columns SalesID, ProductID, SaleDate, and SaleAmount, which SQL query retrieves the average sale amount for each month in the year 2024?

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT MONTH(SaleDate), AVG(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY MONTH(SaleDate);

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT SaleDate, AVG(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024;

options.label: D
options.html: SELECT MONTH(SaleDate), SUM(SaleAmount) FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY SaleDate;

solution:
This query groups the sales data by month and calculates the average sale amount for each month in 2024.

Recommended query (MySQL-style): SELECT MONTH(SaleDate) AS month, AVG(SaleAmount) AS avg_amount FROM Sales WHERE YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 GROUP BY MONTH(SaleDate) ORDER BY MONTH(SaleDate);

  • Filter to the target year using YEAR(SaleDate) = 2024 so only 2024 rows are considered.

  • Extract the month from SaleDate (MONTH(SaleDate) or EXTRACT(MONTH FROM SaleDate)) and GROUP BY that expression to aggregate per month.

  • Use AVG(SaleAmount) to compute the average sale amount per group (month).

  • Optionally alias the output columns (for readability) and ORDER BY the month to present results from January to December.

  • Portability note: functions differ by SQL dialect. In standard SQL and PostgreSQL you can use EXTRACT(MONTH FROM SaleDate) or date_trunc('month', SaleDate) as appropriate.

title: Given table Orders with columns OrderID (PK), CustomerID, OrderDate, and
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Given a table Orders with columns OrderID (PK), CustomerID, OrderDate, and OrderAmount, which of the following queries will return the number of orders placed by each customer? The given table may contains null values.

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderID) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

options.label: B
options.html: SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderAmount) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

solution:
Correct queries that return the number of orders per customer:

  • SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderID) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

    Counts non-null OrderID values per customer. Since OrderID is the primary key and cannot be null, this correctly returns the number of orders for each customer even if other columns contain nulls.

  • SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

    Counts all rows per customer group. COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of null values in other columns, so it also correctly returns the number of orders per customer.

Why the other queries are incorrect:

  • SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderAmount) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

    COUNT(OrderAmount) counts only non-null OrderAmount values. If OrderAmount can be null, this will undercount orders. Use COUNT(*) or COUNT(OrderID) to count orders regardless of nulls.

  • SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderID) FROM Orders;

    This query is missing a GROUP BY clause. Selecting CustomerID together with an aggregate without grouping is invalid in standard SQL and will not produce per-customer counts.

title: Consider table Attendance with columns EmpID, AttendanceDate, and Status ('Present'
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Consider a table Attendance with columns EmpID, AttendanceDate, and Status ('Present' or 'Absent'). Which SQL query returns the percentage of days each employee was present in January 2024?

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT EmpID, (SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS AttendancePercentage FROM Attendance WHERE MONTH(AttendanceDate) = 1 AND YEAR(AttendanceDate) = 2024 GROUP BY EmpID;

options.label: B
options.html: SELECT EmpID, (COUNT(Status = 'Present') / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS AttendancePercentage FROM Attendance WHERE MONTH(AttendanceDate) = 1 AND YEAR(AttendanceDate) = 2024 GROUP BY EmpID;

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT EmpID, (COUNT(*) / SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) * 100 AS AttendancePercentage FROM Attendance WHERE MONTH(AttendanceDate) = 1 AND YEAR(AttendanceDate) = 2024 GROUP BY EmpID;

options.label: D
options.html: SELECT EmpID, (SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Absent' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS AttendancePercentage FROM Attendance WHERE MONTH(AttendanceDate) = 1 AND YEAR(AttendanceDate) = 2024 GROUP BY EmpID;

solution:
Key insight: count present days with a conditional SUM, divide by total days, and multiply by 100. Ensure you avoid integer division and use a sargable date filter.

  • Use SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) to count present days.

  • Divide by COUNT(*) to get the proportion of days recorded for that employee.

  • Multiply by 100.0 or cast to a decimal type to prevent integer division in databases that perform integer arithmetic.

  • Prefer filtering by a date range (for example AttendanceDate >= '2024-01-01' AND AttendanceDate < '2024-02-01') instead of MONTH()/YEAR() for better performance.

Recommended query:

SELECT EmpID, 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN Status = 'Present' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS AttendancePercentage

FROM Attendance

WHERE AttendanceDate >= '2024-01-01' AND AttendanceDate < '2024-02-01'

GROUP BY EmpID;

Notes:

  • Some databases (for example MySQL) allow SUM(Status = 'Present') as a shorter form because the boolean evaluates to 1/0, but the CASE expression is more portable and explicit.

title: Consider database with table Employee having columns EmpID, Name, Department,
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Consider a database with a table Employee having columns EmpID, Name, Department, and Salary. Which of the following queries will list the names of employees who have a salary greater than the average salary in their department?

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT Name FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee);

options.label: B
options.html: SELECT Name FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY Department);

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT Name FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Department = Department);

options.label: D
options.html: SELECT Name FROM Employee E WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Department = E.Department);

solution:
Answer: Use a correlated subquery that references the outer row's department. For example: SELECT Name FROM Employee E WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Department = E.Department);

Why this works:

  • The subquery is correlated because it uses E.Department (the alias from the outer query). For each outer row the subquery computes the average salary only for that employee's department.

  • The subquery returns a single scalar value (the department average) for each outer row, so the comparison Salary > (subquery) is valid.

Why the other queries are incorrect or problematic:

  • A query that compares Salary to (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee) uses the overall average across all departments, so it does not select employees above their own department's average.

  • A query that uses (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY Department) produces multiple average values (one per department). Using that multi-row result where a single scalar is expected causes an error; you would need to join to that grouped result or use a correlated subquery instead.

  • A query that uses WHERE Department = Department inside the subquery is not correlated: it compares the same column within the subquery, which is always true, so the subquery effectively computes an overall average rather than a department-specific average.

Alternative correct approach:

You can precompute department averages and join them to the Employee table, for example: SELECT e.Name FROM Employee e JOIN (SELECT Department, AVG(Salary) AS AvgSal FROM Employee GROUP BY Department) d ON e.Department = d.Department WHERE e.Salary > d.AvgSal;

title: Given two tables and both having column ID, which SQL
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Given two tables A and B, both having a column ID, which SQL statement retrieves all IDs from table A that do not exist in table B?

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID <> (SELECT B.ID FROM B);

options.label: B
options.html: SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID NOT IN (SELECT ID FROM B);

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT A.ID FROM A, B WHERE A.ID != B.ID;

options.label: D
options.html: SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID EXISTS (SELECT ID FROM B);

solution:
Safer recommended solutions to retrieve IDs from A that do not exist in B:

  • Use NOT EXISTS (safe with NULLs): SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.ID = A.ID);

  • Or use a LEFT JOIN and check for missing matches: SELECT A.ID FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.ID = B.ID WHERE B.ID IS NULL;

  • The NOT IN form works when B.ID contains no NULLs: SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID NOT IN (SELECT ID FROM B);

Why NOT IN can be problematic:

  • If the subquery returns any NULL values, the NOT IN condition evaluates to UNKNOWN and may cause no rows to be returned. NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL avoid that pitfall.

Why the other provided queries are incorrect:

  • A query that uses a scalar comparison like SELECT A.ID FROM A WHERE A.ID <> (SELECT B.ID FROM B); is invalid when the subquery returns multiple rows and does not implement the intended set-difference logic.

  • A query that selects from both tables with a condition A.ID != B.ID (a cross join filtered by inequality) produces many rows and duplicates, not the distinct set of IDs in A that are absent from B.

  • A statement that attempts to use EXISTS incorrectly (for example using A.ID EXISTS (SELECT ID FROM B)) has invalid syntax; the correct EXISTS usage is WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.ID = A.ID) or its negation for the not-exists case.

Summary: Prefer NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL for a robust solution; the NOT IN form is acceptable only when you can guarantee there are no NULLs in B.ID.

title: Consider table Products with columns ProductID, ProductName, CategoryID, and Price.
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Consider a table Products with columns ProductID, ProductName, CategoryID, and Price. Which of the following queries will correctly return the product names and prices of the products with the highest price in each category?

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products);

options.label: B
options.html: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Price IN (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID);

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products p WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products WHERE CategoryID = p.CategoryID);

options.label: D
options.html: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID

solution:
Correct approach and explanation:

  • Correct query (correlated subquery): SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products p WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products WHERE CategoryID = p.CategoryID);

  • Why this works: the subquery computes the maximum price for the category of the current row (using p.CategoryID). The outer row is returned only when its Price equals that category-specific maximum. This correctly returns all products that are tied for the highest price within their own category.

  • Alternative correct query (join with derived maxima): SELECT p.ProductName, p.Price FROM Products p JOIN (SELECT CategoryID, MAX(Price) AS MaxPrice FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID) m ON p.CategoryID = m.CategoryID AND p.Price = m.MaxPrice;

  • Why the alternative works: it explicitly pairs each product with the maximum price for its category, avoiding incorrect matches across categories and often performing better for large tables.

Why the other queries are incorrect or problematic:

  • SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products);

    This picks the single overall maximum price across the entire table, not the maximum per category, so it only returns product(s) at the global maximum.

  • SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Price IN (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID);

    This compares prices against the set of maximum prices but does not check CategoryID. A product can match the maximum price value of another category and be returned incorrectly. Example: if one category's max is 300 and another category has a product priced 200 (but its own category's max is 400), a 200-priced product may still appear because 200 is a max in some other category.

  • SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products GROUP BY CategoryID

    This is invalid in standard SQL because ProductName and Price are neither aggregated nor included in GROUP BY. It will error in strict SQL or return indeterminate values in DBMSs that allow nonstandard grouping.

Summary: The correlated subquery that restricts MAX(Price) to the current row's CategoryID is correct; joining with a derived table of category maxima is an equivalent and often efficient alternative. The global MAX and the unqualified IN approach are incorrect for per-category maxima, and the GROUP BY example is a misuse of aggregation.

title: Consider database that has the relation schemas: (MCQ) student(rollno, name,
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider a database that has the relation schemas:       

student(rollno, name, degree, year, gender)
course(courseid, cname, credit, dept)
enroll(rollno, courseid, session, grade)

Assume that every student is enrolled in at least one course, then which of the following queries retrieves the names of all students who have scored ‘A’ in all the subjects they enrolled in:

options.label: A
options.html: SELECT s.name FROM student s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT e.rollno FROM enroll e WHERE e.rollno = s.rollno AND e.grade ≠ 'A' )

options.label: B
options.html: SELECT c.cid FROM course c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT cid FROM enrolled e WHERE e.cid = c.cid AND e.grade = 'A' )

options.label: C
options.html: SELECT c.cid FROM course c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT cid FROM enrolled e WHERE e.cid = c.cid AND e.grade = 'A' )

solution:
Key idea: select students for whom there does not exist any enrollment with a grade that is not 'A'.

  • The inner subquery finds enrollments for the same student that have a non-'A' grade.

  • NOT EXISTS around that subquery removes any student who has at least one such non-'A' enrollment, leaving only students whose every enrollment has grade 'A'.

  • Because the question states every student is enrolled in at least one course, students with no enrollments are not a concern for this query.

Corrected SQL (use <> for not-equal and SELECT 1 in the subquery):

SELECT s.name FROM student s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enroll e WHERE e.rollno = s.rollno AND e.grade <> 'A');

Alternative approach using GROUP BY / HAVING:

SELECT s.name FROM student s JOIN enroll e ON s.rollno = e.rollno GROUP BY s.rollno, s.name HAVING COUNT(*) = SUM(CASE WHEN e.grade = 'A' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END);

title: Consider the following relation scheme: Wholesaler (sid: integer, sname: string,
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider the following relation scheme:
Wholesaler (sid: integer, sname: string, address: string)
Parts (pid: integer, pname: string, color: string)
Catalog (sid: integer, pid: integer, cost: real)
The following query executed:
SELECT C.pid FROM Catalog C, Wholesaler S WHERE S.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' AND C.sid = S.sid AND
C.cost >= ALL (SELECT C2.cost FROM Catalog C2, Wholesaler S2 WHERE S2.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' AND C2.sid = S2.sid)
The output of above query is:

options.label: A
options.html: Find the pids of less expensive parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.

options.label: B
options.html: Find the pids of parts whose cost is more than the cost of parts not supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.

options.label: C
options.html: Find the pids of parts whose cost is less than the cost of parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.

options.label: D
options.html: Find the pids of the most expensive parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.

solution:
Concept: In standard SQL, a condition of the form expr >= ALL (subquery) is the classic way to express "expr is the maximum" without an explicit MAX() aggregate. It keeps a row only if its value is greater than or equal to every single value the subquery returns for the same comparison group -- i.e., it selects whichever row(s) attain that group's maximum, and ties are included because >= allows equality.

  1. The nested subquery filters Catalog rows C2 by S2.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' AND C2.sid = S2.sid, so C2.cost enumerates exactly the costs of the parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate.

  2. The outer query applies the identical filter (S.sname = 'KnowledgeGate' AND C.sid = S.sid) to C, so C ranges over that same set of KnowledgeGate catalog rows.

  3. Because the outer set and the subquery's comparison set are the same group, C.cost >= ALL(...) keeps only the row(s) whose cost is greater than or equal to every cost in that group -- the maximum cost among KnowledgeGate's parts.

  4. SELECT C.pid then returns the pid(s) of exactly those row(s): the most expensive part(s) supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate, with every tied pid included.

Cross-check: suppose KnowledgeGate's parts cost {40, 55, 55, 30}. The subquery's result set is {40, 55, 55, 30}. Testing 40 >= ALL(...) fails (40 is not >= 55), and 30 fails likewise, but each row costing 55 satisfies 55 >= 40, 55 >= 55, and 55 >= 30 -- so both pids costing 55 pass. This confirms the query returns the pid(s) of the top-cost part(s), never a partial or 'less than' subset.

Result: the query returns the pids of the most expensive parts supplied by the wholesaler named KnowledgeGate. (Note: the source text's relation/table-name typos -- e.g. a stray 'Wholesalers'/'Supplies' in the subquery's FROM clause -- have been corrected above to the schema's own 'Wholesaler' relation, which is the only table the query can correctly join against; this does not change the query's semantics or the answer.) This reading assumes, as is standard for this classic exercise, that Catalog.cost values are always populated -- SQL's three-valued logic means a NULL cost among the values ALL(...) compares against could make the predicate evaluate to UNKNOWN for that row, which is outside the intended scope here.

title: Consider the following relations given below: SQL: select sid from
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider the following relations given below:


SQL: select sid from supply S1 where region = 'mumbai' and NOT EXISTS (select pid from parts P1 where colour = 'red' and NOT EXISTS(select pid from catalog C1 where C1.pid = P1.pid and C1.sid = S1.sid))

options.label: A
options.html: select sid of all the suppliers in mumbai region who supply all red parts

options.label: B
options.html: select sid of all the suppliers in mumbai region who supply some red parts

options.label: C
options.html: select sid of some of the suppliers in mumbai region who supply all red parts

solution:
Concept

A subquery of the form NOT EXISTS ( ... WHERE <condition> AND NOT EXISTS ( <correlated match> ) ) is SQL's standard idiom for universal quantification — sometimes called relational division. It holds for an outer row exactly when no element of the inner set fails the correlated match, i.e. every element of that inner set is related to the outer row.

Application

  1. The innermost EXISTS/NOT EXISTS tests, for a specific supplier S1 and a specific part P1, whether the catalog table has a row linking S1.sid to P1.pid — i.e. whether S1 supplies P1.

  2. The middle subquery collects every red part (colour = ‘red’) for which that innermost NOT EXISTS is true — i.e. every red part S1 does NOT supply.

  3. The outer NOT EXISTS is true exactly when that middle set is empty — meaning there is no red part missing from S1's catalog.

  4. Combined with region = ‘mumbai’ in the outer WHERE clause, the query returns every supply row satisfying both conditions: a Mumbai-region supplier for whom no red part is missing, i.e. a supplier who supplies every red part.

Cross-check

  • If the outer NOT EXISTS were replaced by a bare EXISTS (one fewer negation), a row would be selected as soon as a single red part is missing — that would describe suppliers failing to supply at least one red part, not this query.

  • A SELECT ... WHERE statement always returns the complete set of rows for which its condition holds for that row; it has no mechanism to arbitrarily return only part of the qualifying rows.

  • The query's truth value for a given supplier depends only on whether every red part is present among that supplier's catalog rows — a structural, always-computable condition, not one that assumes the whole result is empty.

This is why the query selects the sids of suppliers in the mumbai region who supply all red parts.

title: Consider the following three queries on relation S(A, and R(B,
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider the following three queries on relation S(A, B) and R(B, C)

Q1: SELECT S. A FROM S WHERE S.B NOT IN (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R. B > 5);

Q2: SELECT S. A FROM S WHERE S.B <> ALL (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R. B > 5);

Q3: SELECT S.A FROM S WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R.B > 5 AND R.B = S.B) ;

options.label: A
options.html: The first query is not equivalent to any of the other queries

options.label: B
options.html: The first query is equivalent to the second query only

options.label: C
options.html: The first query is equivalent to the third query only

solution:
Answer: Queries 1 and 2 are equivalent; Query 3 is not equivalent to them.

  • Why queries 1 and 2 are equivalent:

    Both S.B NOT IN (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R.B > 5) and S.B <> ALL (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R.B > 5) require that S.B be unequal to every value produced by the subquery. The subquery uses R.B > 5, which excludes NULLs from its result, so the usual NULL pitfalls inside the subquery do not arise and the two expressions produce the same truth values for all rows.

  • Why query 3 can differ:

    Query 3 uses NOT EXISTS with a correlated equality test (NOT EXISTS (SELECT R.B FROM R WHERE R.B > 5 AND R.B = S.B)). If S.B is NULL then R.B = S.B evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row, so the subquery produces no rows and NOT EXISTS is true — the S row is included. In contrast, the first two queries evaluate comparisons with NULL to UNKNOWN and so exclude the S row. Thus the third query can return rows that the first two do not.

  • Concrete counterexample:

    Take S = { (A=1, B=NULL) } and R = { (B=6) }.

    Evaluations:

    • Query 1: S.B NOT IN (6) -> NULL NOT IN (6) evaluates to UNKNOWN -> row is excluded.

    • Query 2: S.B <> ALL (6) -> NULL <> 6 evaluates to UNKNOWN -> ALL yields UNKNOWN -> row is excluded.

    • Query 3: NOT EXISTS( ... R.B = S.B ...) -> R.B = NULL is UNKNOWN so subquery returns no rows -> NOT EXISTS is true -> row is included.

  • Conclusion: select the answer that states the first and second queries are equivalent and the third is different. The three queries are not all equivalent in the presence of NULLs in S.B.

title: Which of the following SQL query deletes all tuples in
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which of the following SQL queries deletes all tuples in the teacher relation for teachers associated with a department located in the building named 'CSE', as recorded in the department relation?

options.label: C
options.html:
DELETE FROM teacher
WHERE dept_name IN (
SELECT dept_name
FROM department
WHERE building = 'CSE');

solution:
A DELETE statement's WHERE clause can only test columns belonging to the table it deletes from. When the filtering condition instead depends on an attribute stored in a DIFFERENT relation, the standard, portable way to express this is a subquery: first resolve the qualifying values from that other relation, then match the outer DELETE's WHERE...IN clause against the resulting set. (Some dialects also allow a correlated EXISTS or a joined DELETE/USING form for the same logic, but the subquery form is the one offered here.)

  1. The inner subquery, SELECT dept_name FROM department WHERE building = 'CSE', resolves to the set of department names whose department is located in the CSE building.

  2. The outer query, DELETE FROM teacher WHERE dept_name IN (...), then removes every teacher row whose dept_name is a member of that resolved set -- this is the query that satisfies the requirement.

Checking why every other option fails:

  • A query that compares dept_name directly to the building's name 'CSE' mixes two different attributes from two different relations, and is not a syntactically valid IN condition either way.

  • A query that deletes rows from the department relation itself removes department records, not the associated teacher records the question asks for.

  • Since a valid query does satisfy the requirement, the option stating that none of the given queries works does not hold.

The subquery-based DELETE is therefore the query, among those offered, that correctly performs the required deletion.

title: Consider the following relation schema along with the tuples. Employee(name,
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider the following relation schema R along with the tuples.

Employee(name, salary) = {<e1, 10000>, <e2, 5000>, <e3, 2500>, <e4, 7500>, <e5, 8900>, <e6, 9800>}

What is the output of following SQL query?

SELECT name, MAX(salary) FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);
solution:
Concept: A scalar subquery inside a WHERE clause is fully evaluated first, producing a single value that the outer query then filters against. Once the WHERE clause has filtered the rows, any aggregate function (MAX, MIN, COUNT, etc.) in the outer SELECT operates only on that filtered subset of rows, not on the whole table.

Application: working through the query step by step —

  1. Evaluate the inner subquery first: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee scans all six tuples and returns 10000 (the salary of e1).

  2. Apply the outer WHERE filter: keep only rows with salary < 10000. This keeps e2 (5000), e3 (2500), e4 (7500), e5 (8900), and e6 (9800); it drops e1 (10000) because 10000 is not strictly less than 10000.

  3. Apply the outer aggregate MAX(salary) over exactly this filtered set of five tuples — the largest value among {5000, 2500, 7500, 8900, 9800} is 9800, contributed by e6.

  4. So the query returns the single row <e6, 9800>.

Cross-check: sorting the filtered salaries — 2500, 5000, 7500, 8900, 9800 — confirms 9800 is the unique largest value in that set, so no other filtered tuple could produce a larger MAX(salary). (Note: strict ANSI SQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY reject this query outright, since name is not functionally dependent on the aggregate without a GROUP BY. A dialect such as SQLite, which specifically permits a bare column alongside MIN/MAX and deterministically returns the row that produced the extreme value, DOES guarantee this exact pairing — non-strict MySQL, by contrast, only guarantees the aggregate value and leaves the paired name officially unspecified. This question follows that SQLite-style / exam-convention reading, under which the row of the extreme salary is returned together with it — exactly the concept these PYQ-style subquery questions are testing.)

A nested query, also known as a subquery, is a query embedded within another SQL query. It acts as a complete select-from-where block used to provide data for the outer query's conditions.

title: Given the following relational schemas Employee (empId, name, age, sex,
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Given the following relational schemas

Employee (empId, name, age, sex, deptId, advisor)

Department (deptId, DName, head, phoneNo)

Which of the following will be the TRC query to obtain the department names that do not have any female employee?
solution:
Concept

In Tuple Relational Calculus, a universal quantifier must be paired with an implication, (∀s)( P(s) → Q(s) ) — read as 'for every tuple s, IF s satisfies P then s also satisfies Q.' The antecedent P(s) is what restricts the quantification to the tuples of interest (here, the employees of a given department); only those tuples are required to satisfy Q. Pairing ∀ with a bare conjunction instead, (∀s)( P(s) ∧ Q(s) ), asserts something different: that every tuple s in the ENTIRE domain satisfies both P and Q — this is essentially never true for a real database, since tuples that fail P (rows of other relations, employees of other departments, etc.) immediately violate the conjunction. An existential quantifier, by contrast, is correctly paired with a conjunction: (∃s)( P(s) ∧ Q(s) ) = 'there exists some s satisfying both.' De Morgan's law connects the two forms: ¬(∃s)(P(s)) ⇔ (∀s)(¬P(s)).

Application

  1. The requirement: return department names d such that no employee of department d has sex = 'F'.

  2. Correctly written with a universal quantifier, this is (∀s)( (employee(s) ∧ s.deptId = d.deptId) → s.sex ≠ 'F' ) — the implication restricts s to employees of department d before requiring sex ≠ 'F'.

  3. By De Morgan's law this is equivalent to ¬(∃s)(employee(s) ∧ s.deptId = d.deptId ∧ s.sex = 'F') — 'there is no employee of department d with sex = F'.

  4. The given option that negates an existential quantifier with the predicate sex = 'F' is written in exactly this equivalent negated-existential form, so it correctly computes the required department names.

  5. The given option that uses a universal quantifier is written as (∀s)(employee(s) ∧ s.deptId = d.deptId ∧ s.sex ≠ 'F') — a bare conjunction, not an implication. As written it requires every tuple in the entire domain (not just employees of department d) to simultaneously be an employee of department d and non-female. Since the domain always contains tuples that fail this, the query as written is not equivalent to the correct implication form and does not answer the requirement.

  6. The given option that negates an existential quantifier with the predicate sex ≠ 'F' identifies departments with no non-female employee — i.e. departments that are all-female or empty — the opposite of the required condition.

  7. 'None of these' is therefore not correct, since one of the given queries (the negated-existential form with sex = 'F') already correctly answers the requirement.

Cross-check

  • Department with employees Alice (sex='F') and Bob (sex='M'): (∃s)(employee(s) ∧ deptId=d ∧ sex='F') is true (Alice), so the negated form is false — department correctly excluded.

  • Department with only Bob (sex='M'): no employee has sex='F', so the existential is false and the negated form is true — department correctly included.

  • Department with zero employees: the existential is trivially false (no employee exists), so the negated form is trivially true — an empty department is correctly included too, exactly as an empty set vacuously has no female employee. This vacuous inclusion is a shared, harmless property of the correct negated-existential form; it is NOT what disqualifies the conjunction-based universal option — that option is disqualified because a bare conjunction under ∀ forces the entire domain (not just department d's employees) to satisfy both conditions.

Conclusion: department names with no female employee are correctly obtained only by the negated-existential form (¬∃s, sex = 'F'). The universal-quantifier option is a common ∀+AND trap and, as written, is not equivalent to the correct implication form; the negated-existential option with the opposite predicate (¬∃s, sex ≠ 'F') answers a different question (all-female-or-empty departments); and since a correct option exists among the choices, 'None of these' is also wrong.

title: In TRC, which of the following expressions correctly retrieves all
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: In TRC (Tuple Relational Calculus), which of the following expressions correctly retrieves all tuples from the Employee relation where the attribute salary is strictly greater than 50,000?
solution:
We need a Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC) expression of the form {t | P(t)} that returns exactly the Employee tuples whose salary exceeds 50000.

A safe TRC filter combines two parts with conjunction (∧): the membership predicate Employee(t), which binds t to tuples of the Employee relation, and the condition t.salary > 50000.

Therefore the correct expression is: {t | Employee(t) ∧ t.salary > 50000}.

Why the others fail: using ∨ (OR) admits any tuple that is an Employee OR earns more than 50000, so it neither filters Employees nor stays safe. Using → (implication) is vacuously true for every non-Employee tuple, again admitting unwanted tuples. σ salary>50000(Employee) is relational algebra, not TRC. And {t : salary > 50000 || Employee(t)} is malformed (salary is not bound to t) and uses OR.

Hence the answer is {t | Employee(t) ∧ t.salary > 50000}.

title: What does the ACID properties guarantee in database transaction?
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: What does the ACID properties guarantee in a database transaction?
solution: The ACID properties guarantee reliable database transactions through four key principles: Atomicity ensures all-or-nothing execution, Consistency maintains data integrity rules, Isolation prevents concurrent transaction interference, and Durability guarantees committed changes persist permanently.

title: ACID is set of properties that guarantee that database transactions
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: ACID is a set of properties that guarantee that database transactions are processed reliably. Here A stands for
solution:
Concept

In a database, a transaction is a logical unit of work made up of one or more operations. The ACID properties are the four guarantees a transaction system must provide so that data stays valid even when errors, crashes, or power failures occur. ACID is an acronym: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

Applying it to this item

The letter A in ACID stands for Atomicity. Atomicity means a transaction is treated as a single, indivisible "all-or-nothing" unit: either every operation inside it completes successfully and is committed, or — if any operation fails — the whole transaction is rolled back and the database is left exactly as it was before the transaction started. There is no partial result.

Example: a bank transfer debits one account and credits another. Atomicity guarantees that you can never end up with the debit applied but the credit lost — both happen, or neither does.

Why the other terms are not "A"

  • Consistency — the C in ACID; a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, preserving all rules and constraints.

  • Isolation — the I in ACID; concurrent transactions do not interfere with one another, as if each ran alone.

  • Durability — the D in ACID; once a transaction is committed, its effects survive any later system failure.

So among the choices, Atomicity is the property denoted by A; "Access", "Algorithm", and "Affiliation" are not part of the ACID model at all.

title: Which ACID property ensures that transaction is executed entirely or
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction is executed entirely or not executed at all, so that partial updates are not permanently applied if a failure occurs during execution?
solution:
Correct answer: Atomicity.

Atomicity is the ACID property that guarantees a transaction is treated as a single, indivisible unit of work — it is either executed entirely (all of its operations commit) or not executed at all. It is popularly called the “all-or-nothing” rule.

If a failure (system crash, power loss, error, or explicit abort) occurs midway through a transaction, the recovery mechanism rolls back every change the transaction has already made, so no partial updates are left permanently in the database. The classic example is a fund transfer: debiting account A and crediting account B must both succeed; if the credit fails after the debit, atomicity ensures the debit is undone so money is never lost.

The other ACID properties solve different problems: Consistency keeps the database in a valid state with respect to all rules and constraints, Isolation keeps concurrently running transactions from interfering with one another, and Durability guarantees that once a transaction commits, its effects survive subsequent failures. (Recoverability is a schedule property, not one of the four ACID properties.) Hence the property described here is Atomicity.

title: In transactions, write-item command includes the following steps. Arrange the
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
In transactions, a write-item (X) command includes the following steps. Arrange the following steps in correct sequence.

A. Copy item X from the program variable named X into its correct location in the buffer.

B. Store the updated block from the buffer back to disk.

C. Find the address of the disk block that contains item.

D. Copy that disk block into a buffer in main memory.

choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. C,D,A,B

  2. A,C,D,B

  3. C,A,B,D

  4. D,B,C,A
solution:
Correct Sequence for Write-Item Command

To perform a write-item (X) command in a database transaction system, the following logical steps must occur in a specific order to ensure data integrity and proper buffer management.

  1. Find the address of the disk block that contains item (Step C). The system must first locate the specific block on the disk.

  2. Copy that disk block into a buffer in main memory (Step D). Once the address is found, the block is loaded from the disk into a buffer in RAM.

  3. Copy item X from the program variable named X into its correct location in the buffer (Step A). The new data is then written into the specific location within the in-memory buffer.

  4. Store the updated block from the buffer back to disk (Step B). Finally, the modified block in the buffer is written back to the permanent storage on the disk.

Therefore, the correct sequence is C → D → A → B.

title: What is the primary purpose of the COMMIT operation in
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: What is the primary purpose of the COMMIT operation in a database management transaction?

options.label: A
options.html: To permanently apply all changes made during the transaction

options.label: B
options.html: To temporarily save the changes for testing

options.label: C
options.html: To rollback the transaction to its initial state

options.label: D
options.html: To check the consistency of the database schema

solution:
The primary purpose of the COMMIT operation in a database management transaction is to permanently save all changes made during the transaction to the database.


Note for more understanding
In database management systems, transactions are governed by the ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). The COMMIT operation is the mechanical trigger for both Atomicity and Durability.

  1. The Concept of a Transaction: A transaction is a bundle of multiple SQL statements that must execute as a single unit of work. For example, a bank transfer requires deducting money from Account A and adding it to Account B.

  2. Staging Area: While these operations are running, the changes are kept in a provisional state. Other database users cannot see these modifications yet (due to Isolation).

  3. Making it Permanent: If all statements within the transaction execute perfectly without errors, the application issues a COMMIT command. This tells the database engine to write these changes safely from the temporary memory buffers directly onto the hard disk transaction logs.

Once the COMMIT completes, the transaction is officially closed, the changes become permanent, visible to all users, and resilient even in the event of a sudden power failure or system crash.

title: Which of the following concurrency problem exist in the above
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which of the following concurrency problems exist in the above schedule?
solution:
Concept: A transaction schedule can exhibit three classic read/write anomalies over a shared data item. A lost update happens when two transactions each read the same original value before either writes, so one write silently overwrites the other's update. A dirty read happens when a transaction reads a value that another transaction wrote but has not yet committed. An unrepeatable read happens when a single transaction reads the same item twice within its own execution and gets two different values because another transaction updated and committed it in between.

Application: tracing the timeline

  1. T1 reads X at t0, computes X = X - N at t1, and writes the updated X at t2 — completing T1's read-modify-write sequence on X with no commit operation shown afterward.

  2. T2 reads X at t3, immediately after T1's write at t2 (not before it), so T2's read picks up the value T1 just produced rather than the value that existed before T1 started.

  3. T2 computes X = X + M at t4 and writes X at t5, again with no commit operation shown for T2.

  4. Because T2's read at t3 occurs after T1's write at t2 with no commit recorded for T1 in between, T2 has read a value that T1's transaction could still roll back — this is the defining condition of a dirty read.

Cross-check: ruling the other anomalies in or out

  • Lost update needs both transactions to read the original value of X before either writes it. Here T2's only read_item(X) happens at t3, strictly after T1's write_item(X) at t2, so T2 never sees the pre-T1 value of X.

  • Unrepeatable read needs one transaction to read the same item twice with different results. In this schedule, T1 executes read_item(X) exactly once and T2 executes read_item(X) exactly once, so no transaction observes X changing across two reads of its own.

  • Since the lost-update timing is not met and no transaction reads twice, the combined option requiring both a lost update and a dirty read together cannot hold either.

Result: the schedule exhibits a dirty read — T2 reads X immediately after T1's uncommitted write at t2.

title: What are the potential problems when DBMS executes multiple transactions
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
What are the potential problems when a DBMS executes multiple transactions concurrently.

1. The dirty read

2. The durability

3. The phantom read

4. The serializability
solution:
Explanation:

When multiple transactions execute concurrently, certain problems can arise due to interference between them. These include:

1. Dirty read: A transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed.

2. Unrepeatable read: A transaction reads the same data twice, but the value changes between reads due to another transaction.

3. Lost update: Two transactions update the same data, and one overwrites the other's changes.

4. Phantom read: A transaction re-executes a query and gets different sets of rows due to another transaction inserting or deleting rows.

Note: Durability and serializability are not concurrency problems. Durability ensures committed data is not lost, and serializability is a correctness property.

title: Two phase locking protocol has which of the following problem(s)?
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which of the following problem(s) can occur in the Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) protocol?
solution:
Two-phase locking (2PL) protocol ensures serializability by dividing transaction execution into two phases: a growing phase (acquiring locks) and a shrinking phase (releasing locks).

In Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL), all exclusive locks are held until the transaction commits or aborts.

One major issue with Strict 2PL is deadlock. Deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are waiting for each other to release locks, resulting in a standstill. For example, if transaction T1 holds a lock on resource R1 and waits for R2, while T2 holds a lock on R2 and waits for R1, neither transaction can proceed.

Cascading rollback is not a problem in Strict 2PL. Since exclusive locks are not released until commit or abort, no other transaction can read uncommitted data. Therefore, cascading rollbacks are prevented.

Hence, the primary problem associated with Strict 2PL is deadlock, while cascading rollback does not occur under Strict 2PL.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Chances of deadlock.

title: Which of the following is also known as read-write conflict?
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Which of the following concurrency anomalies is also known as a read-write conflict?
solution:
Concept: Concurrency-control theory names a conflict between two transactions on the same data item by the chronological order of their two operations: a read followed later by another transaction’s write is a read-write (R-W) conflict; a write followed later by another transaction’s read is a write-read (W-R) conflict; and a write followed later by another transaction’s write is a write-write (W-W) conflict.

Application: Trace the operations for an unrepeatable read on an item X:

  1. Transaction T1 reads item X.

  2. Transaction T2 writes/updates item X and commits.

  3. T1 reads item X again, later in the same execution, and gets a different value than its first read.

The two operations on X therefore occur in the order read (T1) → write (T2), which is exactly the read-then-write ordering that defines a read-write conflict — so “read-write conflict” is the alternate name for unrepeatable read.

Cross-check against the other anomalies:

Anomaly

Operation order on the item

Conflict type

Dirty read / uncommitted dependency (same anomaly)

write (uncommitted) → read

write-read (W-R)

Lost update problem

write → write

write-write (W-W)

Unrepeatable read

read → write

read-write (R-W)

Result: Only the unrepeatable read matches the read-then-write ordering that defines a read-write conflict, so the correct answer is unrepeatable read.

title: Which of the following is conflict equivalent serial schedule for
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Which of the following is a conflict equivalent serial schedule for the precedence graph given below involving transactions T1, T2, T3, and T4?

(1) T1, T4, T3, T2

(2) T1, T4, T2, T3

(3) T2, T1, T3, T4

(4) T2, T1, T4, T3
solution:
Conclusion: The only conflict-equivalent serial schedule is T1, T4, T2, T3.

Precedence edges:

  • T1 -> T4 (T1 must come before T4)

  • T1 -> T3 (T1 must come before T3)

  • T4 -> T2 (T4 must come before T2)

  • T4 -> T3 (T4 must come before T3)

  • T2 -> T3 (T2 must come before T3)

Deriving the order:

From the edges we must have T1 before T4, T4 before T2, and T2 before T3. Combining these constraints yields the ordering T1 before T4 before T2 before T3, i.e., T1, T4, T2, T3.

Check each candidate sequence:

  • T1, T4, T2, T3 — satisfies all edges, so it is valid.

  • T1, T4, T3, T2 — invalid because it places T3 before T2, violating T2 -> T3.

  • T2, T1, T3, T4 — invalid because it places T2 before T4 (and before T1 in this order), violating T1 -> T4 and T4 -> T2.

  • T2, T1, T4, T3 — invalid because it places T2 before T4, violating T4 -> T2 (and also conflicts with T1 -> T4).

Therefore the only conflict-equivalent serial schedule from the given choices is T1, T4, T2, T3.

title: Consider the following schedule consisting of three transactions in database
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider the following schedule S, consisting of three transactions in a database system:
S: r1(X), w1(Y), r2(Y), w2(Z), c1, w3(X), c2, c3.
How many edges are there in the precedence graph of the given schedule?
solution:
Concept: A precedence graph (serialization graph) for a schedule has one node per transaction. For every pair of operations on the SAME data item, from DIFFERENT transactions, where at least one operation is a WRITE, an edge is drawn from the transaction whose operation appears EARLIER in the schedule to the transaction whose operation appears LATER. Read-write, write-read, and write-write pairs across transactions all create edges; a read-read pair never does. This rule depends only on the RELATIVE ORDER of the two conflicting operations: commit operations (ci) are bookkeeping markers only -- they never create an edge, and a transaction having already committed does not remove or block an edge already established by one of its earlier operations against a later operation of another transaction.

  1. Data item X: the only operations on X are r1(X) at position 1 and w3(X) at position 6, from different transactions (T1 and T3), and one of them is a write, so they conflict. Since r1(X) occurs before w3(X) in the schedule, this creates an edge T1 -> T3. c1 (the commit of T1) occurs at position 5, strictly between r1(X) and w3(X) -- but c1 is not itself a conflicting operation, so it neither creates nor removes an edge; only the relative order of r1(X) and w3(X) matters, and that order is fixed regardless of where the commit falls.

  2. Data item Y: the operations on Y are w1(Y) at position 2 and r2(Y) at position 3, from different transactions (T1 and T2), and one is a write, so they conflict. w1(Y) precedes r2(Y), so this creates an edge T1 -> T2.

  3. Data item Z: only w2(Z) touches Z, from a single transaction (T2). With no other transaction accessing Z, there is no conflicting pair on Z, so no edge is produced.

  4. Commit operations c1, c2, c3 are bookkeeping markers only and never contribute edges by themselves.

Cross-check: Cross-check by scanning every pair of transactions directly: (T1, T2) share data item Y -> one edge; (T1, T3) share data item X -> one edge; (T2, T3) share no common data item -> no possible edge. This independently confirms exactly two edges.

Note: Note on the reported confusion: c1 appearing before w3(X) in the schedule does NOT remove the T1 -> T3 edge. A precedence-graph edge is fixed purely by the order of the two conflicting read/write operations (here, r1(X) before w3(X)); it does not matter that T1 had already committed by the time T3's w3(X) executed. Commit order and conflict order are separate things -- only conflict order (the order of the actual read/write operations on the shared item) determines precedence-graph edges.

Total edges in the precedence graph: 2

Both transactions execute completely and exactly once in any serial order without rollback or failure. What will be the final values of X and Y?
solution:
Step 1 — Note the initial values: X = 200, Y = 100.

Step 2 — Identify which item each transaction modifies:

• T₂ reads Y, computes Y := Y + 20, and writes Y. It touches only Y.

title: Suppose database schedule involves transactions Consider the precedence graph of
subject: Databases
bodyHtml: Suppose a database schedule S involves transactions T1 , T2 , .............,Tn . Consider the precedence graph of S with vertices representing the transactions and edges representing the conflicts. If S is serializable, which one of the following orderings of the vertices of the precedence graph is guaranteed to yield a serial schedule ?
solution:
Main idea: If the schedule is conflict-serializable, its precedence graph has no directed cycles (it is a directed acyclic graph, or DAG).

  • A topological ordering of the DAG arranges transactions so that for every directed edge from one transaction to another, the source transaction appears earlier in the order.

  • Executing transactions serially in any topological order preserves the order of all conflicting operations, so the resulting serial schedule is conflict-equivalent to the original schedule.

  • How to obtain such an order: run any topological sort algorithm (for example, Kahn's algorithm or a DFS-based method using finishing times). If a cycle is detected, the schedule is not conflict-serializable.

Conclusion: A topological ordering of the precedence graph is guaranteed to yield a serial schedule when the schedule is serializable, because it respects all conflict dependencies.

title: Consider the following schedule involving Transactions and r₁(x); r₃(x); r₁(x);
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider the following schedule 'S' involving 3 Transactions T₁, T₂, and T₃:

S: r₁(x); r₃(x); r₁(x); w₁(y); r₂(y); w₂(x); C₃; C₁; C₂

Which of the following is true regarding the above schedule?

options.label: D
options.html: It is a strict schedule, so it is both recoverable and cascadeless

solution:
Answer: The schedule is recoverable but not cascadeless.

  • T2 reads y after T1 writes y (w1(y) occurs before r2(y)), so T2 reads an uncommitted value from T1. Therefore the schedule is not cascadeless.

  • T1 commits (C1) before T2 commits (C2). Because any transaction that reads from another commits only after the writer commits, the schedule is recoverable.

  • The schedule is not strict: strict schedules forbid reading or writing items that were last written by an uncommitted transaction, but here r2(y) occurs before C1.

title: Consider table bank_accounts (account_id, balance). Assume two accounts with account_id
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider table bank_accounts = (account_id, balance). Assume two accounts with account_id as A and B. Also assume that initially both accounts have a balance Rs. 5,000 each. Two transactions T1 and T2 are executed concurrently, both under REPEATABLE READ isolation level. Database uses standard locking mechanism.

  • T1: transfers Rs.1,000 from A to B. DB operation sequence is as follows: BEGIN; READ(A); READ(B); WRITE(A); WRITE(B); END

  • T2: transfers Rs.1,000 from B to A. DB operation sequence is as follows: BEGIN; READ(B); READ(A); WRITE(B); WRITE(A); END

Both transactions read the corresponding account balances, deducts Rs. 1,000 from one account, then adds Rs. 1,000 to the other account and results are written back. Assuming that all interleaving of execution of T1 and T2 are possible and that there are no extraneous factors, which of the following will never occur?

options.label: A
options.html: A's account balance shows Rs. 5,000 and B's account balance shows Rs. 5,000

options.label: B
options.html: A's account balance shows Rs. 4,000 and B's account balance shows Rs. 4,000

options.label: C
options.html: Deadlock is detected and T2 will be rolled back to recover

options.label: D
options.html: A's account balance shows Rs. 4,000 and that of B will have Rs. 6,000

solution:
Two-Phase Locking (2PL) with lock upgrades (shared to exclusive) guarantees serializability among the transactions that commit, and it does this by converting any dangerous overlap into a blocking wait (or a deadlock) rather than letting it complete silently. Concretely: a transaction must hold a shared lock to read an item and must upgrade that to an exclusive lock before writing it; the upgrade is refused for as long as any other transaction still holds a lock on the same item. So the only reachable final states are ones equivalent to a serial execution (both transactions commit) or ones where a lock conflict forces exactly one transaction to abort, leaving only the survivor's effect visible.

Trace the two operation sequences against this rule -- T1: READ(A), READ(B), WRITE(A), WRITE(B); T2: READ(B), READ(A), WRITE(B), WRITE(A):

  1. Serial-equivalent case: one transaction fully commits (and releases its locks) before the other begins its writes. Because one transfers Rs. 1,000 from A to B and the other transfers Rs. 1,000 from B to A, running them one after the other in either order cancels out, leaving A = Rs. 5,000 and B = Rs. 5,000.

  2. Reversed-order case: T1 reads A first and T2 reads B first; since shared (read) locks don't conflict with each other, each transaction can then also acquire a shared lock on the OTHER account before either attempts to write. At that point both transactions hold shared locks on both A and B, and each one's attempt to upgrade to an exclusive lock (needed to write) is blocked by the other's shared lock -- a genuine circular wait, i.e. a deadlock, which the DBMS must detect and resolve by rolling one transaction back.

  3. If the DBMS resolves that circular wait by rolling T2 back FIRST, T2's shared locks are released, T1's blocked upgrade then succeeds, and only T1 goes on to write and commit -- leaving A = Rs. 4,000 and B = Rs. 6,000 (and, symmetrically, rolling T1 back first would let T2 alone finish, leaving A = Rs. 6,000 and B = Rs. 4,000).

  4. The one outcome this locking rule structurally rules out is A = Rs. 4,000 and B = Rs. 4,000 (both accounts net LOWER). That number can only come from an uncontrolled lost update: both transactions reading the original Rs. 5,000 balances before either writes, then each independently overwriting the other's result so the Rs. 1,000 'in transit' is destroyed for both accounts. But that requires both transactions to hold read locks on both items and then write without ever waiting for the other -- exactly the situation step 2 shows is blocked (converted into a wait/deadlock) rather than allowed to complete.

Cross-check with the conservation invariant: A + B must equal Rs. 10,000 in every state reachable from a fully committed-or-rolled-back execution, since each transaction only moves Rs. 1,000 between the two accounts. 5,000 + 5,000 = 10,000 (both commit); 4,000 + 6,000 = 10,000 and 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000 (only one transaction's transfer survives) -- all conserve the total. But 4,000 + 4,000 = 8,000 does not conserve the total, confirming it cannot be a legitimate outcome of two atomic Rs. 1,000 transfers; it is reachable only through an uncontrolled lost update, which the required lock upgrade here prevents.

So the account state that will never occur under this locking scheme is both balances showing Rs. 4,000.

title: Consider the following schedule for transaction and r1(x), r2(y), r3(y)
subject: Databases
bodyHtml:
Consider the following schedule for transactions T1, T2, and T3.

S: r1(x), r2(y), r3(y), w1(x), w3(x), r2(z), w1(x)

The timestamps of T1, T2, and T3 are 30, 10, and 20, respectively.

Which of the following statements is true for this schedule?

options.label: A
options.html: The schedule is allowed under the basic time-stamp but not the Thomas write-stamp protocol

options.label: B
options.html: The schedule is not allowed under any of the basic time-stamp protocol as well as Thomas write.

options.label: C
options.html: The schedule is allowed under both basic time-stamp protocols as well as Thomas write.

options.label: D
options.html: The schedule is allowed under Thomas write time-stamp protocol but not basic time stamp protocol

solution:
Concept: Timestamp ordering executes conflicting operations in transaction-timestamp order. For a data item Q, RTS(Q) records the largest timestamp of any successful reader and WTS(Q) records that of any successful writer.

A read by Ti is permitted only when TS(Ti) is at least WTS(Q). A basic-protocol write requires TS(Ti) to be at least both RTS(Q) and WTS(Q).

Thomas write rule changes only the TS(Ti) < WTS(Q) case by ignoring that obsolete write. It does not relax the TS(Ti) < RTS(Q) rejection test.

Application:

  1. Initially, RTS and WTS are 0 for x, y, and z.

  2. r1(x) has timestamp 30, so it is accepted and sets RTS(x) = 30.

  3. r2(y) and r3(y) are accepted in sequence, so RTS(y) becomes max(10, 20) = 20.

  4. w1(x) has timestamp 30. Since 30 is not less than RTS(x) = 30 or WTS(x) = 0, the write is accepted and WTS(x) becomes 30.

  5. At w3(x), TS(T3) = 20 is less than RTS(x) = 30. This read-timestamp violation aborts T3 under the basic protocol and also under Thomas write rule.

Cross-check: The earlier r1(x) followed by w3(x) creates a conflict edge T1 → T3, but timestamp order requires T3 (20) before T1 (30). The schedule therefore violates timestamp order at the same operation.

Result: The true statement is that the schedule is not allowed under either the basic timestamp protocol or Thomas write rule.
