title: Using adjacency edge selection in DFS find valid traversal Starting
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml:
Using adjacency edge selection in DFS find valid traversal

Starting vertex M and travelling should be done in lexicographic order (while traversing vertex T it should traverse A first than M)
solution:
Key idea: perform a depth-first search (DFS) starting at M. At each vertex, examine its adjacent vertices in lexicographic order and visit the first unvisited one; backtrack when no unvisited adjacents remain.

  1. Start at M. M has adjacent vertices A and T; choose A because A is lexicographically smaller than T.

  2. At A, its adjacents (in lexicographic order) are D, O, P. D is unvisited and smallest, so go to D.

  3. At D, adjacent vertices ordered lexicographically are O, P, R. O is unvisited and smallest, so go to O.

  4. At O, adjacents in lexicographic order are M, P, T. M is already visited, so skip it. The next unvisited is P, so go to P.

  5. At P, the only unvisited adjacent is E, so visit E next.

  6. At E, all adjacents either lead to already visited vertices or form cycles (e.g., E → D). No unvisited adjacents remain, so backtrack to P, then to O.

  7. Back at O, the remaining unvisited adjacent is T, so visit T.

  8. After finishing T, backtrack to earlier vertices. From D the remaining unvisited adjacent is R, so visit R last.

Final traversal: M, A, D, O, P, E, T, R

title: Consider the following graph: Which of the following is not
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml:
Consider the following graph:

Which of the following is not a depth first search traversal of the given graph?

options.label: A
options.html: P, Q, T, V, U, S, R, W

options.label: B
options.html: P, R, S, U, W, V, T, Q

options.label: C
options.html: P, R, S, U, V, W, T, Q

options.label: D
options.html: P, Q, T, V, W, S, R, U

solution:
Concept

Depth-first search (DFS) follows one rule: from the current vertex, move to any one of its still-unvisited neighbours and go as deep as possible; only when the current vertex has no unvisited neighbour left do you backtrack to the most recent vertex that still has one. So at every step the next vertex in the order must be adjacent to the vertex you are currently standing on (after any forced backtracking) — you can never jump to a vertex that is not an edge away from the active vertex.

Graph edges

From the figure the adjacency is:

  • P : Q, R

  • Q : P, T

  • R : P, S

  • S : R, U, W

  • T : Q, V

  • U : S, V

  • V : T, U, W

  • W : S, V

Applying the rule to each sequence

Trace each ordering and check, at every move, that the next vertex is a neighbour of the active vertex.

P, R, S, U, W, V, T, Q : P→R→S→U is fine (each is a neighbour of the previous). Now standing at U, its neighbours are S and V; S is already visited, so the only unvisited neighbour of U is V. DFS is therefore forced to go U→V. But this sequence goes U→W instead, and there is no edge between U and W. This jump is impossible, so this ordering can never be produced by a DFS.

P, Q, T, V, U, S, R, W : P→Q→T→V→U→S→R; at R both neighbours (P, S) are visited, so backtrack to S and finish its last neighbour W. Every move lands on a neighbour of the active vertex — a valid DFS.

P, R, S, U, V, W, T, Q : P→R→S→U→V→W; at W both neighbours (S, V) are visited, backtrack to V and go V→T→Q. Every move is along an edge — a valid DFS.

P, Q, T, V, W, S, R, U : P→Q→T→V→W→S→R; at R both neighbours visited, backtrack to S and finish its last neighbour U. Every move is along an edge — a valid DFS.

Cross-check

Three of the four orderings can be reproduced by a legal DFS; exactly one cannot, because it demands the step U→W where no edge exists. Since the question asks which sequence is not a DFS traversal, the answer is the single impossible ordering: P, R, S, U, W, V, T, Q.

title: Consider the following graph: Consider the following traversing sequence of
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml:
Consider the following graph:

Consider the following traversing sequence of nodes: I. 1 2 3 4 5 6 II. 1 3 5 6 4 2 III. 3 2 1 5 6 4 IV. 5 1 6 2 4 3 How many of the above sequence corresponds to the depth-first search for the graph is ______.
solution:
Answer: 2 sequences correspond to a valid depth-first search traversal: 1 3 5 6 4 2 and 3 2 1 5 6 4.

Key idea: Depth-first search (DFS) always visits an unvisited neighbor and continues as deep as possible, backtracking only when the current vertex has no unvisited neighbors. This produces a LIFO (stack-like) visit order.

  • Sequence 1 3 5 6 4 2 — valid: start at 1, go to neighbor 3, from 3 go to neighbor 5, from 5 go to neighbor 6, from 6 go to neighbor 4. After 4 has no new neighbors, backtrack and finally visit the remaining unvisited vertex 2. Each move either visits a new neighbor or backtracks when no neighbors remain, consistent with DFS.

  • Sequence 3 2 1 5 6 4 — valid: start at 3, go to neighbor 2, from 2 go to neighbor 1, from 1 go to neighbor 5, then 5→6→4 completes the deep-first exploration; backtracking happens only when required. This sequence also respects DFS behavior.

  • Sequence 1 2 3 4 5 6 — not valid for DFS on this graph: this order implies visiting 2 immediately after 1, then jumping to 3 and later to 4,5,6 in a way that requires leaving unexplored neighbors behind without backtracking appropriately. In DFS you must finish exploring a chosen branch (visit its reachable unvisited vertices) before returning to earlier vertices; this sequence does not respect that requirement given the graph's adjacency.

  • Sequence 5 1 6 2 4 3 — not valid for DFS on this graph: after visiting 5 then 1, there is no DFS-consistent way to visit 6 next (without revisiting intermediate vertices) while still treating DFS as deep exploration of neighbors; the order requires illegal jumps or skipping unvisited neighbors that should have been explored before backtracking.

Therefore exactly 2 of the given sequences can arise from depth-first search traversals on this graph.

title: Consider the following statements: Connected components of graph can be
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml:
Consider the following statements:

S₁: Connected components of a graph can be obtained by depth-first traversal but not by breadth-first traversal.

S₂: In DFS traversal every vertex of the graph is visited exactly once.

Which of the following options is correct?
solution:
Concept: In every standard algorithms reference (e.g. CLRS's Depth-First-Search procedure), the “traversal of a graph” — as opposed to a single call from one vertex — loops over ALL vertices and launches a fresh BFS or DFS call from each vertex not yet visited. This outer loop is part of the algorithm's own definition, not an extra assumption: it is exactly what makes DFS (and equally BFS) usable to enumerate connected components, since the vertices reached by one such call are precisely one connected component. Because each vertex's visited flag is set by exactly one of these calls, every vertex ends up visited exactly once over that complete traversal — for BFS just as much as for DFS.

Applying it to S₁ and S₂:

  • S₁ claims only depth-first traversal, not breadth-first traversal, can obtain the connected components. Since breadth-first traversal — restarted from each unvisited vertex the same way — discovers the exact same components, S₁ is false: the technique is not depth-first-exclusive.

  • S₂ claims every vertex of the graph is visited exactly once during DFS traversal. This follows directly from the concept above: the outer loop over all vertices, together with the visited marker set once per call, ensures no vertex is ever marked visited a second time, so S₂ is true.

Cross-check: A single depth-first call started from one arbitrary vertex only reaches that vertex's own component, so on its own it would not cover a disconnected graph — but the standard DFS traversal of a graph always includes the outer restart loop, so the exactly-once property in S₂ refers to (and holds for) that complete traversal, not an isolated single call. Also, a vertex may be encountered as a NEIGHBOUR while a different vertex's adjacency list is being scanned — that can happen from more than one place — but the vertex's own adjacency list is expanded, and its own visited flag switched on, only once, at the moment it is itself visited. Being looked at as someone else's neighbour repeatedly is not the same as being visited repeatedly.

Result: S₁ is false and S₂ is true, so the statement pairing that holds is the one asserting S₂ alone.

title: The maximum possible height of BFS tree, if BFS is
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: The maximum possible height of BFS tree, if BFS is run on a complete bipartite graph Km,n where m≥, n≥1 with starting vertex 'S' is ______.
solution:
Answer: 2

Explanation: A complete bipartite graph splits vertices into two disjoint sets, and every edge joins a vertex from one set to a vertex in the other set.

  • Place the starting vertex S in one partition. S is at distance 0 (the root of the BFS tree).

  • Every vertex in the opposite partition is adjacent to S, so they are discovered at distance 1.

  • Any remaining vertices in S's partition (other than S) are not adjacent to S but are adjacent to vertices in the opposite partition, so they are discovered at distance 2 via those vertices.

  • Thus no vertex can be at distance greater than 2 from S, so the BFS tree height is at most 2. The maximum possible height (for valid m,n with at least one vertex on each side and at least one other vertex in S's partition) is 2.

Note: If the starting partition contains no other vertices (for example m=1 and S is that sole vertex), the BFS tree height would be 1. The question asks for the maximum possible height over valid graphs, which is 2.

Answer: 4

In breadth-first search (BFS), the queue always stores the vertices that have been discovered but not yet processed. The required queue size is the maximum number of such vertices that can appear at any time during the traversal.

  4. After that, processing vertices can only keep the queue size at most 4 or reduce it, and no other level has more than 4 vertices, so the queue is never required to hold more than 4 elements.

Therefore, the minimum queue size needed to perform BFS on this graph is 4.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q161
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: Which data structure is used for BFS in graphs?
solution:
Concept — the frontier's removal order is the traversal order. Breadth-first search visits the vertices of a graph in non-decreasing order of their distance from the source: every vertex at distance d is visited before any vertex at distance d + 1. Any such search keeps its discovered-but-not-yet-explored vertices in a frontier container, and the order in which that container releases elements is exactly the order in which the search explores them. Level-by-level exploration therefore requires a container that releases elements in the same order they arrived — a first-in, first-out (FIFO) discipline.

Application — the standard BFS loop. The classical formulation (CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, §22.2) holds the frontier in a FIFO container:

  1. Mark the source s as visited, set dist(s) = 0, and insert s into the frontier.

  2. While the frontier is not empty, remove the element at its front and call it u.

  3. For every neighbour v of u that is not yet visited, mark v visited, set dist(v) = dist(u) + 1, and insert v at the rear of the frontier.

  4. Stop when the frontier empties; every vertex reachable from s has then been visited exactly once, so the run costs O(V + E) time and O(V) extra space.

Why FIFO produces levels. Vertices at distance 1 are inserted while the source is being explored, and vertices at distance 2 only while a distance-1 vertex is being explored. Because insertion is at the rear and removal is from the front, everything inserted at distance 1 leaves the container before anything inserted at distance 2; the frontier therefore holds vertices of at most two consecutive distances and the visit order is level by level. The structure defined by exactly this insert-at-rear, remove-from-front behaviour is the queue, so a queue is the data structure used for BFS.

Cross-check — trace on a small graph. Take the edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, D–E with source A; the front of the queue is written first.

The visit order A, B, C, D, E gives dist(A) = 0, dist(B) = 1, dist(C) = 1, dist(D) = 2 and dist(E) = 3 — every level finished before the next one starts, which is what BFS must produce. Holding the same frontier in a last-in, first-out container instead changes the order to A, C, D, E, B: a deep descent along one branch, not a level sweep.

Contrast with the other structures named.

  • A stack releases the most recently inserted vertex, so the walk pushes on along one branch and backtracks only at a dead end — that is depth-first search rather than a level sweep.

  • A tree is a hierarchy of parent-child links, a graph shape rather than an insertion-order container; BFS in fact produces such a hierarchy (the BFS tree) as its output, so it is a result of the traversal and not the mechanism that drives it.

  • A hash table fixes each entry's position from its key and keeps no order among entries; BFS commonly uses one as the visited set for fast membership tests, but it cannot supply the ordering the level sweep depends on.

Result. The frontier of a breadth-first search is held in a queue.

title: Level order Traversal of rooted Tree can be done by
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: Level order Traversal of a rooted Tree can be done by starting from root and performing :
solution:
Core idea: Level-order traversal visits nodes level by level starting from the root. Implement it using breadth-first search (BFS) with a queue (FIFO).

Algorithm (queue-based):

  1. Enqueue the root node (if it exists).

  2. While the queue is not empty:

  3. Dequeue the front node and visit it; then enqueue all of its children in order (typically left to right).

Pseudo-code: queue = new Queue(); if (root != null) queue.enqueue(root); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { node = queue.dequeue(); visit(node); for each child of node: queue.enqueue(child); }

Time complexity: O(n), where n is the number of nodes (each node is enqueued and dequeued once).

Space complexity: O(n) in the worst case (the queue may hold an entire level of the tree, which can be proportional to n).

title: What is the time complexity of BFS (Breadth-First Search) in
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: What is the time complexity of BFS (Breadth-First Search) in terms of V (vertices) and E (edges)?
solution:
BFS explores each vertex and edge exactly once using a queue. For V vertices and E edges, this results in O(V + E) time complexity.

Note (For More Understanding)
Here is a detailed explanation of why O(V + E) is the exact time complexity for Breadth-First Search (BFS) when using an adjacency list:

1. Vertex Exploration: O(V)

In BFS, we use a boolean array or set (typically called visited) to keep track of the vertices we have already processed.

  • A vertex is only pushed into the FIFO (First-In, First-Out) queue if its visited status is false.

  • Once it enters the queue, it is marked as visited = true, ensuring it can never enter the queue a second time.

  • Enqueuing and dequeuing a vertex takes constant time, O(1)

  • Since there are V vertices, managing the queue across the entire lifetime of the algorithm takes O(V) time.

2. Edge Exploration: O(E)

When a vertex is popped out of the queue, the algorithm looks at all of its adjacent neighbors to see if they need to be visited.

  • If the graph is represented as an Adjacency List, the algorithm only loops through the actual neighbors connected to that specific vertex.

  • In a Directed Graph, every single edge is looked at exactly once during the entire execution.

  • In an Und undirected Graph, every edge is looked at exactly twice (once from each of the two vertices it connects).

  • Therefore, the total time spent scanning neighbor lists across the entire run is proportional to the total number of edges, giving us O(E) time.

Putting It Together

Because the queue management and edge lookups happen in tandem, we add the two components together. This results in a final linear time complexity of:

Total Time Complexity = O(V + E)

Why it isn't O(V x E): The algorithm doesn't look at all E edges for every vertex. Instead, the total work of looking at edges is distributed across all vertices. Once an edge's origin vertex is done, that edge is never scanned again.

title: Which of the following problems can be solved using Breadth
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: Which of the following problems is guaranteed to be solved by a single standard Breadth First Search (BFS) traversal on the graph as given?

options.label: A
options.html: Finding connected components in a directed graph

options.label: D
options.html: Finding shortest path in an unweighted graph

solution:
Concept

Standard BFS uses a FIFO queue and visits vertices in nondecreasing distance layers from one source. In an unweighted graph, traversing one edge increases path length by exactly one, so first discovery fixes the minimum edge count.

A task that needs extra bookkeeping, a transformed graph, repeated traversals, or a different invariant is not guaranteed by one ordinary BFS traversal on the graph as given.

Application

  1. Start at a source s, set distance(s) = 0, and enqueue s.

  2. When a vertex at distance d is dequeued, every newly discovered neighbor is assigned distance d + 1 and enqueued.

  3. Because the queue processes all vertices at distance d before any at distance d + 1, no later discovery can use fewer edges.

  4. For example, if s is adjacent to a and b, and a is adjacent to t, BFS visits a and b at distance 1 and then t at distance 2; the parent links recover a minimum-edge path s–a–t.

Contrast

  • Finding connected components in a directed graph is ambiguous between weak and strong connectivity; it requires ignoring directions, testing mutual reachability, or running additional traversals.

  • Detecting cycles in a directed graph requires recursion-stack state or indegree processing.

  • Topological sorting requires finishing-time ordering or repeated zero-indegree removal.

Cross-check and result

Each alternative needs an invariant beyond one standard BFS traversal. The guaranteed direct application is finding a shortest path in an unweighted graph.

title: Consider directed acyclic graph with vertices Which of the following
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml:
Consider a directed acyclic graph with vertices v1, v2, v3, v4, v5, v6 shown in the figure below.

The directed edges of this graph are:

  • From v1: v1 → v2, v1 → v3

  • From v2: v2 → v4, v2 → v5

  • From v3: v3 → v4, v3 → v6

  • From v4: v4 → v5, v4 → v6

Which of the following is not a topological order?
solution:
Concept: A topological order of a directed acyclic graph is a linear arrangement of all its vertices in which, for every directed edge u → w, the tail u is written somewhere to the left of the head w. Correctness is therefore decided edge by edge and not by how natural the list looks: a single edge whose head is written before its tail already destroys the property, while two vertices with no directed path between them are free to appear in either order.

Reusable checking method: For any candidate ordering, use the position-map test below. It checks the defining condition directly and needs O(V + E) time when the position map is built once.

  1. Create pos(x), the left-to-right position of every vertex x in the proposed order.

  2. For each directed edge u → w, compare pos(u) and pos(w). A valid topological order requires pos(u) < pos(w).

  3. If even one edge violates the inequality, reject the order; if every edge satisfies it, accept the order.

Adjacency of the given graph:

Vertex

Edges leaving it

v1

v1 → v2, v1 → v3

v2

v2 → v4, v2 → v5

v3

v3 → v4, v3 → v6

v4

v4 → v5, v4 → v6

v5

none

v6

none

Application: apply the definition to the arrangement v3, v2, v4, v1, v6, v5.

  1. Write down where each vertex stands, counting from the left: v3 1st, v2 2nd, v4 3rd, v1 4th, v6 5th, v5 6th.

  2. Take the edge v1 → v2. The definition demands v1 to the left of v2, but v1 stands 4th while v2 stands 2nd, so this edge runs from right to left.

  3. Take the edge v1 → v3. It demands v1 to the left of v3, yet v3 opens the list at 1st and v1 stands 4th, so this edge also runs backwards.

  4. A single backward edge is already fatal, so this arrangement fails the definition.

Cross-check: run the same edge-by-edge test on the three remaining arrangements.

  • v1, v3, v2, v4, v5, v6 — v1 precedes v2 and v3; v2 precedes v4 and v5; v3 precedes v4 and v6; v4 precedes v5 and v6, so all eight edges point rightwards.

  • v1, v3, v2, v4, v6, v5 — this differs from v1, v3, v2, v4, v5, v6 only by swapping the final two vertices, and no edge joins v5 with v6, so every edge still points rightwards.

  • v1, v2, v3, v4, v5, v6 — the vertices stand in index order, and every edge of this graph runs from a smaller index to a larger one, so all eight point rightwards.

Result: The three arrangements just checked all satisfy the definition, so the arrangement that is not a topological order is v3, v2, v4, v1, v6, v5.

Two lessons generalise from this: a directed acyclic graph usually admits several topological orders (here at least three of them), and to reject a candidate arrangement it is enough to exhibit one edge that points leftwards.

  • 1401: first 3 digits = 140, 140^2 = 19600, mid digits = 600, index = 600 % 19 + 1 = 12.

  • 1621: first 3 digits = 162, 162^2 = 26244, mid digits = 244, index = 244 % 19 + 1 = 17.

  • 1444: first 3 digits = 144, 144^2 = 20736, mid digits = 736, index = 736 % 19 + 1 = 15.

  • 2345: first 3 digits = 234, 234^2 = 54756, mid digits = 756, index = 756 % 19 + 1 = 16.

Collision count:

title: In hashing, collision resolution is carried out by close addressing.
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml:
In hashing, collision resolution is carried out by close addressing. Which of the following is close addressing technique -

I. Buckets (for contiguous storage)
II. Chains (for linked storage)
solution:
Hash-table collision resolution splits into two families based on WHERE a colliding key ends up being stored. Open addressing (also called closed hashing) keeps every colliding key inside the hash table's own array, relocating it to another slot within that same array via a probe sequence (linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing) — no extra memory is created. Close addressing (also called closed addressing, or chaining / open hashing) instead creates a separate auxiliary structure for each slot specifically to hold colliding keys — most commonly a linked list — so a colliding key is stored outside the table's own array, in memory allocated only when a collision happens.

Applying that test to the two named techniques: the technique described as contiguous storage places a colliding key into another position within the hash table's own array — no separate collision-handling memory is created for it, matching the open-addressing pattern. The technique described as linked storage creates a new node in a structure attached to the slot specifically to hold the colliding key, outside the table's own array — matching the close-addressing pattern exactly.

This lines up with how the two terms are traditionally split: close addressing (also called closed addressing) names the array-external, per-slot chaining approach, while open addressing (occasionally also called closed hashing — a separate point of terminology overlap) names the in-place, same-array approach. A technique that keeps every key inside the table's own array — however that array is organised — sits in the open-addressing family rather than close addressing.

So the linked-storage technique (Chains) is the close-addressing technique among the two listed here; the contiguous-storage technique (Buckets) belongs to the open-addressing family instead.

title: Which of the following is NOT benefit of using hash

bodyHtml: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of using hash tables for data storage and retrieval ?
solution: Hash tables offer O(1) average-case time complexity for search, insert, and delete operations. However, they do not guarantee constant-time performance in all cases because hash collisions can degrade performance to O(n) worst-case.

title: In hash table, the load factor primarily represents which of
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: In a hash table, the load factor primarily represents which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Ratio of stored elements to the total number of slots

options.label: D
options.html: Total memory occupied by the hash table

solution:
The load factor (denoted alpha) of a hash table measures how full the table is. It is defined as alpha = n / m, where n is the number of entries (keys) currently stored and m is the total number of slots (buckets) in the table.

Therefore the load factor is the ratio of the number of stored elements to the total number of slots. It does not count collisions, hash functions, memory bytes, or key sizes; it is purely a fill ratio.

The load factor matters because it controls performance. As alpha grows, collisions become more likely and average lookup, insert, and delete times rise. For separate chaining the average chain length equals alpha, while open addressing requires alpha < 1 (each slot holds one item) and degrades sharply as alpha approaches 1.

To keep operations close to O(1) on average, implementations rehash (grow the table and redistribute keys) once the load factor exceeds a chosen threshold, commonly around 0.75 for open addressing.

Hence the correct description is: the ratio of stored elements to the total number of slots.

title: Which of the following is not used to calculate Hash
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: Which of the following is not used to calculate Hash Functions?
solution: Folding, modular, and division methods are used to compute hash values. For example, the division method commonly uses h(k) = k mod m. Rehashing is different: it is used after collisions or table resizing to place keys again, not to calculate the original hash function. Hence, Rehashing is the correct answer.

title: Which data structure is typically used to implement hash table
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: Which data structure is typically used to implement hash table ?
solution:
Answer: Array

Why: A hash table is typically implemented as an array of buckets. A hash function maps each key to an index in that array, allowing average-case constant time (O(1)) for lookup, insertion, and deletion.

  • Collision handling: When multiple keys map to the same array index, collisions are handled using strategies such as chaining (each bucket stores a list of entries) or open addressing (probing to find another slot).

  • Buckets can use different internal structures: commonly a linked list for chaining, and some implementations switch to a balanced tree for very large buckets to guarantee better worst-case performance.

Why the other structures are not the typical choice:

  • Linked list: Useful as the per-bucket structure for chaining, but not the overall container that maps keys to positions.

  • Binary tree: Provides ordered operations and O(log n) performance, and may be used inside buckets in some implementations, but is not the typical primary structure for a hash table.

  • Stack: Has LIFO semantics and does not support indexing by a hash; it is not suitable for implementing hash table operations.

title: Consider hashing function that resolves collision by quadratic probing. Assume
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: Consider a hashing function that resolves collision by quadratic probing. Assume the address space is indexed from 1 to 16. Which of the following locations will never be probed if a collision occurs at position 8?
solution:
Answer: 14, 16 and 7 will never be probed.

Reason:

Using quadratic probing, probe positions are given by (start + i^2) mod m, where m = 16 and we map 0 to 16 for 1-based indexing. With start = 8, compute a few values:

  • i = 0 → (8 + 0) mod 16 = 8 (initial probe)

  • i = 1 → (8 + 1) mod 16 = 9

  • i = 2 → (8 + 4) mod 16 = 12

  • i = 3 → (8 + 9) mod 16 = 1

  • i = 4 → (8 + 16) mod 16 = 8 (cycle repeats)

Thus the probe cycle is 8, 9, 12, 1, then back to 8; only positions 8, 9, 12 and 1 are ever probed. Therefore any location not in that set (including 14, 16 and 7) will never be probed.

title: If collision happens for key while inserting an element into
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: If collision happens for a key while inserting an element into a hash table using linear probing, then successive probes are independent of initial probe in
solution:
Explanation:

In Linear Probing:

In linear probing, we linearly probe for next slot.

The successive probing happens linearly after the initial probe position.

Successive probes are dependants of the initial probe of a key.

Hence in linear probing the number of probe sequences possible for a key are m.

The main problem with linear probing is primary clustering, many consecutive elements form groups and it starts taking time to find a free slot or to search an element.

Quadratic probing:

The successive probing happens at a distance which is quadratic

Successive probes are dependants of the initial probe of a key.

Hence in quadratic probing the number of probe sequences possible for a key are m.

There is no primary clustering possible in quadratic probing.

Double hashing:

We use another hash function hash2(x) and look for i*hash2(x) slot in i’th rotation.

If the 2 keys happened to have same probe position they will have the successive probes different depending on the h2.

The succeeding probe sequences are decided by the another hash function.

Hence in double hashing the number of probe sequences possible for a key are m^2.

Next probe displacement will be decided by the second hash function, hence they are independent of initial probe.

Hence there won’t be a primary clustering. No primary clustering because the runs of occupied elements is not going to increase.

And even though 2 elements are having same probe position we are going to have different subsequent probe sequences

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q120
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: Among the open-addressing (probing) collision-resolution techniques, which one minimizes clustering (both primary and secondary) the most ?
solution:
Concept

In open addressing, when a key's home slot is already occupied, the table searches through a defined sequence of alternative slots until an empty one is found. Primary clustering is the tendency for these probe sequences to merge into long runs of occupied slots whenever the step size depends only on a fixed rule shared by every key, so that colliding keys are forced to follow an identical sequence of slots and the cluster grows every time another key joins it. Secondary clustering is a milder, related problem: even once different home slots are given different step sizes (so primary clustering is avoided), keys that happen to share the SAME home slot still take the identical step sequence as one another. A probing scheme minimizes clustering overall to the extent that the step it takes depends on the key itself, not merely on the home slot, so that even keys that collide at the same slot diverge onto different sequences.

Application

  1. Linear probing takes a fixed step of 1 from the previous slot on every collision. Two keys that collide at the same slot therefore probe the exact same sequence of slots from that point onward, so runs of occupied slots merge and grow -- the classic primary-clustering behaviour.

  2. Quadratic probing takes increasing squared steps (1, 4, 9, ...) from each key's own home slot. Keys with different home slots quickly diverge onto different slots, breaking up the long runs of primary clustering; but two keys that share the same home slot still trace the identical squared sequence as each other, which is the separate phenomenon called secondary clustering.

  3. Double hashing computes its step size from a second, independent hash function applied to the key. Even two keys that share the same home slot typically get different step sizes from this second hash, so their probe sequences diverge onto different slots almost immediately. Because the step itself is key-dependent, not just the home slot, double hashing's probe sequences most closely approximate a uniformly random probing order, which minimizes both primary and secondary clustering more than linear or quadratic probing does.

  4. Chaining does not probe the table at all: a collision is resolved by appending the key to an independent linked list (or bucket) attached to its home slot. Since no key is ever redirected to another table slot, there is no probe sequence to converge in the first place -- the phenomenon of primary clustering, which is specifically about probe-sequence behaviour in open addressing, does not arise under chaining.

Cross-check

Among the three open-addressing techniques offered, linear probing exhibits both primary and secondary clustering, since its fixed step and shared home slot force colliding keys onto one shared sequence. Quadratic probing removes primary clustering (different home slots diverge onto different slots quickly) but keeps secondary clustering, since keys sharing a home slot still follow the identical squared sequence as each other. Double hashing removes secondary clustering as well, because even keys sharing a home slot typically get different step sizes from the second hash function, so it minimizes clustering overall the most among the three. Chaining sidesteps clustering altogether through a different collision-resolution mechanism (external lists rather than in-table probing), so it is not a comparison point among the open-addressing techniques being compared here.

Hence, the hashing technique that minimizes clustering (both primary and secondary) the most, among the options offered, is double hashing.

title: Hash function defined h(key)=key mod with linear probing, is used
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: A hash function h defined h(key)=key mod 7, with linear probing, is used to insert the keys 44, 45, 79, 55, 91, 18, 63 into a table indexed from 0 to 6. What will be the location of key 18 ?
solution:
Concept

In open addressing, a hash function fixes only a key’s home slot: h(key) = key mod m, where m is the number of slots. Nothing guarantees that home slot is free.

Linear probing resolves a collision by scanning forward one slot at a time — (h(key) + 1) mod m, then (h(key) + 2) mod m, and so on, wrapping past the last slot back to slot 0 — and storing the key in the first free slot it meets.

So a key’s home slot depends only on its own value, but its final resting slot also depends on which slots the earlier insertions already took. Insertion order is part of the answer.

Application

Here m = 7, so h(key) = key mod 7 and the slots are 0 to 6. Insert the keys in the order given, tracking occupancy as you go.

  1. 44 mod 7 = 2. Slot 2 is free, so 44 is stored at slot 2.

  2. 45 mod 7 = 3. Slot 3 is free, so 45 is stored at slot 3.

  3. 79 mod 7 = 2. Slot 2 holds 44, so probe forward: slot 3 holds 45, slot 4 is free. 79 is stored at slot 4.

  4. 55 mod 7 = 6. Slot 6 is free, so 55 is stored at slot 6.

  5. 91 mod 7 = 0. Slot 0 is free, so 91 is stored at slot 0.

  6. 18 mod 7 = 4. Slot 4 holds 79, so probe forward: slot 5 is free. 18 is stored at slot 5.

  7. 63 mod 7 = 0. Slot 0 holds 91, so probe forward: slot 1 is free. 63 is stored at slot 1.

The table after all seven insertions:

Slot

Key stored

0

91

1

63

2

44

3

45

4

79

5

18

6

55

Cross-check

Search for 18 the same way you inserted it: start at h(18) = 4, find 79 there, step forward to slot 5 and find 18. A successful search retraces the insertion path, which confirms the placement.

Contrast this with the order-free reading: 18 hashes to slot 4, and had 18 been inserted before 79, slot 4 would indeed have been its final home. The same key lands in a different slot purely because 79 arrived first — which is exactly why linear probing must be traced in insertion order.

Key 18 is stored at slot 5.

title: The hash function used in double hashing is of the
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: The hash function used in double hashing is of the form:
solution:
Correct formula: h(k,i) = (h1(k) + i * h2(k)) mod m.

Explanation:

  • h1(k) gives the initial probe position (for i = 0).

  • h2(k) provides a step size that is multiplied by the probe number i, so each successive probe moves by a multiple of h2(k). This helps avoid primary clustering common in linear probing.

  • Choose h2(k) so it is nonzero and preferably relatively prime to m to ensure the probe sequence can cover the whole table (no short cycles). A common choice is h2(k) = 1 + (k mod (m-1)).

Short comparison:

  • Linear probing uses an offset proportional to i (for example h(k,i)= (h1(k)+i) mod m), which causes clustering.

  • Double hashing multiplies i by a key-dependent second hash, producing different probe sequences for different keys and reducing clustering.

Example:

  1. Let m = 10, h1(k) = 3, h2(k) = 4.

  2. i = 0: index = (3 + 0*4) mod 10 = 3

  3. i = 1: index = (3 + 1*4) mod 10 = 7

  4. i = 2: index = (3 + 2*4) mod 10 = 1

  5. i = 3: index = (3 + 3*4) mod 10 = 5

Summary: The defining feature of double hashing is that the second hash function determines the step size and is multiplied by the probe number i to compute successive probe indices.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - December 2009 - source Q25
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: A hash function f defined as f(key) = key mod 7, with linear probing used to resolve collisions. Insert the keys 37, 38, 72, 48, 98 and 11 into the table indexed from 0 to 6. What will be the location of 11 ?
solution:
In open addressing with linear probing, a key's home slot is given by h(key) = key mod m, where m is the table size. If that slot already holds another key, the search moves forward one slot at a time, h(key)+1, h(key)+2, and so on (wrapping past the last index back to 0), stopping at the first empty slot found.

  1. Insert 37: h(37) = 37 mod 7 = 2. Slot 2 is empty, so 37 is placed at slot 2.

  2. Insert 38: h(38) = 38 mod 7 = 3. Slot 3 is empty, so 38 is placed at slot 3.

  3. Insert 72: h(72) = 72 mod 7 = 2. Slot 2 already holds 37, so probe slot 3, which already holds 38, so probe slot 4, which is empty; 72 is placed at slot 4.

  4. Insert 48: h(48) = 48 mod 7 = 6. Slot 6 is empty, so 48 is placed at slot 6.

  5. Insert 98: h(98) = 98 mod 7 = 0. Slot 0 is empty, so 98 is placed at slot 0.

  6. Insert 11: h(11) = 11 mod 7 = 4. Slot 4 already holds 72, so probe the next slot, slot 5, which is empty; 11 is placed at slot 5.

Recount the final table: slot 0 holds 98, slot 2 holds 37, slot 3 holds 38, slot 4 holds 72, slot 5 holds 11, and slot 6 holds 48 - six keys in six distinct slots out of seven, a load factor of 6/7, with no slot reused. Independently, 11 = 7x1 + 4 confirms the home slot is 4; since slot 4 is already occupied by 72, the next slot in the probe order, slot 5, is where 11 comes to rest.

So the key 11 is stored at index 5.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q130
subject: Data Structures
bodyHtml: In a file that uses hash-based organization, overflow chains degrade performance mainly due to which of the following?
solution:
Concept: In hash-based file organization, a hash function maps each record's key to a bucket (a fixed-size disk block). When a bucket's capacity is exceeded, the surplus records cannot fit in the primary bucket, so they are placed in a separate overflow block that is chained to the primary bucket with a pointer — this technique is called overflow chaining. On the standard rotating-disk model used throughout file-organization theory, each block access costs seek time (repositioning the head to the target track) plus rotational latency (waiting for the target sector to arrive) plus transfer time — and across this standard model, seek time is consistently the largest of the three, since repositioning the head to an arbitrary, non-adjacent track takes several times longer than waiting out a partial platter rotation.

Application: To answer a lookup once a bucket has overflowed, the system has to walk the chain:

  1. Read the primary bucket block and scan its records for the key.

  2. If not found and an overflow pointer exists, fetch the linked overflow block from wherever it happens to be allocated on disk.

  3. Repeat step 2 for every further overflow block in the chain until the key is found or the chain ends.

Because overflow blocks are typically allocated at whatever free location is available rather than physically next to their primary bucket, each hop to a new overflow block is effectively a fresh, unpredictable access: it forces the disk head to be repositioned to a different track before that block can be read. To isolate what chaining specifically adds, compare a chained lookup (k block reads) against a non-overflowed lookup (1 block read): both incur one seek and one rotational wait per block visited under the standard model above, so chaining specifically adds (k − 1) extra seeks and (k − 1) extra rotational waits. Since seek time is the larger of the two components on that standard model (commonly several times a rotational wait), these (k − 1) extra seeks contribute far more added latency than the (k − 1) extra rotational waits do. As chains grow longer, it is this larger, repeated seek cost across scattered, non-contiguous blocks — i.e. increased seek time — that dominates the performance penalty specifically caused by overflow chaining.

Cross-check — why the other options are not the mechanism at work here:

  • Bucket alignment issues describe whether a bucket's boundaries coincide with the underlying disk block boundaries — a property fixed by the hashing scheme's design, not something that changes as a chain lengthens.

  • Loss of alphabetical ordering cannot be caused by overflow chaining, because hash-based organization never preserves key order to begin with — that property belongs to ordered/sequential file organization.

  • Rotational latency (waiting for the target sector to spin under the head) also recurs once per extra block access in the chain, exactly like seek does — so it is not absent from the picture. What it lacks is dominance: on the standard model, its per-access magnitude is markedly smaller than the per-access seek cost, so its accumulated contribution across the chain's extra accesses is smaller than the growth in seek time is.

So the correct answer is: increased seek time.

title: In Boolean algebra, rule (X+Y)(X+Z)
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: In Boolean algebra, rule (X+Y)(X+Z) =
solution: Expand (X+Y)(X+Z) using the distributive law to get XX + XZ + XY + YZ. Apply the idempotent law (XX = X) to simplify to X + XZ + XY + YZ. Factor out X from the first three terms: X(1 + Z + Y) + YZ. Since 1 + A = 1 in Boolean algebra, this becomes X(1) + YZ, which simplifies to the final result: X + YZ.

title: Which of the following is not valid Boolean algebra rule?
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Which of the following is not a valid Boolean algebra rule?
solution:
Concept

A Boolean identity is valid only when its two sides evaluate to the same bit for every possible assignment of its variables.

Two reliable checks are to simplify with standard identities or to find a single counterexample; one counterexample is enough to disprove a universal identity.

Application

  1. For X·X = X, the two possible inputs give 0·0 = 0 and 1·1 = 1. This is the idempotent law for AND.

  2. For (X+Y)·X = X, distribute to obtain X·X+Y·X. Idempotence gives X+XY, and absorption gives X.

  3. For X̄+XY = Y, use A′+AB = A′+B with A = X and B = Y. The left side becomes X̄+Y. At X = 0 and Y = 0, the left side is 1 while the right side is 0, so the claimed universal equality fails.

  4. For (X+Y)·(X+Z) = X+YZ, expansion gives X·X+XZ+XY+YZ. Idempotence changes X·X to X, and absorption removes XZ and XY beside X, leaving X+YZ.

Cross-check

The assignment X = 0, Y = 0 directly separates the two sides of X̄+XY = Y as 1 and 0. The other expressions reduce by idempotence, absorption, or distributivity without producing a counterexample.

Result

Therefore, X̄+XY = Y is not a valid Boolean algebra rule.

solution:
Simplify the Boolean expression:

title: Which of the following statement represents commutative law?
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Which of the following statement represents commutative law?
solution:
Concept

A commutative law states that the order of the two operands does not change the result of the operation. In Boolean algebra (as in ordinary algebra), an operation is commutative when swapping the two terms on either side of the operator leaves the value unchanged.

Application

Compare each statement against that definition — we need exactly one operator with its two operands swapped and nothing else changed:

  • X + Y = Y + X : the two operands of the same OR operation are simply interchanged, with no regrouping and no second operator. This matches the commutative law exactly.

Cross-check / Contrast

  • (X + Y) + Z = X + (Y + Z) : the operands keep their order but the grouping (parentheses) is shifted — this is the associative law, not commutation.

  • X . (Y + Z) = (X . Y) + (X . Z) : an AND is spread across an OR of two terms — this is the distributive law.

  • X + X = X : a term combined with itself returns the same term — this is the idempotent law.

Only the statement that interchanges the two operands of a single operation expresses commutativity, so X + Y = Y + X is the commutative law.

title: Dual of Boolean theorem is obtained by
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Dual of a Boolean theorem is obtained by

options.label: D
options.html: Interchanging all zero and ones and . to +

solution:
Concept

In Boolean algebra, the dual of a statement is formed by two simultaneous substitutions: every AND operator (·) is swapped with OR (+) and vice versa, and every constant 0 is swapped with 1 and vice versa. Variables and their complements are left unchanged. The Principle of Duality guarantees that if an identity is valid, its dual is automatically valid too.

Application

Applying the rule to a Boolean theorem requires both swaps together:

  1. Interchange the operators: each · (AND) becomes + (OR) and each + becomes ·.

  2. Interchange the constants: each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0.

  3. Keep all variables exactly as they are.

The correct response is therefore the one that combines an interchange of the constants 0 and 1 with a change between the · and + operators, rather than a substitution that only touches the constants.

Cross-check

Take the identity A + 0 = A. Applying both swaps gives A · 1 = A, which is also a valid identity — confirming the dual needs both substitutions. If only the constants were swapped while the operators stayed put, A + 0 = A would become A + 1 = A, which is false; that is why an operator-only or constant-only transformation cannot be the dual.

title: Boolean Function Minimization Using Algebraic Identities
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Boolean function (X + Y + Z).(X + Y + Z').(X + Z') can be minimized to
solution:
Concept

Two product-of-sums factors that agree in every literal except one variable that appears complemented in one and uncomplemented in the other combine by the rule (A + B)(A + B') = A. Distribution then gives (X + A)(X + B) = X + A.B. The rule A + A.B = A (absorption) only removes a product term that already contains A as a factor.

Application

  1. Group the first two factors, which share (X + Y) and differ only in Z vs Z': (X + Y + Z)(X + Y + Z') = (X + Y), by (A + B)(A + B') = A with A = X + Y, B = Z.

  2. The expression becomes (X + Y)(X + Z').

  3. Apply (X + A)(X + B) = X + A.B with A = Y, B = Z': (X + Y)(X + Z') = X + Y.Z'.

  4. The term Y.Z' is not absorbed in X + Y.Z': absorption would require a standalone summand that is also a factor of the product term, as in Y + Y.Z' = Y. Here the other summand is X, and Y.Z' does not contain X as a factor, so the product term remains.

So the minimized sum-of-products form is X + Y.Z'.

Cross-check

Truth-table check: setting X = 0 collapses the original product to (Y + Z)(Y + Z')(Z') = Y.Z' (the same (A + B)(A + B') = A rule, with A = Y, B = Z), so it is 1 only when Y = 1 and Z = 0, and 0 at the other three X = 0 rows. At Y = 1, Z = 1 this gives Y.Z' = 1.0 = 0, and X + Y.Z' reproduces that same 0, while X + Y would give 0 + 1 = 1 -- so X + Y fails to match the function there, whereas X + Y.Z' matches it at all eight input combinations.

Final result

Therefore, (X + Y + Z)(X + Y + Z')(X + Z') minimizes to X + Y.Z'.

title: De Morgan's law states
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: De Morgan's law states which of the following?
solution:
Concept

De Morgan's laws describe how a NOT (complement) distributes across the two basic connectives. The governing rule is: pushing a complement inside a bracket flips the connective and negates each operand — AND becomes OR and OR becomes AND. They form a matched pair of identities, not a single one.

Application

Apply the rule to each connective in turn:

  1. Complement of a conjunction: (X ∧ Y)' = X' ∨ Y' — the AND flips to OR and each variable is negated.

  2. Complement of a disjunction: (X ∨ Y)' = X' ∧ Y' — the OR flips to AND and each variable is negated.

Each of the two identities just derived is individually one of these two true forms, so neither can be rejected and neither alone is the full law.

Cross-check

Verify by truth values. Take X = 1, Y = 0:

  • (X ∧ Y)' = (1 ∧ 0)' = 0' = 1, and X' ∨ Y' = 0 ∨ 1 = 1 — they match.

  • (X ∨ Y)' = (1 ∨ 0)' = 1' = 0, and X' ∧ Y' = 0 ∧ 1 = 0 — they match.

Both identities hold for every assignment, so the complete statement of De Morgan's law is the pair together.

title: Which one of the following boolean algebraic rule is correct?

solution:
Concept

A Boolean identity is valid only when its two sides have the same value for every assignment of the variables. Complement, absorption, and distributive laws provide algebraic checks, while a truth table supplies an independent exhaustive check.

  • Complement: A · A' = 0 and A + A' = 1.

  • Absorption: A + AB = A and A(A + B) = A.

  • Distributive form: X + YZ = (X + Y)(X + Z).

Application

Apply these identities to each stated rule:

  • A · A' = 1 conflicts with the complement identity, because A · A' is always 0.

  • A + AB = A + B reduces on the left to A by absorption, whereas A + B also depends on B.

  • A + A'B = A + B follows from distribution over the complement, as shown below.

  • A(A + B) = B reduces on the left to A by absorption, so it does not equal B for all assignments.

  1. A + A'B = (A + A')(A + B) by X + YZ = (X + Y)(X + Z).

  2. (A + A')(A + B) = 1 · (A + B) by the complement law.

  3. 1 · (A + B) = A + B by the identity law.

title: Convert the Boolean function F(A, to its simplified SOP form.
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Convert the Boolean function F(A, B, C) = Σ(0, 1, 3, 5) to its simplified SOP form.
solution:
Concept

A sum of minterms identifies exactly the input rows on which a Boolean function equals 1. In a Karnaugh map, adjacent 1-cells are grouped in the largest power-of-two blocks; each block removes the variable that changes within it. The minimal SOP is the smallest set of resulting product terms that covers every listed minterm.

Application

For F(A, B, C) = Σ(0, 1, 3, 5), write each minterm in binary and in canonical product form:

  1. m0 = 000 = A'B'C'

  2. m1 = 001 = A'B'C

  3. m3 = 011 = A'BC

  4. m5 = 101 = AB'C

The largest adjacent pairs on the K-map are:

  • m0 and m1 differ only in C, giving A'B'.

  • m1 and m3 differ only in B, giving A'C.

  • m1 and m5 differ only in A, giving B'C.

The minterms m0, m3, and m5 each require one of these three implicants, so none can be removed. Therefore the minimal SOP is F = A'B' + A'C + B'C.

Cross-check

Truth-table evaluation of A'B' + A'C + B'C gives 1 exactly for ABC = 000, 001, 011, and 101, and 0 for the other four rows. Its on-set is therefore {0, 1, 3, 5}, which matches the given function.

title: Which of the following is an example of Digital Electronic?
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Which of the following is an example of a Digital Electronic?
solution:
Concept: Digital electronics refers to circuits and systems that process, store, or transmit information using discrete binary signals (0s and 1s) rather than continuous analog signals -- any device whose core function depends on binary logic circuitry falls under this category.

Application: Among the choices here, more than one device relies on digital circuitry for its core function: computers process and store data in binary logic, modern mobile phones use digital signal-processing chips for voice, data, and multimedia, and digital cameras use electronic image sensors with digital processing to capture and store images.

Contrast:

  • A choice naming only a computing device treats digital electronics as if it were a single, narrow category, when the category is far broader than one device type.

  • A choice naming only a communication device makes the same narrowing mistake -- it ignores that computing and imaging devices are digital-electronic just as much as a communication device is.

  • A choice naming only an imaging device again picks a single instance of the category rather than recognising that the property holds across several of the listed devices.

  • A choice ruling out every listed device assumes none of them use digital circuitry, which is the opposite of what the definition of digital electronics implies for these devices.

Result: Since the digital-electronics property applies to more than a single device among the choices, no single device captures the complete answer, and 'none of the above' is also wrong since digital electronic devices are genuinely represented in the list -- so the option that acknowledges more than one of them is the accurate and complete answer.

title: Which of the following is Boolean operator
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Which of the following is a Boolean operator ?
solution:
Concept

A Boolean operator is an operation defined on truth values — quantities that can take only the two values 0 (false) and 1 (true) — and whose result is itself a truth value. Boolean algebra is built on exactly three such basic operators: AND, OR and NOT. An arithmetic operator is a different kind of object: it acts on numeric magnitudes and returns a number, whose size depends on how large the inputs are.

Application

Apply that test to each operation named in the list. OR is defined on truth values, and its complete behaviour is fixed by a truth table:

Every entry in the result column is again 0 or 1, so OR maps truth values to a truth value — exactly what the definition of a Boolean operator requires.

Add, Subtract and Multiply are arithmetic operations. They act on numeric magnitudes and return numbers whose size tracks the inputs: 1 + 1 = 2, 0 − 1 = −1, 3 × 4 = 12. None of these results is restricted to the two truth values, so none of these three operations is a Boolean operator.

Cross-check: the “+” and “·” notation

This is where the question is most often misread. In Boolean algebra the OR operation is conventionally written with a plus sign (A + B) and the AND operation with a dot (A · B), and those two operations are sometimes called Boolean addition and Boolean multiplication. That notation is borrowed shorthand, not arithmetic — in Boolean algebra 1 + 1 = 1, while in ordinary arithmetic 1 + 1 = 2. Those Boolean readings exist only while the qualifier “Boolean” is attached: unqualified, “Add” and “Multiply” name the ordinary arithmetic operations. The list also offers “Subtract”, which has no Boolean counterpart at all — so the list is a set of arithmetic operation names with a single logical operator placed among them. The plus symbol appearing in Boolean expressions therefore does not turn the arithmetic operation “Add” into a Boolean operator, and the three basic Boolean operators remain AND, OR and NOT.

Result: of the four operations listed, OR is the Boolean operator.

title: The 'OR' function can be used to transmitted waveform.
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: The 'OR' function can be used to _________ a transmitted waveform.
solution:
Concept

An OR gate can be wired as a gating (control) circuit: the waveform is fed into one input and a control signal into the other. The OR truth table then fixes the output in exactly one of two ways depending on the control input's value — when the control input is 0, the output simply equals the waveform signal; when the control input is 1, the output is forced to a constant high regardless of the waveform.

Application

Applying this to the gate in this item: holding the control input at 0 lets the transmitted waveform pass through unchanged — the enable condition. Holding the control input at 1 overrides the output to a constant high and blocks the waveform — the disable condition. Because the control input can only sit in one state at a time, the same gate performs exactly one of these two actions at any given instant, never both together. Its capability is therefore best described as being able to enable or disable the waveform, depending on the control input's state.

Cross-check

Naming only "enable" or only "disable" each assumes the gate behaves the same way regardless of its control input's value, which contradicts the control role the stem describes. Since the gate's actual behaviour is a standard, well-defined response to that control input (as set out above), there is no basis for treating the situation as one that none of the listed descriptions can capture.

title: Which of the following is an universal gate
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Which of the following is an universal gate ?
solution: A universal gate is a logic gate that can be used to implement any Boolean function without needing any other type of gate. Among the options provided, only the NOR gate and NAND gate possess this property. The NOR gate is universal because it can be combined to create the basic logic functions: NOT, AND, and OR. For instance, connecting both inputs of a NOR gate together creates a NOT gate, while combining multiple NOR gates allows the construction of AND and OR gates. In contrast, the AND gate (Option A) cannot produce a NOT function on its own without an inverter. Similarly, the OR gate (Option B) cannot generate a NOT function independently. The XOR gate (Option D) is also not universal because it cannot implement all basic logic functions like AND or OR without additional components. Therefore, since the NOR gate can replicate any other basic logic gate configuration, it is classified as a universal gate.

title: What are the basic gates in MOS logic family? MOS
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: What are the basic gates in MOS logic family?
solution:
In MOS logic (most cleanly seen in CMOS, where complementary PMOS pull-up and NMOS pull-down networks realize each gate; earlier NMOS/PMOS-only families instead use a switching network to one supply rail plus a load device), a gate's output is produced by transistors switching toward ground or toward the supply rail — and that switching action itself performs a logical inversion. Because this happens in a single stage without any dedicated separate inverting circuit, exactly the gates whose Boolean logic already is an inversion — NAND and NOR — are the ones MOS realizes directly; that is why they are called the basic (and, since either one alone is functionally complete, "universal") gates of the family.

For this question, only one pairing among the given options matches a gate realized directly in a single transistor stage: putting the input transistors in series in the pull-down network gives NAND, and putting them in parallel gives NOR — no extra components are needed. So the basic gates of the MOS logic family are NAND and NOR.

  • AND and OR: these are non-inverting. Realizing them in MOS needs a NAND/NOR stage plus an added inverter, so they are derived gates, not basic ones.

  • NAND and OR: this pairs a directly-realized inverting gate with a non-inverting gate that still needs the extra inverter stage; this mixed pairing does not describe what MOS produces natively.

  • More than one of the above: applying the transistor-level check individually to each pairing shows only one pairing holds; treating several as valid together does not match the check.

  • None of the above: applying the transistor-level check individually to each pairing shows that one of them does hold, so ruling out every pairing does not match the check.

Hence NAND and NOR are the basic gates in the MOS logic family.

2. Second Gate: Inputs are the previous output (X) and X. Output = X ⊕ X = 0.

3. Third Gate: Inputs are the previous output (0) and X. Output = 0 ⊕ X = X.

Therefore, the final output Y is equal to X.

title: Minterm equals to maxterm
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Minterm Σm(1, 3, 5, 6) equals to maxterm
solution:
Concept

Any Boolean function of n variables can be written either as a sum of minterms (the input rows where the output is 1) or, equivalently, as a product of maxterms (the input rows where the output is 0). The two lists are complements over the full set of 2n row indices: an index that is a minterm is NOT a maxterm, and vice versa. So to convert Σm to ΠM, list every index from 0 to 2n − 1 that does NOT appear in the minterm list.

Application

  1. There are 3 variables here (the largest index, 6, needs 3 bits), so the full index set is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

  2. The minterms given are 1, 3, 5, 6 — these are the rows where the function is 1.

  3. The maxterms are the remaining indices where the function is 0: 0, 2, 4, 7.

  4. Therefore Σm(1, 3, 5, 6) = ΠM(0, 2, 4, 7).

Cross-check

Count check: 4 minterms + 4 maxterms = 8 = 23 total rows — consistent. Also verify disjointness: {1, 3, 5, 6} and {0, 2, 4, 7} share no index and together cover every value 0–7, confirming the complement is exact.

title: The logic expression Z).(X is called
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: The logic expression (X + Y + Z).(X + Y + Z′) is called
solution:
Concept

In Boolean algebra a Sum-of-Products (SOP) expression is an OR of AND-terms, while a Product-of-Sums (POS) expression is an AND (product) of OR-terms (sum terms). A POS becomes a standard (canonical) POS when every sum term is a maxterm, i.e. each sum term contains every variable of the function exactly once, either in true or complemented form.

Applying it here

  • The expression is (X + Y + Z)·(X + Y + Z′): two sum terms joined by AND (·), so the outer operation is a product of sums — a POS form.

  • Sum term (X + Y + Z) contains all three variables X, Y, Z; sum term (X + Y + Z′) also contains all three (Z appears complemented). Each term therefore holds every variable exactly once — each is a maxterm.

  • Because every sum term is a maxterm, the product is in canonical / standard POS form, not merely a general POS.

Cross-check / contrast

  • SOP would be an OR of AND-terms such as X·Y + X·Z; the given expression is the opposite arrangement, so any SOP label is ruled out.

  • Plain “POS” is correct in spirit but less precise: it does not require full variables in every term. Since every term here is already a complete maxterm, the exact classification is the canonical/standard POS.

Hence the expression is in Standard POS form.

title: Consider Boolean function of variables. The order of an algorithm
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Consider a general Boolean function of n variables, accessible only by evaluating its output for chosen assignments. In the worst case, the order of an algorithm that determines whether any assignment makes the function output 1 is
solution:
Concept: A Boolean function of n variables is defined over every possible assignment of 0/1 values to those n variables. Since each of the n variables independently takes one of 2 values, the total number of distinct input assignments is 2n. When the function has no exploitable structure (a general, black-box function given only as a truth table or oracle), the only way to be certain whether it ever outputs 1 is to test assignments one by one — in the worst case, every one of the 2n assignments may need to be examined before the question is settled.

Application: Applying this to the question:

  1. Count the input space: n independent Boolean variables produce 2n distinct assignments.

  2. In the worst case (no assignment gives output 1, or the one that does is found last), the algorithm cannot skip any assignment without risking a wrong conclusion, so it may need to evaluate the function at all 2n assignments.

  3. This makes the worst-case running time proportional to 2n — exponential in n.

Cross-check: Compare the growth rates against the size of the assignment space:

  • Logarithmic (log n) and linear (n) grow far slower than 2n: at n = 30, log n ≈ 5 and n = 30, while 2n is over a billion — neither can even enumerate the assignment space, let alone search it exhaustively.

  • Quadratic (n2) is still just a polynomial in n — at n = 30, n2 = 900, again far smaller than 2n ≈ 1.07 billion — so it cannot cover every assignment either.

  • Only exponential growth, 2n, matches the actual size of the assignment space that a worst-case, no-shortcut search must cover.

So the order of the algorithm is 2n — exponential in n. (This mirrors the brute-force approach to Boolean satisfiability: for a general Boolean function with no special structure, no algorithm is known to beat exponential worst-case time.)

title: The maximum number of Boolean expressions that can be formed
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml:
The maximum number of Boolean expressions that can be formed for the function f(x, y, z) satisfying the relation

is _______.
solution:
Concept

A Boolean function of three variables assigns either 0 or 1 to each of the eight possible input triples. If a constraint forces two input triples to have the same output, those two rows form one independent class.

When there are k independent classes and each class can independently receive output 0 or 1, the number of admissible Boolean functions is 2 raised to the power k.

Application

  1. The transformation (x, y, z) → (x̄, y, z̄) flips x and z while keeping y unchanged.

  2. It partitions the eight input triples into four disjoint pairs: (0,0,0) with (1,0,1); (0,0,1) with (1,0,0); (0,1,0) with (1,1,1); and (0,1,1) with (1,1,0).

  3. The relation requires both rows in each pair to share one output, so the truth table has four independent output choices.

  4. Each independent pair may be assigned 0 or 1, giving 24 = 16 admissible Boolean functions.

Cross-check

Applying the transformation twice returns the original triple, so every class has exactly two rows and no row is left unpaired. Thus 8 rows ÷ 2 rows per class = 4 independent classes, confirming the count 16.

Therefore, the required maximum number is 16.

title: Maximum number of binary functions possible for the function f(a,b,c)
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Maximum number of binary functions possible for the function f(a, b, c) satisfying the following relation: f(a, b, c) = f(a', b', c').
solution:
Concept: A Boolean function of n variables is fixed by the single value, 0 or 1, that it writes in each of the 2n rows of its truth table, so with no restriction at all there are 2 raised to the power 2n different functions. Any constraint of the form “these rows must carry the same value” welds those rows into one orbit, and an orbit costs one free choice instead of several. Counting rule: if a constraint splits the truth-table rows into k orbits, the number of functions obeying it is 2k.

Application: Here n = 3, so the truth table has 23 = 8 rows, and the stated relation ties every row to the row obtained by flipping all three input bits.

  1. Write the 8 input rows of a three-variable truth table: 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110 and 111.

  2. Read the relation f(a, b, c) = f(a', b', c') as a rule on rows: the value stored in row (a, b, c) must equal the value stored in the complemented row (a', b', c').

  3. Pair every row with its complement. The four pairs are listed in the table below, and each of the 8 rows appears in one pair.

  4. No row can be its own complement, because a bit never equals its own complement, so the 8 rows split evenly and the number of orbits is 8 ÷ 2 = 4.

  5. Each orbit is filled with one free value, 0 or 1, and the orbits are independent of one another, so k = 4 and the count of admissible functions is 24 = 16.

Row (a b c)

Complement row (a', b', c')

000

111

001

110

010

101

011

100

Cross-check: Count the same thing from the other end: there are 28 = 256 Boolean functions of three variables in all, and each of the 4 complement pairs removes one binary choice, leaving 256 ÷ 24 = 16 functions — the same result the orbit count gives.

Contrast: The rule scales with n: for two variables the relation f(a, b) = f(a', b') folds 4 rows into 2 orbits and leaves 22 = 4 functions, while for four variables it folds 16 rows into 8 orbits and leaves 28 = 256 functions.

title: Total number of boolean functions possible over boolean variables are
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Total number of boolean functions possible over n boolean variables are
solution:
Option A.

The total number of Boolean functions possible over n Boolean variables is 2^{2^n}.

Step-by-Step Explanation

To understand how this formula is derived, we can look at how a truth table is constructed for n variables:

  1. Number of Input Combinations: Each Boolean variable can take one of 2 possible values (0 or 1). Therefore, for n independent Boolean variables, the total number of distinct input combinations (or rows in a truth table) is:

    Total rows = 2×2×2×⋯(n times) = 2^n

  2. Number of Possible Outputs for Each Combination: For each individual row in the truth table, a Boolean function can choose to output either a 0 or a 1 (which means there are 2 choices per row).

  3. Total Number of Functions: Since each of the 2^n rows can have 2 possible outcomes independently, the total number of distinct functions is found by multiplying the choices for each row together:

    Total Functions = 2×2×2×⋯(2^n times) = 2^{2^n}

Example for Clarification

  • For n = 1 variable (say, A):

    • Number of input combinations = 2^1 = 2(The inputs can be 0 or 1).

    • Total possible functions = 2^{2^1} = 2^2 = 4 functions (These are: Always 0, Always 1, Buffer (A), and NOT (A')).

  • For n = 2 variables (say, A and B):

    • Number of input combinations = 2^2 = 4 (The inputs can be 00, 01, 10, 11).

    • Total possible functions = 2^{2^2} = 2^4 = 16 functions (This includes standard gates like AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR, etc.).

title: How many Boolean expressions can be be formed with Boolean
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: How many distinct Boolean functions can be defined on 3 Boolean variables?
solution:
Concept

A Boolean function on n variables assigns an output (0 or 1) to every possible input combination. The governing identity is a two-stage power of two — first compute the number of input rows as 2n, then independently choose either output for each row. Therefore, the number of distinct Boolean functions of n variables equals 2 raised to the power 2n.

Application

  1. Count the input rows. With n = 3 variables, each variable is 0 or 1, so the number of distinct input rows is 23 = 8.

  2. Count the functions over those rows. Each of the 8 input rows is sent independently to 0 or 1, so the number of distinct functions is 2 raised to the row count: 2 to the power 8, written 28.

  3. Evaluate. 28 = 256, so 256 distinct Boolean functions exist.

Cross-check

Test the rule on the known small case n = 2. There the row count is 22 = 4, and 2 raised to 4 is 24 = 16 — the familiar count of 16 two-variable Boolean functions (AND, OR, XOR, NAND, the constants, and so on). The same two-stage rule at n = 3 gives 28 = 256.

title: How many Boolean functions of three variables are there
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: How many Boolean functions of three variables are there ?
solution:
Concept

A Boolean function of n variables assigns an output (0 or 1) to each possible combination of its inputs. With n inputs there are 2n distinct input rows in the truth table, and each row can independently be mapped to either 0 or 1. So the total number of distinct functions is 2 raised to the number of rows: 2(2^n).

Application

  1. Here n = 3, so the number of truth-table rows is 23 = 8.

  2. Each of the 8 rows can independently take the value 0 or 1, giving 28 possible output assignments.

  3. 28 = 256, so there are 256 distinct Boolean functions of three variables.

Cross-check

Sanity check with the formula 2(2^n): for n = 1 it gives 22 = 4 functions, and for n = 2 it gives 24 = 16 functions — both standard, well-known counts. Extending the same pattern to n = 3 gives 28 = 256, which confirms the result.

solution:
The circuit simplifies to f = ¬(A·B).

  1. Let x = NAND(A,B) = ¬(A·B).

  2. The top second-stage NAND has both inputs as x, so its output is NAND(x,x) = ¬(x·x) = ¬x = A·B.

  3. Let y = NAND(C,D) = ¬(C·D). The bottom second-stage NAND has inputs y and x, so its output is NAND(y,x) = ¬(y·x) = (C·D) + (A·B).

title: How many minimum numbers of two input NAND gates are
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: How many minimum numbers of two input NAND gates are required to implement boolean function f= p’qrs?
solution:
To implement the Boolean function f = p'qrs using two-input NAND gates, we need to break down the expression into basic logic operations that can be realized with NAND gates.

Step 1: Generate p' (NOT p). This requires one NAND gate configured as an inverter (both inputs connected to p).

Step 2: Generate qrs. This is an AND of three variables. We can implement this using NAND gates by first computing q AND r, then combining the result with s.

Step 3: Compute qr using a NAND gate followed by an inverter (another NAND gate used as inverter). This takes 2 gates.

Step 4: Compute (qr) AND s. Use a NAND gate on (qr) and s, then invert the output using another NAND gate as inverter. This takes 2 gates.

Step 5: Compute p' AND (qrs). Use a NAND gate on p' and (qrs), then invert the output using a NAND gate as inverter. This takes 2 gates.

Total gate count: 1 (for p') + 2 (for qr) + 2 (for qrs) + 2 (for final AND) = 7 gates.

Note: Each AND operation requires two NAND gates (one NAND followed by an inverter), and each NOT operation requires one NAND gate configured as an inverter.

title: In K-map, each square is represented by
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: For sum-of-products (SOP) simplification, each square of a K-map corresponds to which canonical term?
solution:
Concept

An n-variable Karnaugh map contains 2n cells arranged in Gray-code order. Each cell corresponds to one unique input combination. In canonical SOP form, that combination is written as a product containing every variable once, complemented when its bit is 0 and uncomplemented when its bit is 1; this full product is a minterm.

Application

The stem explicitly asks about SOP simplification. Therefore the canonical term attached to a square is a minterm, so the accepted value is “Min term”.

Contrast

  • Min term: a canonical AND product that identifies one input combination in SOP form.

  • Max term: a canonical OR sum associated with one zero-output combination in POS form.

  • Average term: not a canonical Boolean-algebra term.

  • None of these: a set-level fallback, not a Boolean term.

Cross-check

For two variables A and B, the cell for A = 0 and B = 1 corresponds to A̅B, which contains both variables and is minterm m1. This confirms the SOP interpretation.

Result

Therefore, in SOP simplification each K-map square corresponds to a minterm; the accepted value is “Min term”.

title: What is the primary purpose of using Don’t Care conditions
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: What is the primary purpose of using Don’t Care conditions in Karnaugh Map simplification?

options.label: A
options.html: To mark cells that should not be included in the simplification process

options.label: B
options.html: To indicate cells that have an undefined logic value

options.label: C
options.html: To identify cells that are already in their simplest form

options.label: D
options.html: To mark cells with special logic functions

solution:
Option B:

The primary purpose of using Don't Care Condition conditions in a Karnaugh Map (K-Map) is:

✅ To simplify the Boolean expression further by reducing the number of logic gates required.

Explanation:
Don’t Care conditions represent input combinations that never occur or whose outputs do not matter.
In K-Map simplification, they may be treated as either 0 or 1, whichever helps form larger groups.
Larger groups produce simpler Boolean expressions.

Benefits:

Reduces number of gates
Reduces circuit complexity

title: What is the purpose of the “don’t care” condition in

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.html: To ensure that all possible input combinations are covered in truth tables

solution: The 'don't care' condition in digital logic refers to input combinations that do not affect the output of a circuit. These conditions are used to simplify Boolean expressions, particularly in Karnaugh maps (K-maps). By treating 'don't care' as either 0 or 1, we can group adjacent cells more effectively, leading to a minimized expression. This simplification reduces the number of logic gates required, improving circuit efficiency. Importantly, 'don't care' does not imply priority, nor is it used to ensure truth table coverage; it is solely a tool for optimization.

The circuit consists entirely of NAND gates. We analyze the output step-by-step from left to right.

2. Middle NAND gate: Inputs are the output from step 1, (CD)', and input B. Output = ((CD)' · B)'. Applying De Morgan's Law: (CD)'' + B' = CD + B'.

title: Truth table of Boolean function X.Y.Z X.Y.Z' X.Y.Z X'.Y matches
