bodyHtml: Truth table of Boolean function X.Y.Z + X.Y.Z' + X.Y.Z + X'.Y matches with
solution:
Concept

A sum-of-products expression simplifies by two Boolean identities. Combining: a variable ANDed with both a literal and its complement drops that literal, X.Y.Z + X.Y.Z' = X.Y.(Z + Z') = X.Y, because Z + Z' = 1. Distribution in reverse: a common factor ANDed with a variable and its complement leaves only the common factor, since X + X' = 1.

Application

Simplify X.Y.Z + X.Y.Z' + X.Y.Z + X'.Y step by step:

  1. By idempotency (A + A = A) the repeated term X.Y.Z is absorbed, leaving X.Y.Z + X.Y.Z' + X'.Y.

  2. Factor the first two terms: X.Y.Z + X.Y.Z' = X.Y.(Z + Z'). Since Z + Z' = 1, this is X.Y.

  3. The expression is now X.Y + X'.Y. Factor out Y: (X + X').Y.

  4. Since X + X' = 1, this gives 1.Y = Y.

Cross-check

Build the truth table. The expression is 1 exactly on the rows where Y = 1 (X,Y,Z = 010, 011, 110, 111) and 0 wherever Y = 0, independent of X and Z. That column is identical to the column for Y, confirming the function equals Y.

title: We consider the addition of two complement numbers and binary
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Consider the addition of two n-bit two’s-complement numbers bn−1bn−2…b0 and an−1an−2…a0. An unsigned binary adder is used to add them. The n-bit sum is cn−1cn−2…c0, and the carry-out is cout. Which expression correctly identifies signed overflow?
solution:
Concept

In fixed-width two’s-complement addition, overflow is a signed-range error.

It occurs when both operands have the same sign but the stored sum has the opposite sign. Operands of different signs cannot overflow because their exact sum lies between the two operand values.

Application

  1. Let an−1 and bn−1 be the operand sign bits, and let cn−1 be the sign bit of the stored n-bit sum.

  2. Two negative operands producing a non-negative stored sum give the sign triple (1,1,0), represented by an−1bn−1¬cn−1.

  3. Two non-negative operands producing a negative stored sum give the sign triple (0,0,1), represented by ¬an−1¬bn−1cn−1.

  4. The two cases are mutually exclusive, so OR them: V = an−1bn−1¬cn−1 + ¬an−1¬bn−1cn−1.

Cross-check

The same overflow flag equals the XOR of the carry into the sign-bit position and the final carry-out. A sign-triple truth-table check gives V = 1 only for (1,1,0) and (0,0,1), confirming the Boolean expression above.

Contrast

  • cout · ¬(an−1 ⊕ bn−1) also depends on the final carry, which is not itself a signed-overflow indicator.

  • cout ⊕ cn−1 compares the final carry with the stored sum sign bit, not the carry into and out of the sign-bit position.

  • an−1 ⊕ bn−1 ⊕ cn−1 tests odd parity of three sign-related bits rather than the two same-sign/opposite-result cases.

Therefore, the overflow condition is an−1bn−1¬cn−1 + ¬an−1¬bn−1cn−1.

title: Consider serial adder which adds two n-bit numbers. Let 100ns

solution:
In a serial adder, only one full adder (FA) is used for all bit positions. Each bit is processed sequentially, and the full adder is reused for each stage.

The delay for each bit is equal to the delay of the full adder, which is 100 ns.

Since there are n bits, the total time to compute the sum is the number of bits multiplied by the delay per bit: n × 100 ns = 100n ns.

options.label: A
options.html: XOR of inputs for sum; AND only for carry.

options.label: B
options.html: AND of inputs for sum; XOR, OR, and AND for carry.

options.label: C
options.html: XOR of inputs for sum; XOR, AND, and OR for carry.

options.label: D
options.html: OR of inputs for sum; XOR, AND, and OR for carry.

solution:
A full adder takes three 1-bit inputs: A, B, and carry-in Cᵢₙ. It produces a Sum output S and a Carry-out output Cₒᵤₜ.

Sum output:
S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cᵢₙ
So the sum is generated using XOR logic.

Carry output in the common two-half-adder implementation:
Cₒᵤₜ = (A · B) + (Cᵢₙ · (A ⊕ B))
So the carry path uses XOR to form A ⊕ B, AND gates to form partial carry terms, and an OR gate to combine those terms.

Therefore, the correct option is: XOR of inputs for sum; XOR, AND, and OR for carry.

title: Which logic gates are needed to make half adder.
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Which logic gates are needed to make half adder.
solution:
A half adder is a combinational circuit that performs the addition of two single-bit binary numbers (A and B). It produces two outputs: Sum (S) and Carry (C).

  1. Sum (S): The logic operation for the sum of two bits corresponds to an Exclusive-OR (XOR) operation.

    Sum = A ⊕ B

  2. Carry (C): The carry bit is generated only when both inputs are 1, which corresponds to a logical AND operation.

    Carry = A . B

Therefore, to design a standard half adder, we need exactly one XOR gate (for the Sum) and one AND gate (for the Carry).

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q147
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: A full adder circuit has:
solution:
Concept

A full adder is the combinational circuit used to add binary numbers of more than one bit. Unlike a half adder, which only combines two bits, a full adder is built to accept three single-bit inputs -- the two bits being added at that position, plus a carry bit coming in from the addition of the previous (lower-order) position -- and it produces two output bits: the sum bit for that position and a carry bit to pass on to the next (higher-order) position.

Application

Labelling the three inputs A, B, and Cin (carry-in), and the two outputs S (sum) and Cout (carry-out): S = A XOR B XOR Cin, and Cout = AB + B.Cin + A.Cin. Counting the ports directly from this definition gives exactly 3 inputs (A, B, Cin) and 2 outputs (S, Cout).

Contrast

  • 1 input, 2 outputs -- no adder stage can form a sum from a single input bit; this count does not match any binary-addition circuit.

  • 2 inputs, 1 output -- this is the port count of a plain two-input logic gate, which has no carry-in port and so cannot chain with a neighbouring addition stage.

  • 4 inputs, 1 output -- collapsing to one output line loses the separate carry-out signal that every addition stage must pass forward.

Cross-check

Chaining several full adders by feeding each stage's Cout into the next stage's Cin builds a ripple-carry adder for multi-bit numbers. That chaining is only possible because each stage exposes a dedicated carry-in port alongside the two operand bits -- confirming that 3 inputs and 2 outputs is the structurally necessary port count, not an incidental one.

title: The characteristics of the combinational circuits are: Output at any
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml:
The characteristics of the combinational circuits are:

A. Output at any time is function of inputs at that time

B. Contains memory elements

C. Do not have feedback paths

D. Clock is used to trigger the circuits to obtain outputs

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Answer: A and C only ("Output at any time is function of inputs at that time" and "Do not have feedback paths").

Explanation:

  • Output depends only on current inputs: True. In a combinational circuit, the output value at any time is a pure function of the present input values; there is no storage of past inputs.

  • Contains memory elements: False. Memory elements (flip-flops, latches) store state and are a defining feature of sequential circuits, not combinational ones.

  • Do not have feedback paths: True. Feedback paths can introduce storage or state; pure combinational logic is implemented without feedback loops so outputs remain a direct function of current inputs.

  • Clock is used to trigger the circuits to obtain outputs: False. Clocks are used in sequential circuits to synchronize state changes; combinational circuits do not require a clock to produce outputs.

Conclusion: The correct characteristics are that outputs are functions only of current inputs and that there are no feedback paths; therefore the correct choice lists those two statements.

title: Consider the circuit shown below. Which of the following is
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Consider the circuit shown below. Which of the following is true?
solution:
A 2:1 multiplexer implements one fixed identity: Y = S0′I0 + S0I1 — it passes I0 through when the select line S0 = 0, and I1 through when S0 = 1. When several 2:1 MUXes are cascaded, this SAME identity is applied stage by stage, plugging in each stage’s actual I0, I1 and S0 — which may be a constant, a primary variable, or an earlier stage’s output — never a fresh formula for the whole chain.

  1. Stage 1 (leftmost MUX): I0 = 1, I1 = 0, select S0 = x1. So Y1 = x1’·1 + x1·0 = x1’ — exactly the value already marked on the wire feeding the next stage.

  2. Stage 2 (middle MUX): I0 = Y1 = x1’, I1 = x1 (tapped from the same select line driving stage 1), select S0 = x2. So Y2 = x2’·x1’ + x2·x1 = x1’x2’ + x1x2.

  3. Stage 3 (rightmost MUX): I0 = Y2, I1 = x2 (tapped from stage 2’s select line), select S0 = x1. So f = x1’·Y2 + x1·x2 = x1’(x1’x2’ + x1x2) + x1x2 = x1’x2’ + 0 + x1x2 = x1x2 + x1’x2’.

Cross-check with two input pairs confirms the cascade: at x1 = 0, x2 = 0, stage 1 gives Y1 = 1, stage 2 gives Y2 = 1, stage 3 gives f = 1 — matching x1x2 + x1’x2’ = 1 at (0, 0). At x1 = 1, x2 = 0, stage 1 gives Y1 = 0, stage 2 gives Y2 = 0, stage 3 gives f = 0 — again matching the same expression evaluated at (1, 0). So f is 1 exactly when x1 and x2 agree (the XNOR relation), which is precisely f = x1x2 + x1’x2’, not its complement (the XOR form) and not ‘none’, since a definite expression does exist.

title: Minimum number of multiplexers required to realize the following function,f
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml:
Minimum number of multiplexers required to realize the following function,

f = A'B'C + A'B'C'

Assume that inputs are available only in true form, and Boolean constants 1 and 0 are available.
solution:
Given:

f = A'B'C + A'B'C'

We can factor out the common terms A'B':

f = A'B'(C + C')

Since (C + C') = 1 according to Boolean identity:

f = A'B'

2. Implementation using 2-to-1 MUX

Since the inputs are available only in true form (A, B, C), we cannot directly use A' or B'. We must use the multiplexers to generate the necessary complements or the logic function itself.

A 2-to-1 MUX performs the function: Y = S'I_0 + SI_1 (where S is the select line).

Step 1: Generate A'

To get A' using a 2-to-1 MUX with only true forms available:

  • Select line (S) = A

  • I_0 = 1

  • I_1 = 0

  • Result: A(0) + A'(1) = f{A'}

Step 2: Realize f = A'B'

Now we use a second MUX to implement the AND logic between A' and B':

  • Select line (S) = B

  • I_0 = A' (output from the first MUX)

  • I_1 = 0

  • Result: B(0) + B'(A') = f{A'B'}

3. Conclusion

To realize the function f = A'B' using only true inputs:

  1. One MUX is needed to act as an inverter to create A'.

  2. One MUX is needed to perform the AND operation with B'.

Minimum number of 2-to-1 MUX required = 2.

title: Determine the size of PROM required for implementing the 16-to-1
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Determine the size of PROM required for implementing the 16-to-1 multiplexer.
solution:
A PROM (or any lookup-table memory) implements a Boolean function by storing one output value for every possible combination of its input variables — it does not compute, it only recalls a stored value. So the address space must include every signal that can change the output: PROM size = 2n × m, where n is the number of input (address) lines and m is the number of output lines.

  1. Identify what the output actually depends on: in a 16-to-1 MUX, the output Y equals whichever of the 16 data lines (D0–D15) is currently selected — so Y depends on the values on all 16 data lines, not only on which one is chosen.

  2. Count the select lines needed to choose among 16 data lines: 24 = 16, so 4 select lines (S0–S3) are required.

  3. Total input (address) lines n = data lines + select lines = 16 + 4 = 20.

  4. Number of outputs m = 1 (the single MUX output line).

  5. PROM size = 2n × m = 220 × 1 = 1,048,576 × 1, commonly written as 1M × 1.

Cross-check: if only the 4 select lines were counted (24 × 1 = 16 × 1), the PROM would only be able to reproduce a MUX whose 16 data inputs are fixed constants — a decoder-style ROM, not a true multiplexer with independently variable data inputs. Because the data lines here are variable inputs (not hard-wired constants), all 20 signals must be part of the address, confirming the size 220 × 1 = 1M × 1.

Required PROM size = 1M × 1.

title: Suppose you want to build memory with byte words with
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Suppose you want to build a memory with 4 byte words with a capacity of 221bits. What is type of decoder required if the memory is built using 2K x 8 RAM chips?
solution:
First, calculate the total number of addressable words. The memory capacity is $2^{21}$ bits, and each word is 4 bytes (32 bits). Total words = $2^{21} / 32 = 2^{16}$.

Next, analyze the chip specifications. Each RAM chip is 2K x 8 bits, meaning it has a depth of $2^{11}$ words.

To achieve the required depth, determine how many rows of chips are needed. Rows = Target Depth / Chip Depth = $2^{16} / 2^{11} = 2^5 = 32$.

Finally, determine the decoder requirements. To select one out of 32 rows, a decoder with $\log_2(32) = 5$ input lines and 32 output lines is required.

title: How many to line decoders are required for of decoder?
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: How many 3-to-8 line decoders are required for a 1-of-32 decoder?
solution:
Concept

Decoder expansion: a small n-to-2n decoder can be combined to build a larger one. The number of small decoders needed to supply the outputs equals the big decoder's total outputs divided by one small decoder's outputs. A 3-to-8 decoder has 3 select inputs and 23 = 8 output lines.

Application

  1. A 1-of-32 decoder needs 32 distinct output lines (it activates one of 32 lines).

  2. Each 3-to-8 decoder supplies 8 output lines.

  3. Number of 3-to-8 decoders to cover all outputs = 32 / 8 = 4.

  4. A 5-bit address (25 = 32) splits as the lower 3 bits feeding every 3-to-8 decoder identically and the upper 2 bits choosing which one of the four decoders is active.

  5. The remaining 2 address bits are consumed by the ENABLE inputs already built into each 3-to-8 decoder (e.g. a 74138's enable pins) -- the two bits, in their true and inverted forms (from a single inverter), are wired across the four units' enable pins so that exactly one decoder is active for each of the 4 combinations -- so selecting among the four decoders needs no fifth decoder of any size, only one basic inverter gate.

Cross-check

Four decoders give 4 x 8 = 32 output lines, exactly matching the requirement, with no line wasted. The 2 extra address bits are absorbed by the four decoders' own built-in enable pins (needing just one inverter), not by another decoder unit -- this matches the standard manufacturer expansion scheme (e.g. the 74138 datasheet's 1-of-32 application, which uses exactly four 3-to-8 ICs plus a single inverter). That is why only four 3-to-8 decoders are counted.

Result: 4 three-to-eight decoders are required.

title: How many bit comparator,2 input AND gate input OR gate
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: How many 1-bit comparators, 2-input AND gates, and 2-input OR gates, respectively, are required to design a 2-bit magnitude comparator?
solution:
A magnitude comparator produces three outputs — L for A less than B, E for A equal to B, and G for A greater than B — by comparing two binary numbers bit by bit from the most significant bit downward. When single-bit comparator stages are cascaded for a multi-bit comparison, the higher-order bit's own result is used directly, and the lower-order bit's result is used only when the higher-order bits are equal, via the equality signal E1.

  1. Assign one 1-bit comparator stage to each bit position of the 2-bit numbers, producing outputs (L1, E1, G1) for bit 1 (the more significant bit) and (L0, E0, G0) for bit 0 (the less significant bit) — two 1-bit comparator stages in total.

  2. Combine the equality outputs as E = E1 · E0, since the two numbers are equal only when both bit positions are equal — one 2-input AND gate.

  3. Combine the less-than output as L = L1 + (E1 · L0): the overall result is less-than when bit 1 alone decides it, or when bit 1 is equal and bit 0 decides it — one 2-input AND gate for E1 · L0, plus one 2-input OR gate to combine it with L1.

  4. Combine the greater-than output as G = G1 + (E1 · G0), following the same pattern — one more 2-input AND gate for E1 · G0, plus one more 2-input OR gate to combine it with G1.

  5. Tallying the gates used across the equality, less-than, and greater-than combinations gives three 2-input AND gates (E1·E0, E1·L0, E1·G0) and two 2-input OR gates (for L and for G), on top of the two 1-bit comparator stages from the first step.

Substituting A = 10 (decimal 2) and B = 01 (decimal 1) into these expressions checks the derivation:

Signal

Value

Why

L1, E1, G1

0, 0, 1

Bit 1: A1 = 1, B1 = 0, so A1 is greater than B1

L0, E0, G0

1, 0, 0

Bit 0: A0 = 0, B0 = 1, so A0 is less than B0

E = E1·E0

0

Bit 1 already differs, so the two numbers cannot be equal

L = L1 + E1·L0

0

Bit 1 alone does not indicate less-than, and E1 is 0 so the bit-0 term does not contribute

G = G1 + E1·G0

1

Bit 1 alone already indicates greater-than

The derivation therefore needs 2 one-bit comparator stages, 3 two-input AND gates, and 2 two-input OR gates — matching the "2, 3, 2" option.

title: Determine the Boolean function corresponding to the output signal for
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Determine the Boolean function corresponding to the output signal f for the given logic circuit. Express the function in terms of the circuit’s input variables and the logical operations implemented by the gates.
solution:
Key idea: simplify the NOR network using De Morgan's laws and factoring.

  • The first-level NOR gates produce: (P+Q)’, (Q+R)’, (P+R)’ and (Q+R)’.

  • The top pair are combined by a NOR to give f1 = ((P+Q)’ + (Q+R)’)’ = (P+Q)(Q+R).

  • The bottom pair are combined by a NOR to give f2 = ((P+R)’ + (Q+R)’)’ = (P+R)(Q+R).

  • The final output is the NOR of f1 and f2: f = (f1 + f2)’ = ( (P+Q)(Q+R) + (P+R)(Q+R) )’.

  • Factor out (Q+R): ( (P+Q)(Q+R) + (P+R)(Q+R) ) = (Q+R)( (P+Q) + (P+R) ) = (Q+R)(P+Q+R) = Q+R.

Conclusion: f = (Q+R)’.

title: Assume that the inverter in the network below has propagation
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Assume that the inverter in the network below has a propagation delay of 10 ns and the XOR gate has a propagation delay of 5 ns. Draw the timing diagram for the network showing X, Y and Z. Take Y as initially 1; the waveform for X is given. The number of points where the level changes at output Z (excluding t = 0 ns, if any) up to t = 100 ns is _____.
solution:
Concept

An XOR gate acts as a controlled inverter: with one input held at 0 it passes the other input unchanged (Z = 0 XOR Y = Y), and with one input held at 1 it inverts the other input (Z = 1 XOR Y = NOT Y). Here Z is fed back through the inverter to form Y (Y = NOT Z, delayed by 10 ns), so the whole loop's behaviour is set by the control input X and by the total loop delay = inverter delay + XOR delay = 10 ns + 5 ns = 15 ns. A feedback loop with an ODD number of inversions per cycle oscillates; a loop with an EVEN number of inversions holds its value.

Fixing the starting state (this is what 'ambiguous' reports are about)

With X = 0 the loop has a single inversion, so it has no static rest state and would oscillate on its own; the question removes that ambiguity by giving the prior conditions. Take the prehistory (t < 0) as Y = 1 (given) with Z held at its LOW level, matching the timing diagram. Then trace the start event by event:

  1. t = 0: X = 0 and Y = 1, so Z = X XOR Y = 0 XOR 1 = 1. Z settles HIGH right at the start. (This 0 to 1 change sits at t = 0 and is excluded by the question, so it is not counted.)

  2. t = 10 ns: X rises to 1. Independently, the inverter responds to Z = 1 and drives Y from 1 to 0. These two changes reach the XOR together, and 1 XOR 0 = 1 — the same value Z already holds. So Z does NOT change: the Y edge is exactly cancelled by the X = 1 inversion.

  3. t = 10 to 40 ns: X = 1 keeps the loop non-inverting (Z = NOT Y, Y = NOT Z gives Z(t) = Z(t - 15 ns)), so Z HOLDS its HIGH level. No edges in this whole window.

This is exactly why there is no level change of Z before 45 ns even though Y moves at t = 10 ns.

After X returns to 0

  • From 40 ns onward: X = 0 again, so the loop is once more a single-inversion ring OSCILLATOR: Z(t) = NOT Z(t - 15 ns). Z therefore toggles every 15 ns.

  • First toggle: the held HIGH level flips LOW one loop delay after the oscillation resumes, at t = 45 ns, and then keeps toggling every 15 ns.

Counting the level changes of Z

Following the timing diagram, Z changes level at t = 45 ns, 60 ns, 75 ns and 90 ns (spaced 15 ns apart, the loop delay). Up to t = 100 ns there are no further edges.

Cross-check

The toggles are exactly 15 ns apart, matching the loop delay (10 ns + 5 ns), and they all lie after X falls back to 0 at 40 ns — consistent with the oscillate-only-when-X = 0 rule, while the X = 1 window held Z steady. Counting them: 45, 60, 75, 90.

Number of level changes at Z up to t = 100 ns = 4.

title: Consider an SR flip-flop realized with two cross-coupled NAND gates.
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Consider an SR flip-flop realized with two cross-coupled NAND gates. If the input sequence is 00, 11, then the output sequence will be ___.
solution:
Concept: A latch built from two cross-coupled NAND gates has active-LOW inputs S and R. If either input is 0, that gate's output is forced to logic 1 regardless of the feedback; when both inputs are 1 the latch holds its stored value. The combination S = R = 0 is a forbidden input because it drives BOTH outputs to 1, which violates the rule that Q and Q' must be complementary.

  1. Apply 00 (S = 0, R = 0): each NAND gate has a 0 at one input, so both outputs are forced HIGH. The output pair (Q, Q') = (1, 1), i.e. 11 — the forbidden state.

  2. Now apply 11 (S = 1, R = 1): every gate input tied to the source is 1, so each gate output now depends only on the other gate's output. Starting from (1, 1): each computes NAND(1, 1) = 0, so both outputs fall to 0, giving 00.

  3. With both outputs at 0: each computes NAND(1, 0) = 1, so both outputs rise back to 1, giving 11. The two conditions keep alternating.

  4. With equal gate delays the outputs therefore oscillate 11, 00, 11, 00, so the output sequence is 11, 00, 11, 00.

Cross-check: this astable oscillation is the idealized equal-delay picture of the race that occurs when a NAND latch leaves the forbidden state. In a real device the two gate delays are never exactly equal, so the oscillation collapses and the latch settles to one state that cannot be predicted in advance, which is exactly why S = R = 0 must be avoided. A trace that begins with 00 contradicts the first step (both outputs are forced to 1 first), and any trace containing 10 or 01 is impossible here because the two outputs move together throughout this transition.

Short answer: 0.5 MHz

Explanation:

title: If the data input of positive edge-triggered flip-flop changes from
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: If the data input (D) of a positive edge-triggered D flip-flop changes from 0 to 1 right during the rising edge of the clock signal, what will the resulting output Q be?

options.label: C
options.html: Q may be unpredictable due to timing violation

solution:
For any sequential logic circuit like a D flip-flop to operate reliably, its input signals must adhere to strict timing requirements relative to the clock edge. These are known as setup time and hold time .

  • Setup Time: The minimum time the data input (D) must remain stable before the active clock edge.

  • Hold Time: The minimum time the data input (D) must remain stable after the active clock edge.

If the data input changes right during the rising edge of the clock signal, both setup and hold times are violated. When this happens, the internal master-slave latches fail to settle cleanly into a logic 0 or logic 1 state. Instead, the flip-flop enters a highly unstable state called metastability, where the output Q can oscillate or get stuck at an intermediate voltage level before eventually settling arbitrarily.

Therefore, the output becomes completely unstable and unpredictable.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 4
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: The characteristic equation of a JK flip flop is :
solution:
Concept: The characteristic equation of a flip-flop expresses the next state \(Q_{n+1}\) as a Boolean function of the present state \(Q_n\) and the flip-flop's control inputs. It is obtained by writing out the flip-flop's truth table for every combination of inputs and present state, then reducing that table to a sum-of-products expression -- for a JK flip-flop the cleanest route is to split the table on the present state \(Q_n\) itself.

Application:

  1. Write the JK truth table over J, K, \(Q_n\) -> \(Q_{n+1}\): J=0,K=0 holds (\(Q_{n+1}=Q_n\)); J=0,K=1 resets (\(Q_{n+1}=0\)); J=1,K=0 sets (\(Q_{n+1}=1\)); J=1,K=1 toggles (\(Q_{n+1}=\overline{Q_n}\)).

  2. Isolate the rows where the present state \(Q_n=0\): \(Q_{n+1}\) equals J in every one of them, so the \(Q_n=0\) branch reduces to \(Q_{n+1}=J\).

  3. Isolate the rows where the present state \(Q_n=1\): \(Q_{n+1}\) equals the complement of K in every one of them (K=0 keeps \(Q_{n+1}=1\), K=1 flips it to \(Q_{n+1}=0\)), so the \(Q_n=1\) branch reduces to \(Q_{n+1}=\overline{K}\).

  4. Recombine the two branches with the present state itself acting as the selector -- \(\overline{Q_n}\) selects the J branch and \(Q_n\) selects the \(\overline{K}\) branch -- giving \(Q_{n+1}=J\cdot\overline{Q_n}+\overline{K}\cdot Q_n\).

Cross-check: Substituting the hold case J=K=0 gives \(Q_{n+1}=0\cdot\overline{Q_n}+1\cdot Q_n=Q_n\) (state unchanged), and substituting the toggle case J=K=1 gives \(Q_{n+1}=1\cdot\overline{Q_n}+0\cdot Q_n=\overline{Q_n}\) (state inverted) -- both match the defining hold/toggle behaviour of a JK flip-flop, confirming the derivation.

title: Consider the following sequential circuit?(Assume initial clock is What is

bodyHtml:
Q. Consider the following sequential circuit?(Assume initial clock is 00)

What is the output AB of the circuit after two clock cycle?
solution:
Assumptions:

  • Top flip-flop is a T flip-flop held so it toggles on its active edge (diagram shows its clock with a bubble → negative-edge triggered).

  • Bottom flip-flop is a D flip-flop (positive-edge triggered).

  • The bottom D input is the OR of the top Q and the complement of bottom Q (D = A + not B), as shown by the OR gate and the feedback loop.

Start state (given): A B = 0 0.

  1. Compute D before the first rising edge: D = A OR (not B) = 0 OR 1 = 1.

  2. First rising edge: bottom (D) is sampled → B becomes 1. Top does not change on rising. State now A B = 0 1.

  3. First falling edge: top T flip-flop toggles (T = 1) → A becomes 1. Bottom remains 1. State now A B = 1 1.

  4. Compute D before the second rising edge: D = A OR (not B) = 1 OR 0 = 1.

  5. Second rising edge: bottom samples D → B remains 1. State still A B = 1 1.

  6. Second falling edge: top toggles → A becomes 0. Bottom unchanged. Final state after two full clock cycles A B = 0 1.

Answer: 01

Note: Intermediate states (for example 10 or 11) can appear between edges, but after two complete clock cycles (two rising and two falling edges) the outputs are 01.

title: JK FF has minimum propagation delay(tpd) of ns. What is
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: A JK - FF has a minimum propagation delay(tpd) of 12 ns. What is the modulus value of the counter that can be designed from these FFs which can operate up to 10MHz ?
solution:
Given: t_pd = 12 ns; required operating frequency = 10 MHz.

  • Clock period T = 1/f = 1/10 MHz = 100 ns.

  • For an asynchronous (ripple) counter, the worst-case propagation delay through n flip-flops must be <= one clock period: T >= n · t_pd.

  • Solve for n: n <= T / t_pd = 100 ns / 12 ns = 8.333... so the maximum integer n is 8.

  • Modulus = 2^n = 2^8 = 256.

  • Check: with 9 flip-flops the maximum frequency would be 1/(9·12 ns) ≈ 9.26 MHz, which is below 10 MHz, so 9 flip-flops is not acceptable.

Answer: The correct modulus value is 256.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q110
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: How many minimum flip-flops are required for designing synchronous counter with counting sequence : 0 => 1 => 6 => 10 => 4?
solution:
Concept: When a synchronous counter is designed for an explicitly listed counting sequence of decimal state values (rather than an abstract state diagram left free to be encoded any way), the flip-flop outputs must literally reproduce those decimal numbers in binary. So the minimum number of flip-flops n is the smallest n for which 2n exceeds the largest decimal value that appears anywhere in the sequence — not merely enough to tell the listed states apart.

  1. List the given sequence: 0, 1, 6, 10, 4 (the counter then repeats back to 0).

  2. Write each value in binary using the same register width: 0000, 0001, 0110, 1010, 0100.

  3. Identify the largest value in the sequence: 10.

  4. Check a 3-bit register: it spans 23 = 8 patterns, i.e. decimal 0 through 7. Since 10 > 7, 3 flip-flops cannot hold the value 10.

  5. Check a 4-bit register: it spans 24 = 16 patterns, i.e. decimal 0 through 15. This comfortably holds every value in the sequence, including 10 (binary 1010).

  6. So the minimum register width — and hence the minimum number of flip-flops — is 4.

Cross-check: if only the count of distinct states mattered (a free encoding with a separate output-decoding stage translating internal states to the displayed numbers), ⌈log2(5)⌉ = 3 flip-flops would be enough to distinguish the 5 states 0, 1, 6, 10, 4. But designing "a synchronous counter with counting sequence 0 ⇒ 1 ⇒ 6 ⇒ 10 ⇒ 4" is conventionally read as the register itself producing those decimal outputs directly, with no separate decoder — this is also how this exact question is solved in official exam solutions. Under that convention the register must be wide enough for the value 10, giving 4, not 3.

Result: the minimum number of flip-flops required is 4. Since 4 does not match any of 3, 6, or 5, the correct choice is "None of these".

At every clock edge, each stored bit shifts one position toward Q3, the bit that falls out of Q3 is discarded, and a new bit enters Q0 computed as the XOR of the previous Q1, Q2, and Q3. title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q123
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: What is the binary representation of the decimal number 0.25 ?
solution:
Concept: To convert a decimal fraction to binary, express it as a sum of negative powers of 2 - the first digit after the binary point carries weight 2-1, the second 2-2, the third 2-3, and so on, mirroring how whole-number binary digits carry weights 20, 21, 22 ...

  1. Multiply the fraction by 2: 0.25 × 2 = 0.50. The integer part is 0, so the first digit after the binary point is 0; the remaining fraction 0.50 is carried forward.

  2. Multiply the remaining fraction by 2 again: 0.50 × 2 = 1.00. The integer part is 1, so the second digit is 1; the remaining fraction is now 0, so the conversion stops.

  3. Reading the digits in the order they were generated gives 0.01 in binary.

Cross-check: converting 0.01 back to decimal gives 0 × 2-1 + 1 × 2-2 = 0 + 0.25 = 0.25, which matches the original number, confirming the conversion.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q47
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Which number system uses only the two digits 0 and 1?
solution:
Concept

A positional number system is defined by its radix, or base.

A base-r system uses r distinct digit symbols, and each position has a place value that is a power of r.

Application

Using only 0 and 1 gives two digit symbols, so the radix is 2. A base-2 number system is called binary; therefore the required system is Binary.

Cross-check and contrast

  • Decimal has base 10 and uses the digits 0 through 9.

  • Binary has base 2 and uses exactly the digits 0 and 1.

  • Octal has base 8 and uses the digits 0 through 7.

  • Hexadecimal has base 16 and uses the digits 0 through 9 together with A through F.

Thus, Binary is the answer.

title: What is the binary number for decimal number
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: What is the binary number for decimal number 9?
solution:
Concept — In a base-2 (binary) positional system each digit position carries a weight that is a power of 2. Reading a numeral from right to left the weights are 20, 21, 22, 23, … , and the value of the numeral is the sum of the weights whose digit is 1. Converting a decimal number to binary therefore means writing it as a sum of distinct powers of 2; the mechanical way to find those powers is to divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders from the last division backwards.

Application — Divide 9 by 2 repeatedly and record every remainder:

  1. 9 ÷ 2 = 4, remainder 1 — this remainder is the least-significant bit.

  2. 4 ÷ 2 = 2, remainder 0.

  3. 2 ÷ 2 = 1, remainder 0.

  4. 1 ÷ 2 = 0, remainder 1 — this remainder is the most-significant bit.

Reading the remainders from the last division back to the first gives 10012. The sum-of-powers view gives the same thing: 9 = 8 + 1 = 23 + 20, so the bits at the weights 8 and 1 are set and the bits at the weights 4 and 2 are clear.

  • 01112 sets the weights 4, 2 and 1, giving 710.

title: To convert Gray Code to its binary equivalent, which technique
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: To convert a Gray Code to its binary equivalent, which technique is commonly used?
solution:
Concept

Gray-to-binary conversion uses a prefix Exclusive-OR recurrence. The most significant binary bit is copied from the most significant Gray bit, and every later binary bit depends on the binary bit just obtained and the current Gray bit.

Exclusive OR produces 1 when its two input bits differ and 0 when they are equal. This left-to-right recurrence preserves the Gray-code transition information while recovering the positional binary bits.

Application

Apply the recurrence to Gray code 1011 from the most significant bit to the least significant bit:

  1. Copy the most significant bit: B3 = G3 = 1.

  2. Use the previous binary bit with the next Gray bit: B2 = B3 ⊕ G2 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1.

  3. Continue the recurrence: B1 = B2 ⊕ G1 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0.

  4. For the least significant bit: B0 = B1 ⊕ G0 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1.

Cross-check and contrast

Convert binary 1101 back to Gray code: keep the leading 1, then XOR adjacent binary bits to obtain 1, 0, and 1. This reproduces 1011.

  • Subtraction method: It propagates borrows between digit positions; it is not the prefix-bit recurrence used here.

  • Addition method: It propagates carries between digit positions. Carry-free addition modulo 2 describes XOR, not ordinary binary addition.

  • Exclusive OR (XOR) operation: It supplies the required prefix recurrence and can be implemented as a cascade of XOR gates.

  • Division method: Repeated division generates remainders for radix conversion; Gray-code conversion is a code transformation rather than a change of radix.

Result: The commonly used technique is the Exclusive OR (XOR) operation.

title: Is represented as in which of the following base
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: (1.3125)10 is represented as 1.5 in which of the following bases?
solution:
Concept

In any base b, a numeral is read by place value: the digit before the point counts whole units, and the first digit after the point counts b-ths of a unit.

So the numeral 1.5 written in base b stands for the decimal quantity 1 + 5/b. A digit is legal only when it is smaller than its own base, so the digit 5 can appear only in a base greater than 5.

Application

  1. Call the unknown base b and translate the numeral: 1.5 in base b means 1 + 5/b.

  2. The question says this quantity equals 1.3125 in decimal, so write 1 + 5/b = 1.3125.

  3. Subtract 1 from both sides: 5/b = 0.3125.

  4. Turn the decimal into a fraction: 0.3125 = 3125/10000 = 5/16.

  5. Compare 5/b with 5/16. The numerators are already equal, so the denominators must be equal: b = 16.

  6. Confirm the digit is legal: 5 is smaller than 16, so 5 is a valid digit in this base.

Cross-check

Convert in the other direction, by repeatedly multiplying the fractional part by the base: 0.3125 x 16 = 5.0. The whole part 5 becomes the first digit after the point and nothing is left over.

(1.3125)10 = (1.5)16.

Testing every offered base the same way:

Base

Decimal value of the numeral 1.5

8

1 + 5/8 = 1.625

12

1 + 5/12 ≈ 1.4167

16

1 + 5/16 = 1.3125

18

1 + 5/18 ≈ 1.2778

Only base 16 reproduces 1.3125, so the required base is 16, that is hexadecimal.

title: Decimal to octal conversion
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Determine the octal equivalent of (432267)10.
solution:
To convert a decimal (base-10) integer to octal (base-8), repeatedly divide the number by 8, recording the remainder at each step; the octal digits are the remainders read in reverse order, from the last division to the first.

  1. 432267 ÷ 8 = 54033, remainder 3

  2. 54033 ÷ 8 = 6754, remainder 1

  3. 6754 ÷ 8 = 844, remainder 2

  4. 844 ÷ 8 = 105, remainder 4

  5. 105 ÷ 8 = 13, remainder 1

  6. 13 ÷ 8 = 1, remainder 5

  7. 1 ÷ 8 = 0, remainder 1

Reading the remainders from last to first gives (1514213)8.

Cross-check: expanding (1514213)8 in powers of 8 gives 1×86 + 5×85 + 1×84 + 4×83 + 2×82 + 1×8 + 3 = 262144 + 163840 + 4096 + 2048 + 128 + 8 + 3 = 432267, confirming the conversion.

This computed value, (1514213)8, is the correct answer.

title: What is the OCTAL equivalent of the HEXADECIMAL number (ADF)
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: What is the OCTAL equivalent of the HEXADECIMAL number (ADF)16 ?
solution:
Concept

Hexadecimal and octal are both powers of two — 16 = 24 and 8 = 23 — so binary is the common bridge between them. One hexadecimal digit is exactly four bits, and one octal digit is exactly three bits.

A conversion between the two therefore never needs decimal arithmetic: expand every digit of the source base into its fixed-width bit group, join the bits into one unbroken string, then re-partition that same string into groups of the target width, counting from the right and padding the leftmost group with zeros if it falls short.

Applying it here

  1. Expand each hexadecimal digit of ADF into four bits: A = 1010, D = 1101, F = 1111.

  2. Join them in source order into one binary string: 101011011111, twelve bits in all.

  3. Twelve is a multiple of three, so no leading zeros are needed. Re-partition the same string from the right into three-bit groups: 101 | 011 | 011 | 111.

  4. Convert each three-bit group to its octal digit: 101 = 5, 011 = 3, 011 = 3, 111 = 7.

  5. Read the digits left to right: the octal equivalent is (5337)8.

The same bits, read two ways

Grouping

Bit string

Digits read off

Four bits at a time (hexadecimal)

1010 1101 1111

A D F

Three bits at a time (octal)

101 011 011 111

5 3 3 7

Cross-check with positional weights

Both numerals must expand to the same decimal value. (ADF)16 = 10 × 162 + 13 × 16 + 15 = 2560 + 208 + 15 = 2783, and (5337)8 = 5 × 83 + 3 × 82 + 3 × 8 + 7 = 2560 + 192 + 24 + 7 = 2783. The two agree, so the regrouping is sound.

Where this method usually goes wrong

Two slips account for most errors: re-partitioning the bit string from the left instead of the right, and dropping a leading zero while expanding a hexadecimal digit (writing A as 101 instead of 1010). Either one shifts every group after it and changes the octal digits that come out.

title: The complement of the Octal number is:

bodyHtml: The 8's complement of the four-digit octal number (6100)8 is:

(6100)8 + (1700)8 = (10000)8 = 84, so the required 8's complement is (1700)8.

title: 15th complement of Hexadecimal number is:
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: What is the 15's complement of the hexadecimal number (A10)16?
solution:
Concept

For an n-digit hexadecimal number, the 15's complement is formed by replacing every digit d with F − d.

Equivalently, it is the digit-wise subtraction of the number from an n-digit string of F symbols; no borrowing is needed when each position is handled separately.

Application

  1. Use three F digits because (A10)16 has three hexadecimal digits: FFF.

  2. Compute each position independently: F − A = 5, F − 1 = E, and F − 0 = F.

  3. Write the resulting digits in the original order: (5EF)16.

Cross-check

Taking the 15's complement again gives F − 5 = A, F − E = 1, and F − F = 0, which reconstructs (A10)16.

Result

Therefore, the 15's complement is (5EF)16.

title: What is the octal equivalent of (F3B1) hexadecimal number
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: What is the octal equivalent of (F3B1) hexadecimal number ?
solution:
Concept: A hexadecimal digit is a 4-bit binary pattern (since 16 = 24), while an octal digit is a 3-bit binary pattern (since 8 = 23). So to convert hex to octal, first expand every hex digit into its 4-bit binary form and concatenate all the bits into one binary string; then regroup that same string into 3-bit chunks counted from the right (padding the leftmost chunk with zeros if the total bit-length is not a multiple of 3), and read each 3-bit chunk as one octal digit.

Application — converting (F3B1) hexadecimal to octal:

  1. Expand each hex digit into its 4-bit binary form: F = 1111, 3 = 0011, B = 1011, 1 = 0001.

  2. Concatenate the four groups in order: 1111 0011 1011 0001, giving the 16-bit binary string 1111001110110001.

  3. 16 is not a multiple of 3, so pad two leading zeros to make an 18-bit string, then regroup from the right into 3-bit chunks: 00 1111 0011 1011 0001 → 001 111 001 110 110 001.

  4. Convert each 3-bit chunk to its octal digit: 001 = 1, 111 = 7, 001 = 1, 110 = 6, 110 = 6, 001 = 1.

  5. Reading the digits in order gives the octal number 171661.

Cross-check — an independent route via decimal, instead of binary grouping:

  1. Convert (F3B1) hexadecimal to decimal: 15 × 163 + 3 × 162 + 11 × 16 + 1 = 61440 + 768 + 176 + 1 = 62385.

  2. Convert 62385 to octal by repeated division by 8, tracking each remainder: 62385÷8 = 7798 r1, 7798÷8 = 974 r6, 974÷8 = 121 r6, 121÷8 = 15 r1, 15÷8 = 1 r7, 1÷8 = 0 r1.

  3. Reading the remainders from the last division to the first gives 1 7 1 6 6 1 = 171661 — the same result as the binary-grouping method.

Both independent methods agree: the octal equivalent of (F3B1) hexadecimal is 171661.

title: Which of the following represents

bodyHtml: Which of the following represents (D4)16 ?
solution:
We need the hexadecimal expression whose value equals (D4)16, i.e. 13×16 + 4 = 212 in decimal. Convert each operand to decimal and subtract.

Option 1: (4E)16 − (5B)16 = 78 − 91 = −13, which is negative and cannot equal a positive hexadecimal value.

Option 2: (14E)16 − (7A)16 = 334 − 122 = 212 = (D4)16. This matches the target.

title: (BABA) in hexadecimal is what in octal?
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: (BABA)16 in hexadecimal is what in octal?
solution:
Concept

To convert a hexadecimal number to octal, do not convert digit-by-digit directly — the two bases do not align (16 = 24, 8 = 23). Route through binary: each hex digit expands to exactly 4 binary bits; then regroup the whole binary string into bundles of 3 bits from the right, and each 3-bit bundle is one octal digit.

Application

Step through (BABA)16 using hex = 4 bits per digit:

  1. B = 1011, A = 1010, B = 1011, A = 1010, so the binary string is 1011 1010 1011 1010.

  2. Write it as one run: 1011101010111010 (16 bits). For octal, group in 3s from the right; 16 is not a multiple of 3, so pad two zeros on the left to make 18 bits: 001 011 101 010 111 010.

  3. Read each 3-bit group as an octal digit: 001=1, 011=3, 101=5, 010=2, 111=7, 010=2.

  4. Concatenate: 135272.

Cross-check

Independent decimal check: (BABA)16 = 11x163+10x162+11x16+10 = 45056+2560+176+10 = 47802. And (135272)8 = 1x85+3x84+5x83+2x82+7x8+2 = 32768+12288+2560+128+56+2 = 47802. Both equal 47802, confirming the result.

title: What is the hexadecimal equivalent of the binary number:
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: What is the hexadecimal equivalent of the binary number 10111010?
solution:
To convert a binary number to hexadecimal, group the bits into nibbles of 4, starting from the right, then convert each nibble to its hex digit.

Binary: 1011 1010

Left nibble 1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11 = B

Right nibble 1010 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 10 = A

So 10111010 = BA in hexadecimal.

Check (via decimal): 10111010 = 128 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 186, and 186 = (11 x 16) + 10 = (B x 16) + A = BA. Hence the answer is BA.

title: Convert the hexadecimal number into its binary equivalent.
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Convert the hexadecimal number 1B0 into its binary equivalent.
solution:
Concept

Each hexadecimal digit maps to exactly 4 binary bits (because 16 = 24). To convert a hex number to binary, replace every hex digit independently with its fixed 4-bit pattern and concatenate the groups in the same order. The base-16 to base-2 relationship makes this a direct one-digit-to-four-bits substitution, with no carrying or arithmetic across digits.

Application

The number 1B0 has three hex digits, so the binary result has 3 × 4 = 12 bits. Substitute each digit with its 4-bit group:

Hex digit

Decimal

4-bit binary

1

1

0001

B

11

1011

0

0

0000

Concatenate the groups left to right in the original order:

  1. Digit 1 → 0001

  2. Digit B → 1011

  3. Digit 0 → 0000

  4. Join: 0001 1011 0000 → 000110110000

So 1B0₁₆ = 000110110000₂.

Cross-check

Read the binary value back: 000110110000 groups into 0001 1011 0000 = 1, 11, 0 = 1, B, 0 = 1B0. As an independent check, 1B0₁₆ = 1×256 + 11×16 + 0 = 256 + 176 + 0 = 432, and 000110110000₂ = 256 + 128 + 32 + 16 = 432. Both confirm the result.

Key idea: in two's complement the most significant bit (the sign bit) has negative weight.

solution:
Step 1: Convert (BAC) in base 13 to decimal. B = 11, A = 10, C = 12.

bodyHtml: In an 8-bit computer system using 2's complement representation, the decimal number 26 is subtracted from 22 (i.e. 22 − 26). What is the result expressed in 8-bit binary 2's complement form?
solution:
Step 1 — Compute the arithmetic result: 22 − 26 = −4.

Since the result is negative, it must be written in 8-bit 2's complement form.

Step 2 — Represent the magnitude +4 in 8 bits: 4 = 00000100.

Step 3 — Take the 2's complement to obtain −4: invert all bits of 00000100 → 11111011 (the 1's complement), then add 1 → 11111100.

Therefore −4 in 8-bit 2's complement is 11111100.

Cross-check by adding 22 and −26 directly: 22 = 00010110 and −26 = 11100110; their sum is 00010110 + 11100110 = 11111100, which fits within 8 bits (no carry leaves the 8th bit) and equals −4, confirming the result.

title: The smallest integer that can be represented by an bit
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: The smallest integer that can be represented by an 8-bit number in 2's complement form is
solution:
Concept

In two's-complement form an n-bit number reserves the most significant bit as a sign bit, and the representable values form a fixed, asymmetric range. The smallest (most negative) value is -2n-1 and the largest is 2n-1 - 1. The range is asymmetric because the all-zeros pattern is spent on zero, leaving one extra code on the negative side.

Application

Here n = 8, so apply the formula with the exponent n - 1 = 7:

  1. Most negative value = -27 = -128.

  2. Most positive value = 27 - 1 = 127.

  3. So an 8-bit two's-complement byte spans -128 to +127, which is 256 distinct values.

The question asks for the smallest (most negative) integer, which is -128.

Cross-check

The most-negative pattern is 1000 0000. Negating it in two's complement (invert all bits to 0111 1111, then add 1) gives 1000 0000 again - it maps to itself, confirming there is no +128, and the lone extra negative code is exactly -128. Counting also checks out: 256 total codes split as 128 negative values (-128 to -1) and 128 non-negative values (0 to 127).

Why the other values fail

  • -256 would need a magnitude of 28, but 8 bits cap the negative reach at 27 = 128.

  • 127 is the largest representable value, not the smallest.

  • -255 exceeds the negative reach (it would require 9 bits) and is not a power-of-two boundary of any 8-bit byte.

title: Why are complements (such as and complement) used in digital
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Why are complements (such as 1's and 2's complement) used in digital number systems?

options.label: A
options.html: To facilitate subtraction operations using only addition logic in binary arithmetic.

options.label: B
options.html: To enable accurate representation of decimal fractions in binary format.

options.label: C
options.html: To simplify floating-point arithmetic operations in digital processors.

options.label: D
options.html: To convert hexadecimal values directly into BCD representations.

solution:
Complements simplify arithmetic operations in digital systems by enabling subtraction through addition. They also allow for a unique representation of zero and simplify hardware design in computers.


Note for more understanding

In digital electronics, manufacturing space on a silicon chip is precious. Building a circuit that can perform addition requires logic gates configured as Full Adders. If a computer had to perform subtraction the way humans do (borrowing from the next column), engineers would have to design and build an entirely separate, complex circuit called a Full Subtractor.

Complement arithmetic elegantly solves this hardware bloat through a mathematical trick:

  1. Transforming Subtraction into Addition: Mathematically, subtracting a binary number B from A is identical to adding a negative B:

    A - B = A + (-B)

  3. The Role of 2's Complement: In a 2's complement system, a negative number is represented by inverting all its bits (which is the 1's complement) and adding 1.

  4. Hardware Efficiency: Because of this representation, when the processor needs to execute a subtraction instruction, it can simply route the second operand ($B$) through an inverter (NOT gates) to flip the bits, set the carry-in bit of the initial adder to 1 (completing the 2's complement transformation), and run it through the exact same Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) addition hardware.

This single unified design reduces the number of transistors required on a chip, lowers power consumption, and speeds up computation times.

title: Which of the following is the complement of that is
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Which of the following is the 4's complement of (1011)₅, that is in base 5 number system?
solution: To find the r's complement of a number in base r, we first calculate the (r-1)'s complement and then add 1 to it. Here, we need the 4's complement of (1011)₅ in base 5. First, determine the number of digits: there are 4 digits. The (r-1)'s complement in base r is found by subtracting each digit from (r-1). Since the base is 5, we subtract each digit of (1011)₅ from 4. Subtracting the first digit: 4 - 1 = 3. Second digit: 4 - 0 = 4. Third digit: 4 - 1 = 3. Fourth digit: 4 - 1 = 3. This gives the 4's complement as (3433)₅ directly because in base r, the r's complement is often defined as (r^n - N), but for digit-wise operations in base 5, the complement of a number with n digits is (r^n - N). However, strictly speaking, the 4's complement usually refers to the diminished radix complement (base-1) in some contexts, but here it implies finding the value such that adding it to the original yields 10000₅ (which is 5^4). Let's re-evaluate: The standard definition for r's complement of an n-digit number N in base r is (r^n - N). For 4's complement of a base-5 number, this phrasing is slightly ambiguous. Usually, we calculate the (r-1)'s complement first. If '4's complement' means the complement with respect to base 5 (which is r=5), then it's the 5's complement. If it literally means base 4, that doesn't make sense for a base-5 number. Assuming the question asks for the 5's complement (often confused or typoed as r's where r is base), let's calculate 5's complement: (10000)₅ - (1011)₅. 5-1=4, borrow... actually simpler: (r^n - N). 5^4 = 10000₅. 10000₅ - 1011₅ = (4-1)(4-0)(4-1)(5-1) -> 3, 4, 3, 4? No. Let's do subtraction: 10000 - 1011. Last digit: 5-1=4 (borrow). Next: 4-1=3. Next: 4-0=4. First: 4-1=3. Result (3434)₅? Wait, the correct answer is B: (3433)₅. This implies the question asks for the 4's complement where '4' is (r-1). So it is asking for the diminished radix complement (base 5, r-1 = 4). The rule is: subtract each digit from (r-1) = 4. Digit 1: 4-1=3. Digit 2: 4-0=4. Digit 3: 4-1=3. Digit 4: 4-1=3. Result is (3433)₅. This matches Option B. Options A, C, and D are incorrect because they do not follow the digit-wise subtraction from 4 rule. Option A is too small, C and D contain digits invalid for base 5 (8, 9) or incorrect values.

title: Consider self-complementary weighted BCD code. The decimal digit is represented
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: Consider a self-complementary 6 4 2 -3 weighted BCD code. The decimal digit 6 is represented by ______.
solution:
Key point: compute the weighted sum using weights 6, 4, 2, −3 (left to right).

  • For 0110: 0×6 + 1×4 + 1×2 + 0×(−3) = 4 + 2 = 6, so 0110 represents decimal 6.

  • For 1000: 1×6 + 0×4 + 0×2 + 0×(−3) = 6, so 1000 also evaluates to 6 (this is a second valid weighted representation).

Self-complementary requirement: the bitwise complement of a digit's code must represent 9 minus that digit.

  • Complement of 0110 is 1001, and 1001 evaluates to 3, so 0110 ↔ 1001 is a valid complementary pair representing 6 and 3.

  • Complement of 0111 is 1000, and 0111 evaluates to 3, so 1000 ↔ 0111 is another valid complementary pair. This explains why 1000 can also represent 6 in a different complementary assignment.

Answer: 0110 is the representation for decimal 6 in the self-complementary mapping used in this question.

title: 4-bit BCD code represented by(b )is converted to 4-bit Excess-3
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: A 4-bit BCD code represented by(b3,b2,b1,b0)is converted to 4-bit Excess-3 code represented by (e3e2e1e0). Which one of the following function is NOT correct?
solution:
Approach: Add 3 to the 4-bit BCD value for each decimal digit 0–9 to get the Excess-3 code, then read off each output bit's truth set.

  • e0: ones at decimal inputs 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (minterms {0,2,4,6,8}); equivalently e0 = NOT b0.

  • e1: ones at decimal inputs 0, 3, 4, 7, 8 and zeros at 1, 2, 5, 6, 9; therefore e1 can be written as the product of maxterms π(1,2,5,6,9).

  • e2: ones at decimal inputs 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 and zeros at 0, 5, 6, 7, 8; therefore e2 = π(0,5,6,7,8) (product of maxterms where e2 = 0).

  • e3: ones at decimal inputs 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 (minterms {5,6,7,8,9}) and zeros at 0,1,2,3,4.

Why the given e3 expression is incorrect: the provided form π(5,6,7,8,9) lists maxterms (inputs where the function is 0). But e3 is 1 at 5–9, so those indices are minterms, not maxterms. The correct representations are e3 = Σ(5,6,7,8,9) (sum of minterms) or equivalently e3 = π(0,1,2,3,4) (product of maxterms where e3 = 0).

Conclusion: The incorrect function provided is the one that represents e3 as π(5,6,7,8,9).

title: The minimal function that can detect 'divisible by BCD code
subject: Digital Logic
bodyHtml: The minimal function that can detect a 'divisible by 3' 8421 BCD code digit (representation is D8D4D2D1) is given by
solution:
Concept

To build a minimal digit detector, first mark the output 1 for exactly the target digits (here, digits divisible by 3) and 0 for every other valid digit. Any bit pattern that is not a valid 8421 BCD code (decimal 10–15, i.e. 1010–1111) never occurs as input, so it is treated as a don’t-care on the Karnaugh map — this lets prime implicants be grouped larger than the strict minterms alone would allow, giving a smaller sum-of-products (SOP).

Application

  1. Digits divisible by 3 in 0–9 are 0, 3, 6, 9, with 8421 BCD codes 0000, 0011, 0110, 1001 respectively (output F = 1); every other valid digit — 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 — must give F = 0. The six patterns 1010–1111 never represent a valid digit, so they are don’t-cares (X).

  2. Plot these 16 patterns on a 4-variable K-map with rows = D8D4 and columns = D2D1 in Gray-code order (00, 01, 11, 10) on both axes, and mark the six invalid patterns as X.

  3. The cell for 0000 (digit 0) has no adjacent 1 or X (its row and column neighbours are all 0), so it cannot be grouped with anything and stands alone as the product term D8′D4′D2′D1′.

  4. The cell for 1001 (digit 9) is adjacent to the don’t-cares 1011, 1101 and 1111, forming a size-4 group in which only D8 and D1 stay fixed at 1 (D4 and D2 vary freely), giving the term D8D1.

  5. The cell for 0110 (digit 6) is adjacent to the don’t-care 1110, forming a size-2 group with D4, D2 fixed at 1 and D1′ fixed (D1 = 0, D8 free), giving the term D4D2D1′.

  6. The cell for 0011 (digit 3) is adjacent to the don’t-care 1011, forming a size-2 group with D2, D1 fixed at 1 and D4′ fixed (D4 = 0, D8 free), giving the term D4′D2D1.

  7. Summing these four prime implicants gives the minimal SOP: F = D8′D4′D2′D1′ + D8D1 + D4D2D1′ + D4′D2D1.

Cross-check

  • Digit 0 (0000): only D8′D4′D2′D1′ evaluates to 1, so F = 1, as required.

  • Digit 3 (0011): only D4′D2D1 evaluates to 1, so F = 1, as required.

  • Digit 6 (0110): only D4D2D1′ evaluates to 1, so F = 1, as required.

  • Digit 9 (1001): only D8D1 evaluates to 1, so F = 1, as required.

  • Digits 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8: for each of these, every one of the four terms needs at least one literal that is false at that pattern, so all four terms evaluate to 0 and F = 0, as required.

Hence the four-term expression F = D8′D4′D2′D1′ + D8D1 + D4D2D1′ + D4′D2D1 is the minimal sum-of-products realization of the ‘divisible by 3’ 8421 BCD digit detector.

Excess-3 Code (XS-3 Code)

Concept

Excess-3 code is a non-weighted Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) code obtained by adding 3 to each decimal digit and then converting that sum into 4-bit binary: XS-3 = binary(decimal digit + 3), equivalently XS-3 = BCD + 0011.

It is also a self-complementing, sequential code. A valid 4-bit Excess-3 code always falls in the binary range 0011 to 1100 (since digits 0-9 map to 3-12); any 4-bit pattern outside that range cannot be a valid Excess-3 code.

Other Properties of Excess-3 Code

  • Non-weighted: unlike 8-4-2-1 BCD, its bit positions carry no fixed positional weight.

A set given in set-builder form, {x : conditions on x}, is defined by testing each candidate value of x against every stated condition; only values satisfying all the conditions jointly belong to the set. When two conditions are joined by 'and', a value must pass both to qualify.

title: Which of the following set is uncountable
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Which of the following sets is uncountable?
solution:
Concept. A set is countable if its elements can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers, i.e. arranged in a single list (finite sets are also countable). A set is uncountable if no such listing exists — it is strictly “larger” than the natural numbers. The standard example of an uncountable set is the set of real numbers, proved uncountable by Cantor’s diagonal argument.

Applying this to each offered set:

  • Natural numbers can be listed directly as 1, 2, 3, 4, …, which is itself a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers, so this set is countable.

  • All integers can be listed as 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, 3, −3, …, alternating signs so every integer eventually appears at a fixed position, so this set is countable.

  • Positive rationals p/q can be placed in an infinite grid (numerator × denominator) and traversed along successive diagonals, skipping repeated values; this produces a single list of all of them, so this set is countable.

Conclusion. All three named sets are countable, so the option asserting that none of the listed sets is uncountable is the one that holds. By contrast, the real numbers — had they been offered — would be the uncountable choice, since Cantor’s diagonal argument shows the reals in [0, 1] cannot be exhausted by any list.

title: Which of the following is/are true: The set of real
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Which of the following is/are true:
S1. The set of real numbers is countable
S2. The set of rational numbers is countable
S3. The set of integers is uncountable
S4. The set of real numbers between 0 to ¼ is uncountable
solution:
Definitions: Countable means a set can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers. Uncountable means it is not countable.

  • The set of real numbers is countable: False. The real numbers are uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument shows no complete listing of real numbers is possible).

  • The set of rational numbers is countable: True. Rationals can be enumerated by arranging fractions as pairs of integers (numerator, denominator), ordering those pairs (for example by increasing sum of absolute values) and skipping duplicates, giving a sequence that lists every rational number.

  • The set of integers is uncountable: False. The integers are countable; for example list them as 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, ... which gives a bijection with the natural numbers.

  • The set of real numbers between 0 and 1/4 is uncountable: True. Any nontrivial interval of real numbers has the same cardinality as (0,1). A simple bijection x ↦ 4x maps (0,1/4) to (0,1), and (0,1) is uncountable by Cantor's diagonal argument.

Conclusion: The true statements are the countability of the rational numbers and the uncountability of the real numbers between 0 and 1/4. Therefore, the correct combination is: the statement that the rationals are countable and the statement that the real numbers between 0 and 1/4 are uncountable.

Approach: Let A(n) be the number of subsets of {1, 2, ..., n} in which no two selected elements are consecutive.

  • Do not include n: then the subset can be any valid subset of {1, 2, ..., n − 1}, giving A(n − 1) choices.

  • Include n: then n − 1 cannot be included, so the remaining elements come from {1, 2, ..., n − 2}, giving A(n − 2) choices.

Therefore, A(n) = A(n − 1) + A(n − 2). This is the Fibonacci recurrence.

Base cases: A(0) = 1 for the empty set, and A(1) = 2 for {} and {1}.

Values up to n = 12: A(2)=3, A(3)=5, A(4)=8, A(5)=13, A(6)=21, A(7)=34, A(8)=55, A(9)=89, A(10)=144, A(11)=233, A(12)=377.

Solution: If A ∪ B = A ∩ B then A = B. Proof:

  1. Take any element x in A. Since A ⊆ A ∪ B and A ∪ B = A ∩ B, we have x in A ∩ B, so x is in B. Hence A ⊆ B.

  2. Similarly, take any element x in B. From B ⊆ A ∪ B and A ∪ B = A ∩ B we get x in A ∩ B, so x is in A. Hence B ⊆ A.

Since A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A, we conclude A = B. (The special case A = B = empty set also satisfies the equality, but the general conclusion remains that the two sets are equal.)

title: If A,B,C are any three set, consider the following statement
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: If A,B,C are any three set, consider the following statement , find which one is true?
solution:
Answer: Only the statement "If A Δ C = B Δ C then A = B" is true.

  • Intersection statement (If A ∩ C = B ∩ C then A = B): False. Counterexample: take C = ∅. Then A ∩ C = ∅ = B ∩ C for any A and B, but A and B need not be equal.

  • Union statement (If A ∪ C = B ∪ C then A = B): False. Counterexample: let C be a set that contains both A and B (for instance C = {1,2}, A = {1}, B = {2}). Then A ∪ C = C = B ∪ C, but A ≠ B.

  • Symmetric-difference statement (If A Δ C = B Δ C then A = B): True. Proof: take the symmetric difference of both sides with C. Using associativity of Δ and C Δ C = ∅ we get (A Δ C) Δ C = A and (B Δ C) Δ C = B. Since A Δ C = B Δ C, applying Δ C to both sides yields A = B.

Final answer: (A − B) ∪ (B − C) = ~C ∩ (A ∪ B)

  • Rewrite set differences: (A − B) ∪ (B − C) = (A ∩ ~B) ∪ (B ∩ ~C).

  • Show inclusion into ~C ∩ (A ∪ B): if x is in the union then either x ∈ A ∩ ~B or x ∈ B ∩ ~C. In both cases x ∉ C (if x ∉ B then x ∉ C because C ⊂ B), and x ∈ A ∪ B. Hence every element of the union lies in ~C ∩ (A ∪ B).

  • Show the reverse inclusion: if x ∈ ~C ∩ (A ∪ B) then x ∉ C and x ∈ A or x ∈ B. If x ∈ A and x ∉ B then x ∈ A − B; if x ∈ A and x ∈ B but x ∉ C then x ∈ B − C; if x ∈ B and x ∉ C then x ∈ B − C. Thus every element of ~C ∩ (A ∪ B) lies in (A − B) ∪ (B − C).

  • Combining both inclusions gives the equality: (A − B) ∪ (B − C) = ~C ∩ (A ∪ B).

solution:
Summary of which statements are true and why:

  • Statement: A⊕B = B⊕A — True. Reason: Symmetric difference means "in exactly one of the sets." For any element x, being in A⊕B is the same as being in B⊕A, so the sets are equal.

  • Statement: (A ⊕ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ⊕ C) — False. Counterexample:

    Choose A = {1}, B = {1}, C = {2}.

    Compute left side: A⊕B = ∅, so (A⊕B) ∪ C = ∅ ∪ {2} = {2}.

    Compute right side: B⊕C = {1,2}, so A ∪ (B⊕C) = {1} ∪ {1,2} = {1,2}.

    Since {2} ≠ {1,2}, the equality fails in general.

  • Statement: If A⊕B = A⊕C then B = C — True. Proof: Take symmetric difference with A on both sides: A⊕(A⊕B) = A⊕(A⊕C). Using associativity and the fact that A⊕A = ∅, this gives ∅⊕B = ∅⊕C, i.e. B = C.

  • Statement: A ∩ (B⊕C) = (A∩B)⊕(A∩C) — True. Proof: Element-wise: x is in A ∩ (B⊕C) exactly when x ∈ A and x is in exactly one of B or C. That is equivalent to x being in (A∩B) but not (A∩C), or in (A∩C) but not (A∩B). This description matches membership in (A∩B)⊕(A∩C).

title: Suppose A,B and are events such that P(A) P(B) =P(C)
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Suppose A,B and C are events such that
P(A) = P(B) =P(C) = 1/4
P(A ⋂ B) =P(B⋂ C) = 0 and P( A ⋂ C) =1/8
Probability that one of the events A,B or C occur …….
solution:
Solution:

  1. Use the inclusion–exclusion formula: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A ∩ B) - P(B ∩ C) - P(A ∩ C) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C).

  2. Substitute the given values: P(A) = P(B) = P(C) = 1/4, P(A ∩ B) = 0, P(B ∩ C) = 0, P(A ∩ C) = 1/8.

  3. Determine the triple intersection: P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = 0 because any triple intersection is a subset of A ∩ B, and P(A ∩ B) = 0, so the triple intersection has probability 0.

  4. Compute: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 - 0 - 0 - 1/8 + 0 = 3/4 - 1/8 = 6/8 - 1/8 = 5/8 = 0.625.

  5. Answer: The probability that at least one of A, B, or C occurs is 5/8 (0.625).

title: Question If and are sets, then which of the following
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Which of the following is false, if A and B are sets?
solution:
Conclusion: All the given statements are true. Short proofs for each follow.

  • A \ B^c = A ∩ B: A \ B^c consists of elements in A that are not in B^c. Not being in B^c means being in B, so A \ B^c = A ∩ B. Algebraically: A \ B^c = A ∩ (B^c)^c = A ∩ B.

  • If A ⊂ B then B' ⊂ A': Take any element x in B'. Then x ∉ B. Since A ⊂ B, x cannot be in A, so x ∈ A'. Hence every element of B' is in A', which gives B' ⊂ A'.

  • A \ (A \ B) = A ∩ B: Use complements and De Morgan: A \ (A \ B) = A ∩ (A \ B)' = A ∩ (A' ∪ B) = (A ∩ A') ∪ (A ∩ B) = ∅ ∪ (A ∩ B) = A ∩ B.

Therefore, the choice that asserts 'None of these' is correct because none of the presented statements is false.

title: Consider set How many members of shall be divisible by
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Consider a set A = {1, 2, 3, …….., 1000}. How many members of A shall be divisible by 3 or by 5 or by both 3 and 5 ?
solution:
Solution:

Count how many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by 3 or 5 using inclusion–exclusion.

  • Numbers divisible by 3: floor(1000 ÷ 3) = 333.

  • Numbers divisible by 5: floor(1000 ÷ 5) = 200.

  • Numbers divisible by both 3 and 5 (i.e. by 15): floor(1000 ÷ 15) = 66.

  • Apply inclusion–exclusion: 333 + 200 − 66 = 467.

Answer: There are 467 members of the set {1, …, 1000} divisible by 3 or 5 (or both).

title: If and be any two sets such that then is
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: If A and B be any two sets such that A - B = A, then A ∩ B is
solution:
For any two sets A and B, the set difference A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B} keeps exactly the elements of A that are absent from B. If that result still equals the whole of A, no element of A has been removed — which is possible only when no element of A is present in B at all. Two sets with no elements in common are called disjoint sets.

  1. Write the given condition: A − B = A.

  2. Apply the definition of set difference, A − B = {x ∈ A : x ∉ B}. Setting this equal to A means every element x ∈ A must satisfy x ∉ B — so no element of A lies in B.

  3. Since no element of A is in B, sets A and B have no elements in common; A and B are disjoint.

  4. By the definition of intersection, two disjoint sets share no common elements, so A ∩ B = ∅.

  • A ∩ B = A would require A ⊆ B, i.e. every element of A also lying in B — the exact opposite of what A − B = A gives. The two can agree only in the degenerate case A = ∅, so A is not the value of the intersection in general.

  • A ∩ B = B would require B ⊆ A, i.e. every element of B also lying in A. The given condition says nothing that places B inside A, and the two agree only when B = ∅, so B is not the value in general.

  • A ∩ B = A ∪ B forces A = B, because the intersection is contained in the union and equals it only when the two sets coincide. Together with A − B = A this would need A = B = ∅, so A ∪ B is not the value in general.

  • The stem fixes A and B as any two sets satisfying A − B = A, so the answer must be the value that holds for every such pair — and only ∅ does. The other three coincide with the intersection at most in an isolated empty-set case, never as the general result.

Cross-check with a concrete example: let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {4, 5}. Then A − B = {1, 2, 3} = A, which matches the given condition, and indeed A ∩ B = { } = ∅ — consistent with the general result above.

title: Let are the sets with number of elements respectively, and
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Let A, B are the sets with m, n number of elements respectively, and it is observed that

P (( A X B) U (B X A)) and P (( A X B) U (A X B))

and has equal number of elements.

NOTE: ‘P’ is a power set.

The above condition holds false only if

 l A = B

 ll A = ϕ and B = ϕ

 lll  A = ϕ or B = ϕ or A = B

 lV A = ϕ or B = ϕ
solution:
Explanation and final conclusion:

Compare the sizes of the power sets by comparing the sizes of the underlying sets: if two sets S and T have power sets of the same size, then |S| = |T| because |P(S)| = 2^{|S|}.

Apply this to the problem: the equality of power sets means

  • |(A × B) ∪ (B × A)| = |A × B|.

  • This equality holds exactly when every element of B × A is already in A × B, i.e. when B × A ⊆ A × B.

  • For nonempty A and B, B × A ⊆ A × B forces B ⊆ A and A ⊆ B, so A = B.

  • If A = ∅ or B = ∅, then A × B = ∅ and B × A = ∅, so the two sets are equal and their power sets have equal size.

Therefore the power sets are equal precisely in the cases: A = B, or A = ∅, or B = ∅.

Consequently, the given equality fails exactly when none of those conditions hold, i.e. when A ≠ B and both A and B are nonempty.

Note about the provided options: none of the answer choices precisely state the failure condition 'A ≠ B and A ≠ ∅ and B ≠ ∅'. The correct characterization of the failure case is the complement of {A = B, A = ∅, B = ∅}.

title: If Then no of relation possible on which are not
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: If A ={1,2}, Then no of relation possible on A which are not function?
solution:
Explanation: For the set A = {1, 2}, compute the counts step by step.

  • Number of elements in A is 2, so the Cartesian product A × A has 2 × 2 = 4 ordered pairs.

  • A relation on A is any subset of A × A, so the total number of relations is 2^4 = 16.

  • A function from A to A assigns to each of the 2 elements exactly one image in A, so the number of functions is 2^2 = 4.

  • Therefore the number of relations that are not functions is 16 − 4 = 12.

Answer: 12

title: For every is said to be reflexive relation on set
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: ____ for every a ∈ A is said to be a reflexive relation R on set A.
solution:
Definition: A relation R on a set A is called reflexive if the ordered pair (a, a) is an element of R for every a in A. In symbols: for all a ∈ A, (a, a) ∈ R.

In other words, every element of A is related to itself.

  • Example: If A = {1, 2, 3} and R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2)}, then R is reflexive because (1,1), (2,2), and (3,3) are all in R.

  • Common mistake: Writing (a, a) ∈ A is incorrect, because A contains elements (like a), while R contains ordered pairs (like (a, a)).

title: Consider binary relation on is defined as follows: (a,b)R(c,d) iff
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Consider a binary relation R on Z ✖ Z is defined as follows:   
(a,b)R(c,d) iff a>c and b<d
then which of the following is/are true:
solution:
Relation R on Z x Z is defined by (a,b)R(c,d) iff a > c and b < d.

  • Irreflexive: No pair (a,b) can satisfy (a,b)R(a,b) because that would require a>a and b<b, which is impossible. Hence the relation is irreflexive.

  • Asymmetric: If (a,b)R(c,d) then a>c and b<d. For (c,d)R(a,b) we would need c>a and d<b, which contradicts a>c and b<d. Thus both directions cannot hold, so the relation is asymmetric.

  • Antisymmetric: Antisymmetry requires that if two elements are mutually related then they are equal. Since no distinct pairs can be mutually related (and no element is related to itself), the condition is vacuously satisfied, so the relation is antisymmetric.

  • Transitive (so "Not transitive" is false): If (a,b)R(c,d) and (c,d)R(e,f), then a>c>e implies a>e, and b<d<f implies b<f; therefore (a,b)R(e,f). Hence the relation is transitive.

Conclusion: The relation is irreflexive, asymmetric, and antisymmetric (the latter vacuously). It is also transitive, so the claim that it is not transitive is incorrect.

title: Relation is defined on set with cardinality which is both
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: A relation R is defined on a set A with |A| = 5. If R is both reflexive and antisymmetric, how many such relations are possible?
solution:
Answer: 59049 = 3¹⁰

Reasoning:
A reflexive relation must include all 5 diagonal pairs (a, a), so these pairs are fixed.

For each unordered pair of distinct elements {a, b}, antisymmetry does not allow both (a, b) and (b, a) to be present together. For each such pair, there are exactly three choices: include neither ordered pair, include (a, b) only, or include (b, a) only.

The number of unordered pairs of distinct elements is n(n - 1)/2 = 5 × 4 / 2 = 10. Therefore, the number of reflexive and antisymmetric relations is 3¹⁰ = 59049.

title: The number of Asymmetric relations of set with elements
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: The number of Asymmetric relations of a set with 4 elements ____
solution:
Correct solution: The number of asymmetric relations on an n-element set is 3^(n(n-1)/2).

  • For each unordered pair of distinct elements {i, j} (there are n(n-1)/2 such pairs), there are three possibilities: no ordered pair between them, only (i, j), or only (j, i).

  • Diagonal pairs (i, i) cannot appear in an asymmetric relation, so there are no choices for those.

  • Multiplying the three choices for each unordered pair gives 3^(n(n-1)/2) possible asymmetric relations.

For n = 4, n(n-1)/2 = 6, so the number of asymmetric relations is 3^6 = 729.

title: If relation is both symmetric and anti-symmetric, what can be
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: If a relation R is both symmetric and anti-symmetric, what can be said about R?

options.label: C
options.html: R must contain only elements of the form (a, a)

options.label: D
options.html: R must contain only elements of the form (a, b) where a ≠ b

solution:
Answer: The relation must consist only of pairs of the form (a, a) (i.e., it is a subset of the diagonal).

Reasoning:

  • Symmetry: If (a, b) is in R, then (b, a) must also be in R.

  • Anti-symmetry: If (a, b) and (b, a) are both in R, then a = b.

  • Combining these: if (a, b) were present with a ≠ b, symmetry would force (b, a) too, and anti-symmetry would then force a = b, a contradiction. Therefore no pair with a ≠ b can be in R.

  • Conclusion: R can only contain pairs (a, a). This includes the empty relation or any subset of the diagonal {(a,a) : a is in the set}.

title: Consider relation xRy between times of day such that and
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Consider a relation xRy between times of day such that x and y are at most twenty minutes part. Then which of the following are true?
solution:
Correct properties: Reflexive and Symmetric; not Transitive; not Irreflexive.

  • Reflexive: Every time is at distance 0 from itself, and 0 ≤ 20, so each time is related to itself.

  • Symmetric: If time x and time y differ by at most 20 minutes, then y and x differ by the same amount, so the relation holds in both directions.

  • Not Transitive: Counterexample: 10:00 and 10:20 are related (20 minutes), and 10:20 and 10:40 are related (20 minutes), but 10:00 and 10:40 are 40 minutes apart, which is more than 20, so they are not related. Thus transitivity fails.

  • Not Irreflexive: Irreflexive would require no element to relate to itself, but since every time relates to itself (difference 0 ≤ 20), the relation is not irreflexive.

solution:
Set A = {a, b, c} and
R = {(a, a), (a, b), (a, c), (b, b), (b, c), (c, c)}.

Reflexive: For every element of A, the corresponding diagonal pair is present: (a, a), (b, b), and (c, c). Hence R is reflexive.
