title: Is relation defined over the set of integers as follows
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Let R be a relation on the set of integers Z, defined by aRb if and only if a is a factor of b. Then R is:
solution:
Concept

A relation R on a set is reflexive when xRx holds for every x, symmetric when xRy implies yRx, and transitive when xRy and yRz together imply xRz.

For divisibility, a divides b means that b = ak for some integer k.

Application

  1. Reflexivity: For every integer a, a = a × 1, so a divides itself. Hence aRa holds for every a.

  2. Symmetry: Symmetry need not hold. For example, 2 divides 4, but 4 does not divide 2; thus 2R4 does not imply 4R2.

  3. Transitivity: If a divides b and b divides c, write b = am and c = bn for integers m and n. Then c = a(mn), and mn is an integer, so a divides c.

Cross-check

For instance, 3 divides 6 and 6 divides 18, and indeed 3 divides 18; reversing 3 divides 6 gives 6 divides 3, which is false. Therefore R is reflexive and transitive, but not symmetric.

title: Let be set of non zero natural numbers. Define binary
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Let N be set of non-zero natural numbers. Define a binary relation R on N×N by (m,n)R(s,t) such that, gcd(m,n) = gcd⁡(s,t). The binary relation R is,
solution:
(a) (b) (c)

1. Reflexive:

  • A relation RR is reflexive if (a,b)R(a,b) for all (a,b)∈N×N.

  • Here, gcd(a,b)=gcd(a,b), so (a,b)R(a,b) holds.

  • Conclusion: RR is reflexive.

2. Symmetric:

  • A relation RR is symmetric if (a,b)R(c,d) implies (c,d)R(a,b).

  • If gcd(a,b)=gcd(c,d), then gcd(c,d)=gcd(a,b), so (c,d)R(a,b) holds.

  • Conclusion: RR is symmetric.

3. Transitive:

  • A relation RR is transitive if (a,b)R(c,d) and (c,d)R(e,f) implies (a,b)R(e,f).

  • If gcd(a,b)=gcd(c,d) and gcd(c,d)=gcd(e,f), then gcd(a,b)=gcd(e,f), so (a,b)R(e,f) holds.

  • Conclusion: RR is transitive.

4. Equivalence Relation:

  • A relation is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

  • Since RR satisfies all three properties, it is an equivalence relation.

  • Conclusion: RR is an equivalence relation.

title: Consider relation between vertices in an undirected graph two vertices
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Consider a relation R on the vertices of an undirected graph: two vertices v and w are connected if and only if there is a path between them.

Which of the following properties is/are satisfied by the relation R?
solution:
Answer: The connectedness relation in an undirected graph is symmetric and transitive (and also reflexive), so asymmetric and irreflexive do not hold.

  • Symmetric: If there is a path from v to w, the same sequence of edges can be traversed in reverse to produce a path from w to v (edges are bidirectional). Thus the relation is symmetric.

  • Transitive: If there is a path from v to w and a path from w to u, concatenating those paths yields a path from v to u (repeating vertices is allowed when only existence matters). Therefore the relation is transitive.

  • Asymmetric: Asymmetry would require that whenever v is related to w, w is not related to v. This contradicts the symmetry just explained, so the relation is not asymmetric.

  • Irreflexive: Irreflexive means no vertex is related to itself. But every vertex has a trivial path of length zero to itself, so each vertex is related to itself. Hence the relation is not irreflexive; it is reflexive.

title: Let {x,y,z} and let {(x,x) (y,y), (z,z),(x,y)(y,x), (y,z) be relation
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Let P = {x, y, z} and let R = {(x, x), (y, y), (z, z), (x, y), (y, x), (y, z)} be a relation on P. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Select all that apply.)
solution:
Concept

On a set, a relation R is reflexive if (a, a) ∈ R for every element a; symmetric if (a, b) ∈ R forces (b, a) ∈ R; and transitive if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R force (a, c) ∈ R. R is an equivalence relation only when it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive together. A single missing required pair is enough to break the corresponding property.

Application to this relation

Test each property of R = {(x, x), (y, y), (z, z), (x, y), (y, x), (y, z)} on P = {x, y, z}:

  1. Reflexive: (x, x), (y, y) and (z, z) are all present, so every element relates to itself. R is reflexive.

  2. Symmetric: (x, y) and (y, x) pair up, but (y, z) is present while its mirror (z, y) is missing. R is not symmetric.

  3. Transitive: (x, y) and (y, z) are present, yet the forced pair (x, z) is absent. R is not transitive.

  4. Equivalence: an equivalence relation needs all three properties; since R fails symmetry and transitivity, R is not an equivalence relation.

Selecting the incorrect statements

The question asks which statements are incorrect (false). Judging each by its content:

  • “R is not a reflexive relation” — false, because R is reflexive.

  • “R is not a symmetric relation” — true, because R indeed fails symmetry; this statement is correct, so it is not an answer.

  • “R is a transitive relation” — false, because R is not transitive.

  • “R is an equivalence relation” — false, because R is neither symmetric nor transitive.

Result: the three false (incorrect) statements are “R is not reflexive”, “R is a transitive relation” and “R is an equivalence relation”.

title: Let be the real line. Consider the following subsets of
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Let R be the real line. Consider the following subsets of the plane R×R:

S={(x,y) ∣ y=x+1 and 0<x<2},

T={(x,y) ∣ x−y is an integer}

Which of the following are true?

options.label: A
options.html: Neither S nor T is an equivalence relation on R

options.label: B
options.html: Both S and T are an equivalence relations on R

options.label: C
options.html: S is equivalence relation on R but T is not

options.label: D
options.html: T is equivalence relation on R but S is not

solution:
Answer: T is an equivalence relation on R but S is not.

  • S: S = {(x,y) | y = x+1 and 0 < x < 2}. S is not an equivalence relation. It is not reflexive because for any real number a the pair (a,a) would require a = a+1, which is impossible, so no (a,a) lies in S. S is not symmetric: if (x,y) is in S then y = x+1, but (y,x) would require x = y+1 = x+2, impossible. S is not transitive: if (x,y) and (y,z) are in S then z = x+2, so (x,z) does not satisfy z = x+1 and hence is not in S.

  • T: T = {(x,y) | x−y is an integer}. T is an equivalence relation because it satisfies the three properties:

    1. Reflexive: for every x, x−x = 0, and 0 is an integer, so (x,x) ∈ T.

    2. Symmetric: if x−y is an integer, then y−x = −(x−y) is also an integer, so (y,x) ∈ T.

    3. Transitive: if x−y and y−z are integers, their sum x−z is an integer, so (x,z) ∈ T.

  1. Reflexive: For any integer a, a - a = 0, and 0 is divisible by n. So (a,a) is in the relation for every a.

  2. Symmetric: If a - b is divisible by n, then b - a = -(a - b) is also divisible by n. Hence whenever (a,b) is in the relation, (b,a) is also in the relation.

  3. Transitive: If a - b = n·k1 and b - c = n·k2 for some integers k1,k2, then a - c = (a - b) + (b - c) = n·(k1 + k2), which is divisible by n. Thus whenever (a,b) and (b,c) are in the relation, (a,c) is also in the relation.

Therefore the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation.

title: Consider natural numbers and xRy iff divides x-y. Then which
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Consider natural numbers x and y, xRy iff 11 divides x-y. Then which of the following is false?
solution:
Solution: Show that the relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

  • Reflexive: For any natural number x, x - x = 0 and 11 divides 0, so xRx holds for every x.

  • Symmetric: If 11 divides x - y, then 11 divides y - x because y - x = -(x - y), and divisibility by 11 is unaffected by changing sign.

  • Transitive: If 11 divides x - y and 11 divides y - z, then x - z = (x - y) + (y - z) is a sum of multiples of 11, so it is a multiple of 11; hence xRz.

Conclusion: All three properties hold, so the statement that none of these is false is correct; none of the given properties is false.

title: For set having distinct elements, the number of symmetric as

bodyHtml: For a set having 14 distinct elements, the number of symmetric as well as reflexive relations will be _____________.
solution:
Key idea: For a relation to be both reflexive and symmetric on a set with 14 elements, all diagonal pairs must be included and each unordered distinct pair either appears as both ordered pairs or not at all.

  • Count diagonal (reflexive) pairs: all 14 pairs (a,a) are fixed, so no choice here.

  • Count unordered distinct pairs: number is C(14,2) = 14*13/2 = 91.

  • For each unordered pair {a,b} there are 2 choices: include both (a,b) and (b,a), or exclude both. So there are 2^{91} possibilities coming from these pairs.

Answer: 2^{91}. More generally, for an n-element set the number of relations that are both reflexive and symmetric is 2^{n(n-1)/2}.

title: Suppose set has elements. The number of elements in the
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Suppose a set has 8 elements. The number of elements in the smallest equivalence relation in this set is _______.
solution:
Answer: 8.

Reasoning:

  • Reflexivity requires that every element a of the set satisfies (a,a) in the relation. For a set with 8 elements, this forces at least 8 ordered pairs.

  • The relation that contains exactly those 8 pairs (the identity or equality relation) is reflexive, symmetric (trivially, since each pair is of the form (a,a)), and transitive (trivially), so it is an equivalence relation.

  • Therefore the smallest possible number of elements in an equivalence relation on an 8-element set is 8.

title: Suppose both have equivalence relations. The relation R1∩R2 is:
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Suppose R1 & R2 both have equivalence relations. The relation R1 ∩ R2 is:
solution:
Key idea: The intersection of relations inherits properties that both relations share. If both relations are equivalence relations, their intersection will be reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

  • Reflexive: For any element x, (x,x) belongs to both relations because each is reflexive, so (x,x) is in the intersection.

  • Symmetric: If (x,y) is in the intersection, then (x,y) is in both relations; since both relations are symmetric, (y,x) is in both relations and therefore in the intersection.

  • Transitive: If (x,y) and (y,z) are in the intersection, then they are in both relations; because both relations are transitive, (x,z) is in both and hence in the intersection.

Conclusion: The intersection is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation. Therefore the correct answer is: an equivalence relation.

title: Consider the given relations and on the power set of
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Consider the given relations R1 and R2 on the power set of P(A) of set A as:

R1: ∀a,b ∊ P(A) {(a,b) ∊ R ⇔ a በ b ≠ Φ}

R2: ∀a,b ∊ P(A) {(a,b) ∊ R ⇔ a ሀ b = a}

Which of the following is/are true:

options.label: A
options.html: R1 is Reflexive and Symmetric but not Transitive

options.label: B
options.html: R1 is Equivalence and R2 is Reflexive and Symmetric but not Transitive

options.label: C
options.html: R2 is Equivalence but R1 is Partial relation

options.label: D
options.html: R2 is Not Symmetric but Reflexive and Transitive

solution:
Correct classification and concise reasoning:

  • R1 (a ∩ b ≠ ∅): This relation is symmetric, not reflexive on the whole power set, and not transitive.

    Reasons:

    • Reflexive? No — counterexample: the empty set. ∅ ∩ ∅ = ∅, so (∅,∅) is not in the relation.

    • Symmetric? Yes — intersection is symmetric: if a ∩ b ≠ ∅ then b ∩ a ≠ ∅.

    • Transitive? No — counterexample: a = {1}, b = {1,2}, c = {2,3}. Here a ∩ b ≠ ∅ and b ∩ c ≠ ∅, but a ∩ c = ∅.

  • R2 (a ∪ b = a, equivalently b ⊆ a): This relation is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric, but not symmetric. Therefore it is a partial order on P(A).

    Reasons:

    • Reflexive? Yes — for any a, a ∪ a = a.

    • Symmetric? No — if b ⊆ a it does not generally follow that a ⊆ b. Example: a = {x,y}, b = {x}. Then a ∪ b = a so (a,b) is in the relation, but (b,a) is not.

    • Transitive? Yes — if b ⊆ a and c ⊆ b then c ⊆ a.

    • Antisymmetric? Yes — if b ⊆ a and a ⊆ b then a = b.

Conclusion: The nonempty-intersection relation is symmetric but neither reflexive (on P(A)) nor transitive. The relation a ∪ b = a (b ⊆ a) is reflexive, transitive and antisymmetric (a partial order) and therefore not an equivalence relation.

title: Consider the following relation on the set of positive integers
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Consider the following relation R on the set of positive integers Z:

R = {(a, b) ∈ Z x Z | a ≡ r (mod 7) and b ≡ r (mod 7)} i.e., aRb iff a and b yield the same remainder r when divided by 7. Then R is
solution:
Answer: The relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (an equivalence relation).

  • Reflexive: For any positive integer a, a ≡ a (mod 7), so (a,a) ∈ R.

  • Symmetric: If (a,b) ∈ R then a ≡ b (mod 7). Congruence modulo 7 is symmetric, so b ≡ a (mod 7), hence (b,a) ∈ R.

  • Transitive: If (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ R then a ≡ b (mod 7) and b ≡ c (mod 7). By transitivity of congruence, a ≡ c (mod 7), so (a,c) ∈ R.

Therefore R is an equivalence relation and partitions the positive integers into seven equivalence classes according to the remainder 0 through 6 when divided by 7.

title: Subset of poset is called an antichain, if every two
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: A subset of a poset is called an antichain, if every two elements of this subset are incomparable. How many antichains are there in the poset with the following Hasse diagram?
solution:
Correct count: There are 9 antichains.

Explanation:

  • Comparabilities found in the Hasse diagram: a < b, a < c, b < d, b < e, c < d. By transitivity we also have a < d and a < e.

  • Because a is comparable with every other element, any antichain that contains a can contain only a (no other element).

  • Among the four elements b, c, d, e the forbidden (comparable) pairs are b with d, b with e, and c with d. The allowed incomparable pairs are (b, c), (c, e), and (d, e).

  • No three-element antichain exists because any triple from {b, c, d, e} contains at least one forbidden pair.

  • Counting antichains: the empty set (1), the five singletons {a}, {b}, {c}, {d}, {e} (5), and the three two-element antichains {b, c}, {c, e}, {d, e} (3). Total = 1 + 5 + 3 = 9.

title: The hasse diagram of lattice is shown below. Which of
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: The hasse diagram of a lattice L = {x, a, b, c, d, e, y} is shown below. Which of the following subsets of ‘L’ are sub-lattices of L?
solution:
Definition: A subset S of a lattice L is a sublattice if for every pair of elements in S, their least upper bound (join) and greatest lower bound (meet) computed in the whole lattice L also lie in S. Equivalently, S must be closed under joins and meets (as computed in L).

  • {x, a, c, y}: This is a sublattice. For every pair of elements in this set the join and meet in L remain in the set. For example, the meet and join of a and c in L are x and y respectively, both contained in the set; similar checks hold for other pairs, so the set is closed under joins and meets.

  • {x, d, c, y}: This is not a sublattice. Counterexample: the greatest lower bound (meet) of d and c in the full lattice L is a, which is not in this subset. Because the subset fails to contain that meet, it is not closed under meets and therefore not a sublattice.

  • {x, a, e, y}: This is a sublattice. Key checks such as the meet and join of a and e in L give x and y respectively (both in the subset). All other pairs similarly have their joins and meets inside the subset, so it is closed under the lattice operations.

  • {x, a, b, y}: This is not a sublattice. Counterexample: the least upper bound (join) of a and b in the full lattice L is c, which is not in this subset. Inside the subset the least upper bound of a and b would be y, differing from the join in L. Since the join in L is not contained in the subset, the subset is not closed under joins and thus not a sublattice.

Conclusion: The subsets that are sublattices are {x, a, c, y} and {x, a, e, y}.

title: The function is mapped from natural numbers to integer numbers
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: The function f is mapped from natural numbers to integer numbers and f(x) = x2 - 3x + 3 then what is the function f?
solution:
Given f: N → Z defined by f(x) = x^2 - 3x + 3.

Show not injective:

  • Compute f(1) = 1^2 - 3·1 + 3 = 1 and f(2) = 2^2 - 3·2 + 3 = 1.

  • Two distinct inputs (1 and 2) give the same output, so the function is not injective.

Show not surjective:

  • Check whether 0 is in the image: solve x^2 - 3x + 3 = 0.

  • The discriminant is Δ = (-3)^2 - 4·1·3 = 9 - 12 = -3, which is negative, so there are no real solutions and hence no natural solutions for f(x) = 0.

  • Therefore 0 is not in the image of f, so f is not surjective onto Z.

Conclusion:

  • Since f is neither injective nor surjective, it is not bijective.

  • Therefore the correct choice is that none of the listed properties (injective, surjective, bijective) hold.

title: What is function in terms of relation?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: What is a function in terms of a relation?

options.label: A
options.html: A relation where every element of the domain is related to exactly one element of the codomain

options.label: B

options.label: D
options.html: A relation where some elements of the domain are not related to any element of the codomain

solution:
Definition: In terms of relations, a function is a special type of relation that assigns to every element of the domain exactly one element of the codomain.

  • Key requirement: each input (domain element) has one and only one output (codomain element).

  • Not a function if any input has zero outputs or more than one output.

  • Example of a function: the relation { (1,2), (2,3), (3,2) } where each domain element 1, 2, 3 maps to exactly one value.

  • Non-function examples: { (1,2), (1,3) } (input 1 maps to two outputs) and domain {1,2} with relation { (1,2) } (input 2 has no output).

Therefore, the correct definition is a relation where every domain element is related to exactly one codomain element.

title: Let f:X→Y be function, and be the subsets of Which

bodyHtml: Let f:X→Y be a function, A and B be the subsets of X. Which of the following conditions are true?I.If A⊆B then f(A)⊆f(B)II.fA∩fB⊆f(A∩B)
solution:
Answer: Only the first statement is true.

Proof that the first statement is true: If A ⊆ B and y ∈ f(A), then there exists x ∈ A with f(x) = y. Since A ⊆ B, that x is also in B, so y ∈ f(B). Therefore f(A) ⊆ f(B).

The second statement is false (counterexample):

  • Let X = {1, 2}, Y = {a}, and define f by f(1) = a, f(2) = a.

  • Take A = {1} and B = {2}. Then f(A) = {a} and f(B) = {a}, so f(A) ∩ f(B) = {a}.

  • But A ∩ B = ∅, so f(A ∩ B) = ∅. Hence f(A) ∩ f(B) is not contained in f(A ∩ B).

Related correct inclusion: In general we always have f(A ∩ B) ⊆ f(A) ∩ f(B), but the reverse inclusion need not hold.

title: Let be function from to and be function from to
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Let g be a function from B to C and f be a function from A to B. Which of the following properties of function composition is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.html: If f and g∘f are onto, then g is also onto.

options.label: B
options.html: If f and g∘f are both one-to-one, then g is also one-to-one.

options.label: C
options.html: If f and g are both onto, then g∘f is also onto.

options.label: D
options.html: If f and g are both one-to-one, then g∘f is also one-to-one.

solution:
Concept

For f : A → B and g : B → C, the composition g∘f : A → C is defined by (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)). Surjectivity is tracked by following preimages backward, while injectivity is tracked by pulling an equality backward through the functions.

For injectivity, the composition tests g only on the image f(A). Thus injectivity of g on all of B follows from injectivity of g∘f only when f(A) covers B.

Application

  1. If g∘f is onto, then for every c ∈ C there is an a ∈ A with g(f(a)) = c. Setting b = f(a) gives g(b) = c, so g covers C.

  2. If both f and g are onto, choose b ∈ B with g(b) = c and then a ∈ A with f(a) = b. Hence g(f(a)) = c, so the composition covers C.

  3. If both f and g are one-to-one and g(f(x₁)) = g(f(x₂)), injectivity of g gives f(x₁) = f(x₂), and injectivity of f gives x₁ = x₂.

  4. If only f and g∘f are one-to-one, g is constrained on f(A) but not necessarily on B \ f(A). Thus g can assign the same value to two distinct elements of B when at least one lies outside f(A), without the composition detecting that collision.

Cross-check

Take A = {1}, B = {1, 2}, and C = {0}. Define f(1) = 1 and g(1) = g(2) = 0.

  • The function f is one-to-one because its domain has one element.

  • The composition g∘f maps 1 to 0 and is also one-to-one.

  • The function g is not one-to-one because g(1) = g(2) although 1 ≠ 2.

Result

Therefore, the incorrect property is: if f and g∘f are both one-to-one, then g is also one-to-one.

title: The function is mapped from natural number to integer numbers
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: The function f is mapped from natural number to integer numbers and f(x) = x2 -2x + 3 . Consider N as a natural number and Z as Integer number , what is the function f : N -> Z ? 2, 4, 10, 28, 82, …
solution:
Answer: Injective (assuming the standard convention N = {1,2,...}).

Rewrite the function:

f(x) = x^2 - 2x + 3 = (x-1)^2 + 2

  • Proof of injectivity: Assume f(m) = f(n). Then (m-1)^2 = (n-1)^2, so |m-1| = |n-1|. This gives either m = n or m + n = 2. If natural numbers are taken as 1,2,..., the equation m + n = 2 forces m = n = 1, so in all cases m = n. Therefore f is one-to-one on N = {1,2,...}.

  • Failure of surjectivity: Since (x-1)^2 >= 0, we have f(x) >= 2 for every natural x (with N = {1,2,...}). Thus integers such as 0, 1 and all negative integers are not in the image of f, so f is not onto Z.

  • Edge case about the definition of N: If N is defined to include 0, then f is not injective because f(0) = 3 = f(2). Under that convention the function would fail to be injective.

Conclusion: Under the common convention N = {1,2,...}, f is injective but not surjective onto Z.

For surjectivity: Surjective: For any real y, choose x = (y - 1)/2 which is real. Then f(x) = 2((y-1)/2) + 1 = y, so every y has a preimage. Therefore f is a bijection.

f(x) = x² + 1 — Not injective: For example, f(1) = 1² + 1 = 2 and f(-1) = (-1)² + 1 = 2, so two different inputs give the same output. Hence it is not one-to-one.

Also note: the range of x² + 1 is [1, ∞), so values less than 1 have no preimage; therefore the function is not surjective. Combining these observations, f(x) = x² + 1 is not a bijection.

f(x) = x³ — Injective: If x1³ = x2³ then x1 = x2 (the cube function is strictly increasing), so it is one-to-one.

For surjectivity: Surjective: For any real y, x = ³√y is real and satisfies f(x) = (³√y)³ = y. Thus every real y has a preimage, so f is a bijection.

Conclusion: Exactly two of the given functions are bijections: 2x + 1 and x³.

title: Consider the mapping f:n→N, where is the set of natural

For n∈N, which of the following is true about f?
solution:
Answer: The function is neither injective nor surjective.

Definition: f(n) = n^2 for odd n, and f(n) = 2n+1 for even n.

  • Not injective: distinct inputs can give the same output. For example, f(3)=3^2=9 and f(4)=2·4+1=9.

  • Not surjective: every output is congruent to 1 modulo 4. If n is even (n=2k), then f(n)=2n+1=4k+1≡1 (mod 4). If n is odd (n=2k+1), then f(n)=(2k+1)^2=4k(k+1)+1≡1 (mod 4). Thus the image is a subset of numbers congruent to 1 mod 4, and numbers such as 2, 3, and 4 have no preimage.

Conclusion: Since the function fails to be one-to-one and fails to be onto, it is neither injective nor surjective.

bodyHtml:
Consider the mappings f1 and f2 defined as follows:

f1: ℝ → ℝ, where f1(x) = x2 + x for x ∈ ℝ.

f2: ℤ → ℤ, where f2(y) = 2y for y ∈ ℤ.

Here, ℝ is the set of real numbers and ℤ is the set of integers. Which statement is true?

options.label: A
options.html: f1 is neither injective nor surjective; f2 is injective but not surjective.

options.label: B
options.html: f1 is injective but not surjective; f2 is injective but not surjective.

options.label: C
options.html: Both f1 and f2 are injective as well as surjective.

options.label: D
options.html: f1 is not injective but is surjective; f2 is injective but not surjective.

solution:
Concept

A function is injective when distinct inputs never produce the same output. It is surjective onto its codomain when every codomain element has at least one preimage.

To test these properties, use a repeated-output counterexample for injectivity and characterize the range for surjectivity.

Application

  1. For f1, compare two distinct inputs: f1(0) = 0 and f1(−1) = (−1)2 + (−1) = 0. Hence f1 is not injective.

  2. Complete the square: f1(x) = x2 + x = (x + 1/2)2 − 1/4. Since a square is non-negative, the range of f1 is [−1/4, ∞), not all of ℝ. Hence f1 is not surjective onto ℝ.

  3. For f2, if f2(y1) = f2(y2), then 2y1 = 2y2, so y1 = y2. Hence f2 is injective.

  4. Every value of f2 is even. No odd integer, such as 1, equals 2y for an integer y. Hence f2 is not surjective onto ℤ.

Cross-check

The vertex of x2 + x is at x = −1/2 with minimum value −1/4, confirming the range found above; and f2(ℤ) = 2ℤ confirms that only even integers occur.

Therefore, f1 is neither injective nor surjective, whereas f2 is injective but not surjective.

The statements "A graph G is bipartite if and only has even cycle." and "The degree sum of odd degree vertices must be odd." are incorrect.

  • Statement: Some k-regular graph can be complete graph — True. A k-regular graph on n vertices is complete exactly when k = n − 1, because every vertex must be adjacent to all other n − 1 vertices. Example: the complete graph on 4 vertices (K4) is 3-regular.

  • Statement: In a simple connected graph with more than 2 vertices, it must have at least 2 vertices with same degree — True. For a connected simple graph with n > 2 vertices, possible degrees are 1,2,...,n−1 (only n−1 distinct values) while there are n vertices. By the pigeonhole principle, two vertices must share the same degree.

  • Statement: A graph G is bipartite if and only has even cycle — False. The correct characterization is: a graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd-length cycles. A bipartite graph need not contain any cycle at all (for example, any tree is bipartite), so requiring an even cycle is incorrect.

  • Statement: The degree sum of odd degree vertices must be odd — False. The handshaking lemma implies that the number of vertices with odd degree is even, so the sum of degrees of all odd-degree vertices is even. For example, two vertices of degree 1 have sum 2.

bodyHtml: Let G be a loop-free undirected graph with n vertices. If G has 56 edges and G^C (the complement of G) has 80 edges, then what is the value of n?
solution:
Number of edges in G plus the number of edges in G^C (the complement of G) equals n(n - 1)/2.

56 + 80 = n(n - 1)/2

136 = n(n - 1)/2

272 = n(n - 1)

n^2 - n - 272 = 0

Solve the quadratic: n = (1 + sqrt(1 + 4·272))/2 = (1 + sqrt(1089))/2 = (1 + 33)/2 = 17.

solution:
Key idea: If the two parts of a bipartite graph have sizes a and b with a + b = n, then the maximum possible number of edges is a × b (every vertex in one part connected to every vertex in the other).

Step 1: Express the edge count in one parameter:

  • Let one part have a vertices, so the other has n - a vertices. The number of edges is a × (n - a).

Step 2: Maximize the product a(n - a).

  • The product a(n - a) is a quadratic in a with maximum at a = n/2. Therefore the product is maximized when the two parts are as equal as possible.

Conclusion: For even n take a = n/2, giving maximum edges = (n/2) × (n/2) = n^2/4.

title: Let be complete bipartite graph given below. Which of the
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Let K2,2 be a complete bipartite graph given below, with parts {1, 2} and {3, 4} and edges 1-3, 1-4, 2-3 and 2-4. Which of the following is the total number of paths of length 3 from vertex 1 to vertex 4?
solution:
Concept

In graph theory a path is a walk in which no vertex is repeated; its length is its number of edges. A walk of length k allows vertices (and edges) to repeat, and the count of walks of length k between two vertices equals the [u][v] entry of the k-th power of the adjacency matrix. So "number of paths" and "number of walks" are different quantities, and a path of length 3 must visit 4 distinct vertices.

Setup

The complete bipartite graph K2,2 has parts V1 = {1, 2} and V2 = {3, 4}, with every left vertex joined to every right vertex. Its edges are 1-3, 1-4, 2-3 and 2-4. Because edges only go between the two parts, any path must alternate sides at every step.

Application

A path of length 3 from 1 to 4 uses 4 distinct vertices in the order 1, x, y, 4. Trace the alternation:

  1. From 1 the first step must cross to the right part: the neighbours of 1 are 3 and 4. It cannot be 4 (that is the destination and would leave only 2 edges, repeating vertex 4), so the second vertex is 3.

  2. From 3 the next step crosses back to the left part: neighbours of 3 are 1 and 2. Vertex 1 is already used, so the third vertex is 2.

  3. From 2 the last step crosses to the right part to reach 4: 2-4 is an edge, completing 1 → 3 → 2 → 4.

No other choice of distinct intermediate vertices works, so exactly one simple path of length 3 exists: 1 → 3 → 2 → 4. Hence the count is 1.

Cross-check

Counting walks instead (allowing repeats) gives four: 1→3→1→4, 1→3→2→4, 1→4→1→4 and 1→4→2→4 — this is the adjacency-matrix value A3[1][4] = 4. Three of these repeat a vertex, so they are walks, not paths. Removing them leaves the single simple path, confirming the answer is 1.

title: What is the maximum number of edges in bipartite graph

bodyHtml: What is the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph having 10 vertices?
solution:
To find the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph with 10 vertices, we need to consider the structure of a bipartite graph. A bipartite graph has two disjoint sets of vertices, and edges only exist between vertices of different sets.

The number of edges is maximized when the graph is complete bipartite, meaning every vertex in one set is connected to every vertex in the other set.

For 10 vertices, the maximum number of edges occurs when the two sets are as equal as possible. Splitting 10 vertices into two sets of 5 each gives the maximum number of edges.

The number of edges is then 5 × 5 = 25.

Thus, the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph with 10 vertices is 25.

title: Determine the numbers of undirected labeled simple graphs (connected and
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Determine the numbers of undirected labeled simple graphs (connected and disconnected) with n vertices.
solution:
Counting all labeled simple graphs on n vertices: A simple undirected graph on n labeled vertices is completely determined by choosing, for each of the C(n,2) possible unordered vertex pairs — C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 — whether that pair is an edge or not. Since these C(n,2) choices are made independently and each pair has exactly two outcomes (edge present or edge absent), the total number of distinct labeled simple graphs on n vertices is 2C(n,2).

  1. Count the number of unordered vertex pairs: C(n,2), which equals n(n-1)/2.

  2. Each of these C(n,2) possible edges can independently be present or absent — 2 choices per pair.

  3. Multiply the 2 independent choices across all C(n,2) pairs: total graphs = 2C(n,2).

Why no separate connected-only count is needed here: Every graph on these n vertices is either connected or disconnected — the two categories are exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so the connected graphs and the disconnected graphs together account for every possible graph. Since this question asks for the total across both categories, the count above already includes every disconnected graph and every connected graph; deriving how many of the 2C(n,2) graphs are connected is not needed to answer it.

  • n=2: C(n,2) = 1, so total graphs = 21 = 2 — the empty graph (disconnected) and the single-edge graph (connected); 1 + 1 = 2, matching the total.

  • n=3: C(n,2) = 3, so total graphs = 23 = 8 — enumerating: 1 empty graph and 3 graphs with exactly one edge are disconnected (4 total), while 3 graphs with exactly two edges (paths covering all 3 vertices) and 1 triangle with all three edges are connected (4 total); 4 + 4 = 8, matching the total.

title: Consider the following statements. There is no graph with VG=12
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Consider the following statements.

S1: There is no graph G with VG=12 and EG=28 in which each vertex is of degree either 3 or 4

S2: There is no graph G with VG=12 and EG=28 in which each vertex is of degree either 3 or 6
solution:
Let p be the number of vertices of degree 3. Thus, (12-p) are of degree 4.

By the handshaking lemma, the sum of degrees is twice the number of edges: 2 × 28 = 56.

So, 3p + 4(12-p) = 56.

Simplifying: 3p + 48 - 4p = 56 → -p = 8 → p = -8.

Since p cannot be negative, no such graph exists. Thus, S1 is true.

For S2, assume p vertices have degree 3 and (12-p) have degree 6.

Sum of degrees: 3p + 6(12-p) = 56.

Simplifying: 3p + 72 - 6p = 56 → -3p = -16 → p = 16/3.

Since p is not an integer, no such graph exists. Thus, S2 is true.

Therefore, both S1 and S2 are true.

title: What is maximum number of vertices in graph that has

bodyHtml: What is maximum number of vertices in a graph that has 35 edges and degree of each vertex is greater than or equal to 3?
solution:
Key idea: To maximize the number of vertices, make each vertex degree as small as allowed (each degree is at least 3).

By the handshaking lemma, the sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges, so the sum of degrees is 2E = 2·35 = 70.

If there are n vertices and each has degree at least 3, then the sum of degrees is at least 3n. Therefore 3n ≤ 70, which gives n ≤ 70/3 ≈ 23.33, so n ≤ 23.

We must check whether n = 23 is achievable.

  • Construct degrees so the sum equals 70 while every vertex has degree ≥ 3: take 22 vertices of degree 3 and 1 vertex of degree 4. The sum is 22·3 + 4 = 66 + 4 = 70.

  • Check feasibility in a simple graph: the vertex with degree 4 has degree ≤ n − 1 = 22, so this degree sequence does not violate simple-graph degree bounds.

Therefore the maximum possible number of vertices is 23.

title: What Conclusions may be drawn from the Handshaking theorem?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: What Conclusions may be drawn from the Handshaking theorem?

options.label: A
options.html: The Sum of degrees of all vertices is always even.

options.label: B
options.html: The Sum of degrees of all vertices with odd degree is always even.

options.label: C
options.html: The number of vertices with odd degree is always even

solution:
Handshaking Theorem (key fact): the sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of edges.

Reason:

  • Each edge contributes 1 to the degree of each of its two endpoints, so every edge contributes exactly 2 to the total degree sum. Therefore the total degree sum is 2 × (number of edges), which is even.

  • Consequently, the sum of degrees of all vertices is always even.

  • Because the sum of all degrees is even and the sum of degrees of even-degree vertices is even, the sum of degrees of odd-degree vertices must also be even.

  • From parity: the sum of k odd numbers is odd when k is odd and even when k is even. Since the sum of all odd-degree vertices is even, there must be an even number of odd-degree vertices.

Summary:

  • The sum of degrees of all vertices is always even.

  • The sum of degrees of vertices with odd degree is even.

  • The number of vertices with odd degree is even.

title: For which of the following, Euler Circuit is never possible
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: For which of the following, Euler Circuit is never possible if number of vertices is greater than 2
solution:
Euler circuit condition: A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree.

  • Complete graph K_n: Each vertex has degree n-1. If n is odd then n-1 is even and K_n has an Euler circuit; if n is even then n-1 is odd and K_n does not. So K_n can admit an Euler circuit for some values of n.

  • Cycle graph C_n: Every vertex has degree 2 (even). For n ≥ 3 the cycle is connected, so C_n always has an Euler circuit.

  • n-dimensional cube Q_n: Each vertex has degree n. If n is even then all vertices have even degree and Q_n has an Euler circuit; if n is odd then all vertices have odd degree and Q_n does not. Thus Q_n sometimes admits an Euler circuit.

  • Wheel graph W_n: The hub (central) vertex has degree n-1 and each rim vertex has degree 3. For the standard wheel graphs with n ≥ 4 the rim vertices have degree 3 (odd), so not all vertices are even degree and an Euler circuit is impossible. Therefore wheel graphs do not admit an Euler circuit for the usual range of n (so they are the correct choice for the graph that never has an Euler circuit in the standard definitions).

Conclusion: Among the listed graphs, the wheel graph never admits an Euler circuit under the standard definition (because rim vertices have odd degree), so the wheel graph is the correct answer.

title: Find the number of strong components of the following graph?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Find the number of strong components of the following graph?
solution:
Answer: 2 strongly connected components.

The two strongly connected components are:

  • {A, B, C}: A, B and C form a cycle because there are directed edges from A to B, from B to C, and from C back to A. Therefore each of these nodes can reach every other node in this set.

  • {D, E, F, G, H}: These five nodes form a directed cycle: there are edges D → E, E → F, F → H, H → G and G → D (together with the diagonals E → G and E → H that provide extra connectivity). Because there is a directed path between every pair of nodes in this set, they are strongly connected.

Note: There are downward edges from the top component to the middle/bottom component (for example A → D), but no directed paths back from the lower component to any of A, B or C. That prevents the two sets from merging into a single strongly connected component.

title: Maximum number of edges in simple graph with vertices and
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Maximum number of edges in a simple graph with ‘n’ vertices and ‘k’ components is:
solution:
Concept: For a fixed number of vertices split between two component-sizes a and b (a + b constant), the total edge count C(a,2) + C(b,2) is maximized when a and b are as unequal as possible — because C(x,2) grows quadratically, concentrating vertices into one large component always beats spreading them out. So to maximize edges across exactly k components on n vertices, make one component as large as possible and connect it completely, while every other component is reduced to a single isolated vertex (0 edges).

  1. Let the large component have m vertices; the other k − 1 components share the remaining n − m vertices.

  2. To add zero extra edges from the other k − 1 components, each of them must be a single isolated vertex, so n − m = k − 1, giving m = n − k + 1.

  3. Make the large component a complete graph on m = n − k + 1 vertices; a complete graph on m vertices has m(m − 1)/2 edges.

  4. Substituting m = n − k + 1: edges = (n − k + 1)(n − k + 1 − 1)/2 = (n − k)(n − k + 1)/2.

Cross-check: take n = 5, k = 2. The formula gives (5 − 2)(5 − 2 + 1)/2 = 3 × 4/2 = 6. Directly: a complete graph on 4 vertices (K4) has 4×3/2 = 6 edges plus one isolated vertex, total 6 — and no other 2-component split of 5 vertices beats this (a 3+2 split gives only C(3,2) + C(2,2) = 3 + 1 = 4 edges), confirming the "as unequal as possible" principle.

So the maximum-edge count for n vertices in k components is (n − k)(n − k + 1)/2 — the expression matching this value among the options is correct.

title: Which of the following statements for simple graph is correct?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Which of the following statements for a simple graph is correct?

options.label: C
options.html: Every trail is a path as well as every path is a trail

solution:
Concept

A walk is any sequence of vertices and edges connecting them, where both vertices and edges may repeat. A trail is a walk in which no edge repeats. A path is a walk in which no vertex repeats. In a simple graph, at most one edge joins any pair of vertices, so an edge is uniquely identified by its two endpoint vertices; reusing an edge would force at least one of those two vertices to be revisited. Consequently, a walk that never revisits a vertex can never reuse an edge either, which makes the path condition strictly stronger than the trail condition.

Application

  1. A walk satisfying the path condition has every vertex distinct.

  2. In a simple graph an edge is determined uniquely by its two endpoint vertices, so reusing an edge in the walk would require revisiting at least one endpoint vertex.

  3. Since the path condition rules out revisiting any vertex, it also rules out reusing any edge, so every path automatically satisfies the trail condition.

Cross-check

Testing the reverse direction with a triangle graph on vertices A, B, C: the closed walk A-B-C-A uses the three distinct edges AB, BC, CA, so it satisfies the trail condition, yet it revisits vertex A, so it fails the path condition. This confirms the implication holds only in the path-to-trail direction, not the reverse.

Contrast

  • "Every trail is a path": the triangle trail A-B-C-A above satisfies the trail condition while revisiting vertex A, so this direction does not hold.

  • "Every trail is a path as well as every path is a trail": this needs both directions to hold, but the trail-to-path direction fails as shown above, so the two conditions are not equivalent.

  • "Path and trail have no relation": the path condition (distinct vertices) has just been shown to force the trail condition (distinct edges), so the two are related by containment rather than being unconnected.

The vertex-distinctness of a path always forces edge-distinctness in a simple graph, so every path is a trail, while the converse fails: the correct statement is Every path is a trail.

title: Consider the following graphs: The number of graphs which are
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Consider the following graphs:

The number of graphs which are Euler ____.
solution:
Fact: A graph has an Euler circuit exactly when it is connected and every vertex has even degree.

  • G1: G1 is connected. Each vertex has degree 4 because each adjacent pair of vertices is joined by two edges (one straight and one curved), so every vertex has even degree. Therefore G1 has an Euler circuit.

  • G2: Compared to G1, G2 has an extra diagonal joining two opposite vertices. Those two vertices now have degree 5 (odd), while the other two vertices remain degree 4 (even). A graph with exactly two odd-degree vertices has an Euler trail (a path using every edge once) but does not have an Euler circuit. Hence G2 is not Eulerian in the sense of having an Euler circuit.

  • G3: G3 is not connected (there is at least one vertex not reachable from the others), so it fails the connectivity condition and cannot have an Euler circuit.

Conclusion: Exactly 1 of the given graphs has an Euler circuit (only G1).

title: The length of Hamiltonian Path in connected graph of vertices
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: The length of Hamiltonian Path in a connected graph of n vertices is
solution:
Concept: A Hamiltonian Path in a graph visits every vertex exactly once, without revisiting any vertex and without needing to return to its starting vertex. For any such path linking n vertices in sequence, the number of edges is n-1 — the same principle by which a spanning tree on n vertices always has exactly n-1 edges, since each edge joins one consecutive pair of vertices and a sequence of n items has exactly n-1 consecutive pairs.

Application:

  1. Represent the Hamiltonian Path as an ordered sequence of vertices v1, v2, …, vn, since it visits each of the n vertices exactly once.

  2. Each edge of the path joins one consecutive pair in this sequence: (v1,v2), (v2,v3), …, (vn-1,vn).

  3. Count the consecutive pairs in a sequence of n vertices: there are exactly n-1 such pairs.

  4. Each pair contributes exactly one edge, so the path contains exactly n-1 edges in total.

Cross-check: For n = 3 vertices joined as A-B-C, the Hamiltonian Path has edges AB and BC — 2 edges, matching n-1 = 3-1 = 2. Contrast this with a Hamiltonian Cycle on the same n vertices: a cycle adds one further edge that returns from the last vertex back to the first, closing the sequence into a loop. That extra closing edge is exactly why a Hamiltonian Cycle has n edges — one more than a Hamiltonian Path on the same n vertices.

Therefore, the length of a Hamiltonian Path in a connected graph of n vertices is n-1.

title: Graph with number of vertices greater and equal than three
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
A graph G with number of vertices greater and equal than three i.e. (n≥3) is a Hamiltonian graph,
if the degree of each vertex is greater and equal to ....
solution:
Correct criterion: For a simple graph with n ≥ 3 vertices, if every vertex has degree at least n/2, then the graph is Hamiltonian (Dirac's theorem).

Proof sketch:

  • Assume every vertex has degree ≥ n/2. Let C be a longest cycle in the graph.

  • If C contains all vertices, it is a Hamiltonian cycle and we are done. Otherwise pick a vertex x not on C.

  • Vertex x has at least n/2 neighbors on C. These neighbors divide C into many segments, so two neighbors of x on C are not consecutive along C. By connecting x into C between such nonconsecutive neighbors, one can form a longer cycle that includes x, contradicting the maximality of C.

  • This contradiction implies C must include all vertices; hence the graph is Hamiltonian.

Remarks: The condition is sufficient but not necessary. Also note the maximum possible degree in an n-vertex simple graph is n−1, so suggestions like degree equal to n or multiples of n are impossible.

title: Graph is non-planar if and only if it contains subgraph
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: A graph is non-planar if and only if it contains a subgraph homomorphic to
solution:
Answer: A graph is non-planar if and only if it contains a subgraph homeomorphic to K3,3 or K5.

Explanation (Kuratowski's theorem):

  • Kuratowski's theorem states that a finite graph is non-planar exactly when it contains a subdivision (a homeomorphic copy) of K5 or K3,3.

  • Homeomorphic (a subdivision) means you may replace edges by paths by inserting degree-2 vertices; the resulting graph preserves the same connectivity pattern as the original.

  • K5 is the complete graph on five vertices and K3,3 is the complete bipartite graph with partitions of size three; these two are the minimal forbidden subdivisions for planarity, so every non-planar graph contains a subdivision of one of them.

  • Other graphs mentioned in the choices (for example K2,3 or K6) are not the correct characterization: K2,3 is not one of the two Kuratowski obstructions, and K6, while non-planar, is not required as a subdivision in every non-planar graph.

Therefore the correct characterization is: a graph is non-planar iff it contains a subgraph homeomorphic to K3,3 or K5.

title: Consider finite connected planar graph with vertices with all of
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Consider a finite connected planar graph with n vertices with all of degree 4 and 10 regions. Find the number of vertices in the graph.
solution:
Answer: 8

Step 1: Euler's formula

For any connected planar graph, n - e + r = 2, where n is the number of vertices, e the number of edges, and r the number of regions (including the outer region).

Step 2: Given

  • The graph is connected and planar.

  • All vertices have degree 4.

  • The number of regions is r = 10.

Step 3: Relate vertices and edges

By the Handshaking Lemma, the sum of degrees equals 2e. Since every vertex has degree 4, 4n = 2e, so e = 2n.

Step 4: Solve for the number of vertices

Substitute e = 2n and r = 10 into Euler's formula:

  1. n - e + r = 2

  2. n - 2n + 10 = 2

  3. -n + 10 = 2 ⇒ -n = -8 ⇒ n = 8

Step 5: Verify

  • Edges: e = 2n = 16.

  • Check Euler: 8 - 16 + 10 = 2, which is correct.

title: Any graph is set of vertices and edges i.e., G=(v,e).
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Any graph G is a set of vertices and edges i.e., G=(v,e). Which of the following graphs are planar? (MCQ)

  1. K5

  2. G1=(12,18)

  3. G2=(25,56)
solution:
Planarity criterion: For any simple graph with v ≥ 3, a necessary condition for planarity is e ≤ 3v − 6. If this inequality is violated the graph is definitely non‑planar. If the inequality holds, the graph may be planar (the bound is necessary but not sufficient).

  • Complete graph on 5 vertices: v = 5, e = 10. Compute 3v − 6 = 3×5 − 6 = 9, and 10 ≤ 9 is false. Therefore this graph is non‑planar.

  • Graph with 12 vertices and 18 edges: v = 12, e = 18. Compute 3v − 6 = 3×12 − 6 = 30, and 18 ≤ 30 is true. The edge count passes the necessary bound, so this graph can be planar based on the given information.

  • Graph with 25 vertices and 56 edges: v = 25, e = 56. Compute 3v − 6 = 3×25 − 6 = 69, and 56 ≤ 69 is true. The edge count passes the necessary bound, so this graph can be planar based on the given information.

Conclusion: The two graphs with counts (12,18) and (25,56) meet the necessary inequality and therefore are the graphs that can be planar; the complete graph on 5 vertices is non‑planar.

r = (20 - 14 + 2) = 6 + 2 = 8

Therefore 8 = 1 + rclosed

Therefore rclosed = 7

title: Consider the following statements: There exists no simple, undirected and
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Consider the following statements:

P: There exists no simple, undirected and connected graph with 80 vertices and 77 edges.

Q: All vertices of Euler graph are of even degree.

R: Every simple, undirected, connected and acyclic graph with 50 vertices has at least two vertices of degree one.

S : There exits a bipartite graph with more than ten vertices which is 2-colorable.

What is the number of correct statements among the above statements.
solution:
Answer: 4 — all four statements are correct.

  • P is true. A connected simple graph with n vertices has at least n−1 edges, so for 80 vertices it needs at least 79 edges. Having only 77 edges cannot yield a connected graph.

  • Q is true. An Eulerian graph (one that has an Euler circuit) requires every vertex to have even degree; therefore all vertices of an Euler graph are of even degree.

  • R is true. A simple, connected, acyclic graph is a tree. Any tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves (vertices of degree one), so a tree on 50 vertices has at least two degree-one vertices.

  • S is true. Bipartite graphs are exactly the graphs that can be colored with two colors (2-colorable). There exist bipartite graphs with more than ten vertices (for example, a path with 11 vertices), so the statement holds.

Therefore the number of correct statements is 4.

title: An undirected graph contains nodes named ,...,vn. Two nodes vi
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: An undirected graph G (V, E) contains n (n > 2) nodes named v1 , v2 ,...,vn. Two nodes vi and vj are connected if and only if 0 <│i−j│≤2. Each edge (vi , vj ) is assigned a weight i+j. The cost of the minimum spanning tree of such a graph with 7 nodes is ______?
solution:
Answer: 43

Explanation: Construct the minimum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. For n = 7, edges exist between nodes that are one apart and two apart; each edge between vi and vj has weight i + j.

  • Edges between consecutive nodes vi and vi+1 have weights: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 (these are 2i+1 for i = 1..6).

  • Edges between nodes two apart vi and vi+2 have weights: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 (these are 2i+2 for i = 1..5).

Apply Kruskal: pick the smallest-weight edges that do not form a cycle until all 7 nodes are connected.

  1. Pick edge between v1 and v2 with weight 3.

  2. Pick edge between v1 and v3 with weight 4.

  3. Pick edge between v2 and v4 with weight 6 (connects v4).

  4. Pick edge between v3 and v5 with weight 8 (connects v5).

  5. Pick edge between v4 and v6 with weight 10 (connects v6).

  6. Pick edge between v5 and v7 with weight 12 (connects v7).

Total cost = 3 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 43.

title: Let be graph with vertices, with each vertex labelled by
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Let G be a graph with 5! vertices, with each vertex labelled by a distinct permutation of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4,5. There is an edge between vertices u and if and only if the label of u can be obtained by swapping two adjacent numbers in the label of . Let y denote the degree of a vertex in G, z denote the number of connected components in G, and p denote the number of edges in G. Then y + z + p= ________.
solution:
The graph G has vertices corresponding to all permutations of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The total number of vertices is 5! = 120.

Each vertex represents a permutation, and an edge exists between two vertices if one permutation can be obtained from the other by swapping two adjacent numbers.

Step 1: Find the degree y of a vertex.

For any permutation, the number of adjacent swaps possible is equal to the number of adjacent pairs in the sequence. In a sequence of 5 elements, there are 4 adjacent pairs: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,5).

Thus, each vertex has degree 4. So, y = 4.

Step 2: Find the number of connected components z.

Any permutation can be transformed into any other permutation by a sequence of adjacent swaps. This is a well-known result in permutation group theory: adjacent transpositions generate the symmetric group.

Therefore, the graph is connected, and there is only one connected component. So, z = 1.

Step 3: Find the number of edges p.

Use the handshaking lemma: the sum of the degrees of all vertices is equal to twice the number of edges.

Sum of degrees = number of vertices × degree of each vertex = 120 × 4 = 480.

So, 2p = 480, which gives p = 240.

Step 4: Compute y + z + p.

y + z + p = 4 + 1 + 240 = 245.

Therefore, the final answer is 245.

title: Let be simple undirected complete and weighted graph with vertex

title: Which of the following algebraic structure form group? The set
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Which of the following algebraic structure form a group?

A: The set of integers under Subtraction

B: The set of irrational numbers under multiplication

C: The set of real numbers under subtraction

D: The set of real number under multiplication

How many statements are true _________
solution:
The set of integers under subtraction

  • Closure: Subtraction of two integers is an integer. Satisfied.

  • Associativity: Subtraction is not associative; for example (1 − 2) − 3 = −4, whereas 1 − (2 − 3) = 2. Not satisfied.

  • Identity: 0 is a right identity because a − 0 = a, but 0 is not a two-sided identity (0 − a ≠ a in general). A group requires a two-sided identity. Not satisfied.

  • Inverse: Because associativity and a two-sided identity fail, the inverse axiom is not satisfied for a group.

  • Conclusion: This structure is not a group.

The set of irrational numbers under multiplication

  • Closure: The product of two irrational numbers need not be irrational. For example, √2 × √2 = 2, which is rational. Not satisfied.

  • Associativity: Multiplication is associative. Satisfied.

  • Identity: The multiplicative identity is 1, but 1 is not an irrational number. So the identity is not in the set. Not satisfied.

  • Inverse: Because the identity is not in the set, we cannot have the required inverses for a group. Not satisfied.

  • Conclusion: This structure is not a group.

The set of real numbers under subtraction

  • Closure: Subtraction of two real numbers is a real number. Satisfied.

  • Associativity: Subtraction is not associative, so the associativity axiom fails. Not satisfied.

  • Identity: 0 is a right identity (a − 0 = a) but not a two-sided identity (0 − a ≠ a in general). A group requires a two-sided identity. Not satisfied.

  • Inverse: Without a two-sided identity and associativity, the inverse axiom cannot hold for all elements. Not satisfied.

  • Conclusion: This structure is not a group.

The set of real numbers under multiplication

  • Closure: Product of two real numbers is real. Satisfied.

  • Associativity: Multiplication is associative. Satisfied.

  • Identity: The multiplicative identity 1 is in the set. Satisfied.

  • Inverse: Every nonzero real number has a multiplicative inverse, but 0 does not. Since 0 is in the set and lacks an inverse, the inverse axiom fails for the full set of real numbers.

  • Conclusion: The set of all real numbers under multiplication is not a group. (However, the set of nonzero real numbers under multiplication does form a group.)

Final answer

None of the given algebraic structures form a group. Thus, the number of true statements is: 0

title: Where a*b LCM (a,b). Then is
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60}. Define the operation a * b = LCM(a, b). Then (A, *) is a:
solution:
Step 1: Check for closure. The least common multiple (LCM) of any two elements in A is also an element of A. Since A contains all divisors of 60, the LCM of any two divisors of 60 is a divisor of 60; hence A is closed under the operation *.

Step 2: Associativity. LCM is associative: LCM(a, LCM(b, c)) = LCM(LCM(a, b), c). Therefore, * is associative.

Step 3: Identity element. An identity element e satisfies a * e = a for all a in A. For the LCM operation, e = 1 because LCM(a, 1) = a for all a in A. Thus, 1 is the identity element.

Step 4: Inverses. An inverse of an element a is an element b such that a * b = e = 1. The only element in A with such an inverse is 1 (since LCM(1, 1) = 1). For any a ≠ 1, there is no b in A with LCM(a, b) = 1, so other elements are not invertible.

Step 5: Conclusion. Since A is closed under *, the operation is associative, and A has an identity element 1, but not every element has an inverse, (A, *) is a monoid (a semigroup with an identity element).

title: Let and be two groups. The groups G⨁H is abelian

solution:
Claim: G ⊕ H is abelian if and only if G and H are abelian.

Proof. First suppose G and H are abelian. For any (g1,h1),(g2,h2) in G ⊕ H we have (g1,h1)(g2,h2) = (g1g2,h1h2). Since g1g2 = g2g1 in G and h1h2 = h2h1 in H, this equals (g2g1,h2h1) = (g2,h2)(g1,h1). Hence G ⊕ H is abelian.

Conversely, suppose G ⊕ H is abelian. Let e_H denote the identity in H. For any g1,g2 in G consider (g1,e_H) and (g2,e_H) in G ⊕ H. Their product equality gives (g1g2,e_H) = (g2g1,e_H), so g1g2 = g2g1. Thus G is abelian. The same argument with identities in G shows H is abelian.

Therefore G ⊕ H is abelian precisely when both G and H are abelian.

title: Which of the following options are true if is finite

bodyHtml: Which of the following options are true if G is a finite group of 54 elements?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.html: The size of the largest possible proper subgroup of G is 27.

options.label: D
options.html: The size of the smallest subgroup of G is 5.

solution:
By Lagrange's theorem: the order of any subgroup divides 54.

Therefore the possible orders of subgroups are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 27, 54. Orders 1 and 54 correspond to the trivial subgroup and the whole group.

Existence of a subgroup of order 27:

  • Let n3 be the number of Sylow 3-subgroups. By Sylow's theorems, n3 divides 2 (the factor of 2 in 54) and n3 ≡ 1 (mod 3).

  • The only integer dividing 2 and congruent to 1 modulo 3 is 1, so n3 = 1.

  • Hence there is a unique (and therefore normal) Sylow 3-subgroup of order 27, so a subgroup of order 27 does exist.

Conclusion: The largest possible proper subgroup of G has order 27, so the correct statement is that the size of the largest possible proper subgroup is 27.

Brief notes on the other statements:

  • A group of order 54 is not necessarily cyclic; cyclicity would require an element of order 54, which is not guaranteed.

  • The total number of subgroups depends on the group's structure. For example, a cyclic group of order 54 has one subgroup for each divisor (8 subgroups), so '16' is not generally true.

  • The smallest subgroup has order 1 (the trivial subgroup). Order 5 is impossible because 5 does not divide 54.

A proposition is a declarative statement that is either true or false. To determine if a sentence is a proposition, check if it is a statement (not a question, command, or expression with variables) and has a definite truth value.

  • Case: P is Knight and Q is Knave. Since Q is not a Knight, the conditional has a false antecedent and is therefore true. A Knight can truthfully state a true conditional, so this case is consistent.

  • Case: Both are Knights. Then Q is a Knight, so the antecedent is true, and the conditional requires that P is a Knave. That contradicts P being a Knight, so this case is impossible.

  • Case: P is Knave and Q is Knight. The antecedent is true and the consequent 'P is a Knave' is also true, so the conditional is true. But a Knave cannot utter a true statement, so this case is inconsistent.

  • Case: Both are Knaves. Q is not a Knight, so the antecedent is false and the conditional is true. A Knave cannot make a true statement, so this case is also inconsistent.

Conclusion: The only assignment consistent with the statement and the knight/knave rules is that P is a Knight and Q is a Knave.

title: Which of the following is correct? F1​:(p↔q)∧(¬p↔q) F2:(p∨q)∧(¬p∨q)∧(¬p∨¬q)

F2:(p∨q)∧(¬p∨q)∧(¬p∨¬q)
solution:
Answer: F1 is unsatisfiable; F2 is satisfiable (not valid).

F1: (p↔q) ∧ (¬p↔q) is unsatisfiable because p↔q forces q = p while ¬p↔q forces q = ¬p; together they imply p = ¬p, a contradiction.

  • p↔q means p and q have the same truth value.

  • ¬p↔q means q is the negation of p.

  • Combining them yields p = ¬p, which is impossible, so no assignment satisfies F1.

F2: (p∨q) ∧ (¬p∨q) ∧ (¬p∨¬q) is satisfiable. For example:

  • Take p = false, q = true.

  • Then p∨q = true, ¬p∨q = true, and ¬p∨¬q = true, so all clauses hold.

Conclusion: F1 is unsatisfiable; F2 is satisfiable. The correct statement is the one that reports these facts.

title: Which of the following are tautologies? (ii) (iii) (iv)
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Which of the following are tautologies?

(i) (p ∧ q) → p

(ii) p → (p ∨ q)

(iii) ¬p → (p → q)

(iv) (p ∧ (p → q)) → q

(v) ¬(p → q) → p
solution:
Let's break down each statement to determine if it's a tautology (always true):

(i) (p ∧ q) → p:This is true because if p and q are both true, then p is certainly true. If p and q are not both true, the implication is still true because the antecedent is false.

(ii) p → (p ∨ q):This is always true because if p is true, then p∨q is true regardless of q. If p is false, the implication is true regardless of q (as the antecedent is false).

(iii) ¬p → (p → q):This is true because if p is false, then p→q is true regardless of q. If p is true, the implication still holds.

(iv) (p ∧ (p → q)) → q:This is always true because if p is true, p→q means q must also be true. If p is false, the implication holds automatically.

(v) ¬(p → q) → p:This is true. If p→q is false (meaning p is true and q is false), the implication forces p to be true.

title: Which of the following argument is valid?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Which of the following arguments is valid?

options.label: A
options.html: {p → q, r → s, r ∨ p, ¬q} ⊢ p

options.label: B
options.html: {p → q, r → s, r ∨ p, ¬q} ⊢ q

options.label: D
options.html: {p → q, r → s, r ∨ p, ¬q} ⊢ s

solution:
Concept: An argument (a set of premises together with a conclusion) is valid when the conclusion is a necessary consequence of the premises under truth-preserving rules of inference. Three such rules are used here — Modus Ponens: from P → Q and P, infer Q. Modus Tollens: from P → Q and ¬Q, infer ¬P. Disjunctive Syllogism: from P ∨ Q and ¬P, infer Q.

  1. The premises are: (1) p → q, (2) r → s, (3) r ∨ p, (4) ¬q.

  2. Apply Modus Tollens to (1) and (4): p → q with ¬q gives ¬p.

  3. Apply Disjunctive Syllogism to (3) and the derived ¬p: r ∨ p with ¬p gives r.

  4. Apply Modus Ponens to (2) and the derived r: r → s with r gives s.

Cross-check (proof by contradiction): suppose the conclusion s were false, i.e. ¬s. Then from (2) r → s and ¬s, Modus Tollens gives ¬r. From (3) r ∨ p and ¬r, Disjunctive Syllogism gives p. From (1) p → q and p, Modus Ponens gives q — but premise (4) states ¬q, a direct contradiction. So ¬s is impossible together with the premises, confirming s must hold.

Since every step above follows by a valid rule of inference and an independent contradiction check confirms it, the premises necessarily and only establish the conclusion s — that is the valid argument among those offered.

title: Which of the following is/are correct for given sentence: “No

Which of the following is/are correct for given sentence:

“No student is allowed to carry laptop or mobile”
solution:
Formalization: No student is allowed to carry laptop or mobile can be written as ∀x(student(x) → ¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x))).

  • Equivalence to the conjunction form: apply De Morgan's law ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q to get ∀x(student(x) → ¬carry_laptop(x) ∧ ¬carry_mobile(x)).

  • Equivalence to the disjunction form: rewrite implication p → q as ¬p ∨ q to get ∀x(¬student(x) ∨ ¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x))).

  • Equivalence to the negated-existence form: use the identity ∀x φ ≡ ¬∃x ¬φ and simplify inside:

    Start: ∀x(student(x) → ¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x)))

    ≡ ¬∃x ¬(student(x) → ¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x)))

    Inside: ¬(student → ψ) ≡ student ∧ ¬ψ, so ¬∃x(student(x) ∧ ¬¬(carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x)))

    Double negation simplifies to give ¬∃x(student(x) ∧ (carry_laptop(x) ∨ carry_mobile(x))).

Conclusion: the three formulas above are equivalent and correctly express the sentence. The remaining formula ¬∃x(student(x) ∧ (carry_laptop(x) ∧ ¬carry_mobile(x))) is not equivalent because it only forbids students who carry a laptop and not a mobile, but it does not forbid a student who carries only a mobile. For example, a student carrying only a mobile would violate the original sentence but would satisfy that last formula.

Therefore the correct equivalent formalizations are the conjunction form, the negated-existence form, and the disjunction form given above.

title: Match the following Lists List-I List-II There are at most
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Match the following Lists       

                   List-I                                                                                      List-II
A. There are at most two apples.                               1. ∀x∀y∀z((Apple(x) Λ Apple(y) Λ Apple(z)) → (x =y V x=z V y = z))
B. There are exactly two apples.                                2. ∀x∀y((Apple(x) Λ Apple(y)) → (x = y V y = x))
C. There is at most one apple.                                    3. ∃x∃y(Apple(x) Λ Apple(y) Λ (x ≠ y) Λ ∀z(Apple(z) → ((z= x) V (z = y))))
D. There is exactly one apple.                                     4. ∃x(Apple(x) Λ (Apple(y) → (x = y)))

Codes:
        A    B   C   D
(a)    1     2    3   4
(b)    3     2    1   4
(c)    1     3    2   4
(d)    3     1    2   4
solution:
Let Apple(p) mean: p is an apple.

Interpretation of the formulas:

  • Formula 1: ∀x∀y∀z((Apple(x) ∧ Apple(y) ∧ Apple(z)) → (x = y ∨ x = z ∨ y = z)). This forbids three distinct apples, so there are at most two apples.

  • Formula 2: ∀x∀y((Apple(x) ∧ Apple(y)) → x = y). This forces any two apples to be identical, so there is at most one apple.

  • Formula 3: ∃x∃y(Apple(x) ∧ Apple(y) ∧ x ≠ y ∧ ∀z(Apple(z) → (z = x ∨ z = y))). This asserts there exist two distinct apples and every apple is one of them, so exactly two apples.

  • Formula 4: ∃x(Apple(x) ∧ (Apple(y) → x = y)). Read as intended with universal quantification over y: ∃x(Apple(x) ∧ ∀y(Apple(y) → x = y)). This asserts a unique apple, so exactly one apple.

Final matching and justification:

  • A (There are at most two apples) → Formula 1, because formula 1 rules out three distinct apples.

  • B (There are exactly two apples) → Formula 3, because formula 3 asserts two distinct apples and that no other apples exist.

  • C (There is at most one apple) → Formula 2, because formula 2 makes any two apples identical, allowing at most one.

  • D (There is exactly one apple) → Formula 4 (read with ∀y), because it asserts existence of an apple and that any apple must equal that one.

Therefore the correct code is: A → 1, B → 3, C → 2, D → 4 (the third choice).

title: Which of the above statements are valid?
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml: Which of the above statements are valid?
solution:
We interpret "valid" to mean that the implication is true in every structure with a non-empty domain.

We now analyse each of the four implications:

  1. ∀x ∃y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃y ∀x P(x,y): This implication is not valid. It can be true that for every element x there is some element y (possibly depending on x) with P(x,y), while there is no single element y that works for all x. For example, let the domain be {1, 2} and let P(x,y) mean "x = y". For each x we can choose y = x, so the premise "for every x there exists a y with P(x,y)" is true. However, there is no single element that is equal to both 1 and 2, so there is no y such that P(x,y) holds for all x, and the conclusion fails in this structure.

  2. ∃x ∀y P(x,y) ⇒ ∀y ∃x P(x,y): This implication is valid. If there is some element a such that P(a,y) holds for every y, then for each particular y we can simply choose that same element a as the witness. Thus, for every y there exists an x (namely, a) such that P(x,y) holds, so the conclusion is always true whenever the premise is true.

  3. ∀x ∀y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃x ∃y P(x,y): Assuming the domain is non-empty, this implication is valid. If P(x,y) holds for every pair (x,y), then in particular it holds for at least one concrete pair (a,b) from the domain. Therefore there exist x and y such that P(x,y), so the existential conclusion is guaranteed whenever the universal premise is true in a non-empty structure.

  4. ∀x ∃y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃x ∃y P(x,y): Again assuming a non-empty domain, this implication is valid. If for every x there exists at least one y with P(x,y), then we can choose one particular element a from the domain and a corresponding element b such that P(a,b) holds. These a and b serve as witnesses for the existential statement "there exist x and y such that P(x,y)".

Therefore, the implications that are valid in every structure with a non-empty domain are: ∃x ∀y P(x,y) ⇒ ∀y ∃x P(x,y), ∀x ∀y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃x ∃y P(x,y), and ∀x ∃y P(x,y) ⇒ ∃x ∃y P(x,y).

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q64
subject: Discrete Mathematics
bodyHtml:
Consider the following well-formed formula (WFF) of predicate logic:

∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) → (∃xP(x) → ∃xQ(x))

Which of the following statements about this WFF is correct?

options.label: B
options.html: Valid only if P(x) → Q(x) holds for every x in the domain

solution:
Concept

A predicate-logic formula is called valid — a logical validity, or a "tautology" of predicate logic — when it evaluates to true under every interpretation: every choice of a non-empty domain together with every assignment of meaning to the predicate symbols. One of the standard valid inference patterns is that from ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) and ∃xP(x), one can always derive ∃xQ(x), because the very element witnessing ∃xP(x) can be substituted into the universal conditional to also witness ∃xQ(x).

Application

  1. Take an arbitrary interpretation (any non-empty domain, with any meanings assigned to P and Q). If ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) is false in it, the whole formula is true automatically, since a false antecedent makes any implication true — so this case needs no further work.

  2. So assume ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) is true in this interpretation, and also assume the inner antecedent ∃xP(x) is true — pick a domain element a for which P(a) is true (existential instantiation).

  3. Apply ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)) to this specific a (universal instantiation): P(a) → Q(a) is true.

  4. Since P(a) is true and P(a) → Q(a) is true, modus ponens gives Q(a) is true.

  5. Because Q(a) is true for this element a, ∃xQ(x) is true (existential generalization).

  6. So whenever ∃xP(x) is true, ∃xQ(x) is also true — the inner implication ∃xP(x) → ∃xQ(x) holds, and hence the whole formula holds in this arbitrary interpretation.

Cross-check

Try to falsify the formula instead: a conditional A → B is false only when A is true and B is false. Here that would need ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) true while ∃xP(x)→∃xQ(x) is false, i.e. ∃xP(x) true and ∃xQ(x) false. But ∃xP(x) true gives some element a with P(a) true; combined with ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) being true, this forces Q(a) true, which means ∃xQ(x) is true — contradicting ∃xQ(x) false. No interpretation can falsify the formula, and this argument never used the size of the domain, confirming the result holds for finite and infinite domains alike.

Since the formula evaluates to true under every interpretation, it is always valid — a tautology of predicate logic.

title: Word "ROORKEE" is given to us. What is the probability
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
bodyHtml: A word "ROORKEE" is given to us. What is the probability that same letters will always be together on making the words from the letters of the word taken all at a time ?
solution:
Concept: For a word with repeated letters, the number of distinct arrangements of all its letters equals n! divided by the factorial of each letter's repetition count. To force certain letters to always stay together, bundle each such repeated group into one single unit, arrange the reduced set of units, and take probability as (favourable arrangements) / (total arrangements).

Application

  1. "ROORKEE" has 7 letters: R, O, O, R, K, E, E — R repeats 2 times, O repeats 2 times, E repeats 2 times, and K occurs once.

  2. Total distinct arrangements of all 7 letters = 7! / (2! × 2! × 2!) = 5040 / 8 = 630.

  3. For the favourable case, bundle each repeated pair as one block — (RR), (OO), (EE) — together with K, giving 4 distinct units to arrange.

  4. Arrange these 4 units: 4! = 24 favourable arrangements (no extra internal arranging is needed inside a block since its two letters are identical).

  5. Probability = favourable / total = 24 / 630.

  6. Simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by 6: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 630 ÷ 6 = 105, giving 4/105.

Cross-check: An independent recomputation confirms the total count differently — choosing positions for the repeated letters via combinations: C(7,2) ways to place R, C(5,2) ways to place O among the remaining slots, C(3,2) ways to place E among what is left, and the last slot for K, giving 21 × 10 × 3 × 1 = 630, matching the earlier total. The two fractions 24/630 and 4/105 are also numerically equal (both ≈ 0.0381), confirming the simplification is correct and no arrangement was double-counted, since dividing by 2!×2!×2! in step 2 already accounts for the identical letters inside each pair.

So the probability that the identical letters stay together is 24/630 = 4/105.

title: How many positive integers less than are such that the
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
bodyHtml: How many positive integers less than 10,000 are such that the product of their digits is 210?
solution:
Answer: 54.

Prime factorization: 210 = 2 × 3 × 5 × 7. Digits must be between 1 and 9 (zero is not allowed because it would make the product 0), and we may use the digit 1 to fill extra positions.

  • Four-digit numbers: The primes can be placed as four separate digits giving {2, 3, 5, 7}, or combine 2 and 3 into 6 and use a 1 giving {1, 6, 5, 7}. Any other grouping of the primes produces a factor greater than 9 (for example 2×5 = 10), so these are the only two multisets. Each multiset has four distinct digits, so each yields 4! = 24 permutations, for 24 + 24 = 48 four-digit numbers.

  • Three-digit numbers: The only way to get three digits is to combine two primes into one digit and leave the other prime as separate digits; the only valid digit from combining two primes that stays ≤ 9 is 2×3 = 6, giving {6, 5, 7}. These are three distinct digits, so there are 3! = 6 such numbers.

  • One- and two-digit numbers: Impossible, because 210 cannot be represented as the product of one digit (≤9) or two digits (each ≤9).

Total count: 48 (four-digit) + 6 (three-digit) = 54.

title: Hall has gates. In how many ways, can man enter
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
bodyHtml: A hall has 14 gates. In how many ways, can a man enter the hall through one gate and come out through a different gate?
solution:
Concept

When a task is carried out in stages performed one after another, the total number of ways is the product of the number of choices available at each stage — the fundamental counting principle. If both stages draw from the same pool of k distinct objects and the second stage may not repeat the object chosen at the first, then the first stage offers k choices and the second offers only k − 1, so the number of ordered pairs of distinct objects is k × (k − 1).

This count is exactly the number of ordered selections of 2 distinct objects out of k. Order is part of the arrangement, so a pair taken in one sequence is counted separately from the same pair taken in the opposite sequence.

Applying it here

  1. The pool here is the hall's 14 gates, and the man performs two ordered stages: he picks the gate he enters by, and then the gate he leaves by.

  2. Entry stage: any gate of the hall may be used, so there are 14 choices.

  3. Exit stage: the gate already used to enter is barred, so 13 of the 14 gates remain and there are 13 choices.

  4. By the counting principle the two stages multiply: 14 × 13 = 182 ways.

Cross-check

Count it the other way round as a check. Ignoring the restriction there are 14 × 14 = 196 ordered (entry gate, exit gate) pairs. Exactly 14 of these use the same gate twice, one for each gate, so the admissible count is 196 − 14 = 182, which matches the direct count.

In permutation notation the same figure is 14P2 = 14! / 12! = 14 × 13 = 182.
