solution:
Correct answer: independent

In operating systems, an independent process does not share data/state in a way that lets it affect another process or be affected by another process.

A process that can affect or be affected by another process is called a cooperating process. So the definition in the stem matches independent process.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q28
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: On a Unix system, if five people are currently using the vi editor, how many corresponding vi processes are running?
solution:
Concept

In Unix, a process is an executing instance of a program. Each independently started invocation has its own process identity and execution state.

Several processes may execute the same program code, but shared executable code does not merge those running instances into one process.

Application

  1. Each of the five people starts or uses an independent running instance of vi.

  2. Each running instance corresponds to one process, so the count is 5 × 1 = 5.

Cross-check

A process listing assigns a distinct process ID to each active vi invocation. Five active invocations therefore produce five vi process entries.

Result

The number of corresponding processes is 5.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q30
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: What is a program in execution called?
solution:
Concept

A program is a passive set of instructions stored on secondary storage. When the operating system loads it and begins execution, the active instance—with its own address space, program counter, registers, and resources—is a process.

One program can therefore create multiple processes, each with a distinct execution state.

Application

The stem asks for the name of a program while it is executing. That active instance is a process.

Contrast

  • Procedure: a reusable sequence of instructions that can be invoked within a program.

  • Instruction: one operation executed by a processor.

  • Function: a callable program unit, often with parameters and a return value.

Cross-check

If execution is paused, the operating system saves the active instance’s context in its process control block and later restores it. That runtime state belongs to a process, not to the passive program file.

Therefore, a program in execution is called a process.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q60
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: In an operating system, a process is:
solution:
Concept

An operating system distinguishes a passive program from an active execution context. A process is the dynamic context created while program instructions run; it carries current CPU state, memory references, and allocated resources.

Application

A program in execution has exactly this active context: the operating system tracks its program counter, registers, scheduling state, and resources while the instructions are being carried out.

Contrast

  • A program written in a high-level language is source code that may later be translated or interpreted.

  • The contents of main memory are a collection of stored instructions and data, potentially belonging to several execution contexts.

  • A job in secondary memory is submitted work awaiting admission or loading and does not yet carry an active CPU context.

Cross-check

The same program can be launched more than once, producing separate contexts with different program counters and resource states. This confirms that the dynamic entity, rather than the passive code alone, is the process.

Therefore, a process is a program in execution.

title: What is the full form of the PCB that is

solution: PCB stands for Process Control Block. It is a data structure in the operating system kernel containing information about a specific process.

title: Which of the following statements are TRUE about Process Control
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Which of the following statements are TRUE about Process Control Block (PCB) ?
(A) The PCB contains information about the process state, such as whether it is running, waiting or terminated
(B) The PCB includes the program code and data segments of the process
(C) The PCB stores the process's memory management information, such as page tables and segment tables
(D) The PCB is used to track process scheduling information and CPU registers for process execution
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
solution:
Answer: The correct statements are the ones that say the PCB contains information about the process state, stores memory-management information (such as page tables or segment tables), and is used to track scheduling information and CPU registers for process execution. The statement that the PCB includes the program code and data segments is not correct.

Why the incorrect statement is false:

  • The PCB does not contain the process's actual program code or data segments; those reside in the process address space in memory or on disk. The PCB may hold pointers or references to those regions but not the code/data themselves.

Typical contents of a PCB:

  • Process identifier and current process state (running, waiting, ready, terminated).

  • CPU registers and program counter values needed to resume execution.

  • Scheduling information (priority, pointers in scheduler queues, accounting data).

  • Memory-management information (base/limit or page table/segment table pointers).

  • I/O status and resource allocation information.

Summary:

  • True statements describe process state, memory-management information, and scheduling/CPU-register tracking.

  • The false statement incorrectly claims the PCB stores the program code and data segments themselves.

title: The Unix Operating System Kernel maintains two key data structures
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
The Unix Operating System Kernel maintains two key data structures related to processes, the process table and the user structure. Now, consider the following two statements :

I. The process table is resident all the time and contain information needed for all processes, even those that are not currently in memory.

II. The user structure is swapped or paged out when its associated process is not in memory, in order not to waste memory on information that is not needed.

Which of the following options is correct with reference to above statements ?
solution:
Answer: Both statements are correct.

  • Statement I — The process table is resident all the time: The kernel keeps a process-table (process table) in memory to maintain bookkeeping information (process state, scheduling information, pointers to address space, etc.) for every process. This table must be available even for processes that are not currently loaded into physical memory so the kernel can manage them.

  • Statement II — The user structure can be swapped or paged out: The user structure (often called the u-area in traditional Unix) holds per-process kernel-mode state such as the kernel stack and process-specific kernel data. To avoid wasting physical memory on processes that are not resident, this per-process data may be swapped or paged out when the process is not in memory.

Summary: The process table remains resident for system-wide process management, while the user structure can be moved out of memory when its process is swapped to conserve kernel memory.

title: When process raises an I/O request.
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: When a process raises an I/O request.
solution:
Answer: The process is placed in the device queue for the requested I/O device.

Key points:

  • Each I/O device typically maintains its own device queue to hold processes waiting for that device's operation to complete.

  • When a process issues an I/O request it transitions from running to a waiting (blocked) state and is placed in the appropriate device queue; it is removed from the CPU and is not in the ready queue while waiting.

  • When the I/O completes, the process is moved to the ready queue so it can be scheduled on the CPU.

  • This behavior is different from the job queue (used for newly admitted jobs) and the suspended queue (used for swapped-out processes).

title: In state process diagram processes are executing on running state
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: In the five-state process model, what happens to a running process when it issues a blocking I/O instruction during execution?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.html: The process will move to the ready state.

options.label: D
options.html: None of these; the question is wrong.

solution:
A process-state transition depends on the event that occurs while the process is running.

  • Blocking I/O request: the process moves from running to waiting/blocked because it cannot continue until the I/O event completes.

  • I/O completion: the process moves from waiting to ready and can compete for CPU time again.

  • Termination: the process moves to terminated only when it finishes execution or is explicitly ended.

Therefore, the correct answer is that the process moves to the waiting state.

title: Which of the following transitions is not possible between the
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which of the following transitions is not possible between the process states shown below?
solution: Based on standard process state models: Run → Terminated is valid (process ends). Run → Waiting is valid (blocking for I/O). Run → Ready is valid (preemption). However, a process in the Waiting state must transition to Ready before it can be scheduled to Run; direct transitions from Waiting to Running are not allowed. Thus, Waiting → Run is the impossible transition.

title: Which of the following is NOT process state?
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which of the following is NOT a process state?
solution: A process passes through standard states such as New, Ready, Running, Waiting/Blocked, and Terminated. Ready means waiting for CPU allocation, New means the process is being created, and Running means it is executing on the CPU. “Start” is not a standard process state, so it is the correct answer.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q164
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: A process in the "ready" state is
solution:
In the operating system's five-state process model, every process moves through the New, Ready, Running, Waiting (blocked), and Terminated states as it executes. A process enters the Ready state once it has been loaded into main memory and holds every resource it needs to run except the CPU itself; it then sits in the ready queue until the CPU scheduler dispatches it.

Since a process occupies exactly one of these five states at any instant, the stem's phrase "a process in the ready state" can be matched against the offered descriptions by checking which state each one names:

  1. A process that is holding the CPU and having its instructions carried out is in the Running state, not the Ready state, because a Ready process is waiting for the CPU rather than using it.

  2. A process that has issued an I/O request or is waiting on some event is in the Waiting (blocked) state, not the Ready state, because it cannot proceed until that event completes, regardless of CPU availability.

  3. A process that has completed execution (or been aborted) and had its resources released is in the Terminated state, not the Ready state, because a Ready process is still eligible for future execution.

  4. A process that has every resource it needs except the processor, sitting in the ready queue awaiting dispatch, matches the Ready state exactly.

This matches the scheduler's state-transition rule: the short-term scheduler moves a process from Ready to Running through a dispatch event, and only a process already in the Ready state can be dispatched next — confirming that "ready to run on CPU" is the description that defines the Ready state, distinct from Running, Waiting, and Terminated.

title: How many states can process be in
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: How many states can a process be in
solution: In operating systems, processes typically transition through five standard states: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, and Terminated. This 5-state model is the most comprehensive framework used in academic contexts to describe process lifecycle management.

title: Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE about Long term
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are false about the long-term scheduler?

P: It controls the degree of multiprogramming.

Q: It maintains a good mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes.
solution:
The CPU-scheduling hierarchy has three levels — long-term (job), medium-term, and short-term (CPU) schedulers — each acting at a different queue boundary. The long-term scheduler sits between the job pool (jobs waiting on disk) and the ready queue: it decides which new processes are admitted into main memory to compete for the CPU.

Because it gatekeeps admission, the long-term scheduler has two defining responsibilities: it fixes the degree of multiprogramming (the number of processes resident in memory at once), and it selects new jobs so that the resident set stays a balanced mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes — avoiding a memory full of only one type, which would leave either the CPU or the I/O devices under-used.

Checking statements P and Q against this role:

  • P — controlling the degree of multiprogramming is exactly the admission-control function described above, so P is true.

  • Q — deliberately balancing I/O-bound and CPU-bound admissions is exactly the mix-maintenance function described above, so Q is true.

Both defining responsibilities match, so neither P nor Q is false — a useful cross-check is to see why the near-miss combinations don't fit:

  • "Only P" would require Q to be false, but the balanced-mix objective is textbook long-term-scheduler behaviour, not an exception.

  • "Only Q" would require P to be false, but admission-rate control over multiprogramming is the scheduler's core job, not an exception. (This role is easy to confuse with the medium-term scheduler, which adjusts multiprogramming dynamically by swapping already-admitted processes out — but that doesn't make the long-term scheduler's own admission-based control untrue.)

  • "Both P and Q" would require both to be false, which contradicts both checks above.

Since both P and Q hold, the false-statement set is empty — the correct choice is the option stating neither P nor Q is false.

title: In multi-programmed systems, it is advantageous if some programs such
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
In multi-programmed systems, it is advantageous if some programs such as editors and compilers can be shared by several users. Which of the following must be true of multi-programmed systems in order that a single copy of a program can be shared by several users?

I. The program is a macro

II. The program is recursive

III. The program is reentrant
solution: In multi-programmed systems, sharing a single copy of a program among multiple users requires the code to be reentrant. A reentrant program can be interrupted and entered again without affecting its execution by another user, as it does not modify itself and uses local storage for variables. Macros are compile-time expansions unrelated to runtime sharing, while recursion risks stack conflicts when shared without proper isolation. Therefore, reentrancy (III) is the necessary condition for safe program sharing.

title: Consider the following statements: Short term scheduler selects which process
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Consider the following statements:

S1: The short-term scheduler selects which process moves from the ready state to the running state.

S2: The medium-term scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming.

Which of the following is true?

options.label: B
options.html: S1 is true and S2 is false

options.label: C
options.html: S1 is false and S2 is true

solution:
Concept

Operating-system schedulers make different kinds of process-selection decisions. The short-term scheduler chooses a ready process for the CPU, while the medium-term scheduler swaps processes between main memory and secondary storage.

The degree of multiprogramming is the number of processes resident in main memory. Swapping a process out lowers that number, and swapping it back in raises it; therefore medium-term scheduling can control this degree.

Application

  1. For S1, the short-term scheduler selects a process from the ready queue and dispatches it to the CPU, causing the ready-to-running transition. Hence S1 is true.

  2. For S2, the medium-term scheduler changes how many processes remain in memory by swapping processes out or back in. Hence S2 is true.

Cross-check and contrast

The long-term scheduler also controls the degree of multiprogramming through admission of new jobs. That does not make S2 false: S2 neither says “only” nor limits control to admission, and medium-term swapping independently changes the resident-process count.

  • “S1 is true and S2 is false” overlooks the direct effect of swapping on the number of resident processes.

  • “S1 is false and S2 is true” overlooks the short-term scheduler’s ready-queue dispatch role.

  • “None of the above” does not apply because the offered pair “Both S1 and S2 are true” matches the two scheduler mechanisms.

Therefore, both S1 and S2 are true.

title: On which of the following parameters, context switch is independent
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
On which of the following parameters, context switch is independent of?

(a) hardware support

(b) memory speed

(c) existence of special instructions

(d) process size

(e) number of registers to be copied
solution:
A context switch occurs when the CPU switches from one process to another, involving saving and loading process states. The time required for a context switch depends on the following:

Hardware support (a): Affects efficiency, as some systems have hardware features to speed up the switch.Memory speed (b): Impacts the time taken to save/load context data.Special instructions (c): May reduce the overhead if supported by the CPU.Process size (d): Independent of context switch, as only process state (registers, program counter, etc.) is saved, not the entire process memory.Number of registers to be copied (e): Directly impacts the time needed for context switching. Thus, context switching is independent of the process size (d).

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q41
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which module gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler?
solution:
CONCEPT

Process selection and execution transfer are separate operating-system functions. A short-term scheduler chooses a ready process according to policy, while a dispatch mechanism applies that choice through a context switch and execution-state restoration.

APPLICATION

Here, the process has already been selected by the short-term scheduler. The remaining work is to switch the processor context, enter the required mode, and resume the selected process from its saved instruction address. Those duties belong to the dispatcher. Therefore, the required module is the dispatcher.

CROSS-CHECK AND CONTRAST

  • Interrupt: a signal that redirects execution to an interrupt-service routine so an event can be handled.

  • Dispatcher: the component that performs the context switch, mode transition, and restoration of the execution point.

  • Scheduler: the decision-making component that chooses which ready process should run next.

  • None of the above: a residual-set claim, not the name of an operating-system component.

The two-stage check is therefore: the scheduler selects; the dispatcher carries out the handoff. This confirms Dispatcher as the result.

title: Process waiting time is given with the probability There are
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Process waiting time is given with the probability p. There are n processes in the memory then the CPU utilization is given by,
solution:
Solution: Derivation of CPU utilization when each process waits with probability p.

  • Step 1: The CPU is idle only if every one of the n processes is waiting simultaneously.

  • Step 2: Assuming the waiting status of each process is independent, the probability that all n processes are waiting is p^n.

  • Step 3: CPU utilization is the probability that the CPU is busy, i.e., at least one process is not waiting. That is the complement of all-waiting:

  • Therefore, CPU utilization = 1 - p^n.

Note: This result depends on the independence assumption for process waiting; if waiting events are correlated the formula changes.

solution:
In an operating system, the dispatcher is the module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler.

When switching from one process to another, the dispatcher needs to:

  1. Save the state (context) of the currently running process.

  2. Load the saved state (context) of the newly selected process.

  3. Jump to the proper location in the user program to restart that process.

The total time spent by the dispatcher in stopping one process and starting another running is explicitly defined as Dispatch Latency. Since this overhead occurs during every context switch, operating systems aim to keep this duration as low as possible.

title: Which of the following scheduling algorithms selects the process that
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which of the following scheduling algorithms selects the process that has been waiting the longest?
solution:
First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) is a non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm whose only selection rule is queue position: at every scheduling decision, the CPU is handed to whichever ready process has been sitting in the ready queue the longest -- that is, the process that entered the queue earliest among those still waiting -- regardless of its burst time, priority, or any other attribute.

Apply this to a concrete arrival sequence: P1 arrives at time 0 with burst time 99, P2 arrives at time 1 with burst time 1, and P3 arrives at time 2 with burst time 1.

  1. At time 0, P1 is the only process in the ready queue, so the scheduler dispatches P1.

  2. P2 and P3 arrive at t = 1 and t = 2, but must wait, because FCFS is non-preemptive and never interrupts a running process.

  3. When P1 finishes at t = 99, the scheduler looks at who has been waiting in the queue the longest -- P2, waiting since t = 1 -- and dispatches P2 next, then P3.

  4. The execution order is P1 -> P2 -> P3, decided purely by queue-entry (arrival) order -- even though P1 has the longest burst time, it is P1's arrival order, not its burst time, that gets it scheduled first.

Contrast this with the other listed algorithms, each of which uses a different selection rule:

  • Shortest Job First dispatches by the process's own predicted burst time -- the process needing the least CPU time next runs first -- so how long a process has already waited plays no role.

  • Round Robin cycles every ready process through a fixed time quantum in rotation; the next process to run is whichever is next in the rotation, not whichever has accumulated the most waiting time.

  • Priority Scheduling dispatches by an assigned priority level, so a process can be chosen purely because of its priority value even if other processes have waited far longer.

Only First-Come, First-Served defines its dispatch rule purely in terms of time already spent waiting in the ready queue, which is exactly the criterion the question describes.

solution:
Concept

A FIFO queue follows the first-in, first-out rule: an item is inserted at the rear and removed from the front.

In process scheduling, this means jobs are selected by arrival order; processor demand is not used to reorder them.

Application

The job that entered the ready queue first is at the front of the queue.

FIFO therefore dispatches that earliest-arriving job before jobs that arrived later.

Contrast

  • The last-arrived-first rule corresponds to LIFO or stack-style selection, not FIFO queue removal.

  • Selecting maximum processor need uses a resource-demand criterion rather than arrival order.

  • Selecting minimum processor need uses a resource-demand criterion rather than arrival order.

Cross-check

For arrivals J1, J2, and J3, the queue front is J1, so the dispatch order begins J1, then J2, then J3.

Therefore, FIFO first executes the job that came first in the queue.

solution:
Concept: for any CPU-scheduling policy, Waiting Time = Completion Time − Arrival Time − Burst Time. Non-preemptive Shortest Job First (SJF) selects, whenever the CPU becomes free, the process with the smallest burst time among those already arrived, and runs it to completion without interruption. Applied consistently at every such decision point, this greedy shortest-first rule produces the lowest average waiting time among the non-preemptive policies compared here for this particular batch of processes, as verified by direct computation below.

Application — deriving the non-preemptive SJF schedule:

  1. At time 0, only P1 has arrived, so it runs first: P1 occupies 0–6.

  2. At time 6, P2 (burst 4), P3 (burst 7), and P4 (burst 4) have all arrived; the smallest burst (4) is tied between P2 and P4, so the earlier-arriving one, P4 (arrival 2), runs next: P4 occupies 6–10.

  3. At time 10, P2 (burst 4), P3 (burst 7), and P5 (burst 2, arrived at 7) are available; P5 has the smallest burst, so it runs next: P5 occupies 10–12.

  4. At time 12, only P2 (burst 4) and P3 (burst 7) remain; P2 is shorter, so it runs next: P2 occupies 12–16.

  5. Finally P3 runs from 16 to 23.

  6. Waiting time = Completion − Arrival − Burst for each process: P1 = 0, P4 = 4, P5 = 3, P2 = 8, P3 = 13; sum = 28, average = 28/5 = 5.6 ms.

Policy

Average waiting time

7.6 ms

SJF (non-preemptive)

5.6 ms

Round Robin (quantum 6)

8.4 ms

The total CPU-busy time (6+4+7+4+2 = 23 ms) matches the last completion time under SJF (23), confirming no idle gaps were missed. solution:
Concept

In Non-Preemptive Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling, whenever the CPU is free it picks the ready process with the smallest CPU burst and runs it to completion without interruption. A process's waiting time is the total time it spends in the ready queue before it starts executing; for processes that all arrive at time 0, that equals the sum of the burst times of every process scheduled ahead of it. Average waiting time (AWT) is the mean of the individual waiting times.

Application

All four processes arrive at time 0, so SJF simply orders them by increasing burst time and runs them one after another:

  1. The 3 ms process runs first: it starts immediately, so its waiting time is 0.

  2. The 6 ms process runs next: it waited while the 3 ms process ran, so its waiting time is 3.

  3. The 7 ms process runs next: it waited for 3 + 6, so its waiting time is 9.

title: Let there be four processes whose CPU burst times are
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Let there be four processes P1, P2, P3, P4 whose CPU burst times are 6, 8, 7, 3 ms, respectively, and they arrive at time 0. Which of the following is the average waiting time and order of the process scheduling under the shortest-job-first scheduling?

options.label: A
options.html: Average Waiting time = 7.75 ms; Process order: P1, P4, P3, P2

options.label: B
options.html: Average Waiting time = 7 ms; Process order: P4, P1, P3, P2

options.label: D
options.html: Average Waiting time = 10.25 ms; Process order: P1, P2, P3, P4

solution:
In shortest-job-first (SJF) scheduling with non-preemptive execution, whenever every process is already available (arrives at time 0), the scheduler always picks the process with the smallest burst time next; because the order is decided just once at the start, the waiting time of each process equals the sum of the burst times of every process that runs before it, and the average waiting time is the mean of these four waiting times.

  1. The given burst times are P1 = 6 ms, P2 = 8 ms, P3 = 7 ms, P4 = 3 ms; sorting them in ascending order of burst time gives the execution sequence P4 (3 ms) -> P1 (6 ms) -> P3 (7 ms) -> P2 (8 ms).

  2. P4 runs first, so it waits 0 ms.

  3. P1 runs second, so it waits for P4's entire burst time: 3 ms.

  4. P3 runs third, so it waits for P4 and P1's combined burst time: 3 + 6 = 9 ms.

  5. P2 runs last, so it waits for P4, P1 and P3's combined burst time: 3 + 6 + 7 = 16 ms.

  6. The average waiting time is (0 + 3 + 9 + 16) / 4 = 28 / 4 = 7 ms, with the execution order P4, P1, P3, P2.

As an independent check, the sum of the four waiting times (28 ms) must equal the sum of each process's burst time multiplied by the number of processes still waiting behind it in the queue: (3 x 3) + (6 x 2) + (7 x 1) + (8 x 0) = 9 + 12 + 7 + 0 = 28 ms, which matches, confirming the average of 7 ms.

title: Which of the following best distinguishes Shortest Job First (SJF)
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which of the following best distinguishes Shortest Job First (SJF) from Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) scheduling?

options.label: A
options.html: SJF is non-preemptive, while SRTF supports preemption when a shorter process arrives.

options.label: B
options.html: SJF allows preemption, while SRTF does not.

options.label: C
options.html: SJF is used in real-time systems, whereas SRTF is used in batch systems.

options.label: D
options.html: Both SJF and SRTF operate identically in all CPU scheduling environments.

solution:
Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) are both CPU scheduling algorithms designed to minimize average waiting time by prioritizing processes with the shortest burst times. The fundamental distinction lies in how they handle process execution once started.

SJF is inherently non-preemptive, meaning that once a process begins executing on the CPU, it runs to completion without interruption. Even if a new process arrives with a shorter burst time, the currently running process continues until it finishes.

In contrast, SRTF is the preemptive version of SJF. It continuously monitors the ready queue and allows a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining burst time to preempt (interrupt) the currently running process. This ensures that the CPU is always working on the task expected to finish soonest.

title: The problem of indefinite blocking of low-priority processes is
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: The problem of indefinite blocking of low-priority processes is _____
solution: Starvation is the situation where a process is ready to execute but never gets the processor due to the continuous arrival of higher priority processes.

title: Which scheduling algorithm can cause starvation
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which CPU scheduling algorithm can cause starvation of low-priority processes?
solution:
Concept — starvation (indefinite blocking). A ready process is starved when the scheduling rule lets it be overtaken without any limit, so it may never reach the CPU. Whether a rule permits this turns on one test: is the set of processes that may be dispatched ahead of a waiting process closed at the moment that process joins the ready queue, or can later arrivals keep entering that set forever? A closed set means the wait is bounded; an open-ended set means starvation is possible.

Application. Priority Scheduling always dispatches the ready process holding the best priority value. A process carrying a low assigned priority is passed over by every higher-priority process that becomes ready, and fresh higher-priority processes may keep arriving, so the set ahead of it never closes and its waiting time has no upper bound. That is precisely starvation of low-priority processes, so the answer is Priority Scheduling.

Cross-check — apply the same test to all four dispatch rules.

Algorithm

Dispatch rule

Can later arrivals keep overtaking a waiting process?

First Come First Serve

Earliest arrival time

No — the queue ahead of a process is fixed the moment it arrives, so its wait is bounded.

Round Robin

Cyclic order, fixed quantum q

No — with n ready processes a process waits at most (n − 1)q before its next turn.

Priority Scheduling

Best assigned priority value

Yes — every later higher-priority arrival jumps ahead, with no upper bound on the wait.

Shortest Job First

Smallest predicted next CPU burst

Yes — every later shorter job jumps ahead, so a long job can be postponed.

Why not Shortest Job First? SJF does starve processes, but its victims are long CPU bursts, not low-priority ones — SJF attaches no priority attribute to a process at all. Standard texts do note that SJF can be modelled as priority scheduling with priority equal to the inverse of the predicted burst, which is why the two feel close; this stem, however, is anchored to an explicitly assigned low priority, and Priority Scheduling is itself offered, so the directly named mechanism is the intended answer.

Standard remedy. Aging — steadily improving the priority of a process the longer it has waited — puts an upper bound on the wait and removes starvation from a priority scheduler.

title: Consider the following preemptive priority scheduling algorithms based on dynamically
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Consider the following preemptive priority scheduling algorithms based on dynamically changing priorities. Large priority numbers imply higher priority. When the process is waiting for the CPU in ready queue, its priority changes at a rate 'α'; when it's running, its priority changes at a rate 'β'. All processes are given same priority, when they enter the ready queue. Which one of the CPU scheduling algorithm results from α > β > 0 ?
solution:
All processes start with the same priority. While waiting in the ready queue, their priority increases at rate α, and while executing, it increases at a slower rate β, with α > β > 0.

A running process therefore gains priority slowly, whereas waiting processes gain priority faster. Very soon, a waiting process attains a higher priority than the currently running one, causing preemption.

As a result, the CPU keeps switching between processes, and each process gets to run only for a short duration before being preempted. This creates a time-sharing type of system.

Hence, this behavior closely resembles Round Robin scheduling, where each process gets CPU for a small time and is then preempted.

title: Which of the following scheduling algorithms could result in starvation?
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which of the following scheduling algorithms could result in starvation?
solution:
Answer: Priority scheduling can cause starvation.

Starvation (indefinite blocking) occurs when a process waits forever because other processes are continually favored.

  • Why this happens: In priority scheduling, lower-priority processes can be repeatedly bypassed if higher-priority processes keep arriving, preventing them from ever running.

  • Example: A low-priority background job may never execute if the system continuously receives higher-priority interactive jobs.

  • Prevention: Apply aging, which gradually increases the priority of waiting processes so they eventually obtain CPU time.

Contrast with other algorithms: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) serves in arrival order so starvation does not occur, and Round Robin gives each process regular time slices, making starvation unlikely.

bodyHtml: Three processes P1, P2, and P3 arrive at time 0 with CPU burst times of 12 ms, 8 ms, and 3 ms respectively. Using the Round Robin scheduling algorithm with a time quantum of 5 ms, what is the total waiting time experienced by process P3 (the process with the 3 ms burst)?
solution:
Concept: Round Robin scheduling gives every process one time-quantum turn in cyclic queue order. A process's waiting time before its own first turn equals the sum of the quantum slices used by the processes ahead of it in the initial queue, and once its completion time is known, waiting time = turnaround time − burst time (turnaround = completion − arrival).

Application: Time quantum = 5 ms. Initial queue order: P1 (12 ms), P2 (8 ms), P3 (3 ms), all arriving at t = 0.

  1. t = 0 to 5 ms: P1 takes its first quantum, using 5 of its 12 ms; 7 ms remain and P1 rejoins the back of the queue.

  2. t = 5 to 10 ms: P2 takes its first quantum, using 5 of its 8 ms; 3 ms remain and P2 rejoins the back of the queue.

  3. t = 10 to 13 ms: P3 gets its turn. Its entire 3 ms burst fits inside one quantum, so it finishes completely at t = 13 ms.

  4. P3 needs no further turn: completion = 13 ms, arrival = 0, so turnaround = 13 ms, and waiting time = turnaround − burst = 13 − 3 = 10 ms.

Cross-check: By queue position alone, P3 is third in the initial queue, so before its own first turn it must wait out one full quantum from each of the two processes ahead of it — 5 ms + 5 ms = 10 ms — matching the turnaround-based calculation above.

title: What is the goal of round-robin CPU scheduling algorithm
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: What is the goal of a round-robin CPU scheduling algorithm ?

options.label: B
options.html: Minimize the average waiting time for all processes

solution:
Concept

CPU scheduling algorithms are each designed around a primary objective. Round-robin (RR) is a preemptive, time-sharing algorithm: every ready process is given a fixed time quantum in cyclic order, and a process that does not finish within its quantum is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. Its governing design goal is fair CPU sharing among all processes and good response time for interactive jobs.

Application

Because every process is served in turn for an equal slice, no process waits indefinitely and short interactive tasks get the CPU quickly, which keeps response time low. RR deliberately treats all processes uniformly rather than optimizing any single throughput or completion metric.

Contrast

  • Minimizing the average waiting time is the defining strength of Shortest Job First (SJF/SRTF), which is provably optimal for that metric; round-robin generally produces a higher average waiting time than SJF because of frequent preemption and context switches.

  • Prioritizing long-running processes or favouring I/O-bound versus CPU-bound jobs are properties of priority or specialized schedulers; round-robin gives every process the same quantum regardless of length or I/O behaviour.

  • Maximizing CPU utilization and throughput is a general scheduling concern, but RR can lower throughput because each context switch adds overhead; raw utilization/throughput is not RR's distinguishing goal.

Note

None of the four options above states round-robin's actual objective — fair time-sharing with a good response time. The option that sounds closest, minimizing the average waiting time, is in fact Shortest Job First's defining goal, not round-robin's.

title: What is the primary factor that affects the performance of
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: What is the primary factor that affects the performance of Round Robin scheduling?
solution:
In Round Robin (RR) CPU scheduling, the time quantum is the fixed amount of time a process is allowed to run before being preempted and placed back at the end of the ready queue.

Choosing the right time quantum size is a delicate balancing act that directly dictates the efficiency and responsiveness of the operating system:

  • If the Time Quantum is too large: The algorithm behaves exactly like First-Come, First-Served (FCFS). Processes with long CPU bursts will hold onto the processor for their entire duration, causing shorter, interactive processes to experience high waiting times.

  • If the Time Quantum is too small: The CPU will switch between tasks incredibly quickly. While this provides excellent responsiveness (giving the illusion that all programs are running simultaneously), it triggers a massive amount of context switches. Since saving and loading process states takes CPU cycles, a tiny time quantum forces the system to waste most of its processing power on scheduling overhead rather than actual user programs.

title: In round robin CPU scheduling as time quantum is increased
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: In round robin CPU scheduling as time quantum is increased the average turnaround time
solution: Increasing the time quantum reduces context switch overhead, which lowers turnaround time. However, it also increases waiting times for short processes arriving after long ones. Since the net effect depends on specific process burst times and arrival patterns, the average turnaround time varies irregularly rather than following a fixed trend.

title: Which of the following is true with respect to monitor?
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Which of the following is true with respect to monitor?

i. It ensures deadlock freedom

ii. Monitor is hardware synchronization mechanism
solution:
Answer: Both statements are false.

Explanation:

  • Statement i: "It ensures deadlock freedom" — False. Monitors enforce mutual exclusion within the monitor and provide condition variables for coordination, but they do not automatically prevent deadlocks. Deadlocks can occur when threads wait on conditions in the wrong order or when multiple monitors/locks are acquired inconsistently.

  • Statement ii: "Monitor is hardware synchronization mechanism" — False. A monitor is a software-level abstraction provided by languages or libraries (for example, synchronized blocks in Java or mutexes/condition variables in pthreads). Hardware synchronization primitives are low-level operations such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap.

Therefore, the correct choice is the option that states both statements are false.

solution:
Final answer: Minimum final count = 5, Maximum final count = 15, Sum = 20.

Reasoning:

  • Total attempted increments = 3 threads × 5 iterations = 15.

  • Maximum case: If every increment is serialized so no two increments overlap (no lost updates), all 15 increments take effect, so final count = 15.

  • Minimum case: Each increment is load; inc in a private register; store. In the worst interleaving, for each of the 5 loop iterations all three threads can perform the load before any store, so they all read the same memory value and after their stores only one effective increment occurs per iteration. That gives 1 effective increment × 5 iterations = 5.

  • Therefore minimum final count = 5, maximum final count = 15, and their sum = 20.

title: In order to avoid RACE condition the maximum no of
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: In order to avoid RACE condition the maximum no of process inside the critical section will be:
solution:
Correct answer: none of the above (the maximum number of processes allowed inside the critical section is 1).

Reason: To avoid race conditions, the critical section must satisfy mutual exclusion so that at most one process may execute it at any time.

  • Race condition occurs when multiple processes concurrently access or modify shared data and the final outcome depends on the timing of their execution.

  • To prevent this, mutual exclusion requires that no two processes be inside the critical section at the same time; therefore the maximum number is 1.

  • Why the given choices are incorrect:

  • "More than 2" — incorrect because allowing more than two processes permits concurrent access and can cause race conditions.

  • "2" — incorrect because two concurrent processes can still lead to race conditions; mutual exclusion requires only one.

  • "0" — incorrect because preventing all processes from entering the critical section is unnecessarily restrictive and not required to avoid races.

  • "none of the above" — correct because none of the other choices specify the required value of 1.

title: What is race condition in operating systems
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: What is a race condition in operating systems ?
solution: A race condition occurs when multiple processes or threads access shared data concurrently without proper synchronization mechanisms. This leads to unpredictable outcomes because the final result depends on the timing of process execution.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q106
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: What is the main disadvantage of Peterson’s solution for mutual exclusion?

options.label: B
options.html: It fails on modern multi-core CPUs due to memory reordering

solution:
A correct critical-section solution must satisfy three conditions: mutual exclusion, so no two processes execute in their critical sections at the same time; progress, so a process wanting to enter is not delayed indefinitely by processes not interested in entering; and bounded waiting, so there is a finite bound on how many times other processes enter before a waiting process is served. Peterson's algorithm achieves all three purely through ordinary shared variables — a turn variable and a per-process flag array — with no special hardware instructions, but its correctness proof rests on the memory-access model of the machine: it assumes reads and writes to shared variables complete in the exact order they appear in the program, a property known as sequential consistency.

Modern multi-core and multiprocessor systems do not guarantee that assumption by default. To improve performance, compilers reorder independent-looking instructions and CPUs use per-core caches, store buffers, and out-of-order execution, so a write one process makes to its flag or to turn may not become visible to another core in the same order it was issued, unless the program explicitly inserts a memory barrier or fence. Because Peterson's proof depends entirely on strict ordering of these reads and writes, running the unmodified algorithm on such hardware can let both processes enter the critical section at the same time, breaking mutual exclusion even though the algorithm's logic looks correct on paper.

Checking each remaining option against this reasoning:

  • It does not ensure progress — progress is a formally proven property of Peterson's algorithm under the classical, sequentially consistent model; the algorithm's construction, where each process yields via the flag and turn check, is specifically designed so a process not seeking entry never blocks another. This is not the property affected by moving to modern hardware.

  • It causes external fragmentation — external fragmentation is a memory-allocation phenomenon, the leftover unusable gaps between allocated blocks in contiguous or segmented memory schemes; Peterson's algorithm only reads and writes two small shared variables and has no relation to how memory blocks are allocated.

  • It requires high memory access time — memory access time is a hardware and memory-hierarchy property, governed by cache and RAM latency, independent of which synchronization algorithm a program uses; Peterson's algorithm does not impose any unusual memory-access cost.

Cross-checking against how real systems handle this: production synchronization primitives such as mutexes and spinlocks are built on hardware atomic instructions like test-and-set or compare-and-swap, combined with explicit memory fences, precisely because plain load and store based algorithms like Peterson's cannot be trusted to work correctly on modern multi-core CPUs without such support. This confirms that the main disadvantage lies in Peterson's incompatibility with modern multi-core hardware, not in progress, fragmentation, or memory-access time.

title: Message passing system allows processes to [Asked in Hexaware] This

solution:
Two classic IPC (Inter-Process Communication) models let processes coordinate: a shared-memory model, where processes map a common memory region and read/write it directly (needing explicit synchronization to avoid race conditions), and a message-passing model, where processes exchange information only through discrete send/receive messages routed by the OS, each keeping its own private address space.

The blank asks what a message-passing system specifically allows processes to do. By definition, message passing gives processes a way to communicate purely through message exchange, without ever sharing memory or address space -- that is exactly the capability being tested.

  • Resorting to shared data / sharing data directly describes the shared-memory model -- the alternate IPC technique, not message passing.

  • Naming the recipient or sender is only an addressing detail of how a message is routed (direct vs indirect addressing) -- not the core capability the blank is asking about.

So message passing systems allow processes to communicate with each other without sharing the same address space.

title: Which of the following algorithms is used to solve the
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which of the following algorithms is used to solve the critical section problem for n processes?
solution:
Concept

The critical-section problem requires a synchronization mechanism that guarantees three properties for processes sharing a resource: mutual exclusion (at most one process inside the critical section), progress (a waiting process eventually enters), and bounded waiting (no starvation). A general solution must hold for an arbitrary number of processes, n, not just two.

Applying it here

The Bakery algorithm (Lamport, 1974) gives a classic software solution that works for any number of processes n. Each process that wants to enter the critical section draws a numbered token, much like customers taking tickets at a bakery counter. The process holding the lowest token enters first; ties are broken deterministically by process id. Because every entrant gets a strictly ordered ticket, mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting all hold for n processes without special hardware.

Why the other choices fail

  • Peterson's algorithm: a correct critical-section solution, but defined only for exactly two processes; it does not generalise to n processes on its own.

  • Moore algorithm: there is no established critical-section technique by this name; it is more commonly associated with the Moore finite-state-machine model in sequential-circuit and automata theory, unrelated to process synchronization.

  • Banker's algorithm: a deadlock-avoidance method that decides whether a resource request keeps the system in a safe state; it does not provide mutual exclusion for a critical section.

title: Which of the following is true with respect to strict

options.label: C

solution:
Strict Alternation – Explanation

Strict alternation is a software-only mutual exclusion mechanism that forces two processes (P1, P2) to take turns while entering the critical section (CS).

✅ Guarantees

  • Mutual Exclusion is guaranteed
    Only one process can be in CS at a time.

❌ Does NOT Guarantee

  • Progress

  • Bounded Waiting (sometimes violated indirectly)

Why progress fails?

Because strict alternation forces a process to wait for its “turn”, even if the other process has no intention to enter CS.(Washroom Analogy – Perfect Explanation)

Two persons A and B share a washroom.

Rule:
A will go first, then B, then A, then B… (strict alternation)

This ensures only one person is inside → mutual exclusion is guaranteed ✔️.

But the progress problem appears:

Suppose it's A’s turn, but:

  • A does not want to use the washroom

  • B does want to use it

Still, B is blocked because the rule says “It’s A’s turn.”

So B must wait unnecessarily → progress is violated ❌.

This is exactly the same problem in process synchronization.

title: Consider the following solution of critical section for two processes:
subject: Operating System

Consider the following solution of critical section for two processes:
Boolean val[2] = {false,false};
int turn = 0;
void Pi(){
while(1){
val[i] = true;
turn = j;
while(val[j] && turn == j);
/// critical section////
val[i] = false;
}}
Here val and turn are shared variables between two processes P0 and P1, than which of the following is true about above solution ?

options.label: B
options.html: Satisfy process and bounded wait but not mutual exclusion

options.label: C
options.html: Satisfy mutual exclusion but not process both

options.label: D
options.html: Doesn’t satisfy any of mutual exclusion, process and bounded wait

solution:
while(val[j] && turn == j); condition checks whether the other process wants to enter and if the turn favors the other process; if so, the current process waits. Below is a clearer explanation of the properties satisfied.

  • Mutual exclusion: If both processes try to enter the critical section, both set their flags true. The last assignment to the shared turn variable gives priority to one process, making the other satisfy the while condition (val[j] && turn == j) and wait. Thus both cannot be in the critical section at the same time.

  • Progress: If a process wants to enter and the other does not, the waiting condition is false and it can enter immediately. If both want to enter, the turn variable breaks the tie so some process will enter. Therefore a waiting process is not prevented from entering by a process that is not interested in the critical section.

  • Bounded waiting: When a process is waiting, the other process can enter the critical section at most a bounded number of times before the waiting process gets the turn. For two processes this ensures no starvation and thus bounded waiting holds.

title: Consider the following codes: Assume and are two concurrent process
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Consider the following C code:

Assume p1 and p2 are two concurrent processes that share the global variables x, y and z. Assignment and condition checks are atomic functions. Which of the following is false about p1 and p2:
solution:
Conclusion: The statement "p2 terminates but p1 does not" is impossible.

Reason:

  • When p2 exits its loop it has set z to false by evaluating z = (x != y). That can only happen when x == y at that moment.

  • If x == y then p1's condition (x < y) is false, so p1 cannot still be inside its loop. Therefore p1 must have terminated as well.

Possible and impossible outcomes with short interleavings:

  • p1 terminates but p2 does not — possible. Example: p1 runs first and increments x to 1 (so x == y) and exits. Later p2 runs, increments y to 2 and sets z = true, so p2 can continue indefinitely.

  • p1 and p2 both terminate — possible. Example: p2 increments y to 2 but is paused before updating z; p1 then increments x until x == 2 and exits; when p2 resumes it computes z = (x != y) which is false, so p2 exits too.

  • p2 terminates but p1 does not — impossible, for the reason given above.

  • Both do not terminate — possible. Example: p2 keeps incrementing y faster than p1 increments x, so x never catches up and both loops continue forever.

title: Assume that is the mutex semaphore. Which of the following
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Assume that s is the mutex semaphore. Which of the following order of statements is/are deadlock or violation of mutual exclusion?(assume s=1)
solution:
Summary of which sequences are incorrect and why:

  • Signal(s); critical_section(); Wait(s);

    • Problem: Violation of mutual exclusion.

    • Reason: Signaling before entering increments the semaphore and allows entry into the critical section without an accompanying Wait (acquire). The critical section is not properly protected.

  • Wait(s); critical_section(); Signal(s);

    • Problem: None — this is the correct usage.

    • Reason: Waiting before entering ensures the semaphore is acquired, preserving mutual exclusion; signalling after leaving releases the mutex.

  • critical_section(); Signal(s);

    • Problem: Violation of mutual exclusion.

    • Reason: Entering the critical section without a Wait means the semaphore was never acquired; Signal afterward does not retroactively enforce mutual exclusion.

  • Wait(s); Wait(s); critical_section(); Signal(s); Signal(s)

    • Problem: Deadlock.

    • Reason: The first Wait decrements the mutex from 1 to 0; the second Wait blocks because the semaphore is 0. The process is blocked before it reaches its Signal calls, so it cannot release the semaphore and becomes deadlocked.

Final answer: The sequences that are incorrect (either violate mutual exclusion or cause deadlock) are: Signal(s); critical_section(); Wait(s);, critical_section(); Signal(s);, and Wait(s); Wait(s); critical_section(); Signal(s); Signal(s). The correct usage that preserves mutual exclusion without deadlock is Wait(s); critical_section(); Signal(s).

title: Consider the two process and given below uses the binary

consider the two process p1 and p2 given below uses the binary semaphores r=1, s=0, t=1 :

solution:
Final possible outputs:

  • 6,5,3,1,2,3

  • 6,5,1,2,3,3,1,2,3

Key facts:

  • Initial semaphore values: r = 1, s = 0, t = 1.

  • The first process must start (P(r) succeeds), so it prints 6 and 5 and then does V(s) before printing 3.

Why each output is possible:

  1. For 6,5,3,1,2,3: First process does P(r), prints 6,5, then V(s) (s becomes 1). If the first process continues, it prints 3 and does V(t). Then the second process does P(s), prints 1, does P(t) (t is available), and prints 2,3. This yields 6,5,3,1,2,3.

  2. For 6,5,1,2,3,3,1,2,3: First process does P(r), prints 6,5 and V(s). The second process then takes s, prints 1, does P(t) (consuming the initial t), prints 2,3 and does V(s). Meanwhile the first process was blocked after V(s) and later resumes to print 3 and V(t). The second process can then run again using the V(s) just produced and P(t) (after the V(t)), printing 1,2,3 again. This interleaving across iterations gives 6,5,1,2,3,3,1,2,3.

Why the other listed sequences are impossible:

  • Any sequence that starts with "1" (printing from the second process) before the first process has printed 6 and 5 is impossible because s is initially 0 and only the first process can do V(s) to allow the second process to proceed.

  • Any sequence that shows the second process printing "2" before printing "1" contradicts the code order (the second process prints 1 immediately after P(s)), so such sequences are impossible.

title: Bounded Buﬀer problem: There is set of buﬀers shared by
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Bounded Buﬀer problem: There is a set of buﬀers shared by producer and consumer processes. Producer inserts resources into the buﬀer, and consumer removes resources from the buﬀer. A producer goes to sleep if the buﬀer is full, and a consumer goes to sleep if the buﬀer is empty. Now, consider the following implementation:

Choose the appropriate answer

options.label: C
options.html: Cannot say, the implementation depends on the size of the buﬀer

solution:
Key issue: consumers can enter the critical section and try to remove a resource even when the buffer is empty because there is no semaphore tracking filled slots.

Why this fails:

  • The consumer only uses the mutex for mutual exclusion and does not wait for any indication that an item is available.

  • If a consumer runs when the buffer is empty it will attempt to remove an item from an empty slot (underflow) or otherwise behave incorrectly.

Correct fix:

  • Introduce a semaphore full initialized to 0 to count filled buffers.

  • Keep mutex for mutual exclusion and empty initialized to buffer size N for empty slots.

Initialization:

  • Semaphore mutex = 1

  • Semaphore empty = N

  • Semaphore full = 0

Corrected pseudocode:

  • Producer:

  • P(empty) // wait for an empty slot

  • P(mutex) // enter critical section

  • add resource to buffer

  • V(mutex) // leave critical section

  • V(full) // signal a filled slot

  • Consumer:

  • P(full) // wait for a filled slot

  • P(mutex) // enter critical section

  • remove resource from buffer

  • V(mutex) // leave critical section

  • V(empty) // signal an empty slot

Note: The existing solution text had a wording error saying the consumer should "wait until the buffer is empty". The correct requirement is that the consumer must wait until the buffer is not empty (i.e., until a filled slot exists).

title: Which of the classical IPC problems is not solved using
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which of the classical IPC problems is not solved using semaphore?
solution:
Answer: All of the listed problems can be solved using semaphores.

  • Producer–Consumer: Use a counting semaphore for empty slots (initialized to buffer size), a counting semaphore for filled slots (initialized to 0), and a mutex (binary semaphore) to protect buffer access. This ensures producers wait when the buffer is full and consumers wait when it is empty.

  • Sleeping Barber: Use a counting semaphore to track waiting customers (chairs), a semaphore to signal the barber's readiness, and a mutex for updating the waiting count. Customers block when chairs are available or leave if all chairs are occupied; the barber sleeps when there are no customers.

  • Dining Philosophers: Represent each fork with a binary semaphore and use a strategy to avoid deadlock (for example, a waiter semaphore that limits the number of philosophers who may pick forks, resource ordering, or letting one philosopher pick forks in reverse order). Semaphores model pickup and putdown actions.

Key point: Semaphores provide mutual exclusion and synchronization primitives that, when designed carefully to avoid deadlock and starvation, can be used to solve these classic IPC problems.

bodyHtml:
Let each process Pᵢ, i = 1 to 7 executes the following code.

repeat

P(mutex);

V(mutex);

forever

The process P₈ executes the following code:

repeat

V(mutex);

V(mutex);

forever

What is the maximum number of processes that can be present in the critical section at any point of time?
Given that the initial value of binary semaphore variable “mutex” is 1.
solution:
Concept: A semaphore only guarantees mutual exclusion when every process follows the same protocol: succeed at P(mutex) before entering, then execute the matching V(mutex) after leaving so a permit becomes available for someone else. “Present in the critical section” means a process has passed its own entry step and has not yet executed its own exit step — the CPU can be given to other processes in between, so several processes can be sitting inside the CS simultaneously as long as each one individually cleared its own entry.

Application: Trace one valid interleaving starting from mutex = 1, always letting a released waiter consume a signal before the next signal is issued:

  1. P₁ executes P(mutex): mutex is 1, so it succeeds and mutex becomes 0. P₁ enters the CS and is left paused there (it has not yet reached its own V(mutex)).

  2. P₈ executes V(mutex): mutex goes from 0 to 1. Since P₈'s code never calls P(mutex), it enters the CS unconditionally — P₁ and P₈ are now both inside together.

  3. With mutex back at 1, P₂'s waiting P(mutex) immediately succeeds (mutex: 1 → 0). P₂ enters and stays paused. (P₁, P₂, P₈ inside.)

  4. P₈ signals V(mutex) again to close this pass: mutex goes to 1, and P₃'s waiting P(mutex) immediately consumes it (mutex back to 0). P₃ enters and stays paused.

  5. Looping back, P₈ signals V(mutex) once more to open the next pass: mutex goes to 1, and P₄'s waiting P(mutex) immediately consumes it (mutex back to 0). P₄ enters and stays paused, and P₈ itself re-enters the CS for a second visit — P₁ through P₄ and P₈ (five processes) are now inside.

  6. Repeating this same signal-then-consume pattern twice more releases P₅ (after P₈'s next closing signal) and P₆ (after its next opening signal); each enters and stays paused exactly as before, while P₈ re-enters the CS for a third visit — P₁ through P₆ and P₈ (seven processes) are now inside.

  7. One more signal-then-consume releases P₇, who enters and stays paused. P₈ signals once again — with no waiters left, this final signal simply leaves mutex at 1 — and re-enters the CS for a fourth time.

  8. At this instant P₁ through P₇ (all seven ordinary processes) and P₈ are simultaneously present inside the CS — 8 processes in total. At every step, mutex never had to exceed 1: each of P₈'s signals was consumed by exactly one already-waiting process before the next signal was issued, so this works even under a strictly binary semaphore.

Cross-check: This count is also the maximum possible, because the scenario defines only eight processes in total — P₁ through P₇ running the ordinary code, plus P₈ — and a count of just 1 would only hold if mutex behaved as a correctly-paired binary lock, which it does not here, since P₈ signals without ever waiting.

title: Consider the following synchronization mechanism and choose the appropriate answer:
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: The image shows a synchronization mechanism intended for a uniprocessor. Which statement correctly describes how this mechanism behaves?

options.label: A
options.html: It works on single CPU machines because it disables context switches within the critical region.

options.label: B
options.html: It works on single CPU machines even when there are context switches within the critical region.

options.label: C
options.html: It does not work on single core CPU.

solution:
CONCEPT

On a uniprocessor, only one instruction stream executes at a time. Masking interrupts prevents timer- and interrupt-driven preemption, so the running thread keeps the CPU until interrupts are restored.

This technique can protect a short kernel critical section when the code does not voluntarily block or fault and the previous interrupt state is restored afterward. It does not by itself provide multiprocessor mutual exclusion because another CPU can continue executing.

APPLICATION

  1. Calling acquire masks interrupts on the only CPU before the critical section begins.

  2. While interrupts remain masked, the periodic timer cannot preempt the running thread, so an interrupt-driven context switch cannot place another runnable process on that CPU.

  3. The current thread therefore executes the critical section without another process entering it through preemptive scheduling.

  4. Calling release re-enables interrupts, after which ordinary preemption and context switching may resume.

CROSS-CHECK / CONTRAST

  • “It works on single CPU machines because it disables context switches within the critical region” matches the uniprocessor execution trace: masking interrupts removes the preemption route during that interval.

  • “It works on single CPU machines even when there are context switches within the critical region” assumes away the protection: if another process can be scheduled there, this code has no shared lock-state test to stop that process from entering.

  • “It does not work on single core CPU” conflicts with the mechanism’s intended setting; controlling interrupt-driven preemption on the sole CPU is precisely what makes this limited technique usable.

  • “None of these” does not apply because one concrete statement describes the traced behavior.

Therefore, the appropriate statement is: “It works on single CPU machines because it disables context switches within the critical region.”

title: Consider the following given programs and with execution time of
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Consider the following given programs P1, P2 and P3 with execution time of process x,y and z being 4ms, 3ms and 5ms respectively:

Assume s and t are locks initially in free state and preemptive priority scheduling algorithm is used. Then average turnaround time is ___________: (round off 2 decimal places)
solution:
Key idea: simulate preemptive priority scheduling, track lock acquisition and blocking, then compute completion times and turnaround times.

  • 0–4: Program 1 runs process x (4 ms).

  • 4–5: Program 1 acquires lock s and starts process z (first 1 ms of z).

  • 5: Program 2 arrives (higher priority) and preempts Program 1.

  • 5–9: Program 2 runs its process x (4 ms).

  • 9: Program 2 attempts to lock s but finds it held by Program 1, so Program 2 blocks.

  • 9–13: Program 1 resumes and completes remaining 4 ms of z, then unlocks s.

  • 13: Program 2 (waiting) acquires s and then t, starts its process z at 13.

  • 13–15: Program 2 runs 2 ms of z (of 5 ms).

  • 15: Program 3 arrives (highest priority) and preempts Program 2.

  • 15–19: Program 3 runs its process x (4 ms), then at 19 it tries to lock s but s is held by Program 2, so Program 3 blocks.

  • 19–22: Program 2 resumes and completes remaining 3 ms of z, then unlocks s and t at 22.

  • 22–27: Program 3 (waiting) acquires s and t, runs its z for 5 ms.

  • 27–30: Program 3 runs its process y (3 ms) and completes at time 30.

  • 30–33: Program 2 runs its process y (3 ms) and completes at time 33.

  • 33–36: Program 1 runs its process y (3 ms) and completes at time 36.

Turnaround times:

  • Program 1: completion 36 − arrival 0 = 36 ms

  • Program 2: completion 33 − arrival 5 = 28 ms

  • Program 3: completion 30 − arrival 15 = 15 ms

Average turnaround = (36 + 28 + 15) / 3 = 79 / 3 = 26.333... → 26.33 ms (rounded to 2 decimals).

title: Which makes more sense when it comes to critical section
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Which makes more sense when it comes to critical section problem?

1. “ Spin lock with single core cpu”

2. “Spin lock with multi core cpu”
solution:
Answer: Spin lock with multi core CPU is the better choice in typical cases.

Key idea: spin locks cause busy-waiting; whether that is acceptable depends on the CPU topology and expected wait time.

  • Single-core systems: Busy-waiting blocks the only runnable core. If a thread spins, it prevents the lock holder from running and releasing the lock, so progress stalls. Use blocking synchronization (mutexes or condition variables) instead.

  • Multi-core systems: Other cores can run the thread that will release the lock while one thread spins. For very short critical sections and low contention, spinning can be cheaper than the overhead of sleeping and waking threads.

  • Rule of thumb: Use spin locks only when the expected wait is very short (microseconds) and the overhead of blocking is higher than spinning. Otherwise prefer blocking locks.

title: Which of the below statements is/are false? Mutual statement is
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml:
Which of the below statements is/are false?

1. Mutual statement is guaranteed
2. Deadlock free algorithm
3. Progress is guaranteed
solution:
Assumption: occupied and blocked are initialized to 0, and wakeup unblocks exactly one waiting process. Under these usual assumptions, none of the three statements is false — mutual exclusion, deadlock freedom, and progress are all satisfied. Explanation:

  • Mutual exclusion: Only a process that finds occupied == 0 executes occupied = 1 and proceeds into the critical section. Any process that finds occupied == 1 increments blocked and sleeps. On exit, the exiting process sets occupied = 0 and wakes exactly one waiting process, which is the only waiter that will continue into the critical section next. Therefore at most one process is in the critical section at a time.

  • Deadlock freedom: There is no cycle of processes waiting indefinitely for each other. If a process is in the critical section it will eventually execute the exit code, set occupied = 0 and wake one blocked process. If no process is in the critical section, any arriving process will set occupied = 1 and enter. Because exit always wakes a waiter when one exists, blocked processes are eventually awakened, so the system cannot enter a deadlock where no one can make progress.

  • Progress: If some process wishes to enter and no one is in the critical section, that process sets occupied = 1 and proceeds immediately. If the critical section is occupied, waiting processes are queued conceptually via the blocked count; each exit wakes one waiter, so waiting processes will eventually be woken and enter. Thus a waiting process will make progress rather than being permanently blocked (assuming wakeup is reliable and scheduler eventually runs the woken process).

Caveats and required assumptions: The conclusions rely on occupied and blocked being initialized (commonly to 0), that the check/update of occupied and blocked within the Enter/Exit region is performed atomically as shown, and that wakeup reliably unblocks exactly one waiting process. If those assumptions are violated, behavior can differ.

title: Which mechanism allows processes to exchange data and messages directly
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which mechanism allows processes to exchange data and messages directly?
solution: Shared memory is the correct mechanism because it allows multiple processes to access a common region of physical memory, enabling them to exchange data directly without the overhead of kernel-mediated copying. When processes map the same memory segment, they can read and write data instantly, making it highly efficient for high-volume communication. In contrast, semaphores are synchronization primitives used to control access to shared resources but do not transfer data themselves. Pipes facilitate communication through a unidirectional byte stream, typically requiring the kernel to buffer and relay data between processes rather than allowing direct access. Signals are asynchronous notifications used to alert a process of an event but carry minimal data payload, making them unsuitable for direct message exchange. Therefore, shared memory uniquely supports the requirement of direct data and message exchange between processes.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q92
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Which of the following ensures mutual exclusion in concurrent processes?
solution:
Mutual exclusion requires that when multiple processes or threads share a critical section, at most one of them executes inside it at any instant. Operating systems achieve this through several general mechanisms — semaphore-based blocking, software algorithms such as Peterson's solution, and atomic hardware instructions. Hardware-based approaches use an operation that reads a shared lock variable and updates it in a single indivisible step, so no other process can see or act on an in-between state; the classic hardware primitive for this is the Test-and-Set (TSL) instruction.

Trace how a spinlock built on test-and-set enforces this in practice:

  1. The lock variable starts at false (unlocked), and every process trying to enter the critical section repeatedly calls TestAndSet(&lock) until it returns false.

  2. TestAndSet atomically reads the current value of lock, sets lock to true, and returns the value it read — the read and the write happen as one uninterruptible hardware step.

  3. The first process to call TestAndSet gets back false (lock was unlocked), so its loop exits and it proceeds into the critical section, and lock is now true.

  4. Any other process calling TestAndSet while the first is inside the critical section reads back true (lock is already held), so its loop keeps spinning instead of entering — it can never slip in during the gap between the read and the write, because there is no gap.

  5. When the first process finishes, it sets lock back to false, allowing exactly one waiting process to succeed on its next TestAndSet call.

boolean TestAndSet(boolean *target) {
    boolean rv = *target;
    *target = true;
    return rv;
}

// Each process:
while (TestAndSet(&lock))
    ;              // busy-wait
// critical section
lock = false;

Contrast with the other options: unbuffered I/O only controls when a single process's output is flushed to a device, not how multiple processes coordinate; environment variables are key-value settings copied into a process's own address space at creation time; command-line arguments (argv) are launch-time parameters whose values are fixed when a program starts, though the process may go on reading them repeatedly during its run. None of these three involve a shared, atomically-updated variable, so none can serialize access between concurrently running processes.

Among the options offered here, only an atomic hardware instruction such as test-and-set removes the window in which two processes could both see the lock as free at once; the other three options never touch any shared, atomically-updated variable at all, so none of them can serialize access between concurrent processes.

title: Disabling an interrupt is known as
subject: Operating System
bodyHtml: Disabling an interrupt is known as ______.
solution:
Concept

In an interrupt-driven system, the CPU can selectively ignore an interrupt request by setting a bit in an interrupt-mask register. This act of switching off (disabling) recognition of an interrupt source is called masking. A masked interrupt remains pending or is ignored — the CPU does not jump to its service routine.

Application

"Disabling an interrupt" is, by definition, masking it: the mask bit for that interrupt is set so the processor stops responding to that signal even when it is asserted. Masking can be done in hardware (mask pins/registers on the interrupt controller) or in software (writing the mask register).

Contrast

  • Run, Stop, and Halt all describe execution states of a process or the CPU — whether instructions are being executed — and have nothing to do with switching an interrupt line on or off.

  • Only masking names the mechanism that controls (enables/disables) which interrupt signals the CPU will recognize.
