bodyHtml: Select the figure that is the correct mirror image of the question figure with the mirror held on line XY.
solution:
A mirror image formed across a line is a lateral inversion: every point of the figure maps to a point on the opposite side of the mirror line at the same perpendicular distance, so left-right positions swap while the vertical (up-down) layout stays exactly the same. No part of the figure rotates or turns upside down — only sideways positions reverse.

Applying this to the question figure, whose mirror line XY is vertical:

  • the shaded kite must move from the slanted edge it touches in the question figure to the slanted edge on the opposite side

  • the diagonal arrow must reverse its left-right direction while still travelling the same distance up and down, so it now starts from the edge the kite moves to (the edge opposite the one it touched in the question figure) and points back toward the centre

  • the small cross mark must move to the side away from where it sits in the question figure, staying at the same height

Checking each option against this rule:

  • the figure that leaves the shaded kite on the same slanted edge as the question figure, with only the arrow and cross turned around, is not a full reflection — every element must swap sides together, not just some of them

  • the figure where the shaded kite rests against the edge opposite to the question figure, the arrow runs from that edge back toward the centre, and the cross sits on the side away from its original position, with every element's height unchanged, is the exact lateral inversion of the question figure

  • the figure with the triangle turned upside down applies a top-to-bottom flip, not a left-right one — a mirror held on a vertical line never inverts the figure's vertical layout

  • the figure that moves the shaded kite and the arrow toward the opposite edge but does not reproduce their exact size, angle and spacing is close to a mirror image at a glance, but not an exact point-for-point reflection

So the figure with the kite mirrored to the opposite edge, the arrow reversed toward the centre, and the cross shifted to the other side is the correct mirror image of the question figure about the line XY.

A left-right symmetric character (such as A or 0) looks unchanged after reflection, while an asymmetric character (such as Z, E, B, R, 2, 5, S, or a lowercase s) looks like its own backwards silhouette.

  3. A reliable check for any candidate answer figure: reflect it back a second time. A genuine right-side mirror image restores zEBRA205s exactly, character for character, on that second reflection; any character left undistorted in its normal (non-mirrored) form on the first reflection will show up as a mirrored glyph instead of the original when reflected back a second time.

Cross-check: Applying that second-reflection test to the four answer figures, only one figure restores zEBRA205s exactly — its digit 5 and lowercase s are both correctly mirrored, matching the source figure character for character. In each of the other figures, at least one character (the letter E, the digit 5, or both) is left in its normal upright form instead of its mirror form, so the second reflection produces a distorted string rather than zEBRA205s — confirming those figures are not accurate right-side mirror images.

title: Select the alternative which represents three out of the five

bodyHtml: Select the alternative which represents three out of the five alternative figures which when fitted into each other would form a complete square.
solution:
In a figure-formation (assembling) puzzle, the accompanying key diagram shows the target outline actually being built from three specific pieces. The three correct answer-figures are exactly the three pieces used in that construction: each must be a plain, straight-sided polygon matching one of those pieces in shape. A figure that is not itself a simple triangle -- one whose own outline is concave, notched, or stepped -- cannot match a plain-triangle piece, so it cannot be one of the three correct figures here.

The key diagram shows the square split, using one full diagonal plus a second line from the midpoint of that diagonal to the opposite corner, into three triangular pieces; the accompanying image demonstrates that figures (1), (4) and (5) are exactly the pieces used in that construction. Among the five given figures, only (1), (4) and (5) are plain triangles bounded by three straight sides. Figures (2) and (3) are not triangles at all: figure (2) has a zig-zag outline with an inward, reflex point, and figure (3) has a stepped, L-shaped outline with a right-angle notch -- neither matches any piece of this three-piece construction.

The image above shows this construction: the square split along one full diagonal plus a line from the midpoint of that diagonal to the opposite corner, giving three triangular pieces. Fitting figures (1), (4) and (5) together along their shared edges, exactly as pictured, reconstructs the square.

  • The trio with figures (1), (3) and (4) swaps in figure (3): its stepped, notched outline is not a plain triangle, so it does not match any piece of this three-piece construction.

  • The trio with figures (1), (2) and (5) swaps in figure (2): its zig-zag, reflex-angled outline is not a plain triangle, so it does not match any piece of this three-piece construction.

  • The trio with figures (1), (2) and (4) carries figure (2)'s non-triangular zig-zag outline and also drops one of the pieces this construction actually needs.

Because figures (1), (4) and (5) are the plain triangles matching this construction, while figures (2) and (3) are not triangles at all, the trio of figures (1), (4) and (5) is the one that fits together to form the complete square.

PIECES IN (X): the box holds three pieces — a right triangle in the upper-left (right angle at the top-left, slanted edge sloping down to the right), a mirror-image right triangle in the upper-right (right angle at the top-right, slanted edge sloping down to the left), and one small square near the bottom.

APPLICATION: Check each answer figure against the three pieces by size and by edges — same total area, same edge lengths, only rotation/flipping allowed, no resizing, no gaps, no overlaps:

  1. Add up the areas: the two right triangles plus the square must exactly equal the area enclosed by the answer figure's outline.

  2. In the first answer figure, the one slanted edge (from the top-right corner down to the bend point) matches a triangle's hypotenuse exactly in length and slope.

  4. Every edge and the full enclosed area are accounted for, with nothing left over and nothing overlapping — so the first figure is exactly the one these three pieces can form.

CROSS-CHECK — why the other figures fail:

  • The figure with the deep V-shaped cut in its top edge: one side of that cut runs straight down, the other runs diagonally — an uneven pairing, unlike the two mirror-image triangles, and no square-shaped region is set aside anywhere in it.

Only the first arrangement consumes all three pieces exactly, so it is the figure that can be formed.

title: Choose figure which would most closely resemble the unfolded form
subject: Reasoning
topic: Non Verbal Reasoning (Spatial Aptitude) (Spatial Reasoning) (Visual Reasoning)
bodyHtml: Choose a figure which would most closely resemble the unfolded form of Figure (Z)
solution:
Concept: When a folded paper is unfolded, every mark on the folded layer reappears as its mirror-image reflection across each fold line it was folded through — the reflections must be exactly symmetric and equal in size, and no new marks can appear anywhere else on the sheet, since no cutting occurred here.

Application: Figure X is folded once along the central vertical line to get Y, then Y is folded again along a second line to get Z, leaving a single small triangular crease near the apex of Z. Unfolding step by step:

  1. Unfold the second fold (Z → Y): reflect the crease in Z across that fold line. This produces one symmetric diamond (two mirrored triangular creases joined edge to edge) at the centre of Y, near the apex.

  2. Unfold the first fold (Y → X): reflect that diamond across the central vertical fold line of X. This produces a mirrored copy of it on the other side, giving three evenly spaced, congruent diamond creases across the apex of X — and nothing else on the triangle.

Cross-check: Since both folds are pure mirror reflections with no cuts, the unfolded figure must satisfy three things: (a) it is symmetric about the original central vertical axis, (b) it shows exactly three congruent diamond creases — the reflected copies of the one crease in Z — and nothing more, and (c) no unrelated marks appear elsewhere on the triangle. Checking each option against these three requirements:

  • The option with three uniform, evenly spaced diamond creases and no other marks satisfies all three requirements.

  • An option whose middle marking is split unevenly by an extra line, or that adds small hatched squares near the base, breaks requirements (b) and (c) — an uneven split cannot come from a straight-line reflection, and the squares have no matching crease in Z.

  • An option whose middle marking is flattened into a rounded hump, or that adds small unfilled triangles near the base, breaks (b) and (c) similarly — a reflection preserves the crease's angular shape, and the triangles have no matching crease in Z.

  • An option whose middle marking is compressed narrower than the two flanking creases breaks requirement (b) — a reflection always reproduces the crease at its original size.

Hence, the figure with three symmetric, evenly sized diamond creases and no other marks is the correct unfolded form of Z.

When a flat sheet is folded into a cube, each square becomes one face of the cube and keeps exactly the pattern printed on it. So a picture of the folded cube is valid only if it uses the same face-patterns, in the same numbers, as the sheet, and the patterns meeting at a corner in the picture are faces that are actually next to each other on the sheet.

Sheet (X) has six faces: one plain (blank) face, one face with a single dot, and four faces shaded diagonally into a black half and a white half.

  • Cube (2) shows the plain face, the dotted face, and a diagonally-split face meeting at one corner. The sheet's plain, dotted and split faces are likewise mutually adjacent, so this also matches the sheet.

Since cubes (1) and (2) use only the face-patterns present on sheet (X), arranged the way they actually meet on the sheet, while cubes (3) and (4) each introduce a pattern that does not exist on the sheet, only cubes (1) and (2) can be formed by folding sheet (X).

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q85
subject: Reasoning
topic: Non Verbal Reasoning (Spatial Aptitude) (Spatial Reasoning) (Visual Reasoning)
bodyHtml: Find the odd man out
solution:
In a "find the odd one out" classification question, three of the four given items share a common category or defining property, while exactly one item belongs to a different category. Solving it means identifying the shared property among the majority and checking which single item does not fit that property.

Here, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter are all planets of the solar system — each follows its own primary orbit directly around the Sun. The Moon, however, is not a planet; it is a natural satellite whose primary orbit is around Earth, even though the Earth-Moon system as a whole also moves around the Sun.

  • Earth — a planet of the solar system, orbiting the Sun directly.

  • Mars — a planet of the solar system, orbiting the Sun directly.

  • Jupiter — a planet of the solar system, orbiting the Sun directly.

  • Moon — not a planet; a natural satellite whose primary orbit is around Earth, not an independent orbit around the Sun.

Since three items share the "planet" category and only the Moon does not, the Moon is the odd one out among the four.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q5
subject: Reasoning
topic: Non Verbal Reasoning (Spatial Aptitude) (Spatial Reasoning) (Visual Reasoning)
bodyHtml: Find out the odd word from the following four options:
solution:
Concept: In a classification (odd-one-out) question, three of the four items share a common category, and the correct answer is the one item that does not belong to that category, even if all four look alike on the surface (for example, sharing the same prefix).

Application: All four words here begin with the prefix "micro-", so the prefix itself cannot be the basis for grouping. Look instead at what each word actually denotes:

  • Microfilm — a photographic reproduction of documents or printed pages recorded at a greatly reduced size on a roll or sheet of film, used for long-term archival storage.

  • Microphone — an electro-acoustic device that converts sound waves into an electrical signal, used for amplification, recording, or transmission of audio.

  • Microscope — an optical or electronic instrument that magnifies very small objects, used to examine specimens in a laboratory.

  • Microbe — a microscopic living organism, such as a bacterium, virus, or fungus, studied in biology and medicine.

Cross-check: Grouping the words by what they actually are (not by spelling) shows that Microfilm, Microphone, and Microscope are all man-made technological objects or media used for recording, transmitting, or observing information, while Microbe is a living organism. Since three words share the "man-made technological object" category and one does not, Microbe is the odd word out.

title: RSSB Patwar 2025 Shift 2 Q45
subject: Reasoning
topic: Non Verbal Reasoning (Spatial Aptitude) (Spatial Reasoning) (Visual Reasoning)
bodyHtml: Select a suitable figure from the given alternatives that would complete the following figure matrix:

options.label: A
B
C
D

solution:
A 3×3 figure-matrix item like this one changes its figures along two independent rules that are best read separately: the number of arms radiating from the central dot is fixed within each column and increases by one from column 1 to column 3, and the set of compass directions those arms point in is obtained by rotating Row 1's direction-set by a single fixed angle that stays constant across all three columns of that row, while only the arm's end-style (plain stroke, arrowhead, or hook) changes from row to row.

  1. Arm count by column: every figure in column 1 has 1 arm, column 2 has 2 arms, and column 3 has 3 arms, in all three rows — so the missing figure must have exactly 3 arms.

  2. End-style by row: Row 1's arms end in a plain stroke, Row 2's arms end in an arrowhead, and Row 3's arms end in a small hook — so the missing figure's arms must end in a hook, like the other two Row 3 figures.

  3. Row 1 to Row 2 rotation: comparing matching columns shows every arm direction reverses by 180° — column 1's left arm becomes right, column 2's up-and-right arms become left-and-down, and column 3's left-right-down arms become up-left-right.

  4. Row 1 to Row 3 rotation: using the two completed Row 3 figures, column 1's left arm becomes up, and column 2's up-and-right arms become right-and-down — both changes are a single 90° clockwise turn of the Row 1 arms.

  5. Applying that same 90° clockwise turn to column 3's Row 1 arms (left, right, down): left turns to up, right turns to down, and down turns to left, giving up, left, and down arms with no arm on the right.

This 90° clockwise turn was confirmed independently from column 1 (left → up) and from column 2 (up-and-right → right-and-down) before being applied to column 3, so the predicted missing figure is fixed by two matching data points rather than a single guess.

So the missing figure has three hook-ended arms pointing up, left, and down, with no arm on the right side.

solution:
Concept: In this operator-based figure-reasoning type, each symbol (a filled circle, a target-like circle, a circle with a cross, and an S-curve circle) is a rule defined by one worked example: comparing the box before the arrow with the box after it tells you exactly what that operator does to the box. When two operators are chained one after another, each is applied in the given left-to-right order, and here every operator acts only on the leftmost item of the box, leaving every other item untouched.

Application:

  1. From the top-right worked example, the filled black circle operator's rule is "Shades 1st item": it turns the leftmost item of the box fully black (solid), while the other two items stay exactly as they were.

  2. From the top-left worked example, the target-like circle operator's rule is "Makes 1st item Half size": it shrinks the leftmost item of the box to half its size, while the other two items again stay exactly as they were.

  3. The given box is [a solid black square, an unfilled circle, an unfilled crescent], and it is processed first by the "Shades 1st item" operator, then by the "Makes 1st item Half size" operator.

  4. Applying the shading rule first: the square, being the leftmost item, is already fully black, so shading it makes no visible difference and it stays a solid black square. The circle and the crescent are not the leftmost item, so this operator does not touch them.

  5. Applying the half-size rule next, to that result: the solid black square, still the leftmost item, shrinks to half its size, becoming a small solid black square. The circle and the crescent are still not the leftmost item, so they remain exactly as given: an unfilled circle and an unfilled crescent.

  6. So the final box must show, left to right: a small solid black square, an unfilled (outline) circle, and an unfilled (outline) crescent.

Cross-check: Because both rules explicitly act only on the leftmost item, applying them in the reverse order gives the same result here: halving the solid black square first gives a small solid black square, and shading an already-black square changes nothing further - so the result does not depend on the order for this particular pair of operators.

title: Select the figure from the alternatives which will complete the
subject: Reasoning
topic: Non Verbal Reasoning (Spatial Aptitude) (Spatial Reasoning) (Visual Reasoning)
bodyHtml: Select the figure from the alternatives which will complete the pattern in the given question figure.
solution:
Concept

In a “complete the pattern” grid, the large figure is built from one design rule that is repeated, rotated or reflected across its cells. To find the missing piece, first read the rule from the cells that are already filled, then apply that same rule to the empty cell — the correct choice is the one whose internal elements continue the design exactly, not merely a figure that looks broadly similar.

Reading the rule from the filled cells

The big square is split by a central cross into four corner cells, and a large diamond (a square rotated 45°) joins the mid-points of the four sides. Each filled corner carries two repeated features:

  • a small circle sits in the OUTER corner of the cell — the corner that touches the outer corner of the big square (top-left cell → circle top-left; top-right cell → circle top-right; bottom-left cell → circle bottom-left);

  • the short tick marks lie on the INNER edges of the cell — the edges next to the central cross — pointing toward the centre, while the diamond’s slanting edge cuts off the outer corner triangle that holds the circle.

Applying the rule to the empty cell

  1. The empty cell is the bottom-right one, so its OUTER corner is the bottom-right corner; by the circle rule, the small circle must sit in the bottom-right corner.

  2. Its INNER edges are the top edge and the left edge (both border the central cross); by the tick rule, the short ticks must lie on those two inner edges and point inward.

  3. The diamond’s lower-right slanting edge must run across the cell, cutting off the bottom-right triangle that carries the circle.

The figure that satisfies all three at once — circle in the bottom-right corner, ticks on the inner (top and left) edges pointing toward the centre, and the diagonal cutting the bottom-right corner — is the one that completes the pattern.

Cross-check

Place the chosen figure into the empty cell and rotate the whole big square in quarter-turns: the four corner cells now map onto one another exactly — every circle lands in an outer corner and every tick stays on an inner edge — confirming the design is consistent all the way round.

When a figure is completed by reflection, every point keeps the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line while moving to the opposite side. Line endpoints, triangle orientation, and marker positions must all reflect together; the reflected part must not introduce any new symbol.

Application

The left pair reveals the rule, and the same rule can then be applied to the right pair.

  1. Compare the upper-left and lower-left quadrants: the lower quadrant is the vertical reflection of the upper one across the central horizontal line. The upright triangle becomes inverted, and the hollow circle moves from the upper-right region to the lower-right region.

  2. Reflect the upper-right quadrant in the same way. Its upright triangle must point downward with its vertex at the lower centre; its extra diagonal must run from the upper-left corner toward the right midpoint; and its hollow circle must move from upper-left to lower-left.

  3. The unshaded figure with that inverted triangle, that upper-left-to-right-midpoint diagonal, and the hollow circle in the lower-left preserves every reflected feature.

Cross-check

  • The figure with the hollow circle in the lower-right region places the marker on the wrong side for the reflected right-hand quadrant.

  • The figure made from full crossed diagonals changes the triangle structure instead of reflecting it.

  • The upright-triangle figure keeps the original orientation and leaves the circle in the upper-right region.

Result

The completing value is the unshaded inverted-triangle figure with a hollow circle in the lower-left region and an extra diagonal from the upper-left corner toward the right midpoint.

title: Statement Ramesh has four balls (basketball and football). Statement Two

bodyHtml:
Statement 1: Ramesh has four balls (basketball and football). Statement 2: Two of the balls are red and other two are blue. Statement 3: Half of the balls are basketball.

If the above statements are true then which of the following statement must also be true? I. At least one basketball is red. II. Two of the balls are football. III. The footballs are of blue colour.

options.label: D
options.html: None of these statement is a fact

solution:
To determine which statement must be true based on the provided information, we can break down the facts given:

Step-by-Step Analysis
Analyze Given Statements:

Total Balls: Ramesh has 4 balls.

Color Distribution: 2 balls are red, and 2 balls are blue.

Type Distribution: Half the balls (2 out of 4) are basketballs. Consequently, the remaining 2 balls must be footballs.

Evaluate Conclusions:

Statement I ("At least one basketball is red"): This is not necessarily true. The red and blue colors could be distributed in any combination; for example, both basketballs could be blue, meaning no basketball would be red.

Statement II ("Two of the balls are football"): This is necessarily true. Since there are 4 balls in total and 2 are basketballs, the remaining 2 must be footballs.

Statement III ("The footballs are of blue colour"): This is not necessarily true. We cannot determine the specific color of each ball type; for instance, both red balls could be footballs.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q61
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
Read the statement and the two conclusions, then select the correct option.

Statement

Adversity makes a man wise.

Conclusions

  1. The poor are wise.

  2. A person learns from bitter experience.
solution:
CONCEPT

In statement–conclusion reasoning, a conclusion follows only when it is a direct restatement or a necessary inference from the given statement.

A conclusion that introduces a new class, condition, or assumption is not licensed by the statement.

APPLICATION

  1. Adversity means hardship or bitter experience. Becoming wise through adversity therefore expresses learning from that experience.

  2. The statement does not mention poverty and does not say that every poor person has faced the adversity described. The claim about the poor adds an unstated group assumption.

  3. Thus, conclusion 2 is supported, whereas conclusion 1 is not supported by the statement alone.

CROSS-CHECK AND CONTRAST

  • “Only conclusion 1 follows” depends on equating adversity with poverty and drops the learning-from-experience relation.

  • “Neither 1 nor 2 follows” overlooks the direct relation between adversity, experience, and acquired wisdom.

  • “Both 1 and 2 follow” combines the supported learning relation with the unsupported poverty assumption.

Therefore, only conclusion 2 follows.

solution:
Logical Analysis
Statements:

All fans are brown. (All F are B)

Some brown are chairs. (Some B are C)

Some chairs are plastic. (Some C are P)

Evaluating Conclusions:

Conclusion I: Some brown are fans.

If "All fans are brown," it logically follows that at least "Some brown are fans." This is a valid conversion of the universal affirmative. Conclusion I follows.

Conclusion II: Some chairs are brown.

The statement "Some brown are chairs" can be converted directly to "Some chairs are brown" without losing truth value. Conclusion II follows.

Conclusion III: No chair is plastic.

The statement "Some chairs are plastic" directly contradicts the assertion that "No chair is plastic." Therefore, this conclusion cannot follow.

subject: Reasoning

bodyHtml:
Directions: A statement followed by two arguments numbered (i) and (ii) are given below. Select an option to decide which of the given arguments is strong and which argument is weak in respect to the statement.

Statement: Should there be only one university throughout the country?

Arguments:
(i) Yes. This is the only way to maintain the uniformity in standards of education throughout the country
(ii) No. It is quite difficult to control the university processes administratively in several parts of the country
solution:
To determine the strength of the arguments provided, we must analyze them based on their logical soundness, practicality, and relevance to the statement: "Should there be only one university throughout the country?"

Step-by-Step Analysis
Analyze Argument (i): "Yes. This is the only way to maintain the uniformity in standards of education throughout the country."

Assessment: This is considered a weak argument. While the goal of uniform standards is positive, the claim that having "only one" university is the only way to achieve this is logically flawed. Standards can be maintained through national accreditation bodies, standardized curricula, and regulatory frameworks without centralizing all higher education into a single institution.

Analyze Argument (ii): "No. It is quite difficult to control the university processes administratively in several parts of the country."

Assessment: This is a strong argument. It addresses the practical, logistical, and administrative reality of managing a massive, complex system across diverse geographic regions. Centralizing such an institution would create immense bottlenecks, reduce institutional autonomy, and make it nearly impossible to address regional educational needs effectively.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q48
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
Statement: Should competitive examinations used to select candidates consist only of objective tests?

Arguments:

1. Yes, because assessment through an objective test is reliable.

2. No, because the number of questions to be answered is always very large.

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
solution:
Concept

A strong argument is directly relevant to the policy question, has practical importance, and rests on a defensible premise rather than an unsupported absolute.

For a “should” question, test each argument independently: ask whether it addresses the proposed action and whether its reason would materially support or oppose that action.

Application

  1. Argument 1 links objective tests with reliable assessment. Reliability is directly relevant to selecting candidates because consistent scoring supports fair comparison.

  2. Argument 2 says that the number of questions is always very large. This is an unsupported absolute and does not show that objective testing is unsuitable; test length can be designed independently of question format.

Cross-check

If an objective test contains a moderate number of questions, the reason offered in argument 2 disappears, while the relevance of reliable assessment in argument 1 remains. This confirms that the two arguments do not have equal strength.

Contrast

  • “Only argument 2 is strong” reverses the relevance test by relying on an unsupported claim about test length and excluding a direct assessment-quality consideration.

  • “Neither 1 nor 2 is strong” overlooks the direct connection between reliable scoring and candidate selection.

  • “Both 1 and 2 are strong” treats the unsupported question-volume claim as a necessary disadvantage of objective testing.

Result

Therefore, only argument 1 is strong.

title: Statement: "Z-T.V, the only T.V. which gives the viewers chance
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
Statement: "Z-T.V, the only T.V. which gives the viewers a chance to watch two programmes simultaneously." - An advertisement.

Assumptions:

I. Sale of Z-T.V will increase because of the advertisement.

II. Some people may be influenced by the advertisement and buy Z-T.V.

III. The sale of Z-T.V. may be on the downward trend.
solution:
An assumption in a Statement-and-Assumption question is something that is not stated but is silently taken for granted for the statement to make sense — a background premise, not a fresh prediction. The standard check is the negation test: negate the candidate assumption; if doing so does not touch the validity of the statement, the assumption was never implicit in the first place. A claim that predicts a specific, separate future outcome, rather than describing why the statement is being made at all, is a conclusion to be verified, not a silent premise, and therefore fails this test.

Assumption I claims Z-T.V.'s sales will increase because of the ad. This describes a hoped-for result of the campaign, not a premise the advertisement quietly depends on — an advertiser can run this exact ad, believing in it fully, and still see no rise in sales; the statement does not fall apart if this prediction fails, so I is not implicit. Assumption II claims some viewers may be swayed to buy after the ad. This is the ordinary working premise behind placing any advertisement — a company would have no reason to publicise a claim like this unless it believed the message could reach and influence at least some buyers; this is exactly the kind of background premise the negation test flags as implicit, so II holds. Assumption III claims Z-T.V.'s sales may currently be on a downward trend. Highlighting a distinctive, differentiating feature ("the only T.V. which...") is a common, unstated reason companies advertise at all — when a product's sales are healthy, there is less pressure to publicise a unique selling point this way; so a soft, unasserted concern about sagging sales is a reasonable premise quietly behind the statement, and III holds too.

  • Ruling out every assumption (denying that any premise underlies the statement) overlooks that placing this advertisement at all already presupposes some ordinary premise about its purpose.

  • Treating every assumption as implicit, or keeping the sales-increase claim alongside the persuasion premise, both smuggle in a guaranteed future result as if it were a silent premise — but a predicted outcome must be argued for, not assumed.

Only the two modest, unasserted premises about persuasive intent and a plausible motive for advertising survive the negation test, so "Only II and III are implicit" is the answer that matches the statement's own quiet assumptions.

To determine which statement must be true, we analyze the options based on this rule.\nOption B is correct because a building with a 7th floor necessarily has at least 7 floors. Since 7 is greater than 3, the condition 'more than 3 floors' is satisfied. Therefore, such a building must have a lift, making the presence of lifts on 7th floors logically necessary.\nOption A is incorrect because buildings with exactly 2 or 3 floors are not required to have lifts, but the statement implies they definitely do not, which is an assumption. Option C is wrong because it claims only floors above the 3rd have lifts, ignoring that buildings with more than 3 floors might also have lifts on lower floors. Option D is too broad, as buildings with only 2 or 3 floors might not have lifts at all. Thus, Option B is the only statement that must be true based on the given premises.

title: Statement followed by two assumptions are given below. Select the

A statement followed by two assumptions are given below. Select the assumption(s) from the options which is implicit in the statement. Select : (A) If only assumption (i) is implicit (B) If only assumption (ii) is implicit (C) If both (i) and (ii) are implicit (D) If neither (i) nor (ii) is implicit

Statement: We should work hard to be successful in our life

Assumptions:
i) Being successful in our life is desirable
ii) We will be happy if we work hard
solution:
To determine which assumptions are implicit in the statement "We should work hard to be successful in our life," we need to evaluate whether the assumptions are logically necessary for the statement to be valid.

Step-by-Step Analysis
Analyze the Statement: The statement encourages working hard for the purpose of being successful. This implies that success is a goal that people want to achieve.

Evaluate Assumption (i): "Being successful in our life is desirable."

If success were not desirable, there would be no logical reason to "work hard" to achieve it. Therefore, this is an implicit assumption that underpins the entire motivation of the statement.

Evaluate Assumption (ii): "We will be happy if we work hard."

The statement links hard work to success, not directly to happiness. While many people might believe hard work leads to happiness, the statement itself does not claim this. It is possible to be successful without being happy, or to work hard and not be happy. Thus, this is not an implicit assumption of the statement.

Statement: The civic body put up a large notice board on the beach located at an isolated part of the city, stating "Many picnickers drowned while swimming in the sea during the last few months."

(II) The picnickers may read this and become cautious while entering the sea.

solution:
The board is a warning. The purpose of any warning notice is to inform people so that they act with caution. Hence the civic body assumes that people will read the board and become more careful — Assumption II is implicit.

Assumption I says people may ignore the notice and keep taking risks. If the authority believed people would simply ignore it, there would be no point in putting up the board at all. So Assumption I works against the very reason for the action and is NOT implicit.

Since only Assumption II underlies the statement, the correct response is: only Assumption II is implicit.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q15
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
Statement: “Put a notice on the board informing all employees that they should arrive at the office on time,” an officer tells his assistant.

Assumptions:

  1. All the employees come late.

  2. Employees read such a notice on the board.

  3. Employees will follow the instructions.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
solution:
Concept

An implicit assumption is an unstated condition that must be accepted for a statement, instruction, or proposed action to have its intended purpose. The test is necessity: deny the assumption and ask whether the instruction still makes practical sense.

Application

  1. Assumption 1 is not necessary. The officer may want timely attendance even if only some employees are late or merely as a preventive reminder; the instruction does not require every employee to be late.

  2. Assumption 2 is necessary. A notice can communicate the instruction only if employees are expected to read notices displayed on the board.

  3. Assumption 3 is necessary. Issuing the notice for punctuality presupposes that employees are expected to act on the instruction.

Contrast

  • Assumption 1 is a universal status claim. Denying it still permits the officer to address partial lateness or issue a preventive reminder, so the instruction remains meaningful.

  • Assumption 2 is the communication link. Denying expected notice-reading removes the board’s ability to convey the instruction to employees.

  • Assumption 3 is the intended-response link. Denying any expectation of compliance removes the practical purpose of issuing the punctuality instruction.

Result

Therefore, assumptions 2 and 3 are implicit.

title: Statement: The Chairman stressed the need for making education system
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
Statement: The Chairman stressed the need for making the education system more flexible and regretted that the curriculum has not been revised in keeping with the pace of the changes taking place.

Courses of Action:

  • I. Curriculum should be reviewed and revised periodically.

  • II. System of education should be made more flexible.
solution:
Concept

A course of action is a practical administrative step proposed to remedy a problem or improve a situation described in a statement. A course FOLLOWS when it satisfies two tests: (i) relevance — it addresses a need, grievance or problem that the statement itself actually raises; and (ii) practicability — it is a reasonable, proportionate step, not an extreme, vague or impossible one. Courses are judged independently of one another: two courses can both follow, because a statement that voices more than one concern can warrant more than one remedy. ‘Either-or’ applies only when the two courses are rival substitutes for a single problem, and ‘neither’ applies only when both fail the tests.

Applying it to this statement

  1. Isolate what the statement raises. It carries two distinct concerns: (a) the Chairman STRESSED the need to make the education system more flexible; and (b) he REGRETTED that the curriculum has not been revised to keep pace with change.

  2. Test course I — ‘Curriculum should be reviewed and revised periodically.’ It speaks directly to concern (b), and periodic review is an ordinary, workable administrative measure. It passes both tests.

  3. Test course II — ‘System of education should be made more flexible.’ It speaks directly to concern (a), and it is the very measure the Chairman asked for. It passes both tests.

  4. Combine. Each course clears the tests on its own, and they remedy two different concerns rather than competing for one, so they are complementary, not alternatives.

Cross-check against the other verdicts

  • ‘Only I follows’ and ‘Only II follows’ each drop a course that survives the tests, on the mistaken assumption that a single statement can support just one remedy.

  • ‘Either I or II follows’ would require the two courses to be substitutes for the same problem, so that one makes the other unnecessary — but here they answer two different concerns.

  • ‘Neither I nor II follows’ would require both to fail relevance or practicability, whereas each addresses a concern the statement itself raises.

Hence the correct verdict is: Both I and II follow.

title: Statement is given followed by two courses of actions and
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
A statement is given followed by two courses of action I and II. You have to assume everything in the statement to be true, then decide which of the given courses of action logically follows.

Statement: It is estimated that in this year's International Trade Fair 25 lakh people will visit Pragati Maidan, Delhi.

Courses of action:

I. The Delhi Police should be on high alert and discourage people from visiting the fair.
II. The fair management should have enough ticket booths and shuttle services to avoid long queues.
solution:
Concept

In a Statement–Courses of Action item, a proposed course of action follows only if it is a practical, feasible administrative step that a responsible authority would reasonably take in response to the stated situation, and if it does not work against the underlying purpose implied by the statement. A course of action that is impractical, merely restates the problem, or conflicts with that purpose does not follow, even if it appears superficially related to the situation.

Application to This Item

Statement:
It is estimated that 25 lakh people will visit the International Trade Fair at Pragati Maidan, Delhi.

We need to determine which course of action logically follows.

Analysis of Course of Action I:

“The Delhi Police should be on high alert and discourage people from visiting the fair.”

  • Being on high alert may be reasonable for crowd management.

  • However, discouraging people from visiting the fair is not logical because trade fairs are organized to attract visitors, not prevent them.

Therefore, Course of Action I does not logically follow.

Analysis of Course of Action II:

“The management of the fair should have enough ticket booths and shuttle services to avoid long queues.”

  • A very large crowd is expected.

  • Additional ticket booths and shuttle services would help manage the crowd efficiently.

Therefore, Course of Action II logically follows.

Why the Other Options Don't Hold

  • Both I and II follow — this fails because course of action I's instruction to discourage attendance conflicts with the very purpose of holding a trade fair; grouping it with the genuinely sound course of action II is not justified.

  • Neither I nor II follows — this fails because the ticket-booth and shuttle-service measure genuinely responds to the anticipated 25-lakh crowd and does not conflict with the fair's purpose, so ruling out every course of action is too sweeping a conclusion.

  • Only I follows — this fails because approving the whole of course of action I overlooks that its discourage-attendance clause conflicts with the fair's purpose, even though the high-alert part alone would be reasonable.

Correct Option:
Only II follows

  • It targets the cause (insufficient service capacity) rather than shifting responsibility to customers.

title: Statement: large number of two-wheeler accidents every year result in

title: Directions: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
Directions: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions given beside.

Five weekly trains – Rajdhani Express, Samta Express, Duranto Express, Shatabdi Express and Bhopal Shatabdi Express run on different days of a week starting from Monday and ending on Saturday such that one day of a week was holiday i.e. No train run on that particular day.No train runs between Rajdhani Express and Samta Express. Shatabdi Express runs after but not immediately after Duranto Express, which is not the first train to run. Bhopal Shatabdi runs before Rajdhani Express, which runs on third day of the week. Rajdhani Express runs before Samta Express. First day of the week is not a holiday. Neither Friday nor Saturday is a holiday.

Four of the following five are alike in a certain way and thus form a group. Which of the following does not belong to the group?
solution:
CONCEPT: In day-and-holiday scheduling puzzles, first anchor the entity whose day is stated outright, then use the ordering, running before or after, and adjacency clues to place every other entity relative to that anchor; whichever day is left unassigned is the holiday. When such a puzzle is turned into a four-alike-one-odd-one-out question, the shared property linking four of the five choices is usually ‘a train runs on this day’; the odd one out is the day that fails that property, i.e. the holiday.

  1. Rajdhani Express runs on the third day of the week, i.e. Wednesday (Monday is the 1st day, ... Saturday is the 6th day).

  2. Bhopal Shatabdi Express runs before Rajdhani Express, so it runs on Monday or Tuesday.

  3. Monday (the first day) is not a holiday, and Wednesday is not a holiday either since Rajdhani Express runs there, so the holiday must be Tuesday or Thursday. Friday and Saturday are ruled out by the given clue.

  4. Rajdhani Express runs before Samta Express with no train running between them, so Samta Express must run on the very next train day after Wednesday, skipping over the holiday if it falls in between.

  5. If Tuesday were the holiday, the next train day after Wednesday would be Thursday, so Samta Express would run on Thursday, leaving only Friday and Saturday, two consecutive days, for Duranto Express and Shatabdi Express. Shatabdi Express must run after Duranto Express without running on the immediately following day, which is impossible on two consecutive days. So Tuesday is not the holiday.

  6. This leaves Thursday as the holiday. The next train day after Wednesday is then Friday, so Samta Express runs on Friday.

  7. Duranto Express is not the first train to run, so it cannot run on Monday; it must run on Tuesday or Saturday. If Duranto Express ran on Saturday, no day would remain after it for Shatabdi Express, which must run after it, so Duranto Express runs on Tuesday.

  8. Shatabdi Express must run after Tuesday but not on the very next calendar day; the only day left is Saturday, which satisfies both conditions, so Shatabdi Express runs on Saturday.

  9. The one remaining day, Monday, is assigned to Bhopal Shatabdi Express, consistent with it running before Rajdhani Express (Wednesday).

Day

Train

Monday

Bhopal Shatabdi Express

Tuesday

Duranto Express

Wednesday

Rajdhani Express

Thursday

Holiday (no train)

Friday

Samta Express

Saturday

Shatabdi Express

This arrangement satisfies every clue: no train runs between Rajdhani Express (Wednesday) and Samta Express (Friday) since Thursday is the holiday; Shatabdi Express (Saturday) runs after Duranto Express (Tuesday) but not on the immediately following day; Bhopal Shatabdi Express (Monday) runs before Rajdhani Express; Rajdhani Express runs before Samta Express; and neither Monday, Friday, nor Saturday is a holiday.

A train runs on Monday, Tuesday, Friday, and Saturday, so these four days share the property of having a scheduled train and form the group. Thursday is the day on which no train runs at all, so Thursday does not belong to the group.

title: Kritty Karma, Ishwar Prasad, Harshini are children of Gopal and
subject: Reasoning

bodyHtml: Kritty Karma, Ishwar Prasad, Harshini are children of Gopal and Radha. Gopal works in Secretariat of central government at New Delhi. Kritty Karma was born when Gopal was serving in Tiruchirapalli office. Ishwar Prasad was born in a leading hospital at Kochi. Harshini the only daughter of the couple was born in Gangaram Hospital, New Delhi. Five years before Kritty Karma, Ishwar Prasad was born for the couple. Harshini is the youngest of the three and she is younger than the eldest son by 9 years. Gopal was 26 years old when Ishwar Prasad was born. Gopal and Radha got married eight years before the birth of Kritty Karma. Radha is 2 years younger than Harshini’s father. Harshini is now 20 year old and has secured appointment in Microsoft after studying in Anna University. Find out the age of Radha, Harshini’s mother now?
solution:
The couple has two sons and a daughter.

Let them be called K, P and H. K = Kritty, P = Prasad, H = Harshini

Since P was born 5 years before K, he’s the eldest.

H is 9 years younger than P.

She’s currently 20 years old.

So, P is currently 20 + 9 = 29 years old.

I.e. P was born 29 years ago, when Gopal was 26 years old.

Thus, Gopal’s current age = 26 + 29 = 55 years.

Radha is 2 years younger than Gopal.

So, Radha’s current age is 55 – 2 = 53 years

title: RSSB Patwar 2025 Shift 2 Q96
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
Below is given a passage followed by several possible inferences which can be drawn from the facts stated in the passage. You have to examine each inference separately in the context of the passage, decide upon its degree of truth or falsity and choose your answer accordingly from amongst the alternatives provided thereafter. (Q. No. 94 to 96)

Wind is an inexhaustible source of energy and an aerogenerator can convert it into electricity. Though not much has so far been done in this field, the survey shows that there is a vast potential for developing wind as an alternative source of energy. On this basis, U.P.’s hilly areas have been found to be an ideal place for setting up aerogenerators. In U.P. hills alone, as many as 56 sites have been identified.

Inference to examine: The survey was conducted by the Government of U.P. (Choose the most appropriate option from below)
solution:
In a Statement-and-Inference reasoning question, each inference is judged strictly against the facts stated in the passage, never against outside information. An inference is Definitely True only when it is directly stated or is an unavoidable logical consequence of the passage; Probably True when the stated facts make it more likely than not without confirming it outright; Probably False when the stated facts make it less likely than not without ruling it out; and Definitely False when it contradicts a fact stated in the passage.

The passage reports that a wind survey found vast potential for wind energy and that, on this basis, U.P.'s hilly areas — with 56 specific sites — were identified as ideal for aerogenerators. The passage never names the body that carried out the survey. The finding is presented as regional energy planning: sites are counted specifically for U.P., which is the kind of exercise a state typically initiates or sponsors for its own territory. No other agency — a private company, a central body, or otherwise — is mentioned as the source of the survey.

  • Definitely true would require the passage to name the surveying agency outright; it does not, so certainty is not available.

  • Probably false or Definitely false would require the passage to point to a different agency, or to otherwise work against government involvement; nothing in the passage does either.

So the U.P.-specific framing of the finding supports, without confirming, involvement of the Government of U.P. — making the inference Probably true.

title: If Ram studies, he will pass his exam. Ram fails
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml: If Ram studies, he will pass his exam. Ram fails the exam. Which of the following statements is true?

options.label: B
options.html: Ram did not study for the exam

options.label: C
options.html: Ram may or may not have studied for the exam

solution:
Solution: Use the contrapositive of the conditional statement.

Let S be "Ram studies for the exam" and P be "Ram passes the exam".

We are given S → P (if Ram studies then he will pass) and that Ram failed, i.e. not P.

The contrapositive of S → P is not P → not S, which is logically equivalent to the original conditional. From not P we can therefore conclude not S.

Hence, Ram did not study for the exam.

  • The statement "Ram studied for the exam" is false because it contradicts the conclusion that he did not study.

  • The statement "Ram may or may not have studied for the exam" is incorrect because we can determine he did not study.

  • The statement "None of these" is incorrect because the statement "Ram did not study for the exam" follows from the premises.

title: Statements: The private medical colleges have increased the tuition fees
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
bodyHtml:
Statements:

1. The private medical colleges have increased the tuition fees in the current year by 200 per cent over the last year's fees to meet the expenses.

2. The Government medical colleges have not increased their fees in spite of price escalation.

options.label: A
options.html: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect

options.label: B
options.html: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect

options.label: C
options.html: Both the statements I and II are independent causes

options.label: D
options.html: Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes

solution:
In 'Statement - Cause and Effect' reasoning, two given statements are classified by the causal relationship between them: one statement may be the cause of the other and the other its effect; both may be independent causes with no traceable driving factor of their own; both may be effects of two separate (independent) underlying causes; or both may be effects of one shared/common cause. A statement counts as an effect, not a raw cause, whenever it already carries -- explicitly or by implication -- a reason behind the outcome it reports.

Statement I reports a fee hike and states its own reason inside the sentence, 'to meet the expenses', so the hike is the outcome of rising costs at private colleges, not an unexplained originating action. Statement II reports that government colleges held fees steady 'in spite of' price escalation; holding the line against an expected upward pressure signals a separate, unstated policy consideration, such as keeping medical education affordable, driving that outcome. Neither statement is triggered by the other, since private-college fee policy and government-college fee policy are unrelated administrative decisions, so no cause-effect link runs between Statement I and Statement II.

  • Statement I is the cause and Statement II is its effect, or Statement II is the cause and Statement I is its effect: both require one statement to trigger the other; private and government college fee policies are set independently, so no such link exists.

  • Both statements are independent causes: this fits only when neither statement shows any traceable reason behind it; here, Statement I openly states 'to meet the expenses' as its reason, so it is a resulting action, not an unexplained originating one.

  • Both statements are effects of independent causes: each statement's outcome (the fee hike, the fee freeze) is driven by its own separate factor (rising costs versus an affordability-focused policy); the two colleges' outcomes are unrelated to each other but each is explainable by its own reason.

Since each statement reports an outcome traceable to its own distinct, unstated underlying cause, and neither outcome causes the other, the two statements are best classified as effects of independent causes.

title: Statements: All the goats are tigers. All the tigers are
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Statements:

  1. All the goats are tigers.

  2. All the tigers are lions.

Conclusions:

  1. All the goats are lions.

  2. All the lions are goats.

  3. Some lions are goats.

  4. Some tigers are goats.
solution:
Key idea: The two premises place goats inside tigers and tigers inside lions, so goats are a subset of tigers and tigers are a subset of lions.

  • All the goats are lions — Valid. Because goats ⊂ tigers and tigers ⊂ lions, every goat is a lion.

  • All the lions are goats — Invalid. The premises only place goats inside lions; they do not state that lions have no other members, so you cannot conclude every lion is a goat.

  • Some lions are goats — Valid (assuming classes are nonempty). Since all goats are lions, the goats (if any exist) are lions, so at least some lions are goats.

  • Some tigers are goats — Valid (assuming classes are nonempty). Because all goats are tigers, the goats are members of the tiger class, so at least some tigers are goats.

Conclusion: The correct set of conclusions that follow is: all goats are lions; some lions are goats; and some tigers are goats.

title: Given below are three statements followed by three conclusions. Assuming
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Given below are three statements followed by three conclusions. Assuming these statements to be true, decide which one logically follows:

Statements:

I. All trash barrels are filthy. II. No container is filthy. III. All baskets are containers.

Conclusions:

I. Some baskets are filthy. II. No basket is a trash barrel. III. Some baskets are containers
solution:
Given statements:

  • All trash barrels are filthy.

  • No container is filthy.

  • All baskets are containers.

Conclusion analysis:

  • Some baskets are filthy — Does not follow. Since all baskets are containers and no container is filthy, baskets cannot be filthy.

  • No basket is a trash barrel — Follows. All trash barrels are filthy while containers are not filthy, so trash barrels cannot be containers. Because all baskets are containers, baskets cannot be trash barrels.

  • Some baskets are containers — Follows (with the standard exam convention of existential import). All baskets are containers, so assuming at least one basket exists, some baskets are containers.

Final conclusion: Conclusions "No basket is a trash barrel" and "Some baskets are containers" follow; "Some baskets are filthy" does not follow.

title: Statements: National Aluminium Company has moved India from position of
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Statements: National Aluminium Company has moved India from a position of shortage to self-sufficiency in the metal.

Conclusions:
I.Previously, India had to import aluminium.
II.With this speed, it can soon become a foreign exchange earner.
solution:
Answer: Only conclusion I follows.

Reasoning:

  • The statement says the country was moved from a position of shortage to self-sufficiency in aluminium. Moving from shortage to self-sufficiency implies that previously there was insufficient domestic supply, which typically requires imports to meet demand. Therefore the conclusion that the country previously had to import aluminium follows.

  • The second conclusion asserts that, at the current speed, the country can soon become a foreign exchange earner (i.e., an exporter). The original statement does not mention the rate of increase in production, the existence of a growing surplus, or any time frame. Self-sufficiency only means domestic demand can be met, not that excess for export exists. Therefore the second conclusion is not supported by the given information.

Final conclusion: Only the first conclusion is logically supported by the statement.

title: What conclusion can be drawn from given statement? All apples
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
What conclusion can be drawn from given statement?

All apples are fruits. Some fruits are sweet.
solution:
Conclusion: None of the given statements can be logically concluded from the premises.

Given premises:

  • All apples are fruits.

  • Some fruits are sweet.

Key logical point:

  • A universal statement like "All apples are fruits" does not assert that any apples actually exist.

  • "Some fruits are sweet" is an existential statement that guarantees at least one sweet fruit exists, but it does not say which fruits are sweet.

Analysis of each proposed conclusion:

  1. All apples are sweet. The premises do not support this; there is no information that every apple is sweet.

  2. Some fruits are apples. This cannot be inferred because "All apples are fruits" does not guarantee that any apples exist.

  3. No apples are sweet. Also not supported: the premises do not tell us whether sweet fruits include or exclude apples.

  4. Some apples are sweet. This is possible but not guaranteed by the premises; the sweet fruits mentioned might not be apples.

Final verdict: None of the four statements is logically entailed by the premises. The original solution incorrectly asserted that "Some apples are sweet" follows; this is not a valid deduction without additional information linking sweet fruits specifically to apples.

title: Statements: Some cows are crows. Some crows are elephants. Conclusions:
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Statements: Some cows are crows. Some crows are elephants.

Conclusions:

Some cows are elephants.

All crows are elephants
solution:
Answer: Neither "Some cows are elephants" nor "All crows are elephants" follows from the premises.

Reasoning:

  • Some cows are elephants — Does not necessarily follow. Explanation: The premises state there exist cows that are crows and there exist crows that are elephants, but these "some" groups can be different. For example, one small group of crows could overlap with cows (but not with elephants), while a different group of crows overlaps with elephants. In that case no cow is an elephant.

  • All crows are elephants — Does not follow. Explanation: The premise only asserts that some crows are elephants, which is weaker than asserting every crow is an elephant. There may exist crows that are not elephants.

Conclusion: Because neither statement can be deduced in all cases from the given premises, the correct choice is that neither conclusion follows.

title: Three statements are given followed by four conclusions II, III
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Three statements are given followed by four conclusions I, II, III and IV. You have to consider these statements to be true, even if they seem at variance from commonly known facts. Decide which of the given conclusions logically follows from the given statement.
Statements:

All beetroots are carrots.
All carrots are radishes.
All radishes are white.

Conclusions:

I. All beetroots are white.
II. All white are carrots.
III. All radishes are beetroots.
IV. All carrots are white.
solution:
- The Logic: The statements describe nested relationships (concentric circles): Beetroots inside Carrots, Carrots inside Radishes, and Radishes inside White.
- Checking Conclusion I: Since all beetroots are inside carrots, all carrots are inside radishes, and all radishes are inside white, all beetroots are automatically inside white. (Follows)
- Checking Conclusion II: "All white are carrots" moves from the outermost circle to an inner circle, which is incorrect. Only "some white are carrots" is true. (Does not follow)
- Checking Conclusion III: "All radishes are beetroots" moves from an outer circle to an inner circle, which is incorrect. Only "some radishes are beetroots" is true. (Does not follow)
- Checking Conclusion IV: Since all carrots are inside radishes, and all radishes are inside white, all carrots are automatically inside white. (Follows)
- Therefore, only conclusions I and IV follow.
