title: Decide which of the given conclusions logically follow from the
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Decide which of the given conclusions logically follow from the given statement(s)

Statement:

Some metals are alloys.

No metal is a stone.

Conclusions:

I. No alloy is stone. II. At least some alloys are metals

options.label: A
options.html: Neither conclusion I nor II is true

options.label: D
options.html: Both Conclusion I and II are true

solution:
Concept: Two standard syllogism rules decide conclusions like these. First, a particular affirmative statement ("Some X are Y") converts simply and validly to "Some Y are X" — no second premise or extra condition is needed; a particular negative ("Some X are not Y"), by contrast, never converts this way. Second, a universal claim ("All" or "No") about an entire class can only be drawn from premises that fix that class's whole extent — a premise that establishes merely a partial ("some") overlap with a class can never license a universal statement about that class.

Applying this to the two statements:

  1. "Some metals are alloys" is a particular affirmative (I-type). By the first rule, it converts directly to "Some alloys are metals" — this alone establishes Conclusion II, with no need for the second statement.

  2. "No metal is a stone" excludes stones from the metal class specifically. Since "Some metals are alloys" fixes only a partial overlap between metals and alloys — not that every alloy is a metal — this exclusion covers just that overlap; alloys outside it are never brought under it.

  3. Conclusion I ("No alloy is stone") would need the metal–stone exclusion to hold across the WHOLE alloy class. By the second rule, a partial ("some") premise cannot support that universal a conclusion, so Conclusion I does not follow.

Cross-check with a Venn diagram: draw the alloy circle overlapping the metal circle (as "some" requires), and place the stone circle entirely outside the metal circle. Nothing stops the alloy circle from ALSO overlapping the stone circle in the region lying outside the metal circle — so "no alloy is stone" is never guaranteed, while "some alloys are metals" is fixed the moment the metal-alloy overlap is drawn.

Hence only Conclusion II follows: the correct choice is "Only Conclusion II is true."

title: Four sets of three statements each are given below. Take
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Four sets of three statements each are given below. Take these statements to be true even if they look factually absurd. Select one alternative in which third statement is implied by the first two statements.

options.label: A
options.html: All bats are balls. All stumps are bats. Therefore, all balls are stumps.

options.label: B
options.html: All fruits are flowers. All vegetables are fruits. Therefore all vegetables are flowers.

options.label: C
options.html: All trains are buses. All buses are roads. Therefore, all roads are buses.

options.label: D
options.html: All R's are T's. All T's are Q's. Therefore, all Q's are R's.

solution:
Concept

A categorical syllogism of the form "All A are B" and "All B are C" lets you validly conclude "All A are C" — the subset relation is transitive: A is inside B, and B is inside C, so A must be inside C. The direction matters: you may chain forward through the middle term, but you may NOT reverse a universal statement. From "All X are Y" it does not follow that "All Y are X" (that is illicit conversion).

Application

Examine the pair "All vegetables are fruits" and "All fruits are flowers." Here the middle term is "fruits": vegetables sit inside fruits, and fruits sit inside flowers. Chaining forward, vegetables must sit inside flowers, so "All vegetables are flowers" is a valid conclusion that follows directly from the two premises. The conclusion keeps the same subject-to-predicate direction as the premises, so nothing is reversed.

Cross-check / Contrast

Each of the other three sets draws a conclusion that reverses one of its premises, which is the classic illicit-conversion error:

  • From "All bats are balls" and "All stumps are bats," the only valid conclusion is "All stumps are balls." Concluding "All balls are stumps" reverses the chain and is invalid.

  • From "All trains are buses" and "All buses are roads," the valid conclusion is "All trains are roads." Concluding "All roads are buses" reverses "All buses are roads" and is invalid.

  • From "All R are T" and "All T are Q," the valid conclusion is "All R are Q." Concluding "All Q are R" reverses the chain and is invalid.

Only the vegetables-fruits-flowers set chains the middle term forward without reversal, so it is the alternative whose third statement is genuinely implied by the first two.

title: Four sets of three statements are given below. Suppose these
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Four sets of three statements are given below. Suppose these statements are true even if they differ from known facts. Select the option in which the third statement follows the first two statements.

options.label: A
options.html: All foxes are wild. All jackals are wild. Therefore, all jackals are foxes.

options.label: B
options.html: All fruits are leaves. All flowers are fruits. Therefore, all flowers are leaves.

options.label: C
options.html: All pens are pencils. All rubber are pens. Therefore, all pencils are erasers.

options.label: D
options.html: All buses are roads. All cars are buses. Therefore, all roads are cars.

solution:
Concept:

A categorical syllogism is valid only when its conclusion is forced by its two premises through term chaining. "All A are B" places set A entirely inside set B. When two "All ... are ..." premises share a common middle term, the chain A ⊆ B ⊆ C lets you conclude A ⊆ C — but only in that direction and only for terms that actually appear in the premises.

Two rules decide every such item:

  • Chain rule — the conclusion must run along the inclusion direction (subset → superset), never reversed.

  • No new term rule — the conclusion may use only the terms present in the premises; a fresh term that never appeared cannot be concluded.

Application to each set:

  • foxes ⊆ wild and jackals ⊆ wild: both are inside "wild," but two subsets of the same set need not overlap, so "all jackals are foxes" does not follow.

  • flowers ⊆ fruits and fruits ⊆ leaves: chaining gives flowers ⊆ leaves, so "all flowers are leaves" follows in the correct direction — this is the valid set.

  • rubber ⊆ pens ⊆ pencils: the premises never mention "erasers," so concluding anything about erasers breaks the no-new-term rule.

  • cars ⊆ buses ⊆ roads: this forces "all cars are roads," but the stated conclusion "all roads are cars" reverses the direction (illicit conversion).

Cross-check: Only the flowers–fruits–leaves set keeps both the same terms and the subset → superset direction, confirming it is the one whose third statement is forced by the first two.

title: Two statements are given followed by two conclusions II, III
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Two statements are given followed by four conclusions I, II, III and IV. You have to consider these statements to be true, even if they seem at variance from commonly known facts. Decide which of the given conclusions logically follow/s from the given statement.

Statements:

  1. All judges are lawyers.

  2. Some lawyers are seniors.

Conclusions: I. Some seniors are judges. II. Some seniors are lawyers. III. Some lawyers are judges. IV. Some judges are seniors.
solution:
Concept: Two rules of immediate inference decide which conclusions validly follow from two categorical statements.

  • A particular statement ("some A are B") converts simply to "some B are A" -- no information is lost.

  • A universal statement ("all A are B") converts by limitation to "some B are A", valid once the subject class A is taken to be non-empty (the standard assumption in these questions).

  • No conclusion may validly link two classes unless the class shared between the statements (the middle term) is distributed -- used as the subject of a universal statement -- in at least one of them; appearing only as a predicate, or as the subject of a "some" statement in both places, is not enough (the undistributed-middle fallacy).

Application: Statement 1, "All judges are lawyers", is universal with judges as the distributed subject; statement 2, "Some lawyers are seniors", is particular with lawyers as its (undistributed) subject.

  1. Convert statement 1 by limitation (judges non-empty): "All judges are lawyers" gives "Some lawyers are judges" -- this is exactly conclusion III.

  2. Convert statement 2 simply: "Some lawyers are seniors" gives "Some seniors are lawyers" -- this is exactly conclusion II.

  3. Lawyers is the predicate of the universal statement and the subject of the particular statement -- undistributed in both -- so no statement distributes lawyers, and no valid judges-seniors relationship can be drawn in either direction. Conclusions I and IV therefore do not follow.

Cross-check: Draw the judges circle wholly inside the lawyers circle (per statement 1), then draw the seniors circle overlapping lawyers only in a region placed entirely outside the judges circle (statement 2 only requires some lawyer-senior overlap, not that it touch the judges subset). This diagram satisfies both statements while making I and IV false, and no diagram consistent with the statements can make II or III false, confirming the split.

Result: Only conclusions II and III follow, matching "Only conclusions II and III follow."

Why the other combinations fall short:

  • "Only conclusions I and IV follow" chains the two statements straight through to a judges-seniors claim, ignoring that lawyers is undistributed in both statements.

  • "Only conclusions III and IV follow" keeps the valid judges-lawyers restatement but adds the unsupported judges-seniors claim.

  • "Only conclusions I and II follow" keeps the valid lawyers-seniors restatement but adds the unsupported judges-seniors claim.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q6
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
If the statement “Some residents are voters” is true, consider the following conclusions:

  1. No voter is a resident.

  2. All residents are voters.

  3. Some voters are residents.

  4. No resident is a voter.

Which of the above conclusion(s) follow?
solution:
Concept

An existential affirmative statement says that the two named sets share at least one member. Such a statement permits simple conversion: “Some A are B” implies “Some B are A.”

It does not establish universal inclusion, and it is incompatible with a universal statement that the two sets are disjoint.

Application

  1. Let R be the set of residents and V the set of voters. “Some residents are voters” means that at least one person lies in R ∩ V.

  2. The same shared person is both a voter and a resident, so conclusion 3, “Some voters are residents,” follows by simple conversion.

  3. Conclusion 2 says R is entirely contained in V. One shared member does not prove that every resident belongs to V.

  4. Conclusions 1 and 4 both say R and V are disjoint. That contradicts the given non-empty intersection.

Cross-check and contrast

  • “Only 1 and 2” combines two universal claims that are not established by the existential statement.

  • “Only 2” strengthens “some” to “all,” which is not licensed.

  • “Only 3” preserves the same shared witness while reversing the order of the two classes.

  • “Only 3 and 4” combines the shared-witness claim with a disjointness claim, so the pair is internally inconsistent.

Therefore, conclusion 3 alone follows, so the answer is “Only 3.”

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q7
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Consider the following arguments.

A. No athletes are vegetarians.

B. All football players are athletes.

C. Therefore no football players are vegetarians.

If the statements A and B are true, then the statement C is
solution:
Concept

A categorical syllogism treats each named group as a set. A universal affirmative statement places one set inside another, while a universal negative statement says that two sets have no common member.

If one set is contained in a second set and the second set is disjoint from a third, then the first set is also disjoint from the third. This is a necessary implication, not a probabilistic estimate.

Application

  1. Let F be the set of football players, A the set of athletes, and V the set of vegetarians.

  2. Statement B gives F ⊆ A: every football player belongs to the set of athletes.

  3. Statement A gives A ∩ V = ∅: no athlete belongs to the set of vegetarians.

  4. Because F ⊆ A, any member of F would also be in A. Since A has no member in V, F ∩ V must also be empty.

  5. Therefore statement C follows necessarily: no football player is a vegetarian.

Contrast

  • “Probably true” describes a conclusion supported by likelihood but not forced by the premises.

  • “True” describes a conclusion that holds in every interpretation in which the premises hold.

  • “Uncertain” describes a conclusion for which the premises permit both a confirming model and a countermodel.

  • “Probably false” describes a conclusion disfavoured by evidence but not logically contradicted by the premises.

Cross-check

In a Venn diagram, the football-player circle lies entirely inside the athlete circle, and the vegetarian circle cannot overlap the athlete circle. It therefore cannot overlap the football-player circle either.

Result

Statement C is true because it is logically entailed by statements A and B.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q38
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Which Venn diagram represents the statement “Some men are not great scientists”?
solution:
Concept

In a categorical Venn diagram, shading means that a region is empty, while a cross means that at least one member exists in that region.

The statement “Some A are not B” is existential: it requires at least one member inside A but outside B.

Application

  1. Let one circle represent men and the other circle represent great scientists.

  2. The phrase “some men” requires an existing member of the set of men.

  3. The phrase “are not great scientists” places that member outside the overlap with great scientists.

  4. Therefore, put a cross in the part of the men circle that excludes great scientists.

Cross-check and contrast

  • Shading the overlap would assert that no men are great scientists.

  • Shading the great-scientists-only region would assert that every great scientist is a man.

  • Shading the men-only region would assert that every man is a great scientist.

  • A cross in the men-only region directly represents the required existential member.

Hence, the required representation is the diagram with a cross in the men-only region.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q67
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Which symbol is used to express a universal negative proposition?
solution:
Concept

In traditional categorical logic, a standard-form proposition is classified by quantity (universal or particular) and quality (affirmative or negative). The four forms are conventionally labelled A, E, I, and O.

A proposition with the form “No S are P” ranges over the whole subject class and denies membership in the predicate class.

Application

The phrase “universal negative” corresponds to the form “No S are P.” In the traditional A–E–I–O notation, that form is represented by E.

Contrast

  • A represents “All S are P,” the universal affirmative form.

  • I represents “Some S are P,” the particular affirmative form.

  • O represents “Some S are not P,” the particular negative form.

Result

Therefore, the symbol for a universal negative proposition is E.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q73
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Under the conventional existential-import rule used in aptitude-test syllogisms, if “All successful administrators are intelligent” is true, which of the following statements follows?

options.label: D
options.html: Some intelligent people are not successful administrators

solution:
CONCEPT

A universal affirmative proposition has the form “All S are P”, represented as S ⊆ P. In the conventional syllogism rules used in aptitude tests, the subject class S is treated as non-empty, so the universal affirmative has existential import.

Under subalternation, an A-form proposition therefore supports the corresponding I-form proposition “Some S are P”. It does not support the contrary E-form, the contradictory O-form, or an existence claim about the part of P outside S.

APPLICATION

  1. Let S be the set of successful administrators and I be the set of intelligent people.

  2. The premise “All successful administrators are intelligent” gives S ⊆ I.

  3. By the conventional existential-import assumption, S is non-empty; choose an element x in S.

  4. Since S ⊆ I, the same element x is also in I. Hence at least one successful administrator is intelligent.

CONTRAST

  • “No successful administrator is intelligent” makes S and I disjoint, contrary to S ⊆ I with non-empty S.

  • “Some successful administrators are not intelligent” requires an element of S outside I, contradicting S ⊆ I.

  • “Some intelligent people are not successful administrators” needs an element in I outside S; the premise does not guarantee that region is occupied.

CROSS-CHECK

Draw the S circle entirely inside the I circle and place one witness in S. That witness necessarily lies in both circles, while no witness is forced into the I-only region.

Therefore, the statement that follows is “Some successful administrators are intelligent”.

title: In each of the following questions there are three statements.
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
In each of the following questions there are three statements. Which are followed by three or four conclusions. Choose the conclusions which logically follow from the given statements.

Statements: Some questions are answers. Some answers are writers. All the writers are poets.
Conclusions:
1. Some writers are answers.
2. Some poets are questions.
3. All the questions are poets.
4. Some poets are answers.
solution: Answer: Option B Explanation:

title: In each of the questions below are given few statements
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
In each question below, a few statements are followed by three conclusions. Treat the statements as true, even if they differ from commonly known facts. Use the convention of this exam that every class named in a universal ‘All A are B’ statement is non-empty. Read all the conclusions and decide which logically follow from the statements.

Statements

  • All chairs are tables.

  • All tables are bottles.

  • Some bottles are jars.

  • No jar is a bucket.

Conclusions

I. It is possible that some tables are jars.

II. Some bottles are chairs.

III. Some bottles are not buckets.

options.label: B
options.html: Both conclusions I and II are true

solution:
Concept

In categorical syllogisms, treat each universal statement as a set inclusion and each particular statement as proof that at least one member exists. A possibility conclusion is admissible when it can be added without contradicting any stated inclusion or exclusion.

This item explicitly stipulates existential import for universal statements: if all A are B, then A is non-empty and some B are A. Also, if some B are C and no C are D, those existing B–C members are not D.

Application

  1. Let C, T, B, J, and K denote chairs, tables, bottles, jars, and buckets. From C ⊆ T and T ⊆ B, transitivity gives C ⊆ B. Because the stem stipulates that C is non-empty, choose c in C; then c is also in B. Hence some bottles are chairs, so conclusion II follows.

  2. Some bottles are jars, so choose an existing member x in B ∩ J. No jar is a bucket, hence x is not in K. Thus x lies in B but not in K, so conclusion III follows.

  3. No statement forbids T ∩ J. A table may be placed inside the jar region while every jar remains outside the bucket region and C ⊆ T ⊆ B is preserved. Therefore conclusion I is possible.

Cross-check

A consistent model can contain one chair–table–bottle member and one table–bottle–jar member, with every jar outside the bucket set. The explicit non-empty-class convention rules out an empty chair set; the model satisfies all four statements and supports conclusions I, II, and III.

Therefore, all conclusions follow.

title: In each of the questions below are given few statements
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Directions: Read the statements as true and decide which conclusions logically follow, ignoring commonly known facts.

Statements:

  • All apartments are huts.

  • No hut is a building.

  • All buildings are cottages.

Conclusions:

I. No apartment is a cottage.

II. Some buildings being apartments is a possibility.

options.label: A
options.html: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows.

options.label: C
options.html: Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows.

solution:
Correct answer: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows.

  • Apartment vs building: All apartments are huts, and no hut is a building. Therefore, no apartment can be a building.

  • Conclusion II: This is impossible, because a building being an apartment would also make it a hut, contradicting "No hut is a building."

  • Conclusion I: All buildings are cottages does not mean all cottages are buildings. Apartments may or may not be cottages, so this conclusion is not definite.

Hence, neither conclusion follows.

title: In the following question, some statements are given followed by
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: In the following question, some statements are given followed by some conclusions based on those statements. Taking the given statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance from commonly known facts. Read all the conclusions and then decide which of the given conclusions logically follows the given statements. Statements: I. All F are C. II. No D is F. Conclusions: I. Some C are F. II. All C are D. III. No F is D.
solution:
1. Evaluate Statement I ("All F are C"): This implies F is a subset of C. Consequently, the reverse holds true partially: "Some C are F". Thus, Conclusion I follows.
2. Evaluate Statement II ("No D is F"): This establishes a negative relationship between D and F. Its direct conversion is "No F is D". Thus, Conclusion III follows.
3. Evaluate Conclusion II ("All C are D"): Since we know some C are F (from Step 1), and no F can be D (from Step 2), it is impossible for *all* C to be D. Thus, Conclusion II does not follow.
Final Answer: Option C

title: Identify the features of Aristotelian syllogism from the following It
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Identify the features of Aristotelian syllogism from the following :

(A) It is deductive - inductive and formal material
(B) It is only deductive and formal
(C) The major and minor terms stand apart in the premises
(D) It is verbalistic
(E) Verbal form is not the essence of inference

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
solution: Aristotelian syllogism is deductive and formal; the major and minor terms stand apart in the premises; and it is verbalistic. Hence B, C and D are correct.

title: UGC NET Paper I - July 2016 - canonical question 34
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Given below are two premises and four conclusions are drawn from them (taken singly or together).
Select the code that states the conclusions validly drawn.
Premises :
(i) All religious persons are emotional.
(ii) Ram is a religious person.
Conclusions :
(a) Ram is emotional.
(b) All emotional persons are religious.
(c) Ram is not a non-religious person.
(d) Some religious persons are not emotional.
Codes :
solution:
Concept: A direct syllogism (the Barbara pattern) draws a conclusion from a universal premise "All A are B" together with a particular case "x is A" to validly infer "x is B". Converting a universal affirmative statement -- turning "All A are B" into "All B are A" -- is not a valid inference, and a particular statement that directly contradicts a stated universal premise can never be validly drawn from it. Restating "x is A" in negative form as "x is not non-A" is always a valid immediate inference on its own.

Application:

  1. Ram is emotional combines premise (i), that all religious persons are emotional, with premise (ii), that Ram is a religious person, through the Barbara pattern, so this conclusion follows directly from the two premises.

  2. All emotional persons are religious reverses the subject and predicate of premise (i)'s universal statement; premise (i) alone licenses the direction from religious to emotional, not its reverse.

  3. Ram is not a non-religious person restates premise (ii), that Ram is a religious person, in negative form; this immediate inference needs nothing beyond premise (ii) itself.

  4. Some religious persons are not emotional asserts that some religious persons fall outside premise (i)'s claim that all of them are emotional, directly contradicting that universal premise.

Cross-check:

  • The code combining all four conclusions would require both the reversed premise-(i) statement and the statement contradicting premise (i) to hold at the same time as the two conclusions that do follow from the premises -- a combination inconsistent with the premises.

  • The code keeping only the direct syllogistic conclusion about Ram omits the equally valid negative restatement of premise (ii).

  • The code pairing the direct syllogistic conclusion about Ram with the negative restatement of premise (ii) uses exactly the two conclusions that follow from the premises, leaving out the reversed statement and the contradicting one.

  • The code pairing the reversed premise-(i) statement with the negative restatement of premise (ii) keeps one conclusion that the premises do not license alongside one that they do.

Result: Only the direct syllogistic conclusion that Ram is emotional and the negative restatement that Ram is not a non-religious person are validly drawn from the two premises, so the code "(a) and (c) only" -- pairing exactly these two conclusions -- is the correct answer.

title: You are given two statements and four conclusions. Choose the
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
You are given two statements and four conclusions. Choose the comment about

conclusions from the options given below:
Statements:

All dancers are girls.
All girls are intelligent.

Conclusions:

I. Some girls are dancers.

II. No girl is dancer.

III. Some intelligent are dancers.

IV. All intelligent are dancers.
solution:
Given statements: All dancers are girls. All girls are intelligent.

  • Dancers are a subset of girls (every dancer is a girl).

  • Girls are a subset of intelligent people (every girl is intelligent).

  • By transitivity, dancers are a subset of intelligent people (every dancer is intelligent).

Evaluation of the conclusions:

  1. Conclusion I (Some girls are dancers): Follows. Since dancers are contained within girls, any dancer (if present) is a girl, so there are girls who are dancers.

  2. Conclusion II (No girl is dancer): Does not follow. This contradicts the relation that dancers are girls and thus cannot be concluded.

  3. Conclusion III (Some intelligent are dancers): Follows. Because dancers are intelligent (via girls), any dancer is an intelligent person, so some intelligent people are dancers.

  4. Conclusion IV (All intelligent are dancers): Does not follow. The premises only assert that dancers are intelligent, not that every intelligent person is a dancer.

Final conclusion: Only the statements 'Some girls are dancers' and 'Some intelligent are dancers' follow from the given premises.

title: All flowers are toys. Some toys are trees. Some butterflies
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
All flowers are toys. Some toys are trees. Some butterflies are trees, then

A. No butterfly is flower

B. Some butterflies are toys

C. Some toys are flowers

D. Some trees are flowers

E. Some trees are butterflies

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Concept: A universal statement “All A are B” converts only by limitation to “Some B are A” (never to “All B are A”). A particular statement “Some A are B” converts simply to “Some B are A”, and this holds with full certainty. When a term that links two statements is particular (“some”) in both of them, that term is undistributed in each, so no valid conclusion can be drawn connecting the other two end terms.

  1. Conclusion A (No butterfly is flower): the only path between butterflies and flowers runs through “trees”, but “Some toys are trees” and “Some butterflies are trees” are both particular statements sharing that middle term — it is undistributed in both, so nothing about butterflies and flowers can be validly fixed. Does not follow.

  2. Conclusion B (Some butterflies are toys): for the same reason — two particular premises sharing the undistributed middle term “trees” — no valid link between butterflies and toys can be drawn. Does not follow.

  3. Conclusion C (Some toys are flowers): “All flowers are toys” converts by limitation directly to “Some toys are flowers”. Follows.

  4. Conclusion D (Some trees are flowers): no premise relates trees and flowers directly, and the toys–trees and flowers–toys relations cannot be chained to fix any trees–flowers overlap. Does not follow.

  5. Conclusion E (Some trees are butterflies): a particular statement converts simply, so “Some butterflies are trees” gives “Some trees are butterflies” directly. Follows.

Cross-check: draw flowers entirely inside toys, with toys and trees overlapping in one region and butterflies and trees overlapping in another (possibly different) region — this diagram satisfies every statement. It directly shows the toys–flowers overlap and the trees–butterflies overlap, while the butterflies–flowers and trees–flowers relations stay undetermined, exactly matching the conclusions above.

So only conclusions C and E necessarily follow — the correct choice is “C and E only”.

title: Which of the following statements are so related that if
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Which pair of the following statements is contradictory, i.e. exactly one must be true and the other must be false?

A. All pitcher-plants are carnivores.

B. No pitcher-plants are carnivores.

C. Some pitcher-plants are carnivores.

D. Some pitcher-plants are not carnivores.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
solution:
Correct answer: A and D only

Two categorical statements are contradictory when exactly one of them must be true and the other must be false. They cannot both be true and cannot both be false.

  • A: All pitcher-plants are carnivores. This becomes false if even one pitcher-plant is not a carnivore.

  • D: Some pitcher-plants are not carnivores. This becomes true exactly in that case.

  • A and D are contradictories: if A is true, D is false; if D is true, A is false.

  • A and B are only contraries: they cannot both be true, but they can both be false if some, but not all, pitcher-plants are carnivores.

Hence, only A and D satisfy the required relationship.

title: Choose the Venn diagram from the given options which represents
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Choose the Venn diagram from the given options which represents the correct relationship amongst the following classes:

Pen, Chair, Stationery
solution:
Concept

These are class-relationship (syllogism) diagrams. The link between any two named groups is one of three kinds: one group is wholly a sub-type of the other (one circle drawn entirely inside the other), the groups partly share members (two circles that overlap), or the groups have nothing in common (two circles drawn fully apart). The correct diagram is the one whose circle arrangement matches the real-world relationship of every pair.

Application

Test each pair among Pen, Chair and Stationery:

  • Pen and Stationery: a pen is a kind of stationery, so the whole Pen group sits within the Stationery group — the Pen circle must lie completely inside the Stationery circle.

  • Chair and Stationery: a chair is furniture, not stationery, so they share no members — the Chair circle must stay completely apart from the Stationery circle.

  • Pen and Chair: a pen is not a chair and a chair is not a pen, so these two also share no members — their circles must stay apart.

The arrangement that satisfies all three at once is: one smaller circle fully enclosed by a larger circle, plus a third circle standing entirely on its own, separate from both.

Cross-check

Reject any diagram with overlap (overlap would wrongly claim a chair is partly a pen or partly stationery) and reject any diagram that places two circles inside one outer circle (that would wrongly make a chair a type of stationery). Only the enclosed-circle-plus-one-detached-circle layout keeps Pen inside Stationery while leaving Chair unrelated to both.

title: Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among classes
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among classes given below.

Boys, Students, Athletes
solution:
1. Analyze the Given Classes: The three classes given are "Boys", "Students", and "Athletes".
2. Determine Relationships:
Relationship between Boys and Students: Some boys are students, and some students are boys. This means these two circles must intersect partially.
Relationship between Students and Athletes: Some students are athletes, and some athletes are students. This requires a partial intersection.
Relationship between Boys and Athletes: Some boys are athletes, and some athletes are boys. This also requires a partial intersection.
Combined Intersection: There are individuals who belong to all three categories simultaneously (some individuals are boys, students, and athletes all at the same time).
3. Select the Diagram: A diagram showing three mutually intersecting circles best represents this sharing of traits, which perfectly matches Option 4.

To determine the correct Venn diagram, let’s analyze the relationship between the three terms: Proper Fraction, Numerator, and Denominator.

Mathematical Relationship
A Proper Fraction is defined as a fraction where the numerator is less than the denominator (e.g., 2/3).

A Numerator is a fundamental component of every fraction.

A Denominator is the other fundamental component of every fraction.

Because a fraction is the combination of a numerator and a denominator, both terms are essential parts that constitute the fraction itself. Therefore, the numerator and denominator are both components within the set of a fraction.

Conclusion
Option 2 is the correct choice. It illustrates that both the numerator and the denominator are essential, separate components that reside within the definition of a proper fraction.

title: Which diagram best represents the relationship among Doctor, Women, and
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Which diagram best represents the relationship among Doctor, Women, and Mother?
solution:
In a class-relationship (Venn) diagram, the way two circles are drawn encodes the logical connective between the categories: a universal statement ("every A is B") forces circle A entirely inside circle B; a partial-overlap statement ("some A are B", with also "some A are not B" and "some B are not A") forces the two circles to intersect without either containing the other; and when a third category relates to both groups by such "some" statements on each side, its circle must cross into both regions at once.

  1. “Every mother is a woman” is a universal statement, so the Mother circle must sit entirely inside the Women circle.

  2. “A doctor can be male or female” means Doctor and Women only partly overlap — the Doctor circle must also extend outside the Women circle.

  3. “Some mothers are doctors” means the Doctor circle must also cut into the Mother circle, not just the outer Women region.

  4. Combining all three: the required diagram places a small circle (Mother) wholly inside a larger circle (Women), with a third circle (Doctor) crossing through both the Mother and the Women regions while also extending outside them.

Checking against each incorrect diagram confirms this is the only consistent option:

  • Two separate, non-touching circles inside a third circle would mean no mother is a doctor and every doctor is a woman — this contradicts both “some mothers are doctors” and “a doctor may be a man.”

  • Three fully separate circles with no overlap at all would mean no woman is a mother and no woman is a doctor — this contradicts “every mother is a woman” and the fact that many women are doctors.

  • Two overlapping circles placed entirely inside an outer circle would confine every doctor within the women group, leaving no doctor outside it — this contradicts “a doctor may also be a man.”

So the only diagram consistent with all three facts is the one with the small circle (Mother) wholly inside the larger circle (Women), crossed by a third circle (Doctor).

title: Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among classes
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among classes given below. Boy, Girl, Student
solution:
Concept

A Venn (logic) diagram shows how categories relate by how their circles overlap. Two categories that can never share a member are drawn as separate, non-touching circles (disjoint); a category whose members can also belong to a second category is drawn so the two circles overlap; and a category fully inside another means every one of its members belongs to the larger one.

Application

Test each pair among Boy, Girl and Student:

  • Boy and Girl: no person is both a boy and a girl, so these two categories share no member — their circles must be separate (disjoint).

  • Student and Boy: some students are boys (and some boys are not students), so these two circles must partly overlap.

  • Student and Girl: some students are girls (and some girls are not students), so these two circles must partly overlap as well.

So the matching diagram has two non-touching circles (Boy and Girl) that each overlap a third, central circle (Student), while Boy and Girl never touch each other — the row of three circles in which the middle circle overlaps each of the outer two, and the two outer circles stay apart.

Cross-check

Three fully separate circles would wrongly say no student is a boy or a girl. Three concentric circles (one inside another inside another) would wrongly say every boy is a girl and every girl is a student. A small circle inside a large one with a third circle apart would wrongly make one category a complete subset and leave a category sharing nothing — none of these fits all three real relationships, so they are rejected.

title: Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among classes

bodyHtml:

Brinjal, Banana, Vegetables
solution:
Concept: In a class-relationship (Venn) diagram, one class is drawn INSIDE another only when it is fully contained in it (a subset), and two classes are drawn as separate, non-touching circles when they have nothing in common (disjoint). So before choosing a figure, decide the real-world relationship between each pair of terms.

Apply this to Brinjal, Banana and Vegetables:

  • Brinjal is a kind of vegetable, so every brinjal is a vegetable. Brinjal must sit as a smaller circle wholly INSIDE the Vegetables circle.

  • Banana is a fruit, not a vegetable, so it shares nothing with Vegetables and nothing with Brinjal. Banana must be a separate circle, disjoint from the other two.

Cross-check: the matching figure is the one showing a large circle (Vegetables) with one small circle inside it (Brinjal), and a completely separate circle alongside (Banana) — a big circle enclosing a single small circle plus one detached circle outside.

The other figures encode wrong relationships: three fully separate circles would deny that brinjal is a vegetable; one big circle holding two inner circles would wrongly make banana a vegetable too; three circles nested one inside another would wrongly chain all three as subsets.

title: Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among classes

bodyHtml:
Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among the classes given below.
Boys, Students, Athletes
solution:
CONCEPT: In a Venn diagram, overlapping circles show that sets can share members. When no class is a strict subset of another and membership can overlap in different ways, the suitable diagram uses separate circles that intersect.

The common overlapping part represents members that may belong to all the relevant classes at the same time.

APPLICATION: Boys, students, and athletes are independent classes. Some boys can be students, some students can be athletes, some boys can be athletes, and a boy can also be both a student and an athlete.

So the relationship needs three circles that all overlap each other, including a central common region.

  • Three circles in a chain: it leaves the two end circles without a direct overlap, so it treats one possible pair as unrelated.

  • One large circle with two separate small circles: it makes two classes strict subsets of a third and keeps those two classes apart.

  • One nested pair with a separate circle: it makes one class wholly inside another and treats the third class as unrelated.

Result: the diagram with three mutually overlapping circles best represents Boys, Students, and Athletes.

n(F ∪ W) = (total faculty − faculty not connected to anything) = (150 − 30) = 120

title: In survey where students reported which subjects they like, students
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: In a survey of 100 students, 32 liked Mathematics, 38 liked Business, and 30 liked Literature. The pairwise intersection counts—including students who liked all three subjects—were 7 for Mathematics and Literature, 10 for Mathematics and Business, and 8 for Business and Literature. Five students liked all three subjects. How many students liked exactly one subject?
solution:
Concept: For three sets, a pairwise intersection normally includes members of the three-way intersection unless the question says “exactly two.”

To obtain a single-set-only region, subtract both pairwise intersections involving that set, then add the three-way intersection once because it was subtracted twice.

Application

  1. Mathematics only = 32 − 10 − 7 + 5 = 20.

  2. Business only = 38 − 10 − 8 + 5 = 25.

  3. Literature only = 30 − 7 − 8 + 5 = 20.

  4. Exactly one subject = 20 + 25 + 20 = 65.

Cross-check: The number liking exactly two subjects is (10 − 5) + (7 − 5) + (8 − 5) = 10. Therefore the union contains 65 + 10 + 5 = 80 students, which also equals 32 + 38 + 30 − 10 − 7 − 8 + 5 = 80.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q9
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Out of 120 applicants for a post, 70 are males and 80 have driving licenses. What is the ratio of the minimum to the maximum possible number of males having driving licenses?
solution:
Concept

For two groups A and B within a universe of N people, the smallest possible intersection is max(0, |A| + |B| - N).

The largest possible intersection is min(|A|, |B|), because an intersection cannot exceed the size of either group.

Application

  1. Let A be the 70 male applicants, B be the 80 license holders, and N = 120.

  2. Minimum male license holders = max(0, 70 + 80 - 120) = max(0, 30) = 30.

  3. Maximum male license holders = min(70, 80) = 70.

  4. Required ratio = minimum : maximum = 30 : 70 = 3 : 7.

Cross-check

At the minimum, all 50 non-males can hold licenses, so the remaining 30 license holders are males. At the maximum, all 70 males can hold licenses, which is possible within the total of 80 license holders.

Therefore, the required ratio is 3 : 7.

title: Candidates appeared for examination in three subjects, namely, English Mathematics
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
120 candidates appeared for examination in three subjects, namely, English (E), Mathematics (M) and Science (S). The number of candidates who failed in E, M and S are shown in the diagram given below:

The percentage of candidates who failed in at most two subjects is:
solution:
Key idea: "At most two subjects" means failing in zero, one, or two subjects (everyone except those who failed in all three).

Read the diagram's region counts and sum them:

  • Only English: 13

  • Only Mathematics: 9

  • Only Science: 8

  • English and Mathematics only: 7

  • English and Science only: 8

  • Mathematics and Science only: 10

  • All three subjects: 5

Sum of all regions = 13 + 9 + 8 + 7 + 8 + 10 + 5 = 60. These are the candidates who failed in at least one subject.

Number who failed in at most two subjects = total candidates − those who failed in all three = 120 − 5 = 115.

Percentage = (115/120) × 100 = 95.83%.

Common misunderstandings:

  • Counting only those who failed exactly two gives 25 candidates, which as a percentage is 20.83% (25/120 × 100). That is not what "at most two" asks for.

  • Counting only those who failed one or two subjects gives 55 candidates, which is 45.83% (55/120 × 100). This still excludes those who failed none and so is not the required answer.

Final answer: 95.83%.

title: Ten students and are sitting in row facing west. and
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Ten students A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I and J are sitting in a row facing west. B and F are not sitting on either of the edges; G is sitting to the left of D and H is sitting to the right of J; There are four persons between E and A; I is to the north of B and F is to the South of D; J is between A and D and G is between E and F. There are two persons between H and C.

If G and A interchange their positions then who become immediate neighbours of E?
solution:
Concept

In a linear seating arrangement where everyone faces the same direction, a clue given in compass terms (north/south) must first be converted into the same left/right frame as the other clues, using the shared facing direction: turning 90 degrees clockwise from the direction everyone faces gives everyone's shared right hand. Once every clue speaks the same left-right language, the 'between' and 'edge' clues fix the row order, and any interchange of two seats is resolved by finding who newly occupies the seat next to the person being asked about.

Application

  1. Since every student faces west, each one's right hand points north and left hand points south (turning 90 degrees clockwise from facing west lands on north). So 'I is to the north of B' becomes 'I is to the right of B', and 'F is to the South of D' becomes 'F is to the left of D'.

  2. G is between E and F, and both G (given directly) and F (translated above) sit to the left of D -- so E, G and F form one ordered block, entirely to the left of D, with G sandwiched between the other two.

  3. B and F can never occupy an edge seat, but E carries no such restriction -- so within the E/G/F block, E (not F) must be the one touching the row's edge; the block reads E, then G, then F from that edge inward.

  4. J sits between A and D, and H sits to the right of J -- so D, J, A and H form a chain to the right of the E-G-F block, in that relative order from left to right.

  5. The 'four persons between E and A' clue fixes the gap: with E anchored at the row's left edge, A must sit exactly five seats to its right.

  6. Filling in D (to the right of both G and F) and J (between A and D) gives the order E, G, F, D, J, A for the first six seats.

  7. The remaining clues -- 'two persons between H and C' together with 'I to the right of B' -- place B and I next to each other in seats 8 and 9 (with I to the right of B), and put C and H three seats apart at the two ends of what remains (seats 7 and 10); the given clues do not further distinguish which of C or H takes which end, but neither placement disturbs the seats already fixed for G and A, so it does not affect the answer to this question.

Cross-check

  • Edge check: B sits eighth and F sits third from the left -- neither occupies seat 1 or seat 10, matching the first clue.

  • Between-count check: E (seat 1) and A (seat 6) have G, F, D and J sitting between them -- exactly four people, as required.

  • Gap check: H (seat 10) and C (seat 7) have B and I sitting between them -- exactly two people, as required.

With every clue satisfied, one fully consistent row (left to right) is E, G, F, D, J, A, C, B, I, H (swapping the positions of C and H also satisfies every clue and does not change what follows). Now interchange G (seat 2) and A (seat 6): the row becomes E, A, F, D, J, G, C, B, I, H. E still sits at the extreme left end, so it has only one neighbouring seat -- the one immediately to its right, now occupied by A.

Therefore, after G and A exchange seats, A alone becomes the immediate neighbour of E.

title: Six people are sitting in two parallel rows containing three
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Six people are sitting in two parallel rows containing three people each. In row 1, A, B, and C are seated in order, and in row 2, P, Q, and R are seated in order. B is facing Q, and A is to the immediate left of B. Who is facing A?
solution:
Key facts: two rows facing each other; Row 1 has A, B, C in order; Row 2 has P, Q, R in order.

  • Because B is facing Q, B and Q are opposite each other.

  • A is immediately to the left of B, so the left-to-right order in row 1 is A, B, C.

  • To make B opposite Q while keeping the given orders, row 2 must be left-to-right P, Q, R.

  • Therefore A (left position in row 1) is opposite P (left position in row 2).

Answer: P

title: Directions Study the following information carefully to answer the given
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Directions : Study the following information carefully to answer the given questions:

Ten family members are sitting in two parallel rows containing five people each, in such a way that there is an equal distance between adjacent persons. In row–1 A, B, C, D and E are seated and all of them are facing north. In row-2 P, Q, R, S and T are seated and all of them are facing south. Therefore, in the given seating arrangement each member seated in a row faces another member of the other row.
P faces the one who sits 2nd to the left of his nephew. One person sits between P’s nephew and P’s mother. A is the sister-in-law of D who is not married. S is the granddaughter of B who sits left of P’s mother but not just left. R is the only brother of D who is the only immediate neighbour of B’s wife. Q is the husband of S and sits 2nd to the right of R’s father. A is the daughter of E and faces to the one who sits 2nd to the right of Q’s wife. P is the brother-in-law of R who is the father of C. T’s son sits just right of C’s brother-in-law. A’s father-in-law sits at one of the extreme ends. Both D and A are of same gender but opposite to C’s gender. B is not father of R.

How many persons sit between A’s father and T’s daughter?
solution:
Concept

In a two-parallel-row arrangement, the two rows face each other, so a member of one row faces exactly one member of the other row. “Left” and “right” depend on the direction a person faces: for the north-facing row, left is towards one end and right towards the other, and for the south-facing row these are mirrored. The reliable method is: first fix the family tree (each person’s gender and generation) from the blood- and marriage-relation clues, then seat people using the directional, facing and neighbour clues, and accept only the single layout that satisfies every clue at once.

Building the family tree

  1. R is the only brother of D and is the father of C. D is not married, so the person described as D’s sister-in-law (A) can only be the wife of D’s brother R. Hence A is married to R; A and D are female and C is male.

  2. A is the daughter of E, so E is one of A’s parents. By clue 5, B’s wife sits at an extreme end with D as her only neighbour, which can only be E; hence B and E are husband and wife, making B the other parent — A’s father. The clues “one person sits between P’s nephew and P’s mother” and “P faces the one 2nd to the left of his nephew” also make P a brother of A, consistent with E being the mother of both A and P.

  3. R’s father sits 2nd to the left of Q and at an extreme end. P is only R’s brother-in-law, so R’s father must be T. Thus T is A’s father-in-law, T’s son is R and T’s daughter is D.

Seating the rows

Applying the facing and neighbour clues, the only arrangement that fits is:

Row

Seat 1

Seat 2

Seat 3

Seat 4

Seat 5

Row-1 (North)

B

A

C

D

E

Row-2 (South)

P

R

Q

S

T

Cross-check

  • P faces B, who is 2nd to the left of P’s nephew C — consistent.

  • A faces R, who is 2nd to the right of Q’s wife S — consistent.

  • B’s wife E sits at the extreme end with D as her only adjacent member — consistent.

  • R (T’s son) sits just to the right of Q (C’s brother-in-law) — consistent.

Answer

A’s father is B and T’s daughter is D. Between them sit A and C, so exactly two persons sit between A’s father and T’s daughter.

title: Six participants, and are sitting in two rows, three in
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Six participants — U, V, W, X, Y and Z — are sitting in two rows of three, with each person facing someone in the other row. X is second to the right of Z. W, who is a neighbour of Y, is sitting diagonally opposite X. V is a neighbour of Z. Y is not at the end of any row. If V and U interchange their positions, who would be the neighbours of U in the new position?
solution:
Step 1 — Build one row. "X is second to the right of Z" places Z and X at the two ends of the same row, with one seat between them. Since "V is a neighbour of Z", V takes that middle seat. So this row reads: Z – V – X.

Step 2 — Build the other row. "Y is not at the end of any row", so Y sits in the middle of the opposite row. "W is the neighbour of Y" and W is diagonally opposite X, so W takes the end of that row that lies diagonally across from X. The only person left, U, takes the remaining end. So this row reads: U – Y – W (or W – Y – U), with U opposite Z.

Step 3 — Apply the interchange. V and U swap seats. U moves into V's old middle seat, which sits between Z and X.

Therefore, after the swap, U's neighbours are Z and X, which is option 4.

title: Eight people are sitting in two parallel rows, containing four
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Eight people are sitting in two parallel rows, containing four people each, in such a way that there is equal distance between adjacent persons.

In row 1 – R, S, T and U are seated and all of them are facing south. In row 2 – L, M, N and O are seated and all of them are facing north.

Thus, each person faces another person from the other row. T sits third to the left of U. The person facing T is an immediate neighbour of O. L sits second to the left of O. The person facing M is an immediate neighbour of U. R sits to the immediate right of S. Which of the following represents both people sitting at extreme ends of the line?
solution:
Concept: In a parallel-row (double-row) arrangement the two rows face each other, so a direction word does not carry the same meaning in both rows: whichever way "left" runs for a person in one row, it runs the opposite way for a person in the row facing it. The dependable method is to fix one drawing frame, restate every left/right clue inside that single frame, and start from the clue that admits the fewest placements. Because the rows face each other, the person in seat n of one row always faces the person in seat n of the other row.

Application:

  1. Set the frame. Draw four seats numbered 1 to 4 from left to right for both rows, so that seat n of Row 1 faces seat n of Row 2. Row 1 (R, S, T, U) faces south, so for a Row 1 person "left" runs toward seat 4 and "right" runs toward seat 1. Row 2 (L, M, N, O) faces north, so for a Row 2 person "left" runs toward seat 1 and "right" toward seat 4.

  2. Apply "T sits third to the left of U" in Row 1. Left for this row means moving toward seat 4, so T's seat is three greater than U's seat. In a four-seat row the only fit is U at seat 1 and T at seat 4.

  3. Apply "R sits to the immediate right of S" in Row 1. Right for this row means one seat toward seat 1, so R sits one seat before S. Only seats 2 and 3 remain, which gives R at seat 2 and S at seat 3.

  4. Apply "L sits second to the left of O" in Row 2. Left for this row means moving toward seat 1, so L's seat is two less than O's seat. That leaves two candidates: O at seat 3 with L at seat 1, or O at seat 4 with L at seat 2.

  5. Apply "the person facing T is an immediate neighbour of O". T is at seat 4, so the Row 2 person in seat 4 must sit next to O, and seat 4 has only one neighbour, seat 3. Hence O is at seat 3, which forces L to seat 1, and M and N are left for seats 2 and 4.

  6. Apply "the person facing M is an immediate neighbour of U". U is at seat 1. If M were at seat 4, the person facing M would be T at seat 4, whose only neighbour is S at seat 3, and that is not U. So M is at seat 2, faced by R at seat 2, and R does sit next to U. N therefore takes seat 4.

  7. Read off the two end seats of each row. Row 1 has U at seat 1 and T at seat 4; Row 2 has L at seat 1 and N at seat 4. The people at the extreme ends are therefore U, T, L and N, so the pair whose two names both belong to that set is L and T.

Seat

Row 1 (facing south)

Row 2 (facing north)

Cross-check:

  • For a south-facing person, T at seat 4 is three seats to the left of U at seat 1, and R at seat 2 is immediately to the right of S at seat 3.

  • For a north-facing person, L at seat 1 is two seats to the left of O at seat 3; N at seat 4 faces T and sits next to O; R at seat 2 faces M and sits next to U. All five clues hold.

  • Mirroring the whole diagram, that is numbering the seats the other way round, changes every seat number but leaves the same four people on the end seats, so the result does not depend on which way the rows were drawn.

title: If the position of Manoj is 25th from one end
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: If the position of Manoj is 25th from one end and 23rd from the other end in his class, what is the total number of students in his class?
solution:
Key formula: Total students = position from one end + position from the other end − 1

Apply the formula with the given positions: position from one end = 25 and position from the other end = 23.

Total = 25 + 23 − 1 = 47.

  • Why subtract 1: when you add the two positions the same person is counted twice, so subtracting 1 corrects the double count.

Therefore, the class has 47 students.

title: Read the data given below and based on it answer
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Six girls, Pooja, Qimat, Reeti, Shweta, Tejaswini and Vineeta, are sitting around a circular table. All of them are facing towards the centre of the table (but not necessarily in the same order). Tejaswini is the immediate neighbour of Vineeta and Reeti. Pooja is to the immediate left of Vineeta. Qimat is fourth to the right of Pooja. Shweta is to the immediate left of Pooja. Who is sitting to the immediate left of Shweta?
solution:
Concept

In a circular seating arrangement where everyone faces the centre, "immediate left of X" and "immediate right of X" name the two seats adjacent to X in fixed, opposite rotational directions — left is the clockwise neighbour and right is the anticlockwise neighbour, as viewed from above. Every "nth to the left/right of" clue is just an offset around the circle, so a chain of such clues fixes every seat relative to one reference person.

Application

  1. Fix a direction: number the six seats 0-5 going clockwise, so "immediate left of Y" = seat (Y + 1), and "n-th to the right of Y" = seat (Y − n), all taken mod 6.

  2. Place Vineeta at seat 0 as the reference point.

  3. Pooja is the immediate left of Vineeta, so Pooja = 0 + 1 = seat 1.

  4. Shweta is the immediate left of Pooja, so Shweta = 1 + 1 = seat 2.

  5. Qimat is fourth to the right of Pooja, so Qimat = 1 − 4 = seat −3 ≡ seat 3 (mod 6).

  6. Two seats remain, 4 and 5, for Reeti and Tejaswini. Vineeta's (seat 0) two neighbouring seats are 5 and 1; seat 1 is already Pooja, so Tejaswini — who must neighbour Vineeta — has to occupy seat 5, leaving Reeti at seat 4.

  7. This also satisfies the rest of that clue: Reeti (seat 4) and Tejaswini (seat 5) are adjacent, so Tejaswini neighbours Reeti as well.

  8. The full arrangement, going clockwise from Vineeta, is: Vineeta - Pooja - Shweta - Qimat - Reeti - Tejaswini - back to Vineeta.

  9. The immediate left of Shweta (seat 2) is seat 3, which is Qimat.

Cross-check

  • Pooja is Vineeta's immediate left: seat 0 + 1 = seat 1 = Pooja. Holds.

  • Shweta is Pooja's immediate left: seat 1 + 1 = seat 2 = Shweta. Holds.

  • Qimat is fourth to Pooja's right: seat 1 − 4 ≡ seat 3 = Qimat. Holds.

  • Tejaswini neighbours both Vineeta (seat 0) and Reeti (seat 4): Tejaswini at seat 5 is adjacent to both. Holds.

All four original clues hold simultaneously in this one arrangement, so the seat assignment is unique (up to an overall rotation, which never changes anyone's relative order). Therefore, Qimat is sitting to the immediate left of Shweta.

title: Seven friends and are sitting in circle facing the center.
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Seven friends — A, B, C, D, E, F and G — are sitting in a circle, facing the centre. B is sitting immediately to the right of A and immediately to the left of D. Who is sitting immediately to the right of A?
solution:
Concept

In a circular arrangement, directional clues are read from each seated person’s own point of view. Two immediate-adjacency clues that share a person can be combined into a contiguous block before the unused seats are considered.

Application

  1. Use the direct clue about A: B is immediately to the right of A.

  2. Combine the second clue: B is immediately to the left of D. In the stated rightward direction, the three-person block is A – B – D.

Cross-check

In this block, B has A immediately on one side and D immediately on the other, so both adjacency statements hold together. The positions of C, E, F and G cannot alter this local block.

Result

Therefore, B is sitting immediately to the right of A.

title: Five girls are sitting in circle facing the center. Shivani
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Five girls are sitting in a circle facing the center. Shivani is sitting exactly to the immediate left of Vinay. Anita is sitting between Disha and Vinay. Vibha is sitting exactly to the immediate right of Disha. Who is sitting exactly to the immediate right of Vibha?
solution: 1. Facing the center means "left" is clockwise and "right" is anti-clockwise. 2. Placing them step-by-step: Shivani is immediate left (clockwise) of Vinay. Anita is between Disha and Vinay. Vibha is immediate right (anti-clockwise) of Disha. 3. This creates the clockwise sequence: Vinay -> Shivani -> Vibha -> Disha -> Anita -> (back to Vinay). 4. The person to the immediate right (anti-clockwise) of Vibha is Shivani. Final Answer: Option D

title: Six friends are sitting in circle facing the centre. Bharat
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Six friends are sitting in a circle facing the centre. Bharat is on the left of Vinod. Rajesh is between Bharat and Mukesh. Jayant is between Vinod and Narendra. Who is to the left of Mukesh?
solution:
1. For people sitting in a circle facing the center, 'left' means moving in a clockwise direction.

  2. Build the clockwise sequence: Bharat is on the left of Vinod (Vinod -> Bharat). Rajesh is between Bharat and Mukesh (Vinod -> Bharat -> Rajesh -> Mukesh).

  3. Jayant is between Vinod and Narendra, completing the circle (Narendra -> Jayant -> Vinod).

  4. The complete clockwise order is: Narendra, Jayant, Vinod, Bharat, Rajesh, Mukesh. The person immediately to the left (clockwise) of Mukesh is Narendra.

Final Answer: Option D

title: Seven friends Alice, Bob, Carol, David, Eve, Frank, and Grace
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Seven friends Alice, Bob, Carol, David, Eve, Frank, and Grace are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. Alice is sitting to the immediate right of Bob. Bob and Carol are neighbours. Frank is sitting exactly between David and Eve. Grace is not sitting next to Carol or Eve. Who is sitting between Alice and David?
solution: Bob has Alice on his immediate right, Bob and Carol are neighbours, Frank is exactly between David and Eve, and Grace is not next to Carol or Eve. The only valid circular placement puts Grace between Alice and David.

title: Seven friends, and are sitting around round table facing towards
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Seven friends, A, E, I, O, U, X and Z are sitting around a round table facing towards the center. A is neighbor of E and I. O is not neighbor of I and Z who is second to the left of O and has U and X as neighbours? Who is between A and O?
solution: Solving the circular arrangement gives E as the person sitting between A and O. The result is unchanged under either clockwise orientation convention.

title: Six friends are sitting in circle facing the center. Pramod
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Six friends are sitting in a circle facing the center. Pramod is to the left of Vinod. Tushant is between Pramod and Mayank. Jignesh is in between Vinod and Nitin. Who is to the left of Mayank?
solution:
Concept

When everyone in a circle faces the centre, each person's left hand points along the clockwise direction. So the statement "X is to the left of Y" means X occupies the seat immediately next to Y in the clockwise sense, and "P is between Q and R" means P sits with Q on one side and R on the other.

Application

Fix the seats clockwise using the clues:

  1. "Pramod is to the left of Vinod" places Pramod in the seat clockwise-adjacent to Vinod, so the clockwise pair reads Vinod then Pramod.

  2. "Tushant is between Pramod and Mayank" puts Tushant next to Pramod and Mayank on either side, extending the clockwise run to Pramod, Tushant, Mayank.

  3. "Jignesh is between Vinod and Nitin" puts Jignesh with Vinod and Nitin as neighbours; the only way to close the circle of six is the clockwise order Pramod, Tushant, Mayank, Nitin, Jignesh, Vinod.

  4. The person to Mayank's left is the seat clockwise-adjacent to Mayank, which is Nitin.

Cross-check

Read the final clockwise circle Pramod, Tushant, Mayank, Nitin, Jignesh, Vinod and re-test every clue: Pramod indeed sits just clockwise of Vinod; Tushant has Pramod and Mayank as neighbours; Jignesh has Vinod and Nitin as neighbours. All three conditions hold, confirming that Nitin is to the left of Mayank.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q7
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Six boys are so standing that they form a circle, each facing the centre. Rabi is to the left of Ramen, Subrata is between Abir and Biman, Bimal is between Rabi and Abir. Who is to the left of Bimal?
solution:
Concept. When people stand in a circle and every one of them faces the centre, "left" is a single fixed rotational sense that is the same for all of them: whichever way round the ring one person's left hand points, every other person's left hand points the same way round. A clue of the form "P is to the left of Q" therefore carries two pieces of information at once — P and Q are neighbours, and P is the very next person after Q when you walk around the ring in that left-sense. Chaining enough such neighbour clues fixes the entire cyclic order, after which "who is to the left of X" is answered simply by reading one step onward from X in the same sense.

Application. Take the "left" sense as the direction of travel and build the ring one clue at a time.

  1. "Rabi is to the left of Ramen" makes the two of them neighbours and puts Rabi immediately after Ramen along the direction of travel: Ramen → Rabi.

  2. "Bimal is between Rabi and Abir" makes Bimal a neighbour of both boys. Rabi already has Ramen on one side, so Bimal can only take Rabi's other side, and Abir sits just beyond Bimal: Ramen → Rabi → Bimal → Abir.

  3. "Subrata is between Abir and Biman" makes Subrata a neighbour of both. Abir already has Bimal on one side, so Subrata takes Abir's other side and Biman follows Subrata: Ramen → Rabi → Bimal → Abir → Subrata → Biman.

  4. All six boys are now placed, so Biman closes the ring back onto Ramen. Reading one step onward from Bimal along the direction of travel gives Abir, so Abir stands to the left of Bimal.

Cross-check. Written out as a closed ring, each boy’s two neighbours are:

Boy

On his left

On his right

Ramen

Rabi

Biman

Rabi

Bimal

Ramen

Bimal

Abir

Rabi

Abir

Subrata

Bimal

Subrata

Biman

Abir

Biman

Ramen

Subrata

Every clue checks out against the ring: Rabi does sit on Ramen’s left, Bimal does sit between Rabi and Abir, and Subrata does sit between Abir and Biman. The result is also independent of which rotational sense one chooses to call "left": mirroring the whole circle swaps the two senses, but it relabels every clue at the same time, so Abir still ends up on Bimal’s left.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q12
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Six friends—David, Bhanu, Minto, Krita, John and Nisan—are sitting in a circle with their backs towards the centre. David and Minto are sitting immediately to the left and right of Bhanu, respectively. John is not sitting immediately to the left of David. Nisan is sitting third to the right of Bhanu. Who is sitting second to the left of Bhanu?
solution:
Concept

When people face away from the centre of a circle, their left is in the clockwise direction and their right is in the anticlockwise direction. Fixing one person as a reference removes the effect of rotating the whole circle.

Application

  1. Place Bhanu at a reference seat. Since everyone faces outward, place David immediately clockwise from Bhanu and Minto immediately anticlockwise from Bhanu.

  2. Place Nisan third to Bhanu's right, which is the seat opposite Bhanu.

  3. Two seats remain. The seat immediately to David's left is the clockwise seat next to David. Since John cannot occupy it, Krita occupies that seat and John occupies the other remaining seat.

  4. Moving two seats to Bhanu's left means moving two seats clockwise. That seat is occupied by Krita.

Cross-check

Reading the completed circle in the opposite direction confirms that John is second to Bhanu's right, while Krita is second to Bhanu's left; all four clues remain satisfied.

Result

Krita is sitting second to the left of Bhanu.

title: And are sitting in circle facing the centre. sits third
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: G, H, J, K, L, M and N are sitting in a circle facing the centre. ‘M’ sits third to the right of ‘K’. ‘J’ sits second to the left of ‘N’. ‘L’ is an immediate neighbour of ‘M’. ‘G’ sits immediate right of ‘H’. Only one person sits between ‘G’ and ‘K’. Who sits second to the right of ‘L’?
solution:
Reasoning: place K as reference and use the given constraints to fix all positions.

  • M is third to the right of K, so M is three seats clockwise from K.

  • G sits immediate right of H, and there is exactly one person between G and K. This places G two seats away from K and H immediately left of G.

  • L is a neighbour of M, so L occupies the remaining adjacent seat to M.

  • J sits second to the left of N, which fixes J and N in the two remaining seats.

Final seating (clockwise), starting from K: K, N, L, M, H, G, J

Now count the seats to the right (clockwise) of L: first to the right is M, second to the right is H.

Answer: H

title: DSSSB TGT Special Education Teacher 24 Jun 2025 Shift 3 Q39
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Seven people P, Q, R, S, T, U and V are sitting around a circular table facing the centre.

U sits third to the left of P. R sits third to the right of V. S sits to the immediate right of R. S sits second to the left of U. T sits immediately to the left of P.

Who are the immediate neighbours of Q?
solution:
In a circular seating puzzle where everyone faces the centre, every "X sits nth to the left/right of Y" clue is a fixed directional offset from Y along the circle. Fixing one person as the reference seat and applying each offset in a single consistent rotational direction places every other person; the seats immediately before and after the person asked about then give its immediate neighbours.

Application

  1. Fix P at seat 1 of the 7 circular seats, numbered 1 to 7 in the direction that corresponds to a seated person's left (since everyone faces the centre, moving to a person's right goes the opposite way around the same numbering).

  2. T sits immediately to the left of P, so T takes seat 2 (1 + 1).

  3. U sits third to the left of P, so U takes seat 4 (1 + 3).

  4. S sits second to the left of U, so S takes seat 6 (4 + 2).

  5. S sits immediately to the right of R, so R is one seat further in the left direction than S, taking seat 7 (6 + 1).

  6. R sits third to the right of V, so V is three seats further in the left direction than R: 7 + 3 = 10, which wraps around the 7-seat circle to seat 3.

  7. Seats 1 to 7 are now P, T, V, U, blank, S, R, with only seat 5 left empty, so Q takes seat 5.

Cross-check

  • T immediately left of P: seat 2 minus seat 1 equals 1.

  • U third to the left of P: seat 4 minus seat 1 equals 3.

  • S second to the left of U: seat 6 minus seat 4 equals 2.

  • S immediately to the right of R: from seat 7 (R), one step right lands on seat 6 (S).

  • R third to the right of V: from seat 3 (V), three steps right lands on seat 7 (R), wrapping the same way the arrangement was built.

  • Every one of the five original clues holds in this final order, and it is the only order consistent with all of them together.

With Q fixed at seat 5, the seats on either side of it are seat 4 (U) and seat 6 (S). So the immediate neighbours of Q are U and S.

title: Eight friends and are sitting around square table. Out of
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Eight friends P, Q, R, S, T, V, W and Y are sitting around a square table.

  1. Out of eight, four persons are sitting at the corners of the table and the other four are sitting at the mid-points of each side of the table.

  2. Persons at the corners are facing the centre while the persons at the mid points of side are facing outside.

  3. S is third to the right of P. P is facing the centre.

  4. Y is not sitting beside P or S.

  5. T is third to the right of R.

  6. R is not sitting at the mid-point of any side of the table.

  7. R is also not beside Y.

  8. There is only one person between P and V.

  9. Q is not sitting beside V.


How many people are there between T and Q ?
solution:
Concept: In circular or square seating puzzles, a person's left-right sense depends on which way they face. A person facing the centre has the clockwise direction (as the layout is drawn) as their LEFT, so their RIGHT runs counter-clockwise; a person facing outward has this reversed, with clockwise as their RIGHT. The number of people "between" two seats is counted along the shorter arc joining those two seats.

Application:

  1. Number the eight seats 1 to 8 clockwise, with corners at seats 1, 3, 5, 7 (facing the centre) and mid-points at seats 2, 4, 6, 8 (facing outward). Since P faces the centre, place P at a corner -- seat 1.

  2. P faces the centre, so P's right runs counter-clockwise. S, third to P's right, lands three seats counter-clockwise from seat 1, at seat 6 -- a mid-point.

  3. R never sits at a mid-point, so R must occupy one of the remaining corner seats: 3, 5 or 7.

  4. Only one person separates P and V, so V sits two seats from P along one arc -- seat 3 or seat 7, both corners.

  5. R must be seat 3, 5 or 7, and V must be seat 3 or 7 (clue 6). Testing the four possible pairings against the adjacency clues on Y (clues 2 and 5): V=3 with R=5, V=3 with R=7, and V=7 with R=3 each force Y into a seat that sits beside P, S or R, breaking clue 2 or clue 5. Only V=7 with R=5 leaves a seat for Y that clears every adjacency clue. This pairing also fixes T -- third to R's right, counter-clockwise -- at seat 2.

  6. With P, S, R, T and V fixed, Y cannot sit beside P (seats 8 or 2) or beside S (seats 5 or 7); of the seats still open, Y also cannot sit beside R (seat 4), so Y must take seat 3.

  7. The last two open seats, 4 and 8, remain for Q and W. Since Q cannot sit beside V (seat 8 is beside V's seat 7), Q takes seat 4 and W takes seat 8.

Cross-check: Every clue holds against the seating 1-P, 2-T, 3-Y, 4-Q, 5-R, 6-S, 7-V, 8-W: S is exactly third to P's right, T is exactly third to R's right, Y sits beside neither P nor S, R does not sit beside Y, exactly one person sits between P and V, and Q does not sit beside V.

Result: T occupies seat 2 and Q occupies seat 4; the shorter arc between them (seat 2 to seat 3 to seat 4) passes through only one seat, seat 3. So exactly one person sits between T and Q.

title: Study the following information carefully to answer the given questions:
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Study the following information carefully and answer the question. Eight persons—A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and H—sit around a square table. Four sit at the middle of the sides and face inward, while four sit at the corners and face outward. G sits second to the left of C. Three persons sit between D and B. H sits opposite A but does not sit at the middle of a side. D sits second to the left of A. F sits second to the right of C. E sits immediately to the right of B. Who sits immediately to the right of D?
solution:
Concept

In a mixed-facing seating arrangement, left and right are read from each seated person’s own viewpoint. At a square table, corner seats face outward and side-middle seats face inward, so their clockwise and counterclockwise directions are reversed. A valid answer therefore requires fixing all seats before reading an immediate-neighbor relation.

Application

  1. Number the seats 0 through 7 clockwise and place A at corner seat 0; choosing a starting seat only fixes the rotation and does not change any relationship.

  2. H is opposite A and is not at a side-middle, so H is at corner seat 4. Because A faces outward, A’s left runs counterclockwise; D, second to A’s left, is at corner seat 6.

  3. Three persons sit between D and B, so B is opposite D at corner seat 2. B also faces outward, making B’s immediate right the next clockwise seat; therefore E is at side-middle seat 3.

  4. The remaining side-middle seats are 1, 5, and 7 for C, F, and G. Since C faces inward, C’s second-left position is two seats clockwise and its second-right position is two seats counterclockwise.

  5. If C were at seat 1, G would need occupied seat 3. If C were at seat 5, F would need occupied seat 3. The only consistent case is C at seat 7, which places G at seat 1 and F at seat 5.

  6. The unique clockwise order is therefore A, G, B, E, H, F, D, C. D is at outward-facing corner seat 6, so D’s own right runs clockwise to seat 7, occupied by C.

Cross-check

The final order gives H opposite A, B opposite D with three persons on either arc, D second to A’s left, E immediately to B’s right, G second to C’s left, and F second to C’s right. Every clue holds with no collision, confirming that C sits immediately to D’s right.
