title: Eight friends, and are sitting around square table facing centre.
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Eight friends, P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W are sitting around a square table facing centre. One each is sitting at the midpoints of the sides and one each at the corners of the table. Each person is wearing different colour T-shirt. One in Yellow color is occupying one of the corners. He has the Q in red T-shirt to his immediate left who is second to the right of 'V' in green T-shirt. W in white is opposite 'V' in Green and is between T and R. S in grey T-shirt is between P in black and R in Pink T-shirt. U in Blue T-shirt is diagonally opposite R. Who is wearing yellow T-shirt?
solution:
Concept: In a circular or square seating puzzle where everyone faces the centre, moving clockwise (as the layout is normally drawn) always lands on each person's immediate LEFT neighbour, and moving anticlockwise lands on their immediate RIGHT neighbour -- the reverse of the usual convention for people facing outward. In an 8-seat layout, a seat 4 positions away is 'opposite'; two corners 4 seats apart are 'diagonally opposite'; and when every person but one already has a distinct attribute stated for them directly, the one attribute left over must belong to the one person left over.

Application -- building the seating step by step:

  1. Colours already named directly in the text: P-black, Q-red, R-pink, S-grey, U-blue, V-green, W-white -- seven of the eight friends. Only T has no stated colour, and yellow is the only colour left unassigned, so T is the corner-seated friend in yellow. Label T's seat as seat 1 of 8 (seats 1, 3, 5, 7 are corners; seats 2, 4, 6, 8 are midpoints).

  2. Q is T's immediate left; since facing-centre left means the next seat clockwise, Q takes seat 2.

  3. Q is second to the right of V; right means anticlockwise, so counting two seats anticlockwise from V reaches Q -- this places V at seat 4.

  4. W is directly opposite V (seat 4), so W sits at seat 8 (4 seats away).

  5. W sits between T and R; W's two neighbouring seats are 7 and 1 -- seat 1 is already T, so R must take seat 7.

  6. U is diagonally opposite R; R (seat 7) is a corner, so U takes the corner 4 seats away, seat 3.

  7. S sits between P and R; R's free neighbouring seat is 6, so S takes seat 6, and S's other neighbour, seat 5, is P.

Two friends are sitting in between ‘M’ and ‘S’. ‘R’ is second to the left of ‘J’. ‘S’ is exact left of ‘L’. ‘K’ is third to the left of ‘L’. Who sits fourth to the right to 'K'?
solution:
Solution overview:

  • Place L at a side-mid position.

  • S is immediate left of L. (When facing the centre, left = clockwise.)

  • K is third to the left of L, and Q is immediate right of K and is also at a side-mid.

  • M is immediate right of J, P is second to the left of M, R is second to the left of J, and there are two people between M and S. Also P is not adjacent to L.

One seating arrangement that satisfies all conditions (listed clockwise) is:

  1. L

  2. S

  3. Q

  4. K

  5. M

  6. J

Find who is fourth to the right of K:

  • Remember: when everyone faces the centre, a person's right is the counterclockwise direction.

title: Eight colleagues and are sitting surrounding an octagon table facing
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Eight colleagues H, I, J, K, L, M, N, and O are sitting surrounding an octagon table facing each other at different corners of the table. H is the second left to K. I is the neighbor of M and N. O is second left of N. L is between J and H. J is immediate to M.Who is the third person left to J?
solution:
Concept: When all persons in a circular or polygonal seating arrangement face the centre of the table, moving in the "left" direction from any person corresponds to the clockwise direction as viewed from above. Every clue of the form "X is nth left/right of Y" or "X is the neighbour of Y" is really a positional equation on seat numbers taken modulo the total number of seats. The puzzle is solved by fixing one person's seat as a reference, translating every clue into such an equation, and finding the single arrangement of all persons that satisfies every equation at once.

  1. Fix J's seat as position 0 (the reference point). Number the 8 seats 0-7 running clockwise, and since everyone faces the centre, "left" means increasing position number (clockwise).

  2. "L is between J and H" makes L adjacent to both J and H, so J and H sit on the two sides of L. Checking the two possible placements of L relative to J shows only L at position 7 (with H at position 6) is consistent with the rest of the clues; the other placement later forces H's own clue onto J's seat, which is a contradiction.

  3. "J is immediate to M" places M next to J. With position 7 already taken by L, the only free seat next to J is position 1, so M sits at position 1.

  4. "I is the neighbour of M and N" means M and N are I's two neighbours. With M at position 1, checking both neighbour orders shows I must sit at position 2 (the other order collides with J's seat), which places N at position 3.

  5. The two remaining seats, 4 and 5, go to K and O. "H is second left of K" gives position(K) = position(H) - 2 = 6 - 2 = 4, so K takes position 4.

  6. "O is second left of N" gives position(O) = position(N) + 2 = 3 + 2 = 5, so O takes the last free seat, position 5.

  7. The complete clockwise seating is now fixed. The third person to the left of J is three seats clockwise from J's seat: 0 + 3 = 3, which is N's seat.

  • I is the neighbour of M and N: I (seat 2) sits between M (seat 1) and N (seat 3). Holds.

  • J is immediate to M: J (seat 0) and M (seat 1) are adjacent seats. Holds.

So the third person to the left of J is N.

title: And live on six different floors of the same building.
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: R, E, M, I, N and S live on six different floors of the same building. The lowermost floor in the building is numbered 1, the floor above it, number 2 and so on, till the topmost floor is numbered 6. Only four people live above I. Only S lives above M. N lives immediately above R. What is the sum of the floor numbers of E and N?
solution:
Concept

In a floor-arrangement puzzle, place the absolute clues before the relative ones. In a building of n floors, a clue of the form "exactly k people live above X" pins X to floor n - k, and a clue naming exactly who lives above someone pins both of them at once.

Only after every absolute position is fixed do you fit the relative blocks: a clue of the form "P lives immediately above Q" needs a pair of consecutive floors that are both still free.

Applying it to this building

  1. The six floors are numbered 1 at the bottom up to 6 at the top, and R, E, M, I, N and S occupy one floor each.

  2. Four people live above I, so four floors lie above I. That pins I to floor 6 - 4 = 2.

  3. Only S lives above M, so exactly one floor lies above M and S occupies it. That pins M to floor 5 and S to floor 6.

  4. Floors 1, 3 and 4 are still free, and they must be taken by R, N and E.

  5. N lives immediately above R, which needs two consecutive free floors. Among the free floors 1, 3 and 4 the consecutive pair is 3 and 4, so R is on floor 3 and N is on floor 4. The pair 1 and 2 is unusable because floor 2 already holds I.

  6. E takes the single floor left over, floor 1.

  7. The sum of the floor numbers of E and N is therefore 1 + 4 = 5.

title: And live on six different floors of the same building.
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: S, O, R, B, E and T live on six different floors of the same building. The lowermost floor in the building is numbered 1, the floor above it, number 2 and so on, till the topmost floor is numbered 6. Only two people live above B. Only E lives between S and O. R lives immediately above T. S lives on one of the floors below R. Who lives on floor number 5?
solution:
Concept. A floor-arrangement puzzle is solved by working outward from the most restrictive clue, not by guessing an arrangement. Three clue shapes do almost all the work: "only n people live above P" pins P exactly, because with F floors in all P must stand on floor F - n; "only X lives between P and Q" forces P, X and Q onto three consecutive floors with X in the middle, so they behave as one rigid block; and "R lives immediately above T" forces a rigid pair of adjacent floors. Place the pinned person first, fit the rigid block into whatever consecutive floors remain, then drop the rigid pair into what is left, and use any remaining above/below clue purely as a consistency check.

Application to this question.

  1. The building has six floors, numbered 1 at the bottom up to 6 at the top, and six residents: S, O, R, B, E and T.

  2. Only two people live above B, so exactly two floors lie above B. Therefore B stands on floor 6 - 2 = 4.

  3. Only E lives between S and O, so exactly one resident separates them and that resident is E. S, E and O must therefore occupy three consecutive floors with E in the middle.

  4. Floor 4 is already taken by B, so the runs 2-3-4, 3-4-5 and 4-5-6 are all blocked. The only free run of three consecutive floors is 1-2-3. Hence E stands on floor 2, and S and O take floors 1 and 3 in some order.

  5. Floors 5 and 6 are the only floors still empty, so R and T must fill them. R lives immediately above T, which forces T onto floor 5 and R onto floor 6.

  6. The last clue, S lives on one of the floors below R, is satisfied automatically: S is on floor 1 or 3, and R is on floor 6.

  7. Floor number 5 is therefore occupied by T.

title: And live on six different floors of the same building.
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: F, E, R, P, Q and L live on six different floors of the same building. The lowermost floor in the building is numbered 1, the floor above it, number 2 and so on, till the topmost floor is numbered 6. Only R lives above L. Only E lives below P. How many people live between P and L?
solution:
Concept. In a floor puzzle the word "only" makes a clue an exact count, not a mere comparison. "Only X lives above Y" says the number of people above Y is exactly one, which pins Y absolutely: in a building of n floors numbered 1 at the bottom to n at the top, a person with exactly k people above them lives on floor n − k, and a person with exactly k people below them lives on floor k + 1.

Concept (cont.). Once two floors are pinned, the number of people living strictly between floor a and floor b (with a < b) is b − a − 1. That count depends only on the two pinned floors, never on how the still-unplaced people are distributed among the remaining floors.

Application to this arrangement.

  1. Six people occupy six floors, one person per floor, numbered 1 (lowest) up to 6 (topmost).

  2. "Only R lives above L" → exactly one person lives above L, so L is on floor 6 − 1 = 5, and the single person above, R, is on floor 6.

  3. "Only E lives below P" → exactly one person lives below P, so P is on floor 1 + 1 = 2, and the single person below, E, is on floor 1.

  4. Floors 1, 2, 5 and 6 are now occupied by E, P, L and R, so the two people left, F and Q, take the two floors left, 3 and 4, in some order.

  5. Apply the between-count: with P on floor 2 and L on floor 5, the number of people strictly between them is 5 − 2 − 1 = 2 — the residents of floors 3 and 4.

Final arrangement.

Cross-check and contrast.

  • The two clues fix E, P, L and R uniquely and leave F and Q interchangeable on floors 3 and 4. The arrangement is therefore only partly determined, yet the quantity asked for is fully determined: whichever way F and Q sit, floors 3 and 4 are still the only floors strictly between floor 2 and floor 5, so the count is 2 either way.

  • Common trap: reading "only R lives above L" as the weaker "R lives above L" would allow L on any floor below R and make the count indeterminate. The word "only" is what converts a comparison into an exact count and pins the floors.

  • Sanity check on the endpoints: no one lives above R (floor 6) and no one lives below E (floor 1), which is consistent with R being the single person above L and E the single person below P.

title: Five books and are kept one above the other in

bodyHtml: Five books A, B, C, D and E are kept one above the other in such a way that 'E' is above 'A', 'C' is below 'D', 'A' is above 'D' and 'B' is below 'C'. Which book is kept at the lowermost position?
solution:
Translate each clue into an 'above/below' relation (top of the stack is higher).

E is above A -> E > A. A is above D -> A > D. C is below D -> D > C. B is below C -> C > B.

Linking these gives the single ordering from top to bottom: E, A, D, C, B.

Hence the book at the lowermost position is B.

title: Sukanya is Ayushman’s wife. Lekha is Sukanya’s sister. Nisha is
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Sukanya is Ayushman’s wife. Lekha is Sukanya’s sister. Nisha is Lekha’s mother. Mukesh is Nisha’s husband. Piyush is Nisha’s son. How is Ayushman related to Mukesh?
solution:
Concept: In blood-relation puzzles, a person who marries into a family takes an “in-law” relationship to their spouse’s parents: the husband of a couple’s daughter is their son-in-law. To find how any two people relate, first turn every sentence in the stem into a parent-child or marriage link, build one family tree from those links, then read the relationship straight off the tree.

Application:

  1. Sukanya is Ayushman's wife, so Ayushman and Sukanya are married.

  2. Lekha is Sukanya's sister, so Lekha and Sukanya share the same mother and father.

  3. Nisha is Lekha's mother, and since Sukanya is Lekha's sister, Nisha is Sukanya's mother too.

  4. Mukesh is Nisha's husband, which makes Mukesh Sukanya's father.

  5. Piyush is Nisha's son, so Piyush is Sukanya's brother — Mukesh and Nisha's three children are Piyush, Lekha, and Sukanya.

  6. Ayushman is married to Mukesh's daughter Sukanya, so Ayushman is Mukesh's son-in-law.

Cross-check: Viewed from Mukesh's side: his son Piyush's wife would be his daughter-in-law, while the husbands of his daughters Lekha and Sukanya are his sons-in-law. Ayushman, as Sukanya's husband, falls in that second group, confirming the relationship independently of the step-by-step trace.

Ayushman is Mukesh's son-in-law.

title: Kiran is the father of Ravi. Ravi is the brother
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Kiran is the father of Ravi. Ravi is the brother of Kavya. Then, how is Kavya related to Kiran ?
solution:
CONCEPT: In a family-relation (blood-relations) puzzle, two people who share the same father or mother are siblings. The word 'brother' fixes only the speaker's own gender as male — it does not, by itself, state the other sibling's gender; that comes from the name or wording given, since a father's child is called his son or his daughter depending on that gender.

APPLICATION: Kiran is the father of Ravi, so Ravi is Kiran's child. Ravi is the brother of Kavya, so Ravi and Kavya are siblings who share the same father, Kiran. The name Kavya is a female name, so Kavya is Kiran's daughter, not his son.

CROSS-CHECK — the other options do not fit:

  • Mother-in-law would require a marriage relationship (e.g. being the mother of one's spouse); no marriage appears anywhere in this puzzle, only a father-child link.

  • Sister correctly describes Kavya's relation to Ravi, but the question asks for Kavya's relation to Kiran, a different person.

  • Grandmother belongs one generation above Kiran; Kavya, as Ravi's sibling, is in the same generation as Ravi — one generation below Kiran, not above.

So Kavya is Kiran's daughter.

bodyHtml: A is the brother of B, C is the father of D, E is the mother of B. A and D are brothers. How E relates to C ?
solution:
To determine how E relates to C, we need to map out the family relationships step-by-step.

Step-by-Step Relationship Analysis
Analyze the statements:

"A is the brother of B": A and B are siblings.

"E is the mother of B": Since A and B are siblings, E is also the mother of A.

"A and D are brothers": Since A and D are brothers, they share the same parents. Therefore, E is also the mother of D.

"C is the father of D": Since D is A's brother, C is also the father of A and B.

Determine the final relationship:

E is the mother of the children (A, B, and D).

C is the father of the same children (A, B, and D).

Therefore, E and C are husband and wife.

C and D are sisters: Since C and D are sisters, and we established D is A's child, C is also A's child.

Relationship between B and C:

B is the brother of A.

title: If is the husband of and is the mother of

bodyHtml: If 'P' is the husband of 'Q' and 'R' is the mother of 'S' and 'Q', then what is the relationship between R and P?
solution: P is the husband of Q, so Q is P's wife. R is the mother of S and Q, which means R is the mother of Q. Since Q is P's wife, R (Q's mother) is the mother of P's wife — that is, P's mother-in-law. Hence the correct answer is Mother-in-law.

bodyHtml: 'A' is the father of 'B' and 'C'. 'B' is 'A's son, but 'C' is not 'A's son. What is 'C's relationship with 'A'?
solution: A is the father of both B and C. B is A's son. C is also A's child but is stated not to be A's son, so C must be female. Therefore, C is A's daughter.

title: Is the husband of is the daughter of is the
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: R' is the husband of 'Q', 'P' is the daughter of 'R', 'S' is the husband of 'P', 'E' is the daughter of 'S'. What is the relationship of 'E' to 'Q'?
solution:
Concept

In a blood-relation chain, decode each clue into a parent-child or spouse link first, then read the connection from the named person back to the target by following the chain of links. "Husband/wife" joins two people of the same generation; "daughter/son" moves down exactly one generation. The relationship two generations below a person (their child's child) is grandchild.

Tracing the chain

  1. R is the husband of Q, so R and Q are a married couple in the same generation.

  2. P is the daughter of R (and therefore of Q as well) — P is one generation below Q.

  3. S is the husband of P, so S marries into P's generation; P is still one generation below Q.

  4. E is the daughter of S and P — E is one generation below P, hence two generations below Q.

Result

E is the child of Q's daughter, i.e. two generations below Q and female. A female grandchild is a Grand Daughter, so E is the Grand Daughter of Q.

Cross-check

Count the downward steps from Q: Q → P (one step down) → E (a second step down). Two downward steps and E being female gives exactly "granddaughter", which confirms the result.

title: Is the son of is the granddaughter of who is
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: M is the son of ‘P’, ‘Q’ is the granddaughter of ‘O’ who is the husband of ‘P’. How ‘M’ relates to ‘O’?
solution:
Concept

In a blood-relation puzzle, fix each person's gender and link every stated relationship into a single family chain. A key identity here: if two people are husband and wife, then the child of one of them is also the child of the other; so the child of a person's spouse is that person's own child.

Application

  1. O is the husband of P, so O and P are a married couple and O is male.

  2. M is the son of P. Because O is P's husband, M is the child of O's wife, which by the identity above makes M a child of O too.

  3. M is described as a son, i.e. male, so M is the male child of O. Therefore M is the son of O.

Cross-check

Q being the granddaughter of O is extra information about O's descendants and does not change the M-to-O link; it only confirms O is the head of the family. Reading the chain back the other way, O (P's husband) is the father of M, which is consistent with M being O's son. So the relation of M to O is Son.

title: In family, there are six members and and are married
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: In a family, there are six members A, B, C, D, E and F. A and B are a married couple, A being the male member. D is the only son of C; who is the brother of A. E is the sister of D. B is the daughter-in-law of F, whose husband has died. How is E related to C?
solution:
Concept: In a blood-relation puzzle, fix each person's gender and generation from the explicit clues, then chain the parent–child and sibling links. A child of a person is that person's son (male) or daughter (female); siblings share the same parents, so a sibling of someone's child is also that person's child.

Application — decode the clues step by step:

  1. A and B are a married couple and A is male, so A is the husband and B is the wife.

  2. C is the brother of A, and D is the only son of C. So D is C's child (male).

  3. E is the sister of D. Siblings share the same parents, so E is also a child of C — and since E is a sister, E is C's daughter.

  4. Therefore E is the daughter of C.

Cross-check: B is the daughter-in-law of F (whose husband has died), and B married A, so F is the mother of A and C. The family is consistent: F is the grandmother, A and C are her sons, and E (with brother D) is a child of C. E being D's sister and D being C's son confirms E is C's daughter.

title: Ranjan is the brother of Sachin and Manick is the
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Ranjan is the brother of Sachin and Manick is the father of Ranjan. Jagat is the brother of Priya and Priya is the daughter of Sachin. Who is the uncle of Jagat?
solution:
Concept: To solve a blood-relation puzzle, translate every sentence into a parent-child or sibling link and assemble one family tree, then read the required relation directly off that tree. An uncle is specifically a parent's brother — one generation up, on the sibling line, never the parent or grandparent themselves.

  1. Ranjan is the brother of Sachin, so Ranjan and Sachin are siblings sharing the same parents.

  2. Manick is the father of Ranjan, so — since Ranjan and Sachin are siblings — Manick is also the father of Sachin.

  3. Priya is the daughter of Sachin, so Sachin is a parent of Priya.

  4. Jagat is the brother of Priya, so Jagat is also a child of Sachin, making Sachin the parent of Jagat.

  5. Sachin is Jagat's parent, and Ranjan is Sachin's brother, so Ranjan — the parent's brother — is Jagat's paternal uncle.

Cross-check: Tracing purely from Jagat's side confirms it — his parent is Sachin, and Sachin's sibling is Ranjan, so the parent's-brother slot is filled by Ranjan alone; Sachin himself occupies the parent slot (not the uncle slot) and Manick sits a further generation back as the grandparent, so neither fits the definition of uncle being asked for.

title: Direction: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Direction: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions based on given information.
In a family of eight members, there are two married couples and no child has single parent. K is the brother-in-law of T. Y is the aunt of S. O is the grandson of N. Q is the daughter-in-law of K. P is not the daughter of N. S is not the brother of O. T is the uncle of Y.

How is Q related to N?
solution:
Concept:

In a family-relations puzzle, first fix each person's generation (using clues like grandson, aunt, uncle, brother-in-law) and gender, then read the asked relation off the constructed family tree. An “-in-law” relation always attaches through a marriage link — it is one step removed from the direct blood relation of the same base word (for example, a daughter-in-law is a son's wife, not one's own daughter).

Application:

  1. Q is the daughter-in-law of K, so K has a son and that son's wife is Q. K and the son's mother form the first married couple; the son and Q form the second married couple. The puzzle fixes the whole family at exactly TWO married couples, and “no child has a single parent” means every child in this tree belongs to one of those two couples — so any child of the son and Q could become a parent in turn only by forming a THIRD couple, which the family does not have. This tree is therefore capped at exactly three generations: K's generation, the son's generation, and any children of the son and Q.

  2. K is the brother-in-law of T, so T is the sibling of K's spouse — placing T in K's own generation.

  3. T is the uncle of Y, so T's sibling (K's spouse) is a parent of Y. That makes Y a child of K and K's spouse, and a sibling of K's son.

  4. Y is the aunt of S, so Y's sibling (K's son, married to Q) is a parent of S. S is therefore a child of K's son and Q, in the youngest generation.

  5. O is the grandson of N. A grandson is always two generations below his grandparent, and step 1 fixed this tree at exactly three generations — so only a member of the OLDEST generation (K or K's spouse) can have a grandson; K's own son, being one generation below K, cannot have a grandson within this three-generation limit. All eight names denote eight distinct people, and K already carries his own separate label, so N cannot be K himself. N can therefore only be K's spouse.

  6. With K, N, T, Y and Q now placed, the only unassigned name left is P, and the only role in the tree still without a name is K and N's son (Q's husband, parent of S) — so P must fill that role. “P is not the daughter of N” independently confirms P is male, consistent with being this son rather than a second daughter alongside Y.

  7. N's only grandchildren, through her son P and Q, are S (already fixed in step 4) and O — so O is S's sibling. “S is not the brother of O” then confirms S is female, which fits the tree without contradiction.

Cross-check:

  • Member count: K, N, T, Y, P, Q, S, O — exactly eight people, matching the given family size.

  • Married-couple count: (K, N) and (P, Q) — exactly two couples, matching “two married couples.”

  • “No child has a single parent” holds: Y and P (children of K and N) and S and O (children of P and Q) each have both parents present in the family.

Result:

Q is married to N's son (P), so by definition Q is N's daughter-in-law.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q82
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: A woman is going with a child. On asking the woman about her relation with the child, she replied ‘The child’s mother is the only daughter of my mother’. How is the woman related to the child?
solution:
Concept: In blood-relation puzzles, restate every relationship phrase as a direct kinship link, and resolve a phrase like “the only [relation] of Y” as pointing to one specific family member rather than a separate, unnamed person — then substitute that identity back into the sentence.

Application:

  1. The woman states: “The child’s mother is the only daughter of my mother.”

  2. “My mother” refers to the woman’s own mother.

  3. The woman is herself one of her mother’s children, and her mother has only ONE daughter — so that only daughter can only be the woman herself.

  4. Therefore “the only daughter of my mother” = the woman.

  5. Substituting back: “the child’s mother” = the woman.

Cross-check: If the woman had a sister, her mother would have more than one daughter, which would contradict the word “only” in the statement. So the phrase can only describe the speaker herself, confirming the direct parent link between the woman and the child.

Result: The woman is the child’s mother.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q6
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Given that:

(i) A is the brother of B

(ii) C is the father of A

(iii) D is the brother of E

(iv) E is the daughter of B, then the uncle of D is
solution:
Concept: An uncle is the brother of a person's father or mother, or the husband of that person's aunt. The relation can therefore never be read off a single statement: first fix whose child the person is, and only then look for a brother of that parent. The dependable method for any such data set is to build the family tree generation by generation, fixing each person's generation and gender before answering.

Application — building the family tree:

  1. By statement (iv), E is the daughter of B. So B is a parent, and E stands one generation below B.

  2. By statement (iii), D is the brother of E. Siblings share the same parents, so D is a child of B as well, and D is male.

  3. By statement (i), A is the brother of B. So A stands in B's own generation, as B's male sibling.

  4. By statement (ii), C is the father of A. C therefore stands one generation above A and B, and since A and B are siblings, C is the father of B as well.

  5. Now apply the definition. The parent of D is B, and the brother of B is A. So A is the brother of D's parent, which is exactly what uncle means.

Cross-check — where every person sits in the finished tree:

Person

Generation

Relation to D

C

Grandparent generation

Grandfather of D, being the father of D's parent B

A

Parent generation

Uncle of D, being the brother of D's parent B

B

Parent generation

Parent of D and of E

E

Same generation as D

Sister of D

D

Same generation as E

The person whose uncle is being asked for

Result: the uncle of D is A.

title: Is father of and is son of is brother of
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: A is father of C and D is son of B. E is brother of A. C is sister of D. How is B related to E?
solution:
Step 1: Analyze the relationships given in the problem.

A is the father of C and D.

D is the son of B.

C is the sister of D.

E is the brother of A.

Step 2: Determine the relationship between A and B.

Since A is the father of C and D, and D is the son of B, B must be the mother of C and D (assuming A and B are the parents).

Step 3: Determine the relationship between B and E.

E is the brother of A. Since B is the wife of A, B is the sister-in-law of E.

Conclusion: B is the sister-in-law of E.

हिन्दी उत्तर:

चरण 1: दिए गए संबंधों का विश्लेषण करें।

A, C और D का पिता है।

D, B का पुत्र है।

C, D की बहन है।

E, A का भाई है।

चरण 2: A और B के बीच संबंध निर्धारित करें।

चूंकि A, C और D का पिता है, और D, B का पुत्र है, इसलिए B, C और D की माता होनी चाहिए (यह मानते हुए कि A और B माता-पिता हैं)।

चरण 3: B और E के बीच संबंध निर्धारित करें।

निष्कर्ष: B, E की साली/भाभी है।

title: Girl introduced boy as the son of the daughter of the father of her uncle
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: A girl introduced a boy as the son of the daughter of the father of her uncle. The boy is the girl's ______.
solution:
Concept

Relation-chain puzzles often leave the SIDE of a relative (paternal or maternal) unspecified — e.g. 'uncle' could be either parent's brother. Resolve that kind of ambiguity with two rules together: (1) since this is a single-answer puzzle, the reading that matches an actually offered choice is the intended one — a reading that can only ever land on a relation not in the option list is discarded; (2) among the readings that survive rule 1, the standard convention is to assume no additional unstated relatives — each remaining phrase names the person already required to connect the chain back to the querent, not a hypothetical extra sibling. Apply the general definitions — 'father of X' is X's parent, 'daughter of Y' is Y's female child, 'son of Z' is Z's male child — and sketch a small family tree as you trace the chain.

Step-by-step application

  1. Let U = the girl's uncle; in principle U could be her father's brother or her mother's brother.

  2. If U is the girl's PATERNAL uncle, “the father of U” is her paternal grandfather, and “his daughter” can only be U's sister — the girl's father's sister, i.e. an aunt (never the girl's mother, since the mother married into that family and isn't the paternal grandfather's own daughter). That aunt's son would be a cousin, a relation that isn't among the offered options — so by rule 1 this reading is discarded.

  3. So U must be the girl's MATERNAL uncle. “The father of U” = the girl's maternal grandfather, F.

  4. “The daughter of F” is a sister of U — either the girl's own mother, or a different sister of U (a maternal aunt). By rule 2 (no extra unstated relative), this daughter is the one already required to connect the chain back to the girl: her own mother, M.

  5. “The son of the daughter of F” = M's son, i.e. the girl's mother's son.

  6. A mother's son, being a person distinct from the girl, is the girl's brother.

Cross-check

Checking in reverse: the boy is F's grandson through his mother M; M is F's daughter and a sibling of the maternal uncle U — exactly the family tree the given diagram shows. Both decision points are load-bearing: taking U as the paternal uncle, or taking F's daughter as a different maternal aunt, would each land on a 'cousin' relation that has no matching option — only the fully maternal, direct-lineage reading lands on an offered choice, which is why the standard, published resolution of this well-known puzzle gives 'brother'.

Visual family tree

title: Pointing to photograph, lady said, he is the brother of

bodyHtml: Pointing to a photograph, a lady said, “He is the brother of my husband's father's son.” How is the man related to the lady?
solution:

  2. Now consider "the brother of [that person]": if the inner person is the husband, the brother of that person is the husband's brother. If the inner person is one of the husband's brothers, the brother of that person could be the husband or another brother. In all cases the described man is a male from the husband's generation (a brother of the husband).

  3. Relation to the lady: a male who is the husband's brother is the lady's brother-in-law.

Answer: brother-in-law

bodyHtml: A + B means ‘A is the father of B’, A − B means ‘A is the wife of B’, A × B means ‘A is brother of B’, A ÷ B means ‘A is the daughter of B’. If R − V × T ÷ W, then how is R related to W?
solution:
- Given relation string: R - V × T ÷ W
- Breakdown of relationships from left to right:
- R - V: 'R is the wife of V' (R is female, V is male, and they are a married couple: R(-) ⇔ V(+))
- V × T: 'V is brother of T' (V and T are siblings, sharing the same generation: V(+) — T)
- T ÷ W: 'T is the daughter of W' (T is female, and W is the parent of T: W is one generation above T)
- Generation and family tree tracking: Since V and T are siblings, W is the parent of both V and T. R is married to V, which means R is the wife of W's son.
- Therefore, R is the daughter-in-law of W.

title: If means is the mother of means is the brother
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: If “A 1 B” means A is the mother of B; “A 2 B” means A is the brother of B; “A 3 B” means A is the father of B and “A 4 B” means A is the sister of B, which of the following shows that ‘P is the maternal uncle of Q’?
solution:
To determine which option shows that "P is the maternal uncle of Q," we first need to break down the symbols provided:

1: Mother (A 1 B = A is the mother of B)

2: Brother (A 2 B = A is the brother of B)

3: Father (A 3 B = A is the father of B)

4: Sister (A 4 B = A is the sister of B)

To be a maternal uncle, P must be the brother of Q's mother. Therefore, the chain must show that P is a brother to someone who is the mother of Q.

Step-by-Step Analysis of the Required Chain
P is the brother of M: P 2 M

M is the mother of Q: M 1 Q

Combined chain: P 2 M 1 Q

Looking at the options, we need to find a variation of this logic that confirms the relationship.

title: In certain code language, means is the son of means
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
In a certain code language,

P + Q means 'P is the son of Q',

P & Q means 'P is the husband of Q',

P % Q means 'P is the mother of Q',

and P # Q means 'P is the sister of Q'.

Which of the following mean(s) that F is the father of T?

(I) R % F & S % N & T

(II) R % F & S % N # T

(III) R # F & S % N # T

(IV) R % F + S # N # T
solution:
Concept — In a coded-relationship chain every symbol relates only the two letters standing immediately on either side of it, and the chain is read from left to right. Calling one person the father of another needs two independent facts to hold at the same time: that person has to be male, and the other has to be his child. Maleness comes from a male-specific link such as husband or son. Parenthood can be reached directly through a parent link, or indirectly through marriage, because the husband of a woman who is the mother of a child is that child's father; and since siblings share the same parents, a parent of one sibling is a parent of the other.

So two things have to be located inside a chain before F can be called the father of T:

  • a link that marks F as male, which here can only be the husband link or the son link;

  • a route from F to T that ends in parenthood, either because F is given directly as a parent of T, or because F is the husband of a woman who is the mother of T or of a sister of T.

Applying it — Each statement is decoded link by link, and the last column records what the decoded chain makes F to T.

Statement

Links, read from left to right

What the chain makes F to T

I. R % F & S % N & T

R is the mother of F; F is the husband of S; S is the mother of N; N is the husband of T

F is the husband of N's mother, so F is the father of N; T is the wife of N, which makes F the father-in-law of T

II. R % F & S % N # T

R is the mother of F; F is the husband of S; S is the mother of N; N is the sister of T

N is a sister of T, so N and T are siblings and S is the mother of T as well; F is the husband of S and is therefore the father of T

III. R # F & S % N # T

R is the sister of F; F is the husband of S; S is the mother of N; N is the sister of T

the same core chain: S is the mother of T, so F, being her husband, is the father of T; the link joining R to F adds nothing

IV. R % F + S # N # T

R is the mother of F; F is the son of S; S is the sister of N; N is the sister of T

F is marked as a son and sits one generation below S, N and T; S is a sister of N and N is a sister of T, so T is a sibling of F’s mother, that is F’s maternal aunt or uncle, and in no case his child

Cross-check — Statements II and III carry the same operative sub-chain, F & S % N # T: F is the husband of S, S is the mother of N, and N is the sister of T. That sub-chain is precisely the indirect route to fatherhood set out above, and the point where those two statements differ, R as the mother of F against R as the sister of F, lies outside it and changes nothing. The remaining two break at an identifiable link instead: in I the final link is a husband link, so T arrives as a spouse rather than as a child, and in IV the second link marks F himself as a son.

The statements that mean F is the father of T are therefore II and III.

title: Read the following information carefully and answer the given questions.
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Read the following information carefully and answer the given questions.

‘A + B’ means A is sister of B.
‘A − B’ means A is husband of B.
‘A × B’ means A is brother of B.
‘A ÷ B’ means A is daughter of B.

How is P related to M in the expression M ÷ L − N + P × Q?
solution:
Concept

In a coded-relationship expression, replace each symbol with the relationship it stands for and read the chain one link at a time between adjacent people. Track each person's gender from the relationship words, then trace the path from the first named person to the second.

Applying it to M ÷ L − N + P × Q

  1. M ÷ L means M is the daughter of L, so L is a parent of M.

  2. L − N means L is the husband of N; therefore L is male (M's father) and N is female (M's mother).

  3. N + P means N is the sister of P, so P is a sibling of N — and N is M's mother.

  4. P × Q means P is the brother of Q, which confirms that P is male.

Cross-check

P is male and is the brother of N, who is M's mother. The brother of one's mother is the maternal uncle. Hence P is the maternal uncle of M.

title: Means is father of means is daughter of means is
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
A + B means 'A is father of B' A - B means 'A is daughter of B' A × B means 'A is brother of B' A ÷ B means 'A is sister of B'

If P - V + L × N - V, then how is P related to N?
solution:
In coded blood-relation puzzles, each symbol represents one fixed family relation. To relate two people who are connected through several symbols, decode every adjacent pair from left to right into an actual relation, use those individual relations to build one shared family tree, and then read the relation between the two people directly off that tree.

  1. P − V: P is daughter of V, so V is a parent of P.

  2. V + L: V is father of L, so L is a child of V.

  3. L × N: L is brother of N, so N is also a child of V, and a sibling of L.

  4. N − V: N is daughter of V, confirming N is a female child of V.

  5. V is now fixed as the common father of P, L and N; both P (from step 1) and N (from step 4) are daughters of V.

Cross-check: N's position is fixed twice independently — once through L × N (N is a child of V because L is) and once directly through N − V (N is V's daughter) — and both agree, so the family tree has no contradiction. P's own link to V (step 1) already places her as V's daughter in the same generation as N.

Since P and N are both daughters of the same father, V, P is the sister of N.

title: DSSSB TGT Special Education Teacher 24 Jun 2025 Shift 3 Q25
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
In a certain code language,

‘A ÷ B’ means ‘A is the sister of B’,

‘A # B’ means ‘A is the brother of B’,

‘A + B’ means ‘A is the wife of B’ and

‘A % B’ means ‘A is the father of B’.

How is A related to K if ‘A + B % G ÷ H # K’?
solution:
Concept:

In coded blood-relation puzzles, each symbol stands for one direct family relation (parent-of, sibling-of, spouse-of). To find how one person relates to another placed several links away, decode every symbol in the chain one link at a time, then combine the direct relations using standard family rules: siblings share the same parents, and a person's spouse holds the same parental relation to that person's children.

Application:

  1. Decode each symbol used in ‘A + B % G ÷ H # K’: ‘+’ = wife of, ‘%’ = father of, ‘÷’ = sister of, ‘#’ = brother of.

  2. A + B → A is the wife of B.

  3. B % G → B is the father of G.

  4. G ÷ H → G is the sister of H, so G and H share the same parents.

  5. Since B is the father of G, and H shares G's parents, B is also the father of H.

  6. H # K → H is the brother of K, so H and K share the same parents.

  7. Since B is the father of H, and K shares H's parents, B is also the father of K.

  8. A is the wife of B, and B is the father of K, so A is the mother of K.

Cross-check:

Retracing the chain independently: A's own generation is fixed only by the '+' (wife-of) link to B, so A and B belong to one generation. So G, H, and K are all one generation below A and B, and A's relation to any of them, including K, is that of mother.

title: J's father is N's paternal uncle. M's husband is J's
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: J's father R is N's paternal uncle. M's husband L is J's only paternal uncle. How is M related to N?
solution:
Concept

A paternal uncle is a brother of one's father. The qualifier "only" fixes the exact number of siblings: if a father has just one brother, then any other person described as that father's brother has to be the very same person.

Applying it

  1. R is J's father, and R is N's paternal uncle, so R is a brother of N's father.

  2. L (M's husband) is J's only paternal uncle, which means R — J's father — has exactly one brother, and that brother is L.

  3. From step 1, N's father is a brother of R. Since R has exactly one brother, namely L, N's father must be L.

  4. M is L's wife, and L is N's father, so M is the wife of N's father — that is, N's mother.

Cross-check

Put L as N's father: then R, being L's brother, is correctly N's paternal uncle, and L is indeed J's only paternal uncle. Every statement in the puzzle holds, confirming that M is N's mother.

title: Jayant who is the only son of his father pointed
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Jayant who is the only son of his father pointed to the photograph of a kid and said, ‘he is the grandson of my son’s sister’s mother’s father-in-law. How is Jayant related to that boy?
solution:
Concept: In a chained blood-relation statement such as ‘my X’s Y’s Z’, unpack one relation at a time, starting nearest to the speaker and working outward, before naming the final relative. Two identities matter here: a person’s ‘son’s sister’ is that person’s own daughter, since a son and his sister usually share the same parents; and a married person’s ‘father-in-law’ is their spouse’s father, not a blood relative of their own.

  1. ‘My son’s sister’ is Jayant’s daughter, because Jayant’s son and his sister share the same parents.

  2. That daughter’s mother is Jayant’s own wife.

  3. Jayant’s wife’s father-in-law is her husband’s father, that is, Jayant’s own father.

  4. So the phrase identifies the photographed kid as a grandson of Jayant’s father.

  5. Jayant is stated to be the only son of his father — this detail only does useful work if the ‘grandson’ being pointed to is read as one produced through a son (a grandson via a daughter would make the ‘only son’ fact irrelevant to solving the puzzle), so the intended reading is the grandson through Jayant’s own line.

  6. Since Jayant is his father’s only son, that grandson-through-a-son is Jayant’s own child.

  7. A kid described this way is therefore Jayant’s own son.

Cross-check: If the boy is Jayant’s son, then Jayant’s father is the boy’s grandfather, and Jayant’s father’s grandson through his only son, Jayant, is exactly the boy in the photograph — matching the original statement, and matching the Hindi original’s precise word for this relation, which names a grandson specifically through a son.

Answer: Jayant is the boy’s father.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q17

bodyHtml: Introducing a man to her husband, a woman said, ‘his brother’s father is the only son of my paternal grandfather’. How is the woman related to this man?
solution:
Concept: In blood-relation puzzles, a person and their brother are treated as full siblings who share the same father (the convention this puzzle genre uses unless stated otherwise), so a person's brother's father is simply that person's own father. Also, “the only son of someone's paternal grandfather” identifies that someone's own father directly — a family with exactly one son in that generation leaves no other candidate for the role.

Application:

  1. The woman says: the man's brother's father is the only son of my paternal grandfather.

  2. Her grandfather has only one son, so that son must be the woman's own father.

  3. The man's brother shares the man's father, so "the man's brother's father" is simply the man's own father.

  4. Both phrases describe the same person, so the man's father equals the woman's father.

  5. Two people who share the same father are siblings, so the woman and the man are siblings.

Cross-check: If the woman is the man's sister, her father is also his father. Her grandfather's only son is then her father, and separately, the man's brother's father is also her father — both descriptions land on the exact same person, so the relationship is consistent.

Result: The woman is the man's sister.

title: Person walks km East, then turns degrees to the right
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: A person walks 7 km East, then turns 90 degrees to the right and walks 8 km, then turns left and walks 5 km. In which direction is the person now from the starting point ?
solution:
To find the final direction, let's track the movement step-by-step using a coordinate system, starting at (0, 0).

Step-by-Step Movement Analysis
Movement 1: Walk 7 km East.

New position: (7, 0)

Movement 2: Turn 90 degrees right and walk 8 km. (Turning right from East faces South).

New position: (7, -8)

Movement 3: Turn left and walk 5 km. (Turning left from South faces East).

New position: (7 + 5, -8) = (12, -8)

Determining Direction
Your final position is (12, -8).

Since the x-coordinate (12) is positive, you are East of the starting point.

Since the y-coordinate (-8) is negative, you are South of the starting point.

Combining these, the direction from the starting point is South-East.

title: Clock is so placed that at noon its minute hand
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: A clock is so placed that at 12 noon its minute hand points towards North-east. In which direction does its hour hand point at 1:30 p.m.?
solution:
To determine the direction of the hour hand at 1:30 p.m., we must first calculate the rotation applied to the clock face.

Step-by-Step Analysis
Determine the Clock's Rotation:

Normally, at 12:00 noon, the minute hand points North.

In this scenario, the minute hand points North-East.

North-East is a 45-degree clockwise rotation from North. Therefore, the entire clock has been rotated 45 degrees clockwise.

Determine the Hour Hand's Position at 1:30 p.m.:

On a standard clock, the hour hand at 1:30 is halfway between the 1 and 2 marks.

Each hour mark represents 30 degrees (360 degrees / 12 hours).

At 1:00, the hour hand is at 30 degrees from the vertical (North). At 1:30, it has moved halfway to the 2 o'clock mark (an additional 15 degrees).

Standard position = 30 degrees + 15 degrees = 45 degrees East of North.

Apply the Clock's Rotation:

Since the clock is rotated 45 degrees clockwise, we add this rotation to the standard position.

Total direction = 45 degrees (standard position) + 45 degrees (clock rotation) = 90 degrees from North.

90 degrees from North is East.

title: Mahesh is going towards East. If he has to go
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Mahesh is going towards East. If he has to go towards North, which of the following options should he NOT choose?
solution:
Treat each 'right' as a 90 degrees clockwise turn and each 'left' as a 90 degrees turn the other way. Starting while facing East, the net turning of a full sequence decides the final direction.

From East, ending up facing North needs a net turn equal to one left turn (which is the same as three right turns).

Sequence right, right, left, right, right: the turns add up to a net of three rights, taking him from East to South to West to North - he faces North.

Sequence right, right, left, left, left: the rights and lefts combine to one net left, taking him from East to North - he faces North.

Sequence right, right, right: from East, three rights go South, West, North - he faces North.

Sequence right, left, right, left: every right is cancelled by the left that follows it, so the net turn is zero and he still faces East - this one never reaches North.

So the sequence he should NOT choose is right, left, right, left.

title: Person walks meters North from place. After that he turns

bodyHtml: A person walks 20 meters North from a place. After that he turns right and walks 30 meters. After that he turns right and walks 35 meters. After that he turns left and walks 15 meters and then again turning left walks 15 meters. At what distance and in which direction is he from his initial position?
solution:
Take the starting point as the origin and track the person's coordinates after each leg, using East as positive x and North as positive y. The person begins facing North.

Leg 1 - walks 20 m North: now at (0, 20), facing North.

Leg 2 - turns right (now faces East), walks 30 m: now at (30, 20), facing East.

Leg 3 - turns right (now faces South), walks 35 m: now at (30, -15), facing South.

Leg 4 - turns left (now faces East), walks 15 m: now at (45, -15), facing East.

Leg 5 - turns left (now faces North), walks 15 m: now at (45, 0), facing North.

Final position is (45, 0). The net North-South displacement cancels out (20 North minus 35 South plus 15 North = 0), while the net East-West displacement is 30 + 15 = 45 m East. Hence he is 45 meters East of his initial position.

title: Man is facing North-West. He turns in the clockwise direction,
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: A man is facing North-West. He turns 90° in the clockwise direction, then 180° in the anticlockwise direction and then another 90° in the same direction. Which direction is he facing now?
solution:
Concept

Direction problems are solved on the 8-point compass, read clockwise as N → NE → E → SE → S → SW → W → NW and back to N, where each adjacent point is 45° apart. A clockwise turn moves you along that order; an anticlockwise turn moves you against it (N → NW → W → SW → S …). Apply each turn to the direction you are CURRENTLY facing, one turn at a time, and “the same direction” always refers to the sense of the turn that came immediately before it.

Step-by-step

  1. Start facing North-West.

  2. Turn 90° clockwise: moving clockwise two 45° steps from North-West passes through North and lands on North-East. Now facing North-East.

  3. Turn 180° anticlockwise: a half-turn always points you to the exact opposite direction, so North-East becomes South-West. Now facing South-West.

  4. Turn 90° in the same direction: “same direction” means anticlockwise again. Moving anticlockwise two 45° steps from South-West passes through South and lands on South-East. Now facing South-East.

Cross-check

Track the net rotation in signed degrees (clockwise positive), with North-West at 315°: 315° + 90° − 180° − 90° = 135°. A bearing of 135° is South-East, confirming the result.

title: Shyam walked metres towards south. Then he turned to his

bodyHtml: Shyam walked 20 metres towards south. Then he turned to his left and walked 15 metres. He again turned to his left and walked 20 metres. He then turned to his right and walked 10 metres. How far and in which direction is Shyam from the starting point?
solution:
1. Start Point: Let the starting point be 'A'.
2. First Movement: Shyam walks 20 metres towards South to reach point 'B'.
3. Second Movement: Turning left (towards East), he walks 15 metres to reach point 'C'.
4. Third Movement: Turning left again (now facing North), he walks 20 metres to reach point 'D'. At this point, he is exactly parallel to his starting point line because the northward distance (20m) matches his initial southward distance (20m).
5. Fourth Movement: Turning to his right (towards East), he walks another 10 metres to reach the final point 'E'.
6. Distance Calculation:
Distance from starting point line 'A' to 'D' is equal to BC = 15 metres. Total horizontal distance from A to final point E = AD + DE = 15 metres + 10 metres = 25 metres.
7. Direction Calculation:
Looking from the starting point A, the final point E lies directly towards the East. Hence, the final position is 25 Metres, East.

title: Murari walked km towards North, took left turn and walked
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Murari walked 40 km towards North, took a left turn and walked 20 km. He again took a left turn and walked 40 km. How far and in which direction is he from the starting point?
solution:
Concept

In direction problems, represent each movement as a displacement vector. Take east as the positive x-direction and north as the positive y-direction; west and south then have negative components.

Add horizontal components separately from vertical components. Opposite movements of equal length cancel, and the remaining vector gives both the distance and the direction from the starting point.

Application

  1. Start at (0, 0). Moving 40 km north changes the position to (0, 40).

  2. A left turn while facing north points west. Moving 20 km west changes the position to (-20, 40).

  3. A second left turn while facing west points south. Moving 40 km south changes the position to (-20, 0).

Cross-check

  • The 40 km northward and 40 km southward components cancel: 40 - 40 = 0.

  • The only non-zero component is 20 km westward, so the displacement magnitude is 20 km and its direction is West.

Therefore, Murari is 20 km West of the starting point.

What is the shortest distance between Point Q and Point C? (All turns are 90-degree turns only)
solution:
Concept: A direction-sense path is solved by fixing one origin and two perpendicular axes, then writing every leg as a change in exactly one coordinate — take east as the positive x-direction and north as the positive y-direction.

A left turn rotates the walker 90 degrees anticlockwise, so the facing cycles from north to west to south to east and back to north. Once both endpoints are written as coordinates, the shortest distance between them is the straight line joining them.

Application: track each leg of the two walks as a change in one coordinate.

  1. Place Point C at the origin (0, 0), with east as +x and north as +y.

  2. Tara walks 23 m south from C, reaching (0, -23), and is now facing south.

  3. Facing south, her left turn points her east; walking 10 m east takes her to (10, -23).

  4. Facing east, her next left turn points her north; walking 17 m north takes her to (10, -23 + 17) = (10, -6), which is Point D.

  5. Point P lies 15 m east of D, so P is at (10 + 15, -6) = (25, -6).

  6. Bruce walks 6 m north from P, reaching (25, -6 + 6) = (25, 0), and is now facing north.

  7. Facing north, his left turn points him west; walking 16 m west takes him to (25 - 16, 0) = (9, 0), which is Point Q.

  8. C is at (0, 0) and Q is at (9, 0), so the east-west change is 9 and the north-south change is 0. The straight-line distance is the square root of the sum of the squares of these two changes.

    √(92 + 02) = √81 = 9

Cross-check: Tara ends 10 m east and 6 m south of C, while Bruce ends 16 m west and 6 m north of P. Bruce’s 6 m northward leg exactly cancels Tara’s 6 m southward net displacement, so Q sits on the same east-west line as C and no north-south gap survives.

The whole east-west account is therefore 10 m east from Tara, plus 15 m east from D to P, minus 16 m west from Bruce, giving 9 m east. With the north-south gap zero, the straight-line distance equals that east-west gap.

The shortest distance between Point Q and Point C is 9 m.

The final point (0, 5) lies directly North of the house, so the straight-line distance from the house is 5 m.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q13
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: A person travels 12 km due North, then 15 km due East, after that 15 km due West and then 18 km due South. How far is he from the starting point?
solution:
When a person walks through a sequence of directional legs, the straight-line distance back to the starting point (the resultant displacement) is found by resolving every leg onto two perpendicular axes — North-South and East-West — and combining the legs on each axis. Movements in opposite directions on the same axis cancel each other out (they subtract); if the net displacement on one axis works out to zero, the resultant distance equals just the magnitude of the net displacement on the other axis.

  1. Group the four legs onto the two axes: North (12 km) and South (18 km) lie on the North-South axis; East (15 km) and West (15 km) lie on the East-West axis.

  2. Net East-West displacement = 15 km East − 15 km West = 0 km, so the East and West legs cancel out exactly.

  3. Net North-South displacement = 12 km North − 18 km South = 6 km net towards the South.

  4. Since the East-West component is 0 km, the straight-line distance from the starting point equals the magnitude of the North-South component alone, i.e. 6 km.

As a check, using the general resultant-distance formula, distance = √((net East-West)² + (net North-South)²) = √(0² + 6²) = √36 = 6 km, which matches the direct reading above.

So the person ends up 6 km from the starting point.

title: Two friends Sanjay and Vijay start running from the same
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Two friends Sanjay and Vijay start running from the same place. Sanjay runs 65 m towards the west, then turns left and runs 25 m. In the meanwhile, Vijay runs 20 m towards the north, then turns to his right and runs 35 m, then turns towards the north and runs 45 m. Finally, Vijay takes a left turn and runs 100 m before stopping. What is the minimum distance between Sanjay and Vijay?
solution:
Step 1: Find Sanjay's final position.
Assume the starting point is at the origin (0, 0).
Sanjay runs 65m West (x = -65) and then turns left (South) to run 25m (y = -25).
Sanjay's coordinates: (-65, -25).

Step 2: Find Vijay's final position.
Vijay runs 20m North (y = +20).
Turns right (East) and runs 35m (x = +35).
Turns North and runs 45m (y = 20 + 45 = +65).
Takes a left turn (West) and runs 100m (x = 35 - 100 = -65).
Vijay's coordinates: (-65, 65).

Step 3: Calculate the minimum distance.
Since both have the same X-coordinate (-65), they are on the same vertical line. The minimum distance is the absolute difference between their Y-coordinates:
Distance = 65 - (-25) = 65 + 25 = 90 meters.

Final Answer: Option 1

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q4
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Pavan starts from Point A and drives 10 km towards North. He then takes a

left turn, drives 6 km, turns left and drives 12 km. He then takes a left turn and

drives 9 km. He takes a final left turn, drives 2 km and stops at Point P. How

far (shortest distance) and towards which direction should he drive in order

to reach Point A again?

(All turns are 90-degree turns only unless specified.)
solution:
In direction-sense problems, model every straight segment of the journey as a displacement vector on a compass-aligned coordinate plane, with North taken as the positive vertical axis and East as the positive horizontal axis. A left turn always rotates the current heading 90 degrees anticlockwise (North to West to South to East to North), and a right turn rotates it 90 degrees clockwise. Adding up all the vector displacements gives the traveller's final position, and the straight-line distance plus the compass direction needed to return to the starting point follow directly from the net vertical and horizontal offsets between the final position and the start.

  1. Place Point A at the origin (0, 0). Facing North, Pavan drives 10 km, moving to (0, 10).

  2. Facing North, a left turn changes his heading to West; driving 6 km West moves him to (-6, 10).

  3. Facing West, a left turn changes his heading to South; driving 12 km South moves him to (-6, -2).

  4. Facing South, a left turn changes his heading to East; driving 9 km East moves him to (3, -2).

  5. Facing East, a final left turn changes his heading to North; driving 2 km North moves him to (3, 0), which is Point P.

  6. Comparing P (3, 0) with A (0, 0) shows a vertical offset of 0 km and a horizontal offset of 3 km, with P positioned to the east of A.

As an independent check, sum the North-South legs separately from the East-West legs. North-South: +10 km (North) - 12 km (South) + 2 km (North) = 0 km, so P and A share the same east-west line. East-West: -6 km (West) + 9 km (East) = +3 km, so P lies 3 km east of A. Both methods agree that P is displaced 3 km east of A with no north-south offset.

Since P lies 3 km to the east of A on the same horizontal line, Pavan must drive 3 km to the west to return to Point A.

title: Question: Directions: Each of the questions below consists of question
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Directions: Read the information and answer the given questions.

  • A * B (18m) means A is 8m north of B

  • A% B (24m) means A is 14m south of B

  • A & B (28m) means A is 18m east of B

  • A @ B (35m) means A is 25m west of B

Now, consider the following information:

M * N (16m), O @ P (32m), N & O (36m), Q & P (42m), S @ R (58m), S% T (27m), U% Q (20m), R * U (22m), X * R (30m)

In which direction is M with respect to P?
solution:
In a coded direction-and-distance puzzle, each linking symbol fixes two things at once: a compass direction and a rule for converting the bracketed figure into the actual displacement it represents. Once every symbol's direction and conversion rule is read off the four defining statements, the whole network of relations can be redrawn on a standard grid (north = up, east = right), and any person's position relative to any other follows by adding displacement vectors along a connecting chain of statements.

  1. Read the four defining lines to fix each symbol's direction: '*' = north, '%' = south, '&' = east, '@' = west.

  2. Check the conversion rule from the same four lines: 18m to 8m, 24m to 14m, 28m to 18m, 35m to 25m - every bracketed figure is exactly 10m more than the real displacement, so actual distance = bracketed figure minus 10m.

  3. Apply this rule to the three statements that connect M to P: O @ P (32m) gives O is 22m west of P; N & O (36m) gives N is 26m east of O; M * N (16m) gives M is 6m north of N.

  4. Fix P at the origin (0, 0). Since O is 22m west of P, place O at (-22, 0).

  5. Since N is 26m east of O, N is at (-22 + 26, 0) = (4, 0) - so N is 4m east of P.

  6. Since M is 6m north of N, M is at (4, 0 + 6) = (4, 6) - so M is 4m east and 6m north of P.

  7. A point that is both to the east and to the north of the origin, with neither component zero, lies in the compass direction lying between due east and due north of that origin.

Re-checking just the east-west chain independently confirms this: the 22m westward leg (O to P) and the 26m eastward leg (N to O) combine to a net eastward shift from P to N, and the purely north-south leg (N to M) only ever adds a vertical shift on top of that - it cannot cancel or reverse the horizontal shift. So M can never end up purely north, or west, or south of P; the displacement must carry both an eastward and a northward part.

M lies to the Northeast of P.

title: Amit starts driving from point and drives km towards North.
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Amit starts driving from point A and drives 13 km towards North. Then he turns right and drives 11 km, then turns right and drives 17 km. Then he turns right and drives 15 km. Finally, he turns right and stops at point P after driving 4 km. How much distance (shortest distance) and in which direction does he need to drive to reach point A again? (Until specified, all turns are 90 degree turns only)
solution:
In a direction-sense route-tracing problem, plot every straight-line leg on an X-Y grid with East as the positive x-axis and North as the positive y-axis; a “turn right” always rotates the direction of travel 90° clockwise through the cycle North → East → South → West → North. Once the final point is plotted, the shortest way back to the start is the straight-line distance between the two points, and its direction follows from the sign of the horizontal (east-west) and vertical (north-south) gap between them.

  1. Take A as the origin (0, 0). Travel North 13 km, reaching (0, 13).

  2. Turn right (North → East) and travel East 11 km, reaching (11, 13).

  3. Turn right (East → South) and travel South 17 km, reaching (11, −4).

  4. Turn right (South → West) and travel West 15 km, reaching (−4, −4).

  5. Turn right (West → North) and travel North 4 km, reaching P at (−4, 0).

  6. Compare P(−4, 0) with A(0, 0): both share the same north-south coordinate (0), so there is no residual north-south gap; the east-west coordinates differ by 4, with P sitting 4 km to the west of A.

As an independent check, total the north-south and east-west legs separately instead of plotting points: the north-south legs are +13 (North), −17 (South), +4 (North), which sum to 0 — confirming P is level with A. The east-west legs are +11 (East), −15 (West), which sum to −4 — confirming P is 4 km west of A. Both methods agree.

Since P is 4 km west of A with no north-south offset, the shortest way back from P to A is 4 km towards the East.

title: Given below are two statements: Statement Arguments from analogy are
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
Given below are two statements:
Statement (I): Arguments from analogy are generally deductive, weak or strong
Statement (II): Arguments from analogy are generally inductive and neither valid nor invalid.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.html: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

options.label: C
options.html: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

options.label: D
options.html: Statement II is correct but Statement I is incorrect

solution:
Answer: Statement II is correct and Statement I is incorrect.

  • Why Statement I is incorrect: It claims arguments from analogy are deductive. In fact, analogical arguments are inductive, not deductive.

  • Why Statement II is correct: Arguments from analogy are inductive and therefore are not classified as valid or invalid in the deductive sense. Instead they vary in strength (strong or weak) depending on how relevant and numerous the similarities are.

  • Key takeaway: Assess analogical arguments by their inductive strength (degree of support), not by deductive validity.

title: Identify the word which belongs to the class of given

solution:
In a word-classification reasoning question, three (or more) of the given words share one common category — here, a type of measurement unit — and the task is to find which option shares that same category. The method is: first identify the common attribute of the given words, then test every option against that attribute; the option matching it is the answer, and every other option belongs to a different category.

Grams, Kilograms, and Quintal are all metric units used to measure mass (weight), so the required shared category here is "unit of mass". Checking the options against this category: Tonnes is also a metric unit that measures mass, so it belongs to the same group as the given words.

Since Tonnes is the only option that shares the mass/weight category with Grams, Kilograms, and Quintal, it is the word that belongs to the given class.

The remaining options sit in a different dimension altogether — intelligence, not energy or vitality:

Hence, 'Lazy' is the word that completes the synonym analogy, matching 'Lethargic / Lifeless' the same way 'Clever' matches 'Wise'.

Application

Define the link in the original pair Carnivore : Herbivore. Both words name an animal by the kind of food it eats: a carnivore is an animal whose food is flesh, and a herbivore is an animal whose food is plants. So the hidden bridge is “defined by the food it eats,” and the ordered foods are flesh first, plants second.

Now look for the pair that places those two foods in the same order: the food of a carnivore followed by the food of a herbivore. The pair Flesh : Plant does exactly this — flesh is what the carnivore eats and plant is what the herbivore eats, in matching order — so it carries the identical relationship as the original pair.

Cross-check

Test each alternative against the rule “food of a flesh-eater : food of a plant-eater”:

  • Animal : Bird — this is a category and one of its members (a bird is a kind of animal), which is a class-to-subclass link, not a diet link.

  • Camel : Giraffe — both are plant-eating animals, so there is no flesh-eater versus plant-eater contrast at all.

  • Horse : Lion — these are the animals themselves rather than their foods, and they run plant-eater then flesh-eater, the reverse of the required order.

Only Flesh : Plant restates the carnivore-then-herbivore diet relationship in the correct order, so it is the matching pair.

title: In each of the following question group of three interrelated

In the following question, a group of three interrelated words is given. Choose the word from the given alternatives that belongs to the same group.

Potato : Carrot : Radish
solution:
The three given words form a group based on where their edible parts grow.

Potato (a tuber), carrot (a root) and radish (a root) are all crops whose edible part grows underground.

Among the alternatives, the groundnut (peanut) is the only one that also grows underground: after its flowers are pollinated above the ground, the developing pods bury themselves in the soil and mature below the surface.

Tomato (a fruit on a vine), spinach (a leafy green) and sesame (seed pods on a tall stalk) all grow above the ground, so they do not belong to the group.

Hence the word that belongs to the same group is Groundnut.

title: What is related to 'Sympathy' in the same way as
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: What is related to 'Sympathy' in the same way as 'Virtue' is related to 'Vice'?
solution:
Concept: In a word-pair analogy, first identify the LOGICAL RELATION inside the given pair, then reproduce that exact relation on the new word. Here the relation in Virtue : Vice is ANTONYMY — a virtue is a morally good quality and a vice is its moral opposite. So the task reduces to: find the word that is the OPPOSITE of Sympathy.

Application: Sympathy is the feeling of pity, compassion or fellow-feeling for another's suffering. Its direct opposite is the disposition to be indifferent to — or to enjoy — another's suffering, which is exactly Cruelty. Therefore Cruelty completes the analogy: Virtue : Vice :: Sympathy : Cruelty (good↔bad opposites in both pairs).

Contrast: Compare the other choices against the required ANTONYM test:

  • Kindness — a near-synonym of Sympathy, not its opposite, so it breaks the good↔bad pattern.

  • Emotion — a broader category that Sympathy belongs to (a part–whole link), not an antonym.

  • Charity — an associated benevolent act, again on the same positive side rather than the opposite side.

Cross-check: Only the opposite-meaning word mirrors Virtue → Vice; substituting any positive or category word fails the antonym relation. Hence Cruelty is the answer.

title: Just as 'defeat' is related to 'victory', in the same

solution:
Concept: A word-pair analogy holds only when the SAME relationship that links the first pair links the second. Here 'defeat' and 'victory' are direct antonyms (opposite outcomes of a contest), so the relationship is ANTONYM.

  1. Identify the relationship in the given pair: defeat is the opposite of victory.

  2. Apply the same antonym relationship to 'despair': find the word that means the opposite of despair (a feeling of hopelessness).

  3. The opposite of despair is hope, the expectation that things will turn out well. So despair : hope mirrors defeat : victory.

Cross-check: substitute back — 'defeat is to victory as despair is to hope' reads as one antonym pair mapped onto another, confirming the match.

title: What is related to 'Courage' in the same way as
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: What is related to 'Courage' in the same way as 'Kindness' is related to 'Cruelty'?
solution:
This is an antonym-pair analogy: the second word in the given pair is the opposite of the first, so the missing word must be the opposite of the target word.

'Kindness' and 'Cruelty' are opposite personality traits: a kind disposition versus a cruel one. Applying the same antonym relationship to 'Courage', the missing word must name the disposition of someone who lacks courage.

  • Bravery: means the same as courage (a synonym), so it cannot supply the required opposite.

  • Valour: also means the same as courage (a synonym), so it fails the relationship for the same reason.

  • Fear: names a passing emotion that even courageous people can feel in danger, not the stable character trait of lacking courage.

'Cowardice' is the disposition-word that stands in direct opposition to courage, completing the analogy the same way 'Cruelty' opposes 'Kindness'.

solution:
This item follows the pattern Instrument : Physical quantity it measures : Standard unit of that quantity. For the pattern to hold, all three elements of a pair must correctly correspond to one another - the instrument must actually measure the stated quantity, and the stated unit must actually be the standard unit for that quantity.

In the given set, a thermometer measures temperature, and temperature is expressed in degrees - the instrument, the quantity, and the unit all match. Checking the options against the same triad: a scale measures length, and length is expressed in meters, so every element of this pair corresponds correctly, exactly mirroring the given relationship.

  • Voltmeter : Current : Ampere - a voltmeter actually measures potential difference (voltage), not current, so the instrument and the quantity named here do not correspond.

  • Ammeter : Potential : Volt - an ammeter actually measures current, not potential difference, so the instrument and the quantity named here do not correspond.

  • Barometer : Pressure : Watt - a barometer does measure pressure, but pressure is expressed in units such as the pascal, not the watt, which is the unit of power, so the quantity and unit named here do not correspond.

Scale : Length : Meter is the only pair where the instrument, the quantity it measures, and the unit all correctly correspond, so it shares the same relationship as the given set.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q13
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml:
‘After’ and ‘before’ are converse relational terms: if event X is after event Y, event Y is before event X. Choose the pair that has the same relationship.

After : Before
solution:
Concept

Converse relational terms describe the same relation from opposite viewpoints. If one term expresses a relation from X to Y, its converse expresses that relation from Y to X.

Application

  1. In “After : Before,” if event X is after event Y, event Y is before event X.

  2. Likewise, if person X is person Y’s successor, person Y is person X’s predecessor.

  3. Thus, “Successor : Predecessor” preserves the same converse relation in the same order.

Contrast and cross-check

  • “First : Second” lists ordinal positions in forward order; the two words are not converse descriptions of one relation.

  • “Present : Past” names time periods relative to now; the words do not reverse one relation between two entities.

  • “Contemporary : Historic” gives descriptive time categories rather than converse relational terms.

  • “Successor : Predecessor” passes the converse check: if X is Y’s successor, Y is X’s predecessor.

Therefore, the matching pair is “Successor : Predecessor.”

solution:
Concept

Concept: In a number analogy of the form A : B :: C : D, the two numbers inside each pair are linked by one and the same rule, and you must make the unknown pair obey exactly the rule you extract from the known pair. Here each pair is generated by a single counting index n, where the first number is A = n2 − 1 and the second number is B = n3 + 1.

Hence, the missing number is 59.

title: Three of the following four number pairs are alike in
subject: Reasoning
bodyHtml: Three of the following four number pairs are alike in a certain way and one is different. Pick the odd one out.
solution:
This item asks which of four number pairs breaks a shared numeric relationship. Three pairs will satisfy one common formula linking the two numbers, and the pair that violates it — even by a small margin — is the odd one out. The method is to derive the formula from the pairs that look regular, then test all four pairs against it.

  1. Compute the ratio of the second number to the first number in each pair: 242 ÷ 22 = 11, 128 ÷ 16 = 8, 338 ÷ 26 = 13, and 96 ÷ 14 ≈ 6.86.

  2. For three pairs the ratio equals exactly half the first number (22 ÷ 2 = 11, 16 ÷ 2 = 8, 26 ÷ 2 = 13), so the shared rule is: second number = first number2 ÷ 2.

  3. Apply the rule to every pair: 222 ÷ 2 = 484 ÷ 2 = 242 (matches); 162 ÷ 2 = 256 ÷ 2 = 128 (matches); 262 ÷ 2 = 676 ÷ 2 = 338 (matches); 142 ÷ 2 = 196 ÷ 2 = 98, which does not match the given 96.

Cross-check by direct multiplication (first number × half of first number): 22 × 11 = 242, 16 × 8 = 128, and 26 × 13 = 338 all hold, but 14 × 7 = 98, not 96 — the same mismatch confirmed a second way.

So the pair 14 : 96 fails the shared first-number-squared-over-two relationship that the other three pairs satisfy, making it the odd pair out.
