title: Find the non-context free language among the following.
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: Find the non-context free language among the following.
solution:
To determine which language is not context-free, we analyze each option based on the properties of context-free languages (CFLs). CFLs can be recognized by pushdown automata (PDAs), which use a stack to handle nested or matching structures.

Option A: L = {ωωR ∣ ω ∈ {0,1}∗}

This language consists of palindromes over {0,1}. A PDA can recognize palindromes by pushing symbols onto the stack until the middle, then popping and matching with the reverse. This is a classic context-free language.

Option B: L = {p^n q^n ∣ n ≥ 0}

This language requires matching equal numbers of p and q symbols. A PDA can push a symbol for each p and pop for each q. This is a standard context-free language.

Option C: L = {ωω ∣ ω ∈ {0,1}∗}

This language consists of strings formed by repeating a string twice. A PDA cannot compare the first half with the second half because it cannot store the entire first half in the stack and then compare it with the second half. This language is not context-free.

Option D: L = {p^n q^m r^m s^n ∣ n,m ≥ 0}

This language has two independent matching pairs: p and s must have the same count, and q and r must have the same count. A PDA can use the stack to count p's and then match with s's, and similarly for q and r. This is context-free.

Option E: Question not attempted

This is not a valid language definition and does not represent a formal language. It is not considered in the analysis.

Therefore, the only language that is not context-free is Option C.

हिन्दी उत्तर:

प्रश्न में दिए गए विकल्पों में से एक ऐसा भाषा खोजना है जो संदर्भ-मुक्त नहीं है। संदर्भ-मुक्त भाषाएँ पुशडाउन ऑटोमेटा (PDA) द्वारा पहचानी जा सकती हैं, जो स्टैक का उपयोग करके निष्पादित करती हैं।

विकल्प A: L = {ωωR ∣ ω ∈ {0,1}∗}

यह भाषा {0,1} पर पलिंड्रोमों से बनी है। एक PDA पलिंड्रोम को पहचान सकता है जब तक कि वह स्टैक में पहले आधे भाग के प्रत्येक प्रतीक को डालता है और फिर दूसरे आधे भाग के प्रत्येक प्रतीक के साथ मिलाता है। यह एक मानक संदर्भ-मुक्त भाषा है।

विकल्प B: L = {p^n q^n ∣ n ≥ 0}

इस भाषा में p और q की संख्या बराबर होनी चाहिए। एक PDA प्रत्येक p के लिए एक प्रतीक डाल सकता है और प्रत्येक q के लिए एक प्रतीक निकाल सकता है। यह एक मानक संदर्भ-मुक्त भाषा है।

विकल्प C: L = {ωω ∣ ω ∈ {0,1}∗}

यह भाषा एक शब्द को दो बार दोहराने से बनी है। एक PDA पहले आधे भाग को दूसरे आधे भाग के साथ तुलना नहीं कर सकता क्योंकि यह पूरे पहले आधे भाग को स्टैक में स्टोर नहीं कर सकता और फिर दूसरे आधे भाग के साथ तुलना कर सकता है। यह भाषा संदर्भ-मुक्त नहीं है।

विकल्प D: L = {p^n q^m r^m s^n ∣ n,m ≥ 0}

इस भाषा में दो स्वतंत्र मैचिंग जोड़े हैं: p और s की संख्या बराबर होनी चाहिए, और q और r की संख्या बराबर होनी चाहिए। एक PDA स्टैक का उपयोग कर सकता है p की संख्या गिनने और फिर s के साथ मिलान करने के लिए, और इसी तरह q और r के लिए। यह संदर्भ-मुक्त है।

विकल्प E: प्रश्न अनुसूचित नहीं

यह एक वैध भाषा परिभाषा नहीं है और इसे विश्लेषण में नहीं लिया जाता है।

इसलिए, एकमात्र भाषा जो संदर्भ-मुक्त नहीं है वह विकल्प C है।

title: Consider CFG with no ϵ-productions. Let be the maximum number
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml:
Q. Consider a CFG G with no ϵ-productions. Let k be the maximum number of symbols on the right-hand side of any production in G, ∣P∣ be the number of productions, and ∣T∣ be the number of terminals. Let G′ be the equivalent grammar in Chomsky Normal Form (CNF).

  1. If G has no null productions, then the maximum number of productions in the CNF equivalent of G is (k−1)∣P∣+∣T∣.

  2. The maximum height of the parse tree of any string generated by G′ is at most 2k−1, where k is the maximum number of symbols on the RHS of G.

Choose the correct option: (MCQ)
solution:
Answer: Both statements are False.

Statement 1 — "Maximum number of productions in CNF = (k−1)|P| + |T|":

False. Reason:

  • CNF conversion replaces each RHS of length r by r−1 binary productions, so summing (r−1) over productions gives at most (k−1)|P| for those binary rules. But this accounting omits effects of other steps.

  • Introducing variables to replace terminals contributes at most |T| new terminal rules, but those new variables also appear in binary rules, which the simple formula does not fully count.

  • Crucially, elimination of unit productions can cause long RHS productions to be copied to many nonterminals. Example: if A1 → A2 → ... → An and An → X1 X2 ... Xk, then removing unit productions will add the long RHS to A1, A2, ..., increasing the total number of productions well beyond (k−1)|P| + |T|.

  • Therefore the stated formula is not a guaranteed maximum; it can underestimate the total after full CNF conversion.

Statement 2 — "The maximum height of the parse tree of any string generated by G′ is at most 2k−1, where k is the maximum number of symbols on the RHS of G":

False. Reason:

  • The bound 2k−1 correctly describes the height contributed when a single long RHS of length k is rewritten as a binary tree during CNF conversion (the binary decomposition of that one production).

  • However, whole derivations may apply such productions repeatedly and can nest many such decompositions. For grammars that allow repeated nesting (for example a nonterminal that expands into k nonterminals that again each expand similarly), the parse-tree height grows with the number of nesting steps and can be arbitrarily large.

  • A simple counterexample: a grammar with a recursive production like S → S S (a case with k = 2) yields parse trees whose height increases with the number of derivation steps; there is no absolute bound 2k−1 on the height of all generated strings.

  • Thus 2k−1 is only the size of the local expansion for one production, not a global upper bound for all parse trees of G′.

Summary: Both statements are false. Statement 1 underestimates possible growth caused by unit-production elimination and other CNF steps; Statement 2 confuses the local expansion of one production with the global height of arbitrary derivations.

title: Consider the following CFG, S→aA∣bSS∣SS A→aAb∣bAa∣AA∣ϵ The language generated by
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml:
Consider the following CFG, G:

S→aA∣bSS∣SS

A→aAb∣bAa∣AA∣ϵ

The language generated by G is:

options.label: A
options.html: Set of all strings with at least one 'a'

options.label: B
options.html: Set of all strings with at least two 'a's

options.label: C
options.html: Set of all strings with at least one more 'a' than the number of 'b's

solution:
Grammar:

S → aA | bSS | SS

A → aAb | bAa | AA | ε

Key observation: the nonterminal A generates exactly the strings with an equal number of 'a's and 'b's.

  • Reason for A: ε has equal numbers (zero). The productions aAb and bAa add one 'a' and one 'b' in opposite ends, preserving equality. Concatenation AA also preserves equality, so every string generated by A has #a = #b.

  • Define f(w) = number of 'a's minus number of 'b's. For any string from A, f = 0.

  • S → aA gives strings with f = 1 (one extra 'a' plus a string from A with f = 0).

  • If two strings have f-values x and y from S, then SS yields a string with f = x + y, and bSS yields f = -1 + x + y. Since the base value 1 is achievable, closure under these productions yields all positive integers for f.

  • In particular, f can never be 0 or negative for strings from S, and f = 1 is the minimum possible value, so every S-derived string satisfies f ≥ 1.

Conclusion: The language generated by the grammar is exactly the set of strings where the number of 'a's exceeds the number of 'b's by at least one (i.e., #a(w) = #b(w) + k for some integer k ≥ 1).

Example counterexamples: the single-letter string "a" is in the language (S → aA, A → ε), so any description that requires at least two 'a's is too restrictive. A string like "bbabb" has one 'a' but more 'b's and cannot be produced by the grammar, so descriptions that allow such strings are too permissive.

title: Which of the following CFGs cannot be simulated by an
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: Which of the following CFGs cannot be simulated by an FSM?
solution:
To determine which CFG cannot be simulated by an FSM, we need to check whether the language generated by each CFG is regular or not. An FSM can only recognize regular languages. If a CFG generates a non-regular language, it cannot be simulated by an FSM.

Option A: S→Sa | b

This CFG generates strings of the form b, ba, baa, baaa, etc. This is equivalent to the regular expression b a*. Since this language is regular, it can be recognized by an FSM.

Option B: S→aSb | ab

This CFG generates strings of the form ab, aabb, aaabbb, etc. This is the language a^n b^n, which is not regular. It requires counting the number of a's and matching it with the number of b's, which cannot be done by an FSM. Therefore, this CFG cannot be simulated by an FSM.

Option C: S→abX, X→cY, Y→d | aX

This CFG generates strings starting with ab, followed by c, and then either d or a sequence of a's and c's. The structure is linear and does not require unbounded counting. The language is regular, so it can be recognized by an FSM.

Option D: S→Sb | a

This CFG generates strings of the form a, ab, abb, abbb, etc. This is equivalent to the regular expression a b*. Since this language is regular, it can be recognized by an FSM.

Option E: Question not attempted

This is not a valid CFG and does not represent a grammar. It is not a relevant choice for the question.

Therefore, the CFG that cannot be simulated by an FSM is Option B.

title: Which of the following are decidable? Whether the intersection of
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml:
Which of the following are decidable?

I. Whether the intersection of two regular languages is finite

II. Whether a given context-free language is finite and hence regular.

III. Whether two push-down automata accept the same language

IV. Whether a given grammar is context-free

options.label: B
options.html: I and I I and I I and IV

solution:
Explanation:

Statement I: The intersection of two regular languages is regular (by closure property). Testing whether a regular language is finite is decidable. Therefore, statement I is decidable.

Statement II: The finiteness problem for context-free languages is decidable. Therefore, determining whether a given CFL is finite (and hence regular) is decidable.

Statement III: The equivalence problem for push-down automata (i.e., whether two PDAs accept the same language) is undecidable. Therefore, statement III is not decidable.

Statement IV: Checking whether a given grammar is context-free (i.e., whether it follows CFG rules) is decidable. Therefore, statement IV is decidable.

Thus, statements I, II, and IV are decidable, while III is not.

Classification of L₁: L₁ = {a^i b^j | j = 2i} is deterministic context-free.

Reason: A deterministic pushdown automaton can deterministically handle this language by pushing two stack symbols for each a, then on seeing the first b switching to popping one symbol per b. The input structure a* b* allows a deterministic boundary between phases, so the language is DCFL.

Classification of L₂: L₂ = {a^n b^m | n,m ≥ 1} is regular.

Reason: A finite automaton can accept one or more a's followed by one or more b's, so L₂ is regular (and therefore context-free).

Intersection (L₁ ∩ L₂): The intersection of a deterministic context-free language with a regular language is deterministic context-free, hence context-free.

Therefore L₁ ∩ L₂ is a CFL.

Union (L₁ ∪ L₂): Both L₁ (DCFL) and L₂ (regular) are context-free languages, and context-free languages are closed under union.

Therefore L₁ ∪ L₂ is a CFL.

Complement (L₁'): Deterministic context-free languages are closed under complementation, so the complement of L₁ is also a deterministic context-free language and therefore a context-free language.

Conclusion: Each listed statement is true, so the combined answer that all of these hold is correct.

Consider M is a Turing machine M = ({q₀, q₁, q₂, q₃, q₄}, {a, b}, {a, b, B}, q₀, B, {q₄}) accept the language L = {anbn | n ≥ 0} the transition table for the Rules is

What is the value of * and ** in the transition table? i.e in position q0 B and q3 B
solution:
Answer: q0 on B = (q4, B, R); q3 on B = (q0, B, R)

Reasoning:

  • q0 reading blank: If the tape is empty (the input is λ), the machine must accept immediately. Therefore q0 on B goes to the accepting state q4 and moves right: (q4, B, R).

  • q3 reading blank: State q3 scans left back to the left end after marking a matching pair. When it encounters the left blank it should return to q0 and move right to begin the next pass (or accept if the next step in q0 sees blank). Thus q3 on B should be (q0, B, R).

Example trace for the string "ab":

  1. Start in q0 on tape: a b (with blanks around). q0 reads 'a' and replaces it with B, moving right and entering q1.

  2. q1 moves right over 'a'/'b' until it sees the blank after the input, then transitions to q2 and moves left to find the marked b.

  3. q2 moves left to q3 which scans left to the left blank. When q3 sees the left blank it uses the transition q3 on B -> (q0, B, R) to go back to the start of the next pass.

  4. Back in q0, if the tape now has only blanks the q0 on B -> (q4, B, R) transition moves to the accepting state q4.

Therefore the correct entries are (q4, B, R) for the q0 reading blank position and (q0, B, R) for the q3 reading blank position.

title: The language accepted by the following Turing Machine is &LBA
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: The language accepted by the following Turing Machine is
solution:
Language accepted: All strings consisting of one or more 0s followed by one or more 1s (i.e. {0^n1^m | n ≥ 1, m ≥ 1}).

  • Behavior of the start state (q0): on reading 0 it moves to the state that scans zeros; on reading 1 or blank it halts (reject). So the input must begin with at least one 0.

  • Behavior of the zero-scanning state (q1): it stays on 0s; on the first 1 it transitions to the one-scanning state; on blank it halts (reject). Thus there must be at least one 1 after the initial zeros.

  • Behavior of the one-scanning state (q2): it stays on 1s; if it encounters a 0 it halts (reject); when it sees the blank it moves to the final accepting state. Therefore no 0s are allowed after the first 1.

Example: Trace on the input 0011

  1. Start in q0; read first 0 -> move to q1.

  2. In q1; read next 0 -> stay in q1.

  3. In q1; read first 1 -> move to q2.

  4. In q2; read next 1 -> stay in q2.

  5. In q2; read blank -> go to qf (accept).

Conclusion: The machine accepts exactly those strings with one or more 0s followed by one or more 1s; it rejects strings that start with 1, contain no 1, or have any 0 after the first 1.

title: The next move function of Turing machine is mapping &LBA
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: The next move function δ of a Turing machine M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, B, F) is a mapping
solution:
Correct mapping: δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}

Explanation:

  • Domain Q × Γ: the function takes the current machine state (from Q) and the symbol currently under the tape head (from the tape alphabet Γ).

  • Codomain Q × Γ × {L, R}: the function returns the next state (in Q), the single symbol to write at the current tape cell (from Γ), and the head movement direction (left or right).

Notes on variants:

  • Using Γ* in the output (δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ* × {L, R}) corresponds to a generalized machine that can write a whole string in one step. This is not the standard single-step single-symbol write model.

  • Using Σ in the domain or output is incorrect because Σ is the input alphabet; the head reads and writes tape symbols from Γ (which includes Σ and the blank symbol).

  • For multi-tape machines the signature changes (e.g., δ: Q × Γ^k → Q × Γ^k × {L,S,R}^k), but for the usual single-tape deterministic Turing machine the correct and standard mapping is δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}.

title: Which of the following are false: &ClosureProperties
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: Which of the following are false:

options.label: A
options.html: For two languages L1 and L2, If both are non regular then L1∩L2 is also non-regular.

options.label: B
options.html: Given encodings of 2 DFAs over the same set of alphabets, there is a TM which can tell whether or not they both accept same language or not.

options.label: C
options.html: The set of decidable languages is closed under the subset operation.

options.label: D
options.html: There exist a TM which can simulate the behaviour of any given TM on any given finite input

solution:
Summary: The false statements and explanations are given below.

  • Statement: For two languages L1 and L2, if both are non-regular then L1 ∩ L2 is also non-regular.

    Why this is false: Provide a counterexample. Let L1 = {a^n b^n | n ≥ 0} and L2 = {a^n b^{2n} | n ≥ 0}. Each language is non-regular, but their intersection is empty. The empty language is regular, so the intersection can be regular. Therefore the claim is false.

  • Statement: The set of decidable languages is closed under the subset operation.

    Why this is false: A decidable language can have undecidable subsets. For example, Σ* is decidable, but there exist undecidable subsets of Σ* (take any known undecidable language over the same alphabet). Hence decidability is not guaranteed for arbitrary subsets.

Other statements (true):

  • Given encodings of two DFAs over the same alphabet, there is a Turing machine that decides whether they accept the same language. Reason: construct the product automaton to accept the symmetric difference of the two languages and test emptiness by reachability; this procedure halts.

  • There exists a Turing machine that can simulate the behaviour of any given Turing machine on any given finite input. Reason: a universal Turing machine can read the encoding of any TM and its input and simulate its step-by-step execution.

title: Consider the following two languages, where represents the encoding of
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml:
Consider the following two languages, where ⟨M⟩ represents the encoding of a Turing Machine M:

L1​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that halts on all inputs w where w is a prime-length binary string}
L2​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that, on input ϵ (empty string), visits its initial state at least twice}
Which of the following statements accurately describes the decidability of L1​ and L2​?

options.label: B
options.html: L1​ is undecidable, but L2​ is decidable.

options.label: C
options.html: L1​ is decidable, but L2​ is undecidable.

solution:
This question tests your ability to distinguish between properties of a Turing Machine's language (which Rice's Theorem applies to) and properties of its computation (which Rice's Theorem does not apply to, and which must be analyzed directly, often via reduction).

Analysis of L₁

  • L1​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that halts on all inputs w where w is a prime-length binary string}

  • This language L1​ defines a property of the language L(M) accepted by the Turing Machine M. The property is "M halts on all strings w where ∣w∣ is prime."

  • We can check if this property is "non-trivial" to see if Rice's Theorem applies. A property is non-trivial if someTuring Machines (and their languages) have it, and some do not.

    1. TM that has the property: A simple TM Mhalt​ that halts on all inputs (e.g., it accepts Σ∗). This TM certainly halts on all prime-length strings.

    2. TM that does not have the property: A TM Mloop​ that is designed to loop forever only if the input string has a prime length (e.g., it loops on "10", length 2).

  • Since the property is non-trivial (it's not held by all TMs or by no TMs) and it is a property of the languageL(M), Rice's Theorem states that L1​ is undecidable.

Analysis of L₂

  • L2​={⟨M⟩∣M is a TM that, on input ϵ (empty string), visits its initial state at least twice}

  • This is a property of the TM's computation on a specific input (ϵ), not a property of the language L(M). Therefore, Rice's Theorem does not apply.

  • We must check for decidability by other means, typically by trying to reduce the Halting Problem to L2​.

  • Let's use the ϵ-Halting Problem (HALTϵ​), which is known to be undecidable. HALTϵ​={⟨M⟩∣M halts on input ϵ}.

  • We will construct a new TM M′ from an arbitrary TM M such that: M halts on ϵ⟺M′∈L2​

  • Construction of M′:

    • Let M have an initial state q0​.

    • Create M′ with a new, unique initial state qnew′​.

    • Define the transitions of M′ as follows:

      • On input ϵ, M′ starts in qnew′​. (This is Visit 1 to its initial state).

      • M′ immediately transitions to q0​ (the initial state of M) and begins simulating M on input ϵ.

      • Modify all "halting" transitions in M: If M would enter a halt state (qhalt​), M′ is programmed to instead transition back to qnew′​ and then halt.

  • Analyzing M′'s behavior:

    • Case 1: M halts on ϵ. M′ starts in qnew′​ (Visit 1), simulates M, and when M halts, M′ transitions back to qnew′​ (Visit 2). M′ then halts. In this case, M′ visits its initial state twice. Thus, M′∈L2​.

    • Case 2: M loops forever on ϵ. M′ starts in qnew′​ (Visit 1), simulates M, but the simulation never reaches M's halt state. Since qnew′​ is a new state not in M, the simulation will never re-enter qnew′​. M′ only visits its initial state once. Thus, M′∈/L2​.

  • Since we have successfully created a reduction from the undecidable HALTϵ​ problem to L2​, L2​ must also be undecidable.

Conclusion:

  • L1​ is undecidable (by Rice's Theorem).

  • L2​ is undecidable (by reduction from the Halting Problem).

Therefore, both languages are undecidable.

title: Which of the following are Decidable? {<TM> L(TM) is RE}
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml:
Which of the following are Decidable?

L1 = {<TM> | L(TM) is RE}

L2 = {<TM> | L(TM) has exactly 2025 members}

L3 = {<TM> | M makes different and unique numbers of steps on all inputs}

L4 = {<TM> | L(TM) is non-empty}

L5 = {<TM> | L(TM) is CFL but not DCFL}
solution:
Summary: Only the property that a machine's language is recursively enumerable is decidable (it is true for every Turing machine). The other listed properties are undecidable. Since none of the provided answer choices lists only that decidable language, the choice that says "none" is the correct selection among the given options.

Details by language:

  • L1 = {⟨TM⟩ | L(TM) is RE}: Decidable. Reason: For any Turing machine M, the set L(M) is, by definition, recursively enumerable (it is exactly the language recognized by M). Thus the predicate "L(M) is RE" holds for every encoding ⟨M⟩, so the language of encodings is the set of all encodings and can be decided trivially (always accept).

  • L2 = {⟨TM⟩ | L(TM) has exactly 2025 members}: Undecidable. Sketch of reduction: Given an instance (M,w) of the acceptance problem, construct a machine M' that on any input x first ignores x, simulates M on w, and if M accepts w then accepts exactly a fixed set of 2025 distinct strings (e.g., a fixed 2025-member set); otherwise M' accepts nothing. Then L(M') has size 2025 iff M accepts w. Deciding the 2025-size property would decide acceptance, so it is undecidable.

  • L3 = {⟨TM⟩ | M makes different and unique numbers of steps on all inputs}: Undecidable. Sketch: The property compares halting times across inputs, so one can encode halting/acceptance information into the runtimes on specially chosen inputs. Any algorithm deciding the uniqueness-of-runtime property would resolve halting/acceptance instances; hence it is undecidable.

  • L4 = {⟨TM⟩ | L(TM) is non-empty}: Undecidable. Sketch: Reduce from the acceptance problem. Given (M,w), build M' that on any input simulates M on w and accepts iff M accepts w. Then L(M') is non-empty iff M accepts w. Thus non-emptiness is undecidable.

  • L5 = {⟨TM⟩ | L(TM) is CFL but not DCFL}: Undecidable. Reason: Being a context-free language (or being context-free but not deterministic context-free) is a nontrivial semantic property of the language recognized by a Turing machine. By Rice's theorem (properties of the language recognized by a TM that are nontrivial are undecidable), this decision problem is undecidable.

Conclusion: Only the property in L1 is decidable (it is always true). The other properties L2, L3, L4, and L5 are undecidable. Because none of the provided answer-choices lists exactly that single decidable language, the offered choice that states "none" (i.e., none of the other answer-sets is correct) is the correct selection among the given choices.

solution:
Step 1: Regular grammar to context-free grammar – Every regular grammar is a context-free grammar. Therefore, this conversion is always possible algorithmically.

Step 2: Non-deterministic pushdown automata to deterministic pushdown automata – Not all languages accepted by NPDA can be accepted by DPDA. Hence, this conversion is not always possible algorithmically.

Step 3: Non-deterministic finite state automata to deterministic finite state automata – The subset construction algorithm converts any NFA to an equivalent DFA. This is always possible algorithmically.

Step 4: Non-deterministic Turing machine to deterministic Turing machine – Any NTM can be simulated by a DTM using a breadth-first search of computation paths. This conversion is algorithmically possible.

title: What is the computational complexity of the halting problem? Halting
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: What is the computational complexity of the halting problem?
solution:
The halting problem asks whether a given program will halt on a given input. It was proven by Alan Turing that no algorithm can solve this problem for all possible program-input pairs. This means the problem is undecidable, or not computable. Therefore, the computational complexity is not expressible in standard time complexity classes like O(1) or O(n), as no algorithm exists to compute the answer in finite time.

हिन्दी उत्तर: हाल्टिंग समस्या यह पूछती है कि कोई दिया गया प्रोग्राम दिए गए इनपुट पर रुकेगा या नहीं। एलन ट्यूरिंग द्वारा सिद्ध किया गया है कि कोई भी एल्गोरिदम इस समस्या को सभी संभावित प्रोग्राम-इनपुट जोड़ियों के लिए हल नहीं कर सकता है। इसका अर्थ है कि समस्या अनिर्णायक है, या गणना योग्य नहीं है। इसलिए, गणनात्मक जटिलता को O(1) या O(n) जैसी मानक समय जटिलता श्रेणियों में व्यक्त नहीं किया जा सकता है, क्योंकि किसी भी सीमित समय में उत्तर की गणना करने वाला कोई एल्गोरिदम मौजूद नहीं है।

Given below are two statements:

Statement 𝐼: The problem “Is 𝐿1∧𝐿2=𝜙?” is undecidable for context sensitive languages 𝐿1 and 𝐿2

Statement 𝐼𝐼: The problem “Is 𝑊∈𝐿?” is decidable for context sensitive language 𝐿. (where 𝑊 is a string).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.html: Both Statement 𝐼 and Statement 𝐼𝐼 are true

options.label: B

solution:
Final answer: Both statements are true.

  • Statement I: The problem “Is the intersection of two context-sensitive languages empty?” is undecidable. Reason: The emptiness problem for context-sensitive languages (languages accepted by linear bounded automata) is undecidable, and since context-sensitive languages are closed under intersection, asking whether L1 ∩ L2 = ∅ remains an undecidable question.

  • Statement II: The membership problem “Is a given string w in a given context-sensitive language L?” is decidable. Reason: Context-sensitive languages are exactly those accepted by (nondeterministic) linear bounded automata, which always run within space linearly bounded by the input length and therefore decide membership in finite (PSPACE) time. Membership for context-sensitive languages is decidable (and in fact PSPACE-complete).

Therefore both statements are true.

title: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding Recursive and
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding Recursive (R) and Recursively Enumerable (RE) languages?

options.label: A
options.html: The union of two Recursively Enumerable (RE) languages is always Recursively Enumerable.

options.label: B
options.html: A language L is Recursive if and only if both L and its complement LC are Recursively Enumerable.

options.label: C
options.html: The complement of a Recursive language is always Recursive.

options.label: D
options.html: The complement of a Recursively Enumerable (RE) language is always Recursively Enumerable.

solution:
This question tests your knowledge of the closure properties of Recursive and RE languages.

(A) Union of RE is RE: This is TRUE. If L1​ and L2​ are RE, they are accepted by Turing Machines M1​ and M2​respectively. We can construct a new TM Munion​ that, on input w, simulates M1​ and M2​ in parallel (e.g., by alternating steps). If either M1​ or M2​ accepts, Munion​ accepts. This new TM accepts the union L1​∪L2​.
(B) L is R iff L and LC are RE: This is TRUE. This is the standard theorem defining Recursive languages in terms of RE languages.
If L is R, it's accepted by a total TM M that always halts. L is clearly RE. Its complement LC is also accepted by a total TM M′ (that just flips M's accept/reject states), so LC is also R, and thus RE.
If L and LC are both RE, we have TMs M1​ (for L) and M2​ (for LC). We can run them in parallel on an input w. Since w must be in either L or LC, one of M1​ or M2​ is guaranteed to halt and accept. If M1​accepts, we accept. If M2​ accepts, we reject. This creates a total TM, proving L is Recursive.

(C) Complement of R is R: This is TRUE. As explained in (B), if L is Recursive, it has a total TM M that always halts. A TM M′ for LC can be built by simply swapping the accept and reject states of M. M′ will also always halt, making LC Recursive.
(D) Complement of RE is RE: This is FALSE. This is the key distinction. The set of RE languages is not closed under complementation. If this statement were true, it would imply that for any RE language L, its complement LC is also RE. By the theorem in (B), this would mean every RE language is also Recursive. This is false; the Halting Problem is a well-known example of a language that is RE but not Recursive. Therefore, the complement of an RE language is not guaranteed to be RE.

title: Which of following problems are undecidable? Membership problem in context-free
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml:
Which of following problems are undecidable?

I. Membership problem in context-free languages
II. Whether a given context-free language is regular
III. Whether a finite state automaton halts on all inputs
IV. Membership problem for type 0 languages
solution:
Correct Answer: D (II and IV)

  • II is Undecidable: Checking if a context-free language is regular is a well-known undecidable problem (proven via Rice's Theorem or reduction from the Post Correspondence Problem).

  • IV is Undecidable: Type 0 languages are Recursively Enumerable (RE). The membership problem for $RE$ languages is equivalent to the Halting Problem, which is undecidable.

  • I & III are Decidable: Membership for CFLs is decidable (CYK algorithm). A Finite State Automaton (DFA/NFA) always halts on all inputs because it processes exactly one input symbol per transition and has no infinite loops without consuming input; hence, its halting problem is trivially decidable.

title: Assume statements and defined as: is recursive enumerable where and
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml:
Assume statements S₁ and S₂ defined as:

S₁: L₂ − L₁ is recursively enumerable, where L₁ and L₂ are recursive and recursively enumerable respectively

S₂: The set of all Turing machines is countable

Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.html: S₁ is correct and S₂ is not correct

options.label: C
options.html: Both S₁ and S₂ are not correct

options.label: D
options.html: S₁ is not correct and S₂ is correct

solution:
Two closure results govern this question: recursive languages are closed under complement, and a recursively enumerable (r.e.) language intersected with a recursive language is again r.e.; separately, the set of all Turing machines is countable because each machine has a finite description over a finite alphabet.

  • Recursive (decidable) languages are closed under complement: if L₁ is recursive, its complement L₁′ is also recursive.

  • An r.e. language intersected with a recursive language is r.e.: to recognize membership in the intersection, first run the recursive language's decider, which always halts; only if it accepts do you run the r.e. language's semi-decision procedure — the overall procedure need not halt when the input is not in the intersection, which is exactly what recursive enumerability requires.

  • Every Turing machine has a finite transition-table description over a finite alphabet, so it can be written as a finite binary string; the set of all finite binary strings is countably infinite.

Applying this to the two statements:

  1. S₁: L₁ is recursive, so its complement L₁′ is recursive. L₂ − L₁ = L₂ ∩ L₁′. Since L₂ is r.e. and L₁′ is recursive, this intersection is r.e. — S₁ holds.

  2. S₂: Each Turing machine's description (states, transitions, tape alphabet) is a finite string over a finite alphabet. Enumerating all finite strings by length gives a bijection with a subset of ℕ, so the set of all Turing machines is countable — S₂ holds.

  3. Both statements are true, so the correct choice is 'Both S₁ and S₂ are correct.'

The closure-under-complement and r.e.-intersect-recursive results are standard theorems, independent of this specific L₁, L₂ — so S₁ holds for any such pair, not just this one. For S₂, contrast with the (uncountable) set of all possible languages over an alphabet: that larger set is uncountable, which is exactly why not every language is decidable or recognizable — but the machines themselves, being finite descriptions, remain countable.

title: Which of the following sets is/are uncountable? &LBA
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: Which of the following sets is/are uncountable?

options.label: A
options.html: Set of all languages except RE is countable

options.label: D
options.html: Set of all RE ∪ set of all CFL ∪ set of all regular languages

solution:
Key facts:

  • The set Σ* of all finite strings is countable.

  • The set of all languages over Σ is 2^{Σ*} (the power set of Σ*), which is uncountable (Cantor diagonalization).

  • Recursively enumerable (RE) languages are countable because Turing machines (or their encodings) can be enumerated.

  • Context-free languages (CFL) and regular languages are also countable (grammars, automata, or their encodings can be enumerated).

Consequences:

  • The set described as "set of all languages except RE" (all languages that are not recursively enumerable) is uncountable because 2^{Σ*} is uncountable and removing the countable set RE leaves an uncountable set.

  • The set described as "set of all not RE languages" is the same set and therefore uncountable for the same reason.

  • The set described as "set of all non-regular languages" is uncountable because the regular languages are countable, so their complement in 2^{Σ*} is uncountable.

  • The set described as the union "RE ∪ CFL ∪ regular languages" is countable, since it is a union of countable sets and a countable union of countable sets is countable.

Final summary: the three descriptions that denote complements of countable classes inside the full power set (the first three listed items) are uncountable; the union of RE, CFL and regular languages is countable.

title: Consider the language: is Turing machine} L(M) Complement of {⟨ww⟩
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml:
Consider the language:
L1 = {⟨M⟩ ∣ M is a Turing machine}
L(M) ≤p Complement of {⟨ww⟩ ∣ w∈(a,b)*}
Then L1​ is:
solution:
Interpretation: L1 = {⟨M⟩ | L(M) ⊆ complement({ww | w ∈ {a,b}*}) }.

Key facts:

  • {ww} is decidable. Given an input x, we can check all possible splits (in particular check if its length is even and the two halves are equal), so membership in {ww} is decidable.

  • Hence the complement of {ww} is also decidable and is a nontrivial subset of Σ* (neither empty nor all strings).

Undecidability (Rice's theorem): The property 'L(M) is a subset of this fixed nontrivial decidable set' depends only on the language recognized by M and is nontrivial (some languages satisfy it, some do not). By Rice's theorem, any nontrivial property of the language recognized by Turing machines is undecidable. Therefore membership in L1 is undecidable.

Membership in co-RE:

  • Look at the complement of L1: it consists of all ⟨M⟩ for which there exists a string x with x ∈ L(M) and x ∈ {ww}.

  • To semidecide the complement, enumerate candidate x, decide whether x ∈ {ww} (possible since {ww} is decidable), and simulate M on x; if M accepts and x ∈ {ww}, accept ⟨M⟩. Thus the complement is recursively enumerable.

Conclusion: L1 is undecidable. Its complement is recursively enumerable, so L1 is in co-RE (but not r.e. in general). The original solution claiming decidability is incorrect.

title: If and is undecidable, then what about Find the true
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: If L1 ≤P L2​ and L2 is undecidable, then what about L1​? Find the true statement:

options.label: C
options.html: L1​ may or may not be decidable

solution:
Key idea: If there is a polynomial-time (or many-one) reduction f with x ∈ L1 iff f(x) ∈ L2, then a decider for L2 composed with f would decide L1. Thus if L2 were decidable, L1 must be decidable. However, the fact that L2 is undecidable does not force any particular status for L1.

  • Example where L1 is decidable:

    Let L1 = ∅ (decidable). Since L2 is undecidable it cannot be Σ*, so there exists some fixed string s0 not in L2. Define f(x)=s0 for all x. Then x ∈ L1 is always false and f(x) ∈ L2 is always false, so x ∈ L1 iff f(x) ∈ L2 holds. Thus L1 reduces to L2 even though L1 is decidable.

  • Example where L1 is undecidable:

    Take L1 = L2 (or any known undecidable language that reduces to L2). The identity reduction shows L1 can be undecidable.

Answer: Therefore, L1 may or may not be decidable. Reducibility to an undecidable language does not determine L1's decidability in general.

title: Given some languages &ClosureProperties
subject: Theory of Computation
bodyHtml: Given some languages
solution:
Key facts:

  • L1 is REC (decidable).

  • L2 is RE but not REC, so the complement of L2 is not decidable.

Assume for contradiction that the complement of L2 is polynomial-time reducible to L1.

  1. Then there is a polynomial-time computable function f such that x is in the complement of L2 exactly when f(x) is in L1.

  2. Because L1 is decidable, we can decide membership in the complement of L2 by computing f(x) and running the decider for L1 on f(x).

  3. Hence the complement of L2 would be decidable, contradicting the given that L2 is RE but not decidable.

Conclusion: The reduction cannot exist, so the correct answer is that such a reduction is not possible.

title: Choose the word which best expresses the meaning of given
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word which best expresses the meaning of given word

Dreadfully
solution:
Answer: Incredibly

Explanation: 'Dreadfully' is commonly used as an intensifier meaning 'extremely' or 'very'. 'Incredibly' conveys the same intensifying idea, so it is the best match.

  • Why 'Incredibly' is correct: It expresses a high degree or intensity (e.g., "She was dreadfully tired" = "She was incredibly tired").

  • Why 'Disastrous' is incorrect: It means causing a disaster or great damage and is an adjective, not an adverb that intensifies.

  • Why 'Sad' is incorrect: It denotes feeling sorrow or unhappiness and does not match the intensifying sense of 'dreadfully'.

  • Why 'none of above' is incorrect: A correct synonym is present among the choices, so selecting 'none of above' is not appropriate.

title: Choose the word that best replaces the words highlighted in

CONCEPT

A one-word substitution replaces a descriptive phrase with a noun that preserves the phrase’s exact meaning and grammatical role.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q9
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Choose the word that is closest in meaning (synonym) to the underlined word.

The government introduced several measures to alleviate poverty in rural areas.
solution:
Concept: A synonym question asks for the word that carries the same core sense as the underlined word, so that substituting it preserves the sentence’s meaning. “Alleviate” means to make a problem, hardship, or burden less severe or intense — to lessen its degree, not to remove it fully.

Application: In “The government introduced several measures to alleviate poverty in rural areas,” alleviate describes the intended effect of the measures on poverty: making its severity smaller. Substituting “reduce” — “measures to reduce poverty” — keeps this exact sense of lessening a problem’s extent, so the sentence’s meaning is preserved.

Cross-check: Checking each remaining word against this same sense of lessening severity rules them out:

  • “Increase” denotes a rise in quantity, size, or degree — the reverse of lessening something — so substituting it would flip the sentence’s meaning.

  • “Observe” denotes watching, noticing, or remarking on something, with no sense of a change in magnitude at all.

  • “Ignore” denotes deliberately disregarding something; disregarding a problem does not make it less severe.

So “reduce” is the word that keeps “alleviate”’s sense of lessening severity intact in this sentence.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q6

Ubiquitous describes something that seems to be present or found everywhere. Omnipresent carries the same central idea of being present everywhere, so it is the nearest match.

Contrast and cross-check

  • Rare means seldom encountered; it concerns low frequency.

  • Scarce means insufficiently available; it concerns limited quantity.

  • Unique means being the only one of its kind; it concerns singularity.

Therefore, the nearest synonym is Omnipresent.

title: What is synonymy relation?
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which statement defines the semantic relation of synonymy?
solution:
Concept

Lexical-semantic relations describe how the meanings of words or expressions are connected.

Synonymy is the relation in which two expressions have the same or nearly the same meaning; substitutability can still depend on context and register.

Application

The statement “A denotes the same as B” directly expresses equality or near-equality of meaning, so it represents synonymy.

Contrast

  • “A is part of B” expresses a part–whole relation, known as meronymy.

  • “A is a kind of B” places A under the broader class B, which is hyponymy.

  • “A is superordinate of B” makes A the broader class that includes B, which is hypernymy.

Cross-check

Pairs such as “begin” and “start” can denote the same action in many contexts, confirming the synonymy criterion.

Result: A denotes the same as B.

title: Choose the word that means the opposite of the highlighted
subject: Verbal Ability (English)

solution:
Antonym questions test whether you know a word's core sense precisely enough to state its exact opposite — not just any word that looks or sounds related. Many English words cluster in families sharing a root (here, “-ceed” and “-cede”), so distractors are often built from that root while expressing a different relationship (such as sequence/order) instead of the one actually being tested (direction of movement).

The highlighted word “proceed” means to move forward or carry on in a course of action. Reversing this specific sense of forward movement gives “to move backward, withdraw, or go away” — exactly what “receding” expresses.

  • proceeding — carries the same forward-moving sense as the highlighted word, so it is a near-synonym, not an opposite.

  • succeeding — means coming after in sequence or achieving a goal; this concerns order, not direction of movement.

  • preceding — means coming before in sequence; again an order relationship, not the movement-direction opposite required here.

Because “receding” is the only option that reverses the specific sense of forward movement carried by “proceed,” it is the correct antonym.

solution:
Concept: An antonym is a word whose meaning is opposite to that of the given word. To choose it, first fix the core sense of the given word, then look for the option that reverses that core sense (not one that merely relates to it).

Application: The core sense of ‘precious’ is having great value or worth. The opposite of ‘great value’ is ‘no value’. The choice that names ‘having no worth or use’ is ‘Worthless’, so it is the antonym.

Contrast with the other choices by meaning:

  • Valued – means held to be of worth; this restates the positive sense of precious rather than reversing it.

  • Loved – expresses affection or emotional attachment; this is about feeling rather than worth, a different idea from ‘precious’ (not its opposite).

  • Costly – means expensive or high in price; this is a near-synonym on the value axis, not its opposite.

Result: Only ‘Worthless’ reverses the core sense of value, so it is the antonym of precious.

Application: The target word straight describes a line or path that runs directly, without bending or curving. Negating that core property — directness — gives a line that bends or twists. The word that means “bent, twisted, not in a direct line” is crooked, so it is the antonym of straight.

Contrast with the other choices:

  • “Weak” — opposite of strong; about strength, not the shape of a line.

  • “Short” — opposite of long; about length, not bending.

  • “Long” — opposite of short; also about length, and a line can be long yet still straight.

Only crooked reverses the property of being direct/unbent, which is why it is the correct antonym.
