To determine the correct antonym, we must first clearly define the word "penchant" in the context of the sentence.

Word Analysis
Penchant: A strong or habitual liking for something or a tendency to do something.

Sentence context: "He has a penchant (strong liking/preference) for writing satirical poems."

Antonym required: We need a word that represents a lack of preference, aversion, or dislike for something.

title: Choose the word that means the opposite of the highlighted
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word that means the opposite of the highlighted word in the sentence.

The programme was not organized properly and confusion seemed inevitable.
solution:
Key idea: “Inevitable” means certain to happen or unavoidable.

  • The opposite idea is something that is not certain.

  • “Uncertain” best expresses that opposite meaning.

Answer: Option 0, “uncertain”, is correct.

title: Choose the word that means the opposite of the highlighted
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word that means the opposite of the word in bold in the sentence.

The leading English newspapers are known for their comprehensive coverage of news.
solution:
CONCEPT

An antonym is a word whose meaning contrasts with the central sense of another word in its context.

For an adjective describing coverage, compare the choices on the same semantic axis: breadth, completeness, or sufficiency.

APPLICATION

Here, “comprehensive” describes coverage that includes all or nearly all relevant news. Its contextual opposite is coverage that is insufficient in scope; “inadequate” carries that meaning.

CONTRAST

  • “Indifferent” describes a lack of interest or concern, so it belongs to the axis of attitude.

  • “Difficult” describes something hard to do or understand, so it belongs to the axis of effort.

  • “Impossible” describes something that cannot happen or be done, so it belongs to the axis of possibility.

  • “Inadequate” describes something insufficient in quality, quantity, or scope, so it belongs to the axis of sufficiency.

RESULT

The opposite of “comprehensive” in this sentence is “inadequate.”

title: Choose the word that roughly means the same as the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word that roughly means the same as the underlined phrase in the sentence.

The committee's decision to fund the project was agreed upon by everyone in the committee.
solution:
CONCEPT

A synonym is a word whose meaning is the same as, or very close to, another word or phrase in a particular context.

Context clues identify the intended sense; a word that is merely related to the topic is not necessarily interchangeable.

APPLICATION

The highlighted phrase describes complete agreement among all members of a group. “Unanimous” expresses that shared agreement, so it preserves the sentence’s meaning.

CONTRAST

  • “Divisive” describes something that creates disagreement or separation.

  • “Decided” describes something settled or determined, without saying that every person agreed.

  • “Comprehensive” describes something broad or complete in scope.

CROSS-CHECK

Substitution gives: “The committee’s decision to fund the project was unanimous.” The sentence still states that all committee members agreed, confirming “unanimous” as the result.

title: Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.

The deserted streets brought about a morose feeling into our minds.
solution:
The word 'morose' means gloomy, sullen, ill-humoured, or depressed in mood. We need its antonym (opposite).

'happy' (cheerful, light-hearted) directly opposes the gloomy sense of 'morose', so it is the correct antonym.

'sympathetic' (compassionate toward others) and 'diseased' (ill) describe attitude and health, not mood; 'halting' (hesitant, faltering) describes speech or movement. None of these is the opposite of 'morose'.

title: Choose the word which is closest in meaning to the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word which is closest in meaning to the underlined word in the given sentence.

Bengaluru has a salubrious climate to live in.
solution:
The sentence describes Bengaluru’s climate as “salubrious.” The word salubrious (from Latin salubris, “healthful, wholesome”) means favourable to health or well-being, and it is used especially of climate or air.

Therefore the closest synonym is “healthful” — a healthful climate is one that is good for your health, exactly the idea conveyed by salubrious.

The other options do not fit: “luxurious” relates to comfort and wealth, “hectic” means very busy or frantic, and “unpredictable” means changeable or hard to forecast — none of these carry the sense of being good for one’s health.

title: Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.

What a deceitful man; I am happy that he is behind the bars now.
solution:
The underlined word "deceitful" means dishonest, misleading, or intending to cheat. We need its antonym (opposite).

"Honest" means truthful, sincere, and free from deceit, which is the exact opposite of "deceitful." Hence, "honest" is the correct answer.

The other options do not fit: "fortunate" means lucky, "tasteful" means showing good taste, and "diseased" means affected by illness — none of these relate to truthfulness.

title: Which of the following words used in the passage reinforces
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which of the following words used in the passage reinforces the idea contained in the word, 'DISSONANCE'?
solution:
Concept

This is a vocabulary-in-context question testing the synonym relationship between words. To 'reinforce the idea' of a key word, an option must share or strengthen its core sense. The word DISSONANCE means a harsh, inharmonious clash of sounds, or a lack of harmony and agreement.

Application

Compare each candidate's core meaning against the sense of discord and harsh, jarring sound carried by DISSONANCE:

  • Cacophony means a harsh, jarring mixture of discordant sounds. This is the same sense of clashing, unharmonious noise that DISSONANCE expresses, so it directly reinforces the idea.

  • Aspersions means false or damaging accusations against someone's character; it concerns slander, not sound or harmony.

  • Strategy means a careful plan of action designed to reach a goal; it has no connection to harmony or noise.

  • Transition means the process of changing from one state to another; it concerns change, not discord.

Cross-check

Only one option carries the 'lack of harmony / harsh sound' sense that defines DISSONANCE. Cacophony is the matching synonym (both are listed together as near-synonyms in standard dictionaries), so it is the word that reinforces the idea contained in DISSONANCE.

title: Synonym (Most nearest meaning) of ORATOR is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Synonym (most nearly the same meaning) of ORATOR is
solution:
Concept

A synonym is a word that carries nearly the same core meaning as the target word. For vocabulary derived from Latin/Greek roots, fix the root sense first, then match the option whose definition overlaps that sense most closely.

Application

ORATOR comes from the Latin orare (‘to speak, to plead before an assembly’). An orator is therefore a public speaker — someone who delivers a formal, eloquent speech to an audience. Among the options, ‘Speaker’ denotes exactly a person who speaks to an audience, so it shares the central meaning.

Contrast

  • Reader — one who reads written text; about reading, not addressing an audience by speech.

  • Singer — one who produces music with the voice; melody, not spoken oratory.

  • Critic — one who evaluates or judges works; analysis, not public speaking.

Only ‘Speaker’ overlaps the root sense of delivering speech to an audience, so it is the nearest synonym of ORATOR.

title: Antonym (Most opposite meaning) of the word CELESTIAL is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Antonym (Most opposite meaning) of the word CELESTIAL is
solution:
Concept

An antonym is the word whose meaning is most opposite to the given word. "Celestial" is an adjective meaning relating to the sky or the heavens — divine, heavenly, otherworldly. So its antonym must name what belongs to the ground/earth, not to the heavens.

Application

CELESTIAL = of the heavens / sky. The opposite domain is the earth / worldly realm. The choice that means "belonging to the earth, worldly, terrestrial" is the correct antonym — that is "Earthly."

Contrast with the near-misses

  • "Heavenly" means of or like heaven — a synonym of celestial, not its opposite.

  • "Divine" means godlike / sacred — again a synonym of the heavenly sense, not an antonym.

  • "Supernatural" means beyond the natural / otherworldly — close in sense to celestial, so it is not the opposite either.

Only "Earthly" reverses the heavenly domain, so it is the most opposite in meaning. (Terrestrial / worldly / mundane are the standard dictionary antonyms of celestial.)

title: Choose the word that roughly means the same as the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word that most nearly means the same as the highlighted word in the sentence below.

Students who prepare for their board exams shouldn't neglect the languages.
solution:
The highlighted word is "neglect," which means to fail to give proper care or attention to something that deserves it.

Among the options, "ignore" (to refuse to take notice of / disregard) is the closest in meaning. Standard thesauruses list ignore and disregard as direct synonyms of neglect.

"Abandon" (to desert completely) is too strong, "decline" means to refuse or to decrease, and "fail" means to be unsuccessful — none of these conveys the sense of under-attending. Hence, the correct answer is "ignore."

title: From the option given below, choose the correct synonym which
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
From the options given below, choose the correct synonym which is the nearest in meaning to:

Parsimonious
solution:
Concept

A synonym is a word that carries the same or nearly the same meaning as another word. To pick the nearest synonym, fix the core meaning of the key word first, then match it against each choice by sense, and watch out for antonyms, which mean the opposite.

Application

"Parsimonious" describes someone who is excessively unwilling to spend money or resources, that is, miserly, stingy, or frugal to a fault. The needed word must express this same idea of extreme tight-fistedness.

"Penurious" carries exactly this sense: extremely sparing or stingy with money, and by extension extremely poor. It matches the core meaning of being unwilling to spend.

Contrast

  • Pessimistic: expecting the worst outcome; about a gloomy outlook, not about spending money.

  • Generous: freely giving and open-handed; this is the opposite of being tight with money.

  • Despondent: in low spirits, dejected; an emotional state, unrelated to thriftiness.

Only "Penurious" shares the meaning of extreme miserliness, so it is the nearest synonym of "Parsimonious".

title: From the option given below, choose the correct synonym which
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
From the option given below, choose the correct synonym which is the nearest in meaning:

Persistence
solution:
Concept

A synonym is the word that is nearest in meaning to a given headword. Persistence denotes the quality of continuing firmly and steadily in a course of action, a purpose, or a state, especially in spite of difficulty, opposition, or discouragement.

Application

We need the option that conveys this same idea of steadfast, unyielding continuation of effort. Perseverance means exactly that: continued, determined effort to do or achieve something despite obstacles. It maps directly onto the sense of Persistence, so it is the nearest synonym.

Contrast with the other choices

  • Surcease — a cessation or bringing to an end; this expresses stopping, the opposite of continuing.

  • Interruption — a break or temporary halt in something; again the idea of stopping, not of sustained effort.

  • Accuracy — correctness or precision; a quality about being error-free, unrelated to continuing an effort.

title: From the options given below, choose the correct antonym which
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
From the options given below, choose the correct antonym which is the most opposite in meaning:

Demur
solution:
Concept:

An antonym is the word most OPPOSITE in meaning to the given word. The verb "demur" means to raise an objection, to hesitate, or to express reluctance or disagreement before accepting something. So its strongest antonym is a word that means to accept or consent to something willingly.

Application:

To demur is to push back or withhold agreement. The exact opposite action is to give one's agreement or sanction — "approve". Where demur signals "I object / I hold back", approve signals "I accept / I consent". This direct reversal of the action makes "approve" the most opposite in meaning.

Contrast with the other choices:

  • "Reject" — this means to refuse or turn down, which is close in spirit to objecting; it points in the SAME direction as demur, not opposite to it.

  • "Entrust" — this means to give someone responsibility or to hand something over for safekeeping; it is unrelated to agreeing or objecting.

  • "Allot" — this means to allocate or assign a share; it is about distribution, not about consent or objection.

Cross-check: replacing demur with its opposite in a sentence — "She did not demur" carries the same sense as "She approved" — confirms that approve is the correct antonym.

title: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the underlined word. If you abstain from unnecessary criticism, you will be happier in life.
solution:
Concept

The verb ‘abstain’ means to deliberately hold back from doing something — to voluntarily refrain from or keep away from an action, often one that is tempting or easy to slip into. To choose the best synonym, look for the option that carries this same core idea: refraining from or keeping away from an act.

Applying it here

In ‘abstain from unnecessary criticism’, the sentence urges you to refrain from criticising needlessly. ‘Avoid’ means to keep away from or refrain from something, so replacing the word gives ‘avoid unnecessary criticism’, which keeps the meaning of the sentence intact. So ‘Avoid’ is the word that best expresses the meaning of ‘abstain’.

Why the other words do not fit

  • ‘Indulge’ means to give in to or freely take part in something — the very opposite of holding back.

  • ‘Differ’ means to be unlike something or to disagree with someone; it is about contrast, not refraining from an act.

  • ‘Deny’ means to declare something untrue or to refuse to grant a request; it is about rejecting a claim, not voluntarily keeping away from an activity.

title: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the underlined word. A corrupt officer is a disgrace to the whole department.
solution:
Concept

A synonym question asks for the word whose meaning is closest to the target word in the given sense. The underlined word "disgrace" (as a noun) means the loss of honour or respect that results from dishonourable conduct — in short, a state of dishonour or shame. To answer, match this core sense, not merely a loosely related idea.

Application

In the sentence, "A corrupt officer is a disgrace to the whole department," the corrupt officer brings dishonour upon the department — the department is shamed by the officer's conduct. The word that carries this exact sense of dishonour/loss-of-respect is "shame."

Contrast

  • Disgust — a feeling of strong revulsion or distaste; it describes an emotional reaction, not loss of honour.

  • Disturbance — an interruption of order or calm (a commotion); unrelated to dishonour.

  • Scandal — a publicised incident of wrongdoing that causes outrage; it names an event, whereas "disgrace" names the resulting state of dishonour.

  • Shame — dishonour and loss of respect; this matches the core sense of "disgrace" exactly.

Therefore the word that best expresses the meaning of "disgrace" is "shame."

title: Select the ANTONYM of the given word. FINITE
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the ANTONYM of the given word.
FINITE
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose meaning is the opposite of another word. To find an antonym, fix the core meaning of the given word and look for the option that reverses it.

"Finite" means having limits or bounds — something that can be counted or measured and that comes to an end.

Applying it here

The opposite of "having limits / coming to an end" is "having no limits / never ending." Among the choices, the word that carries this meaning of being without bound is "Endless," which means infinite or limitless. So "Endless" is the antonym of "Finite."

Why the other choices do not fit

  • "Limited" — this is a synonym of "finite" (also means bounded/restricted), so it has the same sense, not the opposite.

  • "Deep" — refers to extent downward or intensity; it is unrelated to the idea of limit versus limitlessness.

  • "Wide" — refers to breadth or extent across; it too is unrelated to whether something has an end.

Cross-check: "finite" and "endless/infinite" are a standard antonym pair (finite ↔ infinite), confirming the choice.

title: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the underlined word. He made some very pertinent comments. They would certainly help us revise the project.
solution:
Concept: In a synonym question you choose the option whose meaning is closest to the target word in the given context. The word ‘pertinent’ describes something that applies to and bears directly on the matter being discussed — to the point and materially useful.

Application: The sentence says the remarks ‘would certainly help us revise the project.’ A remark that genuinely helps revise the work must apply directly to it. The single word that names this quality — applicable to and bearing on the subject — is ‘Relevant’, the standard dictionary equivalent of ‘pertinent’.

Why the other words fall short:

  • ‘Thoughtful’ describes the care or reflection behind a remark — a quality of the speaker, not of its bearing on the topic.

  • ‘Applied’ means put to practical use; it speaks to how something is used, not to its meaning.

  • ‘Related’ conveys only a loose, general association, weaker and vaguer than the precise force of ‘pertinent’.

Therefore the best synonym is ‘Relevant’.

title: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the given word: COHERENT
solution:
Concept

A synonym question asks for the option whose meaning is closest to the given word. "Coherent" describes something that is logically connected and internally consistent, so its parts hold together and follow one another sensibly.

Application

Applying this to the given word, the option that matches "logically connected and consistent" is "Logical". Something coherent is reasoned and orderly, which is exactly what "logical" conveys.

Contrast

  • "Affiliated" means connected through formal membership or association, not consistency of ideas, so it does not capture the meaning.

  • "Convincing" means persuasive or believable; a coherent argument is often convincing, but the two words describe different qualities (consistency versus persuasiveness).

  • "Rambling" means disconnected and wandering, which is the opposite of coherent, so it is an antonym rather than a synonym.

title: Choose the correct synonym (most nearest meaning). 'Docile'
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct synonym (the word nearest in meaning):

'Docile'
solution:
Concept

A synonym is a word that carries the same or nearly the same meaning as another word. To pick the best synonym, fix the core sense of the target word, then choose the option whose meaning matches that sense most closely, rejecting any option that is opposite or unrelated.

Application

The adjective 'docile' describes a person or animal that is easy to manage, teach, or control — quiet, obedient and yielding to the will of others. Its core sense is therefore 'readily controlled or obedient'.

'Submissive' means ready to yield to the authority or will of another, that is, obedient and compliant. This matches the core sense of 'docile' almost exactly, so it is the nearest synonym.

Contrast with the other words

  • 'Stubborn' means refusing to change one's mind or yield — this is the opposite of being easy to control, so it is an antonym, not a synonym.

  • 'Strong' refers to physical or mental power and has nothing to do with obedience, so it is unrelated.

  • 'Changeable' means likely to vary or fluctuate, which describes inconstancy rather than obedience, so it too is unrelated.

Hence the word nearest in meaning to 'docile' is 'submissive'.

title: Choose the correct synonym (most nearest meaning). 'Bemoan'
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct synonym (most nearest meaning).

'Bemoan'
solution:
Concept

A synonym is a word that carries the most nearly the same meaning as the target word. To find it, fix the precise sense of the target word first, then match the option whose core meaning aligns with that sense — not merely a word from the same emotional area.

Application

The verb “bemoan” means to express grief, sorrow, or dissatisfaction about something — to mourn or wail over it aloud. The option that means “to express grief or sorrow about something” is Lament, which matches this sense exactly.

Contrast

  • Soothe — to calm, comfort, or relieve distress. This is the opposite movement: it eases sorrow rather than expressing it.

  • Denounce — to publicly condemn or accuse. It targets blame at a person or act, not personal grief.

  • Loathe — to feel intense dislike or disgust. It names an emotion of hatred, not the act of mourning or grieving.

Only Lament shares the core sense of voicing grief, so it is the nearest synonym of “bemoan.”

title: Choose the correct antonym (most opposite meaning). 'Gargantuan'
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct antonym (most opposite meaning).

'Gargantuan'
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose meaning is the most opposite to that of a given word. The task is not to find a related word, but the word that lies at the far end of the same scale of meaning. For size, that scale runs from extremely large at one end to extremely small at the other.

Application

'Gargantuan' means enormous, gigantic, immense — occupying the 'extremely large' end of the size scale (it comes from Gargantua, the giant in Rabelais's tales). Its most opposite meaning is therefore a word meaning 'extremely small'. 'Dwarf', used to describe something, means very small or stunted in size, which sits at the opposite extreme of the same scale.

Contrast with the near-misses

  • Colossal — means huge or vast; this is a synonym of gargantuan, not its opposite, so it is on the same end of the scale.

  • Humongo — from 'humongous', meaning extremely large; again a synonym of gargantuan, not an opposite.

  • Routinely — an adverb meaning 'as a regular habit'; it has nothing to do with size at all, so it cannot be an antonym of a size word.

Only 'Dwarf' expresses the opposite of large, so it is the correct antonym of 'Gargantuan'.

title: Choose the correct antonym (most opposite meaning). 'Exposition'
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct antonym (most opposite meaning).

'Exposition'
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose meaning is the most directly opposite to that of a given word. To find one, first fix the precise sense of the target word, then look for the offered choice that denotes its reverse, not merely a related or similar idea.

Exposition means a comprehensive setting-forth, explaining, or making-known of an idea, theory, or material in detail (also a public display that puts things on show). Its essence is to reveal and explain openly.

Application

Test each choice against the sense “to set forth and explain openly”:

  • Explanation – to make something clear; this is the same idea as exposition, so it is a synonym, not an opposite.

  • Critique – a detailed evaluation or judgement of something; this is a related analytical act, not the reverse of explaining.

  • Pronouncement – a formal public declaration; this too involves making something known, so it sits on the same side as exposition.

  • Silence – the state of saying nothing, withholding explanation or expression; this is the direct reverse of setting forth and making known.

The word that reverses “open explanation/making-known” is Silence, because it denotes the complete absence of expounding or expression.

Cross-check

Standard thesauruses list “explanation” among the synonyms of exposition and place “silence” on the opposite side. So the choice that holds, Silence, is confirmed as the most opposite in meaning among the four.

title: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the given word.

DEVOUR
solution:
Concept

A synonym question asks for the word closest in meaning to the given word. To solve it, fix the core sense of the headword, then test each candidate for the same core sense rather than a loose association.

Application

The headword "DEVOUR" means to eat or swallow up hungrily and completely; by extension it means to use up or take in entirely. Its core sense is therefore "to take in or use up completely".

Among the candidates, "Consume" carries exactly this core sense — to eat, drink, or use up entirely — so it matches DEVOUR most closely.

Contrast

  • Assign — means to allot a task or give out; it concerns distribution of duties, not eating or using up.

  • Despise — means to look down on or regard with contempt; it is an attitude of scorn, unrelated to the act of consuming.

  • Design — means to plan, sketch, or devise; it concerns creating a plan, the opposite of using something up.

Only "Consume" preserves the core sense of taking in or using up completely, so it is the best synonym for DEVOUR.

title: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the word that best expresses the meaning of the given word. EXOTIC
solution:
Concept

A “best synonym” question asks for the option whose meaning is closest to the headword. The test is substitution: the right answer is the word that could replace the headword in a sentence while keeping the same sense, not merely a word that is loosely associated with it.

Application

The headword EXOTIC means strikingly different from the ordinary — strange, foreign, or not commonly seen. Its core sense is “out of the ordinary.” The option that carries this same meaning is Unusual, which directly denotes “not usual, uncommon, out of the ordinary.” It passes the substitution test: an “exotic plant” and an “unusual plant” both convey something uncommon.

Contrast

Checking the remaining choices against the meaning of “exotic”:

  • Familiar — means well-known and ordinary; this is the opposite of “exotic,” so it is an antonym, not a synonym.

  • Thorough — means complete or carried out in full detail; it describes effort or care, unrelated to strangeness or foreignness.

  • Excessive — means too much in amount or degree; it speaks to quantity, not to being unusual or foreign.

Only the choice meaning “out of the ordinary” matches “exotic,” which is why Unusual is correct.

title: Select the ANTONYM of the given word. COINCIDE
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the ANTONYM of the given word.
COINCIDE
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose meaning is opposite to that of a given word. To find an antonym, first fix the core sense of the target word, then choose the option that expresses the reverse of that sense — not merely a word that is unrelated or that begins with the same prefix.

“Coincide” means to agree, to correspond exactly, or to be in harmony (two opinions, accounts, or events that match each other).

Application

The reverse of “to agree / correspond” is “to differ in opinion / fail to correspond.” Among the choices, “Disagree” carries exactly this opposite sense — to hold a contrary view or to be at variance — so it is the true antonym of coincide.

Contrast

  • “Disappear” means to cease to be visible; it is the opposite of “appear,” not of “agree,” so it does not reverse the sense of coincide.

  • “Disappoint” means to fail to fulfil someone’s hopes; it concerns expectation, not agreement or correspondence.

  • “Disbelieve” means to refuse to accept as true; it is the opposite of “believe,” and has nothing to do with two things matching.

The “dis-” prefix on every choice is a deliberate trap: a shared prefix does not make a word an opposite. Only the option that reverses the meaning of “agree / correspond” qualifies.

title: Select the ANTONYM of the given word. LAVISH
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the ANTONYM of the given word.

LAVISH
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose meaning is opposite to that of a given word. To find one, first fix the precise sense of the cue word, then choose the option that expresses its direct opposite (not a synonym or an unrelated word).

"Lavish" means given, spent, or produced in large, generous, even excessive amounts — abundant and extravagant.

Application

The opposite of "abundant / extravagant" is something scanty and inadequate in quantity. "Meagre" means lacking in quantity or quality — sparse, scanty, deficient — which is the direct opposite of lavish. So the antonym is "Meagre".

Contrast with the other words

  • "Laudable" means deserving praise; it describes worth, not amount, so it is unrelated to the abundant/scanty axis.

  • "Liberal" means generous and free in giving — this is a synonym of lavish, not its opposite.

  • "Excessive" means more than what is needed or proper — again close in sense to lavish, not opposite to it.

title: Select the ANTONYM of the given word. OPPRESSIVE
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the ANTONYM of the given word.
OPPRESSIVE
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word that expresses the opposite meaning of another word. To find the antonym of a word, first fix its core meaning, then look for the option whose meaning directly reverses it. Oppressive describes something cruel, harsh, and unjustly burdensome — typically the behaviour of a tyrannical authority that crushes people. Its opposite is therefore a quality of kindness, mercy and compassion toward people.

Application

The core sense of oppressive is "cruel and merciless toward people." The word that directly reverses this sense is humane, which means "marked by compassion, sympathy and consideration for people." Treating people humanely is the exact opposite of treating them oppressively, so humane is the antonym.

Contrast with the other choices

  • Voluntary means "done of one's own free will." Its true opposite is "compulsory/forced," so it does not reverse the cruelty sense of oppressive.

  • Wise means "having good judgement." Its opposite is "foolish"; it is unrelated to the harshness sense of oppressive.

  • Prosperous means "flourishing or wealthy." Its opposite is "poor/unsuccessful"; it describes financial condition, not treatment of people.

Antonym = Humane.

title: Choose the word that means the opposite of the highlighted
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word that means the opposite of the highlighted word in the sentence.

Rohit's analysis of the poem is profound.
solution:
CONCEPT

An antonym question asks for the word whose meaning directly reverses the highlighted word's sense in this exact context, not merely a dissimilar or generically negative word. First pin down the precise sense the highlighted word carries here, then match that sense's exact opposite.

APPLICATION

Here, "profound" describes Rohit's analysis of the poem as showing great depth of thought and insight. The direct opposite of having great depth is lacking depth, i.e. being shallow or surface-level. This is exactly what "superficial" means, so it reverses "profound" in this context.

CROSS-CHECK / CONTRAST

Checking the other options confirms none of them reverse the sense of depth:

  • "exacting" means demanding great care, precision, or rigor from effort; it describes strictness or thoroughness of the task, not depth of insight, so it does not oppose "profound".

  • "good" is a general positive evaluation of quality; it does not describe depth of thought one way or the other, so it is not an antonym of "profound".

  • "mysterious" means puzzling or hard to understand; it concerns clarity, not the depth of an analysis, so it does not reverse "profound" either.

Result: since only one option reverses the "great depth" sense of "profound" into "lacking depth," that option is the correct antonym.

title: Choose the correct synonyms being the most nearest meaning. Subscribe
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the option that is closest in meaning to the following word.

Subscribe
solution:
A synonym question asks for the option that shares the core dictionary meaning of the given word — not just any everyday association, but the sense a standard dictionary lists as primary or well-established for that word.

'Subscribe' — beyond its narrow everyday use for magazines or services — has a well-established dictionary sense: 'to subscribe to' an opinion, theory, or belief means to give one's consent or support to it, i.e., to hold or share that view. This is the sense tested here, so the option expressing 'share an opinion, view' is the match.

Cross-check / Contrast:

  • 'combine into a whole' — the meaning of 'combine'/'unite', not of holding an opinion.

  • 'join' — the meaning of 'enrol'/'enlist' as a member, a narrower everyday use, not the dictionary sense of agreeing with a view.

  • 'appoint' — the meaning of 'nominate'/'designate' someone to a role, unrelated to expressing agreement.

Hence, 'share an opinion, view' is the closest synonym of 'subscribe' among the given options.

title: Choose the correct synonyms being the most nearest meaning. Compliment
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the option that is nearest in meaning to the given word.

Compliment
solution:
Concept: A synonym question asks you to match the given word to the option that shares its core sense — its central meaning — not just its general topic or emotional field. Words in the same broad topic (people's reactions to someone) can still carry opposite senses (praise vs blame vs confusion), so the match must be on meaning, not topic.

Application: 'Compliment' (noun) is a polite remark that expresses praise, approval, or admiration for someone. Among the given options, 'Admiration' captures exactly this sense of favourable, approving regard, so it is the word nearest in meaning to 'Compliment'.

Cross-check — contrast with the other options:

  • 'Condemnation' means strong disapproval or blame — the opposite sense to praise.

  • 'Criticism' means pointing out faults or shortcomings — again a negative/evaluative sense, not praise.

  • 'Misunderstand' means failing to comprehend something correctly — a sense of confusion, unrelated to praise or approval.

These three distractors do not carry the favourable-regard sense of Compliment, which confirms Admiration as the nearest synonym.

title: Choose the correct antonym being the most opposite meaning. Eradicate
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct antonym being the most opposite meaning.

Eradicate
solution:
Concept: An antonym question asks for the option whose meaning is most directly OPPOSITE to the given word — not a synonym or a word that merely shares its general theme. Fix the exact sense of the given word first, then test every option against that sense; discard any option that restates or reinforces the same meaning.

Application: "Eradicate" means to destroy or remove something completely — to root it out so nothing remains. "Uproot", "Eliminate", and "Dismantle" all describe removing, ending, or taking something apart, so each stays in the same 'destroy/remove' sense as "Eradicate" rather than reversing it. "Implant" means to fix, insert, or establish something firmly in place — the reverse action of removing it entirely — so it is the option whose meaning is most opposite to "Eradicate".

  • "Uproot" shares Eradicate's sense of destroying by pulling out completely, so it reinforces the stem rather than opposing it.

  • "Eliminate" also means to remove or get rid of something fully, again matching rather than reversing the stem's sense.

  • "Dismantle" means to take a structure apart piece by piece, which is still an act of destruction/removal, not its opposite.

Result: Because the required antonym must reverse the 'destroy/remove completely' sense of "Eradicate" into a 'fix/establish' sense, "Implant" is the correct answer.

title: Choose the correct antonym being the most opposite meaning. Esteem
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

Esteem
solution:
An antonym is a word whose meaning is the direct opposite of another word's meaning, not merely different, but reversed. To find it, first pin down the core sense of the given word, then pick the option that stands in polar opposition to that sense, ruling out any option that merely restates or resembles it.

Esteem means a favourable opinion held of someone: high regard, respect, or admiration. The word standing in direct opposition to holding someone in high regard is one that denotes a lack of regard or a low opinion of them.

  • Regard denotes a favourable opinion or high esteem itself, so it restates the given word's meaning rather than reversing it.

  • Respect likewise means holding someone in high esteem, again a synonym, not an opposite.

  • Occasional describes how often something happens, a matter of frequency, and has no bearing on regard or esteem at all, so it cannot be the semantic opposite of Esteem.

The option that denotes a lack of regard, the polar opposite of high esteem, is Disrespect, which is the correct antonym.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q9
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Fill in the blank with the antonym, in context, of the capitalized word in the sentence:

If you wish for PEACE, be prepared for ____.
solution:
An antonym-in-context question asks for a word that is directly opposite in meaning to the capitalized word, chosen so the completed sentence still reads as a coherent, well-known statement (often a contrastive maxim).

The capitalized word here is PEACE. The sentence frame "If you wish for PEACE, be prepared for ____." echoes the classic English maxim "If you want peace, prepare for war" (from the Latin adage Si vis pacem, para bellum), which argues that readiness for conflict is what preserves calm. "Peace" denotes a state of calm and the absence of conflict; its direct antonym is "war", a state of armed conflict and hostility. So the blank is completed by "War".

Checking the other options against this contrast confirms the choice:

  • Misery is the antonym of "happiness", describing emotional suffering — it does not name a state of armed conflict, so it does not complete the "peace vs. ____" maxim.

  • Happiness sits on the same side as "peace" (a positive, calm state); it cannot be the antonym of "peace" itself.

  • Healthy describes physical well-being and has no direct semantic opposition to "peace", so it does not fit the sentence's contrast.

Hence the completed sentence reads: "If you wish for PEACE, be prepared for WAR."

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q10
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning (antonym) to the underlined word.

The witness gave a credible statement before the court.
solution:
An antonym is a word whose meaning is the direct opposite of another word’s meaning. To pick it out among several options, first pin down the specific core sense of the underlined word — not just its general topic — and then find the option that reverses exactly that sense.

Credible means capable of being believed; a credible statement is one that is trustworthy and convincing to a listener.

Applying this to the sentence, unreliable reverses that exact sense: a statement that is unreliable cannot be trusted or believed, which is the precise opposite of a credible statement. This makes unreliable the correct antonym.

  • believable carries the same sense as credible (a synonym, not its opposite).

  • truthful also implies trustworthiness, aligning with credible rather than opposing it.

  • logical describes valid reasoning or consistency of argument, a quality unrelated to whether a statement can be trusted, so it does not oppose credible either.

Hence, the correct antonym of credible is unreliable.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q12
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning (antonym) to the underlined word.

His explanation was too vague to be understood clearly.
solution:
An antonym is a word whose meaning is directly opposite to that of a given word — it is distinct from a synonym, which shares a similar meaning. To identify the antonym among a set of options, each candidate word's own meaning must be checked against the given word's meaning, since word-relation questions often include near-synonyms designed to look plausible.

"Vague" means lacking clarity or precision — indefinite, not clearly or exactly expressed. Checking each option's own meaning: "unclear" describes something not distinctly expressed; "confusing" describes something that causes difficulty in understanding; "uncertain" describes something not known for certain. All three carry a meaning close to "vague" rather than opposite to it. "Precise", however, means exact and sharply defined — the direct opposite of vague.

This is confirmed independently: standard English thesauri list "precise" as the antonym of "vague", while "unclear", "confusing", and "uncertain" are listed among its synonyms — so among the four options, "precise" is the only word carrying the opposite meaning, and the other three restate the same idea as "vague".

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q97
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Read the following passage and select the correct option.

We planned to travel Calcutta towards the end of last November. We arranged tickets for the journey from an agency and began our long cherished journey on the third day of the fourth week. It was a very clear day without a cloud in the sky. We felt very little motion as the vehicle moved smoothly into the air. The hostess brought water bottle for each passenger along with a light meal packet in a card board box. She also served tea or coffee according to the demands of the passengers. One passenger asked her when to open the box. She replied, ‘you can take it now or keep it to be used later’. We did not open the box then and there as we did not feel any urge for we just took our meals.

The appropriate meaning of the word ‘cherished’ is
solution:
A vocabulary-in-context question asks for the dictionary sense of the highlighted word that also fits the sentence's meaning and tone, not merely a word that sounds similar. 'Cherish' (past participle 'cherished') is a verb meaning to hold an idea, a hope, a memory, or a plan in one's mind with care and affection over a period of time; standard dictionaries gloss it as 'to nurture' or 'to hold dear'.

  1. Locate the word in context: the phrase 'our long cherished journey' describes the journey itself as something held in mind with affection over time, rather than describing a physical action performed on it.

  2. Recall the core dictionary sense of 'cherish': to keep and cultivate a feeling, hope, or plan with care over time (e.g. 'to hold dear', 'to nurture an ambition').

  3. Match that sense to the sentence: a journey that has been mentally sustained and looked forward to for a long period corresponds to this sense.

Substituting each candidate word back into the phrase 'our long ___ journey' and comparing the resulting sense to 'held dear / sustained with care over time' confirms the choice:

  • 'carried' describes physically transporting or bearing something from one place to another — a different sense from holding a plan dear.

  • 'nurtured' describes fostering and sustaining something with care over time — the same sense as 'held dear'.

  • 'left' describes departing from or abandoning something — the opposite of continuing to hold it in mind.

  • 'forgotten' describes losing something from memory — again the opposite process of actively sustaining an idea over time.

Result: the sense of 'cherish' that fits — fostering and sustaining something with care and affection over time — matches 'nurtured'.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q76
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Synonym (nearly the same meaning) of FURORE is
solution:
Concept

A synonym is a word that carries nearly the same core meaning as the headword and can replace it in the same kind of sentence without changing what is being said. The dependable method is to fix the headword’s dictionary sense first — including what it is normally used about — and only then test each offered word against that whole sense.

Where a standard dictionary glosses the headword with one particular word, that gloss is the closest equivalent. Other words may sit near the headword in a broad thesaurus range while their own core sense lies elsewhere, so a “nearly the same meaning” item is settled by the direct gloss, not by loose proximity.

Application

FURORE (also spelt furor) means an outbreak of public anger or excitement — a noisy, collective reaction of protest or excited comment about something, as in “the announcement caused a furore”. Its core sense therefore has three parts:

  • it is public — a reaction shown by many people together, not by one person;

  • it is noisy or vehement — anger, indignation or excited comment, not quiet disapproval;

  • it is triggered — it is a reaction to some particular event, decision or announcement.

Tested against those three parts, “uproar” matches on all of them: it names a loud, confused noise made by a crowd and, by extension, a public outburst of protest or complaint about something. It is also the direct dictionary equivalent — Oxford gives uproar as the synonym of furore, Collins glosses the sense as uproar, and Merriam-Webster defines the US form furor as “a sudden outburst: uproar”. The two words are interchangeable in use: “the decision caused an uproar” says the same thing as “the decision caused a furore”.

Cross-check

Each of the other offered words overlaps furore somewhere, but none of them is its direct equivalent:

Word

Its own core sense

Distance from FURORE

Storm

A violent disturbance of the atmosphere, with strong winds and usually rain, thunder or snow; figuratively, a violent commotion or an outburst of strong feeling, as in “a storm of protest”.

Touches furore only through that extended figurative use; its core, defining sense is meteorological, and no dictionary glosses furore as “storm”, so it is the looser match.

Disorder

An absence of order or regular arrangement — confusion or untidiness in how things stand; in public contexts, a breakdown of peaceful conduct, as in “civil disorder”.

Names a state of confusion or lawlessness rather than a noisy collective reaction to a trigger.

Wildness

The quality of being wild — uncultivated, untamed or lacking restraint; used of land left in its natural state and of behaviour that is unruly or unchecked.

Describes a character or manner rather than a public outcry about something.

The substitution test reads the same way: in the frame “the announcement caused a ___”, uproar reproduces “the announcement caused a furore” exactly, while the other words shift the meaning towards weather, confusion or unrestrained behaviour.

Hence the word nearest in meaning to FURORE is uproar.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q77
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Antonym (word most opposite in meaning) of DEFEND is:
solution:
Concept: An antonym is a word whose core sense stands opposite to another word's core sense. For an action verb the antonym names the converse action — the deed that reverses or opposes it — not merely a word with a different meaning, and not a near-synonym drawn from the same field. The dependable test is to place both verbs in one frame, such as "to ___ a fort", and check whether the two readings pull in opposite directions.

Application: "Defend" means to protect a person, place, position or claim from an assault — to ward off a threat and hold ground against an aggressor. Its converse is therefore the verb that names the very aggression being warded off: to set upon a target with force. In one frame, "to defend a fort" and "to attack a fort" describe the two opposed sides of a single engagement, which is exactly the opposition an antonym must capture.

Cross-check against every choice

Word

Core sense

Relation to "defend"

Preserve

keep something in its existing condition, free from loss or decay

belongs to the same protective field, so a near-synonym rather than an opposite

Caress

touch or stroke a person or animal gently and affectionately

belongs to an unrelated field of physical touch, so neither opposite nor synonym

Attack

set upon a person, place or position with force

names the converse action, which is the opposition the stem asks for

None of these

a claim about the option set rather than a word

not applicable, since a listed word does carry the opposite sense

Hence the word most opposite in meaning to "defend" is attack.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q78
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to CHRONIC.
solution:
Concept

An antonym expresses a meaning opposed along the same semantic dimension. For adjectives of duration, compare whether something persists for a long period or lasts only for a limited time.

Application

Chronic means continuing or recurring for a long time. Temporary means lasting for only a limited time and having an expected end. These meanings oppose each other on the dimension of duration.

Contrast

  • Pathetic means arousing pity or being very inadequate; it describes quality or emotional response rather than duration.

  • Mild means limited in intensity or severity; it describes degree rather than duration.

  • Characteristic means typical or distinctive; it describes a defining quality rather than duration.

Cross-check

A dictionary contrast gives long-lasting for chronic and limited-time for temporary, so the opposition remains on the same time axis.

Therefore, the most opposite meaning is Temporary.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q7
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: CAPRICIOUS
solution:
Concept

A synonym is a word that has the same or nearly the same meaning as another word. To identify one, isolate the target word’s core sense and compare every candidate on that same semantic axis.

Application

Capricious describes a person, mood, or action that changes suddenly and unpredictably, often according to impulse. Whimsical can likewise describe behaviour guided by sudden, fanciful, or unpredictable ideas.

Contrast

  • Steadfast denotes firmness and constancy rather than changeability.

  • Cautious denotes careful avoidance of risk through deliberation.

  • Generous denotes willingness to give freely or abundantly.

Cross-check

An antonym check reinforces the distinction: steadfast is close to the opposite of capricious, while whimsical shares its idea of impulse and unpredictability. Therefore, the nearest synonym is Whimsical.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q8
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to ‘OBFUSCATE’.
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose meaning is opposite to that of another word.

To obfuscate means to make something unclear, confusing, or difficult to understand.

Application

Clarify means to make something clear or easier to understand. It therefore expresses the opposite movement in meaning from obfuscate.

Contrast

  • Confuse means to make something difficult to understand, so it is close in meaning to obfuscate.

  • Muddle means to put something into a confused or disordered state, so it is also close in meaning to obfuscate.

  • Clarify means to remove confusion and make the meaning clear, which gives the required opposite sense.

  • Conceal means to hide something from view or knowledge; it does not express the direct opposite of making something unclear.

Cross-check

Replacing obfuscate with clarify reverses the clarity of the information: one makes it obscure, while the other makes it clear.

Therefore, the answer is Clarify.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q9
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: EPHEMERAL
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose core meaning is opposite to that of another word.

For a duration word, compare whether each choice expresses brevity, permanence, or an unrelated quality.

Application

Ephemeral means lasting for a very short time. Eternal means continuing forever or without end, so the two words lie at opposite ends of the duration scale.

Contrast

  • Transient means temporary or passing quickly, which is close in meaning to ephemeral.

  • Short-lived means lasting only briefly, which is also close in meaning to ephemeral.

  • Eternal means lasting without end, which reverses the brief-duration sense of ephemeral.

  • Trivial means unimportant; it describes significance, not duration.

Cross-check

Replacing ephemeral with eternal changes the duration from brief to unending, whereas transient and short-lived preserve the original idea and trivial changes the meaning axis.

Therefore, the most opposite word is Eternal.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q82
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Read the following passage carefully and select the correct answer to the questions given at the end of the passage.

Ecosystems provide people with a variety of goods and services, such as food, clean water, clean air, flood control, soil stabilization, pollination, climate regulation, spiritual fulfillment and aesthetic enjoyment, to name just a few. Most of these benefits are either irreplaceable or the technology necessary to replace them is prohibitively expensive. For example potable fresh water can be extracted by desalinating sea water, but only at great cost.

The rapidly expanding human population has greatly modified the earth’s ecosystem to meet their increased requirements of some goods and services, particularly food, fresh water, timber, fibre and fuel. These modifications have contributed substantially to human well being and economic development. The benefits have not been equally distributed.

Some people have actually been harmed by these changes. Moreover, short-term increases in some ecosystems’ goods and services have come at the cost of long term degradation of others. For example, efforts to increase the production of food and fibre have decreased the ability of some ecosystems to provide clean water, regulate flooding and support biodiversity.

The antonym of the word “Substantially” used in the passage is
solution:
Concept

Antonyms express opposing meanings on the same semantic scale. Degree adverbs can be compared by the amount or intensity they convey.

A high-degree adverb contrasts with a low-degree adverb; words that express a broad extent or a marked degree remain close in meaning rather than opposite.

Application

In the passage, “contributed substantially” means “contributed to a large or considerable degree.” The required opposite must therefore express only a small degree.

Contrast

  • “Extensively” refers to a broad scope or extent.

  • “Largely” means for the most part or to a great extent.

  • “Slightly” means to a small degree.

  • “Significantly” means to a meaningful or noticeable degree.

Result

The antonym is “Slightly.”

title: Select the pair which has the same relationship. CORPOREAL:SPIRITUAL

title: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. Innuendo
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Innuendo
solution: The correct answer is Option D (Insinuation). An innuendo refers to an indirect or subtle remark, often suggesting something derogatory without stating it directly. Similarly, an insinuation is a hint or suggestion of something unpleasant made in an indirect way. Both words share the core meaning of conveying a message through implication rather than explicit statement, making them close synonyms. Option A (Prose) refers to ordinary written language without metrical structure, which is unrelated to the concept of indirect suggestion. Option B (Crude) means rough or unrefined, which describes quality rather than a method of communication. Option C (Ragged) refers to something torn or worn out, which is also irrelevant to the context of verbal implication. Therefore, Insinuation is the most appropriate synonym for Innuendo.

title: Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word. don’t
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the most appropriate antonym of the underlined word. I don’t like to work with people who are not flexible.
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose meaning contrasts with that of another word.

To select an antonym in context, first identify the intended sense of the tested word and then compare each choice with that sense.

Application

Here, flexible describes a person who is adaptable and willing to change. Rigid expresses the contrasting idea of being fixed or unwilling to adapt.

Contrast

  • Capable concerns ability or competence, not adaptability.

  • Malleable conveys readiness to be shaped or adapted, so it is close in sense to flexible.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q80
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

Just as the oceans opened up a new world for clipper ships and Yankee traders, space holds enormous potential for commerce today. The International Space Station (ISS) took 10 years and more than 30 missions to assemble. It is the result of unprecedented scientific and engineering collaboration among five space agencies representing 15 countries. The space station is approximately the size of a football field: a 460-ton, permanently crewed platform orbiting 250 miles above Earth. It is about four times as large as the Russian space station Mir and five times as large as the U.S. Skylab. The idea of a space station was once science fiction, existing only in the imagination until it became clear in the 1940s that construction of such a structure might be attainable by our nation. As the Space Age began in the 1950s, designs of 'space planes' and stations dominated popular media. The first rudimentary station was created in 1969 by the linking of two Russian Soyuz vehicles in space, followed by other stations and developments in space technology until construction began on the ISS in 1998, aided by the first reusable spacecraft ever developed: the American shuttles. Until recently, U.S. research space onboard the ISS had been reserved for mostly government initiatives, but new opportunities for commercial and academic use of the ISS are now available, facilitated by the ISS National Lab.

Find the ANTONYM of the word 'rudimentary'.
solution:
An antonym is a word whose meaning is opposite to another word's meaning. To find the antonym of a word used in a passage, first pin down the sense in which the passage uses that word, then pick the option that expresses the reverse of that sense — not merely a related or similar idea.

In the passage, "rudimentary" describes the very first, most basic version of a space station — one that was still simple and had not yet been developed further. So the word's contextual sense here is "basic, elementary, at an early stage of development." Its antonym must therefore express the opposite sense: "far developed, complex, or sophisticated."

  • "Elementary" names the same basic, early-stage sense as "rudimentary," so it is a synonym, not an antonym.

  • "Basic" names the same plain, foundational, undeveloped state as "rudimentary" — again a synonym.

  • "Simple" likewise describes something uncomplicated and unrefined, matching rather than opposing "rudimentary."

  • "Advanced" describes something far developed, refined, and sophisticated — the reverse of a basic, early stage, which is exactly what an antonym of "rudimentary" must express.

Cross-checking against established dictionaries confirms this: Collins Dictionary lists "advanced" as an antonym of "rudimentary," while "elementary," "basic," and "simple" are documented as synonyms of it in Cambridge and Merriam-Webster.

Hence, "Advanced" is the correct antonym of "rudimentary" among the options offered.

title: Directions: In the question, there are four sentences. Each sentence
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Directions: In the question, there are four sentences. Each sentence has a pair of words/phrases that are italicised and highlighted. Select the most appropriate words or phrases to form grammatically and syntactically correct sentences. Then, from the options given, choose the best one.

(a) The (A) reticent / (B) taciturn boy doesn't want to mix up with strangers.

(b) The (A) exceptionable / (B) exceptional behaviour of the old choleric has been viewed seriously by everyone concerned.

(c) I am simply (A) uninterested / (B) disinterested in your cock and bull story.

(d) The landlord died intestate leaving the (A) descendants / (B) descendents to settle the property dispute at their own.

Note: each option below is a four-letter code, in the order (a)-(b)-(c)-(d), showing which choice -- A or B -- is grammatically correct for that sentence. For example, the option "AAAA" means the (A) word is the correct choice in every one of the four sentences.
solution:
Concept: This item tests commonly confused word pairs -- near-synonyms that look or sound alike but differ in meaning or register, so only one member of each pair fits a given context. The answer options are coded as four-letter sequences (order a to d); each letter is the correct choice, A or B, for that sentence.

Application: working through each sentence's word pair in turn:

  • Sentence (a): "reticent" indicates reluctance to speak or to mingle with others, which is exactly the sense needed for "doesn't want to mix up with strangers." "Taciturn" only means habitually untalkative in general, without that specific stranger-avoiding nuance.

  • Sentence (b): "exceptionable" means objectionable or open to criticism, which matches behaviour that "has been viewed seriously." "Exceptional" means unusually good, the opposite sense.

  • Sentence (c): "uninterested" means not interested or bored, matching a reaction to a tedious story. "Disinterested" means impartial/unbiased, a different idea entirely.

  • Sentence (d): "descendants" is the standard spelling for offspring, which is who "their" refers to. "Descendents" is a non-standard spelling and not the accepted noun form.

Cross-check: contrasting each accepted word against its rejected pair-word by meaning:

Sentence

Correct word -- meaning

Rejected word -- meaning

(a)

reticent -- reluctant to speak/mingle, esp. with strangers

taciturn -- habitually silent by nature, no stranger-specific sense

(b)

exceptionable -- objectionable, open to criticism

exceptional -- remarkably good, outstanding

(c)

uninterested -- not interested, bored

disinterested -- impartial, unbiased

(d)

descendants -- offspring (standard spelling)

descendents -- non-standard/incorrect spelling

Result: every sentence takes its (A) word, so the correct four-letter combination is AAAA -- reticent, exceptionable, uninterested, descendants.

title: The study of pronunciation of words is called
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The study of pronunciation of words is called
solution:
Concept: Different branches of language study describe sounds in different ways. Orthoepy is the study of the accepted, standard pronunciation of words — it tells you how a word ought to be spoken. It is prescriptive: it deals with what counts as correct pronunciation, often in relation to spelling.

Application: The stem asks specifically for the study of the pronunciation of words. That definition matches orthoepy exactly — "orthoepy" comes from Greek orthos (correct) + epos (speech), literally "correct speech", i.e. the study of how words should be pronounced.

Contrast — why the near-misses do not fit:

  • Phonetics studies the physical speech sounds themselves — how they are articulated, their acoustic properties, and how they are heard. It is descriptive and broader than the pronunciation of particular words, so it is the close distractor but not the term for the standard pronunciation of words.

  • Speech is the general act of speaking, not a field of study, so it cannot be the name of this discipline.

  • Voice refers to the sound a person produces, not the study of how words are pronounced.

Result: the study of the pronunciation of words is orthoepy.

title: Choose the word that best replaces the words highlighted in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word that best replaces the words highlighted in the sentence.

RADAR is a word formed from the initial letters of a set of words.
solution:
A word created by joining together the initial letters of a longer name or phrase, and then used as an ordinary standalone word, is classed as an abbreviation — specifically, an acronym, the type of abbreviation that is pronounced as a single word rather than spelled out letter by letter.

RADAR is built exactly this way: it takes the initial letters of RAdio Detection And Ranging and is read as one word. So the phrase “a word formed from the initial letters of a set of words” is best replaced by “an abbreviation.”

  • an anachronism describes something placed in the wrong time period (for example, a clock shown in a medieval painting) — it has nothing to do with how a word is built from letters.

  • an anagram rearranges every letter of one word or phrase to spell a different word (for example, 'listen' becomes 'silent') — RADAR is not a rearrangement of another word's letters, it is built from the first letters of several separate words.

  • an idiom is a fixed multi-word expression with a figurative meaning (for example, 'kick the bucket') — it stays a phrase, not a single word built from initials.

title: Choose the word (or words) that would best replace the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word (or words) that would best replace the words highlighted in the sentence.

They will be celebrating the 25th year of their marriage day.
solution:
In a word/phrase substitution question, the replacement must match the underlined phrase in both sense and grammatical role, not just topic. A word that names a one-time EVENT (a ceremony, a specific day) is not interchangeable with a word that names a RECURRING date tied to that event, even when both relate to the same topic — here, marriage.

The sentence counts ‘the 25th year’ of something happening in their marriage, which only makes sense if that something returns every year. As written, ‘marriage day’ literally names the one specific day the couple got married — a single day cannot have a ‘25th’ occurrence. The word for the yearly return of that date is ‘anniversary’, so ‘marriage anniversary’ — the noun phrase for the yearly recurrence of the wedding date — is the correct replacement: ‘They will be celebrating the 25th year of their marriage anniversary,’ i.e., their 25th wedding anniversary.

A substitution question tests whether the chosen word preserves the MEANING of the underlined phrase, not just whether a mechanical swap reads most smoothly — so surface fluency of the resulting sentence should not be the deciding factor.

Checking each distractor by its own meaning confirms only one term names a yearly-recurring date:

  • ‘marriage’ names the ongoing married relationship/institution itself, not a date; although swapping it in reads smoothly, it drops the day/date-recurrence sense of the original phrase, so it cannot be ‘the 25th’ of anything.

  • ‘marriage function’ names the wedding ceremony/reception — a single social event held once, at the time of the wedding, not something that returns every year.

  • ‘wedding’ is another name for that same one-time marriage ceremony, again not a date that recurs annually.

Because only ‘marriage anniversary’ expresses a date that returns every year, it alone matches the ‘25th year’ framing in the sentence.

title: Select the phrase that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)

I am grateful to my teacher who persistently scolded me for poor spelling.
solution:
Concept

Idioms must be read as fixed units, not word-by-word: the same verb ('pull') takes a completely different sense depending on the particle that follows it (up, through, out, off). To answer, replace the underlined word with each phrase and keep only the one whose established idiomatic meaning equals the underlined word.

Application

The underlined word is scolded, meaning to reprimand or criticise someone for a fault or mistake. Among the phrasal verbs offered, pull (someone) up is the one that idiomatically means to rebuke or criticise a person for something they have done wrong. Substituting it gives: 'my teacher who persistently pulled me up for poor spelling' — which preserves the sense of repeated reprimanding.

Contrast

  • pull through — to recover from or survive a difficult situation (e.g. an illness). This is about helping someone get better, not correcting them.

  • pull out — to withdraw from or rescue someone out of a situation; it carries no sense of reprimand.

  • pull off — to succeed in doing something difficult, or to remove/detach something; unrelated to criticising a fault.

Only pull (someone) up carries the meaning of reprimanding for a mistake, so it is the phrase that best expresses scolded.
