To understand the idiom "Cut Corners", it is helpful to look at its origin and practical application in professional or creative contexts.

Meaning and Usage
The idiom "Cut Corners" means to perform an action or task in the easiest, quickest, or cheapest way possible, often by ignoring rules, safety measures, or high standards. It essentially implies sacrificing quality to prioritize efficiency, speed, or cost-cutting.

title: Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.

I have never __________ in the Raj Bhavan, but I hope to very soon.
solution:
Key idea: The phrase “set foot in” means to enter or visit a place.

  • The sentence says the speaker has never been inside Raj Bhavan but hopes to visit soon.

  • The idiom that expresses entering a place is “set foot”.

Answer: Option 1, “set foot”, is correct.

title: Select the option that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the option that best expresses the meaning of the underlined phrase/group of words. Several houses had to be demolished to decongest the road.
solution:
Concept

A vocabulary-match question asks for the phrasal verb whose dictionary meaning is closest to the underlined word in the same context. To demolish means to deliberately knock down or tear apart a structure, especially a building, until it is destroyed.

Application

In the sentence, houses are being destroyed so the road can be cleared. The standard phrasal verb for deliberately destroying a building is pull down — dictionaries list “pull down” directly as a synonym of “demolish” (for example, “the old houses were pulled down”). So Pulled down is the exact contextual match.

Contrast

  • Put down — to suppress, to write or note something, or to kill an injured animal; it is not used for destroying a building.

  • Turned down — to reject an offer or request, or to reduce volume, heat, or intensity; it does not describe destroying a structure.

  • Broken down — to stop working (a machine), or to split something into parts or decompose; it does not mean to demolish a structure.

Therefore the option that best expresses the meaning of demolished is Pulled down.

title: Find the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom. Value education
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Find the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.

Value education should be a part and parcel of any education system.
solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from the literal sense of its individual words; you must learn the phrase as a single unit. The idiom “part and parcel” denotes something that is an essential, integral and inseparable component of a larger whole — a piece without which the whole is incomplete.

Application

In the sentence “Value education should be a part and parcel of any education system,” the writer is saying that value education is not an optional add-on but a necessary, built-in element of the system. Substituting the meaning gives: “Value education should be an essential part of any education system,” which preserves the intended sense exactly.

Contrast

The near-meanings differ in force:

  • “An essential part” — captures the inseparable, must-have sense the idiom carries.

  • “An important part” — signals high value but still allows the part to be separable or merely significant; the idiom is stronger than “important.”

  • “An additional part” — implies something extra added on, the opposite of being built in.

  • “A plus part” — is not a standard English phrase and conveys no defined idiomatic meaning.

title: Select the appropriate phrase that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. He
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate phrase that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

He is so rude that it is difficult to ________ with him.
solution:
Concept

A phrasal verb is a verb combined with a particle (a preposition or adverb), and the whole unit carries a fixed meaning that is usually different from the literal meaning of its parts. Changing the particle changes the meaning entirely, so the correct choice depends on the relationship the sentence describes.

Application

The sentence describes a person who is rude, so the blank must express the difficulty of maintaining a friendly relationship with him. The phrasal verb "get on with (somebody)" means to have a friendly, harmonious relationship with that person. So "difficult to get on with him" means it is hard to be on good terms with him, which fits a rude person perfectly.

Contrast

  • "get out" means to leave or escape from a place; it does not describe a relationship between people.

  • "get up" means to rise from bed or to stand up; it has nothing to do with how two people relate.

  • "get away" means to escape or to take a short holiday; it expresses departure, not the difficulty of relating to someone.

Only the phrase meaning "have a friendly relationship" matches the idea that a rude person is hard to be on good terms with.

title: Find the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom. When he
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Find the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom. When he was speaking, his father cut him off.
solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose overall meaning cannot be worked out from the literal meaning of its individual words. The phrasal idiom "to cut someone off" has more than one sense, so the correct sense must be chosen from the surrounding context. When it is used about a person who is talking, "to cut someone off" means to stop them mid-speech — that is, to interrupt them before they have finished.

Application

In the sentence "When he was speaking, his father cut him off," the time clause "When he was speaking" tells us the action happened while the son was in the middle of talking. The father broke into the son's speech and stopped him from continuing. That is exactly the speech-related sense of the idiom, so "cut him off" here means interrupted him.

Why the other meanings do not fit here

  • "Disinherited him" — "cut off" can mean to deprive someone of an inheritance, but only in a money/family-legacy context (e.g., "cut off without a penny"); the sentence is about speaking, not money, so this sense does not apply.

  • "Rebuked him" — this means to scold or criticise; the sentence describes the father stopping the speech, not telling the son off, so it does not match.

  • "Isolated him" — to isolate is to separate someone socially or physically; nothing in the sentence suggests cutting the son off from contact with others.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q21
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Choose the correct meaning of the underlined phrase/idiom from the options given below.

The new employee is still trying to learn the ropes in the office.
solution:
An idiom is a fixed expression whose overall meaning cannot reliably be worked out from the literal meaning of its individual words; it instead carries a conventional sense, recorded in standard dictionaries, that speakers use consistently in context. The verb phrase "learn the ropes" (also "know the ropes") is one such idiom; it originates from sailors learning to handle a ship's ropes and rigging.

In the given sentence, "The new employee is still trying to learn the ropes in the office," the phrase describes the new employee's ongoing effort to become familiar with the workplace's tasks, procedures, and routines — in other words, to understand how to do the job.

  • "Avoid responsibilities" names deliberately shirking or dodging assigned duties, not the act of acquiring a new skill.

  • "Teach others" names passing knowledge outward to someone else — the reverse direction of what a newcomer does.

  • "Change the rules" names altering existing procedures or regulations, not learning them.

Independent check: substituting the plain-English gloss — "is still trying to understand how to do her job in the office" — into the original sentence preserves its meaning, confirming this sense of the idiom.

So "learn the ropes" means to understand how to do a job.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q90
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate idiomatic expression from the options to replace the underlined word or words:

For the sake of domestic peace we should abide by wife’s advice.
solution:
Concept: Idiom-replacement questions ask you to match the figurative sense of an underlined word or phrase to the one listed idiom whose established, dictionary meaning best captures that sense — even when the underlined wording is a loose real-world paraphrase rather than a literal gloss of the idiom.

Application: The sentence describes a husband who, for the sake of keeping peace at home, submits to private counsel or reproof from his wife. ‘Curtain lecture’ is the established idiom for exactly this situation — a private reprimand a wife delivers to her husband at home, the term dating from the curtained four-poster bed where such talks historically took place. TPSC’s own official answer key for this paper marks ‘curtain lecture’ as the answer to this question.

Cross-check: The other three idioms describe unrelated situations:

  • ‘Cold feet’ denotes sudden nervousness or reluctance felt just before doing something, not domestic counsel.

  • ‘Cold water’ (as in ‘pour/throw cold water on’ something) denotes discouraging someone’s plan or enthusiasm, not receiving counsel from them.

  • ‘Call a spade a spade’ denotes speaking the plain truth bluntly, describing a manner of speech rather than a specific piece of domestic advice.

Hence ‘curtain lecture’ is the only offered idiom that matches the sentence’s sense.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q83
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Among the options, “cart off” is closest in meaning to:
solution:
Concept

A phrasal verb — a verb together with its particle — behaves as a single lexical unit. Some are largely transparent and others are wholly idiomatic, so the reliable method is never to add the two words together but to look up the sense that dictionaries record for the phrase as a whole.

A “X means” item then asks for the best match among the words actually offered. When no offered word is an exact synonym, the item works as a closest-match item: keep the single word that lies inside the phrase's semantic field and can occupy the same grammatical slot, and let the setting body's official key settle the intended choice.

Application

  1. Recorded sense of the whole phrase. Merriam-Webster gives “to take or drag away without ceremony or by force”; Collins gives “to carry or remove brusquely or by force”; Cambridge gives “to take someone away from a place and transport them somewhere else by using force”; Vocabulary.com gives “take away by means of a vehicle”, with the example “They carted off the old furniture.”

  2. The core common to all four glosses is removal: something or someone is taken away from where it was, typically bodily and typically without ceremony.

  3. Test each offered word against that core. discard also names removal — getting rid of an object by putting it out of use — and it is a verb, so it can occupy the same grammatical slot. disregard is a verb, but its action is mental, and dejected is an adjective describing a mood; neither lies in the removal field at all.

  4. discard is therefore the only offered word inside the phrase's semantic field, and it is the word the official key marks.

Cross-check: how close the match is

  • Be clear about how close the match actually is. discard adds the idea that the thing is unwanted, which “cart off” does not require: thieves can cart off valuable furniture without discarding it, and police cart people off to jail. Strictly, the nearest everyday equivalents are “haul away” or “carry off”, and neither is offered here.

  • That gap is why “None of these” is a live tension on this item. It would be the answer if no offered word lay inside the phrase's semantic field. discard does lie inside it — it is the only offered word that names removal at all — so on a closest-match reading the blanket choice is not selected.

  • The tie is settled by the setting body rather than by argument: the official TPSC final answer key for the Common Written Examination for Sub-Inspector of Excise, held on 30 April 2023, marks discard as the answer to this question, identically in all four booklet series.

Hence, as set and keyed by the commission, “cart off” means discard. For your own vocabulary work carry away the precise sense — to take or carry someone or something away, often forcibly — and remember that “discard” is the nearest of the words offered here rather than a full synonym.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q84
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The idiom “to have an axe to grind” means:

options.label: A
options.html: to have some personal interest to serve

solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose conventional meaning is not normally obtained by taking each word literally.

To interpret an idiom, identify its established figurative sense and test whether that sense makes a natural substitution in context.

Application

The idiom “to have an axe to grind” describes having a private or self-interested motive that influences one’s words or actions. Therefore, “to have some personal interest to serve” expresses the intended meaning.

Contrast

  • “To desert” means to abandon someone, a place, a cause, or a duty.

  • “To break through reserve or stiffness” refers to making an initially formal or awkward interaction more relaxed.

  • “None of these” would apply only if every listed meaning were unsuitable.

Cross-check

In the sentence “He criticised the plan because he had an axe to grind,” the phrase explains a personal motive behind the criticism. This confirms the meaning “to have some personal interest to serve.”

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q85
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: To add fuel to the fire means

options.label: A
options.html: to be conceited or arrogant in behaviour

solution:
Concept — An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is figurative rather than the sum of its individual words. The standard way to recover that meaning is to read the physical picture the words paint and then transfer that picture to human affairs: what the pictured action does to a physical object is what the idiom does to a situation, feeling, or dispute.

Application — The picture here is fuel being poured onto a fire that is already burning. Fuel is not what starts a fire; it is what makes a flame that is already alight burn harder and spread further. Transferred to human affairs, the fire is a state of affairs already under way — a quarrel, an anger, an agitation — and the fuel is a word or act added to it. So the idiom describes saying or doing something that makes an already-running situation more intense. Standard dictionaries gloss it as making an already bad or heated situation worse, and Collins records "agitation" as an established sense of "excitement", so among the meanings offered here the matching one is "to increase the existing excitement".

Contrast — The other meanings offered belong to different English expressions:

  • Conceited or arrogant behaviour is carried by expressions such as to blow one's own trumpet or to be on one's high horse.

  • Extravagant spending is carried by expressions such as to spend money like water or to live beyond one's means.

  • "None of these" would apply if no meaning offered matched the idiom; since the intensifying sense is offered here, it does not apply.

Cross-check — Substitute the meaning back into ordinary use: "His sarcastic remark added fuel to the fire" reads naturally as "his remark made the ongoing quarrel flare up further", and does not read as "his remark made him arrogant" or "his remark made him spend lavishly". The intensifying sense is the one that survives substitution.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q86
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: In the sentence, “The climbers came down from the mountain before sunset,” the phrasal verb “came down” means:
solution:
Concept: A phrasal verb combines a verb with a particle and may express a meaning determined by context. With movement verbs, the particle “down” commonly marks motion from a higher level to a lower level.

Application: The climbers begin on the mountain and move from that higher place before sunset. In this spatial context, “came down” therefore means to move downward or descend.

Contrast: The other expressions describe emotional states rather than physical downward movement:

  • “Calm down” means to become less agitated.

  • “Feel bad” means to experience sadness, guilt, regret, or discomfort.

  • “Feel frustrated” means to experience annoyance when progress is blocked.

Result: The contextual meaning of “came down” is “descend.”

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q10
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The CEO’s speech on the company’s future was just a flash in the pan.
solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose intended meaning differs from the literal meanings of its individual words. To interpret an idiom, use its established figurative sense and the surrounding context.

Application

“A flash in the pan” refers to something that becomes successful or impressive suddenly but does not continue. In the sentence, the speech created an initial impression about the company’s future, but that effect is described as short-lived.

Contrast

  • “A spectacular and lasting success” includes durability, whereas the idiom emphasizes brevity.

  • “A well-planned strategy” describes preparation and method, not the duration of success.

  • “A complete failure” removes the element of initial success that the idiom retains.

Therefore, the idiom means a sudden but temporary success.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q11
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
We have done a lot of work on the report. Let’s call it a day and continue tomorrow.

What does the underlined idiom mean?
solution:
CONCEPT

An idiom is a fixed expression whose intended meaning is different from a purely literal reading of its individual words.

To interpret an idiom, use its conventional meaning and test that meaning against the surrounding context.

APPLICATION

The sentence says that substantial work has already been completed and that the activity will continue tomorrow. In this context, “call it a day” means to stop working on something for the present session.

CONTRAST

  • “announce something as a great achievement” refers to public recognition of an accomplishment, not to ending a work session.

  • “ignore someone’s command” refers to disregarding an instruction, which the sentence does not describe.

  • “resume work” means to begin again after a pause, whereas the sentence places continuation on the following day.

CROSS-CHECK

Replacing the idiom with “stop working for now” preserves the logic: the report work ends today and continues tomorrow. Therefore, the answer is “to stop working on something.”

title: Identify the option that can be substituted as the correct
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Identify the option that can be substituted as the correct idiom for the underlined part of the given sentence.

My cousin sister Neetu had an aerial view of the trade fair from the top of the giant wheel.
solution: An aerial view from above is called a bird's eye view.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q74
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Forty winks
solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose accepted figurative meaning may differ from the literal meanings of its individual words.

Its meaning is determined by established usage, not by adding the dictionary meanings of the words.

Application

In established English usage, “forty winks” means a short sleep or nap, often taken during the day. Therefore, the matching value is “a brief nap or short sleep.”

Contrast

  • “A brief study” concerns a short period of learning or review; it is not the conventional meaning of this idiom.

  • “A brief history” is a concise account of past events or development; it is not the meaning of this expression.

  • “A brief description” is a short account of features or qualities; it is not the established sense of this idiom.

Cross-check

Substituting “a short nap” into “take forty winks” gives the natural sense “take a short nap”; study, history, and description do not fit the established idiomatic use.

Thus, the idiom means “a brief nap or short sleep.”

title: Choose the correct meaning of "Strike while the iron is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the correct meaning of "Strike while the iron is hot" from the given options:

options.label: B
options.html: to take advantage of an opportunity as soon as it exists

solution:
The correct meaning of the idiom "Strike while the iron is hot" is to take advantage of an opportunity as soon as it exists.

Explanation of the Idiom
Idioms often use metaphors derived from historical trades or everyday experiences to convey deeper meanings.

Origin: This phrase originates from the work of a blacksmith. To shape iron effectively, a blacksmith must strike it with a hammer while it is red-hot and pliable. If the iron is allowed to cool, it becomes too hard to mold, and the opportunity to shape it into the desired object is lost.

Metaphorical Meaning: In daily life, this idiom advises that when a favorable situation or a "window of opportunity" arises, you must act immediately to achieve your goal before the situation changes and the opportunity disappears.

title: DSSSB TGT Hindi 17 Aug 2025 Shift 1 Q73
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate proverb for the given situation.

Rohit bragged about winning a competition before the results were announced, but he lost.

options.label: A
options.html: Don't count your chickens before they hatch

options.label: D
options.html: The pen is mightier than the sword

solution:
A proverb-matching question asks you to identify the saying whose figurative meaning best fits the described situation, rather than one that merely shares surface words with it. Each proverb encodes a specific lesson about behaviour or consequence.

Rohit publicly celebrated a win before the competition result was declared, and the outcome went against him. This is exactly the caution captured by “Don’t count your chickens before they hatch” — treating a favourable result as certain before it is confirmed can backfire, precisely as it did for Rohit.

  • “Actions speak louder than words” contrasts spoken claims with actual deeds — it says nothing about celebrating a result too early.

  • “All that glitters is not gold” warns that an attractive appearance can be misleading — it is about deceptive appearance, not about assuming an outcome before it is confirmed.

  • “The pen is mightier than the sword” compares the influence of ideas and writing to physical force — it has no connection to premature celebration of a result.

So the proverb about treating an unconfirmed outcome as already settled is the one that matches Rohit’s situation.

title: The word ‘adolescence’ has been derived from the word ‘adolescent’
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The word ‘adolescence’ has been derived from the word ‘adolescent’ which is a:
solution: The term adolescence comes from the Latin word adolescere, meaning “to grow” or “to grow up.” This origin is widely accepted in developmental psychology.

title: Choose the correct spelling from the options given.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the correct spelling from the options given.
solution:
The correct spelling is accommodate, which has a double “c” and a double “m”: a-cc-o-mm-o-d-a-t-e.

Meaning: to provide space or lodging for someone, or to adjust or adapt to someone’s needs.

  1. To provide space or lodging for someone
    Example: The hotel can accommodate 200 guests.

  2. To adjust or adapt to someone’s needs or requests
    Example: The teacher accommodated the students by extending the deadline.

  3. To fit in or make room for something
    Example: This bag can accommodate all your books.

Tip: Like “committee” and “occurrence”, this word doubles its consonants — keep both the double “c” and the double “m”.

title: Select the word that is spelt INCORRECTLY.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the word that is spelt INCORRECTLY.
solution:
Concept

Standard spelling is determined by established dictionary forms, not by how a word sounds.

When regional variants exist, each recognized form is acceptable; an unrecognized letter pattern is the misspelling.

Application

Compare every offered letter pattern with its standard dictionary form and meaning:

  • “Favaur” is not a standard dictionary spelling. The intended word is “favour” in British English or “favor” in American English.

  • “Fauna” is the standard spelling for the animal life of a region or period.

  • “Faucet” is the standard spelling for a tap or a device that controls liquid flow.

  • “Fault” is the standard spelling for a defect, mistake, or responsibility for an error.

Cross-check

The recognized forms “fauna,” “faucet,” and “fault” retain their standard spellings, whereas “favaur” must be changed to “favour” or “favor.” Therefore, the incorrectly spelt word is “favaur.”

title: Select the option that rectifies the INCORRECTLY spelt word in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the option that rectifies the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.

The philanthropist's benvolence and magnanimity contributed to the establishment of a philanthropic foundation dedicated to alleviating poverty.
solution:
The sentence contains the misspelt word "benvolence", which is missing the second "e". The correct spelling is "benevolence" (meaning kindness or goodwill).

The remaining words in the sentence — "magnanimity", "philanthropic", and "alleviating" — are all spelt correctly, so the option that rectifies the error is "benevolence".

title: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence. While
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.

While the historic building required significant maintanance to accommodate modern needs, its perceived gorgeousness remained a source of civic pride.
solution:
The task is to find the word that is spelt wrongly in the sentence. Each option is one of the words used in the sentence.

The word "maintanance" is incorrect. The correct spelling is "maintenance" (main-ten-ance). Although it derives from the verb "maintain", the "ai" is dropped in the noun, which is why it is a very commonly misspelt word.

The other three words match their dictionary spellings: "perceived" (from perceive: c followed by ei), "gorgeousness" (from gorgeous: the -eous ending plus -ness), and "accommodate" (double c, double m).

title: Select the word that is spelled INCORRECTLY.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the word that is spelled INCORRECTLY.
solution:
Concept

Spelling questions test whether each word matches its standard dictionary form. The reliable method is to recall the word's root and the suffix pattern it uses, then check each given form against that pattern letter by letter. A single wrong vowel or consonant makes the form non-standard.

Application

Apply the root-and-suffix test to each word given here:

  • “Monarchy” comes from monarch + -y; this matches the standard dictionary spelling.

  • “Monetary” is formed from the Latin root moneta and the adjective ending -ary; this matches the standard dictionary spelling.

  • “Monastery” (from Latin monasterium) is a standard dictionary word; its accepted spelling ends in -ery, so it is spelled correctly.

  • “Momentery” is built on the root moment; the standard adjective form takes the ending -ary, giving “momentary”. The form written here uses -ery, so it does not match the dictionary spelling.

Result

Three of the four words match their standard dictionary spelling, while “Momentery” departs from it; the correct adjective from “moment” is spelled “momentary” (ending in -ary, not -ery). Therefore “Momentery” is the word spelled incorrectly.

Cross-check

Standard dictionaries (Merriam-Webster, Cambridge) list “momentary” as the only accepted spelling and have no entry for “momentery”, confirming the result.

title: Which of the following words is wrongly spelled?
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which of the following words is wrongly spelled?
solution:
Answer: The wrongly spelled word is Prepostorous; the correct spelling is preposterous.

Correct spelling and meaning: preposterous — absurd or contrary to reason.

Example: The charges against her were preposterous.

Meanings of the other given words:

  • Callous — correctly spelled; showing an insensitive or cruel disregard for others.

  • Surreal — correctly spelled; describing something strange, dreamlike, or unbelievable.

  • Convenience — correctly spelled; something that saves trouble or makes tasks easier.

title: In the following question, four words are given out of
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: In the following question, four words are given out of which one word is incorrectly spelt. Select the incorrectly spelt word.
solution:
The incorrectly spelt word is "Distrought". The correct spelling is 'distraught'.

Meanings of the given words:

  • Distraught: very worried or upset.

  • Astonish: to surprise or greatly impress.

  • Asthma: a respiratory condition that causes difficulty in breathing.

  • Correlate: to have a mutual relationship or connection.

Therefore, "Distrought" is the incorrectly spelt word; the correct form is 'distraught'.

title: Choose the correctly spelled word that replaces the misspelled word
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correctly spelled word that replaces the misspelled word in the sentence below:

The manager’s consciencious decision to accommodate the supplication of the differently abled employee surprised the entire committee.
solution:
Many English adjectives that carry the –tious/–cious sound are built around the Latin element “-scient-” (as in science, scientist, omniscient), which contributes the ‘t’ even where it is barely heard in speech. “Conscientious” is one such word: it is built on that “-scient-” element, not on the differently spelled word “conscience” (which has no ‘t’). Because the two words look and sound similar, a common misspelling confuses “conscientious” with “conscience” and replaces its ‘t’ with a ‘c’, producing a wrong form that sounds nearly identical but does not match the accepted spelling.

In the given sentence, the word filling this role is printed with that ‘t’ replaced by a ‘c’, so it is the misspelled word the question is asking about. Applying the rule above — “conscientious” takes its ‘t’ from the “-scient-” element, not from “conscience” — the correctly spelled replacement is “conscientious”.

  • “accommodate” is already correctly spelled in the sentence (double ‘c’, double ‘m’); it is not the word that needs replacing.

  • “committee” is already correctly spelled in the sentence (double ‘m’, double ‘t’, double ‘e’); it is not the word that needs replacing.

  • “supplication” is already correctly spelled in the sentence (the standard noun form of “supplicate”); it is not the word that needs replacing.

Since the other three words are already correctly spelled as printed, only the altered word needs correcting, and its correctly spelled replacement is “conscientious”.

title: The following questions consist of sentence. Four of the words
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
The following questions consist of a sentence. Four of the words of each sentence are marked in bold, which may or may not be correctly spelled or appropriate as per context. Option corresponding to miss spelt/inappropriate word is your answer.

A disspassionate external observer would be bewildered by middle-class India's capacity to look away when confronted with enormous injustice and suffering; by our society's cultural comfort with inequality. That the accident of where a child is born still determines her chances in life almost irrevocably.
solution:
Correct answer: the misspelt word is 'Disspassionate'; the correct spelling is 'dispassionate'.

  • What is wrong: 'Disspassionate' has an extra 's'. Remove the second 's' to get the correct form 'dispassionate'.

  • Why this matters: 'dispassionate' means impartial or unemotional, which matches the sentence describing an external observer.

  • Other words in the sentence — 'bewildered', 'enormous', and 'irrevocably' — are correctly spelled and appropriate in context.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q71
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the option that rectifies the underlined incorrectly spelt word in the given sentence.

The theory has been widely critikued in recent philosophical debates, particularly in post-structuralist circles.
solution:
Concept

In English, when a verb already ends in a silent e, the past tense is formed by adding only the suffix -d, not -ed, because the e is already present (for example, argue -> argued, continue -> continued, value -> valued). Verbs built on an -ique base, such as critique, follow the same convention: critique + d = critiqued, with the qu of the base kept intact.

Application

  1. Identify the intended base verb behind the underlined word: critique (to evaluate critically), which ends in a silent e and contains the sequence q-u just before that e.

  2. Apply the silent-e past-tense rule to this base: since critique already ends in e, only -d is added, giving critique + d = critiqued.

  3. Compare this with the underlined spelling critikued, which replaces the qu of the base with a k, so the base itself is misspelled before any suffix is added.

  4. Restoring the base to critique and adding the same -d suffix gives the properly spelled word critiqued.

Cross-check

The same silent-e-plus-d pattern appears in other common verbs: argue -> argued, continue -> continued, value -> valued. This confirms that critique -> critiqued is a regular application of the rule rather than an exception.

Distinguishing the options

  • critiqued keeps the base critique intact and adds only -d after its existing silent e.

  • critiqueed inserts an extra e between the base's existing e and the suffix, giving a doubled e that the silent-e rule does not call for.

  • criticed omits the qu found in critique and instead builds on the root critic together with the suffix -ed, changing the base word itself.

  • cretiqued changes the first-syllable vowel of the base from i to e, altering the root morpheme before any suffix is applied.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 Shift 1 Q68
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Identify and correct the incorrectly spelt words in the given passage.

The treaty relied on mutual deterrence as a stabilizing force, though some saw it as an

anachronysitic approach in a multipolar world. Its language remained belicosely rigid,

leaving little room for renegotiation. Critics argued that the framers had misjudged the

geostretegic realities of the postcolonial era. This resulted in a framework both

outdated and irreconcilabal with emergent doctrines.
solution:
Spelling-correction passages test recognition of standard English orthography for words that are often misspelled. Typical error patterns include an extra or misplaced syllable inserted into a root, a missing doubled consonant, a vowel swapped inside a Greek- or Latin-derived root, and a nonstandard suffix ending in place of the standard one. Solving such an item means isolating exactly which words in the passage are misspelled and knowing the standard spelling that replaces each one, while leaving every already-correct word untouched.

  1. "anachronysitic" (as it appears in the passage) ends in "-ysitic" rather than the standard adjectival suffix "-istic"; correcting the ending gives "anachronistic".

  2. "belicosely" (as it appears in the passage) is missing the doubled "l" that the adjective "bellicose" takes; restoring the double "l" and keeping the adverb suffix "-ly" gives "bellicosely".

  3. "geostretegic" (as it appears in the passage) spells the root after "geo-" as "stret-"; the standard root (from "strategic") is spelled "strat-", giving "geostrategic".

  4. "irreconcilabal" (as it appears in the passage) ends in "-abal"; the standard suffix on this prefix+verb combination ("ir-" + "reconcile") is "-able", giving "irreconcilable".

Every other word in the passage — treaty, deterrence, stabilizing, framework, emergent, and the rest — already follows standard spelling and is not part of the four errors to be fixed.

  • The set "framework, bellicose, geostrategik, irreconcilable" pairs "framework" (a word the passage already spells correctly and is not one of the four errors) with "bellicose" (drops the adverb suffix "-ly" rather than only restoring the missing double "l") and "geostrategik" (still ends in "-ik" rather than "-ic").

  • The set "anachronystic, bellicosely, geostrategic, emergent" leaves the "anachron-" root ending in "-ystic" rather than "-istic", and pairs it with "emergent", a word the passage already spells correctly.

  • The set "treaty, deterrence, geostretegic, stabilizing" lists three words — "treaty", "deterrence", "stabilizing" — that the passage already spells correctly, alongside "geostretegic", which keeps the same "stret-" spelling found in the passage.

The set that corrects all four misspelled words — and only those four — is anachronistic, bellicosely, geostrategic, irreconcilable. Re-reading the passage with this replacement set confirms every other word stays unchanged, and each replaced word now follows a standard pattern: the "-istic" suffix, the doubled "l" in bellicose, the "strat-" root in geostrategic, and the "-able" suffix in irreconcilable.

title: In this question, the sentence is divided into three underlined
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In this question, the sentence is divided into three underlined parts labelled as (A), (B) and (C). Identify the part in which the error is located. If you find no error, your response should be indicated as (D).

The old furnitures (A) was disposed of (B) and the new ones were placed. (C)
solution:
Concept

Some nouns in English are uncountable (mass) nouns: they name something seen as a single, undivided whole rather than as separate items. An uncountable noun has no plural form and is never written with a plural ‑s. “Furniture” is one such noun — it is the collective name for tables, chairs, beds and so on, so it stays singular: we say “some furniture” or “pieces of furniture”, never “furnitures.”

Applying it to this sentence

Test each underlined part for a grammatical error:

  • “The old furnitures” — this adds a plural ‑s to an uncountable noun, which is not allowed. This is the error; it must read “The old furniture.”

  • “was disposed of” — acceptable: “dispose of” is the correct phrasal verb for getting rid of something, and the singular subject “furniture” correctly takes the singular verb “was.”

  • “and the new ones were placed” — acceptable: in this idiom “ones” stands for the implied countable “pieces (of furniture)” and agrees with the plural verb “were,” so this part raises no clear-cut grammatical error.

Cross-check

Replace only the faulty word with its correct form: “The old furniture was disposed of and the new ones were placed.” The single unambiguous mistake — the plural ‑s on an uncountable noun — sits in “The old furnitures.” Because a real error is present, “No error” cannot be the response.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q14
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the correct sentence from the options below:

options.label: D
options.html: The sceneries of Kashmir are very charming.

solution:
An uncountable (mass) noun names a substance, an abstract idea, or a whole category that cannot be individually counted. Such nouns have no plural form, are not preceded by the indefinite article "a/an", and always take a singular verb — even when they end in "-s" (like news) or refer to many items collectively (like furniture). A single instance is instead expressed with a separate countable noun or a "piece/item of ___" phrase.

  1. "I am learning a new poetry." — poetry is uncountable, so it cannot take the article "a"; a single composition is a "poem", not "a poetry".

  2. "These news are good." — news is uncountable despite its "-s" ending, so it needs the singular demonstrative "this" and the singular verb "is", not "these ... are".

  3. "All the furniture was destroyed." — furniture is uncountable, so it combines with the non-count quantifier "all the" and the singular verb "was", which is exactly how this sentence is built.

  4. "The sceneries of Kashmir are very charming." — scenery is uncountable and has no plural form, so "sceneries ... are" is non-standard; the correct form is "the scenery ... is".

Cross-check with the standard non-count test: one can say "much poetry", "much news", "much furniture", and "much scenery", but not "many poetry/news/furniture/scenery" — confirming all four nouns are non-count. Checking each option's article and verb against this non-count behaviour shows that only one sentence keeps both the article usage and the subject-verb agreement correct throughout.

"All the furniture was destroyed." is therefore the grammatically correct sentence.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q20
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.
solution:
Concept

Subject–verb agreement requires a finite verb to match the grammatical number of its subject.

Some nouns end in -s but are grammatically singular. In standard English, “news” is an uncountable singular noun and therefore takes a singular verb.

Application

In “The news is very disturbing,” the singular subject “news” is paired with the singular present-tense verb “is.”

Contrast

  • “The news are very disturbing” uses the plural present-tense verb “are” with the singular noun “news.”

  • “The news were very disturbing” uses the plural past-tense verb “were” with the singular noun “news.”

  • “The news have been disturbing” uses the plural auxiliary “have” with the singular noun “news.”

Hence, the grammatically correct sentence is “The news is very disturbing.”

title: The correct verb form in this sentence is Neither Afzal
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
The correct verb form in this sentence is :
Neither Afzal nor his friends ______ present.
solution:
Concept

When two subjects are joined by neither … nor (or either … or), the verb does not take both subjects together. By the rule of proximity, the verb agrees in number with the subject that stands nearer to it — the one written just before the blank.

Application

  • Subjects joined: Afzal (singular) and his friends (plural).

  • The subject nearer to the blank is his friends, which is plural, so the verb must be plural.

  • The sentence describes a state of being ("… ______ present"), so the linking verb to be is needed — the plural form is were.

Cross-check

  • Read only the nearer subject with the verb: "his friends were present" — grammatical.

  • "his friends was present" sounds wrong, confirming a plural verb is required.

Hence the correct completion is were.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q14
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error:

Neither the manager/nor the employees/was willing/to accept the proposal.
solution:
Concept

With correlative conjunctions such as neither…nor and either…or, a finite verb normally agrees with the subject that is nearer to it.

The method is to identify both coordinated subjects, locate the one closest to the verb, and match the verb’s number with that subject.

Application

  1. The coordinated subjects are “the manager” (singular) and “the employees” (plural).

  2. The nearer subject to the finite verb is “employees”, which is plural.

  3. A plural subject takes “were”, so the clause should read “Neither the manager nor the employees were willing…”. The form “was willing” carries singular agreement.

Contrast

  • “Neither the manager” introduces the first member of the correlative pair.

  • “nor the employees” introduces the second and nearer subject.

  • “was willing” contains a singular finite verb after a plural nearer subject.

  • “to accept the proposal” is the infinitive complement of “willing”.

Cross-check

Replace the coordinated phrase with the nearer subject alone: “The employees were willing to accept the proposal.” This independently confirms the plural verb form. Hence the erroneous segment is “was willing”.

Explanation: When two subjects are joined by "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the subject that is closer to the verb.

Here, the nearer subject is "employees," which is plural, so the plural present verb "are" is required.

  • Key rule: With "neither...nor," match the verb to the nearer subject.

subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.

solution:
Concept: Certain determiners — each, every, either, neither — are distributive determiners. Even though they refer to the members of a group taken one at a time, English grammar requires them to be followed by a SINGULAR countable noun (and a singular verb), never a plural noun.

Application: In the given sentence, the segment ‘every senior citizens’ pairs the distributive determiner ‘every’ with the plural noun ‘citizens’. This determiner–noun mismatch is the grammatical error; the correct form is ‘every senior citizen’ (singular).

  • ‘every senior citizens’ — contains the error: the singular distributive determiner ‘every’ cannot take the plural noun ‘citizens’.

  • ‘will benefit a lot’ — no error: modal ‘will’ + base verb ‘benefit’ + the adverbial ‘a lot’ is correctly formed.

  • ‘from the new scheme’ — no error: preposition ‘from’ + determiner ‘the’ + adjective ‘new’ + noun ‘scheme’ is in standard order.

  • ‘According to the finance ministry,’ — no error: a standard introductory prepositional phrase, correctly set off by a comma.

Cross-check: Replacing the plural noun with the singular restores full agreement: ‘According to the finance ministry, every senior citizen will benefit a lot from the new scheme.’ No other change is needed, confirming the error is isolated to this one determiner–noun pairing.

title: Each of the students aware of the rules.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Each of the students ____ aware of the rules.
solution:
Correct answer: 'is'.

Explanation: The word "each" is singular and requires a singular verb. Therefore, the singular present-tense linking verb "is" correctly agrees with the subject in the sentence: "Each of the students is aware of the rules."

  • "are" — incorrect because it is a plural verb and does not agree with the singular subject "each."

  • "have" — incorrect because it is plural and also does not function as the appropriate linking verb for the adjective "aware."

  • "were" — incorrect because it is plural and past tense, so it does not agree with the singular present context required by "each."

title: Select the segment of the sentence that contains the grammatical
subject: Verbal Ability (English)

Select the segment of the sentence that contains the grammatical error. If there is no error, mark 'No error' as your answer.

Five gallons of oil (A)/ were required to (B)/ get the refinery running.(C)/ No error (D)/.
solution:
Solution

The segment containing the error is the verb phrase "were required to"; the verb should be singular.

Explanation:

The subject "Five gallons of oil" names a quantity or unit of measurement. When a measurement, amount, or period is regarded as a single unit, it takes a singular verb.

Therefore, use the singular verb "was" instead of "were."

Correct sentence: Five gallons of oil was required to get the refinery running.

  • Key rule: When a quantity is treated as a single unit, use a singular verb.

  • Application: "Five gallons of oil" = single quantity → use "was required to."

title: In the following question, one part of the sentence may

title: Fill in the blank with correct word. Good health is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Fill in the blank with correct word.

Good health is everyone's_____coveted possession.
solution:
What the blank needs: a word that expresses the idea that good health is coveted above all other possessions.

  • Very — an adverb that can modify an adjective ("very coveted"). It does not give the superlative meaning needed here and sounds awkward in this context.

  • Most — forms the superlative with "coveted" ("most coveted"), meaning coveted above everything else. This correctly expresses the intended idea.

  • More — a comparative that requires an explicit comparison (for example, "more coveted than wealth"). Without that comparison, it does not fit the sentence.

  • Absolutely — an adverb meaning completely; "absolutely coveted" is not idiomatic here and does not convey the superlative sense needed.

Final answer: Good health is everyone's most coveted possession.

title: Which is the correct comparative form of "happy"?
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which is the correct comparative form of "happy"?
solution:
Answer: happier is the correct comparative form of "happy".

Rule: For adjectives that end in -y after a consonant, change the final -y to -i and add -er to form the comparative.

  • Example: happy → happier

  • Why "more happy" is not preferred: Although understandable, native usage prefers the -er form for this adjective.

  • Why the other forms are wrong: "happyer" is a spelling error; "happiest" is the superlative (most happy), not the comparative.

title: Choose the correct comparative form of "tall."
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the correct comparative form of "tall."
solution:
Answer: taller

Explanation: To form the comparative of the one-syllable adjective 'tall', add "-er" to make "taller." Use "taller" when comparing two people or things.

  • Example: John is taller than Mary.

  • 'Tallest' is the superlative form used to describe the highest degree among three or more (e.g., "She is the tallest in the class").

title: Find out the correct option for the given sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Find out the correct option for the given sentence.

The crow, which was foolish, made an attempt to sing.
solution:
Concept

An adjective describes a noun, whereas an adverb describes a verb, adjective, or another adverb. To preserve meaning during sentence transformation, the modifier’s form and syntactic attachment must clearly identify what it describes; an attributive adjective may appear directly before its noun, while a predicative adjective may follow a linking verb.

Application

The given sentence states that the crow itself was foolish and that it made an attempt to sing. To describe a crow that is itself foolish, the descriptive word must be the adjective "foolish" placed directly before the noun it qualifies: the + adjective (foolish) + noun (crow) + verb phrase (tried to sing). This yields: The foolish crow tried to sing, in which "foolish" correctly attaches to "crow".

Contrast

  • The foolish crow wanted to sing keeps the adjective correct but swaps the verb tried for wanted, which changes the meaning from making an attempt to merely having a desire.

  • The crow tried to sing foolishly turns the describing word into the adverb foolishly, so it now describes the MANNER of singing rather than the crow itself, a different idea.

  • The crow attempted to sing foolishly makes the same adverbial shift and also replaces tried with attempted, again describing how it sang rather than that the crow was foolish.

Result: the form that keeps foolish as an adjective qualifying the crow is the correct sentence, The foolish crow tried to sing.

title: "Rama comes to college regularly". It is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: "Rama comes to college regularly". It is
solution:
Concept

The simple present tense states a habitual or routine action — something that happens repeatedly or as a general truth. For a third-person singular subject it is formed by adding -s/-es to the base verb, and it is often signalled by an adverb of frequency such as always, usually, often or regularly.

Application

Read the sentence: "Rama comes to college regularly."

  • The subject "Rama" is third-person singular, and the verb appears as "comes" — the base verb "come" with -s added, which is the simple-present form for that subject.

  • The adverb "regularly" marks the action as a repeated routine, not a one-time event.

  • A habitual, routine action described in the present is exactly what the simple present tense expresses.

Contrast

  • Past tense would need a past-form verb such as "came" and would place the action in finished time — the sentence has no such marker.

  • Future tense would need "will come" / "shall come" — absent here.

  • Continuous tense would need a form of "be" plus an -ing verb, e.g. "is coming" — the verb here is the plain "comes", not a progressive form.

Therefore the sentence is in the simple present tense.

title: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error, the answer is 'D'. (Ignore - the errors of punctuation,if any) : (A) At the end of the year/(B) every student who had done adequate work/(C) was automatically promoted./(D) No error.
solution:
Correct answer: No error.

Explanation:

  • At the end of the year — this time expression correctly sets when the promotion occurred and causes no grammatical issue.

  • every student who had done adequate work — "every student" is singular (so the singular verb "was" is required). The past perfect "had done" correctly indicates the work was completed before the promotion event.

  • was automatically promoted — this clause correctly uses the past tense (passive) and agrees with the singular subject.

Overall, each part is grammatically correct, so no correction is needed.

title: My neighbour yesterday.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: I ________ my neighbour yesterday.
solution:
Answer: helped

Explanation: The time word "yesterday" indicates a completed action in the past, so the past simple form of the verb is required.

  • Why "helped" is correct: "helped" is the past simple of "help," which matches the past time marker "yesterday."

  • Why "Helping" is incorrect: "Helping" is a present participle or gerund and does not express a completed past action by itself.

  • Why "Was helped" is incorrect: "Was helped" is passive voice and means you received help, not that you gave help to your neighbour.

  • Why "help" is incorrect: The base form "help" does not show past tense and therefore does not agree with "yesterday."

Tip: Look for time expressions (like "yesterday") to choose the correct verb tense.

title: Select the correct tense: had seen him earlier.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the correct tense:

I had seen him earlier.
solution:
Correct answer: Past perfect.

Explanation: The sentence uses 'had' + past participle (had seen), which is the form of the past perfect tense.

  • Structure: had + past participle (e.g., had seen).

  • Meaning: indicates an action completed before another past time or event.

  • Other tenses: Past continuous uses was/were + verb-ing; past perfect continuous uses had been + verb-ing; future perfect uses will have + past participle. None of these match the form had + past participle used in the sentence.

title: Select the correct tense: The boys were severely punished by
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the correct tense:

The boys were severely punished by the principal.
solution:
Tense is identified from the auxiliary-verb pattern in the verb group, not from meaning alone.

In the passive voice, every aspect keeps its own marker and simply adds a form of "be" before the past participle (V3): simple aspect = was/were + V3; continuous aspect = was/were + being + V3; perfect aspect = had been + V3.

Applying this to the sentence:

"The boys were severely punished by the principal." The verb group is only "were punished" — the simple past auxiliary "were" directly followed by the past participle "punished," with no "being" and no "had" anywhere in it.

Correct answer: Simple past (past simple passive).

Why the other tense options don't fit:

  • Past continuous needs "being" between the auxiliary and the participle (was/were + being + V3, e.g. "were being punished"); the sentence has no "being."

  • Past perfect continuous needs "had been being" + V3 (e.g. "had been being punished") — the perfect marker "had been" plus the continuous marker "being" together; the sentence has neither "had" nor "being."

  • Past perfect needs "had" + been + V3 (e.g. "had been punished"); the sentence uses "were," not "had."

title: By the next month, we shall the project.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: By the next month, we shall __________ the project.
solution:
The sentence starts with "By the next month", which refers to an action that will be finished before that time.

Use: Future Perfect tense

  • Structure: subject + shall/will + have + past participle

Example: By the next month, we shall have completed the project.

Notes on the other choices:

  • "Has completed" is incorrect because "has" is third-person singular; with "we" use "have", and the sentence needs the future perfect form (shall/will have + past participle).

  • "Completing" is a present participle and cannot form the future perfect tense by itself.

  • "Completed" on its own is a past participle but needs the auxiliary (shall/will have) to make the future perfect.

title: "She will be coming to office very often". It is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: "She will be coming to office very often". It is
solution:
Concept

A verb tense is identified by its auxiliary structure. The Future Continuous tense describes an action that will be in progress at some point in the future. Its fixed formula is: subject + will be + the present participle (verb + -ing).

Application

Break the verb phrase "will be coming" into its parts:

  1. will — the modal that places the action in the future.

  2. be — the auxiliary that signals the continuous (in-progress) aspect.

  3. coming — the present participle (come + -ing), the ongoing main action.

Pattern matched: will + be + (-ing) = Future Continuous tense.

Cross-check / Contrast

  • Simple Future would read "She will come" — no "be", no "-ing".

  • Present (simple/continuous) would read "She comes" or "is coming" — it never uses "will".

  • Past tense would read "She came" — it points backward in time, not forward.

Only "will be coming" carries the future modal plus the continuous "be + -ing", so the sentence is in the Future Continuous tense.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Next week
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Next week I ________ to visit my cousin.
solution:
Concept

To talk about a plan or intention you already hold for the future, English uses the PRESENT SIMPLE of an intention verb such as "intend", followed by the to-infinitive: "intend to + base verb". The present-simple form carries the future meaning when a future time marker (here, "Next week") is present, so no separate future auxiliary is needed.

Application

The future time marker "Next week" sets the time, and the slot needs an intention verb that combines with "to visit". The natural, grammatical completion is the present simple "intend":

Next week I intend to visit my cousin.

Here "intend" states a present intention about a future visit, and "to visit" is the to-infinitive it governs.

Contrast

  • "will intend" - pairing the future auxiliary with an intention verb is redundant and unidiomatic; an intention is held now, not formed later, so "will intend" is not used.

  • "intending" - the bare -ing participle has no auxiliary (no form of "be"), so it cannot stand as the main verb of the clause and leaves the sentence without a finite verb.

  • "intended" - this is past tense and clashes with the future marker "Next week", producing a tense mismatch.

title: Select the correct tense: Radha will be joining us.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the correct tense:

Radha will be joining us.
solution:
Answer: Future continuous

Explanation:

Structure: 'will' + 'be' + present participle (verb+ing).

Example: In the sentence "Radha will be joining us," the phrase "will be joining" follows this structure.

Meaning: The future continuous tense describes an action that will be in progress at a specific time or during a period in the future.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • Simple future: Uses "will" + base verb (for example, "will join"). It does not show the progressive/ongoing aspect that "will be joining" shows.

  • Past continuous: Uses "was/were" + verb-ing and refers to actions in the past, so it does not match a sentence that uses "will."

  • Past perfect continuous: Uses "had been" + verb-ing to describe an ongoing action before another past event; it is a past form and therefore does not apply to a future action.

title: Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blank. Mohan
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blank.

Mohan Lal ______ asleep while watching TV last night.

The correct answer is c. fell
Correct sentence:
“Mohan Lal fell asleep while watching TV last night.”
Reason:
The phrase “last night” indicates a completed action in the past, so the simple past tense is required.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Whilst one
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Whilst one group was busy cooking, the other ________ wood for the campfire.
solution:
Concept

When two actions happen in the same past time frame, English keeps their tenses in agreement (the sequence-of-tenses rule). If the framing clause is in the past, the action that goes with it in the same narrative is normally in the simple past too — not in the present or the future, which would point to a different time.

Application

The framing clause here is "Whilst one group was busy cooking" — "was" fixes the whole sentence in the past. The blank describes a second action by the other group happening in that same past time, so it must be a finite verb in the simple past:

"Whilst one group was busy cooking, the other collected wood for the campfire."

Contrast with the other forms

  • "will collect" is the simple future — it places the action ahead of now, which clashes with the past framing "was busy".

  • "is collecting" is the present continuous — it describes an action going on now, again out of step with the past clause.

  • "has collected" is the present perfect — it links a past action to the present moment, but here the time is fully past and parallel to "was cooking", so the plain simple past is what fits.

The simple-past form that matches the past time frame is the correct completion.

title: John and are going to the party.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: John and ___ are going to the party.
solution: The sentence is referring to the subject ("John and I"). Subject pronouns such as "I," "you," "he," "she," "it," "we," and "they" are used as the subject of a sentence. Therefore, "I" is the appropriate subject pronoun to use in this instance.

title: DIRECTIONS: Fill in the blank with the right options provided.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
DIRECTIONS: Fill in the blank with the right options provided.

My grandfather left most of his money to an NGO; the rest went directly to my daughter and _____
solution:
Correct sentence: My grandfather left most of his money to an NGO; the rest went directly to my daughter and me.

Key point: Use an object pronoun after a preposition.

  • The pronoun is the object of the preposition "to," so use the object form "me."

  • Test by removing the other noun: "He left it to me" is correct, whereas "He left it to I" is incorrect.

  • "myself" is reflexive and is used when the subject and object are the same person (e.g., "I introduced myself"). That is not the case here.

  • Use "I" only as a subject (e.g., "My daughter and I went to the store").

title: Am older than
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: I am older than ___ .
solution:
Correct answer: her

Key point: "than" can function either as a preposition or as a conjunction, and that determines which pronoun form is appropriate.

  • When "than" functions as a preposition, use the object pronoun: "I am older than her." This is a common and acceptable form.

  • When "than" functions as a conjunction and introduces a clause, use the subject pronoun with the (possibly implied) verb: "I am older than she (is)." Both forms can be grammatical; the conjunctional form keeps the full clause.

  • Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • "hers" is a possessive pronoun (e.g., "That book is hers") and does not serve as the subject or object in this comparative construction.

  • "herself" is a reflexive pronoun used when the subject and object are the same (e.g., "She hurt herself"), which does not apply in this sentence.

title: Choose the correct sentence from the following
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the correct sentence from the following
solution:
Concept

In a comparison using “than”, “than” functions as a conjunction that joins two clauses. The second clause is usually shortened, but its verb is still understood. Because the pronoun after “than” is the subject of that understood verb, it must take the subjective (nominative) case: I, he, she, we, they — not the object case (me, him, her), not the possessive (mine), and not a reflexive (myself).

Application

The sentence “George ran faster than ___” expands to “George ran faster than ___ ran.” The blank is the subject of the recovered verb “ran,” so it needs a subject pronoun:

  • Recover the hidden verb: “… than I ran.”

  • Test by completing the clause: “than I ran” is grammatical; the pronoun acts as a subject, so the subjective form I is required.

Therefore the correct sentence is “George ran faster than I.”

Cross-check

Apply the “add the verb” test to each alternative. “than I ran” works; “than me ran,” “than mine ran,” and “than myself ran” are all impossible, which confirms only the subjective pronoun fits. (Note: in casual modern speech “than me” is widely heard, but formal and exam grammar follows the conjunction rule.)

title: Which pronoun best fits? Either of the boys can do
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Which pronoun best fits?

Either of the boys can do the job ___.
solution:
Answer: himself

"Either of the boys" refers to one boy, so a singular reflexive pronoun is required. Because the antecedent is male, use "himself."

  • Why the correct choice fits: The phrase indicates a single person (either one), so the pronoun must be singular and agree in person and gender with the antecedent.

  • Why the other choices are wrong: "themselves" is plural (does not match the singular sense), "ourselves" is first-person plural (wrong person), and "itself" is for neuter/inanimate antecedents (not people).

title: Neither Jack nor Jane takes seriously.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Neither Jack nor Jane takes ___ seriously.
solution:
Correct answer: themselves

Explanation: "themselves" is a reflexive pronoun that refers back to the plural subjects Jack and Jane and serves as the object of the verb phrase. It is the appropriate form to use when the action relates back to the people mentioned.

  • Why other choices are incorrect:

  • “theirselves” is nonstandard and incorrect; the standard reflexive form is “themselves.”

  • “their” is a possessive determiner (used before a noun) and cannot serve as a reflexive object in this sentence.

  • “Them” is an object pronoun but not reflexive; it does not show that the action applies back to the subjects themselves.

  • Using “themselves” is also a natural, gender-neutral way to refer back to two people together in casual and formal contexts.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. My cousin
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

My cousin felt annoyed with ______ when he saw what had happened due to his ignorance.
solution: The sentence subject is 'My cousin' (third person singular male). The reflexive pronoun must match the subject, making 'himself' correct.

title: Please pass the salt to asks for it.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Please pass the salt to ___ asks for it.
solution:
Correct answer: whoever

Explanation: Choose the form (whoever vs. whomever) based on the pronoun's role inside its own clause.

  • Step 1: Identify the clause: "whoever asks for it" is a clause that acts as the object of the preposition "to."

  • Step 2: Look at the pronoun's role inside that clause: the pronoun is the subject of the verb "asks."

  • Step 3: Use a quick substitution test: replace with he/him. "He asks for it" is grammatical, so use the subject (nominative) form, which is "whoever."

  • Contrast: In a sentence like "Give it to whomever you choose," the pronoun is the object of "choose" inside the clause, so the objective form "whomever" is correct there.

Therefore, the correct choice for the sentence "Please pass the salt to ___ asks for it." is "whoever."

title: Spot an error in the given sentence. (MCQ) (A)Everyone should
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Spot an error in the given sentence.

(A)Everyone should /(B)submit assignments to respective teachers before the last date /(C)in order to maintain/(D)the records properly.
solution:
Correct answer: The phrase "submit assignments to respective teachers before the last date" contains the error.

Corrected sentence: Everyone should submit assignments to their respective teachers before the last date in order to maintain the records properly.

Better wording (optional): Everyone should submit assignments to their respective teachers before the deadline to help maintain proper records.

  • Reason 1: "Respective teachers" needs a possessive determiner. Using "their respective teachers" shows that each person submits to his or her own teacher.

  • Reason 2: The phrases "in order to maintain" and "the records properly" are grammatically acceptable. "In order to" can be shortened to "to" for conciseness, and "the records" plausibly refers to the institution's records.

title: The damage of the building is over $1million
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The damage to the building is -------- over $1 million
solution:
Explanation: The verb phrase "put at" means to calculate or estimate something to be a particular amount or value.

  • Why "put at" is correct: "Put at" is the standard phrase used to estimate an amount. Example: The damage of the building is put at over $1 million.

  • Why the other choices are incorrect: "Put over" is not used to estimate amounts; "put about" usually means to circulate or move around and is not the standard estimate phrase; "put out" means to extinguish or inconvenience and does not fit the context of estimating a value.

Conclusion: Use "put at" to express the estimated amount.

title: The army made foray the enemy zone.

bodyHtml: The army made a foray _______ the enemy zone.

Correct Option
Option C: into

The correct answer is "into" because the sentence requires a preposition indicating movement toward the interior of the enemy zone.

title: Have been thinking about this yesterday.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: I have been thinking about this _______ yesterday.
solution: The correct answer is 'since' because the sentence structure requires a preposition that links the present perfect continuous tense ('have been thinking') with a specific starting point in time. The word 'yesterday' indicates when the action began, and 'since' is specifically used to denote a starting point in time that continues up to the present moment. For example, 'I have been thinking about this since yesterday' correctly implies that the thinking started in the past and is still ongoing.\nOption A ('along') and Option B ('by') are incorrect because they do not function as time markers in this context; 'along' suggests movement or accompaniment, while 'by' typically indicates proximity or agency. Option C ('after') is also incorrect because it refers to a time following an event, which would not logically connect with the present perfect continuous tense indicating ongoing action from a past point. Therefore, 'since' is the only grammatically appropriate choice to complete the sentence.

title: Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank The
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:

The essay was written _______ great detail.
solution:
Correct Option
Option A: in

Detailed Solution
The correct preposition is "in" because the phrase "in great detail" is a standard English expression used to describe thoroughness. Students should recognize common collocations where prepositions pair with specific nouns like "detail".

title: The teacher ordered me to write ink.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The teacher ordered me to write ______ ink.
solution:
Correct Option
Option 2: in

Detailed Solution
The correct preposition to use with "ink" in this context is "in". In standard English usage, when describing the medium of writing, we say "write in ink".

title: The lion sprang the cow.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The lion sprang ______ the cow.
solution:
Correct Option
Option A: upon

Detailed Solution
The sentence "The lion sprang upon the cow" is idiomatic and grammatically sound. The use of "upon" effectively denotes the movement to a position on top of the target, which aligns with the physical action of the lion springing.

title: Fill in the blank with appropriate preposition He saw wounded
