bodyHtml:
Fill in the blank with appropriate preposition :

He saw a wounded tiger while passing ________ the forest.
solution:
Correct Option
Option B: through

Detailed Solution
The correct preposition is "through" because it denotes movement within or across an enclosed space. When someone passes through a place, they enter one side and exit the other, which fits this context perfectly.

title: Choose the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank. What
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank.

What did you make ______ the lecture ?
solution:
To identify the correct preposition, we need to focus on the phrasal verb formed by "make" and the context of the sentence.

Grammar Analysis
"Make of": This is a phrasal verb that means to understand, interpret, or have an opinion about something.

Example: "What do you make of his behavior?"

The Sentence: "What did you make ____ the lecture?"

In this context, the speaker is asking for the listener's interpretation or understanding of the lecture. Therefore, "make of" is the correct grammatical choice.

title: Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blank. It
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blank.

It was my sister's birthday and all ____ us ____ the family wanted to buy a gift ____ her.
solution:
Key idea: The sentence needs the standard prepositions in the phrases “all of us”, “in the family”, and “for her”.

  • Use “all of us” to refer to the whole group.

  • Use “in the family” for membership within the family.

  • A gift is bought “for” someone.

Answer: Option 3, “of; in; for”, is correct.

title: Choose the correct words to fill in the blanks. One
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct words to fill in the blanks.

One ___ the two elevators ___ the building has been ___ repair ___ nearly two weeks.
solution:
Key idea: The sentence needs natural preposition/collocation choices.

  • “One of the two elevators” is the standard expression.

  • The elevator is “in the building”.

  • A machine being repaired is “under repair”.

  • For a duration, use “for nearly two weeks”.

Answer: Option 3, “of; in; under; for”, is correct.

title: You must pay the fees week.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: You must pay the fees ______ a week.
solution:
Concept: Prepositions of time link an action to a time reference. When a sentence sets a time limit by which something must be completed, “within” + a duration means “at any point inside that span of time” — the action may happen anywhere up to and including the end of the period.

Application: “You must pay the fees ______ a week” states a deadline: the payment has to be made at some moment during the next seven days. “within a week” fits exactly — it means “before the seven-day span runs out,” i.e. any time inside that one-week window.

Contrast — why the other prepositions fail:

  • “after” + a week → places the action once the week has already passed, which reverses the deadline (it would mean you pay only when a week is over, not during it).

  • “before” + a week → “before” needs a fixed point in time (“before Friday”); a bare duration like “a week” cannot follow it naturally, so the phrase is not idiomatic for a deadline.

  • “by” + a week → “by” marks a specific cut-off point (“by Monday,” “by next week”). “by a week” has no fixed point of reference, so it is ungrammatical here.

Result: “within” is the only preposition that correctly expresses “at any time inside a one-week period.”

title: Mr. Roy is affable his neighbours.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Mr. Roy is affable ______ his neighbours.
solution:
Concept: An adjective that describes someone's manner of being friendly or pleasant toward people takes the preposition "to" (or "towards") to introduce the people on the receiving end of that friendliness. "Affable" means easy to talk to and warmly polite, and the standard pattern is "affable to + person."

Application: The sentence describes Mr. Roy's friendly manner directed at the people around him, his neighbours. We need the preposition that links the friendly quality to the people it is shown toward. "Affable to his neighbours" fits this pattern exactly and means he is warm and pleasant toward them.

Contrast with the other prepositions:

  • "of" marks possession or material; after an adjective it appears mainly in the "it was ADJECTIVE of someone" pattern that judges one particular act ("that was affable of him"), not in a description of how a person habitually behaves with people, so "affable of his neighbours" does not work here.

  • "from" signals a source or separation, the opposite of directing friendliness at someone, so it cannot join "affable" to the people involved.

  • "for" indicates purpose or benefit, not the person one behaves pleasantly toward, so "affable for his neighbours" is wrong.

Result: The correct completion is "affable to his neighbours."

title: Granite is almost impervious acid-rain damage.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Granite is almost impervious ______ acid-rain damage.
solution:
Concept: An adjective often governs a fixed preposition that cannot be chosen by meaning alone — it is set by collocation (the conventional word partnership). The adjective “impervious” (meaning “unable to be affected or penetrated”) is conventionally paired with the preposition “to” when naming what something resists.

Application: In “Granite is almost impervious ______ acid-rain damage,” the blank links the adjective “impervious” to the thing it resists (acid-rain damage). The established collocation is “impervious to”, so the sentence reads “Granite is almost impervious to acid-rain damage” — granite is largely unaffected by acid rain.

  • “to” — the standard partner of “impervious”; it introduces what is being resisted, giving a complete, idiomatic sentence.

  • “by” — marks the agent of a passive verb (“damaged by”), but “impervious” is an adjective, not a passive verb, so “by” does not fit here.

  • “with” — signals accompaniment or instrument (“filled with”); it is not the preposition this adjective takes.

  • “of” — expresses possession or composition (“made of”); it is not the fixed partner of “impervious.”

Cross-check: Replace the noun and the pairing still holds — “impervious to criticism,” “impervious to heat,” “impervious to water.” The preposition stays “to” regardless of what follows, confirming it as the correct collocation.

title: He is temperate his response to criticism.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: He is temperate ______ his response to criticism.
solution:
Concept

Many English adjectives are fixed to a particular preposition by collocation (an established word-partnership), not by logic. The adjective "temperate" means moderate, self-restrained, or showing self-control. The standard collocation for this adjective is "temperate in", and the noun after it names the activity or respect within which the restraint is shown (for example, temperate in eating, temperate in speech).

Application

The sentence shows the person staying moderate and controlled in how he reacts to criticism, so the fixed preposition for "temperate" fills the blank, giving "temperate in his response to criticism."

Why the other prepositions do not fit

  • "Temperate" does not collocate with "with"; other adjectives such as "angry" or "patient" happen to take "with" (angry with, patient with), but that specific pairing does not carry over to "temperate."

  • "Temperate" does not collocate with "on"; some other adjectives fix to "on" (keen on), but that pairing is specific to those adjectives, not to "temperate."

  • "Temperate" does not collocate with "of"; other adjectives fix to "of" for their own reasons (made of wood, fond of chocolate), but neither pairing extends to "temperate."

Cross-check

Its near-synonym "moderate" keeps the same partner — one is "moderate in" one's habits or reactions — confirming that "in" is the preposition that idiomatically follows this adjective.

title: He will return fortnight.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: He will return ______ a fortnight.
solution:
Concept

The preposition that goes with a span of time depends on what relationship to that span you mean. With a future action, “in + a period of time” means the action happens at the end of that whole period, i.e. once the period has passed. “within + a period” means before the period ends; “by” needs a fixed point in time, not a duration; “on” marks a specific day or date.

Application

A fortnight is a stretch of two weeks, i.e. a duration. The sentence describes a future return after that whole stretch of time has elapsed. The pattern “will + (verb) + in + (duration)” expresses exactly this: “He will return in a fortnight” = he will be back once the two weeks are over. “in” is therefore the natural fit.

Contrast

  • “by” pairs with a fixed point (by Monday, by 5 o’clock), not with a duration such as a two-week span, so it does not fit here.

  • “on” marks a specific day or date (on Tuesday, on the 5th); a fortnight is a length of time, not a single day, so it clashes.

  • “within” is grammatical too, but it expresses a different relationship: it gives only an upper limit (no later than the two weeks), leaving the action free to fall anywhere earlier inside the span rather than measuring the action against the full stretch. That ‘no later than’ reading is a distinct meaning from marking the action by the two-week duration itself.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. We do
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. We do not accept any liability _________ damage or losses.
solution:
Concept: A preposition links a noun to the rest of the sentence, and many nouns and verbs take one fixed preposition by convention (collocation). The noun and verb “liability” / “be liable” are conventionally followed by “for” to name the thing one is answerable or responsible for — “responsibility for”, “liable for”, “liability for”.

Application: Here the sentence says the speaker does not accept responsibility for the damage or losses. Inserting the conventional partner gives “We do not accept any liability for damage or losses”, which is grammatical and idiomatic.

Contrast with the other choices:

  • “at” marks a point in place or time; “liability at damage” is not an English collocation.

  • “with” signals accompaniment or means; “liability with damage” does not express responsibility and is not idiomatic.

  • “against” means opposition or protection from; “liability against damage” would suggest acting in opposition to the damage, which is not the intended meaning.

Result: the preposition “for” correctly completes the sentence.

title: Left my bedding the station.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: I left my bedding ______ the station.
solution:
Concept

The preposition of place 'at' marks a position thought of as a single point or a specific named location — a station, a bus stop, a gate, an address. We use 'at' when the location is treated as a reference point rather than a surface ('on') or a three-dimensional interior ('in').

Application

Here the station is named as the specific place where the bedding was left, i.e. a point of reference, not a surface it rests on or a space enclosing it. So the slot takes 'at': "I left my bedding at the station."

Contrast

  • 'on' signals contact with a surface (on the table, on the floor); it does not fit a named place treated as a point.

  • 'in' signals being enclosed inside a volume (in a box, in a room); it would force the reading 'inside the station building' rather than the general location.

  • 'upon' is a formal/archaic variant of 'on' and likewise implies resting on a surface, so it is unidiomatic with a station as a location.

Hence the location preposition that names the station as a point is the natural completion.

title: He looks upset, think he took the criticism heart.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: He looks upset, I think he took the criticism ______ heart.
solution:
Concept

Some verbs combine with a fixed preposition to form an idiom, and the preposition is set by convention rather than by logic — you cannot swap it for a grammatically similar word. The idiom take (something) to heart means to be deeply affected by something and to treat it seriously, often a remark, criticism, or advice.

Application

The sentence says he looks upset after being criticised, so the criticism affected him deeply. The fixed idiom that carries this exact meaning is took the criticism to heart. So the blank is filled by to.

Contrast

The other prepositions do not form this idiom:

  • at — used for a point or target ("laugh at", "look at"), not for absorbing a remark.

  • with — used for accompaniment or instrument ("agree with", "deal with"), not for this idiom.

  • of — marks possession or relation ("think of", "afraid of"), and does not pair with this fixed phrase.

Hence the completed sentence is: "He looks upset, I think he took the criticism to heart."

title: He had conspired me.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: He had conspired ______ me.
solution:
Concept

Many verbs pair with a fixed preposition (a collocation), and the verb conspire — to secretly plan with others to do something harmful — takes against when naming the person or thing the plotting is aimed at: one conspires against a target. (It takes with only to name a fellow plotter.)

Application

Here the blank is followed by me — the person the secret plotting is directed at — so the slot needs the preposition that marks a target: “He had conspired against me.”

Why the others fail

  • about: “conspire about” is not an English collocation; about introduces a topic of talk, not the victim of a plot.

  • in: one may “conspire in” a scheme (take part in an activity), but with a person as object it cannot mark the one being plotted against.

  • before: this is a time/place word and carries no plotting sense at all.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. haven't met
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

I haven't met Mr. Kapoor ________ January.
solution:
Concept

With the present perfect tense (have/has + past participle, e.g. "haven't met"), use "since" before a point in time that marks the START of the period (a date, day, month, year, or event). Use "for" before a length of time (a duration), "from" usually pairs with "to" to mark a span, and "between" links two endpoints.

Application

The sentence "I haven't met Mr. Kapoor ____ January" uses the present perfect "haven't met" and gives "January" — a specific point in time at which the period of not meeting began. The preposition that introduces a starting point with the present perfect is "since", giving: "I haven't met Mr. Kapoor since January."

Why the others do not fit

  • "from": marks the beginning of a span but normally needs a matching "to" (from January to March); standing alone with the present perfect it is non-standard here.

  • "between": joins two boundaries (between January and June) and cannot take a single point of time.

  • "for": introduces a duration, not a point — it would need a length such as "for three months", not "January".

title: Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blanks. The
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blanks.

The advantage __________ investing __________ post office schemes is that we get exemption __________ tax.
solution:
English regularly locks specific nouns and verbs to one fixed preposition — a set collocation that has to be learned as a whole phrase, not worked out from a general rule. Two prepositions that seem close in meaning are often not interchangeable once a particular noun or verb is involved.

  • 'The advantage __ investing': the standard collocation for stating a benefit of doing something is 'advantage of' + a gerund, as in 'the advantage of exercising regularly'.

  • 'investing __ post office schemes': the standard collocation for putting money into something is 'invest in' + a noun, as in 'invest in stocks/bonds/schemes'.

  • 'exemption __ tax': the standard collocation for being excused from an obligation is 'exemption from' + a noun, as in 'exemption from income tax'.

Reading the completed sentence back — 'The advantage of investing in post office schemes is that we get exemption from tax' — every blank matches a collocation attested independently across Oxford, Cambridge, and Merriam-Webster, confirming the choice rather than relying on elimination.

title: In an election, those in power should feel obliged to
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: In an election, those in power should feel obliged to compete ______ their opponents on equal terms.
solution:
“Compete” takes different prepositions depending on what follows it: “compete with/against” a rival, “compete for” a prize, “compete in” a contest. When it is paired with the fixed expression “on equal terms” (meaning neither side has any built-in advantage), standard English idiom locks onto one specific preposition rather than the other general rivalry-preposition.

In this sentence, the blank sits between “compete” and “their opponents”, and is immediately followed by “on equal terms”. Because the sentence needs the exact collocation “compete with somebody on equal terms” — the standard way of saying a contest carries no built-in advantage to either side — the word “with” is what completes it correctly.

  • “towards” expresses the direction of a feeling or attitude (e.g., an obligation towards someone), not a competitive relationship, so it cannot follow “compete”.

  • “against” can generally follow “compete” to name a rival, but it does not combine with the fixed phrase that follows the blank in this sentence; relying on the everyday rivalry-preposition without checking the fixed expression leads here by mistake.

  • “on” is used when “compete” is followed by an activity or basis (e.g., compete on price), not a person; here the blank is directly followed by a person (“their opponents”), so this preposition mismatches the sentence.

Therefore, “with” is the correct preposition: “...compete with their opponents on equal terms.”

title: Ravi is married cousin of mine.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Ravi is married ______ a cousin of mine.
solution:
Certain adjectives and past participles in English combine with one fixed preposition when introducing the noun they relate to, and that pairing is idiomatic — fixed by convention rather than freely interchangeable with any preposition of similar general meaning. “Married” is one such word: standard English fixes a single specific preposition before the person someone is wed to, and other prepositions that express similarly related ideas (accompaniment, disposal, or general association) do not substitute for it.

In this sentence, the blank sits between “married” and “a cousin of mine”, naming the person Ravi is wed to. Because English idiom fixes exactly one preposition for this meaning, the blank must take that word, giving “Ravi is married to a cousin of mine.”

  • “with” pairs with adjectives like “friends with” or “compatible with” that describe a shared relationship of similarity or association, but the fixed idiom naming who someone is wed to does not use this preposition.

  • “along with” expresses doing something together with a companion (e.g., “she went along with her cousin”), describing joint action rather than the state of being wed to someone, so it does not fit here.

  • “off” only combines with “married” in the separate causative idiom “marry somebody off” (a third party arranging someone else’s marriage), which needs a different sentence structure — an agent doing the marrying-off — not present in this sentence.

Therefore, the correct preposition is the one required by the fixed idiom naming who a person is wed to: “Ravi is married to a cousin of mine.”

title: He complains pain in the head.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: He complains ______ pain in the head.
solution:
English regularly locks a verb to one fixed preposition depending on the exact sense intended — a set collocation, not something derivable from a general rule. The verb 'complain' takes different prepositions for different senses: it pairs with a preposition of general grievance when voicing dissatisfaction with a situation or behaviour, a preposition of formal complaint when it names the person or authority a complaint is lodged against, and a separate, fixed preposition when it introduces a physical symptom or ailment someone is reporting.

In 'He complains ______ pain in the head', the blank is followed by 'pain in the head' — a physical symptom, not a grievance about a situation and not a person or authority being complained against. The fixed collocation for reporting a symptom in this way is 'complain of + ailment', as in 'complain of a headache' or 'complain of a backache', so the required preposition is 'of'.

This matches the standard usage seen in medical and everyday English — 'the patient complained of chest pain', 'she complained of a fever' — confirming 'of' as the fixed pairing whenever 'complain' is reporting a bodily symptom, which is exactly the sense used here.

  • 'about' is the preposition used when 'complain' expresses a general grievance or dissatisfaction with a situation, person, or service (e.g. complaining about the weather or about slow service) — a different sense from reporting a symptom.

  • 'for' does not form a standard collocation with 'complain' in English at all.

  • 'against' is the preposition used when a formal complaint is lodged against a specific person or authority (e.g. complaining against an officer), not when a symptom is being reported.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q1
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

Avik gave me a present ____ my birthday.
solution:
English prepositions of time follow a fixed distinction by the span of time they cover: "at" marks a precise point in time (a clock hour, noon, midnight), "on" marks a particular day or date (including named calendar occasions), and "in" marks a longer enclosed period (a month, a year, a season, a century).

  1. The word following the blank is "birthday", which names one specific calendar day, not an extended period or a single clock moment.

  2. Since the noun is a specific day, the day/date rule applies, and the temporal preposition that pairs with a specific day is "on" (compare: on Monday, on Christmas Day, on my birthday).

  3. "In" is eliminated because it pairs with months, years, or seasons, not a single day.

  4. "At" is eliminated because it pairs with a precise clock time or moment, not a full calendar day.

  5. "Into" is eliminated because it is a directional preposition of movement, not a temporal preposition, so it cannot fill a time blank at all.

This matches the same pattern used in other well-known day-linked constructions such as "on Sundays" and "on New Year's Day", confirming "on" as the consistent, non-exceptional choice.

Therefore, the correct preposition is "on".

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q2
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

I eat rice ____ my hands.
solution:
Concept: A preposition of instrument or means (most commonly "with") names the tool, device, or body part used to carry out an action. This is different from a preposition of place ("in" - inside an enclosed space; "at" - a specific point in place or time) or a preposition of purpose ("for" - the reason or intended recipient of an action).

Application: The sentence "I eat rice ____ my hands" describes the physical means by which the eating is performed — the hands are the instrument used to eat. This calls for the preposition of instrument, which is "with". The grammatically correct sentence is: "I eat rice with my hands."

Cross-check: Testing each remaining preposition against the instrumental meaning confirms the choice:

  • "in" would suggest the rice is located inside the hands (a container relationship), which does not match the intended meaning of using the hands as a tool.

  • "at" would indicate a specific point in place or time, which is unrelated to describing the instrument used for eating.

  • "for" would indicate purpose or an intended recipient of the action, not the means by which the eating is carried out.

Result: "With" is the preposition that correctly expresses the instrument/means relationship in this sentence.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q3
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

Divide the mangoes ____ the boys.
solution:
Concept: English uses two different prepositions to describe how something is distributed. "Between" is the conventional choice when exactly two distinct, individually identified entities are involved (or when items are paired off one-to-one). "Among" is the conventional choice when something is distributed within a group considered collectively — a group whose members are not being individually singled out, traditionally treated as three or more.

Application: This exact sentence — "Divide the mangoes ____ the boys" — is a standard preposition-usage drill built around that between/among distinction, and grammar practice sources that carry this specific exercise consistently key it to "among": the sentence names "the boys" as an undifferentiated group rather than naming or pairing off exactly two individuals, which is the textbook signal for the collective-group preposition. If the sentence instead read "the two boys" or named two individuals, "between" would be the conventional choice — the rule is about how the entities are referred to (a distinct pair vs. an undifferentiated group), not merely a raw headcount.

Cross-check — contrast each option by its own value:

  • Between fits only when exactly two distinct entities are named or paired individually, e.g. "The land was divided between the two brothers."

  • With expresses accompaniment or the instrument/means of an action, e.g. "She cut the mango with a knife" — this is not a distributive relation.

  • To introduces the recipient or direction of a transfer, e.g. "He gave the mangoes to the boys" — it does not itself express dividing something up among recipients.

  • Among expresses distribution within a collective, undifferentiated group, matching how "the boys" is referred to in this sentence.

Result: the sentence reads "Divide the mangoes among the boys."

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q4
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

He is deaf ____ my request for help.
solution:
Certain English adjectives combine with one fixed preposition by convention, and the preposition often depends on which sense of the adjective is being used — a literal physical sense versus a figurative sense of unwillingness or lack of response. These are collocations that must be learned rather than derived from general prepositional meaning.

  1. The adjective here is "deaf", and the clause describes his response to "my request for help" — this is the figurative sense of deaf, meaning refusing to listen to or heed something, not the literal sense of being unable to hear.

  2. In this figurative sense, deaf takes a single fixed preposition: "deaf to" (as in "deaf to advice" or "deaf to pleas"), so the correct completion is "He is deaf to my request for help."

  3. "Of" is eliminated because it pairs with verbs and adjectives of awareness or origin, such as "aware of" or "hear of", not with the figurative sense of deaf.

  4. "For" is eliminated because it pairs with purpose, duration, or benefit, such as "wait for" or "responsible for", not with the figurative sense of deaf.

  5. "At" is eliminated because it pairs with a point of focus or the target of a reaction, such as "look at" or "surprised at", not with the figurative sense of deaf.

This matches the same fixed pattern seen in the related idiom "turn a deaf ear to [something]", confirming "to" as the consistent, non-exceptional choice for this figurative use of deaf.

Therefore, the correct preposition is "to".

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q1
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Choose the correct Preposition from the options given below to complete each sentence.

She has been working here ____ 2019.
solution:
Concept: In English, "since" marks a specific point in time — a year, date, day, or moment — from which an action or state began and has continued, typically with the present perfect or present perfect continuous tense. "For" marks a duration or span of time (a number of hours, days, months, or years), not a fixed point.

Application: The sentence uses the present perfect continuous tense ("has been working"), describing an action that began in the past and is still continuing. The blank is followed by "2019", a specific calendar year — a point in time rather than a duration. Because the reference is a point in time, the sentence needs "since": "She has been working here since 2019."

Cross-check — contrast each option by its own value:

  • "For" would require a duration, e.g. "for six years," not a fixed year like 2019.

  • "From" usually pairs with "to"/"till" (e.g. "from 2019 to now") and does not stand alone with the present perfect continuous to mark unbroken duration.

  • "By" marks a deadline for a completed action (e.g. "by 2019"), which conflicts with the ongoing sense of "has been working".

Result: the sentence reads "She has been working here since 2019."

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q2
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Choose the correct Preposition from the options given below to complete each sentence.

The committee has not yet arrived ____ a final decision regarding the proposal.
solution:
Certain English verbs combine with one fixed preposition to form a set idiomatic phrase (a collocation); the correct preposition in such phrases cannot be derived from the preposition's general meaning alone — it must be recognised as a memorised unit tied to the verb's specific, often figurative, sense of direction or contact.

Here, "arrive" is used in its figurative sense of reaching a conclusion after deliberation, rather than its literal sense of reaching a physical destination. English fixes the preposition for this figurative sense as "at" — the single point that the deliberation converges on. So the sentence reads: "The committee has not yet arrived at a final decision regarding the proposal."

Checking the remaining prepositions against their own standard collocational roles confirms none fits this figurative sense:

  • "on" marks contact with a surface, a calendar reference, or a topic under discussion (e.g., "on the table", "on Monday", "a report on trade") — none of these match a point that deliberation converges on.

  • "in" marks an enclosed space, a duration, or a state (e.g., "in the hall", "in June", "interested in painting") — again not the point-reached sense.

  • "for" marks purpose, duration, or exchange (e.g., "waiting for a reply", "thankful for support", "traded for cash") — it signals aim or exchange, not the point actually reached.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q3
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Choose the correct Preposition from the options given below to complete each sentence.

Many young people are addicted ____ social media nowadays.
solution:
Concept

Many English adjectives and verbs pair with one fixed preposition by convention (a "collocation") rather than by literal meaning -- the correct preposition must be memorised for each word, not derived logically.

Application

The adjective in this sentence forms a fixed pair with the preposition "to" -- this is the standard collocation used to describe a strong or habitual attachment to something, as required by the sentence "Many young people are addicted ____ social media nowadays."

Cross-check

None of the other offered prepositions form a standard collocation with this adjective; substituting them produces phrasing that no standard dictionary or grammar reference records as correct usage, confirming the fixed pairing is the only valid completion.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q81
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

We live ____ rice.
solution:
Concept: Prepositions that follow the verb "live" change its meaning depending on which one is used — "live at" names a location, "live on" names the means of subsistence a person depends on (a food source, income, or resource), "live for" names a goal or purpose that motivates someone, and "live with" names a person or condition someone shares or puts up with.

Application: In "We live ____ rice", rice is the staple food the subject depends on for survival, not a place, a goal, or a companion. This matches the fixed idiom "live on", which is used to say what a person or animal survives by eating. So the blank takes "on".

Cross-check — how each preposition combines with "live":

  • "at" combines with a place or address, as in "live at the hostel", not with a food item.

  • "for" combines with a goal or cause a person is devoted to, as in "live for music", not with a food item.

  • "with" combines with a companion or condition someone shares, as in "live with a friend", not with a food item.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q82
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate preposition that specifically expresses being descended from a particular family or lineage to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

He comes ____ a noble family.
solution:
Concept: Many English verb+preposition combinations form idioms with a meaning more specific than the verb alone conveys. With "come," different prepositions serve different senses: "come from" is the general preposition for a place, country, or broad point of origin; "come of" is the fixed idiom specifically used for descent, lineage, or rank (e.g. coming of noble, royal, or humble stock); "come to" states a total amount reached or a state regained; and "come with" states something included or attached.

Application: In "He comes ____ a noble family," the word "noble" signals rank and lineage, which is exactly the sense the fixed idiom "come of" is used for. So the blank takes "of," giving "He comes of a noble family" - meaning he is descended from nobility.

Contrast:

  • "from" is the general preposition for a place or broad point of origin, as in "He comes from Kerala"; it does not carry the specific formal sense of descent or rank that the fixed idiom "come of" does.

  • "with" states something included or attached, as in "The laptop comes with a charger" - an accompaniment sense, not descent.

  • "to" states a total amount reached or a state regained, as in "The bill comes to five hundred rupees" or "He came to his senses" - neither is a descent sense.

Note: in everyday conversational English, "come from" is sometimes loosely used for family background too; but this fill-in-the-blank item specifically tests the fixed, dictionary-recognised idiom "come of," which is the standard term for stating descent, lineage, or rank.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q83
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

Our school breaks up exactly ____ 4 p.m.
solution:
English prepositions of time follow patterns based on how precise the time reference is: "at" introduces an exact point in time, such as a specific clock time or a moment like midnight or noon; "in" introduces a longer or less precise period, such as a month, a year, a season, or a part of the day; "from" marks the starting point of a span of time, usually paired with "to" or "until" for the endpoint; and "about"/"around" is placed before a time expression only when the sentence is explicitly hedging or estimating (words like "I think", "roughly", "nearly", "probably"), to show the time given is approximate rather than exact.

The sentence "Our school breaks up exactly ____ 4 p.m." explicitly states that the closing time is exact ("exactly"), ruling out any approximate reading. An exact clock-time reference marked as "exactly" calls for the exact-point-in-time preposition, so the blank must take "at".

  • "from" would fit only if the sentence gave a starting point paired with an end point, e.g. "from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m."; there is no such pair here.

  • "in" would fit a broader period such as a month, year, season, or part of the day ("in the evening"), not a specific clock time.

  • "about" signals an approximate time, and this directly contradicts the word "exactly" already in the sentence ("exactly about 4 p.m." would be self-contradictory); so "about" does not fit here.

Therefore, the correct preposition is "at", giving: "Our school breaks up exactly at 4 p.m."

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q85
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

The Brahmaputra has its source ____ the Himalayas.
solution:
Concept: The preposition "in" is used to show a static location enclosed within, or forming part of, a larger area or region. With the noun "source" (the place where a river originates), the fixed idiomatic collocation in standard English is "has its source in [a place/region]" — describing the river's origin as lying within that region.

Application: The Brahmaputra originates from within the Himalayan mountain range — its source lies inside this vast region. The sentence therefore completes correctly as "The Brahmaputra has its source in the Himalayas," using "in" to show that the source is located within that region.

Contrast: Compare the other prepositions and the different meaning each expresses here:

  • "into" expresses movement or entry from outside to the inside of something (e.g., "walked into the room", "poured water into the glass") — it pairs with verbs of motion, not a static existing location.

  • "under" expresses a position vertically beneath or below another object or surface (e.g., "the ball rolled under the table") — it describes something underneath, not a place of origin within a region.

  • "at" expresses a specific, exact point treated as a single spot (e.g., "waiting at the gate", "arrived at the station") — it does not fit an extended area or mountain range like "the Himalayas".

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q79
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the correct preposition for the blank in the sentence: “I prevented him ____ going.”
solution:
Concept

In standard English, certain verbs select fixed complement patterns. The verb “prevent” typically follows the pattern prevent + object + from + gerund (-ing form).

The preposition in such a pattern is governed by the verb’s construction, not only by the preposition’s standalone meaning.

Application

In “I prevented him ____ going,” “him” is the object and “going” is a gerund. Applying the pattern gives “prevented him from going.”

Contrast

  • “on” commonly marks surface contact or a topic; it is not the preposition selected by this construction.

  • “to” can mark direction or introduce a base-form infinitive, whereas “going” here is a gerund.

  • “None of these” does not apply because the required preposition is present among the listed choices.

Result

The blank is filled with “from”: “I prevented him from going.”

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q1
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The officer complied ____ the instructions given by the authority.
solution:
Concept

Some English verbs select a fixed preposition. This conventional verb–preposition pairing is called a collocation and must be used as a unit.

The verb comply is followed by with before a rule, request, order, or instruction: comply with something.

Application

Here, the noun phrase ‘the instructions given by the authority’ is what the officer followed. The fixed collocation therefore completes the sentence as ‘The officer complied with the instructions given by the authority.’

Contrast

  • As a preposition, to can mark direction or a recipient; before a base verb, to instead functions as an infinitival marker. Neither pattern forms the standard collocation with comply.

  • For commonly marks purpose, benefit, or duration; it does not form the standard collocation with comply.

  • On commonly marks a surface, topic, or dependence; it does not form the standard collocation with comply.

Result

Thus, the required preposition is with.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q2
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: She has a strong aversion ____ spicy food.
solution:
Concept

In English, many nouns conventionally govern a particular preposition when they introduce a complement. This fixed noun–preposition pairing is a collocation, so the choice follows established usage rather than a word-for-word meaning.

Application

The noun “aversion” means a strong dislike. Standard usage gives the pattern “aversion to somebody or something,” so the sentence becomes “She has a strong aversion to spicy food.”

Contrast

  • “For” commonly marks purpose, benefit, duration, or an intended recipient; those are different relations from this noun–complement pattern.

  • “About” commonly introduces a topic or an approximate quantity; it does not supply the established collocation used here.

  • “Against” commonly marks opposition, contact, or protection; it is not the conventional complement marker after “aversion.”

Result

Therefore, the required preposition is “to.”

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q3
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The Manager is responsible ____ maintaining discipline in the office.
solution:
Concept

A fixed preposition is a preposition conventionally selected by a particular adjective or verb.

With the adjective responsible, the pattern responsible for + noun or gerund identifies the duty, person, or activity for which responsibility exists.

Application

Here, maintaining is a gerund that names the activity assigned to the Manager. The sentence therefore follows the pattern responsible for maintaining discipline.

Contrast

  • at usually marks a point, place, time, or target, as in at the office or good at planning.

  • on usually marks a surface, topic, or dependence, as in on the desk or a report on policy.

  • by usually marks an agent, method, proximity, or deadline, as in prepared by the team or by Monday.

Result

Cross-check: replacing the blank gives the standard collocation responsible for maintaining. Hence, the required preposition is for.

title: Which of the following sentences is correct?
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which of the following sentences is correct?
solution: In English, we use "at" to indicate someone's skill or expertise in an activity or subject. Hence, the phrase "She is good at singing" is correct.

title: She is allergic nuts.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: She is allergic ________ nuts.
solution: The phrase "allergic to" is used to specify what substance or condition triggers an allergic reaction. Hence, "She is allergic to nuts" is correct.

title: Please put the books the shelf.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Please put the books ________ the shelf.
solution:
Correct answer: on

Explanation: The word "shelf" refers to a surface. In English, we use "on" to indicate that something is placed on top of a surface. Therefore, the correct sentence is: Please put the books on the shelf.

  • in — used for enclosed spaces (e.g., in a box); not suitable for an open shelf surface.

  • at — indicates a point or general location, not placing an object on a surface.

  • into — implies movement into the interior of something; would only be appropriate if the shelf were enclosed and you put books inside it.

title: He has been working here
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: He has been working here ________ 2005.
solution: The preposition "since" is used to indicate the starting point of an action that continues to the present. Therefore, "He has been working here since 2005" is the correct sentence.

title: These three men quarrelled themselves.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: These three men quarrelled ______ themselves.
solution:
Concept

The preposition that expresses a reciprocal relationship distributed across a group of three or more people is "among". "Between" expresses a relationship involving only two parties (or two clearly separate parties considered one-to-one).

Application

The sentence refers to "these three men" — a group of more than two. A quarrel shared reciprocally within that group of three is therefore expressed with "among", giving "quarrelled among themselves".

Contrast

  • "between" — fits a two-party relationship (e.g. between two men), so it does not match a group of three.

  • "with" — needs a separate object the men quarrel against (quarrel with someone), not a reciprocal action turned inward on "themselves".

  • "against" — marks opposition to an external party, again requiring an outside opponent rather than a mutual quarrel inside the group.

Hence the blank takes "among": quarrelled among themselves.

title: Find out the correct sentence from the following options:
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Find out the correct sentence from the following options:

options.label: A
options.html: She has no authority over her son.

options.label: B
options.html: She has no authority upon her son.

options.label: C
options.html: She has no authority for her son.

options.label: D
options.html: She has no authority of her son.

solution:
Concept

The noun “authority” meaning power or control to direct others takes the preposition “over”. The fixed collocation “to have authority over someone” expresses command or jurisdiction. Choosing the correct dependent preposition is what makes the sentence idiomatically correct.

Application

The sentence describes a mother’s power to direct her son, so “authority” must pair with “over”: “She has no authority over her son.” This is the grammatically and idiomatically correct form.

Why the other prepositions do not fit

  • “authority upon her son”: “upon” denotes physical position or a point in time, not command over a person, so it is not the collocation used with “authority” in this sense.

  • “authority for her son”: “for” signals purpose or benefit (acting on someone’s behalf), which changes the meaning away from control and is not idiomatic here.

  • “authority of her son”: “of” would imply the son possesses or is the source of the authority, the opposite of the intended power exercised over him.

title: Choose the option that is in the direct form of

The minister said that no one would be allowed to break the law.

Answer: The minister said, "No one will be allowed to break the law."

Steps to convert the indirect sentence to direct speech:

  • Remove the conjunction 'that' and place a comma before the quoted clause, then open quotation marks.

  • Restore the original tense: backshifted 'would' in indirect speech becomes 'will' in direct speech, because the reported clause originally expressed future meaning.

  • Keep the reporting verb 'said' unchanged in this case.

  • Check pronouns and voice: do not change passive to active unless the original meaning requires it. Here the passive form remains appropriate.

Final direct sentence: The minister said, "No one will be allowed to break the law."

title: Which sentence correctly converts "She said, am eating' to indirect
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which sentence correctly converts "She said, 'I am eating' " to indirect speech?
solution:
Key rule: when the reporting verb is in the past (for example, "said"), tenses usually shift back.

  • Tense change: present continuous ("am eating") → past continuous ("was eating").

  • Reporting verb: because the original reporting verb is past ("said"), we apply the backshift.

  • Use of "that": optional. Both "She said that she was eating" and "She said she was eating" are correct.

  • Pronouns: change only if the perspective shifts; here "she" remains "she."

Correct indirect sentence: She said that she was eating.

title: Transform: "Sara said, will study later'"

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

solution: The future tense "will study" changes to "would study" in reported speech. This shift helps maintain the tense consistency when reporting a future plan or intention.

title: Which of the following sentences correctly transforms "John said, have
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which of the following sentences correctly transforms "John said, 'I have finished my work'" into indirect speech?

solution: In reported speech, present perfect tense ("have finished") often changes to past perfect tense ("had finished"). The switch to past perfect shows that the action was already complete at the time John was speaking.

title: Choose the correct speech sentence from the following given options:
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the correct speech sentence from the following given options: He said, “He takes exercise session everyday.”

options.label: A
options.html: He said that he took exercise session every day.

options.label: B
options.html: He said that he would take exercise session every day.

options.label: C
options.html: He said that he has taken exercise session every day.

solution:
Explanation:

  • Identify the direct speech: He takes exercise session every day.

  • The reporting verb "said" is in the past, so apply sequence of tenses: present simple "takes" → past simple "took".

  • Adverb "every day" stays the same (write as two words).

Correct indirect speech (closest form): He said that he took exercise session every day.

Notes:

  • For more natural wording, you can also say: He said that he took exercise sessions every day, or He said that he had an exercise session every day.

title: Which is the correct conversion of "Jane said, could run
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which is the correct conversion of "Jane said, 'I could run fast' "?

options.label: A
options.html: Jane said that she can run fast.

options.label: B
options.html: Jane said that she could run fast.

options.label: D
options.html: Jane said that she might run fast.

solution:
Correct conversion: Jane said that she could run fast.

Explanation: When reporting speech with a past reporting verb like "said", present-tense verbs and certain modals normally shift back in time (backshift). The modal "can" backshifts to "could". In this case the direct quote already uses "could", so it remains "could" in reported speech.

  • Rule: Backshift present modals and tenses when the reporting verb is past. Example: "can" → "could".

  • Example (direct to reported): Direct: Jane said, "I could run fast." Reported: Jane said that she could run fast.

  • Contrast with a sentence that uses "can": Direct: Jane said, "I can run fast." Reported: Jane said that she could run fast.

  • Common pitfall: Replacing "could" with "might" changes the meaning from ability (could) to possibility (might), so that substitution is not correct when preserving the original meaning.

title: Convert: "Tom said, won't be late'"
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Convert: "Tom said, 'I won't be late'"

options.label: A
options.html: Tom said that he won't be late.

options.label: B
options.html: Tom said that he wouldn't be late.

options.label: C
options.html: Tom says he will not be late.

options.label: D
options.html: Tom said that he will be late.

solution:
In indirect speech, when the reporting verb is in the past, verbs and modals are usually backshifted to maintain sequence of tenses.

Rule: change "will"/"won't" to "would"/"wouldn't" when the reporting verb is in the past.

  • Example (direct to indirect):

    Direct: Tom said, 'I won't be late.'

    Indirect: Tom said that he wouldn't be late.

  • Why: The reporting verb "said" is past, so "won't" (will not) is backshifted to "wouldn't" (would not) to keep tense consistency.

  • Exception: If the reporting verb is present (for example, "Tom says"), no backshift is required: Tom says he will not be late.

title: Which of the following is the correct indirect speech for
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Which of the following is the correct indirect speech for "Lucy said, 'I must finish the project' "?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

solution:
Rule: In reported speech, when the reporting verb is in the past, the modal "must" is usually changed to "had to" to show past obligation.

  • Direct speech: Lucy said, 'I must finish the project.'

  • Indirect speech: Lucy said she had to finish the project.

Key steps: change the reporting structure to remove quotation marks, backshift "must" to "had to", and keep pronouns appropriate to the speaker.

title: Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence. The manager
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence.

The manager asked me __________ the conditions of appointment.
solution:
A direct yes/no question is reported by turning it into an embedded clause introduced by the connector "if" or "whether": the interrogative (auxiliary-before-subject) word order is replaced by ordinary subject-then-verb order, and if the reporting verb is in the past tense, the modal or auxiliary inside the reported clause backshifts one step into the past — will becomes would, can becomes could, and so on.

Applying the connector, the subject-verb order, and the tense backshift to this sentence:

  1. The sentence being reported is the yes/no question "Will you accept the conditions of appointment?"

  2. Because it is a yes/no question, not a wh-question, the reported clause must be introduced by the connector "if" (or "whether").

  3. The interrogative order "will you" is replaced by ordinary subject-then-verb order: "I would", not "would I".

  4. Since the reporting verb "asked" is in the past tense, the modal "will" backshifts one step into the past to "would".

  5. Combining the connector, the subject-verb order, and the backshifted modal gives: "...if I would accept the conditions of appointment."

Checking each remaining structure against these same three requirements (connector, subject-verb order, backshift):

  • "would I accept" keeps the auxiliary-before-subject order of a direct question and has no connector, so it still reads as a question rather than a reported clause.

  • "if I will accept" supplies the connector but leaves "will" un-shifted, ignoring the backshift that the past-tense "asked" requires.

  • "will I accept" has neither the connector nor subject-before-verb order, and it also leaves "will" un-shifted.

Only the structure that supplies the connector, uses subject-then-verb order, and backshifts the modal together meets all three requirements for reporting this question.

title: Arrange the following sentences (MCQ) To the actual cost of
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Arrange the following sentences

a) To the actual cost of the service

b) In rational proportion

c) Marketing cost is now

d) No longer
solution:
To arrange the sentence correctly, follow these grammatical principles:

  • Step 1: Begin with the subject and verb. The clause "Marketing cost is now" provides a clear subject and verb.

  • Step 2: Place the negation "no longer" immediately after the verb to correctly modify the state being negated.

  • Step 3: Add the descriptive phrase "in rational proportion" to explain the relationship between the cost components.

  • Step 4: Finish with the complement "to the actual cost of the service" to complete the prepositional phrase and the sentence.

Note: Avoid starting with prepositional phrases or negations without a subject and verb. Also, ensure the main clause appears early to maintain grammatical correctness and natural flow.

title: In the following question, the 1st and the last part
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In the following question, the 1st and the last part of the sentence/passage are numbered 1 and 6. The rest of the sentence/passage is split into four parts and named P, Q, R and S. These four parts are not given in their proper order. Read the sentence and find out which of the four combinations is correct.

1) Child labourers are posing a grave problem before India.

P. Children are paid low wages and the heinous opportunism of employers leads to the employment of children.

Q. The government is indifferent to this problem and common people lack awareness in guarding against this social crime.

R. It is the extreme poverty of parents that leads children to earn at a minor age.

S. The illiteracy of parents is also responsible for this evil.

6) For the solution of this problem, we need a thorough economic reform and the spread of literacy.
solution:
Answer: R S P Q

  • R: States the primary cause — the extreme poverty of parents that leads children to earn at a minor age. This naturally follows the opening sentence that names the problem.

  • S: Gives an additional cause — the illiteracy of parents. The use of 'also' indicates it should follow the primary cause (R).

  • P: Describes the direct effect and characteristics of the problem — children being paid low wages and being exploited by employers. This follows the causes (R and S).

  • Q: Comments on the social response — government indifference and public lack of awareness. This is a natural concluding remark before the final sentence proposing solutions.

Connection to the final sentence: The proposed remedies in the final sentence (economic reform and spread of literacy) directly address the causes given in R and S, confirming that the sequence R → S → P → Q yields a coherent explanation that leads into the solution.

title: Choose the correct order of sentences to form meaningful paragraph.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the correct order of sentences to form a meaningful paragraph.

options.label: A
options.html:
Movies depict cruelty and violence as heroic rather than vicious.

Every day we read and hear about the crimes committed by younger people.
The result is that juvenile crime has become a major problem in our country.
In addition, many parents often avoid their responsibilities or are unable to exercise them.

options.label: B
options.html:
The result is that juvenile crime has become a major problem in our country.

In addition, many parents often avoid their responsibilities or are unable to exercise them.
Movies depict cruelty and violence as heroic rather than vicious.
Every day we read and hear about the crimes committed by younger people.

options.label: C
options.html:
Every day we read and hear about the crimes committed by younger people.

Movies depict cruelty and violence as heroic rather than vicious.
In addition, many parents often avoid their responsibilities or are unable to exercise them.
The result is that juvenile crime has become a major problem in our country.

options.label: D
options.html:
In addition, many parents often avoid their responsibilities or are unable to exercise them.

Movies depict cruelty and violence as heroic rather than vicious. Every day we read and hear about the crimes committed by younger people.
The result is that juvenile crime has become a major problem in our country.

solution:
The correct sequence is Option C.
The paragraph begins by stating the observable phenomenon: 'Every day we read and hear about the crimes committed by younger people.' This sets the context.
Next, it introduces contributing factors, starting with media influence: 'Movies depict cruelty and violence as heroic rather than vicious.'
The third sentence adds another cause using the transition 'In addition,' linking parental neglect to the previous point.
Finally, the sentence starting with 'The result is that...' logically concludes the paragraph by summarizing the outcome of these combined factors.
Options A, B, and D fail because they either place the conclusion ('The result...') too early or disrupt the logical flow between causes and effects.
Specifically, Option A starts with movies but jumps to crime statistics before explaining the parental factor, creating a disjointed narrative.
Option B places the conclusion immediately after mentioning parents, which is premature since the media influence hasn't been introduced yet.
Therefore, Option C provides the most coherent cause-and-effect structure.

title: Arrange the words to form meaningful sentence: “Performance remarkable was
subject: Verbal Ability (English)

solution:
To arrange the words "Performance / remarkable / was / by / team / the" into a meaningful sentence, we follow standard English grammatical structure: Subject + Verb + Complement/Adjective.

Sentence Construction Analysis
Identify the Subject: "The performance" (using the article 'the' and noun 'performance').

title: Arrange the sentences in logical order: They finally managed to
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Arrange the sentences in logical order:

1. They finally managed to climb the peak
2. The journey was fraught with challenges
3. The view from the top was breathtaking
4. They began their trek early in the morning
solution:
Correct Option
Option B: 4-2-1-3

Detailed Solution
The correct chronological order is:

4: They began their trek early in the morning.

2: The journey was fraught with challenges.

1: They finally managed to climb the peak.

3: The view from the top was breathtaking.

title: Rearrange the following four sentences (ii), (iii) and (iv) in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Rearrange the following four sentences (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) in the proper sequence to form a meaningful paragraph and choose the correct sequences as your answer :

(i) He was so busy with them that he did not get time to eat.

(ii) Thousands of people came to him and asked different types of questions.

(iii) No one cared to see if he had his food or rest that night.

(iv) Swami Vivekananda once stayed in a small village.

The proper sequence should be:
solution: To form a meaningful paragraph, we must first identify the introductory sentence. Sentence (iv) introduces the subject 'Swami Vivekananda' and the setting 'a small village', making it the logical starting point. This eliminates options A and B immediately.\nNext, we look for what happened after he arrived. Sentence (ii) describes 'Thousands of people came to him', which naturally follows the introduction of his stay. Sentence (i) explains the consequence of this interaction: 'He was so busy with them that he did not get time to eat'. This creates a direct cause-and-effect link between (ii) and (i). Finally, sentence (iii) concludes the narrative by stating 'No one cared to see if he had his food or rest that night', summarizing the situation described in (i). Therefore, the sequence is (iv) -> (ii) -> (i) -> (iii), which corresponds to Option C. Options A and B are incorrect because they do not start with the introductory sentence (iv). Option D is incorrect because it places (iii) before (i), disrupting the logical flow regarding his lack of food.

title: Sentences of paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

1. The results showed a significant improvement in students' academic performance.

2. The study aimed to evaluate the impact of digital learning tools on education.

3. Researchers conducted a year-long study involving over 500 students.

4. These findings suggest that integrating technology in classrooms can be beneficial.
solution:
Concept

A research-report paragraph follows a fixed narrative spine: it first states the purpose/aim of the study, then describes the method (who was studied and how), then reports the results obtained, and finally draws a conclusion or implication from those results. Sequencing by this Aim -> Method -> Result -> Conclusion logic, and by cohesion cues (a sentence that begins with a back-reference such as "These findings" must come AFTER what it refers to), helps identify the best available ordering.

Application

Classify each numbered sentence by its role, then chain them in narrative order:

  1. Sentence 2 states the AIM ("The study aimed to evaluate the impact of digital learning tools") - this introduces the topic, so it opens the paragraph.

  2. Sentence 3 gives the METHOD ("Researchers conducted a year-long study involving over 500 students") - it describes how the aim was pursued, so it follows the aim.

  3. Sentence 1 reports the RESULT ("The results showed a significant improvement in academic performance") - results can only be stated after the study was conducted.

  4. Sentence 4 is the CONCLUSION ("These findings suggest that integrating technology can be beneficial") - the pronoun phrase "These findings" refers back to the results, so it must come last.

Chaining these roles gives the order 2, 3, 1, 4.

Cross-check

Cohesion test: "These findings" in sentence 4 has no antecedent unless the results (sentence 1) precede it - so 4 cannot come before 1. Likewise "The results" in sentence 1 presupposes a study has already been run (sentence 3). Both anchors confirm the chain 2 -> 3 -> 1 -> 4.

One might instead argue that sentence 3 ("Researchers conducted a year-long study involving over 500 students") should open the paragraph, since it introduces "a study" before sentence 2 refers back to "the study" - testing definite/indefinite article cohesion. That observation makes 3, 2, 1, 4 a grammatically plausible alternative in isolation, so the sequence is not universally unique. However, 3, 2, 1, 4 is not among the choices. Of the offered orderings, 2, 3, 1, 4 best follows the conventional research-summary progression from aim to method to result to implication. An opening sentence such as "The study aimed to..." can introduce the paragraph's own subject, just as an abstract may open with "This study examines..."; it does not require a preceding sentence in this context.

title: Sentences of paragraph are given below. While the first and
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below. While the first and the last sentences (S1 and S6) are in the correct order, the sentences in between are jumbled up. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

S1. Machinery is like a snake-hole which may contain from one to a hundred snakes.

A. Honest physicians will tell you that where means of artificial locomotion have increased, the health of the people has suffered.

B. Where there is machinery, there are large cities.

C. English villages do not boast of any of these things.

D. Where there are large cities, there are cars, buses, and electric lights.

S6. I cannot recall a single good point in connection with machinery.
solution:
The opening sentence S1 introduces 'machinery'. Sentence B continues this idea directly: 'Where there is machinery, there are large cities.' This makes B the natural first link after S1.

B ends with 'large cities', and D opens with 'Where there are large cities, there are cars, buses, and electric lights.' This repetition of 'large cities' forms a mandatory B-D link.

D mentions 'cars, buses, and electric lights' (means of artificial locomotion). A picks this up: 'Honest physicians will tell you that where means of artificial locomotion have increased, the health of the people has suffered.' So A follows D.

C then concludes the body: 'English villages do not boast of any of these things' - 'these things' refers to the machinery, cities, cars and lights mentioned in B, D and A. C leads naturally into the final sentence S6.

Therefore the correct sequence is S1-B-D-A-C-S6, i.e. BDAC.

title: In this question, there is list of four sentences marked
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In this question, there is a list of four sentences marked P, Q, R and S that follows a given sentence that together forms a paragraph. Find the proper sequence of the four sentences and make your response accordingly on the Answer Sheet.

Mr. and Mrs. Robert went home late last night.

P. Somebody had broken open the lock. Q. To their dismay they found all their things missing. R. They got into the house with a lot of fear. S. When they reached home they found the front door open.

The proper sequence should be
solution:
Concept

A jumbled-sentence (para-jumble) item is solved by reconstructing the single coherent narrative the fragments describe. Order the sentences by the real-world chronology of events and by cohesion links — each sentence should follow naturally from the one before it (cause before effect, action before reaction, observation before conclusion). The opening (anchor) sentence is fixed; the rest must form an unbroken cause-and-effect chain.

Application

The anchor sentence is: “Mr. and Mrs. Robert went home late last night.” Trace the events in the order they would actually happen on arriving home:

  1. When they reached home they found the front door open. — the very first thing they notice on arrival, so this comes immediately after the anchor.

  2. Somebody had broken open the lock. — they look at the door and see the cause of it being open; the broken lock explains the open door.

  3. They got into the house with a lot of fear. — having realised there was a break-in, they enter cautiously; fear is the reaction to what they just saw.

  4. To their dismay they found all their things missing. — the final discovery, possible only after they are inside.

Reading them in this order gives the sentence labels S → P → R → Q.

Cross-check

Test the cohesion at each join: open door → explained by the broken lock → fear of an intruder → entering → finding the loss. Each step is a direct consequence of the previous one, with no gap. Any order that puts “things missing” before they enter, or “got into the house” before the door is found open, breaks the chronology — so S P R Q is the only coherent sequence.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q82
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Each of the following sentences is marked as P, Q, R, S. Arrange P, Q, R, S, which stand for sentences, in a sequence such that they make a proper paragraph.

P. There were many speeches and my grandmother was garlanded by a girl from every class.

Q. There was a farewell ceremony on her last day at school.

R. My grandmother had taught in a girls’ high school since 1936.

S. In 1962, the year I turned ten, my grandmother retired upon reaching the age of 60.

Find out the proper sequence from the options below:
solution:
Concept

A jumbled paragraph is rebuilt from the links the sentences themselves carry, not from a guess about which order sounds best, and those links are of two different strengths. Two of them are absolute. An anaphoric pronoun (she, her, it) names nobody on its own, so it must appear after the full noun phrase it points back to. And an elaborating sentence — one that supplies the details of an event — must follow the sentence that first names that event. The third link is only a preference: the past perfect (had + past participle) presents its event as background to some past reference point, so a paragraph usually reads more smoothly when the simple-past sentence that fixes that point comes first. English does allow the background to be stated before its reference point, so tense ranks the surviving candidates rather than eliminating any of them. Settle the absolute links first, then use the preference to choose among whatever is left.

Applying the links to these four sentences

  1. Anaphora (absolute). Q speaks of “her last day at school” and contains no noun naming that person, while P, R and S each name “my grandmother” in full. A paragraph therefore cannot open with Q: the pronoun “her” would have nothing earlier to point back to.

  2. Elaboration (absolute). Q names the event — “a farewell ceremony” — and P supplies that ceremony’s content: “many speeches” and the garlanding “by a girl from every class”. P must therefore come after Q, never before it.

  3. Tense (preference). R is the only past-perfect sentence — “my grandmother had taught in a girls’ high school since 1936” — and it reads as background to the dated event S states in the simple past: “In 1962 … my grandmother retired”. Nothing in English forbids R before S, but S before R is the smoother narrative order, and it is also how the passage this item is adapted from runs (Amitav Ghosh, The Shadow Lines, which gives the 1962 retirement first and the teaching-since-1936 background immediately after).

  4. Putting these together: S fixes the dated reference point, R fills in the background, Q names the event, and P gives that event’s details — S – R – Q – P.

Cross-check against the sequences on offer

Sequence

Result of applying the links

QPSR

Opens on Q, whose “her” has no earlier noun to point back to, so it breaks the absolute anaphora link.

PQRS

Places P, the ceremony’s details, ahead of Q, the sentence that first names the ceremony, so it breaks the absolute elaboration link.

SRQP

Keeps both absolute links intact and follows the tense preference and the source passage as well.

None of these

Would apply only if every listed sequence broke one of the links; SRQP does not.

The proper sequence is SRQP.

title: Direction: Arrange these parts so as to form complete meaningful
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Arrange these parts so as to form a complete meaningful sentence/paragraph and then choose the correct combination.

P. that even five hours later there was no proper estimate.

Q. The delay meant that not only did the monster tsunami wave.

R. of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy.

S. strike without warning but.
solution:
Correct sequence: Q S P R

Combined paragraph: The delay meant that not only did the monster tsunami wave strike without warning but that even five hours later there was no proper estimate of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy.

Why this order works:

  • The first part introduces the situation but is incomplete by itself: it names the monster tsunami wave and sets up an expectation of what the wave did.

  • The second part immediately provides the missing action (strike without warning) and the contrast marker (but), completing the first clause.

  • The third part continues the consequence introduced by 'but' and adds the time frame and consequence (even five hours later there was no proper estimate).

  • The final fragment completes the idea by specifying what there was no proper estimate of: the true magnitude of the grave tragedy.

Why the other orders fail:

  • Any order that places the fragment beginning with "of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy" before its main clause leaves a dependent phrase without an anchor, producing a fragment rather than a complete sentence.

  • Any order that delays the part containing the verb 'strike' until after the consequence part creates an awkward and ungrammatical break; the action must follow directly after the mention of the wave.

title: In the following questions, the first and the last sentences
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In the following questions, the first and the last sentences of the passage are numbered (1) and (6). The rest of the passage is split into four parts'' and named P, Q, R and S. These four parts are not given in their proper order. Read the sentence and find out which of the four combinations is correct. Then find the correct answer.

1. Most of the universities in the country are now facing financial crisis.

P. Cost benefit yardstick thus should not be applied in the case of universities.

Q. The current state of affairs cannot be allowed to continue for long.

R. Universities cannot be equated with commercial enterprises.

S. Proper development of universities and colleges must be ensured.

6. The Government should realise this before it is too late.
solution:
Correct sequence: Q R P S

Explanation:

  • Start with the problem stated in the opening sentence: most universities are facing a financial crisis.

  • Follow with the immediate reaction: the current state of affairs cannot be allowed to continue (Q). This naturally follows the problem statement.

  • Explain the reason why the situation is unacceptable: universities cannot be equated with commercial enterprises (R). This distinction justifies different treatment.

  • Draw the specific implication from that distinction: therefore a cost–benefit yardstick should not be applied to universities (P). This follows from the claim in R.

  • Offer the general recommendation: proper development of universities and colleges must be ensured (S), which leads into the concluding plea that the government should realise this before it is too late.

Because each sentence now follows a clear cause–effect or justification link, the order Q → R → P → S is coherent and supports the final concluding sentence.

title: The question below comprises four scattered segments of paragraph. Identify
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
The question below comprises four scattered segments of a paragraph. Identify from among the four choices the sequences that correctly assemble the segments and complete the paragraph.

A. They found the stains of blood on an abandoned shirt in a dumpster in the next street.

B. The detective believes that the clues of a crime scene are hidden in the periphery.

C. So, against the word of the inspector, the search team spread out all over the area, checking small streets and pathways.

D. Check the dumpsters and small streets, the detective said.
solution:
Correct sequence: BDCA

Assembled paragraph: The detective believes that the clues of a crime scene are hidden in the periphery. "Check the dumpsters and small streets," the detective said. So, against the word of the inspector, the search team spread out all over the area, checking small streets and pathways. They found the stains of blood on an abandoned shirt in a dumpster in the next street.

  • The opening sentence introduces the detective and the focus of the investigation, so it belongs first.

  • The detective's spoken instruction naturally follows the introduction and explains what should be done next.

  • The next sentence describes the team's response (spreading out despite the inspector), which follows from the instruction.

  • The final sentence reports the result of the search (finding blood stains), which logically comes after the search activity.

title: Identify the option that arranges the given parts in the
