Identify the option that arranges the given parts in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

a) In Shakespeare’s hands, English drama

b) that first shone forth in his early history plays

d) achieved a matchless brilliance

title: The question below has six sentences of paragraph with the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
The question below has six sentences of a paragraph with the first and the last sentence being in the correct place. Rearrange the four sentences A,B,C,D in order to form a coherent paragraph.

1. The concept of a ‘nation-state’ assumes a complete correspondence between the boundaries of the nation and the boundaries of those who live in a specific state

A. Then there are members of national collectivities who live in other countries, making a mockery of the concept.

B. There are always people living in particular states who are not considered to be (and often do not consider themselves to be) members of the hegemonic nation.

C. Even worse, there are nations which never had a state or which are divided across several states.

D. This, of course has been subject to severe criticism and is virtually everywhere a fiction.

6. However, the fiction has been, and continues to be, at the basis of nationalist ideologies.
solution:
Concept:

For a sentence-rearrangement (para-jumble) item, each movable sentence carries a linking cue — a pronoun or demonstrative ('this', 'the concept'), a sequencing word ('then', 'even worse', 'however'), or a logical relation — that only makes sense once its antecedent has already been stated. Solving the item means matching each cue to the one sentence that already supplies that antecedent, which fixes a single valid order between the given first and last lines.

Applying it to this passage:

  1. Sentence 1 states the assumption behind the term 'nation-state': that the boundaries of the nation and the boundaries of the state are assumed to coincide.

  2. D follows immediately after 1, because 'This, of course, has been subject to severe criticism and is virtually everywhere a fiction' can only be referring back to the assumption just stated in 1 — no other sentence has introduced anything yet for 'This' to point to.

  3. B comes next, giving the first concrete mismatch: people living in a state who are not treated as (and do not consider themselves to be) members of the dominant nation.

  4. A follows with 'Then', a continuation word that needs a mismatch example already on the table — exactly what B supplies — and adds a second mismatch: members of a national group living in other countries.

  5. C escalates with 'Even worse', which needs two prior examples to escalate past — satisfied only once B and A have both been stated — introducing nations that never had a state, or that are split across several states.

  6. 6 then closes with 'However', contrasting against the strongest point just made in C: despite all these mismatches, the fiction persists as the basis of nationalist ideology.

Cross-check:

  • D's 'This' has only sentence 1 as a possible antecedent, so D must follow 1 directly.

  • A's 'Then' needs a mismatch example already stated — available only once B precedes it.

  • C's 'Even worse' needs two escalatable examples already in place — available only once B and A precede it.

  • 6's 'However' needs the strongest, most negative point just made — available only once C precedes it.

Every one of these four checks is satisfied only by the order D-B-A-C, so the passage reads 1-D-B-A-C-6.

title: DIRECTIONS: Rearrange the following sentences and into meaningful paragraph and
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
DIRECTIONS: Rearrange the following sentences (A), (B), (C), (D), (E) and (F) into a meaningful paragraph and then answer the question given below it.

A. Environment Education unit of Centre for Science & Environment has always been working towards providing easy to understand reading material.

B. Their new publication on this subject is an attempt to lend teachers a helping hand.

C. It unfolds in two sections: Climate change: how to make sense of it all

D. And natural resources how to share & care.

E. However, they are introduced to students not as a paragraph to memorize but as an activity to do.
solution:
Explanation:

Begin with the sentence that introduces the subject: "Environment Education unit of Centre for Science & Environment has always been working towards providing easy to understand reading material." This establishes the unit that the rest of the paragraph discusses.

Next, place the sentence that mentions the new publication so that "their" clearly refers to the unit: "Their new publication on this subject is an attempt to lend teachers a helping hand."

Then put the two sentences that list the publication's sections consecutively because they form a pair: "It unfolds in two sections: Climate change: how to make sense of it all" followed by "And natural resources how to share & care." The second sentence begins with "And," so it must directly follow the first.

Finish with the concluding sentence that begins with "However": "However, they are introduced to students not as a paragraph to memorize but as an activity to do." The word "However" signals a concluding comment, so this sentence belongs at the end.

  • Do not start with a sentence that is clearly a continuation (for example, a sentence beginning with "And").

  • Keep paired sentences that together describe a single idea next to each other (the two-section list must be consecutive).

  • Ensure pronouns have clear antecedents: place the sentence that introduces the subject before the sentence that uses 'their'.

Final paragraph in the correct order:

Environment Education unit of Centre for Science & Environment has always been working towards providing easy to understand reading material. Their new publication on this subject is an attempt to lend teachers a helping hand. It unfolds in two sections: Climate change: how to make sense of it all. And natural resources how to share & care. However, they are introduced to students not as a paragraph to memorize but as an activity to do.

title: The four sentences (labelled given below, when properly sequenced would
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) given below, when properly sequenced would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequence of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the four numbers as your answer.

1. Conceptualisations of ‘women’s time’ as contrary to clock-time and clock-time as synonymous with economic rationalism are two of the deleterious results of this representation.

2. While dichotomies of ‘men’s time’, ‘women’s time’, clock-time, and caring time can be analytically useful, this article argues that everyday caring practices incorporate a multiplicity of times; and both men and women can engage in these multiple-times

3. When the everyday practices of working sole fathers and working sole mothers are carefully examined to explore conceptualisations of gendered time, it is found that caring time is often more focused on the clock than generally theorised.

4. Clock-time has been consistently represented in feminist literature as a masculine artefact representative of a ‘time is money’ perspective
solution:
Correct sequence: 4 → 1 → 3 → 2.

Why this order works:

  • Sentence 4 introduces the representation. — it states that clock-time is represented as a masculine 'time is money' perspective, providing the topic and context.

  • Sentence 1 follows by referring to that representation. — it uses "this representation" and discusses two deleterious results, so it logically comes immediately after the description in sentence 4.

  • Sentence 3 provides a specific finding that complicates the representation. — it reports that caring time can be more clock-focused than theorised, giving evidence that nuances the earlier claims.

  • Sentence 2 serves as the concluding generalization. — it argues that everyday caring practices involve multiple times and that both men and women can engage in them, which is an appropriate closing statement after the evidence and discussion.

Overall flow: introduce the commonly held representation, mention its negative consequences that follow from that representation, present a finding that complicates or qualifies the representation, and finish with a broader argumentative conclusion.

title: Read the sentences and choose the option that best arranges
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Read the sentences and choose the option that best arranges them in a logical order.

1. The moral will arise when, for the reasons we saw earlier, this negation has to be negated; the individual moral will understands that it is the existence of the universal will, which is therefore internal to it.

2. This constitutes a negation, because the individual will is understood not to be the existence of the universal will.

3. This says that in abstract right, as we have just seen, the individual will take its freedom (the universal will that has being in itself) to exist independent of (that is, in opposition to) itself and its particular contents.

4. Rather, the universal will is thought to exist outside any individual will, in the contracts that bind a number of property-owning wills together, and in the punishments that enforce breaches of those contracts.
solution:
Concept: In a Para Jumble drawn from a longer passage, the sentence that opens the excerpt is the one whose pronouns or connectors do not depend on anything found in the OTHER given sentences, even if it carries a phrase that points further back into the source text the excerpt was drawn from. Every other given sentence is placed by tracing its referential and logical-connector words to an idea stated in one of the other given sentences.

Application: Sentence 3's phrases "This says that" and "as we have just seen" point back to material from before this four-sentence excerpt begins, not to anything in sentences 1, 2 or 4 -- so among the four given sentences it is the one that can open without waiting on any of the others. Sentence 2 opens with "This constitutes a negation", where "this" refers directly to the separation of individual and universal will just stated in sentence 3, so 2 follows 3. Sentence 4 opens with "Rather", a contrast connector that corrects the negation just named in sentence 2 by re-describing where the universal will actually exists (in contracts and punishments), so 4 follows 2. Sentence 1's clause "this negation has to be negated" explicitly needs the negation already named in sentence 2 (and refined in sentence 4) to be on the table, and it states the paragraph's conclusion (the moral will arising), so sentence 1 can only come last, after 3, 2 and 4. This gives the order 3, 2, 4, 1.

Cross-check: Reading the assembled paragraph end to end (3, 2, 4, 1) produces one continuous argument with no dangling pronoun or connector left unresolved among the four given sentences, confirming the sequence.

title: Directions: Rearrange the following sentences and in the proper sequence
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Directions 135 -140

Rearrange the following sentences A, B, C, D, E, and F in the proper sequence to form a meaningful paragraph; then answer the questions given below.
A. Moving eastward, we encounter the Indo-Aryan languages like Hindi, Bengali, and Assamese, which dominate the Northern and Eastern plains, originating from Sanskrit.
B. This journey reveals a fascinating tapestry of linguistic evolution, influenced by migrations, invasions, and cultural exchanges over millennia.
C. India's linguistic landscape is incredibly diverse, showcasing a remarkable transition in languages from its far northwest to the easternmost regions.
D. Further south and east, the Dravidian family, including Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam, forms a distinct and ancient branch, unrelated to the Indo-Aryan group.
E. In the far northwest, languages like Kashmiri, Punjabi, and Sindhi, belonging to the Indo-Aryan family, show strong influences from Persian and Arabic due to historical interactions.
F. Beyond these, the Northeast is home to numerous Tibeto-Burman languages, reflecting its geographical proximity and cultural ties with Southeast Asia.


135 Which of the following should be the FIRST sentence after rearrangement?
solution:
Concept: A sentence-rearrangement (para-jumble) passage always opens with a topic sentence — one that states the paragraph's overall theme and scope in general terms, without any transitional word (like 'moving', 'further', 'beyond these') or backward-referring phrase (like 'this journey') that would presuppose content already given. Every other sentence must be anchored to this opening sentence by directional or referential connectors.

Application:

  1. Sentence C sets the theme in general terms — "India's linguistic landscape is incredibly diverse, showcasing a remarkable transition in languages from its far northwest to the easternmost regions." — introducing the west-to-east scope that the rest of the paragraph fills in.

  2. Sentence E specifies the starting point of that transition — "In the far northwest, languages like Kashmiri, Punjabi, and Sindhi, belonging to the Indo-Aryan family, show strong influences from Persian and Arabic due to historical interactions." — directly matching C's 'far northwest' reference, so E follows C.

  3. Sentence A continues with the explicit transition marker 'Moving eastward,' moving from the northwest group in E to the Indo-Aryan languages of the plains, so A follows E.

  4. Sentence D continues with 'Further south and east' — a comparative marker that requires the earlier northwest-to-eastward point already established — introducing the Dravidian family.

  5. Sentence F extends further with 'Beyond these' — the Northeast Tibeto-Burman languages — continuing from D.

  6. Sentence B closes with 'This journey reveals...,' a reflective summary that can only follow after the geographic tour (C-E-A-D-F) has already been described.

Cross-check: Re-reading the paragraph in this order — C (theme), then E (far northwest), then A (moving eastward), then D (further south and east), then F (beyond these, Northeast), then B (this journey reveals) — every connector resolves cleanly to the immediately preceding sentence with no dangling reference, confirming the sequence. Since the paragraph must open with the general topic-setting sentence, sentence C is the first sentence.

title: Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence. The government
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence.

The government helps the poor by providing them loans at __________ rates of interest.
solution:
CONCEPT

Degrees of comparison in English have three forms — positive (low), comparative (lower/less), and superlative (lowest/least). An intensifier such as "very" combines only with the positive-degree form of a gradable adjective (very low, very good); it does not combine with a comparative form (less, lesser), because a comparative already expresses a degree of comparison and cannot be intensified in that same way.

APPLICATION

The blank needs a word or phrase describing "rates of interest" that fits the sentence's meaning — that loans are offered to the poor on affordable terms. "Low" is the positive-degree adjective for interest rates, and "very low rates of interest" is the standard, natural collocation used in everyday and banking English to describe rates that make loans affordable.

CROSS-CHECK — why each other option misses the mark

  • "very less" pairs the intensifier "very" with "less", which is already a comparative form — this combination is not standard English.

  • "mainly lesser" pairs "lesser" (a comparative adjective normally placed before a noun, as in "the lesser evil") with "mainly" ("for the most part"); the resulting phrase is not idiomatic and does not fit describing a rate.

  • "mostly less" pairs "mostly" ("in most cases") with the comparative "less"; this combination does not form a standard adjective phrase either.

Only "very low" correctly pairs the intensifier with the positive-degree adjective, producing the standard phrase "very low rates of interest."

title: Select the word you consider most appropriate for the blank
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the word you consider most appropriate for the blank space and indicate your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly:
Many people today have fallen into utter confusion of values with the result that they cannot ______ the good from the bad.
solution:
Concept

A fill-in-the-blank of this type is solved by collocation and meaning, not by a single word's dictionary gloss. Test two things: (1) which verb forms an idiomatic pattern with the preposition that follows the blank, and (2) which verb's meaning fits the idea the sentence is building. Here the blank is followed by "the good FROM the bad", and the surrounding idea is "confusion of values" — an inability to tell right from wrong.

Application

  • The frame is "cannot ______ the good FROM the bad". The verb must legally take the pattern "___ X from Y" and mean to perceive a difference between X and Y.

  • "differentiate" fits both tests: "differentiate X from Y" is a standard collocation meaning to recognise or show the difference between them — exactly the discernment the "confusion of values" calls for.

So the sentence reads: "...they cannot differentiate the good from the bad" — they can no longer tell right values from wrong ones.

Contrast

  • "divide" — to split into parts; works for physical separation, not for telling categories apart in the mind.

  • "see" — does not take "see X from Y" in a distinguishing sense; not idiomatic here.

  • "alter" — to change/modify; about altering something, not about discerning right from wrong.

title: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate word. Eggs

solution:
Explanation: The phrase 'sold by the dozen' is a common fixed expression in English. Here, 'by' indicates the unit or grouping used for sale — meaning 'per dozen' (often referring to the price or the way items are packaged).

  • Why 'by' is correct: 'by' expresses measure or rate (e.g., sold by the dozen, sold by the pound).

  • Why the other choices are wrong: 'to' indicates direction or purpose; 'at' indicates location or time; neither expresses a unit of sale.

  • Note on 'in': You can say 'sold in dozens' to mean sold in groups of twelve, but the more natural collocation for pricing or units is 'sold by the dozen.'

Examples:

  • Eggs are sold by the dozen.

  • Some stores sell eggs in dozens (less common when referring to pricing).

title: In the following question, the sentence given with blank to
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In the following question, the sentence given with blank to be filled in with an appropriate word. Select the correct alternative out of the four and indicate it by selecting the appropriate option.

It __________ to me that her husband was incurable.
solution:
Answer: occurred

Key idea: The phrase "It occurred to me that..." is idiomatic English meaning "the thought came into my mind." This makes "occurred" the appropriate choice for the blank.

  • happened — means "took place" (an event). It does not mean "came into my mind," so it is not suitable here.

  • occurred — means "came into the mind" in the idiom "It occurred to me that..." and correctly expresses that a thought arose.

  • suggested — normally implies that something or someone led you to think something (an external source or implication), so it is not the natural choice for a spontaneous thought in this sentence.

  • flashed — appears in the phrase "it flashed across my mind," meaning a sudden image or idea, but "It flashed to me that..." is not the usual collocation here.

Therefore, "occurred" is the most appropriate word to complete the sentence: "It occurred to me that her husband was incurable."

title: DSSSB TGT Special Education Teacher 24 Jun 2025 Shift 3 Q83
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The glass pane of my window ____ this morning.
solution:
Concept: In vocabulary-in-context fill-in-the-blank questions, when every option is grammatically valid (here, all four options are simple past-tense verb forms), the blank is decided by meaning alone — the verb chosen must describe an action or event that is realistically possible for the subject of the sentence.

Application: The subject of the blank is 'the glass pane of my window'. A glass pane is a rigid, fragile object, and the everyday event that can happen to it 'this morning' is that it broke — separated into pieces or cracked. Among 'lived', 'rang', 'broke', and 'grew', only 'broke' describes something that can happen to a glass pane, so the sentence reads: 'The glass pane of my window broke this morning.'

Cross-check: Substituting each remaining option confirms this — a glass pane cannot 'live' (living applies to organisms), cannot 'ring' (ringing describes a sound-producing object like a bell or phone), and cannot 'grow' (growing applies to living things or increasing quantities); only 'broke' produces a sentence that makes sense.

  • lived: an inanimate glass pane does not exist as a living being over time, so this verb does not fit the sentence's subject.

  • rang: a breaking glass pane produces a shattering sound, not the resonant ringing sound this verb describes, so it does not fit.

  • grew: a fixed glass pane does not increase in size or maturity, so this verb does not fit.

title: Choose the most appropriate answer and fill in the blank.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the most appropriate answer and fill in the blank.

Hardly _______ drunk the magic liquid when she began to see everything in strange and vivid colours.
solution:
Correct answer: had she

Why this is correct:

When a sentence begins with negative or limiting adverbials such as 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely', subject and auxiliary verb invert: auxiliary + subject + main verb. Because the action of drinking was completed before the later past action ('began'), use the past perfect: had + past participle.

Example: Hardly had I seen the thief when he started running.

Applied here, the correct sentence is: Hardly had she drunk the magic liquid when she began to see everything in strange and vivid colours.

  • she had — Incorrect because it keeps the subject before the auxiliary; inversion is required after 'Hardly'.

  • has she — Incorrect because present perfect ('has') does not match the sequence of past events; past perfect ('had') is needed here.

  • she had had — Incorrect because it retains wrong word order and uses 'had had', which is not the appropriate form for the verb 'drink' in this context.

title: Fill in the blank with suitable words from the options.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Fill in the blank with suitable words from the options.

In the Middle Ages, the ____ of the great cathedrals did not enter into the architects’ plans; almost invariably a cathedral was positioned haphazardly in ____ surroundings.
solution:
Concept: A semicolon joins two independent, closely related clauses; unlike a comma or conjunction, it does not itself signal WHETHER the relationship is elaboration, consequence, or contrast — that relationship must be inferred from the clauses' own wording and any signal words present. So the first task is to read both clauses and identify, from their content, what logical relationship the writer intends, and then fill both blanks with words that stay consistent with that relationship.

Application: Here the signal words "did not enter into the architects' plans" and "haphazardly" show the second clause is explaining the CONSEQUENCE of the first clause's lack of planning, not contrasting it: because the architects never planned the placement, and because that placement was haphazard, the cathedral often ended up standing somewhere that clashed with, rather than complemented, its setting. So the first blank needs a word meaning "position/placement", and the second needs a word meaning "out of harmony with the surroundings" — exactly the sense carried by "situation" (a word that can denote a building's location) paired with "incongruous" (mismatched, out of keeping with its surroundings).

Cross-check — why the other pairings break the semicolon's logic:

  • "location - apt": "apt" means fitting or well-suited, which assumes a careful, deliberate placement — the opposite of what "haphazardly" tells us happened.

  • "ambience - salubrious": "salubrious" describes something as healthy or wholesome, a quality the sentence never raises; an unplanned setting says nothing about whether it was healthful.

  • "durability - convenient": "durability" concerns how long something lasts, not where it is built, so it cannot answer a blank about placement; "convenient" again wrongly implies a suitable, considered site.

Only the pairing that keeps the placement unplanned and the resulting surroundings mismatched satisfies the logic the semicolon sets up.

title: Choose the correct word to fill in the blank: His

solution:
Answer: so

Rule used: Use so + adjective/adverb + that + result when the first part shows degree and the second part shows the result.

  • Here, persuasive is the adjective.

  • The clause that it changed everyone's perspective gives the result.

  • So the correct construction is: His argument was so persuasive that it changed everyone's perspective.

Why the other words do not fit:

  • too usually pairs with to + verb, not with this “that” clause.

  • very only intensifies the adjective; it does not link to the result clause.

  • much is not used naturally before the adjective “persuasive” in this sentence.

Therefore, the correct word is so.

title: Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the blank.

She isn't your sister, _______?
solution:
A question tag mirrors the main clause and flips its polarity: a negative statement takes a positive tag, and a positive statement takes a negative tag. The tag also repeats the auxiliary or be-verb of the statement together with its subject pronoun.

Here the statement 'She isn't your sister' is negative and uses the present be-verb 'is' (contracted in 'isn't'), with the subject 'she'. So the tag must be positive, use 'is', and keep the pronoun 'she' — giving 'is she?'.

Complete sentence: 'She isn't your sister, is she?' The other auxiliaries ('did', 'will', 'can') do not appear in the statement and so cannot form the tag.

title: Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the blank.

You are not coming to the party, ___________?
solution:
A question tag must be formed using the same auxiliary verb as the main clause, and its polarity must be the opposite of that clause.

Here the statement is "You are not coming to the party" — it is negative and uses the auxiliary verb "are" (the be-verb in the present continuous "are coming"). Since the statement is negative, the tag must be positive, and it must reuse the same auxiliary "are" with the pronoun "you".

This gives the positive tag "are you?". The other options use the wrong auxiliaries — "will you" (future/request), "do you" (simple present) and "did you" (simple past) — none of which match the auxiliary "are" in the statement, so the completed sentence is: "You are not coming to the party, are you?"

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q28
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: Choose the most appropriate qualifying word from the options given below to complete each sentence correctly.

The child was ____ excited to visit the science museum.
solution:
A qualifying word (a degree adverb or intensifier) modifies an adjective to show the extent of a quality. English degree adverbs differ along two axes: POSITION — pre-modifiers such as very, totally, and deeply are placed BEFORE the adjective they intensify, while enough is a post-positive modifier that must follow the adjective or adverb it qualifies (for example, "old enough", "good enough"); and REGISTER/COLLOCATION — standard collocation dictionaries record that a given pre-modifier is conventionally paired with adjectives of a particular semantic type in formal written English, even though looser combinations may occur in casual speech.

The instruction explicitly asks for the MOST APPROPRIATE qualifying word, not merely a word that is grammatically possible in isolation. This licenses ruling out an option that is only acceptable in a casual/spoken register, or one whose usual collocation range does not cover the given adjective, even if that option is not strictly ungrammatical everywhere. In "The child was ____ excited to visit the science museum," the blank sits directly before the adjective "excited", so any post-positive word is ruled out by position alone; among the remaining pre-modifiers, the most appropriate one is the one whose dictionary-recorded collocation range covers an ordinary positive, gradable emotional adjective like "excited" in standard written English, without needing an informal register or a mismatched semantic class.

  • Enough is ruled out purely by word order: as a post-positive modifier it must follow the adjective it qualifies ("excited enough"), so it cannot fill a slot immediately before an adjective.

  • Totally conventionally intensifies adjectives with an absolute or all-or-nothing sense ("totally destroyed", "totally different"); standard dictionaries label its use with an ordinary gradable adjective as an informal, colloquial sense, so it is not the most appropriate choice for a standard written-English completion exercise even though it can appear in casual speech.

  • Deeply's standard collocation range in dictionaries covers serious, introspective, or negative emotional adjectives ("deeply concerned", "deeply moved", "deeply disturbed"); it is not the conventional intensifier for an upbeat, everyday adjective like excited, so it is not the most appropriate choice here even where an isolated instance might occur.

Very is the register-neutral, general-purpose intensifier whose dictionary-recorded collocation range covers ordinary gradable adjectives across both formal and informal English without any semantic-class restriction, making it the most appropriate qualifying word: "The child was very excited to visit the science museum" is the standard, correctly qualified sentence.

title: Fill in the blank in the given sentence by choosing
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Fill in the blank in the given sentence by choosing the correct option.

A thief is a thief, _______ he steals a diamond or a cucumber.
solution:
Answer: whether

Explanation:

The sentence means that a person remains a thief regardless of which item they steal. "Whether" is used to introduce alternatives (diamond or cucumber) and correctly expresses that idea.

Why the other choices are wrong:

  • "Since" indicates a reason (because), not a choice between alternatives, so it does not fit the sentence.

  • "So" indicates a result or consequence and cannot introduce alternatives, so it is inappropriate here.

  • "Because" gives a reason and changes the meaning; it does not present alternative possibilities.

Complete sentence: A thief is a thief, whether he steals a diamond or a cucumber.

title: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
Travellers to space go beyond the orbit of the earth and ______ the orbit of the moon. On the other ______, the suborbital tourist will travel in a rocket ______ the International Space Station only. Space travel is not possible for everyone, ______ suborbital tourism is a possible alternative.
solution:
Answer: reach, hand, up to, but (Note: 'up to' is normally written as two words.)

Explanation:

  • First blank: 'reach' is present tense and matches 'Travellers to space go', which is a general statement. 'Reached' is past tense and does not fit the present-tense context.

  • Second blank: 'hand' completes the idiom 'on the other hand'. The idiom uses the singular 'hand', not 'hands'.

  • Third blank: 'up to' indicates extent or maximum height reached (as in 'up to the International Space Station'). 'Onto' would imply landing on the station and 'into' would imply entering it, both of which change the intended meaning.

  • Fourth blank: 'but' provides the contrast between 'Space travel is not possible for everyone' and 'suborbital tourism is a possible alternative.' 'Because' or 'since' would state a reason, and 'and' would merely add information without contrast.

Complete corrected sentence: Travellers to space go beyond the orbit of the earth and reach the orbit of the moon. On the other hand, the suborbital tourist will travel in a rocket up to the International Space Station only. Space travel is not possible for everyone, but suborbital tourism is a possible alternative.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q68
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Raj is an ______ student.
solution:
Concept

When a blank falls between an article ('a'/'an') and a noun, the word that fills it must be an adjective, because the article + adjective + noun sequence is the standard pattern in English for describing a noun. The chosen word must also carry the part of speech required by that sentence position, not merely resemble a fitting word.

Application

In 'Raj is an ______ student,' the word 'student' is a noun preceded by the article 'an', so the blank needs an adjective that can meaningfully describe a student. Among the options, 'intelligent' is an adjective, and it correctly occupies the article + ___ + noun position while also supplying a sensible descriptive quality for a student.

Contrast

  • 'intelligible' — an adjective, but it means able to be understood or comprehended (used for speech, writing, or an explanation), not a quality describing a person's mental ability.

  • 'intelligence' — a noun. English does allow a noun to modify another noun attributively in some fixed collocations (e.g. 'an engineering student'), but 'intelligence' is not conventionally used to modify 'student' this way; it names an abstract quality rather than functioning as a descriptive modifier, so it cannot fill the adjective slot the sentence needs.

  • 'intelligently' — an adverb, so it modifies verbs, not nouns, and therefore cannot occupy the adjective slot before 'student'.

Reading the completed sentence back — 'Raj is an intelligent student' — confirms it is grammatically well-formed (article + adjective + noun) and semantically coherent, while each of the other options fails on either grammar or meaning.

title: There is probability that he was charged with being that

Explanation: The first blank needs an adjective meaning 'insane' because the clause describes being regarded as acting like a madman, so 'deranged' fits perfectly.

The second blank follows the phrase 'boasted themselves of', which requires a noun. The words paired in the sentence are qualities (soberness and wisdom), so the noun 'prudence' (meaning careful judgment or wisdom) is the correct fit.

Why the other word pairs fail:

  • rococo, demented — 'rococo' is irrelevant in meaning; 'demented' is an adjective but the second blank requires a noun after 'boasted themselves of'.

  • prudish, covert — 'prudish' does not mean 'mad', and 'covert' is an adjective rather than the required noun describing a wise quality.

title: The meeting was to discuss the new project proposal.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: At the scheduled time, all committee members assembled, and the meeting was ______ to discuss the new project proposal.
solution:
CONCEPT: In sentence completion, select the word whose established meaning and grammatical use match the context. A passive form such as “was + past participle + to + verb” can express that an event was organized for a stated purpose.

APPLICATION: The context says the members assembled at the scheduled time, so the meeting took place as planned. “Convene” means to call people together for a formal meeting; therefore “was convened to discuss” expresses the intended purpose.

  • convened: means formally called together for a meeting or session.

  • postponed: means moved to a later scheduled time.

  • cancelled: means called off so that it does not take place.

title: Fill in the blanks, choosing appropriate word from the options
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Fill in the blanks, choosing appropriate word from the options given below :

Hindus believe that ______ from the cycle of birth and re-birth can be attained only by good deeds.
solution:
To fill in the blank appropriately, we need to understand the concept of liberation in Hindu philosophy.

Analysis of the Terminology
Samsara: This is the ongoing cycle of birth, death, and rebirth in Hindu belief.

Moksha: This represents the ultimate spiritual goal, which is liberation or release from the cycle of Samsara.

Deliverance: In this context, "deliverance" serves as the English equivalent for liberation or release from this cycle.

title: Select the appropriate phrase that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. In
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the appropriate phrase that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.
In view of the situation in his country, he had to ________ his departure for an indefinite time.
solution:
CONCEPT

A phrasal verb is a verb combined with a particle (here, put with through / in / out / off), and the particle changes the whole meaning. To complete a sentence correctly, the phrasal verb's meaning must match the situation described by the rest of the sentence.

APPLICATION

The sentence says he had to do something to his departure "for an indefinite time" because of the situation in his country. "An indefinite time" signals that the planned event is being moved to a later, unspecified date. The phrasal verb meaning "to postpone / defer to a later time" is put off. So the sentence reads: "he had to postpone his departure for an indefinite time."

CONTRAST

  • put through = connect a phone call / make someone undergo something — no sense of delay.

  • put in = install / submit / devote time — does not mean to defer an event.

  • put out = extinguish / publish / inconvenience — does not mean to defer an event.

  • put off = postpone / defer to a later time — the meaning the sentence requires.

Therefore the correct phrase is put off.

title: Complete the sentence with the appropriate word. Pedestrians should be
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Complete the sentence with the appropriate word.

Pedestrians should be __________ when walking on the roads on rainy days, as the roads get slippery.
solution:
In a sentence-completion (fill-in-the-blank) question testing vocabulary in context, the blank must be filled with the word whose meaning logically matches the situation set up by the rest of the sentence — in particular, a reason clause (introduced by 'as' or 'because') that explains WHY a certain quality or behaviour is required.

Here, the reason clause 'as the roads get slippery' explains why a particular quality is expected of pedestrians walking in the rain: slippery roads increase the risk of falling or being involved in an accident, so pedestrians need to be careful and alert to that danger. The word 'cautious' means exactly this — careful, watchful, and mindful of possible danger — so it is the word that logically completes the sentence.

  • 'dangerous' describes a risky or hazardous quality that a thing or situation (such as the roads themselves) can have; it does not describe how a person behaves, so it cannot logically complete 'Pedestrians should be __________' as a description of safe conduct.

  • 'clever' means mentally sharp or quick-witted, a quality about intelligence that has no bearing on the physical care needed to avoid slipping on wet roads.

  • 'smart' likewise refers to intelligence or sharpness of mind, not to watchfulness or care in the face of a physical hazard, so it does not fit the safety context set up by the reason clause.

Reading the completed sentence back — 'Pedestrians should be cautious when walking on the roads on rainy days, as the roads get slippery' — the reason clause and the chosen word line up logically: slippery roads are the hazard, and being cautious is the appropriate protective response, confirming the fit.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q65
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The ______ conduct of the minister helped in the de-escalation of a very tense situation at the border.
solution:
Sentence-completion (vocabulary-in-context) items test whether a word's dictionary meaning and connotation fit the tone and outcome described in the sentence -- a near-synonym can still be wrong if its connotation clashes with the sentence's stated result.

The sentence says the minister's conduct "helped in the de-escalation of a very tense situation" -- a positive, conflict-reducing outcome. Only a word describing a tactful, conciliatory manner produces that outcome, so "diplomatic conduct" fits: diplomatic behaviour is careful, tactful, and aimed at avoiding offence or conflict, which is exactly what de-escalates tension.

  • "Abrasive" conduct is harsh and grating -- such behaviour would inflame tension rather than ease it.

  • "Belligerent" conduct is hostile and combative -- the opposite of behaviour that reduces conflict.

  • "Tactless" conduct is insensitive to others' feelings and risks causing offence, not calming a tense situation.

title: Reality is often stranger than
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Reality is often stranger than _______.
solution: Fiction is the most appropriate word in this situation.

title: It was intrinsic to their grand passion that there should
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: It was intrinsic to their grand passion that there should be _____, both were adept at slamming doors and _____ off into the night.
solution:
Correct words: rows, storming

Explanation: The sentence needs a noun meaning "quarrels" in the first blank and a verb form meaning "leave angrily" in the second blank.

  • rows: A British informal term meaning quarrels or fights; fits the first blank because the sentence describes passionate people prone to arguments.

  • storming: From the phrasal verb "storm off," meaning to leave in anger. The participle "storming" parallels "slamming" in the sentence and naturally completes the phrase "slamming doors and storming off into the night."

  • Why the other word choices fail: Words like "marches," "offers," or "records" do not mean quarrels, and alternatives like "muttering," "overrunning," or "snapping" do not convey the same clearly angry, dramatic departure that "storming off" does.

Grammar note: "rows" as a plural noun fits after "there should be," and "storming" (a present participle) parallels "slamming," making the sentence balanced and idiomatic.

title: Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.

I was quite __________ after I heard that we were going to Singapore for a week's holiday.
solution:
Key idea: “Keyed up” means excited, eager, or nervous in anticipation.

  • A planned holiday to Singapore is a reason to feel excited.

  • “Kicked off”, “knocked off”, and “held off” do not fit this emotional context.

Answer: Option 2, “keyed up”, is correct.

title: Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blanks. the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blanks.

__________ the eve __________ the Prime Minister's visit, there was tight security __________ the airport and en route __________ the venue.
solution:
Concept: English relies on a large set of fixed prepositional phrases (collocations) — such as "on the eve of" an event, "at" a transit hub, or "en route to" a destination — where the preposition is fixed by convention with the surrounding words rather than derived from one universal rule. These phrases must be recognised as whole units; substituting a different preposition, even one that sounds plausible in isolation, breaks the fixed expression.

Applying it: Filling each blank means matching it to the fixed phrase it belongs to:

  1. "____ the eve ____ the Prime Minister's visit" refers to the period immediately preceding a major event — this fixed phrase takes the preposition used for occasions and events, not the one used for an exact clock-time or a deadline.

  2. The second blank in that same phrase stays constant across every option ("of"), linking "eve" to the event it precedes.

  3. "tight security ____ the airport" places security presence at a transit hub — this takes the preposition used for being present at a specific point or hub, not the one used for enclosure within a larger space.

  4. "en route ____ the venue" — "en route" is a fixed phrase that is always followed by the preposition marking a stated destination.

Combining the four words needed for these fixed phrases gives exactly the sequence in the keyed option: "On; of; at; to."

Comparing the choices:

  • "At; of; in; along" — opens with the point-in-time preposition (as in "at noon"), which does not attach to "eve" in this fixed phrase, and closes with "along," which describes moving alongside something rather than arriving at a stated destination.

  • "By; of; at; in" — opens with the deadline-marking preposition (as in "submit by Friday"), a sense that does not fit a period immediately preceding an event, and ends with the enclosure preposition for "the venue" rather than the one "en route" requires.

  • "In; of; in; to" — opens with the enclosure/broader-time preposition (as in "in the morning"), which likewise does not attach to "eve" here, and repeats that same enclosure preposition for "the airport," where the transit-hub phrase requires a different one.

Only the sequence that keeps every blank inside its own fixed phrase reads naturally end to end, matching the keyed option "On; of; at; to."

title: Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.

My former colleague is __________ now because he has no job and he has to support his family.
solution:
CONCEPT

An idiom-based sentence-completion question tests whether a fixed phrase carries the specific meaning the context needs. An idiom's meaning is conventional rather than a literal sum of its words, so the right choice is decided by matching the situation the sentence describes, not any single keyword in isolation.

APPLICATION

The sentence describes someone who has no job and must support his family — a description of a difficult, troubling circumstance for him. The idiomatic phrase that conventionally means being in a difficult or awkward situation is in a spot, which is exactly the sense this blank needs.

CONTRAST

  • in charge conventionally means holding responsibility or authority over something or someone; it describes control, not hardship, so it does not match a person who has lost his job.

  • in check conventionally means kept under control or restrained — typically used for an emotion, a cost, or a process; it does not describe someone's employment or family situation.

  • in favour conventionally means in agreement with or supportive of something; it expresses approval, which is unrelated to job loss or the burden of supporting a family.

Therefore the correct phrase is in a spot.

title: Complete the sentence with the appropriate word. Students should pay
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Complete the sentence with the appropriate word.

Students should pay __________ to the explanations given by the teachers in the classroom.
solution:
Concept: English fixes many verbs to one particular noun by convention rather than by pure meaning — these are called collocations. The verb "pay" is fixed with the noun "attention" ("pay attention to"), meaning to direct one's mind, eyes or ears carefully toward something; a different noun that means something similar cannot simply replace "attention" in this verb slot, because the pairing is fixed by usage, not logic.

Applying it: The sentence needs a noun that completes the fixed phrase "pay __________ to" in the sense of listening carefully to the teachers' explanations. "Attention" is exactly the noun this verb is fixed with, giving the standard idiom "pay attention to": "Students should pay attention to the explanations given by the teachers in the classroom."

Comparing the choices:

  • "concentration" belongs with a different verb pattern — one "concentrates on" something or works "with concentration" — not "pays concentration to" it.

  • "notice" is fixed with the reverse verb: one "takes notice of" something, never "pays notice to" it.

  • "focus" is fixed with the preposition "on" ("focus on", "keep focus on"), not with the verb "pay".

Only the option that completes the fixed "pay ... to" phrase fits the sentence, matching how leading dictionaries (Collins, Oxford Learner's, Merriam-Webster) define this collocation.

title: Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.

She likes to wear clothes that would make her __________ in a group.
solution:
CONCEPT

An idiom-based sentence-completion question tests whether a fixed phrasal verb carries the specific meaning the sentence's context needs. Many phrasal verbs share the same base verb but attach a different particle, and each particle change produces an unrelated, conventional meaning — so the correct choice is decided by matching the situation described in the sentence, not by the shared base verb.

APPLICATION

The sentence describes a person who deliberately wears clothes so that she is noticed as different from everyone else "in a group" — that is, she wants to be distinct or noticeable rather than blend in. The phrasal verb that conveys "to be noticeably different or prominent" is the one that fits this sense exactly.

CROSS-CHECK — why each other phrase misses the mark

  • "stand for" means to represent or symbolize something — unrelated to being noticeable in a group.

  • "stand to" is not a general-purpose phrasal verb on its own; it appears only in fixed patterns such as being in a position to gain or lose something, or the military sense of being on alert — none of which describes a distinguishing effect of clothing.

  • "stand by" means to support someone loyally, or to remain ready/waiting — again unrelated to appearing distinct from others.

Only the phrase meaning "to be noticeably different or prominent" satisfies the sentence, confirming the answer independently of the other three.

title: After much confrontation they gave
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

After much confrontation they gave ______.
solution:
CONCEPT

Phrasal verbs formed with "give" change meaning completely depending on the particle that follows: give in, give out, give away, and give off are four distinct idioms with different senses — surrendering, distributing or running out, donating or revealing, and emitting, respectively.

APPLICATION

The sentence describes "much confrontation" — sustained conflict or resistance. The natural outcome of prolonged resistance is eventually to stop resisting, so "gave in" — meaning yielded or surrendered under pressure after opposition — is exactly the sense the sentence needs.

CROSS-CHECK — why each other option is not correct

  • "give out" means to distribute something (give out prizes) or, for a supply or device, to become exhausted or stop working — it does not describe yielding in a dispute.

  • "give away" means to donate something free of charge or unintentionally reveal a secret — neither sense fits a confrontation being resolved by surrender.

  • "give off" means to emit or produce something such as heat, light, or a smell — it describes emission, not conceding a conflict.

Only "gave in" carries the sense of yielding after resistance, so it correctly completes the sentence.

title: Directions: Complete the sentences in the following question with most
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Directions: Complete the sentences in the following question with most appropriate choice.

Of the sword and pen, the ____ is more powerful.
solution: The phrase 'Of the sword and pen' refers to two items, so we need a word that means 'the second of the two'. The correct word is 'latter', which is used specifically to refer to the second of two items mentioned. 'Last' refers to the final item in a sequence, not the second of two. 'Later' refers to time, not order in a pair. 'Last one' is informal and not appropriate in formal comparisons. Therefore, 'latter' is the most appropriate choice.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q61
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The scientist's ______ to detail ensured the accuracy of the experiment.
solution:
English has several near-synonym nouns for mental engagement with a task — attention, concentration, focus, and observation — but each one pairs with a specific fixed preposition, forming a set collocation rather than a free combination.

Here the blank is immediately followed by "to detail", which signals a fixed-phrase test: the established English collocation is "attention to detail", a set phrase used to describe a careful, meticulous working style. "Attention" is therefore the word that correctly completes the sentence.

Why the others do not fit the same slot:

  • "Concentration" collocates with the preposition "on" (e.g., "concentration on a task"), not "to".

  • "Focus" collocates with the preposition "on" (e.g., "focus on a task"), not "to".

  • "Observation" collocates with the prepositions "of" or "about" (e.g., "observation of a phenomenon"), not "to".

title: Bernard prefers the toast with knife.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Bernard prefers ______ the toast with a knife.
solution:
Answer: Buttering

Explanation:

  • A gerund is a verb form that acts as a noun. "Buttering" names the action and serves as the object of the verb "prefers."

  • Using the gerund fits the sentence: "Bernard prefers buttering the toast with a knife."

  • Why the other choices are wrong:

    • "to buttered" is ungrammatical; the infinitive would be "to butter" (base verb), not "to buttered."

    • "of butter" is a prepositional phrase and does not provide the verb or verbal noun required after "prefers."

    • "buttered" is a past participle/adjective and cannot function as the verbal noun needed here. A different structure would be required to use "buttered" correctly (for example, "Bernard prefers his toast buttered").

  • Note: "prefer" can take either a gerund or an infinitive with similar meaning, so "Bernard prefers to butter the toast with a knife" is also grammatically acceptable. The given correct choice uses the gerund form.

title: Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the blank.

You have not been here before, _______?
solution:
A question tag mirrors the auxiliary verb of the main clause and reverses its polarity: a negative statement takes a positive tag, and a positive statement takes a negative tag.

Here the main clause is "You have not been here before" — present perfect ("have ... been") and negative ("not"). The tag must therefore reuse the auxiliary "have" in the positive form and keep the subject pronoun "you."

The complete sentence is: "You have not been here before, have you?" Tags such as "will you," "would you," or "had you" do not match the present-perfect auxiliary of the statement.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. The last
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

The last rays of the sun ________ fading away when I reached home.
solution:
Concept

Two grammar rules govern this blank. First, subject-verb agreement: the verb must match the number of its true subject (a plural subject takes a plural verb). Second, tense: an action that was already in progress at a particular past moment takes the past continuous form, "was/were + -ing".

Application

  1. Find the subject: the verb belongs to "The last rays" (the head noun is the plural "rays"), not to the singular "the sun" inside the of-phrase. So the subject is plural.

  2. Fix the tense: the clause "when I reached home" is simple past, and the rays were already in the process of fading at that moment, so the blank needs the past continuous.

  3. Combine plural + past continuous: the required auxiliary is "were", giving "The last rays of the sun were fading away when I reached home."

Cross-check the alternatives

  • "Are" is present tense, which clashes with the past-time marker "when I reached home".

  • "Will be" is future tense, but the event is set in the past, not the future.

  • "Was" is singular and cannot agree with the plural subject "rays".

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. You are
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.
You are annoyed with me, _________?
solution:
Concept

A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement to invite confirmation. In the standard confirmation tag, polarity reverses: an affirmative statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. The tag reuses the SAME auxiliary (helping) verb that appears in the main clause, followed by the matching subject pronoun. (A same-polarity echo tag exists only in marked, emphatic speech and is not the neutral completion expected here.)

Application

Read the statement and identify its parts:

  1. Main clause: "You are annoyed with me" — this is affirmative (no negation).

  2. Auxiliary verb: "are" (the present form of be used with the subject "you").

  3. Subject pronoun: "you".

  4. Because the statement is affirmative, the tag must be negative: take the same auxiliary "are", make it negative ("are not" -> contracted "aren't"), then add the pronoun: "aren't you?"

This yields: "You are annoyed with me, aren't you?"

Cross-check

Two quick checks confirm the form. First, polarity: the statement is positive, so the tag is negative — satisfied by "aren't." Second, auxiliary agreement: the main clause uses "are," so the tag must also use "are," not "do" or "don't" (which belong to ordinary action verbs, not to the verb "be"). Both checks point to "aren't you?"

title: Choose the word or phrase which best completes the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the word or phrase which best completes the sentence.

Hold the rifle firmly against your shoulder, ………………………………..

options.label: A
options.html: and then you should take careful aim

options.label: B
options.html: and then you have to take careful aim

options.label: C
options.html: and then you will have to take careful aim

solution:
Answer: and then take careful aim

Explanation:

  • Both clauses are commands (imperative mood). The first clause instructs the reader to 'Hold the rifle firmly against your shoulder,' so the second clause should also be an instruction using the base verb form.

  • 'and then take careful aim' is concise and parallel to the first command; it correctly continues the sequence of direct instructions.

  • Why the other choices are not appropriate:

  • 'and then you should take careful aim' changes the tone to advice rather than a direct command and breaks the parallel imperative structure.

  • 'and then you have to take careful aim' adds an explicit subject and expresses obligation, changing tone and structure compared with the direct instruction.

  • 'and then you will have to take careful aim' places the action in the future and implies a future necessity, which alters the meaning and does not fit the immediate sequence of commands.

title: DIRECTIONS: Fill in the blank with the right options provided.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
DIRECTIONS: Fill in the blank with the right options provided.

Both of them ___________since their childhood.
solution:
Correct sentence: Both of them have been working here since their childhood.

Why this is correct:

  • The word "since" refers to a specific point in time in the past (their childhood).

  • To show an action that started at that past point and continues to the present, use a present perfect form. The present perfect continuous (have been + verb-ing) emphasizes ongoing activity and duration.

  • The plural subject "Both of them" requires "have" (not "has").

Why the other choices are wrong:

  • "are working here": This is present continuous (action happening now) and does not express continuation from a past starting point.

  • "work here": Simple present states a habitual/general fact and cannot alone show that the activity began in the past and continues to now with "since".

  • "are liking to work": Unnatural/incorrect because "like" is normally stative and not used in continuous forms; also the tense does not show continuation from a past point.

Summary: Use the present perfect continuous "have been working" to show an action that started in the past (their childhood) and continues up to now.

title: The new jobs that result of governmental incentives to large
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The new jobs that ______ a result of governmental incentives to large co-operations.
solution:
Correct sentence: The new jobs that are being created come as a result of governmental incentives to large co-operations.

Why this is correct:

  • The clause "that are being created" is a present progressive passive relative clause modifying "jobs," indicating the jobs are currently in the process of being created.

  • The phrase "come as a result of" is the correct idiom meaning "are caused by." "Come" must be followed by "as" in this expression.

  • Placing the relative clause before the main verb keeps the sentence clear: modified noun (jobs) + relative clause + main clause (come as a result of...).

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • "are being created come" is missing the word "as" after "come," so the idiom is broken and the sequence is ungrammatical.

  • "were created to come" uses past tense and an infinitive that do not convey the intended ongoing causation; the idiom "come as a result of" is required instead of "to come."

  • "are created to come as" misorders the verb and the idiom, producing a phrase that does not fit standard English usage here.

Note: The word "co-operations" in the original sentence is likely a typo; the standard word in this context is "corporations."

title: The Super twenty just__1___ their first baseball game of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
The Super twenty just__1___ their first baseball game of the new season; I believe there is much to be 2_ about. Although they lost, it was against an excellent team that had won the championship last year. The Super twenty fell behind early but___3___ excellent teamwork and____4__ back to tie the game. The team had 15 hits and scored 8 runs, which was excellent! Unfortunately, they made 5 fielding errors, which kept the other team in the lead the entire game The game ended with the umpire ___5__ a bad call, and if the call had gone the other way, The Super twenty might have actually won the game. It wasn't a victory, but I say The Super twenty look like they have a shot at the championship, especially if they___6__ to improve.

Fill in the blank 4 with most suitable word
solution:
"came" is the most suitable word for this blank

Answer: came

Completed sentence: The Super twenty fell behind early but showed excellent teamwork and came back to tie the game.

  • Why 'came' is correct: The passage is in the past tense, and 'came back' is the correct past-simple phrasal verb to describe the team’s comeback.

  • Why 'come' is wrong: The base form does not match the past-tense narration and would require an auxiliary to be correct.

  • Why 'will come' is wrong: Future tense conflicts with the description of past events.

  • Why 'had come' is wrong: Past perfect implies the comeback occurred before another past event; here the simple sequence calls for past simple, so 'had come' is unnecessary and changes the meaning.

title: Read the following passage carefully and answer the following questions:Radium
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the following questions:
Radium is a white powder that has the appearance of table salt. A pound of it is worth a thousand pounds of gold. Radium is very expensive because it is very scarce. A pinch of it is worth a small fortune. There are only a few spoons in the world. But radium is so potent that excess amounts are dangerous. A pound or two gathered in one spot will kill anyone who approaches. With radium, scientists hope to learn how to change one element into another. Changing other metals into gold will be attractive and profitable. But it would be more valuable to learn how to get all the energy from atoms to do human work.

Can radium be dangerous if in excess amounts?

options.label: A
options.html: No, it is safe in any amount

options.label: B
options.html: It depends on how it is used

options.label: D
options.html: It is only dangerous to certain individuals

title: Desert is basically wilderness or wasteland. There is little moisture
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
Read the passage carefully and answer the given question:
A desert is basically a wilderness or a wasteland. There is little moisture and poor soil such as sand, gravel or rock. There are few plants to offer shade. Deserts can be described as harsh places. Many are burning hot by day and cold by night.

Every continent has deserts. Much of the western United States is a desert. A desert region called The Outback covers Central Australia. The southern tip of South America is largely desert. Northern Africa is covered by the Sahara, a desert as big as the mainland United States. The Arabian Peninsula, between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, is almost entirely desert. A large part of central Asia, from China to the Caspian Sea, is mostly desert. Deserts cover 1/8 of our planet.

The popular belief is that a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter. But this is not entirely correct. For those who have studied it, the desert can be a beautiful place. It is home to a variety of people, animals and plants that have learnt to live under hot and dry conditions. A desert is not always a flat, unchanging wasteland of dry sand. It may have mountains and hills. It may have an oasis, big or small. An oasis is like a green island in the middle of a desert where a spring or a well gives plants and trees a better chance to grow.

All living things need water in order to survive. The few plants and animals that live in deserts have developed the ability to require less water than most plants and animals. Desert plants have adapted to heat and dryness of the desert. Plants such as cacti have special means of storing and conserving water. They often have few or no leaves. Some plants have gotten used to arid environments by growing extremely long roots, allowing them to acquire moisture at or by the water table.

The desert animals also have found a way to solve the heat and water problems the desert environment creates. Camels can drink a lot of water at one time. They can live without water for days together. The reason is they sweat very little. We sweat because we must keep our body temperature constant. We sweat when it gets hot, and this cools the body. Camels can stand a high body temperature. They don't need to sweat and can therefore retain the water they drink for long periods of time.

Q. What is the popular belief about the climatic conditions of a desert?

options.label: A
options.html: It is a region surrounded by mountains and hills.

options.label: B
options.html: It is sandy where no rain falls and no vegetation grows.

options.label: C
options.html: A variety of animals and plants live there.

options.label: D
options.html: It has vast land which is used for cultivation of flowers.

solution:
The passage states:
“The popular belief is that a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter.”

This means people generally think deserts are sandy, dry places with almost no rain or vegetation.
Correct Answer:
(b) It is sandy where no rain falls and no vegetation grows.

A large part of central Asia, from China to the Caspian Sea, is mostly desert. Deserts cover 1/8 of our planet.

The popular belief is that a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter. But this is not entirely correct. For those who have studied it, the desert can be a beautiful place. It is home to a variety of people, animals and plants that have learnt to live under hot and dry conditions. A desert is not always a flat, unchanging wasteland of dry sand. It may have mountains and hills. It may have an oasis, big or small. An oasis is like a green island in the middle of a desert where a spring or a well gives plants and trees a better chance to grow.

All living things need water in order to survive. The few plants and animals that live in deserts have developed the ability to require less water than most plants and animals. Desert plants have adapted to heat and dryness of the desert. Plants such as cacti have special means of storing and conserving water. They often have few or no leaves. Some plants have gotten used to arid environments by growing extremely long roots, allowing them to acquire moisture at or by the water table.

The desert animals also have found a way to solve the heat and water problems the desert environment creates. Camels can drink a lot of water at one time. They can live without water for days together. The reason is they sweat very little. We sweat because we must keep our body temperature constant. We sweat when it gets hot, and this cools the body. Camels can stand a high body temperature. They don't need to sweat and can therefore retain the water they drink for long periods of time.

Q. The desert region called ‘The Outback’ is located in:
solution: The Outback is a desert region in Central Australia, making option (c) the only correct choice.

bodyHtml:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow. Critical appreciation is central to literary analysis, encouraging readers to explore the layers of meaning, symbolism and themes in a text. It involves a detailed examination of elements such as structure, language, characters and themes to understand the author's intentions and messages. Analysing a work's structure reveals how its narrative organisation enhances its impact. For instance, the fragmented structure of William Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury mirrors the disjointed consciousness of its characters, offering insights into human psychology and complexity. Language analysis focuses on how diction, syntax, imagery and figurative language convey ideas and evoke emotions. In Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, the stream-of-consciousness style immerses readers in characters' inner thoughts, providing an intimate perspective of their experiences. Character analysis is pivotal, as characters embody the themes and messages of a text. By examining their motivations and relationships, readers uncover the underlying conflicts and dilemmas driving the narrative. For example, Fyodor Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment wrestles with guilt and morality, prompting reflection on justice and redemption. Themes and motifs offer insights into the author's worldview and social commentary. Identifying recurring themes deepens understanding of the text's messages. George Orwell's 1984 critiques totalitarianism, warning against the loss of individual freedoms. In conclusion, critical appreciation demands a discerning approach, enabling readers to analyse and interpret a text's complexities. By exploring its structure, language, characters and themes, readers can appreciate the artistry and depth of the author's work.

Which of the following statements represents a fact given in the passage?

options.label: A
options.html: Historical context has little relevance in the analysis of literary works.

options.label: B
options.html: The central theme of the passage is the impact of technology on modern literature.

options.label: C
options.html: The process of critical appreciation involves examining the structure, language, characters and themes of literary works.

options.label: D
options.html: Literary criticism is primarily concerned with personal opinions rather than objective analysis.

solution:
The question asks which statement is a fact actually stated in the passage. Test each option against the text.

Option about historical context: the passage never mentions historical context, so nothing supports it.

Option about technology and modern literature: the passage is about critical appreciation through structure, language, characters and themes; technology is never discussed.

Option about critical appreciation examining structure, language, characters and themes: the passage states directly that critical appreciation 'involves a detailed examination of elements such as structure, language, characters and themes to understand the author's intentions.' This is a near-verbatim restatement of the text, so it is the fact given in the passage.

Option about personal opinions over objective analysis: the passage describes a careful, discerning, detailed approach, not an opinion-driven one, so this is not stated.

Hence the correct choice is the statement that critical appreciation involves examining the structure, language, characters and themes of literary works.

bodyHtml:
Read the passage carefully. Select the answer from the four alternatives given below each question.

The human body can tolerate only a small range of temperature, especially when the person is engaged in vigorous activity. Heat reactions usually occur when large amounts of water and/or salt are lost through excessive sweating following strenuous exercise. When the body becomes overheated and can not eliminate this excess heat, heat exhaustion and heat stroke are possible.

Heat exhaustion is generally characterised by clammy skin, fatigue, nausea, dizziness, profuse perspiration, and sometimes fainting, resulting from an inadequate intake of water and the loss of fluids. First aid treatment for this condition includes having the victim lie down, raising the feet 8 to 12 inches, applying cool, wet cloths to the skin, and giving the victims sips of salt water over a 1-hour period.

Heat stroke is much more serious; it is an immediate life-threatening situation. The characteristics of heat stroke are a high body temperature (which may reach 106° F or more); a rapid pulse; hot and dry skin; and a blocked sweating mechanism, victims of this condition may be unconscious, and first-aid measures should be directed at quickly cooling the body. The victim should be placed in a tub of cold water or repeatedly sponged with cool water until his or her temperature is sufficiently lowered.

Question: The most immediate concern of a person tending to a victim of heat stroke should be

options.label: A
options.html: get salt into the victim's body

solution:
Concept

In a reading-comprehension question, the correct option is the one the passage itself supports — not what sounds medically reasonable in general. So first locate where the passage talks about the exact situation in the stem (here: first aid for heat stroke) and let that text decide the priority.

Applying it to this passage

The passage treats heat stroke as the serious case: it calls it "an immediate life-threatening situation" and lists a high body temperature that "may reach 106° F or more" together with a blocked sweating mechanism. Crucially, it states that for heat stroke "first-aid measures should be directed at quickly cooling the body," and that the victim should be cooled "until his or her temperature is sufficiently lowered."

So the passage names cooling the body — i.e. bringing the dangerously high temperature down — as the immediate priority. That matches the option "lower the victim's temperature."

Why the other options do not fit

  • "get salt into the victim's body": giving sips of salt water is the passage's first aid for heat EXHAUSTION (loss of water and salt), a different and less urgent condition; the passage never assigns it to heat stroke.

  • "raise the victim's feet": raising the feet 8 to 12 inches is again part of the heat-exhaustion treatment in the passage, not the heat-stroke priority.

  • "lower the victim's pulse": a rapid pulse is only listed as a symptom/characteristic of heat stroke; the passage never directs the rescuer to act on the pulse itself, so it is a description, not the stated first-aid goal.

Cross-check

The only action the passage explicitly prescribes for heat stroke is rapid cooling, and it ends by tying success to the temperature being "sufficiently lowered" — confirming the intended answer.
