Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A new study published in Science provides clear evidence of organic matter on Mars’s surface. NASA’s rover Curiosity collected the data, confirming earlier findings that Mars once had carbon-based compounds essential for life. These organic molecules were found in Gale Crater, an area that may have been a lake over three billion years ago. The rocks containing the organics also had sulfur, which might have preserved them despite harsh surface radiation. While the presence of organic molecules doesn’t prove ancient life—since they could form through non-living processes—it is a significant discovery. About five years ago, Curiosity also detected methane, a basic organic molecule and natural gas component, in the Martian atmosphere. Methane only lasts a few hundred years, suggesting an unknown source replenishes it. Its levels fluctuate seasonally, possibly due to underground icy crystals releasing gas.

These findings indicate Mars is more active than thought and might be becoming more habitable. Future missions, like ESA’s Exo Mars and NASA’s Mars Rover, aim to explore the soil and atmosphere further, potentially answering if life ever existed on Mars.

Q. The passage’s tone when describing future missions can best be described as:
solution:
Correct Option
Option A: Optimistic

Detailed Solution
Analysis of the Tone: The passage maintains an optimistic tone when discussing future missions by focusing on the potential for new scientific discoveries.

Evidence from the Text: The passage describes future missions, such as ESA's Exo Mars and NASA's Mars Rover, as "aiming to explore the soil and atmosphere further" with the goal of "potentially answering if life ever existed on Mars". This language conveys hope and positive anticipation regarding future exploration.

title: The passages given below are followed by set of questions.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
The passages given below are followed by a set of questions. Choose the most appropriate answer to each question.

Ask an American schoolchild what he or she is learning in school these days and you might even get a reply, provided you ask it in Spanish. But don’t bother, here’s the answer: Americans nowadays are not learning any of the things that we learned in our day, like reading and writing. Apparently, these are considered fusty old subjects, invented by white males to oppress women and minorities.

What are they learning? In a Vermont college town, I found the answer sitting in a toy store book rack, next to typical kids’ books like ‘Heather Has Two Mommies and Daddy Is Dysfunctional’. It’s a teacher’s guide called ‘Happy To Be Me’, subtitled ‘Building Self, Esteem’.

Self-esteem, as it turns out, is a big subject in American classrooms. Many American schools see building it as important as teaching reading and writing. They call it “whole language” teaching, borrowing terminology from the granola people to compete in the education marketplace.

No one ever spent a moment building my self-esteem when I was in school. In fact, from the day I first stepped inside a classroom, my self-esteem was one big demolition site. All that mattered was “the subject,” be it geography, history, or mathematics. I was praised when I remembered that “near”, “fit”, “friendly”, “pleasing”, “like” and their opposites took the dative case in Latin. I was reviled when I forgot what a cosine was good for. Generally, I lived my school years beneath a torrent of castigation so consistent I eventually ceased to hear it, as people who live near the sea eventually stop hearing the waves.

Schools have changed. Reviling is out, for one thing. More important, subjects have changed. Whereas I learned English, modern kids learn something called “language skills.” Whereas I learned writing, modern kids learn something called “communication ”. Communication, the book tells us, is seven percent words, 23 percent facial expression, 20 percent tone of voice, and 50 percent body language. So this column, with its carefully chosen words, would earn me at most, a grade of seven percent. That is if the school even gave out something as oppressive and demanding as grades.

The result is that, in place of English classes, American children are getting a course in How to ‘Win Friends and Influence People’. Consider the new attitude toward journal writing: I remember one high school English class when we were required to keep a journal. The idea was to emulate those great writers who confided in diaries, searching their souls and honing their critical thinking on paper.

‘Happy To Be Me’ states that journals are a great way for students to get in touch with their feelings. Tell students they can write one sentence or a whole page. Reassure them that no one, not even you, will read what they write. After the unit, hopefully, all students will be feeling good about them and will want to share some of their entries with the class.

There was a time when no self-respecting book for English teachers would use “great” or “hopefully” that way. Moreover, back then, the purpose of English courses (an antique term for “Unit”) was not to help students “feel good about themselves.” Which is good, because all that reviling didn't make me feel particularly good about anything.

The attitude of the author can be best described as
solution: The author contrasts traditional education with modern approaches, criticizing the shift toward self-esteem and emotional expression. The tone is critical and nostalgic, reflecting a resistance to change and a preference for rigorous academic standards. This aligns with a reactionary attitude, which opposes modern reforms and idealizes the past.

Direction: Read the passage and answer the questions based on it.

RICHARD WRIGHT, the father figure of African American literature, both nurtured and was rejected by his two most conspicuous heirs, Ralph Ellison and James Baldwin. Wright, who took Ellison under his wing in New York in the late 1930s, told his acolyte to stop copying him, that he was mimicking, not cultivating his own style. Ellison responded that he was trying to learn to write well by imitating his mentor. That was when they were close. Baldwin, too, started out as a pupil and an admirer who saw Wright poised to be the greatest Black writer in the United States.

Though it happened slowly, by 1941, Ellison betrayed signs of feeling that Wright, affiliated off and on with the Communist Party, wrote fiction that was too ideological and not sensitive enough to nuance: Wright wanted to testify to the monstrosities of white supremacy, rather than the power of Black resilience. Ellison grew committed to the poetry of American democracy, despite how badly it was sullied; he swore by the virtues of individualism. Calling Wright “Poor Richard,” Baldwin joined Ellison in lamenting their mentor’s failure to see the beauty of Black people. The two of them never ceased to love Wright’s prose, but they came to reject his perspective.

I admit I’ve been inclined to share their verdict, based on Wright’s first novel, Native Son, published in 1940, which I read again and again in classes before and during college. I’ve parroted the notes I took in lectures, and I’ve taught a version of those lectures myself: Bigger Thomas was a protagonist stripped of any redeeming qualities, so distorted by the conditions of racism that he became an avatar more than a character, and an unsettling representation of Blackness.

My assessment of Wright has begun to shift over the past couple of years. I’ve read 12 Million Black Voices (1941)—his reflections on the Great Migration, accompanied by Farm Security Administration photographs taken during the Depression—and been struck by his broad sympathy. And I’ve reread Black Boy (1945), a memoir I hadn’t touched since my final year of high school in the Northeast, in a writing seminar led by a teacher born, like me, in Birmingham, Alabama. Wright reached for the very core of the human condition in his portrait of growing up destitute in the Deep South during the early 20th century and then making his way north: abundance everywhere and terrible hunger, tragedy mixed with the quotidian in the most disorienting ways. The experience he evoked might not have been every Black life, but it was indeed a part of Black life. In Mississippi, the

land could swallow you whole. In Chicago, a rat might bite you, because after all, you were made to live in slums no different from rattraps. Wright was showing us something true, if not absolute—how, with the plantation breathing at your back and deferred dreams before you, a tragedy happened. Now I’m even more convinced that Wright deserves to be looked at with fresh eyes.

All of the following statements can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.html: The protagonist, Bigger Thomas, is portrayed as a pessimistic character who is an unsettling reflection of Blackness.

options.label: B
options.html: Wright grew up extremely poor in the Deep South in the early twentieth century and then moved north.

options.label: C
options.html: Bigger Thomas, a character devoid of any negative traits, was the protagonist in Wright's first book, Native Son.

options.label: D
options.html: The author was moved by Wright's broad sympathy after reading his book 12 Million Black Voices.

solution:
Correct answer: The statement that Bigger Thomas was "devoid of any negative traits" cannot be inferred from the passage.

Explanation:

The passage describes Bigger Thomas as "a protagonist stripped of any redeeming qualities, so distorted by the conditions of racism that he became an avatar more than a character, and an unsettling representation of Blackness."

This means he is portrayed as lacking positive or redeeming traits, not as lacking negative traits. The choice that says he was devoid of negative traits reverses the meaning and is therefore not supported by the passage.

Why the other statements can be inferred:

  • The portrayal of Bigger Thomas as pessimistic and an unsettling reflection of Blackness is supported by the phrase describing him as stripped of redeeming qualities and an unsettling representation.

  • Wright's own background of extreme poverty in the Deep South and his move north is stated when the passage says he portrayed "growing up destitute in the Deep South during the early 20th century and then making his way north."

  • The narrator being moved by Wright's broad sympathy is supported by the line that the narrator had "been struck by his broad sympathy" after reading 12 Million Black Voices.

Therefore, the only statement that cannot be inferred is the one that incorrectly claims Bigger Thomas was devoid of negative traits.

title: Assertion Social media platforms are able to control the type
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
Assertion A: Social media platforms are able to control the type of content that will appear in a reader's feed.
Reason R: They do so because they are quite concerned about individual likes and dislikes of users.

options.label: A
options.html: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.

options.label: B
options.html: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.

options.label: C
options.html: A is correct but R is not correct.

options.label: D
options.html: A is not correct but R is correct.

solution:
Conclusion: The assertion is correct; the reason is not correct.

Why the assertion is correct:

  • The passage explicitly says social media platforms "decide which article will appear in which readers feed," indicating they control the content users see.

Why the reason is incorrect:

  • The passage explains platforms use their size and information advantage and that they choose feed content "to maximize advertising revenues." This shows the motive is commercial (ad revenue), not a concern for individual likes and dislikes.

Implication: The assertion is supported by the passage, but the stated reason does not accurately describe the motive given in the passage; therefore the assertion is true and the reason is false.

title: What is of no value for assessing social realizations?
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml: What is of no value for assessing social realizations?
solution:
Answer: Utilities

  • Key reason: The passage explains that assessing social realizations involves taking substantive freedoms and capabilities into account, rather than focusing solely on pleasures or utilities.

  • Therefore, utilities (pleasures or outcomes people end up having) are of no value by themselves for assessing social realizations.

  • Brief elimination of other choices:

    • Ignoring the values of freedom: Contrary to the passage, which stresses the importance of freedoms.

    • Capabilities of people: Central to the capability approach and to assessing social realizations.

    • Inability to use the freedom given: Relevant, since capabilities include the opportunity and ability to use freedoms.

title: The difficulty with the proposed high-speed train line is that
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
The difficulty with the proposed high-speed train line is that a used plane can be bought for one-third the price of the train line, and the plane, which is just as fast, can fly anywhere. The train would be a fixed linear system, and we live in a world that is spreading out in all directions and in which consumers choose the free-wheel systems (cars, buses, aircraft), which do not have fixed routes. Thus a sufficient market for the train will not exist.

Which of the following, if true, most severely weakens the argument presented above?

options.label: A
options.html: Cars, buses, and planes require the efforts of drivers and pilots to guide them, whereas the train will be guided mechanically.

options.label: B
options.html: Cars and buses are not nearly as fast as the high-speed train will be.

options.label: C
options.html: Planes are not a free-wheel system because they can fly only between airports, which are less convenient for consumers than the high-speed train's stations would be.

options.label: D
options.html: The high-speed train line cannot use currently underutilized train stations in large cities.

options.label: E
options.html: For long trips, most people prefer to fly rather than to take ground-level transportation.

solution: The argument claims a used plane is better than a fixed train line because it can fly anywhere. The weakness is that planes are not truly free-wheel systems: they operate between airports, which may be less convenient than train stations.

title: Question: Directions: Each of the questions below consists of question
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
Directions: Study the passage carefully and answer the given questions.

In recent years, India has witnessed a rapid transformation driven by digital innovation, infrastructure expansion, and a renewed focus on sustainability. The government's push toward digital public infrastructure, such as UPI, Aadhaar-enabled services, and online governance platforms, has significantly improved service delivery and financial inclusion, particularly in semi-urban and rural areas. At the same time, large-scale infrastructure projects, including highways, metro networks, renewable energy parks, and logistics corridors, aim to boost economic growth and employment. However, this rapid development has also raised concerns regarding environmental impact, data privacy, and equitable access to opportunities. While startups and technology-driven enterprises have benefited from policy support and increased investor confidence, traditional sectors and small businesses often struggle to adapt to fast-changing regulations and digital requirements. As global economic uncertainties persist and climate challenges intensify, policymakers face the task of balancing growth with inclusivity, innovation with regulation, and development with long-term sustainability.

Which of the following can be most reasonably inferred from the paragraph?

options.label: A
options.html: Digital public infrastructure has completely eliminated economic inequality in India.

options.label: B
options.html: Infrastructure growth alone is sufficient to ensure long-term sustainability.

options.label: C
options.html: Rapid development brings both opportunities and challenges that need careful management.

options.label: D
options.html: Traditional businesses will inevitably shut down due to digital transformation.

options.label: E
options.html: Environmental concerns are no longer relevant in modern development policies.

solution:
Concept: In inference-based reading comprehension, the correct choice is the statement that follows reasonably from what the passage actually says — it neither adds certainty the passage does not claim (words like completely, alone, inevitably, no longer) nor contradicts any detail in the passage. An inference must be supported by the passage as a whole, not just one sentence taken in isolation.

Application: The passage presents digital and infrastructure gains (UPI, Aadhaar-enabled services, highways, metro networks, renewable energy parks) that boost growth and employment, alongside genuine concerns it names explicitly — environmental impact, data privacy, unequal access, and traditional/small businesses struggling to adapt. It closes by saying policymakers must balance growth with inclusivity, innovation with regulation, and development with sustainability. Taken together, this is exactly a picture of rapid development bringing both opportunities and challenges that require careful management — the inference stays within what every sentence of the passage already supports.

Why the other options overreach:

  • “Completely eliminated economic inequality” goes far beyond the passage, which only says financial inclusion has “improved” — it also says small businesses and traditional sectors continue to struggle, so inequality has clearly not been eliminated.

  • “Infrastructure growth alone is sufficient” for sustainability contradicts the passage's own environmental-impact concern and its closing point that growth must be actively balanced with sustainability — sustainability is not treated as automatic.

  • “Traditional businesses will inevitably shut down” overstates the passage's wording that they “struggle to adapt” — a struggle to adapt is not the same as a certain, inevitable closure.

  • “Environmental concerns are no longer relevant” is the reverse of the passage, which explicitly lists environmental impact as a live concern that policymakers must weigh against growth.

Cross-check: Re-reading the passage sentence by sentence confirms every other option is either an unsupported absolute claim or a direct contradiction, while the opportunities-and-challenges reading is corroborated by both halves of the passage (the gains listed in the middle, and the balancing act named at the end).

title: ISRO 2023 Aptitude Q84

संपूर्ण संयुक्त राज्य अमेरिका (यूएस) की आबादी के लिए औसत जीवन प्रत्याशा 73.9 वर्ष है, लेकिन हवाई में जन्म लेने वाले बच्चे औसतन 77 वर्ष जीवित रहेंगे, और लुइसियाना में जन्म लेने वाले बच्चे औसतन 71.7 वर्ष जीवित रहेंगे। इसलिए, यदि लुइसियाना के एक नवविवाहित जोड़े को हवाई में अपना परिवार शुरू करना था, तो उनके बच्चों के लुइसियाना में रहने पर परिवार की तुलना में अधिक समय तक जीवित रहने की उम्मीद की जाएगी।

title: Read the following passage and answer the given questions. Providing
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
Read the following passage and answer the given question.

Providing stable freshwater supplies is a priority for every country in the world. Yet stable supplies are increasingly hard to come by in many countries, as water-related risks increase. For example, recent droughts threatened GDP growth in the United States. Monsoon floods killed hundreds and displaced thousands in India. Increased competition for water may impact energy production in China, and the list goes on.

World Resources Institute’s Aqueduct project recently evaluated, mapped, and scored water risks like these in 100 river basins and 180 nations – the first such country-level water assessment of its kind. We found that 36 countries face extremely high levels of baseline water stress. This means that more than 80 percent of the water available is withdrawn annually by agricultural, domestic, and industrial users, leaving businesses, farms, and communities vulnerable to scarcity. Such situations severely threaten national water security and economic growth – especially if a country does not have adequate water-management plans in place. This information is highly relevant for a country’s economy, environment, and communities.

It’s also important for countries to understand the underlying natural factors that drive their water-related risks and respond accordingly. Extremely high levels of baseline water stress, for example, don’t necessarily mean that a country will fall victim to scarcity. Armed with the right information, countries facing extremely high stress can implement management and conservation strategies to secure their water supplies.

Singapore, for example, has the highest water stress ranking. The country is densely populated and has no freshwater lakes or aquifers, and its demand for water far exceeds its naturally occurring supply. Yet the country is consistently held up as an exceptional water manager. Singapore invests heavily in technology, international agreements, and responsible management, allowing it to meet its freshwater needs. Advanced rainwater capture systems contribute 20 percent of Singapore’s water supply, 40 percent is imported from Malaysia, grey water reuse adds 30 percent, and desalination produces the remaining 10 percent of the supply to meet the country’s total demand. These forward-thinking and innovative management plans provide a stable water supply for Singapore’s industrial, agricultural, and domestic users – even in the face of significant baseline water stress.

Singapore is held up as an example of water management. Match the strategy (a–c) with the actual practice (i–iii).

Strategy

Practice

a. Use of technology

i) Import from Malaysia

b. International agreement

ii) Rainwater capture

c. Responsible management

iii) Desalination and grey water use
solution:
Concept

In a match-the-following comprehension item, each label on the left must be paired with the practice on the right that the passage explicitly links to it. The correct mapping is fixed by what the text states, not by guesswork: read the sentence that names each strategy and see which concrete practice it describes.

Application

The passage states that Singapore meets its water needs through three named approaches — technology, international agreements, and responsible management — and then describes the concrete practices behind them. Pair each strategy with the practice the passage attaches to it:

Strategy

Practice in the passage

Why

a. Use of technology

Rainwater capture

“Advanced rainwater capture systems” are an engineered, technology-driven method.

b. International agreement

Import from Malaysia

Water bought from another country rests on a treaty/agreement between the two nations.

c. Responsible management

Desalination and grey water use

Reusing grey water and desalinating supply are deliberate, sustainable management choices.

This gives the mapping a – ii, b – i, c – iii.

Cross-check

Test the pairing against the passage once more: import from Malaysia is the only practice involving a second country, so it must belong to the international-agreement strategy; rainwater capture is the engineered system, so it fits the technology strategy; the remaining pair – grey water reuse and desalination – then matches responsible management. All three line up, confirming a – ii, b – i, c – iii.

title: Saving energy means saving money. Homeowners and renters know this
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
Saving energy means saving money. Homeowners and renters know this basic fact, but they often don't know what kinds of adjustments they can make in their homes and apartments that will result in savings.

For those willing to spend some time and money to reap long-term energy savings, an energy audit is the way to go. An energy auditor will come into your home and assess its energy efficiency. The auditor will pinpoint areas of your home that use the most energy and offer solutions to lower your energy use and costs. Trained energy auditors know what to look for and can locate a variety of flaws that may be resulting in energy inefficiency, including inadequate insulation, construction flaws, and uneven heat distribution.

There are quicker and less costly measures that can be taken as well. One way to save money is to replace incandescent lights with fluorescents. This can result in a savings of more than 50% on your monthly lighting costs. When it's time to replace old appliances, it's wise to spend a bit more for an energy-efficient model, and be sure that you are taking advantage of energy-saving settings already on your current refrigerator, dishwasher, washing machine, or dryer.

Windows provide another opportunity to cut your energy costs. Caulk old windows that might be leaky to prevent drafts, and choose double-paned windows if you're building an addition or replacing old windows.

Most areas of your home or apartment offer opportunities to save energy and money. The results are significant and are well worth the effort.

According to the passage, which of the following would an energy auditor do?
(A). Locate a variety of flaws that may result in energy inefficiency and fix them.

(B). Check for construction flaws

(C). Look for problems with heat distribution

(D). Offer solutions to lower your energy costs

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution: According to the passage, an energy auditor will "pinpoint areas of your home that use the most energy and offer solutions to lower your energy use and costs." The text explicitly states auditors can "locate a variety of flaws," including "construction flaws" and "uneven heat distribution." Thus, checking for construction flaws, looking for problems with heat distribution, and offering solutions to lower costs are correct. However, the text does not state auditors "fix" flaws themselves, only that they offer solutions. Therefore, the combination of options regarding construction flaws, heat distribution, and offering solutions is accurate.

title: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
Read the following passage and answer the questions based on it:

Project Tiger has recently completed fifty years. On this occasion, this major news was repeatedly shown how the number of these tigers, which was 2,967 in the year 2018, became 3,167 in the year 2022. This hides the bitter truth: the people of India are not ready to make any kind of compromise with their Western lifestyle to save the tigers. Most middle-class Indians would not like to give up the habit of driving towards the hills located on multi-lane highways for their second investment home or the national animal.

You cannot even change the requirements (needs) of the tiger - because it is a large, solitary animal. A tigress needs about 15 square kilometers of space with a good prey base. If she gives birth to cubs, those cubs will need additional space. Data shows that 30 percent of the tiger population lives outside protected areas, i.e., among us. The more we fragment their habitats through urbanization, highways, and industrial parks, the more they will be forced to go towards unprotected areas.

We have to bring a change in our thinking. I advocate achieving these three results by the 75th anniversary of Project Tiger. First, instead of unbridled growth in the number of tigers, India can identify and achieve a metric (measurement) that is not much more than the current number. Remember, about 1000 tigers are roaming in fields and villages, if it becomes more than this, it will become a disaster. Second, making better what we have protected. It is important to keep the protected tiger habitat undisturbed. Keeping in mind the investment made in keeping the unprotected ecosystem intact should be economically viable and part of other programs like CSR. Third, it is essential to reduce conflict with humans. Monitoring and communication are important parts of this. Compensation for killed livestock should be evaluated quickly and compensation should be given at the market rate. In the next 25 years, we have to consider quality.

According to the author, which of the following should not be the objective on the 75th anniversary of Project Tiger?
(A) Keeping protected habitats intact.
(B) Maintaining the tiger population at approximately the current level.
(C) Sufficient compensation should be given for livestock killed by tigers.
(D) Focusing on numbers (quantity) instead of quality.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution: The passage explicitly advocates for quality over unbridled growth in the tiger population. The author suggests maintaining current numbers to avoid disaster, protecting habitats, and ensuring livestock compensation. Option D contradicts this by prioritizing quantity over quality, making it the correct choice for what should not be an objective.

title: The rapid urbanization of developing countries has led to increased
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
bodyHtml:
The rapid urbanization of developing countries has led to increased environmental degradation. Urban areas are experiencing unprecedented growth, which has resulted in deforestation, loss of biodiversity, and heightened air pollution. In response to this, governments are introducing policies aimed at sustainable development. However, the success of these initiatives depends heavily on public participation and effective implementation. While some argue that economic growth should take precedence, others believe that environmental conservation is critical for long-term prosperity.

Which of the following statements best describes the author’s perspective on urbanization?

options.label: A
options.html: Urbanization is a necessary evil for economic development.

options.label: B
options.html: Urbanization has only negative effects on the environment.

options.label: C
options.html: Urbanization poses environmental challenges, but sustainable policies can mitigate its impact.

options.label: D
options.html: Urbanization should be completely halted to protect the environment.

solution:
Answer: Urbanization poses environmental challenges, but sustainable policies can mitigate its impact.

Why this is best:

  • The passage notes specific environmental problems linked to urbanization, such as deforestation, loss of biodiversity, and increased air pollution.

  • It also states that governments are introducing sustainable development policies and that success depends on public participation and effective implementation, indicating a belief that impacts can be mitigated.

  • This choice captures the balanced view in the passage: recognition of environmental challenges combined with confidence in policy responses.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • Saying urbanization is a necessary evil for economic development presents an imbalanced trade-off and fails to reflect the passage’s emphasis on mitigation through policy and public involvement.

  • Claiming urbanization has only negative effects ignores the passage’s mention of government policies aimed at sustainable development and the possibility of reducing harm.

  • Arguing that urbanization should be completely halted is an extreme position not supported by the passage, which instead focuses on managing impacts rather than stopping urban growth outright.

title: One of the following sentences is grammatically correct. Identify the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
One of the following sentences is grammatically correct.

Identify the sentence.

options.label: A
options.html: Many a man have succumbed to this temptation.

options.label: B
options.html: Fifteen minutes are allowed to each speaker.

options.label: C
options.html: It was one of the best speeches that have ever been made in the Parliament.

options.label: D
options.html: He not only lost his ticket, but also his luggage.

solution:
Correct sentence: It was one of the best speeches that have ever been made in the Parliament.

Reason: The phrase 'one of the' is followed by a plural noun ('speeches'), and the relative clause 'that have ever been made' refers to that plural noun; therefore the plural verb 'have' is correct.

  • For 'Many a man have succumbed to this temptation.': 'Many a' takes a singular verb, so write 'Many a man has succumbed to this temptation.'

  • For 'Fifteen minutes are allowed to each speaker.': Time periods are often treated as a single amount and take a singular verb; better: 'Fifteen minutes is allowed to each speaker.' More natural: 'Each speaker is allowed fifteen minutes.'

  • For 'He not only lost his ticket, but also his luggage.': Maintain parallel structure with correlative conjunctions. Better: 'He not only lost his ticket but also lost his luggage.' Or: 'He lost not only his ticket but also his luggage.' The comma is unnecessary in the short construction.

Conclusion: The given sentence about one of the best speeches is grammatically correct because the relative clause correctly agrees with the plural noun 'speeches'.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options.

This is one of the five books that was launched yesterday at the Vigyan Bhawan.
solution: The correct answer is Option D (that was). The sentence contains a subject-verb agreement error in the relative clause. The phrase 'one of the five books' indicates that there are multiple books, making 'books' a plural noun. Consequently, the verb in the relative clause modifying 'books' must also be plural. Therefore, 'that was' is incorrect and should be changed to 'that were'. Options A ('one of the'), B ('This'), and C ('at') are grammatically correct in this context. 'One of the' correctly introduces a plural noun phrase, 'This' serves as an appropriate demonstrative pronoun for the singular subject 'one', and 'at' is the correct preposition to indicate location. The error lies solely in using the singular verb 'was' instead of the plural 'were'.

Hostility/ between the rival groups/ have increased/ since the last elections.
solution:
Key idea: The singular subject “Hostility” needs a singular verb.

  • The phrase “between the rival groups” only modifies the subject; it does not make the subject plural.

  • The correct verb phrase is “has increased”.

Answer: Option 1, “have increased”, contains the error.

title: Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.

In the front room/ of our house/ there's/ two chairs and a sofa.
solution:
Key idea: The verb must agree with the real subject that follows: “two chairs and a sofa”.

  • “Two chairs and a sofa” is plural.

  • “There is/there’s” is singular.

  • The correct form is “there are two chairs and a sofa”.

Answer: Option 0, “there’s”, contains the error.

title: Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.

Many of our staff / find it difficult to / follow her as she / don't speak clearly.
solution:
Concept: A negative auxiliary must agree in person and number with its subject: plural subjects (and "I"/"you") take "don't", while a singular third-person subject (he/she/it, or a singular noun) always takes "doesn't", never "don't".

Application: The clause "as she don't speak clearly" has the singular third-person subject "she". Since "she" is singular, the auxiliary must be "doesn't", not "don't" — the phrase should read "doesn't speak clearly".

Cross-check: None of the other segments show an agreement, tense, or reference problem:

  • "Many of our staff" — "many of" gives the collective noun "staff" a plural sense, so a plural verb correctly follows.

  • "find it difficult to" — this verb phrase correctly agrees with that plural subject and is idiomatically standard.

  • "follow her as she" — the pronoun "she" clearly and correctly refers back to "her", the person already named in the clause.

Result: the error is the mismatched auxiliary — it should read "doesn't speak clearly", not "don't speak clearly".

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q12
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Identify the erroneous part of the following English sentence: Each of the participants / have submitted / their report / before the deadline.
solution:
Concept

In subject–verb agreement, the verb agrees with the grammatical head of the subject, not with a nearby noun inside an ‘of’ phrase.

Distributive words such as ‘each’ are grammatically singular, so they take a singular verb form.

Application

In ‘Each of the participants’, the head is ‘each’; ‘participants’ belongs to the intervening prepositional phrase. Therefore the present-perfect auxiliary must be ‘has’, giving ‘Each of the participants has submitted their report before the deadline.’

Contrast

  • ‘Each of the participants’ is the subject phrase; ‘each’ controls agreement.

  • ‘have submitted’ is the verb phrase; ‘have’ must change to ‘has’ for the singular head.

  • ‘their report’ is acceptable with singular ‘they’ as a gender-neutral possessive in modern English.

  • ‘before the deadline’ is a correctly formed time phrase.

Cross-check

Remove the intervening phrase ‘of the participants’: ‘Each has submitted’ remains grammatical, whereas ‘Each have submitted’ does not.

Result

The erroneous segment is ‘have submitted’; it should be ‘has submitted’.

title: Choose the correct sentences from the given alternatives. am used
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct sentences from the given alternatives.
I am used to get up early.

options.label: A
options.html: I am used to getting up early

options.label: B
options.html: I am used in getting up early

options.label: C
options.html: I am used for getting up early

solution:
Correct Option
Option A: I am used to getting up early

Detailed Solution
The phrase "used to" indicates a habit and must be followed by a gerund (a verb ending in -ing), rather than the base form. Therefore, "getting" must be used instead of "get" to match this grammatical rule correctly.

title: Find out which part of the sentence has error. When
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Find out which part of the sentence has error. When he entered the classroom the lecture already was beginning.
solution:
Correct Option
Option B: Already was beginning

The error lies in the phrase 'Already was beginning'. In English grammar, adverbs of frequency or time like 'already' typically precede the main verb but follow auxiliary verbs in continuous tenses. The correct word order should be 'was already beginning' to maintain proper syntax within the past continuous tense. The phrase 'When he entered' is grammatically correct as it sets up a time clause, and 'the classroom the lecture' does not constitute an error in itself. Therefore, option B is incorrect due to improper adverb placement.

title: In the following questions, one part of the sentence may
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In the following questions, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the 'No error' option.

I have never see (A)/ her so happy (B)/ about anything ever before. (C)/ No error (D)
solution:
Answer: The error is in the first part of the sentence: 'I have never see'.

Identification and correction:

  • The verb 'see' is the base form; with 'have' (present perfect) we need the past participle 'seen'.

  • Corrected sentence: I have never seen her so happy about anything ever before.

Grammar rule: Use the present perfect with 'never' as: have/has + past participle (e.g., have never seen).

Why the other parts are not errors:

  • The phrase 'her so happy' correctly uses the object pronoun and adjective phrase to describe her state.

  • The phrase 'about anything ever before' is grammatical. Although 'ever before' can be redundant when used with 'never', this redundancy is stylistic rather than a grammatical error.

title: Spot an error in the given sentence. (A)Roshni saw man/(B)
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Spot an error in the given sentence.

(A)Roshni saw a man/(B) quarrelling with a lady,yesterday/(C)but did not recognise whom it was due to darkness/(D)no error.
solution: The error lies in part (C) of the sentence. The relative pronoun 'whom' is used incorrectly because it is the subject of the clause 'it was'. In such cases, the subjective case 'who' should be used instead of the objective case 'whom'.

title: Each question gives sentence with part of the sentence underlined
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Each question gives a sentence with a part of the sentence underlined that may contain an error. Four alternative substitutes are given for the underlined portion. Identify the choice that replaces the underlined part to form a logically and grammatically correct statement and mark its number as your answer.

As these changes in the rock are greatest at the surface and diminish downward, we infer that they have been caused by agents that were working downward in the surface.

options.label: A
options.html: we infer that they have been caused by agents that were working downward in the surface.

options.label: B
options.html: we are inferring that they have caused by agents working downward from the surface.

options.label: C
options.html: we infer so they have been caused by agents working downward on the surface.

options.label: D
options.html: we infer that they have been caused by agents working downward from the surface.

solution:
Correct sentence: "we infer that they have been caused by agents working downward from the surface."

Why this is correct:

  • The phrase "we infer that" uses the simple present to state a general conclusion drawn from observation, which is appropriate here.

  • "have been caused" is the present perfect passive. It correctly indicates that the changes were caused in the past but the result is relevant now; passive voice correctly focuses on the changes themselves.

  • "working downward from the surface" uses the preposition "from" to show the origin of the agents and the participle "working" to describe their action. This combination is precise and natural.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • "we infer that they have been caused by agents that were working downward in the surface." This version uses the preposition "in the surface," which is incorrect for indicating origin; "from the surface" is correct. The clause "that were working" is unnecessarily wordy and shifts the temporal framing.

  • "we are inferring that they have caused by agents working downward from the surface." This version is ungrammatical because it omits "been" after "have," so the passive is incorrect (it should be "have been caused"). "We are inferring" is also less natural for a general conclusion, but the primary error is the missing auxiliary.

  • "we infer so they have been caused by agents working downward on the surface." The phrase "we infer so" is not a grammatical connector here and disrupts the sentence structure. In addition, "working downward on the surface" suggests movement along the surface rather than downward from it; use "from the surface" to indicate origin.

title: In this section each sentence is underlined and labelled in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In this section each sentence is underlined and labelled in four separate sections-P, Q, R, S. Identify the section in which the error is located. If you feel that there is no error, section 'S' will signify a 'No error' response.

I find it difficult (P) / to cope up with (Q) / your demands (R) / No error. (S)
solution:
Correct Option
Option B: Q

Detailed Solution
The error is located in section Q. The phrase "cope up with" is incorrect; it should be "cope with".

title: Find out the part of the sentence which has error.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Find out the part of the sentence which has error.

John has been working on the pilot project since two years.
solution: The error lies in the phrase 'pilot project since two years'. In English grammar, the preposition 'since' is used to indicate a specific starting point in time (e.g., since 2021, since Monday), whereas 'for' is used to denote a duration or period of time (e.g., for two years, for three hours). The sentence describes the duration of John's work on the project, which is 'two years'. Therefore, using 'since' before a duration is incorrect. The sentence should read: 'John has been working on the pilot project for two years.' Options A and B are grammatically correct as they form a proper present perfect continuous structure ('has been working') followed by the prepositional phrase 'on the'. Option D is incorrect because there is a clear grammatical error in part C. Thus, option C is the correct choice as it identifies the misuse of 'since' with a time duration.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q13
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: The teacher asked/the students/that why they were late/for the class.
solution:
Concept

An indirect question introduced by a wh-word uses that wh-word as its connector. A declarative complementizer such as that is not placed before why, what, when, or where. The embedded clause also follows statement word order.

Application

The reporting frame is “The teacher asked the students.” The reported question asks for a reason, so why must introduce the embedded clause: “why they were late.” Placing that before why gives two competing connectors.

Contrast

  • “The teacher asked” is the reporting clause, with teacher as its subject and asked as the reporting verb.

  • “the students” is the object of asked and names the people addressed.

  • “that why they were late” contains competing connectors; retain why and remove that.

  • “for the class” is a prepositional phrase expressing the class context associated with lateness.

Result

The erroneous segment is “that why they were late.” The corrected sentence is: “The teacher asked the students why they were late for the class.”

title: Directions: Read the sentence to find out whether there is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Directions: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error, the answer is ‘E”. (Ignore – the errors of punctuation, if any)

Jane was sitting with her mother and sisters, (A) /reflecting about what she had heard, and doubting whether (B)/ she was authorized to mention it when Sir George himself appeared, sent by his lovely daughter, (C)/ to announce her engagement with the family (D) No error (E).
solution:
Explanation:

To announce her engagement with the family should be replaced with ’to announce her engagement to the family.’

Used to indicate the place, person, or thing that someone or something moves toward, or the direction of something.

We use with to mean ‘having’ or ‘possessing’.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

title: Directions: In the following question, there is sentence given with
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Directions: In the following question, there is a sentence given with four words marked as (A), (B), (C) and (D). These words may or may not be placed in their correct order. Four options with different arrangements of these words are given. Mark the option with the correct arrangement as your answer. If no rearrangement is required, mark option (5) as your answer.
Despite the eagerness (A) seen among parents and students towards schools, children’s basic literacy (B) levels have taken a big hit, with their reading ability as compared (C) to numeracy skills declining (D) much more sharply and dropping to pre-2012 levels.
solution:
Concept: In word-rearrangement questions like this one, four words in a sentence are marked (A)-(D). The task is to check whether every marked word already occupies its correct grammatical slot -- as a noun, a modifier, or a participle -- so that the sentence's subject, its comparative phrase, and its participial clause all stay intact. Test each offered swap: if trading two marked words breaks grammatical agreement or destroys the meaning, that swap is wrong. If the original order already reads as one coherent, grammatical sentence and every offered swap breaks it, the correct answer is that no rearrangement is required.

Checking each marked word in its given place:

  1. eagerness (A) is the head noun of "the eagerness seen among parents and students towards schools" -- correctly a noun following "the", modified by the participle "seen".

  2. literacy (B) correctly modifies "levels" in "children's basic literacy levels" -- a standard noun-noun compound, just like "literacy levels" is normally used.

  3. compared (C) completes the standard comparative phrase "as compared to numeracy skills".

  4. declining (D) is the main participle governing "much more sharply and dropping to pre-2012 levels" -- describing what is happening to reading ability.

Testing each offered swap confirms none of them work:

  • A-B: gives "the literacy seen among parents and students" and "children's basic eagerness levels" -- "eagerness levels" is not an idiomatic collocation, and "literacy seen among" makes no sense.

  • D-A: gives "the declining seen among parents and students" and "...to numeracy skills eagerness much more sharply" -- "declining" cannot sit as a plain noun after "the", and "eagerness much more sharply" is meaningless.

  • C-B: gives "children's basic compared levels" and "reading ability as literacy to numeracy skills declining" -- "compared" cannot function as an adjective before "levels", and "as literacy to numeracy skills" breaks the comparison structure.

  • C-D: gives "reading ability as declining to numeracy skills" and "...skills compared much more sharply and dropping" -- "declining" cannot slot into the "as ___ to" comparison, and "compared much more sharply" does not pair naturally with "and dropping".

Cross-check: Reading the sentence straight through with all four words in their original places: parents and students are keen on schooling, yet children's foundational literacy has suffered, with reading ability -- as compared to numeracy skills -- declining much more sharply and dropping to pre-2012 levels. This is one complete, coherent statement with no broken agreement and no dangling phrase.

Answer: Since every marked word is already in its correct grammatical slot, and every offered swap breaks the sentence, no rearrangement is required.

title: In the following question, some part of the sentence may
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select
the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'.


"Goa is not so better as (A)/ I thought it to be," (B)/ said Ragini to Nooran. (C)/ No error (D)
solution:
Corrected sentence: "Goa is not as good as I thought it to be," said Ragini to Nooran.

Key points:

  • Use the structure as + base adjective/adverb + as to compare equality: e.g., "The thief ran as fast as he could."

  • Do not combine "so" with a comparative form like "better" ("so better as" is incorrect). Comparative adjectives (better, more interesting) normally pair with "than" (e.g., "Goa is better than I thought") or, in negation, use "not as + adjective + as" (e.g., "not as good as").

  • Note: "so...as" can appear in negative clauses with the base adjective (e.g., "He is not so tall as his brother"), but it is not correct to use it with a comparative form like "better".

title: Read the sentence below to find out if there is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Read the sentence below to find out if there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error, the answer is (E). (Ignore errors in punctuation, if any.)
A third group of people would probable (A)/ accuse both the power plant (B)/ and the research institute of poisoning (C)/ the world by using and storing toxic nuclear waste (D)/ No error (E)
solution:
Concept: In English, adverbs — not adjectives — modify verbs, including a modal-verb + main-verb phrase such as “would ___ accuse”. An adjective can modify only a noun or pronoun; using it to modify a verb is a grammatical error.

Application: Check each underlined part of the sentence against this rule:

  • (A) “would probable accuse” — “probable” is an adjective used to modify the verb “accuse”; the modal-verb phrase needs the adverb “probably” (“would probably accuse”). This is the grammatical error.

  • (B) “accuse both the power plant” — correctly begins the “accuse ... of ...” construction; no error.

  • (C) “and the research institute of poisoning” — “of poisoning” correctly uses the gerund after the preposition “of”, and the “both ... and ...” structure is parallel; no error.

  • (D) “the world by using and storing toxic nuclear waste” — “using” and “storing” are parallel gerunds after the preposition “by”; no error.

Cross-check: Replacing “probable” with “probably” — “A third group of people would probably accuse both the power plant and the research institute of poisoning the world by using and storing toxic nuclear waste” — reads as a grammatically correct sentence, confirming part (A) is the only error and the answer is (A).

title: Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence. Friendship built
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence.

Friendship built on business is __________ business based on friendship.
solution:
Key idea: The sentence compares two things, so it needs the comparative form “better than”.

  • “Best” is superlative and is not followed by “than” in this structure.

  • “Better than” is the correct comparative phrase.

Answer: Option 1, “better than”, is correct.

title: Alice never have and ever will take such wrong measures.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Alice never have and ever will take such wrong measures.
solution:
Explanation

The structure of this sentence requires maintaining parallel negative structures. The correct phrasing combines "never had taken" with "nor will ever take" to ensure the negative aspect is consistently applied throughout the entire statement.

title: Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.

India and Sri Lanka / have / many large number of / educated workers than Brazil.
solution:
Correct answer: the segment 'many large number of'.

The sentence compares the number of educated workers in two groups (India and Sri Lanka vs Brazil) using 'than'. A comparison with 'than' must be supported by a comparative form. The phrase 'many large number of' provides no comparative and is itself ill-formed: it wrongly stacks 'many' (which goes straight before a plural noun, e.g. 'many workers') on top of the quantifier 'a large number of'. English uses one or the other, never both together.

The corrected sentence reads: 'India and Sri Lanka have a larger number of educated workers than Brazil' (or 'India and Sri Lanka have more educated workers than Brazil').

The remaining segments are fine: 'India and Sri Lanka' is a valid compound subject, the plural verb 'have' agrees with it, and 'educated workers than Brazil' is well-formed once the comparative is restored. Hence the error lies only in 'many large number of'.

title: Select the correct sentence from the following. [This test belongs
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Select the correct sentence from the following.

options.label: B
options.html: I have learnt this lesson word by word.

solution:
Concept: A sentence is grammatically correct only when it avoids semantic redundancy (pairing two words that already mean the same thing), uses idiomatic collocations correctly (the fixed word-partnerships native speakers actually use, such as learning something 'by heart', not 'word by word'), follows the correct pattern after 'know' when expressing ability ('know how to + verb', not 'know' + a gerund), and uses the correct causative structure 'get/have + object + past participle' when the subject arranges for someone else to perform an action.

Application:

  • He made a blunder mistake. — 'Blunder' already means 'a serious mistake', so adding 'mistake' after it repeats the same idea; this is a redundancy error.

  • I have learnt this lesson word by word. — 'Word by word' means reading, translating, or repeating something literally; the idiom for memorizing something exactly is 'by heart', so this pairing is wrong here.

  • She does not know swimming. — 'Know' expressing ability takes the pattern 'know how to + verb' (or the modal 'can'); a bare gerund after 'know' is not standard usage.

  • He got his daughter married. — This follows the causative pattern 'get + object + past participle' correctly, showing the subject arranged for the action to happen.

Cross-check: Substituting the causative frame with 'have' — 'He had his daughter married' — keeps the same acceptable meaning, confirming the structure is sound; none of the other three sentences can be made correct without changing a word, so exactly one sentence in the set is grammatically flawless.

Result: The grammatically correct sentence is 'He got his daughter married.'

title: Choose the correct alternative of the sentence from given sentences.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose the correct alternative of the sentence from given sentences. They now walked on in silence, each of them deep in their thoughts.

options.label: A
options.html: They now walked into in silence, each of them deep in their thoughts.

options.label: B
options.html: They started walking in silence and thinking something.

options.label: C
options.html: They now walked on in silence, both of them were thinking

solution:
Concept: In error-spotting / sentence-correction questions, check a candidate sentence against three common failure patterns — (1) a redundant/doubled preposition (e.g. two prepositions doing the same job), (2) a comma splice, where two independent clauses are joined by a bare comma instead of a conjunction, semicolon, or subordinate structure, and (3) unidiomatic phrasing. A separate, legitimate structure — the verbless (absolute) construction, e.g. "noun + adjective/participle phrase" attached by a comma — correctly describes a simultaneous state without needing its own verb. A sentence with none of these errors should be left unchanged.

Applying this to the given sentence, "They now walked on in silence, each of them deep in their thoughts.": "walked on" is the finite main-verb phrase, and "each of them deep in their thoughts" is precisely this verbless absolute construction — it has no redundant preposition, no comma splice (it is not a second independent clause, so a comma correctly attaches it), and no unidiomatic wording. The sentence is therefore already grammatically sound.

  • "walked into in silence" doubles the preposition ("into" plus "in"), which is ungrammatical redundancy.

  • "started walking in silence and thinking something" replaces the absolute construction with the unidiomatic phrase "thinking something."

  • "walked on in silence, both of them were thinking" joins two independent clauses with a bare comma — a comma splice.

Since the given sentence contains none of these errors, the correct choice is to make no changes to it.

title: In the question below, sentence is given with four words
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
In the question below, a sentence is given with four words highlighted. These four words may not be in their correct positions. The sentence is then followed by options with the correct combination of words that should replace each other in order to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct. Find the correct combination of the words that replace each other.

Be careful (A) not to microwave (B) the hot plate (C) when you take the food out of the touch (D).
solution:
Concept

In a word-interchange sentence, the marked word forms stay unchanged, but each word’s grammatical role is determined by the slot into which it moves. A valid swap must make every affected slot fit both the surrounding grammar and the intended meaning.

The method is to identify what kind of word each slot requires, test the proposed exchanges, and then read the complete sentence again for coherence.

Application

The structure “Be careful not to ___ the hot plate” requires a verb naming the action to avoid. The word “touch” supplies that action. The structure “take the food out of the ___” requires the name of the appliance containing the food; “microwave” supplies that noun.

  1. Exchange “microwave” and “touch” while leaving “careful” and “the hot plate” in place.

  2. Read the resulting sentence: “Be careful not to touch the hot plate when you take the food out of the microwave.”

  3. Check the grammar: “touch” follows the infinitive marker “to,” and “microwave” follows the preposition “of” as the object noun.

  4. Check the meaning: avoiding contact with a hot plate is a sensible warning, and food can be removed from a microwave.

Cross-check

  • Moving “careful” would break the adjective complement after “Be.”

  • Moving “the hot plate” would remove the object of “touch.”

  • Leaving all four words unchanged would retain the mismatched phrases “microwave the hot plate” and “out of the touch.”

Therefore, the required interchange is B-D.

title: Read each sentence to find out whether there is any
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Read each sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is ‘No error’, the answer is (e). (Ignore errors of punctuation, if any).

Spunky and full of spirit (A)/, the little girl is known (B)/ for always doing things that (C)/ others are afraid to does (D)/.
solution:
Concept

When a verb follows the infinitive marker “to”, it must appear in its base (first) form — “to + base verb” (to go, to do, to see). The base form never takes the third-person singular ‑s/‑es ending; subject–verb agreement is carried by the finite verb of the clause, not by an infinitive. Adjectives such as “afraid”, “willing”, and “able” are completed by a to-infinitive, so the same rule applies.

Application

  1. Split the sentence into its marked parts and locate every verb form.

  2. In the part “others are afraid to does”, the adjective “afraid” is followed by the to-infinitive “to + verb”.

  3. The verb after “to” must be the base form “do”. The inflected “does” is the third-person singular present, which an infinitive can never take.

  4. Correct it to “others are afraid to do”. This single change makes the sentence grammatical.

Cross-check (the other parts)

  • “Spunky and full of spirit” — a correct introductory participial/adjectival phrase describing the subject.

  • “the little girl is known” — correct singular subject with the passive “is known”.

  • “for always doing things that” — correct: the preposition “for” is properly followed by the gerund “doing”.

Hence the grammatical error lies in the part “others are afraid to does” (“to does” → “to do”).

title: Directions In the following questions, sentence is given which is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Directions: In the following question, a sentence is divided into parts. The sentence may or may not be grammatically or contextually correct. To make the sentence correct, interchange the positions of the phrases and select the required interchange. If no interchange is required, select “No interchange required.”

The small savings scheme, (A)/ investment avenues in India (B)/ is arguably one of the most popular(C)/ which offers guaranteed returns along with tax benefit(D)
solution:
Concept

A relative clause beginning with “which” should directly follow the noun phrase it modifies. In a linking-verb construction, the subject is followed by the linking verb and then its complement.

The expression “one of the most popular” must be completed by a plural count-noun phrase that names the class being described.

Application

  1. Take “The small savings scheme” as the subject noun phrase.

  2. Place “which offers guaranteed returns along with tax benefit” immediately after that noun phrase, so the relative clause clearly modifies the scheme.

  3. Continue with “is arguably one of the most popular” as the linking-verb construction.

  4. Complete the construction with “investment avenues in India,” the plural noun phrase required after “one of the most popular.”

Cross-check and contrast

The reconstructed sentence is: “The small savings scheme, which offers guaranteed returns along with tax benefit, is arguably one of the most popular investment avenues in India.” It is grammatically complete and preserves the intended meaning.

  • A–C gives the segment order C–B–A–D, which does not keep the subject, its relative clause, and the linking-verb complement together.

  • A–D gives the segment order D–B–C–A, beginning with the relative clause instead of the noun it modifies.

  • A–D and B–C gives the segment order D–C–B–A, again separating the modifier from its noun and disturbing the clause structure.

  • No interchange keeps A–B–C–D, leaving “investment avenues in India” between the subject and the clause that modifies it.

Therefore, the required interchange is B–D.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q13
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Direction: In the following question, a part of the sentence is underlined. Below are given alternatives to the underlined part which may improve the sentence. Choose the correct alternative. In case no improvement is needed, choose the option that says "No improvement".

Had I realised how close I was to the precipice, I would not have taken that step.
solution:
Concept: A third-conditional sentence ("If + subject + had + past participle, subject + would not have + past participle") can be rephrased in formal English by inverting the subject and the auxiliary "had" and dropping "if": "If I had realised" becomes "Had I realised", with no change in meaning or grammatical correctness.

Application

The underlined clause "Had I realised" places the auxiliary "had" before the subject "I" and omits "if" — exactly the inversion pattern for "If I had realised". The main clause, "I would not have taken that step", uses "would not have + past participle", the standard result-clause form that pairs with a past-perfect if-clause. The tenses of the two clauses match correctly as written.

Cross-check

  • "If I would have realised" places the modal-perfect "would have" inside the if-clause itself, alongside the conditional word "if" — a doubled conditional marker not used in the standard if-clause.

  • "Had I been realised" puts "realised" in the passive voice, making the subject "I" the receiver of the action rather than the one performing the mental act of realising.

  • "If I realised" uses simple past tense in the if-clause, which is the tense that pairs with "would" (not "would have") in a result clause — a different tense-pairing from "would not have taken".

  • The original "Had I realised" keeps the inverted, "had"-fronted form paired correctly with "would not have taken".

Since the sentence is already grammatically correct as written, "No improvement" is the right choice.

title: Unless we do not know where to go we can't
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Unless we do not know (1) where to go (2), we can't find (3) that restaurant. (4) No error (5)
solution:
Correct segment: The first segment "Unless we do not know" is incorrect.

Reason: "Unless" already introduces a negative condition. Adding "do not" creates a double negative, which is ungrammatical in this context. Remove the extra negation or replace "unless" with "if".

Corrected versions:

  • Unless we know where to go, we can't find that restaurant.

  • If we do not know where to go, we can't find that restaurant.

Note: The other segments—"where to go", "we can't find", and "that restaurant"—are grammatically correct and require no changes.

title: Each question consists of four sentences on topic Some sentences
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
Each question consists of four sentences on a topic. Some sentences are grammatically incorrect or inappropriate. Select the option that indicates the grammatically incorrect and inappropriate sentence(s).

A. It was a tough situation and Manasi was taking pains to make it better.

B. Slowly her efforts gave fruit and things started improving.

C. Every one complimented her for her good work.

D. She was very happy and thanked everyone for their help.
solution:
Concept:

These ‘spot the error’ items test whether a sentence uses natural, idiomatically correct English — not just grammar rules, but the conventional collocations native speakers use: which preposition follows a given verb, and which verb pairs with a given noun in a fixed expression. A sentence can be structurally grammatical and still be judged incorrect here if it swaps the conventional word for a wrong one.

Checking each sentence:

  • A — ‘taking pains to make it better’ is correct: ‘take pains to do something’ is the standard idiom for making a great effort. No error.

  • B — ‘her efforts gave fruit’ is incorrect: the fixed collocation for an effort succeeding is ‘bear fruit’ (past tense ‘bore fruit’), not ‘give fruit’. ‘Gave fruit’ breaks this idiom.

  • C — ‘complimented her for her good work’ is incorrect on two counts: the verb ‘compliment’ conventionally takes the preposition ‘on’, not ‘for’, when naming the reason for praise (the standard form is ‘complimented her on her good work’); and ‘every one’, written as two words, is the phrase used before an ‘of’ construction (‘every one of them’) — as a stand-alone subject meaning ‘everybody’ it should be the single word ‘everyone’.

  • D — ‘thanked everyone for their help’ is correct: ‘thank someone for something’ is itself the standard collocation, and ‘everyone’ is rightly written as one word here, so this sentence needs no change.

Cross-check:

Substituting the corrected forms — ‘her efforts bore fruit’ and ‘Everyone complimented her on her good work’ — reads naturally, which confirms the fault lies in the verb-idiom, preposition, and one-word-pronoun choices, not in the sentence structure.

So the sentences that are grammatically incorrect and inappropriate are B and C together, while A and D are perfectly correct as written.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q89
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Find the correct sentence among the options given below.
solution:
A sentence is grammatically correct only when it satisfies every rule that applies to it at once: the preposition a verb needs to complete its meaning, subject-pronoun agreement, the article chosen by the SOUND of the following word (not its spelling), and the tense form matched to its time-marker. A lapse in any one of these makes a sentence incorrect, even when the rest of it reads smoothly.

Checking the time marker “since” against the verb form used to describe an action that started at a fixed point and is still continuing shows that “has been raining since morning” fits the present perfect continuous rule precisely: the fixed starting point (“morning”) is paired with the matching continuous form “has/have been + verb-ing”, with no missing preposition and no pronoun or article slip anywhere in the sentence.

  • “This is a chair to sit.” — the verb “sit” needs a preposition (on/in) to name the surface or space being sat upon, as in “sit on a chair”; that preposition is missing here.

  • “One should do his duty.” — the indefinite pronoun “one” is referred back to, in formal usage, by the matching possessive “one’s”, not by the personal possessive “his”.

  • “He is a M.A in English.” — the abbreviation “M.A.” is pronounced “em-ay”, a vowel sound, so it takes the article “an”, not the consonant-sound article “a”.

So the sentence built on the correctly matched tense and time-marker, with no preposition, pronoun, or article slip, is the correct one among the four: “It has been raining since morning.”

title: Sentence is divided into six parts, from the given six
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml:
A sentence is divided into six parts, from the given six parts two parts are error free and remaining four parts are erroneous. You have to find that combination of two parts which do not contain any error

Gadkari unveiled the much-awaited (A)/ Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernization Program (B) /or “Vehicle Scrapping Policy” which are (C)/ aimed on creating an ecosystem (D)/ for phasing out of unfitted and (E) /polluted vehicles, in the Lok Sabha.(F)
solution:
Answer: the two error-free parts are the clause "Gadkari unveiled the much-awaited" and the phrase "Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernization Program".

Corrections for the erroneous parts:

  • For the phrase "or "Vehicle Scrapping Policy" which are": replace "are" with "is" because "policy" is singular (correct: "which is").

  • Replace "aimed on creating an ecosystem" with "aimed at creating an ecosystem"; also use the single-word spelling "ecosystem".

  • Replace "unfitted" with "unfit" and remove the unnecessary "of" after "phasing out" (correct: "phasing out unfit and polluting vehicles").

  • Replace "polluted" with "polluting" because vehicles cause pollution (correct: "polluting vehicles"). Also remove the unnecessary comma before "in the Lok Sabha."

Corrected sentence:

Gadkari unveiled the much-awaited Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernization Program or "Vehicle Scrapping Policy" which is aimed at creating an ecosystem for phasing out unfit and polluting vehicles in the Lok Sabha.

title: Choose CLOSEST word “MAYHEM”
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Choose CLOSEST word “MAYHEM”
solution: "Havoc" is closest in meaning to "mayhem."

title: Find the word that names necessary part of the given
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Find the word that names a necessary part of the given word : guitar
solution:
Answer: Strings. A guitar requires strings to function because the instrument produces sound through the vibration of its strings.

  • Why strings are necessary: The strings vibrate when plucked or strummed, creating the tones and pitches we hear; without strings a guitar cannot produce its characteristic sound.

  • Why the other choices are not correct: A teacher is a person who may teach playing, a band is a group of musicians that may include a guitar, and songs are musical pieces performed on the instrument; none of these are physical components required for the guitar itself to exist or function.

title: In each of the pair given in options, the 2nd
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: In each of the pair given in options, the 2nd term is related to the first term in a certain way except one. Which is the odd one out?
solution:
To determine the odd one out , we need to evaluate the relationship between the two terms in each pair.

Analysis of Relationships
Option 1 (Fiction-Novels): Novels are a specific subset or form of fiction. This follows a category-subset relationship.

Option 2 (Literature-Poems): Poems are a specific form of literature. This also follows a category-subset relationship.

Option 3 (Science-Geography): Geography is often categorized under the broader umbrella of science (or social science, depending on the context of the classification system used). This is intended to follow a category-subset relationship.

Option 4 (Calculation-History): Calculation is a mathematical process, while History is a social science subject. These terms do not share the category-subset relationship found in the other options.

Conclusion
The correct answer is Option 4 because it is the only pair where the second term is not a subset of the first.

title: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate alternative: He
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate alternative: He is like a body without a soul, eye without light or flower without _______.
solution: The sentence uses a series of similes to describe something incomplete or lifeless. The structure compares 'a body without a soul' and 'an eye without light' to 'a flower without...'. In this context, the missing word must represent an essential quality that gives a flower its value or completeness. While petals are physical parts, fragrance is the defining characteristic that makes a flower appealing and complete in a poetic sense. 'Smell' is too generic, while 'colour' is less critical than the scent in this specific literary parallel. Therefore, 'Fragrance' best completes the analogy of a flower lacking its most cherished attribute.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q88
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
bodyHtml: ‘Doctor’ is related to ‘Stethoscope’. In the same way ‘Painter’ is related to
solution:
A 'word analogy' item pairs two words that share a specific relationship, then asks you to complete a second pair using the same relationship. One common relationship type is profession : primary instrument — the second word names the physical tool or instrument that a person in that profession principally uses to do their work.
